In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah al-Nisa' is Madani, except for one verse. It was revealed in Makkah in the year of the Conquest, concerning Uthman ibn Talhah al-Hajabi, and it is His saying: (Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to their owners) [[See p. 255 of this part]] as will be explained later. Al-Naqqash said: It was also said that it was revealed at the time of the Prophet's ﷺ migration from Makkah to Madinah. Some people have said that His saying, Exalted is He, (O mankind), wherever it occurs, is Makki, and this was said by Alqamah and others. So it is likely that the beginning of the surah is Makki, and whatever was revealed after the migration is Madani. Al-Nahhas said: This surah is Makki. I say: The correct view is the first, for in Sahih al-Bukhari, it is narrated from Aisha that she said: Surat al-Nisa' was not revealed except while I was with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, meaning that he had consummated the marriage with her. There is no disagreement among the scholars that the Prophet ﷺ consummated his marriage with Aisha in Madinah. Whoever examines its rulings knows that it is undoubtedly Madani. As for the one who said that His saying, (O mankind), wherever it occurs, is Makki, this is not correct, for al-Baqarah is Madani and in it is His saying, (O mankind), in two places [[See vol. 1 p. 235 and vol. 2 p. 207]], as has already passed. And Allah knows best.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿O mankind, fear your Lord, who created you from a single soul and created from it its mate and spread from both of them many men and women. And fear Allah, through whom you ask one another, and the wombs. Indeed Allah is ever, over you, an Watcher.﴾ (1)

There are six issues (in some copies: seven; the issues are six, and the third appears to be the one beginning: "and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i recited", making them seven).

The first issue: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord, who created you﴾. The derivation of (al-nas, mankind), and the meaning of taqwa, al-Rabb, al-khalq, al-zawj and al-batth have already been discussed in (al-Baqarah), so there is no point in repeating them [[See vol. 1 pp. 136, 161, 226, 310 and vol. 2 p. 196]]. The verse also contains an alert to the Maker. He said (wahidah) in the feminine, in agreement with the word nafs. The word nafs is feminine even when it refers to a male. It is also permissible in speech to say (min nafsin wahidin), and this is according to the sense, since the intended meaning of nafs is Adam, peace be upon him. This was said by Mujahid and Qatadah. It is also the reading of Ibn Abi Ablah, (wahid) without the ta' marbutah.

(Wa-batha) [its meaning [[from B, J, Z, T and D]]] means he scattered and spread across the earth, and from it comes (wa-zaraabiyyu mabthuthah) [[See vol. 2 p. 33]], and it has already been discussed in (al-Baqarah) [[See vol. 2 p. 196]]. (Minhuma) means Adam and Hawwa'. Mujahid said: Hawwa' was created from the qusayra of Adam. The qusayra means the lowest ribs; it was also said it is the rib adjacent to the flank between the side and the belly. In a hadith: "Woman was created from a crooked rib," which has already passed in al-Baqarah.

(Rijalan kathiran wa-nisa'an): He confined their offspring to two kinds, which implies that the hermaphrodite is not a kind, but has a human reality that returns him to one of these two kinds, so he is attached to one of them, according to the consideration of lacking or having extra organs, as has already been mentioned in (al-Baqarah) [[See vol. 1 p. 301]].

The second issue: His saying, Exalted is He, (And fear Allah, through whom you ask one another, and the wombs). He repeated the command to be wary as an emphasis and to alert the hearts of those addressed. (Alladhi) is in the accusative position as an attribute. (Al-arham) is coordinated. That is: fear Allah by not disobeying Him, and fear the wombs by not severing them. The people of Madinah read (tasa'alun) with the ta' assimilated into the sin. The people of Kufa read it by dropping the ta' because two ta's come together, and by lightening the sin, because the meaning is known, as in His saying, (wa-la ta'awanu 'ala al-ithm) [[See vol. 6 p. 47]] and (tunazzal) and the like.

The third issue: Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, Qatadah, al-A'mash and Hamzah read (al-arhami) in the genitive. [Perhaps this is the start of the third issue in a copy with seven issues.] Grammarians have discussed this. As for the Basrans, their leaders said: It is a solecism (lahn), and it is not permissible to recite with it. As for the Kufans, they said: It is ugly (qabih), and they did not go beyond this, nor did they mention the reason for its ugliness, as al-Nahhas said, as far as I know. Sibawayh said: It is not coordinated upon a pronoun in the genitive, because it is like tanwin, and tanwin is not coordinated upon. A group said: It is coordinated upon the pronoun, for they used to ask one another by them, a man would say: "I ask you by Allah and by the womb." This is how al-Hasan, al-Nakha'i and Mujahid explained it, and it is the correct view in this question, as will come. Some people weakened it, including al-Zajjaj, and they said: It is ugly to coordinate an apparent noun upon a pronoun in the genitive without repeating the genitive particle, as in His saying, (fa-khasafna bihi wa-bidarihi al-ard) [[See vol. 13 p. 317]], and (marartu bihi wa-Zayd) is ugly. Al-Zajjaj said, quoting al-Mazini: Because the coordinated and the coordinated-upon are partners, each occupying the position of the other, so just as it is not permissible to say (marartu bi-Zayd wa-ka), so it is not permissible to say (marartu bika wa-Zayd). As for Sibawayh, it is in his view ugly and not permissible except in poetry, as he said:

Today you have come close to deriding us and insulting us, so go, for what is with you and the days of wonder (?)

He coordinated (al-ayyam) upon the kaf in (bika) without the ba' out of necessity. Likewise another's saying:

We hang our swords on pillars like these, and between them and the Ka'bah is a wide, open expanse.

He coordinated (al-Ka'bah) upon the pronoun in (baynaha) out of necessity. Abu Ali said: That is weak by analogy. In the book al-Tadhkirah al-Mahdiyyah [[in B, T and Z: al-Muhadhdhabah]] it is narrated from al-Farisi that Abu al-Abbas al-Mubarrad said: If I prayed behind an imam who recited (ma antum bi-musrikhiyya) [[This is the reading of Hamzah. See vol. 9 p. 357]] and (ittaqu Allah alladhi tasa'aluna bihi wa-al-arham), I would take my sandals and leave. Al-Zajjaj said: The reading of Hamzah, despite its weakness and ugliness in Arabic, is a grave error in the fundamentals of the religion, for the Prophet ﷺ said: "Do not swear by your fathers." If swearing by other than Allah is not permissible, how then is it permissible by the womb? I have seen Isma'il ibn Ishaq go to the view that swearing by other than Allah is a grave matter, and that it is specific to Allah, Exalted is He. Al-Nahhas said: The saying of some that (wa-al-arham) is an oath is an error in both meaning and grammar, for the report from the Prophet ﷺ indicates the accusative. Shu'bah narrated from Awn ibn Abi Juhayfah, from al-Mundhir ibn Jarir, from his father, who said: We were with the Prophet ﷺ until people from Mudar came, barefoot and naked, and I saw the face of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ change because of their poverty. Then he prayed the noon prayer and addressed the people, saying: "O mankind, fear your Lord," until "and the wombs," then he said: "A man gave a dinar of his, a man gave a dirham of his, a man gave a sa' of his dates," and he mentioned the hadith [[The narration in Sahih Muslim, Kitab al-Zakah: "A man gave from his dinar, from his dirham, from his garment, from a sa' of his wheat, from a sa' of his dates." It has no repetition. It is the same narration and chain.]]. So the meaning of this is the accusative, for he urged them to maintain the ties of their kinship. Also, it is authentically reported from the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever swears, let him swear by Allah or let him be silent." This refutes the view of the one who said the meaning is "I ask you by Allah and by the womb." Abu Ishaq said: The meaning of (tasa'aluna bihi) is that you demand your rights by Him, and there is no meaning for the genitive with this either. I say: This is what I have come across of the statements of the scholars of language in prohibiting the reading (wa-al-arham) in the genitive, and Ibn Atiyyah chose it. It was rejected by the Imam Abu Nasr Abd al-Rahim ibn Abd al-Karim al-Qushayri, who chose coordination and said: Such speech is rejected by the leading scholars of the religion, because the readings which the leading reciters transmitted are established from the Prophet ﷺ by mass transmission (tawatur) known to the specialists, and when something is established from the Prophet ﷺ, whoever rejects it has rejected the Prophet ﷺ, and considers ugly what he was reciting, and this is a dangerous position, and linguists and grammarians are not to be followed in it, for Arabic is received from the Prophet ﷺ, and no one doubts his eloquence. As for what has been mentioned from the hadith, there is room for examination, for he, peace be upon him, said to Abu al-Ushara [[In Tahdhib al-Tahdhib: Abu al-Ushara al-Darimi, from his father, from the Prophet ﷺ: "If you had stabbed her in the thigh, it would have sufficed you." The hadith is in the chapter on slaughter]]: "By your father, if you had stabbed her in the flank." Then the prohibition came only regarding swearing by other than Allah, and this is seeking intercession through another by the right of kinship, so there is no prohibition in it. Al-Qushayri said: It has also been said that this is an oath by the womb, meaning "fear Allah and the right of the womb," as you say: "Do such-and-such, by the right of your father." And in the revelation there came: (By the star), (by the mountain), (by the fig), (by your life) [[Qur'an 15:72]], and this is artificial. I say: There is no artificiality in it, for it is not far-fetched that (wa-al-arham) belongs to this category, so He swore by them as He swore by His creatures that point to His oneness and His power, as an emphasis for them, until He joined them with Himself. And Allah knows best.

Allah may swear by whatever He wills, prohibit what He wills, and permit what He wills, so it is not far-fetched that this is an oath. The Arabs swear by kinship. It is also valid that the particle ba' is intended and omitted, as it was omitted in the saying:

Ill-omened ones, they do not reform a tribe, nor is there a messenger whose crow brings anything but separation.

So it is genitive even though no ba' precedes it. Ibn al-Dahhan, Abu Muhammad Sa'id ibn Mubarak, said: The Kufan permits coordinating an apparent noun upon a genitive pronoun and does not prohibit it, and from this is his saying:

Woe to you, one who calls to me or is sent forth from the swift asses of the grazing ground, a heavy-chested, thick-bodied one.

And from this:

So go, for what is with you and the days of wonder.

And another's saying:

And between them and the Ka'bah is a wide, open expanse.

And from this:

So enough for you and al-Dahhak is a sharp, Indian sword.

And another's saying:

He sought the horizons of the sky but found no ascent into them, nor a seat on earth.

And another's saying:

There is no destruction in it and in the affairs of what was decreed by its unseen fate.

And another's saying:

I pass by the battalion, not knowing whether my death was in it or in another.

In "siwaha" the position is genitive by "fi." On this basis some interpreted His saying, Exalted is He, (And We made for you therein means of livelihood, and [for] those for whom you are not providers) [[See vol. 10 p. 12]], so they coordinated upon the kaf and the mim. Abd Allah ibn Yazid read (wa-al-arhamu) in the nominative, as a beginning, with the predicate omitted, its estimate being: "and the wombs are deserving of being joined." It may also be an exhortation (ighra'), for some Arabs put the one exhorted in the nominative. Al-Farra' recited:

Indeed, a people among them are Umayr and the sons of Umayr, and among them al-Saffah,
Truly they are worthy of meeting when the valiant one calls, the weapon, the weapon.

It has also been said that (wa-al-arham) in the accusative is coordinated upon the position of (bihi), since its position is accusative, and from this is his saying:

We are not mountains, nor iron.

They used to say: "I adjure you by Allah and by the ties of kinship (al-raḥim)." The more apparent view is that it is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb, as we mentioned.

The third issue: The community (al-milla) is agreed that maintaining the ties of kinship (ṣilat al-raḥim) is obligatory, and that severing them is forbidden. It is established that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Asma', when she asked him: "Shall I maintain ties with my mother?" (na'am, "Yes") "Maintain ties with your mother." So he commanded her to maintain ties with her, though she was a disbeliever. Then the scope of this extended to maintaining ties with a disbeliever, until the matter reached Abu Hanifa and his companions, who held that relatives (dhawu al-arham) inherit when there are no agnatic heirs (ʿasaba) and no fixed-share heirs (farḍ musammā), and that they are freed upon being purchased by a relative out of respect for the ties of kinship. They supported this with what Abu Dawud related, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever owns a relative within the prohibited degrees, he is free." This is also the view of most scholars. It is narrated from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) and ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud, and no opponent among the Companions is known for them. It is also the view of al-Hasan al-Basri, Jabir ibn Zayd, ʿAta', al-Shaʿbi and al-Zuhri, and al-Thawri, Ahmad and Ishaq adopted it.

Among our scholars (the Malikis) there are three opinions on this: The first: that it is specific to fathers and grandfathers. The second: "the two sides," meaning siblings. The third: like the view of Abu Hanifa. Al-Shafiʿi said: Only his children, his fathers and his mothers are freed upon him; his siblings and none of his relatives and kin (lukhma) are freed upon him. The correct view is the first, because of the hadith we mentioned, which al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i also reported. The best of its chains is the version of al-Nasa'i, which he related from the hadith of Damra, from Sufyan, from ʿAbdullah ibn Dinar, from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever owns a relative within the prohibited degrees, he is freed upon him." This is a established hadith by the transmission of reliable narrators from reliable narrators, and none of the imams has impugned it with a defect that would require abandoning it, except that al-Nasa'i said at its end: "This is a munkar hadith." Others said: "Damra alone narrated it." This is the meaning of munkar and shadh in the terminology of the hadith scholars. But Damra is trustworthy and reliable, and the solitary narration of a reliable narrator does not harm it. And Allah knows best.

The fourth issue: They differed on this topic regarding those within the prohibited degrees through fosterage (dhawu al-mahram min al-radaʿa). Most scholars said they do not fall under the implication of the hadith. Shurayk al-Qadi said they are freed. The people of the literal reading (ahl al-Zahir) and some theologians held that a father is not freed upon his son if the son owns him, and they argued with His (peace be upon him) saying: "A child does not repay his father, unless he finds him enslaved and buys him and frees him." They said: When the purchase is valid, ownership is established, and the owner has the right of disposal. This is ignorance on their part of the objectives of the Sharia, for Allah the Exalted says: "And to parents, goodness" (wa-bil-walidayni ihsanan). He has linked worship of Him with goodness to parents in obligation, and it is not goodness that his father remains in his possession and under his authority. Then it is obligatory for him to free him, either for the sake of ownership, in acting upon the hadith ("he buys him and frees him"), or for the sake of goodness, in acting upon the verse. The meaning of the hadith according to the majority is that when the child became the cause of his father's freedom by purchasing him, the Sharia attributed the freeing to him as though he had performed it. As for the scholars' disagreement about who is freed by ownership, the basis of the first view is what we have mentioned of the meaning of the Book and the Sunna; the basis of the second view is extending the close prohibited relative to the father mentioned in the hadith, and no one is nearer to a man than his son, so it is applied to the father; and the brother is close to him in this, because he traces through paternity, for he says: "I am the son of his father." As for the third view, its basis is the hadith of Damra, which we have mentioned. And Allah knows best.

The fifth issue: His saying, the Exalted: "and the wombs" (wal-arḥām). Al-raḥim is a term for all relatives without distinction between the prohibited and others. Abu Hanifa considers the prohibited relative in preventing the retraction of a gift, and retraction is permitted with respect to paternal cousins, although severance exists and kinship is present, and for this reason inheritance, guardianship and other rulings are attached to it. So restricting it to the prohibited degrees is an addition to the text of the Book without any basis. They regard that as abrogation (naskh), especially since it contains an indication of the reason being severance, and they have permitted it with respect to paternal cousins and the children of maternal uncles and aunts. And Allah knows best.

The sixth issue: His saying, the Exalted: "Indeed, Allah is ever a watcher (raqiban) over you." That is, a guardian (ḥafiẓan), according to Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid. Ibn Zayd said: knowing (ʿalīman). It was said: raqiban means guarding (ḥafiẓan), and it was said: in the sense of the form fāʿil. So al-Raqib is one of the attributes of Allah the Exalted. Al-raqib means the guardian and the one who waits; you say: raqabtu arqubu raqbatan and raqabanan when I waited. And al-marqab is a high, elevated place upon which the watcher stands. And al-raqib is the third arrow of the seven arrows that have shares (anṣiba); it is said that al-raqib is a kind of snake, so it is a shared (mushtarak) term. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verse 2:

There are five issues in this.

The first: His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And give the orphans their property﴾. By "orphans" He means those who were orphans (formerly), like His saying: (And the sorcerers were thrown down prostrate [[See vol. 7, p. 260.]]). There is no sorcery with prostration, so likewise there is no orphanhood with puberty [[The hadith: "There is no orphanhood after reaching maturity (ihtilam)."]]. And the Prophet ﷺ was called "the orphan of Abu Talib," by way of continuing the designation of what had been.

(And give) means "give." And ītā' (giving) is "al-i'ṭā'" (bestowing). One says "li-fulān atw," meaning a gift. Abu Zayd said: "atawtu al-rajul ātūhu itāwatan," and it is a bribe (ri'shah). The orphan is one who has not reached puberty (al-ḥulm), and this has been discussed fully in (al-Baqarah) [[See vol. 2, p. 14.]]. This verse is addressed to the guardians and the executors. It was revealed, according to the view of Muqatil and al-Kalbi, concerning a man from Ghatafan who [had a great deal of wealth belonging to a young orphaned nephew of his. When the orphan reached maturity he demanded the wealth, but his paternal uncle refused him, so this was revealed. The uncle said: "We seek refuge in Allah from the great sin [[al-ḥawb: sin.]]!" and returned the wealth. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever is protected from the avarice of his own soul and returns [wealth] in this manner, then he will dwell in his abode," meaning his Paradise. When the youth took the wealth, he spent it in the way of Allah. Then he (peace be upon him) said: "The reward has been secured and the burden remains." It was asked: "How, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "The reward has been secured for the boy, and the burden remains upon his father," because he was a polytheist.

The second: The giving of the orphans their property occurs in two ways. One: providing food and clothing for as long as the guardianship lasts, since this is not possible except in that manner for one who does not deserve full taking and independent control, such as a child or a foolish adult. The second: giving by enabling them and handing the property over to them, which occurs upon testing and guidance. In this case the naming is metaphorical; the meaning is "the one who was an orphan," and this is the continuation of the designation, like His saying, the Exalted: (And the sorcerers were thrown down prostrate), meaning those who had been sorcerers. And the Prophet ﷺ was called "the orphan of Abu Talib." When the guardian verifies his maturity (rushd), it becomes forbidden for him to withhold his property from him, and he would be disobedient.

Abu Hanifah said: When he reaches twenty-five years of age, his entire property is given to him in every case, because he becomes capable of being a grandfather.

I say: Since Allah, the Exalted, did not mention in this verse the perceiving of maturity (rushd), and mentioned it in His saying, the Exalted: (And test the orphans until they reach marriageable age; then if you perceive in them maturity (rushd), hand over to them their property). Abu Bakr al-Razi al-Hanafi said in Ahkam al-Quran: Since rushd is not restricted in one place and is restricted in another place, it is obligatory to apply both. So I say: When he reaches twenty-five years and he is foolish, in whom maturity has not been perceived, it is obligatory to hand the property over to him; and if he is below that, it is not obligatory, acting upon both verses [[See al-Jassas, Ahkam, vol. 1, p. 489, and vol. 2, p. 49, on the difference in wording.]].

And Abu Hanifah said: When he reaches his rushd [[From b, w and t. In the others: ashuddah.]], he becomes fit to be a grandfather; and when he becomes fit to be a grandfather, how is it valid to give him property on the basis of the cause of orphanhood and by the name of orphan? Is that not in the extreme of remoteness?

Ibn al-Arabi said: This is false and has no basis, especially according to his principle, which holds that the prescribed measures (muqaddarat) are not established by analogy but are taken from the textual source, and there is no text in this matter. The positions of the scholars concerning interdiction (al-ḥajr) will come, Allah willing.

The third: His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And do not substitute the bad for the good﴾. That is, do not substitute the fat sheep from the orphan's property with the lean one, nor the good dirham with the counterfeit one. In the Jahiliyyah, because they had no religion, they did not scruple about the property of orphans; they would take the good and the best of the orphans' property and replace it with the inferior of their own property, saying: "A name for a name, and a head for a head," so Allah forbade them from that. This is the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, al-Zuhri, al-Suddi and al-Dahhak, and it is the apparent meaning of the verse. It has also been said: the meaning is: do not eat the orphans' property, which is forbidden and bad, and leave the good, which is your own property. Mujahid, Abu Salih and Badhan said: Do not hasten to eat the bad of their property and leave waiting for the lawful provision from Allah. Ibn Zayd said: The people of the Jahiliyyah did not give inheritance to women and children, and the eldest would take the inheritance. Ata': Do not profit from your orphan who is under your care while he is a deceived child. These two views are outside the apparent meaning of the verse, for it is said: "tabaddala al-shay' bi al-shay'," meaning he took it in its place, and from it comes "al-badal" (substitute).

The fourth: His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And do not eat their property along with your property﴾. Mujahid said: This verse prohibits mixing in expenditure, for the Arabs used to mix their expenses with the expenses of their orphans, so they were forbidden from that, and then it was abrogated (naskh) by His saying: (If you mix with them, they are your brothers) [[See vol. 3, p. 62.]]. Ibn Furak said, from al-Hasan: The people interpreted in this verse the prohibition of mixing, so they avoided it on their own account, and so it was lightened for them in the verse of al-Baqarah [[See vol. 3, p. 62.]]. A group of later scholars said: "ila" here means "ma'a" (with), like His saying, the Exalted: (Who are my helpers in the way of Allah [[See vol. 18, p. 89.]]). And al-Qutabi recited:

They block the doors of the tents with horses
along with tethered mares, firmly bound by their halters.

[[The verse is by Salamah ibn al-Hushab describing horses; he means horses tied at their courtyards. The 'unun are shelters with which the horses are screened from wind and cold; the awasir are tethers, singular asirah, a rope buried in the ground projecting from it like a loop to which the tethered animal is tied.

(From Lisan al-Arab, entries akhā and asar.)]]

This is not a good reading. The skilled scholars said: "ila" remains in its own sense and carries the meaning of addition, meaning: do not add their property and combine it with your property in eating. So they were forbidden from regarding the orphans' property as their own property, so that they would take authority over it by eating and benefiting.

The fifth: His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Indeed, that is a great sin (ḥūban kabīran)﴾. "Indeed, that" refers to the eating.

(Was a great sin) means a great sin, according to Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and others. It is said: "ḥāba al-rajul yaḥūbu ḥūban" when a man sins. Its original sense is driving away camels, so sin was called ḥūb because one is driven away from it and by it. It is said in supplication: "Allahumma-ghfir ḥawbatī," meaning my sin. Al-ḥawbah is also need, and from it in supplication: "ilayka arfa'u ḥawbatī," meaning my need. Al-ḥawb is loneliness (wahshah), and from it is his saying (peace be upon him) to Abu Ayyub: "Indeed, the divorce of Umm Ayyub is a ḥawb." And in it there are three dialects: ḥūban with a damma on the ḥa, which is the reading of the majority and the dialect of the people of the Hijaz. Al-Hasan read ḥawban with a fatha on the ḥa. Al-Akhfash said: it is the dialect of Tamim. Muqatil: it is the dialect of the Abyssinians.

Al-ḥūb is the verbal noun, and likewise al-ḥiyabah. Al-ḥūb is also a noun. Ubayy ibn Ka'b read ḥāban as a verbal noun like al-qāl. It may also be a noun like al-zād. Al-ḥawʾab (with a hamza after the waw) is a wide place, and al-ḥawʾab is also a water-source. It is said: "alḥaqa Allahu bihi al-ḥawbah," meaning poverty and need, and from it their saying: "bāta bi-ḥaybat sū'," and the origin of the ya' is waw. Tahawwaba fulan means he worshipped and cast sin from himself. Al-taḥawwub is also grief, and it is also a loud shout, like driving away. Fulan yatahawwabu min kadhā means he suffers pain from such-and-such. Tufayl said:

"So taste as we tasted on the morning of Muhajjar [[Muhajjar (like mu'azzam or muhdath): name of a place; in the Diwan: "in our bellies."]]
the rage in our livers, and the tahawwub."

There are fourteen issues concerning it.

The first: His saying, exalted is He, "(And if you fear) " is a conditional clause, and its answer is "(then marry)." That is, if you fear that you will not be just regarding their dowries and their maintenance, ﴿then marry what seems good to you of women﴾, that is, others than them.

Al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated, and the wording is Muslim's, from Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, from A'isha, concerning the words of God, exalted is He: "And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans, then marry what seems good to you of women, two, three, or four" (4:3). She said: "O son of my sister, it refers to the orphan girl who is under the guardianship of her guardian and shares in his property. He is attracted by her wealth and her beauty, so her guardian wants to marry her without being just regarding her dowry, giving her what others would give her. So they were forbidden to marry them unless they act justly towards them and give them the highest customary dowry, and they were commanded to marry other women who seem good to them." And she mentioned the hadith.

Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: "For this reason we say that it is permissible for the guardian (wasi) to buy from the orphan's property for himself, and to sell to himself without favoritism. The principal (muwakkil) has the right to review what his agent (wakil) buys for himself or sells from it. The ruler (sultan) has the right to review what the guardian does in such matters. As for the father, no one has authority over him unless favoritism becomes evident in him, and then the ruler may object to him." The discussion of this has already passed in (al-Baqara) [[See vol. 3, p. 62.]].

Al-Dahhak, al-Hasan and others said: the verse abrogates (nasikha, abrogating) what existed in the pre-Islamic period and at the beginning of Islam, namely that a man could marry as many free women as he wished, so the verse restricted them to four. Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and others said: the meaning is, "And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans, then similarly be wary regarding women," because they used to be scrupulous regarding orphans but not regarding women. The word "khiftum" (you fear) is among the words with opposite meanings (addad), for the feared thing may be certain to occur or may be only probable, so the scholars differed on the interpretation of this fear. Abu Ubayda said: "khiftum" means "you were certain." Others said: "khiftum" means "you suspected." Ibn Atiyya said: "This is what the skilled scholars have chosen, that it retains its meaning of suspicion and not certainty. The sense is: whoever suspects that he will fall short in justice toward an orphan girl, let him turn away from her." And "tuqsituu" (act justly) means "ta'dilu" (you act equitably). It is said: "aqsata al-rajul" when a man acts equitably, and "qasata" when he oppresses and wrongs his companion. God, exalted is He, said: "As for the unjust (al-qasitun), they will be fuel for Hell" (72:15), meaning those who transgress. And he, peace be upon him, said: "Those who act justly (al-muqsitun) in their judgments will be on pulpits of light on the Day of Resurrection," meaning those who are equitable. Ibn Wathhab and al-Nakha'i read "taqsutu" with a fatha on the ta', as though the sense were an added particle, as if He said: "And if you fear that you will act unjustly."

The second: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿then marry what seems good to you of women﴾. If it is said: how does "ma" (what) come for human beings when its original use is for what does not reason? There are five answers to this. The first: "man" (who) and "ma" (what) may interchange. God, exalted is He, said: "By the heaven and He who built it" (91:5), meaning "and He who built it." And He said: "Among them is one who walks on his belly, among them one who walks on two legs, and among them one who walks on four" (24:45). So "ma" here refers to those who reason, namely women, by His saying afterward "of women," specifying what was indefinite. Ibn Abi Abla read "man tāba" (who is good), referring to those who reason. The second: the Basrans said: "ma" is used for descriptions, just as it is used for what does not reason. One says: "What is with you?" and it is answered: "Pleasant and generous." So the meaning is: marry the good of women, that is the lawful, and what God has forbidden is not good. In the revelation: "And what is the Lord of the worlds?" (26:23), and Moses answered according to what was asked, as will come. The third: some people reported that "ma" in this verse is temporal, meaning "as long as you find marriage agreeable." Ibn Atiyya said: "In this view there is weakness." The fourth answer: al-Farra' said: "ma" here is a verbal noun (masdar). Al-Nahhas said: "This is very far-fetched and not valid; it would be: marry the good woman." Al-Jawhari said: "tāba al-shay yatību tība wa tayyaban." Alqama said:

"As though its fragrance in the nose is perfumed musk" [[This is the second half of a line whose first half is: "They carry a citron, its fragrance spread with ambergris."]]

The fifth answer: what is meant here is the contract, that is, "marry with a good marriage." Ibn Abi Abla's reading refutes the three preceding views. Abu Amr ibn al-Ala' reported that when the people of Mecca heard thunder they said: "Glory to what the thunder glorifies," meaning "Glory to Him whom the thunder glorifies." Similar is their saying: "Glory to what subjected this to us," meaning "to Him who subjected this to us."

All scholars of the sciences agree that His saying, exalted is He, "And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans," has no implicit meaning (mafhum, an implied converse). For the Muslims agree that whoever does not fear injustice toward orphans may marry more than one: two, three, or four, just as one who fears it may. This shows that the verse was revealed in answer to one who feared that, and that its ruling is more general than that.

The third: Abu Hanifa relied on this verse to permit the marriage of an orphan girl before puberty. He said: she is an orphan only before puberty; after puberty she is a divorced woman, not an orphan. The proof is that if He meant the adult woman, He would not have forbidden taking less than her customary dowry, because she would choose that, and it would be permissible by consensus. Malik, al-Shafi'i and the majority of scholars held that this is not permissible until she reaches puberty and is consulted, for His saying: "And they ask you concerning women" (4:127). "Women" is a term that applies to adults, as "men" applies to adult males; the term "man" does not include a child, so likewise the term "women," and "woman" does not include a little girl. He also said: "concerning the orphans of women" (4:127), and the meaning there is the orphans here, as A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said. So the adult orphan is included in the verse, and she is not married except with her consent, and a young girl is not married off since she has no consent. When she reaches puberty, marriage to her is permitted, but she is not married except with her permission. This is as al-Daraqutni narrated from the hadith of Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Nafi', from Ibn Umar, who said: "My maternal uncle Qudama ibn Maz'un married me to the daughter of his brother Uthman ibn Maz'un. Al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba entered upon her mother, persuaded her with wealth, and proposed to her. Her case was brought to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. Qudama said: 'O Messenger of God, she is my brother's daughter, and I am the guardian of her father, and I did not fall short in regard to her. I married her to one whose excellence and kinship I know.' The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, said to him: 'She is an orphan, and the orphan has more right over her affair.' So she was taken from me, and he married her to al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba." Al-Daraqutni said: "Muhammad ibn Ishaq did not hear it from Nafi'; he heard it from Umar ibn Husayn from him." Ibn Abi Dhi'b narrated it from Umar ibn Husayn, from Nafi', from Abdullah ibn Umar, that he married the daughter of his maternal uncle Uthman ibn Maz'un. He said: "Her mother went to the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, and said: 'My daughter dislikes that.' The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, commanded him to separate from her, and he separated from her." And he said: "Do not marry orphans until you consult them. If they remain silent, that is their consent." So after Abdullah, al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba married her.

This refutes what Abu Hanifa says, that once she reaches puberty she does not need a guardian, based on his principle that a guardian is not a condition for the validity of marriage. This has already been mentioned in (al-Baqara) [[See vol. 3, p. 72.]], so there is no meaning in their saying that this hadith refers to a non-adult girl because of His saying "except with her permission," for then mention of the orphan would have no purpose. And God knows best.

The fourth: In A'isha's interpretation of the verse is a point of jurisprudence which Malik relied on: the customary dowry (sadaq al-mithl), and the return to it in cases where a dowry is invalid and there is deception regarding its amount, based on her saying: "less than the customary dowry." It follows that the customary dowry must be known for every class of people according to their circumstances. Malik said: "People have matches (manakih) that are known to them and they are known to them," that is, dowries and equals (akfa'). Malik was asked about a man who married off his daughter, [wealthy [[Addition from Ahkam al-Quran of Ibn al-'Arabi.]]], to a poor nephew of his, and her mother objected. He said: "I see that she has something to say about this." He allowed her to speak on this until he would appear, from his perspective, to have something that would remove the mother's objection to him. It is also narrated as "la ara" (I do not see) with an added alif, but the first is more sound. It is permissible for someone other than an orphan girl to be married for less than her customary dowry, because the verse concerns only orphans. This is its implicit meaning, and a non-orphan is different.

The fifth: When the orphan girl reaches puberty and the guardian acts justly regarding her dowry, it is permissible for him to marry her, and he will be both the one who marries and the one who gives in marriage, according to what A'isha explained. This is the view of Abu Hanifa, al-Awza'i, al-Thawri and Abu Thawr, and it was said by the Successors al-Hasan and Rabi'a, and it is the view of al-Layth. Zufar and al-Shafi'i said: it is not permissible for him to marry her except with the permission of the ruler, or that a guardian of hers who is closer to her in kinship than he is, or equal to him in lineage (al-qa'dad, lineage), marries her to him. As for him taking charge of both sides of the contract himself, so that he is both the one who marries and the one who gives in marriage, that is not permitted. They argued that guardianship is a condition of the contract, based on his, peace be upon him, saying: "There is no marriage except with a guardian and two just witnesses." So the enumeration of the one who marries, the one who gives in marriage, and the witnesses is obligatory, and if two of them coincide, one of those mentioned is dropped. There is a third view on this question: that she entrusts her affair to a man who marries her to him. This was narrated from al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba, and Ahmad also held it, as Ibn al-Mundhir mentioned.

The sixth: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿what seems good to you of women﴾, means what is lawful for you, according to al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr and others. The phrase suffices with the time when marrying is permitted, since the forbidden women are many. Ibn Ishaq, al-Jahdari and Hamza read "tāba" with imala (a vowel shift toward i), and in the codex of Ubayy it is "tība" with a yaa, and this is the evidence for imala.

(مِنَ النِّساءِ) [min al-nisa'] is evidence that the word *nisa'* (women) is applied only to those who have reached puberty (*al-hulm*). The singular of *nisa'* is *niswah*, but *niswah* has no singular from its own form; instead one says *imra'ah* (a woman).

**The seventh issue:** God's words, ﴿*mathna wa-thula<u>th</u> wa-rubaa*﴾ (﴿two, or three, or four﴾). Their place in the grammatical analysis (*i'rab*) is in the accusative, as a substitute (*badal*) for (*ma*), which is indefinite and not inflected (*la yanșarif*), because it is a derived form (*ma'duulah*) and used as an adjective. This is what Abu 'Ali said. Al-Tabari said: they are definite, because the definite article (*al-*) does not enter them, and they stand in the same position as *Umar* regarding definiteness. This was stated by al-Kufi, but al-Zajjaj rejected this view. It has also been said that they are not inflected because they are derived from their own form and meaning: *uhad* is derived from *wahid wahid* (one by one), *mathna* from *ithnayn ithnayn* (two by two), *thulath* from *thalathah thalathah* (three by three), and *rubaa* from *arba'ah arba'ah* (four by four). Each of these has two forms: *fu'al* and *maf'al*. One says *uhad* and *mawhad*, *thunaa'* and *mathna*, *thulath* and *matlath*, *rubaa'* and *marba'*. The same applies up to *ma'shar* and *'ushar*. Abu Ishaq al-Tha'labi recorded a third form: *uhad*, *thuna*, *thulth*, and *rub'*, like *Umar* and *Zufar*. Al-Nakha'i recited this verse in this way. Al-Mahdawi related from al-Nakha'i and Ibn Wathhab the reading *thulatha wa-rub'a* (without an alif in *rub'a*), so it is a shortened form of *rubaa*, for lightness, as the poet said:

*A torrent came from the side of God, rushing with the rage of a garden that has been fenced in.*

[The verb *haruda yahrudu* means: he intended.]

Al-Tha'labi said: this pattern is not extended beyond four except by a line from al-Kumayt:

*They did not ask you to pause until you shot, above the men, ten qualities.*

He means: you stabbed ten. Ibn al-Dahhan said: some stop at what is heard, which runs from *uhad* to *rubaa*, and they do not consider the line because it is anomalous. Abu 'Amr ibn al-Hajib said: one says *uhad*, *mawhad*, *thunaa'*, *mathna*, *thulath*, *matlath*, *rubaa'*, and *marba'*. Whether one says this beyond that up to nine is disputed. The soundest view is that it is not established, and al-Bukhari stated this explicitly in his *Sahih*.

That these forms are derived from their meaning means they are not used in a context where ordinary (non-derived) numbers are used. You say: *jaa'ani ithnan wa-thalathah* (two and three came to me). *Mathna* and *thulath* are not permitted unless a plural noun precedes them, as in: *jaa'ani al-qawm uhad wa-thunaa' wa-thulath wa-rubaa'* (the people came to me one, two, three, and four at a time) without repetition. In this verse, and here, they are in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*), and they may function as an adjective. An example of these numbers functioning as adjectives is God's words: ﴿*ulii ajnihatin mathna wa-thulatha wa-rubaa'*﴾ (﴿bearers of wings, two, three, or four﴾). Here *mathna* etc. are adjectives of *ajnihah* (wings), which is indefinite.

Sa'idah ibn Ju'ayyah said:

*But my family lives in a valley whose companions are wolves that seek people, two by two and one by one.*

[*Tabghi al-nas* means: they seek them.]

Al-Farra' recited:

*We killed by him, among those who were two and one, with four of you and a fifth one.*

[In al-Farra's *Ma'ani al-Qur'an* the text reads:
*And the youth enamored with his remembrance, we killed by him, among those who were two and one, with four of you and a fifth one, and a spear-wielder in the darkness of the night, a spear of Ma'bad.*
So it is in *Sharh al-Sabil*.]

Thus he described wolves, which are indefinite, with *mathna* and *mawhad*. The same applies to al-Farra's line, meaning: we killed by him people. Therefore these words are not inflected whether definite or indefinite. Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' permitted their inflection when used as numbers, on the basis that they are indefinite. Al-Akhfash claimed that if one uses them as a proper name, he inflects them in both definite and indefinite contexts, because the derivation (*'adl*) has been removed from them.

**The eighth issue:** Know that this number, *mathna wa-thulatha wa-rubaa'*, does not indicate permission for nine, as those whose understanding of the Book and the Sunnah is deficient have said, and who turned away from what was upon the early generations of this community. They claimed that the conjunction *wa* (and) is inclusive, and strengthened this by the fact that the Prophet ﷺ married nine and combined them in his marriage. Those who have fallen into this ignorance and made this statement are the Rafidah and some of the Zahiriyyah. They made *mathna* equal to *ithnayn*, and likewise *thulatha* and *rubaa'*. Some of the Zahiriyyah went even further in ugliness, saying it is permitted to combine eighteen, relying on the claim that derived forms of this kind convey repetition, and *wa* signifies combination. So they took *mathna* to mean two by two, and likewise *thulatha* and *rubaa'*. All of this is ignorance of the language and the Sunnah, and a contradiction of the consensus (*ijma'*) of the community (a unanimous agreement of Muslim scholars that serves as a source of law). No one among the Companions (*sahabah*) or the Successors (*tabi'un*) is reported to have combined more than four in marriage. Malik in his *Muwatta'*, al-Nasa'i and al-Daraqutni in their *Sunan* reported that the Prophet ﷺ said to Ghaylan ibn Umayyah al-Thaqafi, who had embraced Islam while he had ten wives: "Choose four of them and divorce the rest." In the *Kitab Abi Dawud*, from al-Harith ibn Qays, who said: "I embraced Islam while I had eight wives, and I mentioned that to the Prophet ﷺ, and he said: 'Choose four of them.'" Muqatil said: Qays ibn al-Harith had eight free wives, and when this verse was revealed, the Messenger of God ﷺ ordered him to divorce four and keep four. Thus he said "Qays ibn al-Harith," but the correct name is al-Harith ibn Qays al-Asadi, as Abu Dawud mentioned. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan related in *Kitab al-Siyar al-Kabir* that it was al-Harith ibn Qays, and this is the one known among jurists. As for what was permitted to the Prophet ﷺ in this matter, that is among his specific privileges, as will be explained in (*al-Ahzab*) [see vol. 14, p. 212].

As for their claim that *wa* is inclusive: this has indeed been said, but God addressed the Arabs in the most eloquent of their languages. The Arabs do not refrain from saying *tis'ah* (nine), and they say *ithnayn*, *thalathah* and *arba'ah*. Likewise, they find it objectionable when someone says: "Give so-and-so four, six, eight," and does not say "eighteen." In this context *wa* is a substitution: that is, marry three in place of *mathna*, and four in place of three. For this reason it is linked by *wa* and not by *aw* (or). Had it been *aw*, it would have been permissible that the one who has *mathna* not have *thulath*, and the one who has *thulath* not have *rubaa'*. As for their claim that *mathna* requires two, *thulath* three, and *rubaa'* four, this is an arbitrary judgment that the people of the language do not agree with, and it is their ignorance. Likewise, the ignorance of others that *mathna* requires two by two, *thulath* three by three, and *rubaa'* four by four. They did not know that *ithnayn ithnayn*, *thalathan thalathan*, and *arba'an arba'an* are a restriction on the number, whereas *mathna*, *thulath*, and *rubaa'* are the opposite. In the derived number according to the Arabs there is an added meaning not present in the original. When they say *jaa'at al-khayl mathna* (the horses came in pairs), they mean two by two, that is, they came paired. Al-Jawhari said: the same applies to derived numbers. Others said: when you say *jaa'ani qawm mathna*, or *thulath*, or *uhad*, or *'ushar* (the people came to me in pairs, or threes, or singly, or in tens), you mean they came to you one by one, or two by two, or three by three, or ten by ten. This meaning is not present in the original, because when you say *jaa'ani qawm thalathah thalathah* (a people came to me three by three), or *qawm 'ashrah 'ashrah* (ten by ten), you have restricted the number of the people by saying "three" and "ten." But when you say *jaa'uni rubaa'* and *thunaa'*, you have not restricted their number; you only mean they came to you four by four or two by two. Whether their number is large or small in this matter, restricting each form to the least that it implies, according to their claim, is arbitrary.

**The ninth issue:** As for the disagreement of the scholars of the Muslims concerning one who marries a fifth wife while he has four: Malik and al-Shafi'i said: he is liable to the prescribed punishment (*hadd*) if he knew it was unlawful. Abu Thawr also held this view. Al-Zuhri said: he is stoned if he knew, and if he was ignorant, the lesser of the two punishments applies, which is flogging. She is owed her dowry, they are separated, and they may never reunite. Another group said: he is not liable to any punishment in any of this. This is the view of al-Nu'man. Ya'qub and Muhammad said: he is punished in the case of a forbidden kinship (*dhat al-mahram*), but not in other forms of marriage. This is like marrying a Magian woman, or five women in one contract, or marrying a woman in a temporary marriage (*mut'ah*), or marrying without witnesses, or marrying a slave woman without the permission of her master. Abu Thawr said: if he knows that it is unlawful for him, he must be punished for all of these except marrying without witnesses. There is a third view stated by al-Nakha'i concerning a man who deliberately marries a fifth wife before the waiting period of the fourth of his wives has ended: he receives one hundred lashes and is not exiled. This is the opinion of our scholars (*'ulama'una*) concerning the fifth wife, as reported by Ibn al-Mundhir. How much more so for one beyond her.

**The tenth issue:** Al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar mentioned: Ibrahim al-Hizami related to me from Muhammad ibn Ma'n al-Ghifari, who said: a woman came to Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, and said: "O Commander of the Faithful, my husband fasts during the day and prays at night, and I dislike to complain about him, for he is doing the work of obedience to God, Mighty and Majestic." Umar said to her: "What a fine husband you have!" She kept repeating her complaint, and he kept repeating his answer. Ka'b al-Asadi said to him: [He is Ka'b ibn Sawar al-Azdi; see *Usd al-Ghabah*.] "O Commander of the Faithful, this woman is complaining about her husband for keeping away from her bed." Umar said: "Just as you understood her words, judge between them." Ka'b said: "Bring me her husband." He was brought, and Ka'b said to him: "Your wife here is complaining about you." He said: "Is it about food or drink?" He said: "No." The woman said:

*O judge, wise in your right guidance, his mosque has distracted my beloved from my bed.*
*His devotion has made him averse to my resting place; so judge the judgment, Ka'b, and do not delay it.*
*He does not sleep by day or by night; so I am not praising him in matters of women.*

Her husband said:

*Devotion made me averse to her bed, while the bridal chamber (*hujal*) is adorned, for I am a man whom what has been revealed has overwhelmed.*
*In the chapter of the Bee and in the seven long surahs (*al-tiwal*), and in the Book of God is a dreadful warning.*

[*Hujal* is the plural of *hujlah*, a tent decorated for the bride with clothing, beds, and curtains. *Al-sab' al-tiwal* are the long surahs of the Qur'an: al-Baqarah, Ali 'Imran, al-Nisa', al-Ma'idah, al-An'am, and al-A'raf, and they differed about the seventh. Some said it is Bara'ah and al-Anfal, counted as one surah, and others said it is Yunus. *Tiwal* is the plural of *tuwla*. In some copies: "al-Naml" instead of "al-Nahl."]

Ka'b said:

*Indeed, she has a right over you, O man; her share is in four, for whoever understands.*
*So give her that, and set aside your excuses.*

Then he said: "Indeed Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has permitted you to marry women, two, three, or four. So you have three days and nights in which you may worship your Lord." Then Umar said: "By Allah, I do not know which of your two matters is more remarkable: your understanding of them, or your judgment between them. Go, for I have appointed you judge (qada') of Basra."

Abu Hudba Ibrahim ibn Hudba related to us from Anas ibn Malik, who said: A woman came to the Prophet ﷺ complaining about her husband, and she said: "I do not have what women have. My husband fasts all the time." He said: "For you there is a day, and for him there is a day: one day for worship and one day for the wife."

The eleventh issue: His words, exalted is He: ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly, then [marry] one﴾. Al-Dahhak and others said: [justice is] in inclination, love, intercourse, companionship, and distribution of time among the four, the three, or the two wives, so [marry] "one." He thus forbade the increase that leads to failing to be just in distribution and in good companionship. This is evidence for the obligation of that, and Allah knows best.

It is also recited in the nominative (marfu'): fawahidatun, meaning "then one is sufficient" (fihi kifaya aw kafiya), and al-Kisa'i said: "fawahidatun tuqni'" (one is enough to content). It is also recited in the accusative (mansub) by supposing a verb, meaning: "then marry one" (fankihu wahidatan).

The twelfth issue: His words, exalted is He: ﴿or what your right hands possess﴾, meaning the female slaves (al-imaa'). It is coordinated (ma'tuf) upon "one," meaning: if he fears that he will not be just with one, then [he may have] what his right hand possesses. In this is evidence that possession of the right hand gives no right to sexual intercourse or to a turn of distribution, because the meaning is: "If you fear that you will not be just" in distribution, "then one, or what your right hands possess," so He made all of what the right hand possesses one category. Thereby it is negated that female slaves have a right to intercourse or to distribution. However, justice toward the right hand's possessions remains obligatory, through the duty of good treatment of them (husn al-malaka) and kindness to the slave. Allah attributed the possession to the right hand because it is a description of praise, and the right hand is specially associated with good qualities because of its strength. Do you not see that it is the one that gives charity? As the Prophet ﷺ said: "Until his left hand does not know what his right hand spends." It is also the one that makes covenants and pledges, and the oath (al-ulya) was named "yamin" (right hand) because of it. It is also the one that receives the banners of glory, as the poet said:

"When a banner is raised for glory, / 'Arabah al-Awsi receives it with the right hand."[[The verse is by al-Shammakh, praising 'Arabah al-Awsi. Before it:
"I saw 'Arabah al-Awsi aspiring / to good deeds, unmatched among peers."]]

The thirteenth issue: His words, exalted is He: ﴿That is nearer to your not being unjust﴾, meaning: that is closer to your not deviating from the truth and not oppressing, according to Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and others. It is said: "'ala al-rajul ya'ulu" when he oppresses and deviates. From this is the saying: "'alat al-sahm 'an al-hadaf," meaning the arrow deviated from the target. Ibn Umar said: "Indeed he is 'a'il (unjust) in measure and weight." The poet said:

"They said: 'We followed the Messenger of Allah,' and they discarded / the word of the Messenger and deviated (ya'ulu) in the scales."

That is, they acted unjustly. Abu Talib said:

"With a balance of truth that does not cheat a barleycorn, / and whose weigher's measure is not unjust (ghayr 'a'il)."[[In J: yakhis. In Ibn Atiyya a variant:
"With a balance of justice that does not cheat a barleycorn, / and a true weigher whose weighing is not unjust."]]

He means "not deviating." Another said:

"Three souls and three she-camels / the time has burdened (la-qad 'ala al-zaman) my dependents."[[By al-Hutay'a. In it is another witness: the number three is masculine with "nafs" (feminine) because it is taken to mean "person." "Thalath dhawd" are she-camels that he used to support his dependents, and they were exhausted. In B, Y, and T, D: "nahnu thalatha," which is the reading in al-Aghani vol. 2 p. 173.]]

That is, [time] was unjust and deviated. "'Ala al-rajul ya'il" means he became poor and became dependent (a'ala). From this is the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And if you fear poverty (3ayla)﴾.[[See vol. 8 p. 106.]] From this is the saying of the poet:

"The poor man does not know when his wealth will come, / and the wealthy man does not know when he will become poor."[[By Uhayha ibn al-Jullah; after it:
"And you do not know, when you have resolved on a matter, / in which land the resting place will overtake you."]]

He is 'a'il, and the people are 'ayla. Al-'ayla and al-'ala are poverty. "'Alani al-shay'" means: it overpowered me and weighed upon me. "'Ala al-amr" means: it became severe and intensified.

Al-Shafi'i said: "allā ta'ūlū" means: that your dependents not multiply. Al-Tha'labi said: "No one else said this; it is only said: 'a'ala yu'ilu when his dependents increase." Ibn al-'Arabi claimed that "'ala" has seven meanings with no eighth: it means "mala" (inclined); second, "zada" (increased); third, "jara" (oppressed); fourth, "iftaqara" (became poor); fifth, "uthqila" (was burdened), related by Ibn Duraid. Al-Khansa' said:

"And what 'ala it (the tribe) he will suffice (the tribe) for."[[In her diwan:
"It was not closer, but he will suffice the tribe what burdened it."]]

Sixth: "'ala" means to support the expense of dependents, and from this is his saying ﷺ: "Begin with those you support (ta'ulu)." Seventh: "'ala" means to overpower, and from it: "'ila sabruhu," meaning his patience was overcome. It is said: "a'ala al-rajul" means his dependents increased.[[In B and H: "sabri."]] But "'ala" in the sense of "his dependents increased" is not sound.

I say: As for al-Tha'labi's statement that no one else said it, al-Daraqutni in his Sunan related it from Zayd ibn Aslam, and it is the statement of Jabir ibn Zayd. These are two imams from the scholars and leaders of the Muslims who preceded al-Shafi'i to it. As for what Ibn al-'Arabi mentioned about restriction and that it is not sound, it is not correct. We have mentioned that "'ala al-amr" means it became severe and intensified, related by al-Jawhari. Al-Harawi said in his two Gharibs: "Abu Bakr said: It is said 'ala al-rajul fi al-ard ya'ilu fiha,' meaning he traveled in it [[In T: when]]." Al-Ahmar said: "'alani al-shay' ya'ilunī 'ayl wa ma'il, when it has rendered you helpless."

As for "'ala" meaning "his dependents increased," it is mentioned by al-Kisa'i, Abu 'Umar al-Duri, and Ibn al-A'rabi. Al-Kisa'i, Abu al-Hasan 'Ali ibn Hamza, said: The Arabs say "'ala ya'ulu" and "a'ala yu'ilu," meaning his dependents increased. Abu Hatim said: Al-Shafi'i was more knowledgeable in the language of the Arabs than we are, and perhaps this is a dialect. Al-Tha'labi the exegete said: Our teacher Abu al-Qasim ibn Habib said: I asked Abu 'Umar al-Duri about this, and he was an unchallenged imam in the language, and he said: "It is the dialect of Himyar," and he recited:

"Indeed death seizes every living being / without doubt, even if he walks (amsha) and 'ala."

He means: even if his livestock and his dependents increased. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: "The Arab expressions have become so numerous that I feared I might take from a solecist (lahin) a solecism." Talha ibn Musarrif recited "allā tu'īlū" [with the causative form], and this is the proof of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him. Ibn 'Atiyya said: Al-Zajjaj and others criticized the interpretation of "'ala" as derived from "'iyal" (dependents) by saying: Allah has permitted a multitude of concubines, and in that is an increase of dependents; so how can it be closer to not having many dependents? This criticism is not correct, because concubines are merely property that may be disposed of by sale, whereas the dependents that burden are free women with obligatory rights. Ibn al-A'rabi reported that the Arabs say: "'ala al-rajul" when his dependents increase.

The fourteenth issue: Whoever permitted a slave (mamluk) to marry four women has relied on this verse, because Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So marry what seems good to you of women, two, three, or four﴾, meaning what is lawful, and He did not specify a slave from a free man. This is the view of Dawud and al-Tabari, and it is the well-known position of Malik, and the substance of his school according to his Muwatta', and so Ibn al-Qasim and Ashhab related from him. Ibn al-Mawwaz mentioned that Ibn Wahb related from Malik that a slave may marry only two, and he said: this is the view of al-Layth. Abu 'Umar said: Al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa and their companions, al-Thawri, and al-Layth ibn Sa'd said: A slave may not marry more than two. Ahmad and Ishaq also held this. It is related from Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ali ibn Abi Talib, and Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf regarding the slave who may not marry more than two, and I know of no dissenter among the Companions regarding it. It is also the view of al-Sha'bi, Ata', Ibn Sirin, al-Hakam, Ibrahim, and Hammad. The argument for this view is sound analogy (qiyas) with his divorce and his prescribed punishment (hadd). Everyone who holds that his punishment is half that of a free man, and his divorce is two pronouncements, and his ila' (vow of abstention) is two months, and similar rulings, it is not far-fetched to say: he is inconsistent in his statement "may marry four." And Allah knows best.

**Ten issues (masa'il) arise from this verse.**

**The first issue:** the words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿And give the women their dowries (ṣadaqāt)﴾. *Ṣadaqāt* is the plural; the singular is *ṣadaqah*. Al-Akhfash said: The Banu Tamim say *ṣudqah*, with the plural *ṣudqāt*, and if you wish you may open the first letter, or you may make it sukun. Al-Mazini said: It is said *ṣidāq al-mar'ah* (with a kasra), and it is not said with a fatha. Ya'qub and Ahmad ibn Yahya related the fatha from al-Nahhas.

The address in this verse is to the husbands. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Juraij. Allah commanded them to give the bridal gifts voluntarily, as a gift (*nihlah*) from them to their wives. It was also said that the address is to the guardians (*awliyā'*). This was said by Abu Salih. The guardian used to take the woman's dowry and give her nothing, so they were forbidden from this and commanded to hand it over to them.

In al-Kalbi's narration: In the Jahiliyyah, when a guardian married off a woman, if she was among his kinsfolk (*'ashirah*, in some manuscripts *'ashirah*), he would not give her any of her dowry, great or small; and if she was a stranger, he would carry her on a camel to her husband and give her nothing beyond that camel. Then this was revealed: ﴿And give the women their dowries as a gift﴾.

Al-Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman related from his father that a man from Hadramawt claimed that the verse refers to *al-mutashāghirūn*, those who would marry one woman to another (in exchange), so they were commanded to set dowries. But the first view is more apparent, because the pronouns are all one and they refer, as a whole, to the husbands, since He said: ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans﴾ up to His saying ﴿And give the women their dowries as a gift﴾. This requires the consistency of the pronouns, and that the first be the same as the last.

**The second issue:** this verse indicates that the dowry is obligatory for the woman. This is agreed upon, and there is no disagreement about it, except what was related from some of the scholars of Iraq, that if a master marries his slave to his female slave, no dowry is required. This is not correct, because of the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And give the women their dowries as a gift﴾, which is general. And He said: ﴿So marry them with the permission of their families and give them their due compensation according to what is reasonable﴾. [See p. 141 of this part.]

The scholars also agreed that there is no limit to its being much. They disagreed about its minimum, as will come in explanation of His saying: ﴿And you have given one of them a great amount (qintār)﴾. [See p. 98 of this part.]

Al-Jumhur read *ṣadaqātihinna* with a fatha on the ṣād and a ḍammah on the dāl. Qatadah read *ṣudqātihinna* with a ḍammah on the ṣād and sukun on the dāl. Al-Nakha'i and Ibn Thabbat read it with ḍammah on both and in the singular: *ṣudqatahunna*.

**The third issue:** the words of the Exalted: ﴿nihlah﴾. *Al-nihlah* and *al-nuhlah*, with a kasra or ḍammah on the nūn, are two dialects. Its origin is from giving: *nahaltu fulānan shay'an* means I gave so-and-so something. So the dowry is a gift from Allah the Exalted to the woman.

It was also said: *nihlah* means with good will from the husbands, without dispute. Qatadah said: the meaning of *nihlah* is an obligatory duty. Ibn Juraij and Ibn Zayd said: a prescribed obligation. Abu 'Ubayd said: *nihlah* is only something specified and known.

Al-Zajjaj said: *nihlah* means as a religious obligation. *Al-nihlah* also means religion and creed. It is said: "This is his *nihlah*," meaning his religion. This is appropriate even though the address is to the guardians who used to take it in the Jahiliyyah, until some woman said about her husband:

*He does not take the ḥulwān from our daughters.*

She meant: he does not do what others do. So Allah took it from them and commanded that it be given to the women.

*Nihlah* is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the husbands, with an implied verb from its own root, its estimate being *anḥalūhunna nihlah* (give them a gift). It was also said it is in the accusative as an explanation (tafsīr). It was also said it is a verbal noun of a different kind from the original, in the position of a circumstantial state.

**The fourth issue:** the words of the Exalted: ﴿But if they give you willingly some of it, then consume it﴾ [*fa-in ṭibna lakum ʿan shay'in minhu nafsan fa-kulūhu*]. The address is to the husbands. By its generality it indicates that a woman's gift of her dowry to her husband is permissible, whether she is a virgin or a previously married woman. This is the view of the majority of jurists. Malik prohibited a virgin from giving her dowry to her husband and made that a matter for the guardian, even though the right belongs to her.

Al-Farra' claimed that the address is to the guardians, because they used to take the dowry and not give the woman any of it, so it was not permitted for them to take from it except what the woman's soul was content with. The first view is more correct, because there was no prior mention of guardians, and the pronoun in *minhu* refers to the dowry. Ikrimah and others also said this.

The reason for the verse, as mentioned, is that some people were reluctant that anything they had given to their wives should return to them, so this was revealed: ﴿If they give you willingly﴾.

**The fifth issue:** the scholars agreed that if a woman who has full legal capacity over herself gives her dowry to her husband, it is valid and she has no right to take it back. However, Shurayh held that she may take it back, and he argued with the saying: ﴿But if they give you willingly some of it﴾, and if she is seeking it, her soul is not content with it. Ibn al-'Arabi said: This is false, because she has been content and he has consumed it, so she has no claim. The intended meaning is not the actual act of eating; rather it is a metaphor for making lawful and taking as lawful. This is clear.

**The sixth issue:** if she stipulates to him at the time of the marriage contract that he will not marry another woman over her, and she reduces some of her dowry for that, then if he marries another woman over her, she has no claim against him according to the narration of Ibn al-Qasim, because she stipulated what it is not permissible to stipulate. Like the people of Barirah, who stipulated that 'A'ishah would free her while the *wala'* would belong to the seller. The Prophet ﷺ validated the contract and nullified the condition. Likewise here, the reduction of part of the dowry is valid, and the stipulation is void.

[Editor's note in the source: "As it stands in the originals. It should read: 'and what he undertook is void,' though by 'marriage' he may mean the state that the contract established."]

Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam said: If what remains of her dowry is equal to the customary dowry of women like her or more, she has no claim against him for anything. But if she reduced some of her dowry, and then he married another over her, she has a claim against him for the full customary dowry, because he made a condition upon himself and took in exchange something which it was obligatory for her to take from him, so it is obligatory upon him to fulfil it, based on the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "The Muslims are bound by their conditions."

**The seventh issue:** the verse is evidence that manumission cannot be the dowry, because it is not property, since the woman cannot give it away and the husband cannot consume it. This is the view of Malik, Abu Hanifah, Zufar, Muhammad and al-Shafi'i.

Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ishaq and Ya'qub said: it may be a dowry, and the woman has no other dowry besides freedom, based on the hadith of Safiyyah [she was Safiyyah bint Huyayy ibn Akhtab, whom the Messenger of Allah ﷺ took captive], narrated by the imams, that the Prophet ﷺ freed her and made her freedom her dowry. It was also related from Anas that he did this, and he was the narrator of the hadith of Safiyyah.

The first group answered: There is no proof in the hadith of Safiyyah, because the Prophet ﷺ had a special privilege in marriage, that he could marry without a dowry. He intended Zaynab, who had become unlawful to Zayd, so he entered upon her without a guardian and without a dowry. So one should not argue from such a case. And Allah knows best.

**The eighth issue:** the words of the Exalted: ﴿nafsan﴾. It was said that it is in the accusative as a specification (*tamyīz*). Sibawayh and the Kufans do not permit that what is in the accusative as a specification be placed before its governor. Al-Mazini and Abu al-'Abbas al-Mubarrad permitted this when the governing word is a verb. And he recited:

*wa-mā kāna nafsan bil-firāqi taṭību*

[This is the second half of a verse by al-Mukhabbal al-Sa'di; the first half is: *atahjuru Layla bil-firāqi ḥabībahā*.]

In the Revelation there is: ﴿their eyes humbled, they will come out﴾ [see vol. 17, p. 125]. On this basis it is permitted to say: *shaḥman tafaqqa'at* (fat burst open) and *wajhan ḥasunat* (a face became beautiful). The companions of Sibawayh said: *nafsan* is in the accusative by an implied verb whose estimate is "I mean a soul," and it is not in the accusative as a specification; if this is the case, there is no proof in it. Al-Zajjaj said the transmitted reading is: *wa-mā kāna nafsī*.

All agree that it is not permitted to place the specification before its governor when the governing word is not inflected, like *'ishrūna dirhaman* (twenty dirhams).

**The ninth issue:** the words of the Exalted: ﴿then consume it﴾ [*fa-kulūhu*]. The intended meaning is not the actual act of eating; rather it means permission, by whatever way. This is what is meant by His saying in the verse after it: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly﴾. The intended meaning is not eating itself, but since eating is among the most common forms of enjoying property, the transactions were expressed by eating. A parallel is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿When the call is made for prayer on the day of Friday, then hasten to the remembrance of Allah and leave off trade﴾ [see vol. 18, p. 97]. It is known that the act of trade is not intended; what is intended is whatever distracts one from the remembrance of Allah the Exalted, such as marriage and other things. But trade was mentioned because it is the most important of what occupies a person from the remembrance of Allah the Exalted.

**The tenth issue:** the words of the Exalted ﴿hanī'an marī'an﴾ [wholesome and pleasant] are in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the pronoun in *fa-kulūhu*. It was also said they are adjectives of an implied verbal noun, meaning: eating that is wholesome, with the goodness of souls. *Hanaa'ahu al-ṭa'ām wal-sharāb yahna'uhu*, and *mā kāna hanī'an*, and *laqad hanu'a*; the verbal noun is *al-hany'*. Anything that comes without hardship or toil is *hanī'*. *Hanī* is the active participle of *hanu'a*, like *ẓarīf* from *ẓaruf*. *Hanī yahna'u fahuwa hani'* on the pattern of *faʿila*, like *zamin*. *Hannaʾanī al-ṭaʿām* and *marra'anī* by way of assimilation; when *hanna'anī* is not mentioned, you say *am'ara'anī al-ṭa'ām* with an alif, meaning it was digested. Abu 'Ali said: This is like what came in the hadith: "Return with burdens (*ma'zūrāt*) not rewarded (*ghayr ma'jūrāt*)," where the waw of *mawzūrāt* was changed to alif to match the form of *ma'jūrāt*.

Abu al-'Abbas, from Ibn al-A'rabi, said: It is said *hani'a* and *hanna'anī* and *marra'anī* and *am'ara'anī*, and *marī'anī* is not said; this was transmitted by al-Harawi. Al-Qushayri related that it is said *hani'anī* and *mari'anī* with a kasra, *yahna'unī* and *yamra'unī*, but this is rare.

It was also said: *hanī'an* means without sin, and *marī'an* means without illness. Kuthayyir said:

*Hanī'an marī'an ghayra dā'in mukhāmiri*
*li-'Azzata min a'rāḍinā mā istaḥallat*

A man entered upon 'Alqamah while he was eating something his wife had given him from her dowry, and he said to him: "Eat, the wholesome and the pleasant."

It was also said: *al-hanī'* is the good, easily swallowed thing that is not disturbed by anything; and *al-marī'* is that whose outcome is praised, fully digested, not harmful or injurious. The meaning is: you will not fear any demand for it in this world, nor any consequence in the Hereafter.

This is supported by what Ibn 'Abbas related from the Prophet ﷺ, that he was asked about this verse: ﴿But if they give you willingly some of it, then consume it﴾, and he said: "When she gives the gift to her husband willingly, not under compulsion, no authority will rule against you concerning it, and Allah the Exalted will not hold you accountable for it in the Hereafter."

It was related from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "When one of you complains of something, let him ask his wife for a dirham of her dowry, then let him buy honey with it and drink it with rainwater, and Allah the Mighty and Majestic will combine for him the wholesome, the pleasant and the blessed water." [In another manuscript: "dirhams"; this does not fit with what follows.]

And Allah knows best.

There are ten issues in this verse.

**The first issue:** When Allah, exalted is He, commanded that the wealth of orphans be handed over to them in His words, ﴿And give the orphans their property﴾, and that the alms be delivered to their recipients, He made clear that the foolish (safih) and the one who has not reached maturity may not be given his property. The verse thus establishes the guardianship (wasi), the custodian (wali) and the caretaker (kafil) for orphans. The scholars agreed that appointing a free, Muslim, trustworthy and upright person as a executor (wasi) is permissible. They differed concerning appointing a free woman as executor. The majority of scholars said that appointing her is permissible. Ahmad argued from the fact that ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, appointed Hafsa as executor. It is narrated from ʿAta' ibn Abi Rabah that, concerning a man who appointed his wife as executor, he said: "A woman may not be an executor. If it is done, the matter is transferred to a man from his people." They differed concerning appointing a slave as executor. Al-Shafi'i, Abu Thawr, Muhammad and Yaʿqub prohibited it, while Malik [[omitted from T.]], al-Awza'i and Ibn ʿAbd al-Hakam permitted it. This is also the view of al-Nakha'i when a man appoints his slave. The discussion of this matter has already been fully covered in (al-Baqara) [[see vol. 2, p. 257 and following.]].

**The second issue:** His words, Exalted is He, ﴿the foolish﴾. The linguistic meaning of safah (foolishness) has already been discussed in (al-Baqara) [[see vol. 1, p. 205.]]. The scholars differed concerning who these foolish ones are. Salim al-Aftas narrated from Saʿid ibn Jubayr that he said: "They are the orphans; do not give them your property." Al-Nahhas said: "This is among the best of what has been said concerning the verse." Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid narrated from Abu Malik that he said: "They are the young children. Do not give them your property, lest they squander it and you are left with nothing." Sufyan narrated from Humayd al-A'raj from Mujahid that he said: "They are the women." Al-Nahhas and others said: "This view is not sound. The Arabs only say safa'ih or safihat for women, because that is the more common plural of the form fa'ila." It is also said: "Do not entrust your wealth to a partner in a mudaraba arrangement, nor to an agent who does not know how to trade well." It is narrated from ʿUmar that he said: "Whoever has not gained understanding (of the rules) should not trade in our market." This is the meaning of His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not give the foolish your property﴾, meaning those ignorant of the rulings. It is also said: "Do not hand it over to unbelievers." For this reason the scholars disliked that a Muslim should appoint a dhimmi (protected non-Muslim) as agent for buying and selling, or entrust wealth to him as a mudaraba partner. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "The foolish here means everyone who deserves to be placed under restriction (hajr)." This is a comprehensive view. Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: "As for placing the foolish under restriction, the foolish person has several conditions: a condition in which he is restricted because of his youth; a condition in which he is restricted because of lack of reason, through insanity or otherwise; and a condition in which he is restricted because of his poor management of his own property. As for the one who is unconscious, Malik considered it good not to restrict him, because what afflicts him passes quickly. Restriction may apply to a person's own right and may apply to the right of others. The one restricted in his own right is the one we have mentioned. The one restricted in the right of others is the slave, the debtor, the sick person with respect to two-thirds of his property, the bankrupt, the married woman with respect to her husband's right, and the virgin with respect to herself. There is no disagreement concerning restricting the child and the insane. As for the adult, because he does not manage his own property well and it cannot be assured that he will not waste his property improperly, he resembles the child, and there is a disagreement on this which will come. There is no difference between whether he wastes his property on sins or on acts of devotion and permissible things. Our companions differed concerning someone who wastes his property on acts of devotion: some of them restrict him, and some do not restrict him. As for the slave, there is no disagreement about him.
