The debtor has what is in his hand taken away for his creditors, by the consensus of the Companions, and because of ʿUmar's action with Usayf of Juhayna [[see the entry for s-f-ʿ in al-Qamus and al-Taj.]], which Malik mentioned in al-Muwatta'. The virgin, as long as she is in seclusion, is restricted, because she does not manage her own affairs well. But once she marries and people come to her and she goes out and her face is seen, she knows what is harmful from what is beneficial. As for the married woman, it is because the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'It is not permitted for a woman whose husband holds her marital bond to dispose of her property except for a third of it.'" I say: As for the one ignorant of the rulings, even if he is not restricted, because he develops his property and does not manage it well, the wealth is not handed over to him, because of his ignorance of valid and invalid sales, and what is lawful and unlawful in them. Likewise the dhimmi is similar in his ignorance of sales, and because of the fear of dealing with him in usury and other things. And Allah knows best. They differed concerning the reason the property is attributed to those addressed, while it belongs to the foolish. It was said: He attributed it to them because it is in their hands and they are the ones who manage it, so it is ascribed to them figuratively, as in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿then greet one another﴾ and His words ﴿then kill yourselves﴾. It was also said: He attributed it to them because it is of the same kind as their property, for wealth has been made common among creation, passing from hand to hand and from ownership to ownership; that is, it belongs to them when they need it, just as your wealth protects your honor, safeguards you, enhances your standing, and by it your affairs are sustained. A second view, held by Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan and Qatada, is that the intended meaning is literally the property of those addressed. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Do not give your property, which is the means of your livelihood, to your wife and your son, leaving yourself poor, looking at them and at what is in their hands. Rather, you should be the one who spends on them." On this view, the foolish are women and young children, the young offspring of a man and his wife. This is consistent with the view of Mujahid and Abu Malik concerning the foolish.

**The third issue:** The verse indicates the permissibility of placing the foolish under restriction, because of Allah's command to that effect in His words: ﴿And do not give the foolish your property﴾. He also said: ﴿But if the one who has the debt is foolish or weak﴾ [[see vol. 3, p. 385.]]. Thus He established guardianship over the foolish just as He established it over the weak. The meaning of "weak" refers to the minor, and the meaning of "foolish" refers to the adult who has reached maturity, because safah is a term of blame, and a person is not blamed for what he has not acquired, and the pen is lifted from one who has not reached maturity, so blame and sin are negated from him. This was stated by al-Khattabi.

**The fourth issue:** The scholars differed concerning the actions of the foolish person before he is placed under restriction. Malik and all his followers except Ibn al-Qasim said: The foolish person's actions and commands are all valid until the ruler (imam) intervenes. This is also the view of al-Shafi'i and Abu Yusuf. Ibn al-Qasim said: His actions are not valid even if the ruler does not intervene. Asbagh said: If his foolishness is apparent, his actions are rejected; if his foolishness is not apparent, his actions are not rejected until the ruler places him under restriction. Sahnun argued for Malik's view, saying: "If the actions of the foolish were rejected before restriction, the authority would not need to place anyone under restriction." The argument of Ibn al-Qasim is what al-Bukhari narrated from the hadith of Jabir that a man freed a slave who had no property other than him, and the Prophet ﷺ annulled it, and he had not placed the man under restriction before that.

**The fifth issue:** The scholars differed concerning placing an adult under restriction. Malik and the majority of jurists said: He is to be placed under restriction. Abu Hanifa said: One who reaches maturity while sound of mind is not placed under restriction, unless he is squandering his property. If he is such, his property is withheld from him until he reaches twenty-five years of age. Once he reaches that age, it is handed over to him in every case, whether he is squandering or not, because a woman may conceive from him at twelve years of age, then he may father a child at six months, and so he becomes a grandfather, and I would be ashamed to place under restriction one who is fit to be a grandfather. It is also reported from him that during the period of withholding property, if he reaches maturity while squandering, his disposals are valid absolutely, and the property is withheld only as a precaution. All of this is weak in both reasoning and transmission. Al-Daraqutni narrated: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn al-Hasan al-Sawwaf told us; Hamid ibn Shu'ayb told us; Shurayh ibn Yunus told us; Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim, who is Abu Yusuf al-Qadi, told us; Hisham ibn ʿUrwa told us from his father, that ʿAbd Allah ibn Ja'far came to al-Zubayr and said: "I have bought such-and-such a sale, and ʿAli wants to go to the Commander of the Faithful and ask him to place me under restriction in this matter." Al-Zubayr said: "I am your partner in the sale." So ʿAli went to ʿUthman and said: "Ibn Ja'far has bought such-and-such a sale, so place him under restriction." Al-Zubayr said: "I am his partner in the sale." ʿUthman said: "How can I place under restriction a man whose partner in the sale is al-Zubayr?" Ya'qub said: "I hold to restriction and consider it valid, and I place under restriction and invalidate the sales of the one restricted, whether he buys or sells. If he buys or sells before restriction, I validate his sale." Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim said: "Abu Hanifa does not place anyone under restriction and does not uphold restriction." So ʿUthman's words, "How can I place a man under restriction," are evidence of the permissibility of placing an adult under restriction. ʿAbd Allah ibn Ja'far was born by his mother in the land of Abyssinia, and he was the first child born in Islam there. He came with his father to the Prophet ﷺ in the year of Khaybar and heard from him and memorized from him. Khaybar took place in the fifth year after the Hijra. This refutes Abu Hanifa's view. His argument will come, if Allah, exalted is He, wills.

**The sixth issue:** His words, Exalted is He: ﴿which Allah has made for you a means of support﴾, meaning for your livelihood and the well-being of your religion. There are three dialectal forms of (allati): al-lati, alti with a kasra on the ta, and alt with the ta sukun. For its dual there are also three forms: allatani and allata with the nun deleted, and allatanni with the nun doubled. As for the plural, its forms will come in their place in this surah, if Allah wills [[see p. 82 of this part.]]. Qiyam and qiwam mean what sustains you, with the same meaning. One says: So-and-so is the qiyam (support) of his family and the qiwam (mainstay) of his household, meaning he is the one who manages their affairs, that is, he sets them right. When the qaf of qiwam is pronounced with a kasra, they change the waw to a ya'. The reading of the people of Medina is (qiyaman) without an alif. Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: qiyaman and qiwaman have the same meaning as qiyaman, and it is in the accusative on their view as a verbal noun, meaning: "And do not give the foolish your property, by which your affairs are set right, so that they may stand by it as support." Al-Akhfash said: The meaning is "standing for your affairs," taking it as a plural. The Basran grammarians said: qiyaman is the plural of qimah, like dimah and diyam, meaning that Allah made them values for things. Abu ʿAli rejected this view and said: It is a verbal noun like qiyam and qiwam, and its root is qiwam, but it irregularly reverted to the ya', as the irregular plural jiyad is from jawad and similar forms. Qiwaman, qiwaman and qiyaman all mean firmness in a good state and continuity in that. Al-Hasan and al-Nakha'i read (allati) [[from b, j, h, w and t.]] in the plural of allati, while the common reading is (allati) in the singular form. Al-Farra' said: "In Arabic speech the most common usage is: 'the women who' (al-nisa' allawati) and 'the wealth which' (al-amwal allati)," and similarly for other things besides wealth, as al-Nahhas reported.

**Seventh:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And provide for them therein and clothe them﴾. It has been said that the meaning is: make provision for them therein, or make it obligatory for them therein. This applies to the maintenance and clothing that a man is obliged to provide for his wife and his young children. This is evidence for the obligation of a father to maintain his child and of a husband to maintain his wife. In al-Bukhari, on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Prophet ﷺ said: "The best charity is that which leaves one self-sufficient. The upper hand is better than the lower hand. Begin with those whom you support. A wife says: 'Either feed me or divorce me.' A slave says: 'Feed me and employ me.' A son says: 'Feed me. To whom are you leaving me?'" They said: "O Abu Hurayrah, did you hear this from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ?" He said: "No, this is from the pocket [[In al-'Asqalani's commentary on al-Bukhari: that is, from his own accumulation, indicating that it is his own deduction from what he understood of the raised hadith together with the reality. It is also narrated as 'from my pocket'. Vol. 9, p. 440.]] of Abu Hurayrah!" Al-Muhallab said: Maintenance of one's family and dependents is obligatory by consensus (ijma', the scholarly consensus), and this hadith is a proof for that.

**Eighth:** Ibn al-Mundhir said: They differed regarding the maintenance of children who have reached maturity but have no property and no earnings. One group said: The father must maintain his male children until they reach puberty, and his female children until they marry and are consummated with. If he divorces her after consummation, or she dies, she has no maintenance from her father. If he divorces her before consummation, she remains entitled to her maintenance.

**Ninth:** There is no maintenance for a grandchild upon the grandfather. This is the view of Malik. Another group said: He maintains his grandchildren until they reach puberty and menstruation. After that he is under no obligation to maintain them unless they are disabled. This applies equally to males and females, as long as they have no property. It applies equally whether they are his children or the children of his children, however far down, as long as they have no father other than him who is able to maintain them. This is the view of al-Shafi'i. Another group made maintenance obligatory for all children and for adult men and women who have no property by which they can be independent of the maintenance of a parent, based on the apparent meaning of his saying, peace be upon him, to Hind: "Take what suffices you and your child, in a reasonable manner." In the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, "The son says: 'Feed me. To whom are you leaving me?'" indicates that only one who has no capacity for earning and trade says this. Whoever has reached the age of puberty does not say this, because he has reached the limit of striving for himself and earning for himself, by the evidence of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿until, when they reach marriageable age﴾ [4:6], the verse. He made the attainment of marriageable age the limit in this matter. In his saying: "The wife says: 'Either feed me or divorce me'" there is a response to those who say that marriage is not dissolved on account of poverty, that the wife must bear patience, and that maintenance remains a debt upon him by the ruling of the judge. This is the view of Ata and al-Zuhri. The Kufans also held this view, relying on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if someone is in hardship, then let there be postponement until a time of ease﴾ [2:280]. They said: It is therefore obligatory to wait until he is well-off. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And marry off the single among you﴾ [24:32], the verse. They said: He, exalted is He, urged the marrying off of the poor, so it is not permissible for poverty to be a cause of separation, while preventing him from marriage is disapproved. But they have no proof in this verse, as will be explained in its proper place. The hadith is explicit on the point of disagreement. It has also been said: The address is to the guardian of the orphan, that he should maintain him from his property which is under his care, according to what preceded regarding the disagreement over attributing the property. So the guardian maintains the orphan according to the amount of his property and his condition. If he is young and his property is large, he appoints for him a wet-nurse and nurses, and expands his maintenance. If he is older, he provides for him fine clothing, tasty food and servants. If it is less than that, then according to his means. If it is less than that, then coarse food and clothing sufficient to meet the need. If the orphan is poor with no property, it is obligatory upon the ruler to provide for him from the bayt al-mal (public treasury). If the ruler does not do so, it becomes obligatory upon the Muslims, the closest relatives first, then the next closest. His mother has the closest claim to him, so it is obligatory upon her to nurse him and look after him, and she does not seek reimbursement from him or from anyone. This was discussed in al-Baqarah at His saying: ﴿And mothers suckle their children﴾ [2:233] (see vol. 3, pp. 160–161).

**Tenth:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And speak to them a kind word﴾. He intended softening the address and a gracious promise. Scholars differed regarding "kind word". It has been said: its meaning is, supplicate for them: "May Allah bless you, protect you, and provide for you, and I am watching over you, and this caution will return its benefit to you." It has also been said: its meaning is to promise them a good promise, meaning: if you become rightly guided, we will hand over your property to you. And a father says to his son: "My property will go to you, and you, God willing, will be its owner when you have attained maturity and I have known your conduct."

**Question 1:** There are seventeen issues in this verse. The first is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And test the orphans﴾. *Al-ibtila'* means testing (*al-ikhtibar*), and it has been discussed before [[See the thirteenth issue, vol. 1, p. 387.]]. This verse addresses everyone, explaining how to hand over their wealth. It was also said that it was revealed concerning Thabit ibn Rifa'ah and his paternal uncle. Rifa'ah died and left a son who was still young. Thabit's uncle came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "My nephew is an orphan in my care. What is lawful for me from his wealth, and when should I hand his property over to him?" Then Allah revealed this verse.

**Question 2:** The scholars differed over the meaning of testing (*ikhtibar*). It was said that it means the guardian (*wasi*) observes his orphan's character, listens to his aims, and so gains knowledge of his ability, his competence in looking after his affairs, and his management of his wealth, or his neglect of these [[The waw here means "or."]]. If he perceives good in him, our scholars and others said: there is no harm in giving him a portion of his wealth that allows him to dispose of it. If he makes it grow and manages it well, the testing has taken place, and the guardian must hand over all his wealth to him. If he manages it badly, the guardian must keep his wealth in his safekeeping. No scholar holds that when the guardian tests the child and finds him mature (*rashid*), the guardianship is lifted and he must hand over his property and give him full freedom to dispose of it, based on His saying: ﴿until they reach marriageable age﴾. A group of jurists said: a young person is either a boy or a girl. If he is a boy, the guardian entrusts him with the household expenses for a month, or gives him a small amount to spend, so that he may learn how he manages and disposes of it, while the guardian still watches over it so that he does not waste it. If he wastes it, the guardian bears no liability. When he sees him acting prudently, he hands over his property to him and calls witnesses against him. If she is a girl, the guardian gives her what is given to the mistress of a household: managing her house and overseeing its affairs, including spinning, supervising the spinners in distributing cotton and their wages, and ensuring the yarn is delivered and of good quality. If he finds her sensible, he also hands over her property to her and calls witnesses against her. Otherwise, both remain under restriction (*hajr*) until their maturity of judgment is evident. Al-Hasan, Mujahid and others said: test them in their intellects, their religion, and the growth of their wealth.

**Question 3:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿until they reach marriageable age﴾, meaning the age of sexual maturity (*al-hulm*), as in His saying: (And when the children among you reach puberty [[See vol. 12, p. 308.]]), meaning the state of puberty (*al-bulugh*) and the age of marriage. Puberty occurs through five things: three shared by men and women, and two specific to women, namely menstruation and pregnancy. Scholars have not disagreed that menstruation and pregnancy are signs of puberty, and that obligations and rulings apply upon them. They differed concerning the three shared signs. As for the growth of hair and age: al-Awza'i, al-Shafi'i and Ibn Hanbal said that fifteen years is puberty for one who has not experienced ihtilam (sexual maturity through emission). This is also the view of Ibn Wahb, Asbagh, Abd al-Malik ibn al-Majishun, Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz and a group of the people of Madinah, and Ibn al-Arabi chose it. According to them, the legal punishments (*hudud*) and obligations (*fara'id*) apply to one who reaches this age. Asbagh ibn al-Faraj said: What we hold is that the limit of puberty by which obligations and punishments become binding is fifteen years. This is the most preferred and best position in my view, because it is the age at which a person receives a share in jihad and is considered for combat. He cited the hadith of Ibn Umar, when he was presented to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the day of the Trench at fifteen years of age, and was permitted [[That is, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) presented him to examine his condition.]], but was not permitted on the day of Uhud because he was fourteen. Muslim recorded it. Abu Umar ibn Abd al-Barr said: This applies to one whose birth date is known. As for one whose birth date is unknown, or whose age is uncertain or denied, the ruling follows what Nafi' related from Aslam from Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that he wrote to the commanders of the armies: "Do not impose the jizyah except on those upon whom the *mawasi* have passed [[Mawasi is the plural of *mawsa*, meaning the growth of pubic hair, on which the razor passes. Among the Children of Israel this was equivalent to Muslims and to circumcision.]]." Uthman said concerning a boy who stole: "Look: if his loincloth has turned dark, cut off his hand." [[His loincloth is a metaphor for the private parts, meaning that they have darkened with hair. The Arabs call the black colour green.]] Atiyyah al-Qurazi said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) presented the Banu Qurayzah, and whoever had grown hair he killed, according to the ruling of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh [[His ruling concerning them was that their men be killed, their women and children taken captive. The Prophet (ﷺ) had said to him: "You have ruled concerning them by the ruling of Allah from above the seven heavens." See his biography in al-Isti'ab.]], and whoever had not grown hair he spared. I was among those who had not grown hair, so he left me. Malik, Abu Hanifah and others said: no ruling applies to one who has not experienced ihtilam until he reaches an age that no one reaches without experiencing ihtilam, and that is seventeen years. Then the penal obligations apply to him when he commits what makes them binding. Malik once said: his puberty is when his voice deepens and the hair above his upper lip sprouts. A second report from Abu Hanifah says nineteen years, and this is the more well-known. He said concerning a girl: her puberty is at seventeen years, and then she is subject to scrutiny. Al-Lu'lu'i related from him eighteen years. Dawud said: Age does not establish puberty unless ihtilam occurs, even if he reaches forty years. As for hair growth: some said it is used as evidence of puberty. This was related from Ibn al-Qasim and Salim, and Malik once said so, and al-Shafi'i in one of his two opinions, and Ahmad, Ishaq and Abu Thawr also held this. It was also said that it is puberty, but it is applied to unbelievers so that whoever has grown hair is killed and whoever has not is counted among the offspring (*dhurriyyah*). This is what al-Shafi'i said in his other opinion, based on the hadith of Atiyyah al-Qurazi. The greenish down and the fine hair are not considered; only coarse hair establishes the ruling. Ibn al-Qasim said: I heard Malik say: "My practice follows the hadith of Umar ibn al-Khattab: if the *mawasi* had passed over him, I would impose the hadd on him." Asbagh said: Ibn al-Qasim told me: "And I prefer that the hadd not be imposed on him except when both hair growth and puberty are present together." Abu Hanifah said: no ruling is connected to hair growth, and it is neither puberty nor an indication of puberty. Al-Zuhri and Ata' said: there is no hadd on one who has not experienced ihtilam. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, and Malik once inclined to it, and some of his companions held it. Its apparent meaning is that hair growth and age are not considered. Ibn al-Arabi said: "If the hadith of Ibn Umar is not evidence regarding age, then every number of years they mention is mere assertion. The age which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) permitted is more deserving than an age he did not consider, and no evidence in the Shari'ah supports it. Likewise, the Prophet (ﷺ) considered hair growth in the case of the Banu Qurayzah. So who can excuse one who abandons two matters that the Prophet (ﷺ) considered, interprets [the texts] to suit himself, and considers what the Prophet (ﷺ) did not consider in wording, when Allah has not given him any standing in the Shari'ah?" I say: This is his view here, but in Surah al-Anfal he said the opposite, since he did not refer to the hadith of Ibn Umar there, and interpreted it as our scholars did: its implication is the distinction between one who is able to fight and receives a share, who is fifteen years old, and one who is not able to fight, who receives no share and is counted among the dependants. This is what Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz understood from the hadith. And Allah knows best.

**Question 4:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then if you perceive in them maturity (*rushd*), hand over to them their property﴾. *Anastum* means you saw and perceived, and from it is His saying: (He perceived a fire from the side of the mount [[See vol. 13, p. 280.]]), meaning he saw and perceived. Al-Azhari said: The Arabs say: "Go and *istanis* whether you see anyone," meaning look and see. The poet al-Nabigha said:

... a wild ox that is alone [[Completion of the verse: "As though my saddle, when the day had passed away with us, on the day of al-Jalil, was on a lone (wahd) ox." The wahd means solitary.]]. He meant a wild bull that looks about to see whether a hunter is watching, so that it may beware of him. It is also said: *ānastu*, *aḥassa* and *wajadtu* have one meaning. From this is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And if you perceive in them maturity of judgment﴾, meaning, if you know. The original sense is *abṣartum* (you saw). The common reading is *rushdan* (rushdan) with a *ḍamma* on the *rā'* and a sukūn on the *shīn*. As-Sulamī, ʿĪsā, ath-Thaqafī and Ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with them, read *rashadan* with a *fatḥa* on the *rā'* and the *shīn*, and both are dialectal forms. It is also said: *rushdan* is the verbal noun of *rashada*, and *rashadan* is the verbal noun of *rashida*, and likewise *al-rashād*. And Allah knows best.

The fifth issue: The scholars differed in interpreting *rushdan*. Al-Ḥasan, Qatādah and others said: soundness in intellect and religion. Ibn ʿAbbās, as-Suddī and ath-Thawrī said: soundness in intellect and the preservation of property. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and ash-Shaʿbī said: a man may be taking hold of his beard while he has not reached *rushd*, so his property is not handed to an orphan even if he is an old man, until his *rushd* is perceived in him. Likewise ad-Ḍaḥḥāk said: the orphan is not given (his property) even if he reaches a hundred years, until his sound management of his property is known. Mujāhid said: *rushdan* means in intellect specifically. Most scholars hold that *rushd* does not occur except after puberty, and that if he does not attain *rushd* after reaching the age of puberty, even if he grows old, the interdiction (*al-ḥajr*, legal restriction on disposal of property) does not lift from him. This is the view of Mālik and others. Abū Ḥanīfa said: a free adult who has reached the stage of men is not placed under interdiction, even if he is the most dissolute of people and the greatest squanderer, so long as he is sensible. Zufar ibn al-Hudhayl also said this, and it is the view of an-Nakhaʿī. They argued for this with what Qatādah narrated from Anas, that Ḥibbān [[Ḥibbān: with a *fatḥa* on the *ḥā'*; it was mentioned in vol. 3, p. 386, where it reads: "and in his intellect". That is another narration.]] ibn Munqidh used to buy, and in his judgment there was weakness. It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, place him under interdiction, for he buys while there is weakness in his judgment." The Prophet ﷺ summoned him and said: "Do not buy." He said: "I cannot refrain." So he said to him: "When you trade, say: 'No deception,' and you have the option for three days." They said: when the people asked him to place him under interdiction because of the loss in his dealings, and he, peace be upon him, did not do so, it is established that interdiction is not permissible. There is no proof for them in this, because he was specifically exempted in that matter, as we have explained in *al-Baqarah* [[Ḥibbān: with a *fatḥa* on the *ḥā'*; it was mentioned in vol. 3, p. 386, where it reads: "and in his intellect". That is another narration.]], so others are different from him. Ash-Shāfiʿī said: if he corrupts his property and his religion, or corrupts his property but not his religion, he is placed under interdiction. If he corrupts his religion but sets his property right, then there are two views: one, that he is placed under interdiction, and this is the choice of Abū al-ʿAbbās ibn Surayj; the second, that he is not placed under interdiction, and this is the choice of Abū Isḥāq al-Marwazī, and it is the more apparent view in the school of ash-Shāfiʿī. Ath-Thaʿlabī said: what we have mentioned about the interdiction of the foolish (*safīh*) is the view of ʿUthmān, ʿAlī, az-Zubayr, ʿĀ'ishah, Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar, may Allah be pleased with them all. Among the Successors is Shurayḥ, and this is what the jurists said: Mālik, the people of Madina, al-Awzāʿī, the people of Syria, Abū Yūsuf, Muḥammad, Aḥmad, Isḥāq and Abū Thawr. Ath-Thaʿlabī said: our companions claimed consensus (*ijmāʿ*) on this question.

The sixth issue: Once this is established, know that the handing over of property occurs with two conditions: perceiving *rushd* and puberty. If one of them is found without the other, it is not permissible to hand over the property. This is the explicit wording of the verse. It is also the narration of Ibn al-Qāsim, Ashhab and Ibn Wahb from Mālik regarding the verse, and it is the view of the majority of jurists, except Abū Ḥanīfa, Zufar and an-Nakhaʿī, for they dropped the requirement of perceiving *rushd* upon reaching twenty-five years of age. Abū Ḥanīfa said: because he is *jadd* (of substance). This indicates the weakness of his view and the weakness of what Abū Bakr ar-Rāzī argued in *Aḥkām al-Qur'ān* from applying the two verses as mentioned earlier, for this belongs to the category of the absolute and the restricted, and the absolute is referred back to the restricted by agreement of the scholars of legal theory. And what does being *jadd* avail if he is not *jadd*, that is, of good fortune? However, our scholars made a condition for a girl that the husband consummates the marriage with her together with puberty, and at that point the testing of *rushd* occurs. Abū Ḥanīfa and ash-Shāfiʿī did not accept this, and they held that testing applies to males and females alike, as mentioned earlier. Our scholars distinguished between them, saying: the female differs from the boy because she is veiled, does not deal with affairs, and does not come forth because of her virginity; therefore for her the existence of marriage is awaited, for by it all her intentions are understood. The male is different, for through his dealings and his contact with people from his youth until his puberty, testing is applicable to him, and his intellect is complete at puberty, so the purpose is achieved. What ash-Shāfiʿī said is more correct, for the mere intercourse, by insertion of the glans, does not increase her in *rushd* if she already knows all her affairs and intentions and does not squander her property. Then our scholars added: after her husband has entered her, a period of time must pass in which she tests her circumstances. Ibn al-ʿArabī said: her scholars mentioned many views in determining it, among them five years, six years and seven years for the one with a father. For the orphan who has no father and no guardian over her, they set one year after consummation. For the one placed under guardianship, they set it as indefinite until her *rushd* is established. There is no proof in all of this, and fixing the number of years for the one with a father is difficult, and even more difficult is fixing a year for the orphan. As for the continuation of interdiction over the one under guardianship until her *rushd* becomes clear, so that the guardian releases her from it or the judge releases her from it, this is the apparent meaning of the Qur'an. The whole purpose of this falls under the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And if you perceive in them maturity of judgment﴾, so the consideration of *rushd* is required, but the perception of it differs according to the differing condition of the one who is mature. So understand this, build upon it, and avoid the arbitrary judgment for which there is no proof.

The seventh issue: They differed regarding what the one with a father does during that period. It was said: what she does is treated as rejected, since the interdiction remains, and what she does after it is treated as valid. Some said: what she does during that period is treated as rejected, unless soundness becomes evident in it, and what she does after that is treated as valid, unless foolishness becomes evident in it.

The eighth issue: They differed on whether handing over property to the one under interdiction requires the authority (*sulṭān*) or not. One group said: it is necessary to refer the matter to the authority, and his *rushd* is established before him, and then his property is handed to him. Another group said: this is left to the judgment of the guardian, without needing to refer it to the authority. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: the correct view regarding the guardians of our time is that one cannot dispense with referring it to the authority and establishing *rushd* before him, because it has been reported that guardians collude so that the child is declared mature, and the one under interdiction is cleared, despite his foolishness and his lack of discernment at that time.

The ninth issue: If property is handed over to him upon the existence of *rushd*, and then he returns to foolishness through the appearance of squandering and poor management, the interdiction returns to him according to us, and according to ash-Shāfiʿī in one of his two views. Abū Ḥanīfa said: it does not return, because he is an adult and sensible, as evidenced by the permissibility of his confession in matters of *ḥudūd* and *qiṣāṣ*. Our proof is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And do not give the foolish your property, which Allah has made for you a means of support﴾, and the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿But if the one who owes the debt is foolish, or weak, or unable to dictate himself, then let his guardian dictate with justice﴾ [[See vol. 3, p. 376.]], and He did not distinguish between one who is placed under interdiction as foolish and one for whom this occurs after release.

The tenth issue: The guardian may do with the orphan's property what the father was permitted to do, such as trade, entrusting capital (*ibḍāʿ*), buying and selling [[In vol. C: in trade or capital.]]. He must pay the zakat from all his property: cash, crops, livestock and the zakat al-fiṭr. He pays on his behalf the compensation for crimes (*arsh al-janāyāt*), the value of what has been destroyed, the maintenance of his parents, and all other obligatory rights. He may marry him off and pay his dowry on his behalf, buy for him a slave-girl whom he may take as a concubine, and make settlements for him and against him in a manner that is in his best interest. If the guardian pays some of the creditors while there remains from the property a remainder that covers what is owed of the debt, the guardian's act is valid. If the remaining property is then lost, the other creditors have no claim against the guardian, nor against those who were paid. If the creditors take the whole property, and then other creditors come, then if the guardian knew of the remaining debt, or the deceased was known to have the remaining debt, the guardian is liable to these creditors for what they would have received in the pro-rata distribution, and he recovers it from those who were paid their debts. If he did not know of it, and the deceased was not known to be in debt, then the guardian is not liable. If the guardian pays the debt of the deceased without witnesses, he is liable. But if he takes witnesses and much time passes until the witnesses die, then he is not liable. What was already mentioned in *al-Baqarah* [[See vol. 3, p. 65.]], at the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And if you mix with them, they are your brothers﴾, contains enough of the rulings concerning the guardian in spending and other matters, and all praise is due to Allah.

The eleventh issue: The saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And do not consume them extravagantly and hastily, fearing that they will grow up﴾ does not mean that consuming their property without extravagance is permissible, so that it would have a *dalīl al-khiṭāb* (implication by inference). Rather, the meaning is: do not consume their property, for that is extravagance. Allah, glorified and exalted, forbade the guardians from consuming the property of orphans except what is obligatory or permissible for them, as will be explained. *Isrāf* in language means excess and going beyond the limit. It was already discussed in *Āl ʿImrān* [[See vol. 4, p. 231.]]. *Sarf* is error in spending. From this is the saying of the poet [[The verse is by Jarīr praising the Umayyads. Hunayda: a name for every hundred camels.]]:
They gave Hunayda, driven by eight (camels), 
with no deficiency in their giving, and no excess.
meaning they do not err in the places of giving. Another said:
And one of them said, while the horses trampled them: 
"You have been extravagant!" and we replied: "We are indeed extravagant."
An-Naḍr ibn Shumayl said: *sarf* is squandering, and *sarf* is heedlessness. More explanation of the meaning of *isrāf* will come in *al-Anʿām* [[See vol. 7, p. 110.]], Allah willing.

(And [do not consume their property hastily] "wa-bidaran") means: and hastening before they grow up. It refers to the time of puberty. Bidar and mubadara are like qital and muqatala. It is conjoined to "israfan" (wastefully). "An yakbaru" is in the accusative position governed by "bidaran", meaning: do not seize the property of your ward while considering it booty, consuming it, and saying, "I will hasten [to take it] before he grows up, lest he become rightly guided and take his property." This is related from Ibn 'Abbas and others.

The Twelfth [issue]: His Exalted saying: ﴿And whoever is rich, let him abstain﴾, etc. Allah the Exalted explained what is permitted to them from their property: He commanded the wealthy to refrain, and permitted the poor guardian (wasi) to eat from the property of his ward according to what is customary (bil-ma'ruf). It is said: 'affa al-rajul 'an al-shay' and esta'affa when he refrained. Al-isti'faf from something is leaving it. From it is His Exalted saying: ﴿And let those who cannot find marriage keep themselves chaste﴾ [see vol. 12, p. 243]. And al-'iffah is refraining from what is not permitted and what is not obligatory to do. Abu Dawud related from the hadith of Husayn al-Mu'allim, from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, that a man came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "I am poor, I have nothing, and I have an orphan in my care." He said: [The Prophet] said: "Eat from the property of your orphan without being wasteful, extravagant, or accumulating [wealth]" (mutaththil [[mutaththil: accumulating; it is said: mal mawthul, meaning collected, having a root].]).

The Thirteenth [issue]: The scholars differed regarding who is addressed by this verse and what is meant by it. In Sahih Muslim, from 'A'isha regarding His Exalted saying: ﴿And whoever is poor, let him eat according to what is customary﴾, she said: It was revealed concerning the guardian of the orphan who manages and looks after him: if he is in need, it is permitted for him to eat from it. In another narration: "in proportion to his property, according to what is customary." Some of them said: what is meant is the orphan: if he is wealthy, he should provide for him generously and abstain from his property; and if he is poor, he should spend on him according to his means. This was said by Rabi'a and Yahya ibn Sa'id. The first view is the view of the majority and is the correct one, because the orphan is not addressed with disposing of his property due to his young age and his immaturity. And Allah knows best.

The Fourteenth [issue]: The majority differed regarding what "eating according to what is customary" is. Some people said: it is a loan: if he is in need he borrows, and repays when he becomes well-off. This was said by 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ubayda, Ibn Jubayr, al-Sha'bi, Mujahid, and Abu al-'Aliya, and it is the view of al-Awza'i. He should not borrow more than his need. 'Umar said: "Indeed, I have placed myself in relation to Allah's property in the position of the guardian in relation to the orphan's property: if I am wealthy I abstain, and if I am poor I eat according to what is customary; then when I become well-off I repay." 'Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak related from 'Asim, from Abu al-'Aliya, regarding (And whoever is poor, let him eat according to what is customary): he said: as a loan, then he recited: ﴿And when you hand over their property to them, call witnesses against them﴾.

A second view: it is related from Ibrahim, 'Ata', al-Hasan al-Basri, al-Nakha'i, and Qatada: there is no repayment obligation upon the poor guardian for what he eats according to what is customary, because that is the right of management (haqq al-nazar), and the jurists hold this view. Al-Hasan said: "It is a provision from Allah for him: he eats what satisfies his hunger, and clothes himself with what covers his nakedness, and does not wear fine linen or silk garments." The evidence for the soundness of this view is the consensus of the Muslim community that the imam who manages the affairs of the Muslims is not obligated to repay what he eats according to what is customary, because Allah the Exalted has prescribed his share in Allah's property. So there is no proof for them in 'Umar's saying "then when I become well-off I repay," even if it were authentic.

It is also related from Ibn 'Abbas, Abu al-'Aliya, and al-Sha'bi that eating according to what is customary is like benefiting from the milk of livestock, employing slaves, and riding animals when this does not harm the principal property, just as one applies tar to a mangy camel (yahna'u al-jarba'a [[hana'a al-ibil: smeared them with tar, a kind of pitch]]), searches for a lost animal (yanshudu al-dallah), plasters the pool (yalut al-hawd [[lat al-hawd: coated it with mud and repaired it]]), and harvests the dates (yajudhdh al-tamr). As for the principal properties and their capital, the guardian has no right to take them. All of this is consistent with the view of the jurists that he takes an amount equal to the wage of his work; and a group held this, and said that this is what is customary, and there is no repayment upon him, and anything beyond that is forbidden.

Al-Hasan ibn Salih ibn Hayy (also said Ibn Hayyan) distinguished between the guardian appointed by the father and the guardian appointed by the judge: the guardian appointed by the father may eat according to what is customary, whereas the guardian appointed by the judge has no access whatsoever to the property. This is the third view. A fourth view related from Mujahid: he said: "He is not permitted to take a loan or anything else." He held that the verse is abrogated, abrogated by His Exalted saying: ﴿O you who have believed, do not consume your properties among yourselves in falsehood, except that it be trade by mutual consent among you﴾ [see p. 149 of this volume], and this is not trade.

Zayd ibn Aslam said: the concession in this verse is abrogated by His Exalted saying: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly﴾, etc. Bishr ibn al-Walid related from Abu Yusuf who said: "I do not know; perhaps this verse is abrogated by the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿O you who have believed, do not consume your properties among yourselves in falsehood, except that it be trade by mutual consent among you﴾."

A fifth view, which is the distinction between residence and travel: it is prohibited when he is staying with him in the city; but if he needs to travel on account of it, he may take what he needs, and not accumulate anything. This was said by Abu Hanifa and his two companions, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad.

A sixth view: Abu Qilaba said: "Let him eat according to what is customary from what the produce yields, but as for liquid cash (al-mal al-nadd [[al-nadd: the dirham and dinar according to the people of the Hijaz; it is called nadd when it turns into cash after having been goods]]), he has no right to take anything from it, whether as a loan or otherwise."

A seventh view: 'Ikrima related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding (And whoever is poor, let him eat according to what is customary): he said: "If he is in need and compelled." Al-Sha'bi said: likewise, if it is for him like blood and the flesh of swine, he takes from it; and if he finds [something else], he stops. Al-Nahhas said: this has no meaning, because when he is compelled to this extent, he may take whatever sustains him from his orphan's property or others', whether near or far. Ibn 'Abbas also said, as did al-Nakha'i: what is meant is that the guardian should eat according to what is customary from his own property so that he does not need the orphan's property; the wealthy abstains through his wealth, and the poor restricts himself so that he does not need his orphan's property. Al-Nahhas said: this is among the finest of what has been related in the interpretation of the verse, because people's property is inviolable and nothing of it may be made lawful except by a decisive proof.

I say: Al-Kiya al-Tabari, in his Ahkam al-Quran, chose this view, saying: "Some of the early scholars imagined from the ruling of the verse that the guardian may consume from the child's property an amount that does not reach the limit of extravagance; but that contradicts what Allah has commanded in His saying: ﴿Do not consume your properties among yourselves in falsehood, except that it be trade by mutual consent among you﴾. That does not hold concerning [the property of the orphan]. So His saying: ﴿And whoever is rich, let him abstain﴾ refers to [consuming] his own property, not the orphan's property. Its meaning is: and do not consume the orphans' property together with your own; rather, limit yourselves to consuming your own property. This is indicated by His Exalted saying: ﴿And do not consume their property along with your own property; indeed, that is a great sin﴾. And it is made clear by His Exalted saying: ﴿And whoever is rich, let him abstain; and whoever is poor, let him eat according to what is customary﴾ that the matter is limited to what suffices, so that he does not need to consume the orphan's property. This is the full meaning of the verse."

Therefore we have found clear verses (muhkamat) that forbid consuming the property of another without his consent, especially in the case of the orphan. We have also found that this verse admits several meanings, so interpreting it in accordance with the requirement of the clear verses is necessary. If someone who supports the view of the early predecessors (salaf) says: the judges take their wages for their work for the Muslims, so why should the guardian (wasi) not be likewise when he works for the orphan, and why should he not take a wage in proportion to his work? It is said to him: know that none of the salaf permitted the guardian to take from the orphan's property while the guardian is wealthy, unlike the judge, and this is the difference between the two issues. Moreover, what the jurists, judges and caliphs who manage the affairs of Islam take does not have a specific owner. God has assigned that lost property to categories of people with specific attributes, and judges are among them. The guardian, however, takes by his work the property of a specific individual without that individual's consent, and his work is unknown and his wage is unknown, and this is far from entitlement.

I say: Our shaykh, the Imam Abu'l-Abbas, used to say: if the orphan's property is large and requires great management, such that it occupies the guardian away from his needs and affairs, then a wage for his work is prescribed for him from it. If it is trivial and does not occupy him from his needs, then he should not eat anything from it, except that it is recommended for him to drink a little milk and eat a little food and butter, not harmful to the orphan and not excessive, but in accordance with the customary leniency in such matters. Our shaykh said: what I have mentioned about the wage and the taking of a small amount of dates [[In ج: السن (teeth/age).]] and milk, each of these is known, so it is valid to interpret the verse in accordance with that. And God knows best.

I say: abstaining from it is more excellent, God willing. [As for what the divider of inheritance (qadi al-qisma) takes and calls rasm (customary fee), and what his followers plunder, I do not know any justification for it or any permissibility, and they are included in the generality of His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly only consume fire into their bellies﴾ [[This addition is found only in manuscript أوح.]].]

The fifteenth issue: His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And when you hand over to them their property, then have witnesses over them﴾. God, the Exalted, commanded calling witnesses as a means of safeguarding and of removing suspicion. According to a group of scholars this witnessing is recommended, since the word of the guardian is accepted because he is trustworthy. Another group said: it is obligatory, and this is the apparent meaning of the verse, and he is not trustworthy such that his word would be accepted, like an agent (wakil) who claims he has returned what was given to him, or a depositary (mudi'), and he is only trusted by the father; whenever the father entrusts him, his word is not accepted regarding anything else. Do you not see that if the agent claims that he has handed over to Zayd what he was ordered to hand over, his word is not accepted except with evidence, despite his probity? Likewise the guardian. Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, and Ibn Jubayr held that this witnessing is only regarding the guardian's handing back what he borrowed from his orphan's property while he was poor, once he becomes wealthy. Ubayda said: this verse is evidence for the obligation of repayment upon the one who consumed (the property). The meaning is: if you borrowed or consumed, then call witnesses when you are obligated to pay. The correct view is that the wording covers this and other cases. The apparent meaning is that what is intended is: when you have spent something on the one under guardianship, then call witnesses, so that if a dispute arises it is possible to establish evidence. For every property received in trust with witnesses, one is not released from it except by witnessing its return, because of His saying: ﴿then call witnesses﴾. So if he returned it to the one from whom he received it without witnesses, he does not need witnesses for returning it if its receipt was without witnesses. And God knows best.

The sixteenth issue: Just as the guardian and the custodian are obligated to protect the orphan's property and make it grow, so too he is obligated to protect the child in his person. He protects the property by controlling it, and he protects the body by disciplining it. This matter has already been discussed in (al-Baqarah) [[See vol. 3, p. 62.]]. It is related that a man said to the Prophet ﷺ: "I have an orphan in my custody; may I eat from his property?" He said: "Yes, without accumulating property (mutaʾaththil) and without protecting your property with his property." He said: "O Messenger of God, shall I strike him?" He said: "Strike him as you would strike your own child." Ibn al-Arabi said: even though it is not established with a continuous chain (musnad), no one can find an alternative to it. [Mutaththil: accumulating.]

The seventeenth issue: His saying: ﴿And sufficient is God as Reckoner﴾, meaning: God is sufficient as a reckoner of your deeds and as one who recompenses them. In this there is a warning to everyone who denies a right. The letter ba' (in "bi-Allah") is superfluous (za'idah), and the phrase is in the nominative position.

**Fifth issue:** [This passage has five issues.] **The first:** When Allah the Exalted mentioned the matter of orphans, He connected it with the mention of inheritance. The verse was revealed concerning Aws ibn Thabit al-Ansari. He died and left a wife called Umm Kuhha and three daughters from her. Two men, who were paternal cousins of the deceased and his executors, called Suwayd and 'Arfajah, came forward, took his property, and gave nothing to his wife or his daughters. In the Jahiliyyah they did not give inheritance to women or to small children, even if they were male. They said: "None receives a share except one who fights on horseback, thrusts with the spear, strikes with the sword, and seizes the spoils." Umm Kuhha reported this to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he summoned the two men. They said: "O Messenger of Allah, her son does not ride a horse, does not carry a burden, and does not strike an enemy." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Go away until I see what Allah will reveal to me concerning them." Then Allah revealed this verse in refutation of them, to nullify their saying and their conduct born of ignorance. For the small heirs ought to have had a better claim to the property than the adult heirs, since they cannot manage it or attend to their own interests. Instead they reversed the ruling, nullified the wisdom, and went astray by their desires and erred in their opinions and their conduct.

**The second:** Our scholars said: In this verse there are three benefits. The first is the explanation of the cause of inheritance, which is kinship. The second is the generality of kinship, whatever its form, whether near or distant. The third is the general statement of the prescribed share. This is made specific in the verse of inheritance, so this verse paved the way for the ruling and nullified that corrupt opinion until the clear explanation came.

**The third:** It is established that when Abu Talhah gave his property, Bi'r Ha' (Bayraha'), as charity and mentioned this to the Prophet (ﷺ), he said to him: "Place it among the poor of your relatives." So he gave it to Hassan and Ubayy. Anas said: "And they were closer to him than I was." Abu Dawud said: It has reached me from Muhammad ibn Abdullah al-Ansari that he said: Abu Talhah al-Ansari is Zayd ibn Sahl ibn al-Aswad ibn Haram ibn 'Amr ibn Zayd Manat ibn 'Adi ibn 'Amr ibn Malik ibn al-Najjar. Hassan ibn Thabit ibn al-Mundhir ibn Haram and they meet in the third forefather, who is Haram. Ubayy ibn Ka'b ibn Qays ibn 'Ubayd ibn Zayd ibn Mu'awiyah ibn 'Amr ibn Malik ibn al-Najjar. The Ansari said: Between Abu Talhah and Ubayy there are six forefathers. He said: 'Amr ibn Malik gathers Hassan, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, and Abu Talhah. Abu 'Umar [Ibn 'Abd al-Barr] said: In this there is that which decides concerning kinship, that it is whatever is within this lineage and the like, and whatever is below it is more fitting to be called kinship.

**The fourth:** The saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿From what is little or much of it, a prescribed share﴾. Allah the Exalted established for the daughters a share in the inheritance but did not specify how much it is. So the Prophet (ﷺ) sent to Suwayd and 'Arfajah that they should not distribute anything from the property of Aws, for Allah has given his daughters a share but has not specified how much it is, until I see what our Lord reveals. Then the verses were revealed: ﴿Allah enjoins you concerning your children...﴾ up to His saying ﴿...the great triumph﴾. So he sent to them both: "Give Umm Kuhha an eighth of what Aws left, and to his daughters two-thirds, and to you both the remainder of the property."

**The fifth:** Our scholars have used this verse for the division of what is left (by the deceased) among the heirs according to the prescribed shares when there is in it a change from its original state, such as a bathhouse, a house, an olive threshing floor [[In z: this is the place where grains are trodden and food is gathered. In h, w, and a: bdh, perhaps from their saying: "tamr badh", meaning scattered. In d, j, wwb, hh, and t: bd. It is not apparent in meaning.]], and a house whose benefits are nullified by the acknowledgment of those entitled to shares in it. Malik said: That is divided, even if the portion of none of them has anything from which they can benefit, based on His saying the Exalted: ﴿From what is little or much of it, a prescribed share﴾. This is also the saying of Ibn Kinanah, and al-Shafi'i held this view, and the saying of Abu Hanifah is similar to it. Abu Hanifah said: In a small house shared between two people, if one of them seeks division and the other refuses, it is divided for him. Ibn Abi Layla said: If among them there is someone who does not benefit from what is allotted to him, it is not divided. Every division that involves harm to one of them and not the other is not divided. This is the saying of Abu Thawr. Ibn al-Mundhir said: It is the more sound of the two sayings. Ibn al-Qasim narrated it from Malik, as Ibn al-'Arabi mentioned. Ibn al-Qasim said: I hold that everything that cannot be divided, such as houses, dwellings, and bathhouses, and whose division entails harm and from which no benefit is gained once divided, should be sold, and there is no pre-emption (shuf'ah) in it, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Pre-emption applies to everything that is not divided; but when the boundaries are set, there is no pre-emption." Thus the Prophet (ﷺ) made pre-emption apply to everything in which the setting of boundaries is possible, and tied pre-emption to what is not divided but in which boundaries can be set. This is the indication of the hadith.

I say: Among the proof for this view is what al-Daraqutni transmitted from the hadith of Ibn Juraij: Siddiq ibn Musa informed me, from Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr, from his father, from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "There is no 'ta'diyah' (dividing and causing harm) upon the heirs except what division can bear." Abu 'Ubayd said: It means that a man dies and leaves something which, if divided among his heirs, would cause harm to all of them or to some of them. He says: So it is not divided, such as a precious gem, a bathhouse, a shawl, and what is similar to these. And "ta'diyah" means separation; it is said: "I divided (ʿadhaytu) the thing" when I separated it. From this is His saying the Exalted: ﴿Those who have made the Qur'an into fragments﴾. And He said the Exalted: ﴿without causing harm﴾, so He negated harm. Likewise the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There should be no harming nor reciprocating harm." Also, the verse does not address division at all; the verse only requires that the small and the great each have a portion and share, whether little or much, in refutation of the Jahiliyyah, so He said: ﴿For men there is a share﴾ and ﴿for women there is a share﴾. This is very evident. As for the actual setting aside of that share, it is derived from another proof: that the heir says, "A share has become due to me by the saying of Allah, mighty and majestic, so enable me to have it," and his partner says to him: "As for your being enabled to take it exclusively, that is not possible, because it would lead to harm between me and you through the spoiling of the property, the change of its form, and the reduction of its value, so the weighing (of considerations) takes place." The more apparent view is that division is dropped in what nullifies the benefit and reduces the property, along with the evidence we have mentioned. And Allah is the Granter of success.

Al-Farra' said: ﴿a prescribed share﴾ is like your saying: "an obligatory division" and "a binding right," so it is a noun in the sense of the verbal noun, and for this reason it is in the accusative. Al-Zajjaj said: It is in the accusative as a circumstantial state, meaning: for these people there are shares in the state of being prescribed. Al-Akhfash said: That is, Allah made that a share for them. And "al-mafrud" means the determined, obligatory.

**First issue:** Allah the Exalted explains that whoever is not entitled to any inheritance but attends the division, and is among the relatives, orphans, or needy who do not inherit, should be honoured and not deprived, if the property is large. If the estate is real property or is small and does not admit a gift (*ar-radkh* here means a small gift) [[Ar-radkh here: a small gift.]], they should be given an apology. If the gift is small, there is a great reward in it: a dirham precedes a hundred thousand dirhams [[In manuscript J: a dirham precedes seven hundred thousand dirhams.]]. On this view the verse is *muhkamah* (definitive, not abrogated). This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas. A group of the Successors (*tabi'un*) acted upon it, including 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr and others, and Abu Musa al-Ash'ari ordered it. However, it is related from Ibn 'Abbas that the verse is *mansukhah* (abrogated), abrogated by the words of Allah the Exalted: ("Allah instructs you concerning your children: for the male, what is equal to the share of two females"). Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: it was abrogated by the verse of inheritance and the verse of bequest. Among those who said it is abrogated were Abu Malik, 'Ikrimah, and al-Dahhak. The first view is more sound, for the verse clarifies the entitlement of the heirs to their shares and the recommendation (*istihbab*) of sharing with those present who have no share. Ibn Jubayr said: people have neglected this verse. Al-Hasan said: but people were stingy. In al-Bukhari, it is related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding Allah's words: ("And when the division is attended by relatives, orphans, and the needy") that he said: it is definitive and not abrogated. In another narration he said: people claim that this verse was abrogated, but no, by Allah, it was not abrogated; rather, it is among the things people have been careless about. There are two kinds of guardian (*wali*): a guardian who inherits, and that is the one who gives sustenance; and a guardian who does not inherit, and that is the one who speaks with kindness and says: "I cannot give you anything." Ibn 'Abbas said: when the estates were being divided, Allah commanded the believers to maintain their kinship ties and to give to their orphans and needy from the bequest; if there was no bequest, then something was given to them from the inheritance. Al-Nahhas said: this is the best of what has been said about the verse, that it is a matter of recommendation (*nadb*) and encouragement to do good and to give thanks to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. A group said: this gift (*radkh*) [[Radkh: a small gift.]] is obligatory as a binding duty: the heirs give these categories whatever their souls are content to give, such as household utensils, an old garment, and whatever is light. Ibn 'Atiyyah and al-Qushayri related this view. The sound position is that this is a matter of recommendation, because if it were an obligation, it would mean an entitlement in the estate and a sharing in the inheritance, where one party's portion is known and the other's is unknown. That contradicts wisdom and causes disputes and the severing of ties. A group went to the view that the one addressed and intended in the verse are those present who divide their property by bequest, not the heirs. This is related from Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, and Ibn Zayd. So when a sick person wishes to distribute his property by bequests and someone who does not inherit is present, he should not deprive him. And this, Allah knows best, applies where bequests were obligatory and the verse of inheritance had not yet been revealed. The sound view is the first, and it is upon it that reliance is placed.

**Second issue:** If the heir is a minor who cannot manage his property, some said that the guardian of the minor heir may give from the property of his ward as much as he sees fit. It was said: he should not give, but should say to those present at the division: "I have no share in this property; it belongs to the orphan. When he reaches maturity, I will inform him of your right." This is the well-known view. This applies if the deceased did not bequeath anything to him; if he did bequeath something, what was bequeathed is paid to him. 'Ubaydah and Muhammad ibn Sirin held that the provision (*rizq*) in this verse means preparing food for them to eat, and they did so: they slaughtered a sheep from the estate. 'Ubaydah said: were it not for this verse, this would have come from my own property. Qatadah related from Yahya ibn Ya'mur, who said: three definitive verses (*muhkamat*) have been neglected by people: this verse; the verse of seeking permission ("O you who have believed, let those whom your right hands possess ask your permission") [[See vol. 12, p. 302.]]; and His words: ("O mankind, indeed We have created you from male and female") [[See vol. 16, p. 340.]].

**Third issue:** The pronoun in Allah's words ﴿minhu﴾ ("from it") refers to the sense of the division, since it carries the meaning of property and inheritance, as in His words: ("Then he extracted it from his brother's bag") [[See vol. 9, p. 235.]], meaning the drinking cup, since *as-suwa'* is masculine. From the same usage is his statement, peace be upon him: "Beware the supplication of the wronged, for there is no barrier between it and Allah." Here he used the masculine pronoun in reference to the sense of supplication. [[In the manuscripts B, D, Z, T, H, and Y: "Fa-innahu laysa baynahu" (the masculine form). The narration resembles that of Mu'adh in the two Sahihs, and it has no masculine pronoun. Allah knows best. In manuscripts A, J, and H: "baynaha" (the feminine form).]] Likewise is his statement to Suwayd ibn Tariq al-Ju'fi when he asked him about wine: "It is not a remedy, but a disease," where he referred the pronoun to the sense of drink. Many examples like this exist. It is said: "He divided the property with him (*qasamahu al-mal*), and they divided it between themselves (*taqasamaha*), and they shared it (*iqtasamaha*)." The noun *al-qisma* (division) is feminine, and *al-qasm* is the verbal noun of "I divided the thing and it was divided (*fa-nqasama*)." The place is *maqsim*, like *majlis*. "Time divided them (*taqassamahum al-dahr*), so they dispersed," meaning it separated them and they went apart. *At-taqsim* means separation. And Allah knows best.

**Fourth issue:** Allah's words ﴿wa-qulu lahum qawlan ma'rufan﴾ ("and speak to them words of kindness"). Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it is said to them, "Take it, may it be blessed for you." It was also said: say, "With the provision, I wish it were more than this." And it was said: with the provision there is no need for an excuse. Yes, but if nothing is given to them, then at least a kind word and some form of apology.

**Two issues arise here.**

**The first issue:** the statement of God Most High, ﴿And let them fear﴾. The alif was dropped from (لْيَخْشَ) because of the jussive (jazm) with the imperative. According to Sibawayh, it is not permissible to omit the imperative lam (lam al-amr, the lam of command) by analogy with the prepositional particles (huruf al-jarr), except in poetic necessity (darurat al-shi'r). The Kufans permitted omitting the lam together with the jussive, and they recited:

*Muhammad, ransom yourself with every soul,*
*if you fear anything of calamity (tabalan).* [[The verse is attributed to Hassan and also to Abu Talib. Tabalan means evil consequence; its root is wabal, with the waw changed to ta'. Al-Khizana, vol. 3, p. 680.]]

The original is *li-tafdi* (let him ransom), and the object of (لْيَخْشَ) is omitted because the context indicates it. The word (خافُوا) is the answer (jawab) to (لَوْ), and the sense is: if they had left (behind weak offspring), they would have feared for them. It is permissible to omit the lam in the answer to (لَوْ).

Scholars differed in the interpretation of this verse. One group said: this is an admonition to guardians (al-awsiya'), meaning: treat orphans as you would wish your own children to be treated after you. This was said by Ibn Abbas, and for this reason God Most High said: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly...﴾ [Qur'an 4:10].

Another group said: the meaning is all people. God commanded them to fear God regarding orphans and the children of others, even if they are not in their own guardianship, and to speak to them in gentle terms, just as each of them wishes his own child to be treated after him. Among this is what al-Shaybani related, who said: "We were at Constantinople in the army of Maslama ibn Abd al-Malik. One day we sat in a group of scholars, among them Ibn al-Daylami, and they discussed the terrors of the last times. I said to him: 'O Abu Bishr' [[In B, H and T: Abu Bisr. Both are attested, as in al-Tahdhib. The story regarding the interpretation of this verse is clearer in al-Tabari.]], I wish I had no child." He said to me: "What is it to you? No soul that God has decreed to come forth from a man will fail to come forth, whether he loves it or hates it. But if you want to be safe concerning them, then fear God regarding others' children." Then he recited the verse.

In another narration: "Shall I direct you to a matter which, if you attain it, God will save you from [its harm], and if you leave children after you, God will protect them on your account?" I said: "Yes!" Then he recited this verse, ﴿And let those fear who, if they left behind them weak offspring...﴾ to its end.

I say: Among what conveys this meaning is what Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi related from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever gives charity well will cross the Sirat, and whoever fulfils the need of a widow, God will provide successors for his estate" (akhlafa Allahu fi tarikatihi). [[In Y: akhlafahu Allah. ]]

A third opinion, held by a group of exegetes: this refers to a man at the point of death, to whom those present at his bequest say: "God will provide for your child, so consider your own self. Bequeath your wealth in the way of God, give charity and free slaves," until he exhausts most of his wealth or all of it, which harms his heirs. So they were forbidden from this. The verse is then as if it says to them: "Just as you fear for your heirs and descendants after you, so fear for the heirs of others, and do not push them to squander their wealth." This was said by Ibn Abbas, Qatada, al-Suddi, Ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak and Mujahid.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr related from Ibn Abbas that he said: "When a man is present at the making of a bequest, it is not appropriate to say to him, 'Bequeath your wealth,' for God Most High provides for your child. Rather, he should say, 'Set aside something for yourself and leave something for your child.' This is the meaning of His statement: ﴿So let them fear God﴾."

Miqsam and Hadrami said: it was revealed concerning the reverse of this, namely that those present say to the dying man: "Hold back for your heirs, and keep for your child, for no one has a better claim to your property than your children," and they forbid him from bequeathing, so that the close relatives and everyone entitled to a bequest are harmed by this. It was then said to them: "Just as you fear for your descendants and are pleased when they are treated well, so likewise speak correctly on behalf of the needy and the orphans, and fear God regarding harm to them."

These two opinions are based on the time when the bequest was obligatory, before the revelation of the verses of inheritance. This was related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibn al-Musayyab.

Ibn Atiyya said: Neither of these two opinions applies to all people. Rather, people are of two kinds: one of the two statements suits one kind, and the other statement suits the other. When a man leaves heirs who are self-sufficient and wealthy, it is good to encourage him to bequeath, and he is directed to set aside something for himself. When he leaves heirs who are weak, neglected and poor, it is good to encourage him to leave them (the estate) and to take precautions, for his reward for intending this is like his reward for [giving to] the needy. The consideration is for weakness, so one must incline toward it.

I say: This distinction is correct, because of the Prophet's statement (peace be upon him) to Sa'd: "Your leaving your heirs wealthy is better than leaving them in poverty, begging from people." If a person has no child, or has a child who is wealthy and independent of his father in himself and his property, then he is secure regarding him. In that case, it is best for the person to send forward his wealth ahead of himself, so that those who come after him do not spend it on what is not proper, and its burden then falls upon him.

**The second issue:** the statement of God Most High: ﴿And let them speak a fitting word﴾. Al-sadid means justice and what is right in speech. That is: instruct the sick person to pay from his wealth what is owed to him in obligatory rights, then bequeath to his relatives an amount that does not harm his young heirs.

It was also said: the meaning is "say to the dead a just word," which is to prompt him with *la ilaha illa Allah* (there is no god but God). One should not command him to say it; rather, one says it to oneself so that he hears it and is prompted by it. The Prophet (ﷺ) said this: "Prompt your dying with *la ilaha illa Allah*." He did not say "command them," because if he were commanded to do so, he might become angry and deny it.

It was also said: the intended meaning is the orphan, that they should not rebuke him (la yanharuhu), and should not treat him with contempt. [[In T, Ya and Z: meaning, do not scold him and do not belittle him.]]

**First issue:** Concerning this verse there are three matters. The first is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly﴾. It is related that it was revealed concerning a man from Ghatafan called Mirthad ibn Zayd, who was in charge of the property of his nephew, who was a young orphan, and consumed it. So God, exalted is He, revealed this verse concerning him. This was said by Muqatil ibn Hayyan. For this reason, the majority (al-Jumhur) said that the intended people are the guardians (al-awsiya') who consume what is not permitted to them from the orphan's property. Ibn Zayd said: It was revealed concerning the disbelievers who did not give inheritance to women or to children. The taking of property in all its forms is called "consuming" (akl), because the aim is consumption, and most destruction of things occurs through it. The bellies (al-butun) were specifically mentioned to show their deficiency and to censure them by the opposite of noble character. He called what is eaten "fire" because of what it leads to, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, I see myself pressing wine﴾ [Q. 12:36], meaning grapes. It was also said: "fire" means unlawful, because the unlawful necessitates the Fire, so God named it by its name. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated, saying: The Prophet ﷺ told us about the night he was taken on the Night Journey (Isra'). He said: "I saw people who had lips like the lips of camels, and an angel had been appointed over them who would take hold of their lips, then place in their mouths a stone of fire that would come out from their lower parts." I said: "O Jibril, who are these?" He said: "They are those who consume the property of orphans unjustly." Thus the Book and the Sunnah both indicate that consuming the property of an orphan is among the major sins (al-kaba'ir). The Prophet ﷺ also said: "Avoid the seven destructive sins," and he mentioned among them "consuming the property of an orphan."

**Second issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly﴾. Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim, in the narration of Ibn 'Abbas, read the yā' with a ḍammah (yuṣlawna), in the passive form, from aṣlāhu Allāhu ḥarra al-nār iṣlā' (God caused them to be burned by the heat of the Fire). God, exalted is He, said: ﴿I will cast him into Saqar﴾ [Q. 74:26]. Abu Haywa read it with a ḍammah on the yā' and a fatḥah on the ṣād, with shaddah on the lām, from al-taṣliyah, due to the repetition of the action time after time. Its evidence is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then burn him in the Blaze﴾ [Q. 69:31]. From this is their saying: "I burned him (ṣallaytuhu) time after time." And "tasallaytu" means: I warmed myself by the fire. He said:

*And I have warmed myself at the heat of their war,*
*As the one afflicted by cold warms himself from the frost.*

[The qirṣ: intense cold; the maqrūr: one whose limbs are struck by severe cold so that he cannot work.]

The rest read the yā' with a fatḥah, from ṣaliya al-nār, yaṣlāhā, ṣalan and ṣilā'an. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿None will burn therein except the most wretched﴾ [Q. 92:15]. Al-ṣilā' is being warmed near the fire or being in direct contact with it. From this is the saying of al-Harith ibn 'Abbad:

*I was not among its fuel, God knows,*
*But today I am roasting in its heat.*

Al-sa'ir: the blazing embers.

**Third issue:** This is one of the verses of threat (ayat al-wa'id), and there is no proof in it for those who declare people to be disbelievers because of sins. What Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah, i.e. the orthodox majority) believe is that this threat applies to some of the disobedient, who are burned and then die, unlike the people of the Fire who neither die nor live. This is a reconciliation between the Book and the Sunnah, so that reports in both do not conflict with their true meaning, that some of them are forgiven by God's will, according to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, God does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [Q. 4:48]. The same applies to everything that comes to you of this meaning. Muslim narrated in his Sahih from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "As for the people of the Fire, who are its people, they will not die in it nor live. But some people will be touched by the Fire because of their sins, or he said because of their wrongdoings, and God will cause them to die a death, until when they become charcoal, intercession will be permitted, and they will be brought in groups (ḍabā'ir), group after group, and they will be scattered along the rivers of Paradise. Then it will be said: O people of Paradise, pour water upon them, and they will sprout like a seed sprouts in the flood-deposit of a torrent." [Al-ḥabbah: a single seed of what is not eaten, like the seeds of herbs; ḥamīl al-sayl: what the torrent carries of foam and mud.] A man from the people said: "As if the Messenger of God ﷺ had been [grazing [in the desert]."

There are thirty-five issues in this passage.

**First: Allah's words, ﴿Allah enjoins you concerning your children﴾.** Through this verse, Allah explains what He had made general in His words, "For men there is a share, and for women there is a share." This shows that clarification may be delayed beyond the time of the question. This verse is a pillar of the religion, a foundation of the rulings, and a "mother" of the verses, for the obligatory shares (*fara'id*, the fixed inheritance shares) are of great standing. It is said that they are a third of knowledge, and it is also narrated that they are half of knowledge. It is the first knowledge to be removed from people and forgotten. Al-Daraqutni narrated from Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Learn the obligatory shares and teach them to the people, for it is half of knowledge, and it is the first thing that is forgotten, and it is the first thing that will be taken away from my community." [[So in al-Daraqutni.]]

It is also narrated from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: "Learn the Qur'an and teach it to the people; learn the obligatory shares and teach them to the people; learn knowledge and teach it to the people, for I am a man who will be taken away, and knowledge will be taken away, and tribulations will appear, until two people dispute over an inheritance share and cannot find anyone to judge between them." [[In Kashf al-Khafa: "fa-la yajidan," and in another copy: "la yuwjad."]]

Once this is established, know that the obligatory shares were the greatest part of the knowledge of the Companions and the greatest subject of their discussions, but people neglected it.
