In the school there is another opinion of his: that such an act is harm and is rejected. And with Allah is success.

**Thirty-fourth issue:** His saying ﴿a bequest﴾ (*wasiyya*): it is in the accusative as a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial state (*hal*), and the governing verb is ﴿He enjoins upon you﴾ (*yusikum*). It is also permissible for "without causing harm" to govern it. The meaning is that harm falls upon it or because of it, so the attribution is figurative (*tajawwuz*), as said by Ibn 'Atiyya. It was mentioned that al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan recited: ﴿without causing harm a bequest﴾ with the genitive construction, as you say "a brave fighter of war" (*shuja'u harb*). And *bada* (the fair skin) of the bare body is in the words of Tarafa ibn al-'Abd [[*Bada*: fair and soft. "The bare body": her body uncovered from her garments. The verse:
"Wide at the collar of her gown, from her, a companion,
in the restraint of the drinking companions, fair of the bare body."]]. The meaning according to what we have mentioned is figurative speech for the soundness of the meaning. Then He said: ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Forbearing﴾, meaning: All-Knowing of the people of inheritance (*ahl al-mirath*) [[In some manuscripts: "All-Knowing regarding the matter of inheritance, All-Forbearing."]], All-Forbearing toward those among you who are ignorant. Some of the earlier readers recited: ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise﴾ [[I have not found this in the non-canonical readings, so it is not to be relied upon.]], meaning: All-Wise in the distribution of inheritance and bequest.

**Thirty-fifth issue:** His saying ﴿These are the limits of Allah﴾: *tilka* (these) means *hadhihi* (this), that is, these are the rulings of Allah, which He has made clear to you so that you may know them and act by them.

﴿And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger﴾ in the division of inheritances, acknowledging them and acting by them as Allah, exalted is He, commanded, ﴿He will admit him into gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾: this clause is in the accusative position as a qualifier of *jannat* (gardens). His saying: ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger﴾, meaning in the division of inheritances, so he does not divide them and does not act by them, ﴿and transgresses His limits﴾, that is, opposes His command, ﴿He will admit him into a Fire, to abide therein forever﴾. If by disobedience disbelief is intended, then "abiding forever" is taken in its literal sense; if by it the major sins and the overstepping of Allah's commands are intended, then "abiding" is used figuratively for a certain period, as you say: "May Allah make His dominion eternal (*khallada*)." Zuhayr said:
"Nothing is lasting among the calamities, nor eternal, except the firm mountains."
[[Its first half: "Ala la ara 'ala al-hawadith baqiyan"]]
This meaning has already been discussed in more than one place.

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir recited ﴿nudkhiluhu﴾ with *nun* in both places, in the sense of attribution to Himself, glorified be He. The rest recited it with *ya'* in both places, because the name of Allah, exalted is He, has already been mentioned.

There are thirty-five issues in this passage.

**First: Allah's words, ﴿Allah enjoins you concerning your children﴾.** Through this verse, Allah explains what He had made general in His words, "For men there is a share, and for women there is a share." This shows that clarification may be delayed beyond the time of the question. This verse is a pillar of the religion, a foundation of the rulings, and a "mother" of the verses, for the obligatory shares (*fara'id*, the fixed inheritance shares) are of great standing. It is said that they are a third of knowledge, and it is also narrated that they are half of knowledge. It is the first knowledge to be removed from people and forgotten. Al-Daraqutni narrated from Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Learn the obligatory shares and teach them to the people, for it is half of knowledge, and it is the first thing that is forgotten, and it is the first thing that will be taken away from my community." [[So in al-Daraqutni.]]

It is also narrated from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: "Learn the Qur'an and teach it to the people; learn the obligatory shares and teach them to the people; learn knowledge and teach it to the people, for I am a man who will be taken away, and knowledge will be taken away, and tribulations will appear, until two people dispute over an inheritance share and cannot find anyone to judge between them." [[In Kashf al-Khafa: "fa-la yajidan," and in another copy: "la yuwjad."]]

Once this is established, know that the obligatory shares were the greatest part of the knowledge of the Companions and the greatest subject of their discussions, but people neglected it. Mutarrif narrated from Malik that Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said: "Whoever does not learn the obligatory shares, divorce and the pilgrimage, how will he be superior to the people of the desert?" Ibn Wahb said, from Malik: "I used to hear Rabi'a say: Whoever learns the obligatory shares without knowing them from the Qur'an, how quickly he will forget them." Malik said: "And he spoke the truth."

**Second:** Abu Dawud and al-Daraqutni narrated from Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Knowledge is three things, and anything beyond that is surplus: a clear (*muhkama*) verse, an established sunna, or a just obligatory share." Al-Khattabi Abu Sulayman said: The "clear verse" is the Book of Allah, and he stipulated clarity (*ihkam*) because some verses are abrogated (*mansukh*) and are not acted upon; rather, one acts upon the abrogating verse (*nasikh*). The "established sunna" is what is authentically established from the Prophet (ﷺ) among the established traditions. As for his words "or a just obligatory share," it has two possible interpretations. One is that it refers to justice in distribution, so that it is balanced according to the shares and portions mentioned in the Book and the Sunna. The other is that it is derived from the Book and the Sunna and their meaning, so that this obligatory share equals what is taken from the Book and the Sunna, since it has the same meaning as what is taken from them explicitly.

Ikrima narrated: Ibn Abbas sent to Zayd ibn Thabit asking him about a woman who left a husband and her two parents. He said: "The husband has half, and the mother has a third of what remains." Zayd said: "Do you find this in the Book of Allah, or do you say it by opinion?" He said: "I say it by opinion; I do not prefer a mother over a father." Abu Sulayman said: This is from the category of balancing the obligatory share when there is no explicit text. He did this by comparing it with what was explicitly stated, which is the words of Allah: ﴿And his parents inherit from him, so his mother has a third﴾. When he found the mother's share to be a third, and the remaining property was two-thirds for the father, he apportioned the half remaining after the husband's share over the whole estate, as when there is no son or a sharer with the parents. So he divided it between them in three parts: one part for the mother and two parts for the father, and this is the remainder. This was more just in distribution than giving the mother a third of the whole estate from the remaining half, and leaving the father what remained, which is a sixth, thereby preferring her over him, so that she receives more than the father, though she is subordinate to him in the original (*asl*) inheritance, while he is the one given precedence and preference in the original. This is more just than what Ibn Abbas adopted, namely giving the mother a full third and reducing the father's right to a sixth. So Ibn Abbas abandoned his view, and most jurists went to Zayd's opinion.

Abu Umar said: Abdullah ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said regarding a husband and two parents: the husband has half, the mother has a third of the whole estate, and the rest goes to the father. He said regarding a wife and two parents: the wife has a quarter, the mother has a third of the whole estate, and the rest goes to the father. This was also the view of Shurayh the judge, Muhammad ibn Sirin, Dawud ibn Ali, and a group among them Abu al-Hasan Muhammad ibn Abdullah al-Faradi al-Misri, known as Ibn al-Labban, in both cases. He claimed it was the analogy (*qiyas*) of the view of Ali regarding the *mushtaraka* case. In another place he said that this was also narrated from Ali.

Abu Umar said: The well-known and widely established view from Ali, Zayd, Abdullah and the rest of the Companions and the majority of scholars is what Malik laid down. Among the arguments for them against Ibn Abbas is this: when the two parents share in inheritance and there is no one else with them, the mother has a third and the father two-thirds. Likewise, when they share in the half that remains after the husband, they are in it in the same way, one-third and two-thirds. This is sound in reasoning and analogy.

**Third:** Reports differ regarding the occasion of the revelation of the verse on inheritance. At-Tirmidhi, Abu Dawud, Ibn Majah and al-Daraqutni narrated from Jabir ibn Abdullah that the wife of Sa'd ibn al-Rabi' said: "O Messenger of Allah, Sa'd was killed and left two daughters and his brother. His brother took what Sa'd left, and women are only married for their wealth." He did not answer her at that session. Then she came to him again and said: "O Messenger of Allah, what about the two daughters of Sa'd?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Call his brother to me." He came, and [the Prophet] said to him: "Give the two daughters two-thirds, give the wife an eighth, and what remains is yours." This is the wording of Abu Dawud. In the version of at-Tirmidhi and others: "Then the verse on inheritance was revealed." He said: "This is a sound hadith."

Jabir also narrated: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and Abu Bakr visited me in Bani Salima, walking, and they found me unconscious, so he asked for water, performed ablution, then sprinkled some of it on me, and I regained consciousness. I said: 'What should I do with my property, O Messenger of Allah?' Then the verse was revealed: ﴿Allah enjoins you concerning your children﴾." Al-Bukhari and Muslim reported this in their Sahihs. At-Tirmidhi also reported it, and in his version: "I said, 'O Prophet of Allah, how should I divide my property among my children?' He did not answer me at all, and then the verse was revealed: ﴿Allah enjoins you concerning your children: for the male, the like of the share of two females﴾," up to the end of the verse. He said: "This is a hasan sahih hadith."

In al-Bukhari, Ibn Abbas narrated that the reason for this revelation was that property used to belong to the children, while the bequest was for the parents, so this was abrogated by these verses.

Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: it was revealed concerning Umm Kahha, which we have mentioned. As-Suddi said: it was revealed on account of the daughters of Abd al-Rahman ibn Thabit, brother of Hassan ibn Thabit. It is also said that the people of the Jahiliyya did not give inheritance except to one who fought wars and battled the enemy, so the verse was revealed to make clear [[in B: "as a reminder"]] that each child, small or great, has his share. It is not unlikely that it was an answer for all of them, and for this reason its revelation was delayed. And Allah knows best.

Al-Kiya al-Tabari said: It has been reported in some traditions that what the Jahiliyya did, namely withholding inheritance from minors, continued in the early period of Islam until this verse abrogated it. But it has not been established for us that the Sharia included this; rather, the opposite was established, for this verse was revealed concerning the heirs of Sa'd ibn al-Rabi'. It is also said that it was revealed concerning the heirs of Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas. The first is more sound according to the transmitters. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took back the inheritance from the paternal uncle, and if that had been established earlier in our Sharia, he would not have taken it back. It has never been established in our Sharia that a child was not given inheritance until he fought on horseback and defended the sacred domain.

I say: Likewise Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi said: The revelation of this verse indicates a wonderful point, which is that what the Jahiliyya did in taking property was not, in the early period of Islam, a silently accepted and affirmed ruling, for if it had been an affirmed ruling, the Prophet (ﷺ) would not have ruled against the uncle of the two girls to return what he had taken from their property, because when rulings have taken effect and then abrogation comes, it only applies to the future and does not invalidate what came before. Rather, it was an injustice that was removed. This is what Ibn al-Arabi said.

**Fourth: ﴿Allah enjoins you concerning your children﴾.** The Shafi'is said: the words of Allah, ﴿Allah enjoins you concerning your children﴾, are literal regarding children of the loin (*awlad al-sulb*, direct children). As for their inclusion by way of metaphor, if someone swears that he has no child while he has a son's child, he does not break his oath; and if he bequeaths to "the children of so-and-so," the children of his children are not included. Abu Hanifa says: they are included if he has no direct child. It is well known that words are not altered by what they say.

**Fifth:** Ibn al-Mundhir said: When Allah said, ﴿Allah enjoins you concerning your children﴾, the apparent meaning of the verse requires that the inheritance go to all children, believing and disbelieving. But when it was established from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "A Muslim does not inherit from a disbeliever," it became known that Allah intended some children and not others. So a Muslim does not inherit from a disbeliever, nor does a disbeliever inherit from a Muslim, according to the apparent meaning of the hadith. [[This is the view of the majority; some hold that a Muslim inherits from a disbeliever, and Mu'adh and Mu'awiya judged this way, to the point that someone said: "How excellent is what Mu'awiya judged: they inherit from the People of the Book, but they do not inherit from us, just as one may marry from them but they may not marry from us." See Fath al-Bari, vol. 12, p. 43, Bulaq edition.]]

I say: When Allah said, ﴿concerning your children﴾, the captive in the hands of the disbelievers was included, for he inherits as long as his life is known to be upon Islam. This was the view of the entire body of scholars, except al-Nakha'i, who said: the captive does not inherit. If his life is not known, his ruling is the ruling of the missing person (*mafqud*).

The inheritance of the Prophet (ﷺ) was not included in the general meaning of the verse, because of his words: "We do not leave inheritance; what we leave is charity." Its explanation will come in (Surat Maryam [[See vol. 11, p. 78.]]), Allah willing.

Likewise, one who intentionally kills his father, his child, his brother or his paternal uncle is not included, by the Sunna and the consensus of the Muslim community, and he does not inherit from the property or the blood money of the one he killed, as has been explained earlier in (al-Baqara [[See vol. 1, p. 456.]]). If the killing was by error, he has no share of the blood money, and he inherits from the property according to Malik's view, but does not inherit, according to al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Sufyan and the people of opinion, neither from the property nor from the blood money, as has been explained earlier in al-Baqara [[See vol. 1, p. 456.]]. Malik's view is more sound, and this is the view of Ishaq and Abu Thawr, and it is the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, Mujahid, al-Zuhri, al-Awza'i and Ibn al-Mundhir, because the inheritance of those whom Allah made heirs in His Book is established and is not excluded except by a Sunna or a consensus. Every disputed matter is referred back to the apparent meaning of the verses that concern inheritance.

The Sixth Issue: Know that in the early days of Islam inheritance was earned through several causes: alliance (al-hilf), emigration (al-hijrah), and contractual pacts (al-mu'aqadah). Then this was abrogated (naskh), as will be explained, God willing, in this surah at His words: ﴿And for each We have appointed heirs﴾ [[p. 165 of this part.]]. The scholars agreed that when there are children together with someone who has a prescribed share (fard musamma), that person is given his share, and the remainder of the estate goes to the male, who receives the equivalent of two females' shares. This is based on the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "Give the prescribed shares to their rightful owners," related by the imams. He meant the prescribed shares mentioned in the Book of God. They are six: one half, one quarter, one eighth, two thirds, one third, and one sixth.

One half is the share of five: the daughter of the loins (ibnat al-sulb), the son's daughter (ibnat al-ibn), the full sister (al-ukhtu al-shaqiqah), the consanguine sister (al-ukhtu li-l-ab), and the husband. All of these receive it when they are alone and not excluded (mahjub) by someone who blocks them from it.

One quarter is the share of the husband when there is a descendant (al-hajib), and the share of the wife or wives when there is none.

One eighth is the share of the wife or wives when there is a descendant.

Two thirds is the share of four: two or more daughters of the loins, two or more daughters of a son, two or more full sisters, or two or more consanguine sisters. All of these receive it when they are alone and not excluded by someone who blocks them.

One third is the share of two categories: the mother when there is no child, and the siblings from the mother's side (uterine siblings), who receive it when there are two or more of them. Two or more uterine siblings also receive one third. This is one third of the whole estate. As for one third of what remains, that is the mother's share in the case of a husband or wife together with both parents. In that case the mother receives one third of what remains, and this has already been explained. In the matters of the grandfather together with the siblings, when there is a sharer present and one third of the remainder is more beneficial to him.

One sixth is the share of seven: the two parents, the grandfather together with a child or a son's child, the grandmother or grandmothers when they are together, the son's daughter(s) together with a daughter of the loins [[that is, one or more]], the consanguine sisters together with a full sister, and one uterine sibling, whether male or female.

All these prescribed shares are taken from the Book of God, except the share of the grandmother and grandmothers, which is taken from the Sunnah.

The causes that make these shares due by inheritance are three: established lineage (nasab thabit), a valid marriage (nikah munaqid), and manumission patronage (wala' 'ataqah). All three may combine, so that a man is a woman's husband, her patron, and her paternal cousin. Two of them may combine, but no more, such as when he is her husband and her patron, or her husband and her paternal cousin. Then he inherits by two aspects, and if he is alone he takes the whole estate: half by marriage and half by patronage or by lineage. Similarly, a woman may be a man's daughter and his freed slave, so that if she is alone she takes the whole estate: half by lineage and half by patronage.

The Seventh Issue: There is no inheritance except after the payment of debts and bequests. When the deceased dies, the specific rights are removed from his estate first, then what is required for his shroud and burial, then the debts according to their order of priority, then the bequests are carried out from one third, and whatever is similar to them, also according to their order. The remainder is inherited by the heirs.

Their total number is seventeen. Ten are men: the son, the son's son however far down, the father, the father's father, which is the grandfather, however far up, the brother, the brother's son, the paternal uncle, the paternal uncle's son, the husband, and the patron of the benefit (mawla al-ni'mah). Seven women inherit: the daughter, the son's daughter however far down, the mother, the grandmother however far up, the sister, the wife, and the female patron, who is the freed woman.

One of the learned men has versified them, saying:

"If you wish to gather the heirs, together with the female heirs,
ten from among the males, and seven persons from among the females.
They are, and I have confined them in the verse:
the son, the son's son, and the paternal uncle's son,
and the father among them, in order,
and the grandfather before the near brother,
and the nearest brother's son, then the uncle,
the husband, and the master, then the mother,
and the son's daughter after her, and the daughter, and wife, and grandmother, and sister,
and the freed woman, I mean the manumitted one.
Take them to yourself as a verified count."

The Eighth Issue: When He said ﴿concerning your children﴾, this includes every child who exists, or who is a fetus in its mother's womb, whether near or distant, male or female, except the disbeliever, as has already been explained. Some said: this word is literal (haqiqah) for the nearer and metaphorical (majaz) for the more distant. Others said: it is literal for all of them, since it derives from procreation, but they inherit according to closeness of relation to him [[in another manuscript: "to them"]]. God says: ﴿O children of Adam﴾ [[see vol. 7, p. 182]]. The Prophet ﷺ said: "I am the master of the children of Adam," and he said: "O children of Isma'il, shoot, for your father was an archer." However, the customary usage prevailed in applying this term to the nearer persons, in accordance with that literal sense.

If there is a male among the children of the loins, the children of a child receive nothing. The scholars agreed on this. If there is no male among the children of the loins but there are children of a son, the daughters of the loins are given first, up to two thirds, and then the remaining one third is given to the son's children if they are equal in degree, or if the male is lower than the females above him, so that the male receives the equivalent of two females' shares. This is the view of Malik, al-Shafi'i, and the people of opinion (ashab al-ra'y). Most scholars among the Companions, the Successors, and those after them held this view, except for what is reported from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: if the male among the son's children is at the level of a female child, she is returned to, and if he is lower than her, she is also returned to, taking into account His words: ﴿If they are women more than two, then for them is two thirds of what he left﴾, so He did not assign to the daughters, however many they are, more than two thirds.

I say: Ibn al-'Arabi thus reported this detail from Ibn Mas'ud. But Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Baji reported from him that what remains after the daughters of the loins goes to the sons of the son, not to the daughters of the son, and they did not make a distinction. Ibn al-Mundhir related this from Abu Thawr, and Abu 'Umar related something similar. Abu 'Umar said: Ibn Mas'ud differed on this and said: when the daughters have completed two thirds, the remainder goes to the sons of the son, not to their sisters, nor to those above them among the daughters of the son, nor to those below them. Abu Thawr and Dawud ibn 'Ali adopted this view, and something similar is reported from 'Alqamah.

The evidence of those who adopted this view is the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Divide the property among the people entitled to the prescribed shares according to the Book of God, and whatever the prescribed shares leave, give it to the nearest male." Al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others transmitted it.

The evidence of the majority is God's saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿God enjoins you concerning your children: for the male, the equivalent of the share of two females﴾, because a son's son is a child. From the perspective of reasoning and analogy: whoever makes the males of his degree residuaries (ya'ussib) in the whole estate must also make them residuaries in the surplus, as with the children of the loins. Therefore the son's son must share with his sister, just as the son of the loins shares with his sister.

If someone argues for Abu Thawr and Dawud that the daughter of a son, since she inherits nothing of the surplus after the two thirds when alone, is not made a residuary by her brother, the answer is that when her brother is with her, she becomes strengthened by him and becomes a residuary together with him. The apparent meaning of His words ﴿God enjoins you concerning your children﴾ includes them, since they are of the children.

The Ninth Issue: His saying ﴿If they are women more than two, then for them is two thirds of what he left﴾, to the end of the verse. God prescribed for one female one half, and prescribed for more than two females two thirds, but He did not prescribe for two females a prescribed share stated in His Book. So the scholars disputed what the proof is that makes two females entitled to two thirds. It was said: it is consensus (ijma'), but this is rejected, because the authentic report from Ibn 'Abbas is that he gave two daughters one half, since God, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿If they are women more than two, then for them is two thirds of what he left﴾, and this is a condition and a consequence. He said: so I do not give two daughters two thirds.

It was also said: two daughters receive two thirds by analogy to two sisters, for when God, Glorified is He, said at the end of the surah: ﴿And if he has a sister, then for her is one half of what he left﴾, and He said: ﴿If they are two, then for them is two thirds of what he left﴾, the two daughters were joined to the two sisters in sharing two thirds, and sisters beyond two were joined to daughters in sharing two thirds. This was objected to: that this is explicitly stated concerning sisters, and consensus has been formed on it, so it is granted in that case.

It was also said: there is in the verse something indicating that two daughters receive two thirds, namely that when one female alone with her brother takes one third, we know that two females take two thirds. This argument was used by Isma'il al-Qadi and Abu al-'Abbas al-Mubarrad. Al-Nahhas said: this argument is an error according to the people of analysis, because the disagreement concerns two daughters and not one. The opponent would say: if he left two daughters and a son, the two daughters have one half, so this is evidence that this is their prescribed share.

It was also said: the word ﴿fawq﴾ ("above") is superfluous, meaning: if they are two women. Compare His words: ﴿Strike above the necks﴾ [[see vol. 7, p. 378]], meaning the necks. Al-Nahhas and Ibn 'Atiyyah rejected this view and said: it is wrong, because in the speech of the Arabs adverbs and all nouns may not be added without meaning. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: and because His words ﴿Strike above the necks﴾ is the eloquent form, and "above" is not superfluous; rather it establishes the meaning, since a blow to the neck must fall above the bones at the joint, not on the brain. As Durayd ibn al-Simmah said: "Lower it away from the brain and raise it above the bone; thus have I always struck the necks of heroes." [[in the Sirah of Ibn Hisham, vol. 2, p. 852, Europe edition: "Raise it above the bone and lower it away from the brain, for thus I used to strike the men."]]

The strongest argument that two daughters receive two thirds is the authentic hadith transmitted concerning the occasion of revelation.

The dialect of the people of the Hijaz and Banu Asad is al-thuluth and al-rubu' up to al-'ashr (one third and one quarter up to one tenth). The dialect of Banu Tamim and Rabi'ah is al-thulth, with the lam pronounced with a sukun, up to al-'ashr. It is said: "thallatha al-qawma uthallithuhum" (I made the people three), and "thallatha al-darahima uthallithuha" (I completed the dirhams to three), and "athlatha hiya" (she made them three). Except that they said for the hundred and the thousand: "amma'aytuha" and "alaftuha," and "amma'at" and "allafat."

The Tenth Issue: His saying ﴿And if she is one, then for her is one half﴾. Nafi' and the people of Madinah read ﴿wahidatun﴾ ("one") in the nominative, meaning "it occurred and happened," so it is the complete (tammah) verb, as the poet said:

"When winter comes, wrap me warm,
for winter wears down the old man."

And the rest read it in the accusative (بالنصب). Al-Nahhas said: this is a good reading (qira'ah), meaning that even if the one left behind or the newborn is a single girl, as in ﴿فَإِنْ كُنَّ نِسَاءً﴾ ("if they are women"). When the daughters of the loins (بنات الصلب) are accompanied by daughters of a son (بنات الابن), and the daughters of the loins are two or more, they exclude the daughters of the son from inheriting by the fixed share (bi-l-fard), because the daughters of the son have no entitlement to inherit by the fixed share except in the case of two-thirds. If there is one daughter of the loins, then the daughter of a son or the daughters of a son inherit together with the daughters of the loins to complete the two-thirds, because it is a fixed share that two daughters or more inherit. The daughters of a son take the place of daughters when the latter are absent, and likewise the sons of sons take the place of sons in exclusion and inheritance. When there is no one among them entitled to the one-sixth, it goes to the daughter of a son, and she has more right to the one-sixth than the full sister of the deceased. This is the view of the majority of jurists among the Companions and the Successors, except what is narrated from Abu Musa and Sulayman ibn Abi Rabi'ah, that the daughter receives one-half and the other half goes to the sister, and the daughter of a son has no right to it. It is authentically reported from Abu Musa something indicating that he retracted this view, narrated by al-Bukhari: Adam narrated to us, Shu'bah narrated to us, Abu Qays narrated to us, I heard Huzayl [[So it is vocalised in Usd al-Ghabah and in the margin of al-Tahdhib; in j, w and t: Hudhayl with a dhal, and this is not established.]] ibn Shurahbil say: Abu Musa was asked about a daughter, a daughter of a son, and a sister. He said: The daughter receives one-half and the sister receives one-half, and go to Ibn Mas'ud, for he will agree with me. Ibn Mas'ud was asked and informed of Abu Musa's view, and he said: Then I would have gone astray, and I am not among the rightly guided! I judge in this matter by what the Prophet ﷺ judged: the daughter receives one-half, the daughter of a son receives one-sixth to complete the two-thirds, and what remains goes to the sister. We came to Abu Musa and informed him of Ibn Mas'ud's view, and he said: Do not ask me as long as this scholar is among you. If there is with the daughter of a son or the daughters of a son a son at her level or below her, he residualises her (عصّبها), so the second half is between them, the male receiving the equivalent of the share of two females, however much it amounts to, contrary to Ibn Mas'ud as mentioned earlier, when the daughters of the loins have taken their two-thirds, or the daughter of the loins and the daughters of the son have taken the two-thirds. The same applies to a sister of the full blood, and sisters and brothers of the paternal half: the full sister receives one-half and the remainder goes to the brothers and sisters, so long as what reaches them from the division does not exceed one-sixth; if it exceeds one-sixth, they are given one-sixth to complete the two-thirds, and it is not increased beyond that. This is also the view of Abu Thawr.

The eleventh issue: if a man dies and leaves a pregnant wife, the estate is withheld until it becomes clear what she delivers. The people of knowledge agreed that when a man dies and his wife is pregnant, the child in her womb inherits and is inherited from if it emerges alive and cries out (استهل) [[Istahalla al-sabiyy: he raised his voice in crying at birth.]]. They all said: if it emerges dead, it does not inherit. If it emerges alive but does not cry out, one group said: it has no inheritance, even if it moves or sneezes, so long as it does not cry out. This is the view of Malik, al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, Ibn Sirin, al-Sha'bi, al-Zuhri and Qatadah. Another group said: when the newborn's life is known by movement, crying, suckling or breathing, its rulings are those of a living person. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, Sufyan al-Thawri and al-Awza'i. Ibn al-Mundhir said: what al-Shafi'i said is open to reasoning, but the report prevents it, which is the saying of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "There is no newborn who is born except that Satan pricks him, and he cries out from the prick of Satan, except Ibn Maryam and his mother." This is a report, and abrogation (naskh) does not apply to a report.

Second: when Allah the Exalted said ﴿فِي أَوْلَادِكُمْ﴾ ("concerning your children"), it included the khunthā (hermaphrodite, one who has two sexual organs). The scholars [[In b: the people of knowledge.]] agreed that he is inherited from by the place from which he urinates: if he urinates from where a man urinates, he inherits the share of a man, and if he urinates from where a woman urinates, he inherits the share of a woman. Ibn al-Mundhir said: I do not know of anything from Malik on this; indeed Ibn al-Qasim mentioned that he was reluctant to ask Malik about it. If he urinates from both, the criterion is the one that comes first, as said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, Ahmad and Ishaq; this is also reported from the people of opinion (ra'y). Qatadah narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib that he said concerning the khunthā: he is inherited from by the place from which he urinates; if he urinates from both together, then from whichever of them comes first; if he urinates from both simultaneously, then half a male's share and half a female's share. Ya'qub and Muhammad said: whichever of them he emits more from, he inherits accordingly, and this is reported from al-Awza'i. Al-Nu'man said: if it comes out from both together, he is ambiguous (mushkil), and I do not look at which of them is more. It is reported from him that he withheld judgment when it was like this. It is also reported from him that he said: when it is ambiguous, he is given the lesser of the two shares. Yahya ibn Adam said: if he urinates from where a man urinates and menstruates as a woman menstruates, he inherits from where he urinates, because in the report it says: he is inherited from by his urination. According to al-Shafi'i's view: if it comes out from both together without either preceding the other, he is ambiguous, and he is given the share of a female, and the rest is withheld between him and the other heirs until his condition becomes clear or they reconcile. This is also the view of Abu Thawr. Al-Sha'bi said: he is given half the share of a male and half the share of a female; this is also the view of al-Awza'i, and it is the school of Malik. Ibn Shas said in his al-Jawahir al-Thaminah, according to the school of Malik, scholar of Madinah: the khunthā is considered if he has two sexual organs, the female's and the male's, by urination from both; the ruling is given to whichever he urinates from. If he urinates from both, the greater quantity from either is considered; if the situation is equal, precedence is considered; if it happens from both together, the growth of a beard or the size of the breasts and their resemblance to women's breasts is considered; if both conditions combine, the situation at puberty is considered: if menstruation is found, he is ruled accordingly; if only wet dreams are found, he is ruled accordingly; if both are found, he is ambiguous. Likewise, if he has neither organ, neither the one specific to men nor the one specific to women, but only a place from which he urinates, then he is awaited until puberty; if a distinguishing sign appears, that is decisive, otherwise he is ambiguous. Then, wherever we rule him ambiguous, his share of inheritance is half of the shares of a male and a female. I say: these are the signs they mentioned in the ambiguous khunthā. We have already pointed to a sign in al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 302.]] and at the beginning of this surah, which attaches him to one of the two categories, namely the consideration of the ribs, which is reported from ʿAlī (رضي الله عنه) and by which he ruled. Some of the learned virtuous scholars versified the ruling on the khunthā in many verses, the first of which is [[So it is in all the manuscripts, and it appears that the verse is joined to a preceding one.]]:

"And that he is judged by his conditions: by the breast, the beard, and urination."

And in it he says:

"If his conditions are equal and do not become clear, and his signs remain ambiguous, then his share of the nearest heir's estate is six-eighths of the portion,
this is the one who deserves to be ambiguous, with what it has of punishment.
It is obligatory in truth that he not marry, as long as he lives in this world, nor be married,
since he is not of pure offspring, nor has he come to be among the men."

"And all that I have mentioned in the verse, the eminent people of knowledge have said it,
but a group among them refused to speak of it, and a blameworthy person did not incline to it,
because of the extent of the disgrace that appears in mentioning it and its manifest ugliness."

"And in his hidden matter has passed the ruling of the Imam al-Murtada ʿAli:
that if his ribs are fewer, he should follow the men,
in inheritance, marriage, ihram, in Hajj, prayer and rulings;
and if he has one rib more than the males, then he is among the females,
for women have an extra rib over men, so take this benefit,
since it was taken from Adam in what preceded, for the creation of Hawwa, and this saying is true,
upon it, from what the Messenger said, may our Lord send blessings upon him, is the proof."

Abu al-Walid Ibn Rushd said: The ambiguous hermaphrodite (al-khunthā al-mushkil) cannot be a husband or a wife, nor a father or a mother. It has been said that a person has been found who has a child from his front (the womb) and a child from his back (the loins). Ibn Rushd said: If this is established, he inherits from his son by his loins (ṣulb) the full inheritance of a father, and from his son by his womb (baṭn) the full inheritance of a mother. But this is far-fetched, and God knows best.

In Sunan al-Daraqutni, on the authority of Abu Hani' Umar ibn Bashir, who said: Amir al-Sha'bi was asked about a newborn that was neither male nor female, having neither the characteristics of a male nor those of a female, that emerged from its navel in the manner of urine and excrement. Al-Sha'bi was asked about its inheritance, and he said: Half the share of a male and half the share of a female.

The thirteenth issue: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And for his parents﴾, means for the two parents of the deceased. This is an allusion to something not mentioned, and it is permissible because the context indicates it, as in His saying, ﴿until it [the sun] was hidden by the veil﴾ [[See vol. 15, p. 192.]], and ﴿Indeed, We revealed it during the Night of Decree﴾ [[See vol. 20, p. 129.]]. (The sixth) ﴿al-sudus (one-sixth)﴾ is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada') in its grammatical analysis (i'rab), and what precedes it is its predicate. Likewise (the third and the sixth). Likewise ﴿half of what he left﴾, likewise ﴿then for you is a quarter﴾, likewise ﴿and for them is a quarter﴾, likewise ﴿then for them is an eighth﴾, and likewise ﴿for each one of them is a sixth﴾.

Al-abawān is the dual of al-ab (father) and al-abah (mother). The word "umm" (mother) suffices, so that it is not necessary to say "abah" for her. Among the Arabs there are those who treat two different things as if they were alike, giving precedence to one of them over the other because of its lightness or its fame. This is attested in well-known names, such as their saying for the father and mother: al-abawān (the two parents). For the sun and moon: al-qamarān (the two moons). For night and day: al-malawān (the two smooth ones). Likewise al-'Umarān for Abu Bakr and 'Umar, may God be pleased with them both. They gave precedence to the moon over the sun because the masculine form is lighter, and they gave precedence to 'Umar over Abu Bakr because the days of 'Umar were long and became famous. Whoever claims that by al-'Umarān he meant 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, his statement is worthless, because they used the dual "al-'Umarān" before 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz was seen. Ibn al-Shajari said this.

The ascendant ancestors are not included in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And for his parents﴾, in the way that descendants are included in His saying ﴿your children﴾, because His saying ﴿for his parents﴾ is a dual term that does not admit of generality or plurality, unlike His saying ﴿your children﴾. The evidence for the soundness of this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If he has no child and his parents are his heirs, then for his mother is one-third﴾. The higher mother is a grandmother, and it is agreed (bi-ijma') that one-third is not prescribed for her. Therefore the exclusion of the grandmother from this term is certain, while its inclusion of the grandfather is disputed.

Among those who said that the grandfather is a father, and by him excluded the brothers, was Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may God be pleased with him, and none of the Companions opposed him in this during his lifetime. They disagreed about this after his death. Among those who said he is a father were Ibn 'Abbas, 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, 'A'isha, Mu'adh ibn Jabal, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Abu al-Darda', and Abu Hurayrah. All of them consider the grandfather, in the absence of the father, to be equal to the father; they exclude all the brothers by him and do not inherit alongside him anything. This was also said by 'Ata', Tawus, al-Hasan, and Qatadah. Abu Hanifah, Abu Thawr, and Ishaq also adopted this view. Their proof is His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿the religion of your father Abraham﴾ [[See vol. 12, p. 99.]], ﴿O children of Adam﴾ [[See vol. 7, p. 182.]], and His saying, peace be upon him: "O children of Isma'il, shoot, for your father was an archer."

'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Zayd, and Ibn Mas'ud held that the grandfather inherits alongside the brothers, and that he is not reduced from one-third alongside full brothers or paternal brothers, except alongside those entitled to fixed shares (dhawu al-furud); in that case he is not reduced at all from one-sixth, according to Zayd's view. This is the view of Malik, al-Awza'i, Abu Yusuf, Muhammad, and al-Shafi'i. 'Ali would give the brothers and the grandfather a share up to one-sixth, and would not reduce it below one-sixth, alongside those with fixed shares or others. This is the view of Ibn Abi Layla and a group.

The scholars agreed (ajma'a) that the grandfather does not inherit alongside the father, and that a son excludes his father. They placed the grandfather in the position of the father regarding exclusion and inheritance in all cases where the deceased leaves no father nearer to him. The majority held that the grandfather excludes the sons of brothers from the inheritance, except for what is reported from al-Sha'bi, from 'Ali, that he treated the sons of brothers in sharing (al-muqasamah) as brothers. The evidence for the majority's view is that this is a male who does not make his sister an 'asabah (agnatic heir), so he does not share with the grandfather, like the paternal uncle and the paternal cousin.

Al-Sha'bi said: The first grandfather to inherit in Islam was 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him. The son of 'Asim ibn 'Umar died and left two brothers, and 'Umar wished to take the property exclusively, so he consulted 'Ali and Zayd about this. They gave him an example, and he said: "Had your opinions not agreed, I would not have seen that he be my son and I not be his father." Al-Daraqutni narrated from Zayd ibn Thabit that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab asked permission to enter upon him one day, and he granted it, while his head was in the hand of a slave-girl who was combing it. He withdrew his head, and 'Umar said to him: "Let her comb you." He said: "O Commander of the Faithful, had you sent for me, I would have come to you." 'Umar said: "It is only my need. I came to you so that you would consider the matter of the grandfather." Zayd said: "No, by God! [[His saying: 'No, by God!' means: the statement in this matter is not what should be said concerning this incident as you say.]] What you say about it!" 'Umar said: "It is not a revelation, that we should add to it or subtract from it. It is only an opinion that you hold [[His saying: 'It is not a revelation' means: what has passed between me and you concerning it is not a Qur'anic text, such that opposing it or adding to it or subtracting from it is forbidden. His saying: 'It is only an opinion that you hold' means: you say it by your opinion and I say it by my opinion.]]. If I find that it agrees with me, I will follow it; otherwise there will be no fault on you concerning it." Zayd refused, and he left angry, saying: "I came to you thinking you would be finished with my need." Then he came to him again at the same hour as the first time, and he kept at him until he said: "I will write for you about it." He wrote it on a piece of leather (qatab) [[al-qatab (with the qaf and the taa' vowelled as usual): the intestines.]] and gave him an example: "Its example is that of a tree that grows on a single trunk; a branch emerges from it, then from the branch another branch emerges. The trunk waters the branch. If you cut the first branch, the water returns to the branch, and if you cut the second, the water returns to the first." 'Umar brought it and addressed the people, then he read the piece of leather to them and said: "Indeed, Zayd ibn Thabit has said a statement about the grandfather, and I have enforced it." He said: 'Umar was the first grandfather to be such, and he wanted to take all the property, the grandson's property, to the exclusion of his brothers; then after that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, divided it.

The fourteenth issue: As for the grandmother, the scholars agreed (ajma'a) that the grandmother has one-sixth when the deceased has no mother. They agreed that the mother excludes her own mother and the father's mother. They agreed that the father does not exclude the mother's mother. They disagreed about the inheritance of the grandmother when her son is alive. One group said: The grandmother does not inherit when her son is alive. This is reported from Zayd ibn Thabit, 'Uthman, and 'Ali. Malik, al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, Abu Thawr, and the people of opinion (ashab al-ra'y) also said this. Another group said: The grandmother inherits alongside her son. This is reported from 'Umar, Ibn Mas'ud, 'Uthman, 'Ali, and Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, and it was said by Shurayh, Jabir ibn Zayd, 'Ubayd Allah ibn al-Hasan, Sharik, Ahmad, Ishaq, and Ibn al-Mundhir. He said: Just as the grandfather is excluded only by the father, so the grandmother is excluded only by the mother. Al-Tirmidhi narrated from 'Abd Allah, concerning the grandmother alongside her son: "She is the first grandmother whom the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, fed a sixth [[In b and y: 'her sixth'.]] alongside her son, while her son was alive." And God knows best.

The fifteenth issue: The scholars differed about the inheritance of grandmothers. Malik said: Only two grandmothers inherit, the mother's mother and the father's mother, and their mothers. Abu Thawr narrated the same from al-Shafi'i, and a group of the Successors (tabi'un) said this. If one of them stands alone, then the sixth is for her; if both are present and their kinship is equal, then the sixth is between them. The same applies if they are many, when they are equal in degree (al-qu'dud). All of this is agreed upon. If the one from the mother's side is nearer, she alone has the sixth, to the exclusion of others; if the one from the father's side is nearer, the sixth is shared between her and the one from the mother's side, even if the latter is more distant. Only one grandmother from the mother's side inherits. The grandmother never inherits the mother of the mother's father under any circumstances. This is the view of Zayd ibn Thabit, and it is the best-attested of what has been reported from him on this matter. It is also the view of Malik and the people of Madina. It was said: The grandmothers are mothers, so when they are present together, the sixth goes to the nearest of them, just as when fathers are present together, the one nearest to the deceased has the greatest right to the inheritance; likewise the sons, the brothers, the sons of brothers, and the sons of paternal uncles: when they are present together, the one nearest has the greatest right to the inheritance; so likewise the mothers. Ibn al-Mundhir said: This is the most correct, and I hold it. Al-Awza'i used to make three grandmothers inherit: one from the mother's side and two from the father's side. This is the view of Ahmad ibn Hanbal, reported by al-Daraqutni from the Prophet, peace be upon him, as a mursal (a report lacking a Companion in its chain). It is also reported from Zayd ibn Thabit the reverse of this: that he used to make three grandmothers inherit: two from the mother's side and one from the father's side. The view of 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, is like the view of this Zayd. Both of them would give the sixth to the nearer of them, whether from the mother's side or the father's side, and no one who is not of her degree (qu'dud) shares it with her. This is the view of al-Thawri, Abu Hanifah and his companions, and Abu Thawr. As for 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas, they used to make all four grandmothers inherit. This is the view of al-Hasan al-Basri, Muhammad ibn Sirin, and Jabir ibn Zayd. Ibn al-Mundhir said: Every grandmother who, when traced back to the deceased, has a father between two mothers in her lineage, does not inherit, according to the view of everyone from the people of knowledge who is reported to us.

The sixteenth issue: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿for each one of them is a sixth﴾: He prescribed for each of the two parents, when there is a child, a sixth, and He left the child unspecified, so that male and female are equal in it. If a man dies and leaves a son and two parents, then for his parents, each one of them has a sixth, and what remains is for the son. If he leaves a daughter and two parents, then for the daughter is one-half, for the two parents two sixths, and what remains goes to the nearest agnatic heir (ʿaṣabah), who is the father, in accordance with the saying of the Messenger of God, peace be upon him: "Give the fixed shares to their owners, and what remains is for the nearest male." Thus the father's entitlement is united from two sources: agnatic succession (al-ta'ṣīb) and fixed share (al-far).

al-Qurtubi, *al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*, on surahs 4:11–14 (part 5 of 7):

(﴿But if he has no child and his parents inherit from him, then for his mother is one-third﴾) So the Exalted, may His remembrance be exalted, informed us that when the two parents inherit from him, the mother has one-third. By His saying, ﴿and his parents inherit from him﴾, and by His informing us that the mother has one-third, He indicates that the remainder, which is two-thirds, goes to the father. This is like saying to two men: "This property is between you two." Then you say to one of them: "You, so-and-so, have one-third of it." You have thereby specified that the other has two-thirds, by the explicit wording of your speech. Also, the force of the wording in His saying, ﴿and his parents inherit from him﴾, indicates that the two of them stand alone apart from all the sharers, whether children or others, and there is no disagreement on this.

I say: On this basis, the two-thirds is a fixed, specified share (fard) for the father and he does not become an 'asabah (residuary heir). Ibn al-'Arabi mentioned that the reasoning behind the father being given one-third is the absence of male offspring, the support (nusrah), and the obligation of maintenance (mu'nah) upon him, while the mother is assigned a share because of kinship. I say: This is refuted, for those (reasons) exist during his lifetime, so why is the sixth withheld (from the father)? What appears is that the sixth is withheld during his lifetime only for the sake of ease for the child and to safeguard his property, since removing a portion of his property may be burdensome to him. Or it is a matter of ta'abbud (devotion, a rule to be followed without knowing its full reason), and this is the best thing that is said. And Allah is the Granter of success.

The Seventeenth Issue: If it is asked: what is the benefit of the addition of the waw (conjunction) in His saying, ﴿and his parents inherit from him﴾, when the apparent wording would have been: "If he has no child, his parents inherit from him"? It is said to him: He intended by its addition the informing, to clarify that this is a matter established and fixed, so He informs of its stability and firmness. Thus the state of the two parents when they stand alone is like the state of two children: for the male is the equivalent of the portion of two females. By this, the father combines two entitlements: the share (sahm) and the residuary (ta'sib), since the brothers are excluded (hajb) just as a child excludes them. This is justice in ruling and clearly wise. And Allah knows best.

The Eighteenth Issue: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿so for his mother is one-third﴾. The people of Kufa read (فَلِإِمِّهِ, *fa-li-immihi*) with a kasra on the initial letter of the mother's word. This is a dialect (lughah) related by Sibawayh. Al-Kisa'i said: It is the dialect of many of Hawazin and Hudhayl. Because the lam was kasra and was attached to the word, they disliked a damma after a kasra, so they replaced the damma with a kasra, since there is no fi'il (verb pattern) of this form in the language. Whoever reads with damma (لِأُمِّهِ, *li-ummihi*) keeps it in its original form. Also, the lam is separated, since it enters upon a noun. This is what al-Nahhas said in full.

The Nineteenth Issue: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿but if he has brothers, then for his mother is one-sixth﴾. The brothers exclude the mother from the one-third to the one-sixth, and this is hajb al-nuqsan (exclusion that reduces a share). This applies whether the brothers are full (ashiqqa') or consanguine by the father or uterine by the mother, and they have no fixed share. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he used to say: The sixth from which the brothers exclude the mother goes to the brothers. It is also narrated from him, in agreement with the view of the people, that it goes to the father. Qatadah said: The father took it to the exclusion of them, because he supports them, takes charge of their marriage, and provides for them.

The scholars agreed that two brothers or more, whether males or females, from a father and mother, or from a father, or from a mother, exclude the mother from the one-third to the one-sixth. The exception is what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, that two brothers are in the ruling of one. And the mother is not excluded by fewer than three. Some people have held that sisters do not exclude the mother from the one-third to the one-sixth, because the Book of Allah speaks of brothers (ikhwah), and the inheritance strength of females is not like the strength of males, such that analogy (i'tibar) would require their inclusion. Al-Kiya al-Tabari said: What their statements imply is that they (the sisters) do not enter together with brothers, for the word "brothers" in its absolute sense does not encompass sisters, just as the word "sons" (banin) does not encompass daughters. This implies that the mother is not excluded by one brother and one sister from the one-third to the one-sixth, and this contradicts the consensus of the Muslims. And if they (the sisters) are intended in the verse along with brothers, they are intended even when alone.

All of them argued that the least plural is two, because the dual is the joining of one thing to its like, so the meaning requires that it is a plural. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Two and what is above them is a jama'ah (group)." It is related from Sibawayh that he said: I asked al-Khalil about the saying "how beautiful are their faces (ma ahsana wujuhihima)?" He said: "Two is a jama'ah." The verse of the poet is also established:

*And a desert, terrifying and far, two-fold (qadhafayn), two barren stretches (martayn),*
*whose backs are like the backs of two shields.*

Al-Akhfash recited:

*When the two women came to us with the news,*
*they said: "Indeed the matter has become known among us."*

And another said:

*He is greeted with peace by the wealthy of a people,*
*while the poor man is withheld the greeting.*
*Is death not equal between them*
*when they die and are in the graves?*

The discussion of the dispute between ʿUthmān and Ibn ʿAbbās arose at this point. ʿUthmān said to him: "Your people have veiled it," meaning the Quraysh, "and they are the people of eloquence and rhetorical skill." Among those who said that the minimum of the plural is three, even though he did not say so here, were Ibn Masʿūd, al-Shāfiʿī, Abū Ḥanīfa and others. And God knows best.

**The twentieth point: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿after any bequest he makes or debt﴾.** Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir and ʿĀṣim [[in the narration of Abū Bakr]] read *yūṣā* with a fatḥa on the ṣād. The rest read it with a kasra, and likewise the second instance. The reports from ʿĀṣim differ concerning both. The kasra is the choice of Abū ʿUbayd and Abū Ḥātim, because the deceased was mentioned before this. Al-Akhfash said: What confirms this is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿yūṣīna﴾ and ﴿tūṣūna﴾.

**The twenty-first point: If it is said: What is the wisdom in mentioning the bequest before the debt, when the debt takes precedence over it by consensus (ijmāʿ, scholarly agreement)?** Al-Tirmidhī narrated from al-Ḥārith, from ʿAlī, that the Prophet (ﷺ) judged regarding the debt before the bequest, while you [[thus in al-Tirmidhī, and in B, W, Z and T; in others: "you recite" (*taqrafūna*), which is not sound]] affirm the bequest before the debt. He said: The practice of the majority of the people of knowledge is in accordance with this, that one begins with the debt before the bequest. Al-Dāraquṭnī narrated from the ḥadīth of ʿĀṣim ibn Ḍamra, from ʿAlī, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The debt comes before the bequest, and there is no bequest for an heir." Abū Isḥāq al-Hamdhānī narrated both of them.

The answer has five aspects. The first: what was intended was to place these two clauses before the inheritance, and their order relative to each other was not intended; therefore the bequest was placed first in wording. The second answer: since the bequest is less binding than the debt, He mentioned it first out of concern for it, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿it leaves out nothing small or great﴾ [[see vol. 10, p. 418]]. The third answer: He placed it first because of how frequently it occurs and happens, so it became like something necessary for every deceased person, given the explicit ruling of the Sharia concerning it; and He delayed the debt because of its rarity, for it may occur and it may not occur. So He began with mentioning what is unavoidable, and joined by the conjunction what may occur at times. What strengthens this is the use of *aw* (or) for the conjunction; if the debt were constant, the conjunction would have been *wa* (and). The fourth answer: the bequest was placed first because it is the share of the poor and weak, and the debt was delayed because it is the share of a creditor who demands it with strength and authority, and he has a claim regarding it. The fifth answer: since the bequest is initiated by the deceased himself, he placed it first, whereas the debt is established, to be paid whether or not he mentions it.

**The twenty-second point: When this is established, al-Shāfiʿī relied on it for giving precedence to the debt of zakat and the debt of pilgrimage over the inheritance.** He said: If a man neglected his zakat, it is obligatory to take it from the principal of his estate. This is apparent at first thought, because it is one of the rights, so its payment after death is obligatory, like the rights of human beings, especially since the zakat is spent upon human beings. Abū Ḥanīfa and Mālik said: If he bequeathed it, it is paid from his third; if he remained silent about it, nothing is taken from him. They said: Because that would necessitate leaving the heirs in poverty, except that he might deliberately leave all of it, so that when he dies, it consumes all his wealth and the heirs have no right.

**The twenty-third point: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Your fathers and your sons﴾.** It is in the nominative case as the subject (*mubtadaʾ*), and the predicate is implied; its estimate is: they are those among whom the inheritance is divided, and they are those who receive.

**The twenty-fourth point: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You do not know which of them is nearer to you in benefit﴾.** It was said: In this world, through supplication and charity, as is reported in the narration: "A man is indeed raised in rank by the supplication of his child after him." And in the sound ḥadīth: "When the son of Adam dies, his deeds are cut off except for three: an ongoing charity, knowledge from which benefit is derived, or a righteous child who prays for him" [[the ḥadīth: "When the son of Adam dies, his deeds are cut off except for three: an ongoing charity, knowledge from which benefit is derived, or a righteous child who prays for him."]]. It was also said: In the Hereafter, for the son may be superior and intercede for his father; this is related from Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḥasan. Some exegetes said: If the son is higher in rank than his father in the Hereafter, he asks God and his father is raised to him; likewise the father if he is higher than his son. Its explanation will come in (*al-Ṭūr*) [[see vol. 17, p. 66]]. It was also said: in this world and the Hereafter, reported by Ibn Zayd. The wording requires this.

**The twenty-fifth point: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿an obligation﴾.** *Farīḍatan* is in the accusative as an emphatic verbal noun (*maṣdar*), since the meaning of ﴿He enjoins upon you﴾ is "He prescribes upon you." Makkī and others said: it is an emphatic circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), and the governing word is ﴿He enjoins upon you﴾; but that is weak. The verse is connected to what preceded it, because He informed the servants that they are relieved of the burden of exerting their own effort in determining the bequest to relatives, since they are united in kinship. That is, fathers and sons benefit one another in this world through support and consolation, and in the Hereafter through intercession. When this is established for fathers and sons, it is established for all relatives. Thus if the division were left to individual judgment, it would be necessary to consider the wealth of each one of them, and at that point the matter would fall outside control, since circumstances differ. So the Lord, blessed and exalted is He, made clear that it is better for the servant not to be left to his own judgment regarding the measures of inheritance, but that the measures be determined by the Sharia. Then He said: ﴿Indeed, God is ever Knowing﴾, that is, of the division of inheritances, ﴿Wise﴾, who has decreed its division and made it clear to its people. Al-Zajjāj said: ﴿Knowing﴾ means knowing things before their creation, ﴿Wise﴾ in what He determines and executes of them. Some said: God, glory be to Him, has always been and always will be, and His report about the past is like His report about the future. The view of Sībawayh is that they saw wisdom and knowledge, and it was said to them: God, mighty and majestic, has been so always, as you have seen.

**The twenty-sixth point: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And for you is half of what your wives leave﴾, [and the following] two verses.** The address is to men. The "child" here refers to the children of the loins and their children, however far down they descend, males and females, one or more, by consensus. The scholars agreed that the husband has a half share if there is no child or child's child, and a quarter if there is one. The wife inherits from her husband a quarter if there is no child, and an eighth if there is one. They agreed that the ruling for one wife, two, three or four is the same: a quarter if he has no child, and an eighth if he has one child, and that they share in this, because God, mighty and majestic, did not distinguish between the ruling for one of them and the ruling for all of them, just as He distinguished between the ruling for one of the daughters and the ruling for one of the sisters, and the ruling for all of them.

**The twenty-seventh point: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if a man leaves an inheritance by kalāla, or a woman﴾.** *Kalāla* is a verbal noun from *takallalahu al-nasab*, meaning kinship surrounded him. From it comes *al-iklīl* (the crown), and it is also a lunar mansion because it surrounds the moon when the moon is in it. From it also comes *al-iklīl*, which is the crown and the band encircling the head. So if a man dies leaving neither a child nor a parent, his heirs are *kalāla*. This is the statement of Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, ʿUmar, ʿAlī and the majority of the people of knowledge. Yaḥyā ibn Ādam narrated from Sharīk, Zuhayr and Abū al-Aḥwaṣ, from Abū Isḥāq, from Sulaymān ibn ʿAbd, who said: "I have not seen them except that they agreed and concurred that *kalāla* is one who dies leaving neither a child nor a parent." Thus said the author of *Kitāb al-ʿAyn*, Abū Manṣūr the linguist, Ibn ʿArafa, al-Qutabī, Abū ʿUbayd and Ibn al-Anbārī. The father and the son are two sides of a man, so when they are gone, kinship surrounds him. From this it is said: a "crowned garden" (*rawḍa mukallala*) when it is encircled by blossoms. They recited:

His dwelling is a crowned garden,
around it grow the *ayhaqān* and the *dhurq* [[*al-ayhaqān*: wild rocket. *al-dhurq*: a herb like raw watercress. In *al-Lisān*: he said once: *al-dhurq* is a plant like the mountain *kurrāt*, fine, with at its top small heads containing grey, sweet seeds, eaten fresh, which herders love and bring to their families; and it has small blades with a black skin that peels to reveal a white, truly sweet, very watery flesh that people eat. The editor said: it is called *ajīz* in the Maghrib, appearing in fertile seasons.]]

meaning two plants. And Imruʾ al-Qays said:

O friend, do you see a flash of lightning that I show you its gleam,
like the flashing of two hands in a cloud that is encircled [[*wamḍ al-barq*: it shone. *ka-lamʿ al-yadayn*: like the signalling of the hands. *al-ḥabī*: the cloud that stretches across. *al-mukallal*: that in whose sides there is lightning like a crown.]]

So they called the relatives *kalāla*, because they surround the deceased from all sides while they are not of him, nor is he of them; and their surrounding him is that they are connected with him in lineage [[from J, B and Y; in A, H and T: "they are connected"]]. As an Arab said: "I have much wealth, and my heir is a *kalāla* whose lineage is distant." And al-Farazdaq said:

You inherited the spear of glory, not from *kalāla*,
from the two sons of Manāf, ʿAbd Shams and Hāshim.

And another said:

Indeed the father of a man is the most protective of him,
but the client of *kalāla* does not become angry.

[[He meant that the father becomes angry for him when he is wronged. The clients of *kalāla* are the brothers, the paternal uncles, the paternal cousins and the rest of the relatives, who do not become angry for a man in the way a father does.]]

It was also said: *kalāla* is derived from *kalāl*, which means fatigue, as if the inheritance comes to the heir from a distance and with exertion. Al-Aʿshā said:

So I swore I would not lament for her from a *kalāla*,
nor from a weary one, until I meet Muḥammad.

[[*al-wajā*: the exhausted.]]

Abū Ḥātim and al-Athram narrated from Abū ʿUbayda, who said: *kalāla* is everyone whom a father, a son or a brother does not inherit from; for that is *kalāla* in the view of the Arabs. Abū ʿUmar said: Abū ʿUbayda's mention of the brother here alongside the father and the son as a condition for *kalāla* is an error with no basis, and no one other than him mentioned it as a condition for *kalāla*. It is narrated from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb that *kalāla* is the one who has no child specifically, and it is narrated from Abū Bakr, then they both retracted that. Ibn Zayd said: *kalāla* is both the living and the dead. From ʿAṭāʾ: *kalāla* is the wealth. Ibn al-ʿArabī said: This is a strange statement with no basis. I say: it has a basis that becomes clear through the grammatical analysis (*iʿrāb*) just below [[in D, W, T and Z; also in J and H]]. It is narrated from Ibn al-Aʿrābī that *kalāla* are the distant paternal cousins. From al-Suddī that *kalāla* is the dead person, and from him a view like that of the majority. These statements have their aspects made clear through *iʿrāb* (grammatical analysis). Some of the Kufans recited ﴿yūraththu kalāla﴾ with a kasra on the rāʾ and a shadda. Al-Ḥasan and Ayyūb recited *yūrithu* with a kasra on the rāʾ and without a shadda, according to different transmissions from them. According to these two readings, *kalāla* can only be the heirs or the wealth. Thus the grammarians of meanings (*aṣḥāb al-maʿānī*) have related. The first is from *waritha*, and the second from *awritha*. *Kalāla* is its object, and *kāna* is in the sense of "occurred." Whoever recites *yūraththu* with a fatḥa on the rāʾ may hold that *kalāla* is the wealth, the estimate being: he is inherited with the inheritance of *kalāla*, so it is an adjective of an elided verbal noun. It is also permissible that *kalāla* be a noun for the heirs, and it is the predicate of *kāna*, so the estimate is: one who has heirs. It is also permissible that *kāna* be complete in the sense of "occurred," with *yūraththu* as an adjective of "a man," "a man" being the subject of *kāna*, and *kalāla* in the accusative as an explanation or a circumstantial clause, on the basis that *kalāla* is the deceased, the estimate being: a man who is inherited from, whose kinship surrounds the deceased.

**Twenty-eighth issue:** Allah, exalted is He, mentions the *kalala* (the heirless deceased, leaving neither descendant nor ascendant) in His Book in two places: at the end of the surah and here. In neither place does He mention any heir other than siblings. As for this verse, the scholars unanimously agree that the siblings meant in it are the maternal siblings, because of His saying: ﴿But if they are more than that, they share in the third﴾. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas used to recite it as: ﴿And he has a brother or sister from the mother﴾. There is no disagreement among the people of knowledge that the inheritance of full siblings or consanguine siblings (sharing only the father) is not like this. Their consensus therefore indicates that the siblings mentioned at the end of the surah are the siblings of the deceased through both parents or through the father, because of the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And if they are siblings, men and women, then the male has the equivalent of the share of two females﴾ [[See vol. 6, p. 28.]]. They have not disagreed that the inheritance of maternal siblings is not like this. Thus the two verses indicate that all siblings together are a *kalala*.

Al-Sha'bi said: "The *kalala* is whoever, among the heirs other than the child and the parent, is a sibling or another of the 'asaba (agnatic relatives)." This was also said by Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Zayd and Ibn 'Abbas, and it is the first opinion with which we began. Al-Tabari said: "The correct view is that the *kalala* are those who inherit from the deceased other than his child and his parent, because of the soundness of the report of Jabir: I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, only a *kalala* inherits from me; should I bequeath all my wealth?' He said: 'No.'"

**Twenty-ninth issue:** The lexicographers said: one says "a man *kalala*" and "a woman *kalala*." It is not made dual or plural, because it is a verbal noun (*masdar*), like *al-wakala*, *al-dalala*, *al-samaha* and *al-shaja'a*. He used the singular pronoun in His saying ﴿And he has a brother﴾ and did not say "for both of them." The mention of the man and the woman continued according to the Arab custom: when they mention two names and then speak about them, and both are equal in the ruling, they sometimes attach the pronoun to one of them and sometimes to both together. You say: "Whoever has a boy and a girl, let him be kind to him, to her, and to both of them, and to them." Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer, and indeed it is difficult﴾ [[See vol. 1, p. 371.]]. He also said: ﴿If he is rich or poor, then Allah is more entitled to both of them﴾ [[See p. 410 of this part.]]. It is permissible to say "more entitled to them" (*awla bihim*), according to al-Farra' and others. For a woman one says *mar'a*, which is the original form. The word *akh* (brother) originally was *akhu*, as shown by *akhawan* (two brothers). It was elided and changed contrary to the regular pattern. Al-Farra' said: the first letter of *ukht* (sister) is vowelled with a *damma* because the elided letter is a waw, and the first letter of *bint* (daughter) is vowelled with a *kasra* because the elided letter is a ya'. This elision and its explanation are also contrary to regular analogy.

**Thirtieth issue:** His saying ﴿But if they are more than that, they share in the third﴾: This sharing requires equality between the male and the female, even if they are many. When they take through the mother, the male is not given preference over the female. This is a consensus among the scholars. There is no place in the shares of inheritance where male and female are equal except in the inheritance of maternal siblings. If a woman dies leaving her husband, her mother and her maternal brother, then the husband has a half, the mother has a third, and the maternal brother has a sixth. If she leaves two brothers and two sisters (from the mother)—the case remaining the same—then the husband has a half, the mother has a sixth, and the two brothers and two sisters share a third, and the division is complete. This is the view of most of the Companions, because they reduced the mother's share from a third to a sixth by the presence of the brother and sister. As for Ibn 'Abbas, he did not accept *'awl* (the increase of the shares beyond the original sum). If he had given the mother a third, the case would have needed *'awl*, and he did not accept that.

*'Awl* [[The share is raised: its portions exceed the original base of calculation according to the number of heirs.]] is mentioned in another place, and this is not its place.

If she leaves her husband, maternal siblings, and a full sibling (sharing both parents), then the husband has a half, her maternal siblings have a third, and what remains goes to her full brother. The same applies to anyone who has a prescribed share: he is given it, and the remainder goes to the 'asaba if anything is left over.

If she leaves six siblings of differing parentage, this is the *Himariyya* [[From their saying: "Suppose our father was a donkey," as will come.]], also called *al-Mushtaraka* (the "shared" case). Some people said: the maternal siblings have a third, the husband has a half, the mother has a sixth, and the full sibling and the sister (from both parents), and the consanguine brother and sister, drop out. This is narrated from Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Musa, al-Sha'bi, Sharik and Yahya ibn Adam, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal also held it. Ibn al-Mundhir preferred it, because the husband, the mother and the two maternal siblings are holders of prescribed shares, and nothing remains for the 'asaba.

Other people said: the mother is one person, "Suppose their father was a donkey!" and they shared the third among them. This is why it is called *al-Mushtaraka* and *al-Himariyya*. This was narrated from Umar, Uthman, Ibn Mas'ud also, Zayd ibn Thabit, Masruq and Shurayh, and Malik, al-Shafi'i and Ishaq also held it. This case does not work out if the deceased is a man.

This is a body of the science of inheritance contained in the verse, and Allah is the One who grants success in guidance.

In the pre-Islamic period, inheritance was based on manhood and strength: they would give inheritance to men to the exclusion of women. Allah, exalted is He, annulled this by His saying: ﴿For men there is a share of what they have earned, and for women there is a share﴾, as already mentioned. Also in the pre-Islamic period and at the beginning of Islam, inheritance was by *al-muhalafa* (the alliance-pact). Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those with whom your oaths have bound you﴾, as its explanation will come [[See p. 165 of this part.]]. Then after the alliance, it became by emigration (*hijra*). Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those who believed but did not emigrate—you have no guardianship of them until they emigrate﴾ [[See vol. 8, p. 55.]], and it will come. There, if Allah wills, the discussion of the *dhawu al-arham* (blood relatives) and their inheritance will come. In Surat al-Nur [[See vol. 12, p. 195.]] will come the inheritance of the child of the *mula'ana* (the child of the li'an-oath couple) and the child of fornication, and the *mukatab* (slave under a manumission contract), by the power of Allah, exalted is He.

Most scholars hold that the prisoner whose life is known has an inheritance that stands, because he is within the body of Muslims to whom the rules of Islam apply. It has been narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab that he said regarding a prisoner in the hands of the enemy: he does not inherit. The inheritance of the apostate has already been mentioned in Surat al-Baqara [[See vol. 3, p. 49.]]. And praise be to Allah.

**Thirty-first issue:** His saying ﴿without causing harm﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*), and the governing verb is "bequeaths" (*yusa*): he bequeaths it without causing harm, that is, without introducing harm upon the heirs. It is not appropriate for him to bequeath a debt that he does not owe in order to harm the heirs, nor to acknowledge a debt. The harm returns to the bequest and to the debt. As for its return to the bequest: it is by exceeding a third, or by bequeathing to an heir. If he exceeds, it is returned, unless the heirs permit it, because the prohibition is for their rights, not for the right of Allah, exalted is He. If he bequeaths to an heir, it reverts to inheritance. The scholars agreed that a bequest to an heir is not permissible. This was already discussed in Surat al-Baqara [[See vol. 2, p. 257.]].
