[See vol. 6, p. 174, where the disagreement on this matter is discussed.] For this reason our scholars said: the male thief, the female thief, and the slanderer, when they repent, and when testimony is established against them, the prescribed punishments are carried out upon them.

It has also been said that "upon" (ʿalā) means "from" (min), i.e., "Repentance is only from Allah for those..." This was stated by Abu Bakr ibn 'Abdus. And Allah knows best. The discussion of sincere repentance and the things one repents from will come in (Surat) al-Tahrim. [See vol. 18, p. 197 and following.]

**The second issue: Allah's words, ﴿those who do evil in ignorance﴾.** The word "evil" (al-su') in this verse, and in (Surat) al-An'am where He says: ﴿Whoever among you does evil in ignorance﴾ [6:54], includes disbelief and acts of disobedience. Therefore everyone who disobeys his Lord is ignorant until he desists from his disobedience. Qatadah said: "The companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) agreed that every act of disobedience is done in ignorance, whether it is done deliberately or out of ignorance." Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, Mujahid and al-Suddi said the same. It is also narrated from al-Dahhak and Mujahid that they both said: "Ignorance here means deliberate action." Ikrimah said: "All the affairs of this world are ignorance," meaning the particular worldly matters that take one outside obedience to Allah. This statement agrees with His words: ﴿The life of this world is nothing but play and amusement﴾ [47:36]. [See vol. 16, p. 257; vol. 6, p. 414; and vol. 17, p. 254.]

Al-Zajjaj said: "His words ﴿in ignorance﴾ mean their choosing fleeting pleasure over lasting pleasure." It has also been said: "in ignorance" means they do not know the reality of the punishment. This was mentioned by Ibn Furak. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This view is weak, and it has been refuted."

**The third issue: Allah's words, ﴿Then they repent soon﴾.** Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi said: "Its meaning is before illness and death." It is narrated from al-Dahhak that he said: "Whatever comes before death is 'soon'." Abu Mijlaz, al-Dahhak also, 'Ikrimah, Ibn Zayd and others said: "Before witnessing the angels and the throes of death (al-sawq) [the throes of death: the extraction, as if the soul is being driven out of the body], and before a person is overpowered by himself."

Mahmud al-Warraq excellently said:

*Send ahead for yourself a hoped-for repentance, before death and before the tongue is bound.*

*Hasten with it, lest the souls be pawned [one says: a pledge is pawned when one cannot redeem it; he means: hasten to repent before the opportunity is lost], for they are a treasure and a gain for the one who turns back and does good.*

Our scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, said: "Repentance is valid at this time because hope remains, and remorse and a firm resolve to abandon the act are still valid from him." Al-Tirmidhi narrated from Ibn 'Umar that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah accepts the repentance of the servant as long as he has not begun the death rattle (yughargir)." He said: "This is a good, strange hadith." The meaning of "as long as he has not begun the death rattle" is: as long as his soul has not reached his throat, so that it becomes like something gargled. This was stated by al-Harawi. It has also been said: the meaning is that they repent shortly after committing the sin without persisting in it. The one who hastens to repent while healthy is more excellent and closer to what he hopes for than one who does righteous deeds. "Far" (al-bu'd) is completely death, as one says:

*And where is a place of distance except my place?*

This is the second half of a verse by Malik ibn al-Rayb al-Mazini. Its first half is:

*They say: "Do not be far," while they bury me.*

Salih al-Murri narrated from al-Hasan who said: "Whoever reproaches his brother for a sin from which he has repented to Allah, Allah will afflict him with it." Al-Hasan also said: "When Iblis descended he said: 'By Your might, I will not leave the son of Adam as long as the soul is in his body.' Allah, the Exalted, said: 'By My might, I will not withhold repentance from the son of Adam as long as his soul has not begun the death rattle.'"

**The fourth issue: Allah's words, ﴿Nor is repentance﴾.** Allah, glorified is He, has negated that those present at death, at the time of despair, are included in the ruling of penitents, just as Pharaoh, when he was in the surge of water and drowning, was not benefited by what he showed of faith. This is because repentance at that time is of no benefit, since it is a state in which obligation has ceased. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Zayd and the majority of exegetes.

As for disbelievers who die in their disbelief, they have no repentance in the Hereafter, and the reference to them is in His words: ﴿For those We have prepared a painful punishment﴾, which is eternal abiding. If the reference in His words is to all of them, then for the disobedient it is a punishment without eternal abiding, and this is on the basis that the "evil deeds" are what falls short of disbelief. That is, repentance is not for those who did evil deeds short of disbelief and then repented at the time of death, nor for those who died as disbelievers and then repented on the Day of Resurrection. It has also been said: "The evil deeds here are disbelief," so the meaning is: repentance is not for the disbelievers who repent at death, nor for those who die while they are disbelievers.

Abu al-'Aliyah said: "The first part of the verse was revealed concerning the believers: ﴿Repentance is only with Allah﴾. The second part concerns the hypocrites."

﴿Nor is repentance for those who do evil deeds﴾: meaning, acceptance of repentance is not for those who persisted in their actions.

﴿Until, when death comes to one of them﴾: meaning, the choking (al-sharaq), the death rattle (al-nazʿ), and witnessing the Angel of Death. [The word translated as choking: in the text, the variant readings differ; some copies read "al-sawq."]

﴿He says: "Indeed I have repented now"﴾: for this there is no repentance.

Then He mentioned the repentance of disbelievers, saying: ﴿Nor for those who die while they are disbelievers, for them We have prepared a painful punishment﴾, meaning, a painful and eternal punishment. This has already been mentioned. [See vol. 1, p. 198.]

There are eight issues.

**The first issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, it is not lawful for you to inherit women against their will﴾. This is connected to what was mentioned before concerning wives. The aim is to negate injustice toward them and harm to them, and the address is to the guardians (awliya').

The "an" (that) here is in the nominative position, governed by "yahillu" (it is lawful), meaning: it is not lawful for you to inherit women. "Karhan" (against their will) is a verbal noun in the accusative position serving as a circumstantial qualifier (hal).

The reports and the statements of the exegetes differ regarding the occasion of its revelation. Al-Bukhari reported from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding ﴿O you who believe, it is not lawful for you to inherit women against their will, nor should you prevent them from marrying, so that you may take back part of what you have given them﴾, that he said: "In the past, when a man died, his guardians had more right to his wife. Some of them would marry her if they wished, or they would give her in marriage if they wished, or they would not give her in marriage if they wished. They had more right to her than her own family. So this verse was revealed concerning that." Abu Dawud also transmitted it with the same meaning.

Al-Zuhri and Abu Mijlaz said: "It was their custom that when a man died, his son from another wife, or his closest male relative (asabah), would throw his garment over the woman, and thereby he became more entitled to her than she was to herself and than her guardians. If he wished, he would marry her without a dowry, except the dowry that the deceased had given her. If he wished, he would give her in marriage to someone else and take her dowry, giving her nothing. If he wished, he would prevent her from marrying so that she would ransom herself from him with what she had inherited from the deceased, or until she died and he inherited her. So Allah, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿O you who believe, it is not lawful for you to inherit women against their will﴾."

Thus the meaning is: it is not lawful for you to inherit them from their husbands, so that you would become their husbands.

It was also said: "If the heir arrived first and threw a garment over her, he had more right to her. But if she got ahead of him and went to her family, she had more right to herself." This was said by al-Suddi.

It was also said: "A man would have an old woman with him, while his desire was for a young woman. He would dislike parting from the old woman because of her wealth, so he would keep her and not approach her, until she ransomed herself from him with her wealth, or until she died and he inherited her wealth." So this verse was revealed. And the husband was commanded to divorce her if he disliked her company, and not to keep her by force. This is what is meant by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is not lawful for you to inherit women against their will﴾.

The purpose of the verse is to eliminate what they practised in their jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic ignorance), and to ensure that women are not treated like property that is inherited from men the way property is inherited.

"Karhan" (with a dammah on the kaf) is the recitation (qira'ah) of Hamzah and al-Kisa'i. The rest read it with a fathah. Both are dialectal forms. Al-Qutabi said: "Al-karh (with a fathah) means compulsion (al-ikrah), and al-kurh (with a dammah) means hardship (al-mashaqqah). It is said: 'Do that willingly or unwillingly (karhan),' meaning willingly or under compulsion."

The address is to the guardians. It was also said that the address is to the husbands of women when they detain them, with bad treatment, hoping to inherit from them, or so that they will ransom themselves with part of their dowries. This view is more sound, and Ibn 'Atiyyah chose it. He said: "The proof of this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿unless they commit a clear immorality﴾. When a woman commits a clear immorality, it is not permissible for the guardian to detain her until he takes her wealth, by consensus (ijma') of the community. Rather, that right belongs to the husband, as will be explained in the issue after this."

**The second issue:** His saying: ﴿nor should you prevent them from marrying﴾. The meaning of "al-'adl" (prevention) has already been mentioned, and that it means to restrain, in Surat al-Baqarah. [See vol. 3, p. 159.]

**The third issue:** ﴿unless they commit a clear immorality﴾. People differed about the meaning of "fahishah" (immorality). Al-Hasan said: it is adultery (zina). If a virgin commits adultery, she is flogged one hundred times and exiled for one year, and she returns to her husband what she took from him. Abu Qilabah said: if a man's wife commits adultery, there is no harm in his harming her and making things hard for her until she ransoms herself from him. Al-Suddi said: if they do that, take their dowries. Ibn Sirin and Abu Qilabah said: it is not lawful for him to take a ransom from her unless he finds a man upon her body, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿unless they commit a clear immorality﴾.

Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak and Qatadah said: the "clear immorality" in this verse is hatred and defiance (nushuz). They said: when she is defiant (nashazat), it is lawful for him to take her wealth. This is the position of Malik. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "However, I do not recall any linguistic evidence that 'fahishah' in the verse means defiance."

Others said: "Fahishah" is foul speech with the tongue and bad conduct in word and deed, and this has the same meaning as defiance. Some scholars permit taking wealth from a defiant wife by way of khul' (divorce by compensation), but they hold that he should not exceed what he gave her, relying on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so that you may take back part of what you have given them﴾.

Malik and a group of scholars said: the husband may take from the defiant wife everything she owns. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "Adultery is harder on the husband than defiance and harm, and all of these are immoralities that make taking wealth lawful."

Abu 'Umar said: "The statement of Ibn Sirin and Abu Qilabah is, in my view, of no weight, because 'fahishah' can mean foul speech and harm. That is why a foul-mouthed person is called fahish and mutafahhish. Moreover, if he discovers immorality from her, he may perform li'an (mutual oath of condemnation) against her, or divorce her if he wishes. But as for harming her until she ransoms herself with her wealth, that is not permitted to him. I know of no one who said that he may harm her and mistreat her until she seeks khul' from him, if he finds her committing adultery, except Abu Qilabah." And Allah knows best.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿But if you fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah﴾, meaning in maintaining good companionship and in fulfilling the wife's rights to the husband and the husband's rights to her, ﴿there is no blame on either of them for what she gives up to ransom herself﴾. [See vol. 3, p. 125.]

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, also said: ﴿And if they willingly give you a part of it, then consume it with satisfaction and ease﴾. [See p. 23 of this volume.] These verses are the foundation of this topic.

'Ata' al-Khurasani said: "If a man's wife committed a immorality, he would take back from her what he had given her and expel her. Then that was abrogated (naskh) by the prescribed punishments (hudud)."

A fourth opinion: ﴿unless they commit a clear immorality﴾ means: unless they commit adultery, in which case they are confined to their homes. This would be before the abrogation. This is similar to the view of 'Ata', and it is weak.

**The fourth issue:** If we adopt the view that the address in the prohibition of preventing marriage is to the guardians, then its jurisprudence is that whenever it is established against a guardian that he is preventing marriage, the judge (qadi) examines the matter of the woman and her husband. The exception is a father regarding his daughters. If he is preventing for a legitimate reason, he is not opposed, by a single opinion. This applies to the suitor and suitors. If his prevention is established, there are two opinions in the school of Malik: first, that he is like the other guardians, and the judge marries her to whomever he wishes from the suitors and seeks his consent. The second opinion: he is not to be interfered with.

**The fifth issue:** Since ﴿clear (mubayyinah)﴾ is read with a kasrah under the ya' by Nafi' and Abu 'Amr, while the rest read it with a fathah on the ya', and Ibn 'Abbas read "mubinah" with a kasrah under the ba' and a sukun on the ya', from abana al-shay' (to make something clear). It is said: abana al-amr bi-nafsihi, abnahu, and bayyana and bayyantuhu. All these recitations are eloquent dialects.

**The sixth issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And live with them in kindness﴾, meaning in accordance with what Allah has commanded regarding good companionship. The address is to everyone, since everyone has companionship, whether a husband or a guardian. But the intended object of this command is mostly husbands. It is like His saying: ﴿then either keep them in kindness﴾. [See vol. 3, p. 127.] This includes giving her what is due to her of the dowry and maintenance (nafaqah), not frowning in her face without cause, speaking to her gently, neither harshly nor coarsely, and not showing inclination to another woman.

"Al-'ishrah" (companionship) means mixing and intimacy. From it is the saying of Tarafah:

*Even if her dwelling has moved far away once,*
*I am still faithful to the pledge of a beloved companion.*

Ibn Manzur says: He made the beloved a group, like a mixture and a crowd. He lived with her in companionship (mu'ashara), and the people lived together and mutually kept company (ta'ashara and i'tasharu). Allah, glorified is He, commanded good companionship with women when they are married to them, so that there would be (adamah [[Adamah: mixing, close association.]]) between them, and their companionship would be complete, for it is more soothing to the soul and more pleasant for life. This is obligatory upon the husband, but it is not binding on him in judicial terms (fi al-qada' [[Qada': judgment, i.e., whether it is enforceable by a judge.]]). Some of them said: it means that he should beautify himself for her as she beautifies herself for him.

Yahya ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Hanzali said: I came to Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah, and he came out to me wearing a red cloak, and his beard was dripping with (al-ghaliyah [[Al-ghaliyah: a type of perfume compounded of musk, ambergris, aloes-wood and oil.]]). I said: What is this? He said: This cloak, my wife threw it over me, and she anointed me with perfume, and indeed they (women) desire from us what we desire from them.

Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: I love to adorn myself for my wife just as I love that she adorn herself [the woman [[From manuscripts J, T, Z, H.]]] for me. This falls within what we have mentioned.

Ibn Atiyyah said: To the meaning of the verse one refers to the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): (Enjoy her, though there is crookedness in her), meaning: let there be no bad treatment from you despite her crookedness, for from it (her crookedness) opposition arises, and by it discord occurs, and it is the cause of khul' (divorce initiated by the wife).

The seventh issue: Our scholars cited the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And live with them in kindness﴾ as evidence that if a woman cannot be served by one servant, then he must provide her with servants sufficient for her needs, like the daughter of a caliph or a king and those similar to them, for whom one servant is not enough, and that this is living with them in kindness. Al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifah said: He is only obligated to provide one servant, and that suffices her for serving herself, and there is no woman in the world for whom one servant does not suffice. This is like a fighter who has several horses, yet he is given a share only for one horse, because he cannot fight except on one horse. Our scholars said: This is an error, because women like the daughters of kings, who have extensive service needs, cannot be served by one servant, since she needs someone to wash her clothes, prepare her bed [[In J, H, T, Y: "her kitchen" (matbakhuha).]], and other things that one person cannot manage. This is clear. And Allah knows best.

The eighth issue: The saying of the Exalted: ﴿if you dislike them﴾, meaning because of ugliness or bad character, without her committing an immoral act or nushuz (disobedience), in which case he is encouraged to show forbearance, for perhaps the matter will lead to Allah granting him righteous children from her. (An [[Here (أَنْ) is in the nominative case, governed by (عَسَى).]]) is in the nominative case governed by (عَسَى), and (أَنْ) with the verb forms a verbal noun.

I say: From this meaning is what was reported in Sahih Muslim from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: (A believing man should not hate a believing woman; if he dislikes one trait in her, he will be pleased with another), or he said (another [[Or: "other than it."]]).

The meaning: that is, he should not hate her with a total hatred that would drive him to separate from her; rather, he should not do so, but should overlook her faults for her good qualities and disregard what he dislikes for the sake of what he loves.

Makhul said: I heard Ibn Umar say: A man will seek Allah's guidance (istikharah), and it is chosen for him, and then he becomes displeased with his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, and it is not long before he looks at the outcome, and then he finds that it was chosen for him.

Ibn al-Arabi mentioned, saying: Abu al-Qasim ibn Habib informed me in al-Mahdiyyah, from Abu al-Qasim al-Suyuri, from Abu Bakr ibn Abd al-Rahman, who said: Shaykh Abu Muhammad ibn Abi Zayd had a standing in knowledge and religion, and in rank and recognition. He had a wife with bad companionship who fell short in his rights and harmed him with her tongue. He was asked about her matter and was urged to be patient with her, and he would say: I am a man whom Allah has completed His blessing upon, in the soundness of my body, my knowledge, and what my right hand possesses. Perhaps she was sent as a punishment for my sin, and I fear that if I separate from her, a punishment worse than her will befall me.

Our scholars said: In this is evidence for the disliking of divorce despite its permissibility. And it is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: (Indeed Allah does not dislike anything He has permitted except divorce and eating, and indeed Allah dislikes the stomach when it is filled).

**Sixth issue (or: six issues in this passage):**

**First issue:** When the previous verse mentioned the separation whose cause is the wife, it followed with the separation whose cause is the husband, and explained that if he wants to divorce her without *nushuz* (disobedience) and without ill treatment, he is not permitted to demand property from her.

**Second issue:** The scholars differed when both spouses want separation and there is *nushuz* and ill treatment from both sides. Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the husband may take property from her if she is the one who caused the separation, and his own causing of it is not taken into account. A group of scholars said: it is not permissible for him to take property unless she alone is at fault with *nushuz* and she asks for the separation on that basis.

**Third issue:** Allah's words, ﴿And you have given one of them a great amount (qintar)﴾, the verse. This is evidence for the permissibility of excess in dowries (*mughalah fi al-muhur*), because Allah does not give an example except with something permissible. Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, gave a sermon and said: "Beware! Do not exaggerate in the dowries of women. If it were a source of honour in this world or piety before Allah, the one most entitled to it would have been the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He never gave any of his wives or daughters a dowry exceeding twelve *uqiyyah*."

A woman stood up and said to him: "O Umar, Allah gives us and you deprive us! Does Allah, the Exalted, not say: ﴿And you have given one of them a great amount, do not take anything from it﴾?"

Umar said: "A woman was right and Umar was wrong."

In another report: "Umar lowered his head and then said: 'Every person is more knowledgeable than you, O Umar!'"

In another: "A woman was right and a man was wrong." And he abandoned the objection.

Abu Hatim al-Busti reported it in his *Sahih Musnad*, from Abu al-Ajfa al-Sulami, who said: Umar addressed the people, and he mentioned it up to his words "twelve *uqiyyah*," but he did not mention "a woman stood up to him," to the end.

Ibn Majah also reported it in his *Sunan*, from Abu al-Ajfa, and he added after his words "*uqiyyah*": "A man burdens his wife with the dowry until she develops resentment toward him in his heart, and he says: 'I have strained myself for you until the *alaq* of the waterskin, or the *araq* of the waterskin.' And I was an Arab *muwallad* (a man of mixed or later Arab lineage), I do not know what *alaq al-qirbah* or *araq al-qirbah* is."

Al-Jawhari said: "*Alaq al-qirbah* is a dialectal variant of *araq al-qirbah*." Another said: "It is said that *alaq al-qirbah* is its *isam*, the thing by which it is hung. He means: 'I strained myself for you even to the *isam* of the waterskin.' And *araq al-qirbah* is its water. He means: 'I endured hardship for you until I travelled and needed the water of the waterskin, which is its water during travel.' It is also said: *araq al-qirbah* is that he says: 'I toiled and exerted myself for you until I sweated the sweat of the waterskin,' which is its flowing."

It was also said: they used to carry water on camels, hanging it on them and taking turns with it, and this caused hardship and strain on the back. So the two terms were explained by this: *al-araq* and *al-alaq*.

Al-Asmai said: "*Araq al-qirbah* is an expression meaning hardship." He said: "I do not know its origin." Al-Asmai also said: "I heard Ibn Abi Tarafah, who was among the most eloquent people I have seen, say: 'I heard our shaykhs say: I met from so-and-so *araq al-qirbah*,' meaning hardship."

He recited to me a verse by Ibn al-Ahmar:

*It is not an insult that is counted, and its pardon*
*is the sweat of the waterskin on the weary riding-camel.*

Abu Ubayd said: he meant that a man hears a word that angers him, and it is not an insult for which the speaker can be held to account. "And I have brought it to him like the sweat of the waterskin." Then he said "like the sweat of the waterskin" because he could not complete the verse with it. Then he said "on the weary riding-camel," and its meaning is that the waterskin is hung on the riding-camel during their journeys.

This meaning resembles what al-Farra used to narrate. He claimed that they were in the desert on their journeys, carrying water and hanging it on camels, taking turns with it, and this involved fatigue and hardship on the back. Al-Farra used to render this explanation of *alaq al-qirbah* with the letter *lam*.

Some people said: the verse does not indicate the permissibility of excess in dowries, because the example of the *qintar* is by way of exaggeration, as if He said: "And you have given this enormous amount which no one gives." This is like the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever builds a mosque for Allah, even as small as the nest of a sand-grouse (*mafhas qatah*), Allah will build for him a house in Paradise." It is known that there is no mosque as small as a sand-grouse's nest.

The Prophet (ﷺ) also said to Ibn Abi Hadrad, when he came asking him for help with his dowry. He asked him about it and he said: "Two hundred." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) became angry and said: "It is as if you were quarrying gold and silver from the side of a *harrah* or a mountain." (*Harrah*: land of black, crumbling stones.)

Some people deduced from this a prohibition of excess in dowries. This does not follow. The Prophet's (ﷺ) rebuke of this man who was marrying was not a rebuke because of excess and extravagance in dowries. Rather, the rebuke was because he was poor at that time, and so he brought himself to need help and asking. This is disliked by consensus.

Umar gave Umm Kulthum, daughter of Ali and Fatimah, may Allah be pleased with them all, a dowry of forty thousand dirhams.

Abu Dawud reported from Uqbah ibn Amir that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to a man: "Are you content that I marry you to so-and-so?" He said: "Yes." And he said to the woman: "Are you content that I marry you to so-and-so?" She said: "Yes." So he married one of them to the other, and the man consummated the marriage with her, but he had not set a dowry for her and had not given her anything. He was among those who witnessed al-Hudaybiyah, and he had a share at Khaybar. When death came to him, he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) married me to so-and-so, but I did not set a dowry for her and did not give her anything. I call you to witness that I have now given her from her dowry my share at Khaybar." So she took his share and sold it for one hundred thousand.

The scholars have agreed that there is no limit on the highest dowry, based on Allah's words: ﴿And you have given one of them a great amount﴾. They differed concerning the minimum, and this will come at His words: ﴿that you seek with your wealth﴾.

The discussion of the *qintar* as a quantity was already presented at (Al-Imran; see vol. 4, p. 30).

Ibn Muhaysin recited ﴿wa-ataytum ihdahunna﴾ with *wasl* (connecting) the *alif* of *ihdahunna*, and this is a dialect. From it is the saying of the poet:

*And you hear from beneath the dust-cloud its *azmal* (sound)*

And the saying of another:

*If I do not fight, then cover me with a face-veil.*

**Fourth issue:** Allah's words, ﴿then do not take from it anything﴾. Bakr ibn Abd Allah al-Muzani said: the husband may not take anything from a wife who seeks *khul'* (divorce by compensation), based on Allah's words, ﴿do not take﴾, and he considered it abrogating (*nasikhah*) the verse of al-Baqarah.

Ibn Zayd and others said: it is abrogated (*mansukhah*) by His words in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿And it is not lawful for you to take anything of what you have given them﴾. (See vol. 3, p. 136.)

The correct view is that these verses are definitive (*muhkamah*), and there is no abrogating or abrogated element in them, and all of them build upon one another. Al-Tabari said: they are definitive. There is no sense in Bakr's statement, since if she gives the compensation voluntarily, the Prophet (ﷺ) permitted Thabit to take back from his wife what he had given her.

*Buhtanan* is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*). *Wa-ithman* is coordinated with it. *Mubinan* is an attribute of it (*min na't-hi*).

**Fifth issue:** Allah's words, ﴿And how could you take it﴾, the verse. This is a reason (*ta'lil*) for the prohibition of taking [property] when the couple has been alone together (*khalwah*).

Some scholars said: *ifda'* (intimate contact) means that when she is with him under a single blanket, whether he has had intercourse with her or not. This was related by al-Harawi, and it is the view of al-Kalbi.

Al-Farra said: *ifda'* means that the man and the woman are alone together and he has intercourse with her.

Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, al-Suddi and others said: *ifda'* in this verse means intercourse. Ibn Abbas said: "But Allah is Generous and uses euphemism."

The original meaning of *ifda'* in the language is mixing together, and a mixed thing is called *fada*. The poet said:

*I said to her: "O aunt, the she-camel is yours,*
*and dates mixed (*fada*) in my bag, and raisins."*

(*Aybah*: a leather bag used for carrying harvested crops to the threshing ground, and for holding garments.)

It is also said: "The people are *fawda fada*," meaning they are mixed together with no leader over them.

Assuming that the meaning of *afda* is to be alone, even if he did not have intercourse: does the dowry become fixed by the mere occurrence of being alone? Our scholars differed on this in four views:

1. It becomes fixed by mere seclusion.
2. It is not fixed except by consummation.
3. It becomes fixed by seclusion in the house of the bridal transfer (*bayt al-ihda'*).
4. A distinction between his house and her house.

The correct view is that it is fixed by seclusion in general. This is the view of Abu Hanifah and his companions. They said: if he is alone with her in a valid seclusion, the full dowry and the *iddah* (waiting period) become obligatory, whether he consummated with her or not. This is based on what al-Daraqutni reported from Thawban, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever uncovers the veil of a woman and looks at her, the dowry becomes obligatory."

Umar said: "If he closes a door and lets down a curtain and sees her private parts, the dowry becomes obligatory, and she must observe the *iddah*, and she has the inheritance."

It was narrated from Ali: "If he closes a door and lets down a curtain and sees her private parts, the dowry becomes obligatory."

Malik said: if he remains with her for a long time, like a year or so, and they both agree that there was no intimate contact, and she demands the full dowry, it is hers.

Al-Shafi'i said: she has no *iddah*, and she is entitled to half the dowry.

This has already been discussed in (al-Baqarah; see vol. 3, p. 205).

**Sixth issue:** Allah's words, ﴿And they have taken from you a solemn covenant﴾. There are three views concerning it.

- It is his, peace be upon him, saying: "Fear Allah regarding women, for you have taken them under the trust of Allah, and you have made their private parts lawful by the word of Allah." This was said by Ikrimah and al-Rabi.
- The second: Allah's words, ﴿then either keep them in kindness or release them with goodness﴾. This was said by al-Hasan, Ibn Sirin, Qatadah, al-Dahhak and al-Suddi.
- The third: the bond of marriage, which is a man's saying: "I have married and possessed through the bond of marriage." This was said by Mujahid and Ibn Zayd.

Some people said: the solemn covenant is the child.

And Allah knows best.

**Sixth issue (or: six issues in this passage):**

**First issue:** When the previous verse mentioned the separation whose cause is the wife, it followed with the separation whose cause is the husband, and explained that if he wants to divorce her without *nushuz* (disobedience) and without ill treatment, he is not permitted to demand property from her.

**Second issue:** The scholars differed when both spouses want separation and there is *nushuz* and ill treatment from both sides. Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the husband may take property from her if she is the one who caused the separation, and his own causing of it is not taken into account. A group of scholars said: it is not permissible for him to take property unless she alone is at fault with *nushuz* and she asks for the separation on that basis.

**Third issue:** Allah's words, ﴿And you have given one of them a great amount (qintar)﴾, the verse. This is evidence for the permissibility of excess in dowries (*mughalah fi al-muhur*), because Allah does not give an example except with something permissible. Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, gave a sermon and said: "Beware! Do not exaggerate in the dowries of women. If it were a source of honour in this world or piety before Allah, the one most entitled to it would have been the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He never gave any of his wives or daughters a dowry exceeding twelve *uqiyyah*."

A woman stood up and said to him: "O Umar, Allah gives us and you deprive us! Does Allah, the Exalted, not say: ﴿And you have given one of them a great amount, do not take anything from it﴾?"

Umar said: "A woman was right and Umar was wrong."

In another report: "Umar lowered his head and then said: 'Every person is more knowledgeable than you, O Umar!'"

In another: "A woman was right and a man was wrong." And he abandoned the objection.

Abu Hatim al-Busti reported it in his *Sahih Musnad*, from Abu al-Ajfa al-Sulami, who said: Umar addressed the people, and he mentioned it up to his words "twelve *uqiyyah*," but he did not mention "a woman stood up to him," to the end.

Ibn Majah also reported it in his *Sunan*, from Abu al-Ajfa, and he added after his words "*uqiyyah*": "A man burdens his wife with the dowry until she develops resentment toward him in his heart, and he says: 'I have strained myself for you until the *alaq* of the waterskin, or the *araq* of the waterskin.' And I was an Arab *muwallad* (a man of mixed or later Arab lineage), I do not know what *alaq al-qirbah* or *araq al-qirbah* is."

Al-Jawhari said: "*Alaq al-qirbah* is a dialectal variant of *araq al-qirbah*." Another said: "It is said that *alaq al-qirbah* is its *isam*, the thing by which it is hung. He means: 'I strained myself for you even to the *isam* of the waterskin.' And *araq al-qirbah* is its water. He means: 'I endured hardship for you until I travelled and needed the water of the waterskin, which is its water during travel.' It is also said: *araq al-qirbah* is that he says: 'I toiled and exerted myself for you until I sweated the sweat of the waterskin,' which is its flowing."

It was also said: they used to carry water on camels, hanging it on them and taking turns with it, and this caused hardship and strain on the back. So the two terms were explained by this: *al-araq* and *al-alaq*.

Al-Asmai said: "*Araq al-qirbah* is an expression meaning hardship." He said: "I do not know its origin." Al-Asmai also said: "I heard Ibn Abi Tarafah, who was among the most eloquent people I have seen, say: 'I heard our shaykhs say: I met from so-and-so *araq al-qirbah*,' meaning hardship."

He recited to me a verse by Ibn al-Ahmar:

*It is not an insult that is counted, and its pardon*
*is the sweat of the waterskin on the weary riding-camel.*

Abu Ubayd said: he meant that a man hears a word that angers him, and it is not an insult for which the speaker can be held to account. "And I have brought it to him like the sweat of the waterskin." Then he said "like the sweat of the waterskin" because he could not complete the verse with it. Then he said "on the weary riding-camel," and its meaning is that the waterskin is hung on the riding-camel during their journeys.

This meaning resembles what al-Farra used to narrate. He claimed that they were in the desert on their journeys, carrying water and hanging it on camels, taking turns with it, and this involved fatigue and hardship on the back. Al-Farra used to render this explanation of *alaq al-qirbah* with the letter *lam*.

Some people said: the verse does not indicate the permissibility of excess in dowries, because the example of the *qintar* is by way of exaggeration, as if He said: "And you have given this enormous amount which no one gives." This is like the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever builds a mosque for Allah, even as small as the nest of a sand-grouse (*mafhas qatah*), Allah will build for him a house in Paradise." It is known that there is no mosque as small as a sand-grouse's nest.

The Prophet (ﷺ) also said to Ibn Abi Hadrad, when he came asking him for help with his dowry. He asked him about it and he said: "Two hundred." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) became angry and said: "It is as if you were quarrying gold and silver from the side of a *harrah* or a mountain." (*Harrah*: land of black, crumbling stones.)

Some people deduced from this a prohibition of excess in dowries. This does not follow. The Prophet's (ﷺ) rebuke of this man who was marrying was not a rebuke because of excess and extravagance in dowries. Rather, the rebuke was because he was poor at that time, and so he brought himself to need help and asking. This is disliked by consensus.

Umar gave Umm Kulthum, daughter of Ali and Fatimah, may Allah be pleased with them all, a dowry of forty thousand dirhams.

Abu Dawud reported from Uqbah ibn Amir that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to a man: "Are you content that I marry you to so-and-so?" He said: "Yes." And he said to the woman: "Are you content that I marry you to so-and-so?" She said: "Yes." So he married one of them to the other, and the man consummated the marriage with her, but he had not set a dowry for her and had not given her anything. He was among those who witnessed al-Hudaybiyah, and he had a share at Khaybar. When death came to him, he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) married me to so-and-so, but I did not set a dowry for her and did not give her anything. I call you to witness that I have now given her from her dowry my share at Khaybar." So she took his share and sold it for one hundred thousand.

The scholars have agreed that there is no limit on the highest dowry, based on Allah's words: ﴿And you have given one of them a great amount﴾. They differed concerning the minimum, and this will come at His words: ﴿that you seek with your wealth﴾.

The discussion of the *qintar* as a quantity was already presented at (Al-Imran; see vol. 4, p. 30).

Ibn Muhaysin recited ﴿wa-ataytum ihdahunna﴾ with *wasl* (connecting) the *alif* of *ihdahunna*, and this is a dialect. From it is the saying of the poet:

*And you hear from beneath the dust-cloud its *azmal* (sound)*

And the saying of another:

*If I do not fight, then cover me with a face-veil.*

**Fourth issue:** Allah's words, ﴿then do not take from it anything﴾. Bakr ibn Abd Allah al-Muzani said: the husband may not take anything from a wife who seeks *khul'* (divorce by compensation), based on Allah's words, ﴿do not take﴾, and he considered it abrogating (*nasikhah*) the verse of al-Baqarah.

Ibn Zayd and others said: it is abrogated (*mansukhah*) by His words in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿And it is not lawful for you to take anything of what you have given them﴾. (See vol. 3, p. 136.)

The correct view is that these verses are definitive (*muhkamah*), and there is no abrogating or abrogated element in them, and all of them build upon one another. Al-Tabari said: they are definitive. There is no sense in Bakr's statement, since if she gives the compensation voluntarily, the Prophet (ﷺ) permitted Thabit to take back from his wife what he had given her.

*Buhtanan* is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*). *Wa-ithman* is coordinated with it. *Mubinan* is an attribute of it (*min na't-hi*).

(*Aybah*: a leather bag used for carrying harvested crops to the threshing ground, and for holding garments.)

2. It is not fixed except by consummation.

4. A distinction between his house and her house.

The correct view is that it is fixed by seclusion in general. This is the view of Abu Hanifah and his companions. They said: if he is alone with her in a valid seclusion, the full dowry and the *iddah* (waiting period) become obligatory, whether he consummated with her or not. This is based on what al-Daraqutni reported from Thawban, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever uncovers the veil of a woman and looks at her, the dowry becomes obligatory."

Umar said: "If he closes a door and lets down a curtain and sees her private parts, the dowry becomes obligatory, and she must observe the *iddah*, and she has the inheritance."

**Sixth issue:** Allah's words, ﴿And they have taken from you a solemn covenant﴾. There are three views concerning it.

- It is his, peace be upon him, saying: "Fear Allah regarding women, for you have taken them under the trust of Allah, and you have made their private parts lawful by the word of Allah." This was said by Ikrimah and al-Rabi.
- The second: Allah's words, ﴿then either keep them in kindness or release them with goodness﴾. This was said by al-Hasan, Ibn Sirin, Qatadah, al-Dahhak and al-Suddi.
- The third: the bond of marriage, which is a man's saying: "I have married and possessed through the bond of marriage." This was said by Mujahid and Ibn Zayd.

Some people said: the solemn covenant is the child.

And Allah knows best.

**First issue: the prohibition in ﴿And do not marry what your fathers married of women﴾.** It is said that people used to marry their father's wife with her consent, until the verse ﴿O you who believe, it is not lawful for you to inherit women against their will﴾ was revealed. Then this verse was revealed: "And do not marry what your fathers married." It thereby became forbidden in all circumstances, because *nikah* (marriage, a term that covers both contracting marriage and sexual intercourse) applies to both. If the father married a woman or had intercourse with her without a marriage contract, she becomes forbidden to his son, as will be explained later, God willing.

**Second issue: the meaning of ﴿mā nakaḥa﴾ (what they married).** It has been said that it refers to the women. It has also been said that it refers to the contract, meaning the corrupt marriages of your fathers that contradict the religion of God, since God has perfected the form of marriage and detailed its conditions. This is the view chosen by al-Ṭabarī (the exegete). According to this reading, *min* (of) is connected to *tankiḥū* (marry), and *mā nakaḥa* is a verbal noun (masdar). He said: "If its meaning were 'do not marry the women whom your fathers married,' the position of *mā* would have to be *man* (whoever)." Accordingly, the prohibition falls only on marrying the same kind of corrupt marriage that their fathers contracted. The first view, however, is more sound, and *mā* then means *alladhī* (which) and *man* (whoever). The evidence for this is that the Companions understood the verse in that sense, and from it they derived the prohibition on sons marrying their fathers' wives.

Among the Arabs there were tribes that were accustomed to a son succeeding his father in marriage to his wife, and this custom was binding among the Anṣār, while among the Quraysh it was permitted by mutual consent. Do you not see that ʿAmr ibn Umayya married his father's wife after his death, and she bore him Musāfir and Abū Muʿayṭ? She had also borne children to Umayya, including Abū al-ʿĪṣ and others, so the sons of Umayya were the brothers of Musāfir and Abū Muʿayṭ and their paternal uncles.

From this practice: Ṣafwān ibn Umayya ibn Khalaf married, after his father's death, his wife Fākhita bint al-Aswad ibn al-Muṭṭalib ibn Asad, and Umayya had been killed leaving her behind. Also from this: Manẓūr ibn Zabbān married Mulayka bint Khārija, who had been under his father Zabbān ibn Sayyār. Also from this: Ḥiṣn ibn Abī Qays married his father's wife Kubayša bint Maʿn. And al-Aswad ibn Khalaf married his father's wife.

Al-Ashʿath ibn Sawwār said: Abū Qays died, and he had been one of the righteous Anṣār. His son Qays then proposed to his father's wife. She said: "I regard you as a son, but I will go to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to consult him." She went to him and informed him, and God revealed this verse.

Among the Arabs there was also someone who married his daughter, namely Ḥājib ibn Zurāra, who became a Magian and committed this act. Al-Naḍr ibn Shumayl mentioned this in his book *al-Mathālib*. God therefore forbade the believers what their fathers had practised of this custom.

**Third issue: ﴿illā mā qad salaf﴾ (except what has already passed).** *Salaf* means what has gone before and passed. *Salaf* also means those of your forefathers and kin who preceded you. This is a discontinuous exception (*istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ*), meaning: "But what has already passed, leave it and abandon it." It has also been said that *illā* here means *baʿda* (after), meaning "after what has passed," as God says: ﴿They will not taste death therein except the first death﴾, meaning after the first death. It has also been said that *illā mā qad salaf* means *wa-lā mā salaf* (and not what has passed), as in His saying: ﴿It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake﴾, meaning "nor by mistake." It has also been said that the verse contains inversion (*taqdīm wa-taʾkhīr*), its meaning being: "Do not marry what your fathers married of women; indeed it was an abomination and a hatred and an evil way, except what has already passed." It has also been said that the verse contains an implied clause (*iḍmār*) relating to ﴿And do not marry what your fathers married of women﴾: if you do so, you will be punished and held to account, except for what has already passed.

**Fourth issue: ﴿innahu kāna fāḥisha wa-maqtan wa-sāʾa sabīlā﴾ (indeed it was an abomination and a hatred and an evil way).** He followed it with severe and successive censure, which is evidence that it is an act that has reached the extreme of ugliness. Abū al-ʿAbbās said: "I asked Ibn al-Aʿrābī about *nikāḥ al-maqt* (the marriage of hatred), and he said: it is when a man marries his father's wife after divorcing her or after his death. This man is called *al-ḍayzan* (one who competes with his father for his wife)." Ibn ʿArafa said: "When an Arab man married his father's wife and she bore him a child, the child was called *al-maqtī*." The root of *maqt* is hatred, from *maqatahu yamqutuhu maqtan*, so he is *mamqūt* and *maqīt*. The Arabs used to call the son of a man by his father's wife *maqīt*, and God named this marriage *maqt* because it is a hatred that befalls its doer.

It has also been said that the verse means the prohibition of a man having intercourse with a woman whom his fathers had intercourse with, except what has already passed of the fathers' fornication with women in the Jahiliyya, not in the manner of lawful marriage; for their marriage to such women is permitted to you. And that you may lawfully marry, by a contract of marriage, those whom your fathers had illicitly had intercourse with: this was said by Ibn Zayd. According to this reading, the exception is a continuous one (*istithnāʾ muttaṣil*), and it is a basis for the view that fornication does not make a woman forbidden, as will be explained later.

And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verse 23 (part 1 of 4):

There are twenty-one issues in this verse. The first: His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers and your daughters﴾ to the end of the verse. That is, marrying your mothers and marrying your daughters. In this verse God the Exalted mentions which women are lawful and which are unlawful, as He mentioned the prohibition of the wife of the father. God has forbidden seven by lineage, and six by suckling and affinity [[In another manuscript: "from among suckling"]]. The widely transmitted Sunnah added a seventh, which is combining a woman with her paternal aunt, and the consensus explicitly confirmed it. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Seven are forbidden by lineage and seven by affinity," and he recited this verse. 'Amr ibn Salim, mawla of the Ansar, said the same, and said: the seventh is His saying: ﴿and the married women﴾. The seven forbidden by lineage are: mothers, daughters, sisters, paternal aunts, maternal aunts, daughters of a brother, and daughters of a sister.
The seven forbidden by affinity and suckling are: mothers by suckling, sisters by suckling, mothers of wives, stepdaughters [[al-raba'ib: singular rabibah, the rabibah of a man is the daughter of his wife from another husband.]], wives of sons, combining two sisters, and the seventh: (and do not marry what your fathers married). Al-Tahawi said: all of this is from the clear (muhkam) and agreed-upon matters, and marrying any one of them is not permitted by consensus, except the mothers of wives with whom their husbands have not consummated the marriage. For the majority of the early scholars held that the mother becomes forbidden by the contract upon the daughter, and the daughter becomes forbidden only by consummation with the mother; and this is the view of the majority of the leading jurists in the regions. A group of the early scholars said: the mother and the stepdaughter are equal; neither of the two becomes forbidden except by consummation with the other. They said: the meaning of His saying: (and the mothers of your wives) is: those with whom you have consummated.
(and your stepdaughters who are in your guardianship, born of your wives with whom you have consummated). They claimed that the condition of consummation applies to both the mothers and the stepdaughters. This was transmitted by Khilas [[Khilas (with a kasra on the kha and light lam): Ibn 'Amr al-Hajari.]] from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib. It is also related from Ibn 'Abbas, Jabir and Zayd ibn Thabit, and it is the view of Ibn al-Zubayr and Mujahid. Mujahid said: consummation is intended in both cases. The view of the majority differs from this, and it is upon this that the ruling and the legal opinion rest. The people of Iraq were strict in this matter to the point that they said: if he had intercourse with her unlawfully, or kissed her, or touched her with desire, her daughter becomes forbidden to him. According to us and according to al-Shafi'i, it is only forbidden by a valid marriage, and the unlawful does not make the lawful unlawful, as will come. The hadith of Khilas from 'Ali is not a basis for proof, and its transmission is not sound according to the people of hadith scholarship; the sound report from him is like the view of the majority. Ibn Jurayj said: I said to 'Ata': "A man marries a woman, then does not see her and does not have intercourse with her until he divorces her, or until her mother becomes lawful to him?" He said: "No, she is unconditional, whether he consummated or did not consummate." I said to him: "Did Ibn 'Abbas read: (and the mothers of your wives with whom you have consummated)?" He said: "No, no." Sa'id related from Qatada from 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: (and the mothers of your wives), he said: "They are unspecified (mubhamah); they become forbidden by the contract upon the daughter." Likewise Malik related in his Muwatta' from Zayd ibn Thabit, in which: "Zayd said: 'No, the mother is unspecified [without a condition [[addition from the Muwatta']]], and the condition applies only to the stepdaughters.'" Ibn al-Mundhir said: this is the sound view, because all mothers of wives are included in His saying: (and the mothers of your wives). This view is supported grammatically: when two predicates differ in their governing element, their qualifier cannot be the same. The grammarians do not permit: "I passed by your women, and I fled from the women of Zayd, the charming ones," with "the charming ones" as a qualifier of both your women and the women of Zayd. Likewise in the verse, (allati) cannot be a qualifier of both together, because the two predicates differ; but it is permitted in the sense of "I mean" (a'ni). Al-Khalil and Sibawayh recited:
Indeed there are with her Akal or Rizam ...
two Khuwayribayn who crush the skulls
"Khuwayribayn" means two thieves, in the sense of "I mean." "Yanqufan" means they break; naqafta ra'sahu means I broke his head. It has also come explicitly from the hadith of 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb from his father from his grandfather from the Prophet ﷺ: "If a man marries a woman, it is not lawful for him to marry her mother, whether he consummated with the daughter or not. And if he marries the mother and does not consummate with her, then divorces her, he may marry the daughter." Recorded by [[In another manuscript: Muslim recorded it.]] in the two Sahihs.

The second: When this is established and confirmed, know that prohibition is not a attribute of the things themselves, and things are neither the locus nor the source of lawfulness and unlawfulness. Rather, legal obligation attaches to the commands and prohibitions concerning the actions of the responsible persons, of movement and stillness. But since things are the locus of actions, the command, prohibition and ruling are attributed to them and linked to them figuratively, in the sense of metonymy, by naming the locus instead of the act that takes place in it.

The third: His saying: ﴿your mothers﴾. The prohibition of mothers is general in every case and is not restricted in any respect. For this reason the scholars call it "the unspecified" (al-mubham), meaning there is no door to it and no path to it, because the prohibition is closed and firm. The same applies to the prohibition of daughters, sisters, and those mentioned among the forbidden. "Ummahat" is the plural of "ummah"; it is said umm and ummah with the same meaning, and the Qur'an came with both. Its explanation was given before in al-Fatihah [[See vol. 1, p. 112.]]. It is said that the original of umm is ummah, on the pattern fu''alah like qubbarah and hummarah for two birds, and it was dropped and returned in the plural. The poet said:
My mothers are Khindif, and al-Dawas is my father
It is also said that the origin of al-umm is ummah, and they recited:
I accepted her from a people of yours who for long
returned to them in calamities, all together.
Its plural is ummat. The poet al-Ra'i said:
The swift camels of Mundhir and Muharriq were
their mothers, and their stallions were fine.
So umm is a name for every female to whom you owe birth. It includes the mother of your mother (dunyah) [[It is said: he is my cousin dunyah and dunya, with or without tanwin, and dunya with a damma and shortened vowel when he is a close cousin, i.e., closely related by lineage.]], her mothers, her grandmothers, the father's mother and his grandmothers, however high they ascend. Bint is a name for every female to whom you have a birth-relation. If you wish, you may say: every female whose lineage returns to you by birth, by one degree or more. This includes the daughter of the loins, her daughters, the daughters of sons, however low they descend. Ukht is a name for every female who shares with you both your roots or one of them. Banat is the plural of bint; the original is bunayyah, and the usage is ibnah and bint. Al-Farra' said: the ba' of bint was given a kasra so that the kasra would indicate the ya', and the alif of ukht was given a damma to indicate the dropped waw, since the original of ukht is akhawah, and the plural is akhawat. "Ammah" is a name for every female who shares with your father or your grandfather his roots or one of them. If you wish, you may say: every male whose lineage returns to you, his sister is your paternal aunt. The paternal aunt may also be on the mother's side, being the sister of your mother's father. "Khalah" is a name for every female who shares with your mother her roots or one of them. If you wish, you may say: every female whose lineage returns to you by birth, her sister is your maternal aunt. The maternal aunt may also be on the father's side, being the sister of your father's mother. "Bint al-akh" is a name for every female to whom your brother has a birth-relation, directly or through an intermediary; likewise bint al-ukht. These are the seven forbidden by lineage. Nafi', in the transmission of Abu Bakr ibn Abi Uways, read with shadda on the kha' of "al-akh" when the alif and lam are present, with transfer of the vowel.

The fourth: His saying: ﴿and your mothers who have suckled you﴾. It is in prohibition like those we mentioned. The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "What is forbidden by lineage is forbidden by suckling." 'Abd Allah read (wa-ummahatukumu al-lai) without a ta', as in His saying: (wa-allai ya'isna min al-mahid [[See vol. 18, p. 162.]]). The poet said:
Of those who have not performed pilgrimage, seeking reward, but rather that they might kill the innocent, the heedless.
(arda'nakum). When a woman suckles a child, she becomes forbidden to him, because she is his mother; her daughter, because she is his sister; her sister, because she is his maternal aunt; her mother, because she is his grandmother; the daughter of her husband, the owner of the milk, because she is his sister; her sister, because she is his paternal aunt; his mother, because she is his grandmother; and the daughters of her sons and daughters, because they are the daughters of his brothers and sisters.

The fifth: Abu Nu'aym 'Ubayd Allah ibn Hisham al-Halabi said: Malik was asked about a woman: may her brother by suckling perform the pilgrimage with her? He said: Yes. Abu Nu'aym said: Malik was also asked about a woman who married, and her husband consummated with her. Then a woman came and claimed that she had suckled both of them. He said: they shall be separated, and what she took from him is hers, and what remains on him, he owes nothing. Then Malik said: the Prophet ﷺ was asked about the like of this and ruled accordingly. They said: "O Messenger of God, she is a weak woman." The Prophet ﷺ said: "Is it not said that so-and-so married his sister?"

The sixth: Prohibition by suckling occurs only when the suckling takes place within the two years, as has passed in (al-Baqarah [[See vol. 3, p. 161.]]). With us there is no difference between little and much suckling, provided it reaches the intestines, even a single sucking. Al-Shafi'i required two conditions for suckling: the first, five feedings, based on the hadith of 'A'ishah who said: "Among what God sent down were ten known feedings that make prohibition; then they were abrogated by five known feedings, and the Messenger of God ﷺ died while they were among what is recited from the Qur'an." The point of the evidence from it is that she established that the ten were abrogated by five, so if prohibition attached to less than five, that would be an abrogation of the five. Neither a single report nor analogy is accepted against this, because it is not abrogated by them. In the hadith of Sahlah [[She is Sahlah bint Suhayl, wife of Abu Hudhayfah ibn 'Utbah. Abu Hudhayfah had adopted (Salim), the mawla of Abu Hudhayfah, and she came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "O Messenger of God, we used to regard Salim as a son, and he would enter upon me while I was in a single garment, and we have only one room." The Messenger, peace be upon him, said to her: "Suckle him ... etc." See the Muwatta'.]]: (suckle him five feedings, by which prohibition is established). The second condition: that it be within the two years. If it is beyond them, it does not make prohibition, because of His saying: (two complete years for whoever wishes to complete the suckling [[See vol. 3, p. 160.]]). After completion and perfection there is nothing. Abu Hanifah considered six months beyond the two years. Malik considered a month or so. Zufar said: as long as he is sustained by milk and has not been weaned, it is suckling, even if three years pass over him. Al-Awza'i said: if he is weaned at a year and his weaning is firm, there is no suckling after it. Al-Layth ibn Sa'd stood alone

...from among the scholars, to the view that suckling as an adult (rada' al-kabir) establishes the prohibition of marriage. This is the view of Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her. It is also reported from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, but there is also a report from him that indicates he retracted this view. This is what Abu Husayn related from Abu 'Atiyya, who said: A man came from Medina with his wife, and she gave birth, and her breast swelled. He began to suck it and spit it out, and a mouthful of it entered his stomach. He asked Abu Musa, who said: "She has become unlawful to you (bant minka). Go to Ibn Mas'ud and inform him." He did so, and Ibn Mas'ud came with the Bedouin to Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and said: "Do you consider this gray-haired man (al-ashmat) [[al-shamt: whiteness of the hair of the head mixed with its blackness. It was also said: the beard.]] a suckling child? Only what makes flesh and bone grow is prohibited by suckling." Al-Ash'ari said: "Do not ask me about anything while this scholar is among you." His saying "Do not ask me" indicates that he retracted that view.

Aisha argued from the story of Salim, the freed slave of Abu Hudhayfa, who was a grown man. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to Sahla bint Suhayl: "Suckle him." This was transmitted by al-Muwatta' and others. A group deviated and took ten sucklings as the criterion, relying on the fact that among what was revealed was: "ten sucklings." It seems they had not received the abrogating text (al-nasikh, the text that abrogates, i.e., naskh).

Dawud (al-Zahiri) said: It is not prohibited except by three sucklings, and he relied on the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "A single suckling or two sucklings do not make prohibited" [[al-imlaja: a single instance of suckling. It means that a single sip or two sips do not establish the prohibition that complete suckling establishes.]]. Muslim related it. This is also transmitted from Aisha and Ibn al-Zubayr, and Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu Thawr and Abu Ubayd also held this view. It is a reliance on dalil al-khitab (the argument from implication of speech), which is disputed.

The rest of the jurists (a'immat al-fatwa) held that a single suckling establishes the prohibition once it is confirmed, as we mentioned, relying on the minimum that the term "suckling" applies to. This was strengthened by the practice found in Medina and by analogy to in-law relations (al-sihr), on the basis that it is a supervening meaning that requires the permanence of the prohibition, so a number is not stipulated for it, like in-law relations.

Al-Layth ibn Sa'd said: The Muslims agreed that a little or a lot of suckling establishes the prohibition in infancy, in what breaks the fast of the one fasting. Abu Umar (Ibn Abd al-Barr) said: Al-Layth was not aware of disagreement on this matter.

I say: The most explicit text in this chapter is his (ﷺ) saying: "A single sip does not make prohibited, nor do two sips," which Muslim recorded in his Sahih. It explains the meaning of His Exalted saying: ﴿And your mothers who have suckled you﴾, that is, who suckled you three sucklings or more. However, it is possible to apply it to the case where the arrival of the milk into the infant's stomach is not confirmed, based on His saying: "ten known sucklings, and five known sucklings." So describing them as "known" is only a precaution against what might be suspected or doubted to reach the stomach. The implication of this speech indicates that if the sucklings are not known, they do not establish the prohibition. And Allah knows best.

Al-Tahawi mentioned that the hadith of the single and double sucking does not hold, because Ibn al-Zubayr sometimes narrates it from the Prophet (ﷺ), sometimes from Aisha, and sometimes from his father, and such inconsistency causes it to be dropped. It is also reported from Aisha that only seven sucklings establish the prohibition. And it is reported from her that she ordered her sister Umm Kulthum to have Salim ibn Abd Allah suckle ten times. The same was reported from Hafsa, and it was reported from her (three), and it was reported from her (five), as al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said; and it is related from Ishaq.

The seventh issue: His Exalted saying: ﴿And your mothers who have suckled you﴾. It is used as evidence by those who deny the milk of the stallion (labam al-fahl), namely Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and Abu Salama ibn Abd al-Rahman. They said: The milk of the stallion does not establish any prohibition on the side of the man. The majority said: His Exalted saying ﴿And your mothers who have suckled you﴾ indicates that the stallion is a father, because the milk is attributed to him, since it flowed because of his offspring. This is weak, for the child was created from the water of both the man and the woman, while the milk is from the woman and did not come out of the man. What comes from the man is only intercourse, which is the cause of the water being released from him. When the child is weaned, Allah creates the milk without it being attributed to the man in any way; for this reason the man has no right to the milk, the milk belongs only to her. So it is not possible to derive this from analogy with the water. And the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "What is prohibited by blood relation is prohibited by suckling" requires prohibition through suckling, and the connection of suckling to the man does not appear as clearly as the connection of the water to him and suckling from her. Yes, the basis for this is the hadith of al-Zuhri and Hisham ibn Urwa, from Urwa, from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her: that Aflah, brother of Abu al-Qu'ays, came asking permission to enter upon her, and he was her uncle through suckling, after the veil had been revealed. She said: "I refused to allow him in. When the Prophet (ﷺ) came, I informed him, and he said: 'Let him enter upon you, for he is your uncle; may your right hand be dust-covered.'" Abu al-Qu'ays was the husband of the woman who had suckled Aisha, and this too is a single report (khabar wahid). It is possible that Aflah was a foster-brother (rada'i labān) with Abu Bakr, and that is why he said: "Let him enter upon you, for he is your uncle."

In summary, the matter is problematic and knowledge is with Allah, but the practice is according to it, and caution in prohibition is preferable. Moreover, His Exalted saying: ﴿And lawful for you is what is beyond that﴾ strengthens the view of the opponent.

The eighth issue: His Exalted saying: ﴿And your sisters through suckling﴾. This refers to the sister by both father and mother, namely the one whom your mother suckled with your father's milk, whether she suckled her with you, or was born before you or after you. The sister by father only, not by mother, is the one whom your father's wife suckled. The sister by mother only, not by father, is the one whom your mother suckled with the milk of another man. Then He mentioned prohibition through marriage-alliance (al-musaharah), saying: ﴿And the mothers of your wives﴾. The relations by marriage are four: the wife's mother, her daughter, the father's wife, and the son's wife. The wife's mother is prohibited to her daughter's husband by the mere valid contract, as has been mentioned before.

The ninth issue: His Exalted saying: ﴿And your stepdaughters who are in your guardianship, born of your wives with whom you have consummated marriage﴾. This is independent in itself. His saying "born of your wives with whom you have consummated marriage" does not refer to the first group, but refers to the stepdaughters, since it is the nearest mentioned, as has been mentioned before. The rabība (stepdaughter) is the daughter of a man's wife from another man; she was named so because he raises her in his lap, so she is marbūba, on the pattern fa'īla in the sense of maf'ūla. The jurists agreed that a stepdaughter is prohibited to her mother's husband if he has consummated the marriage with the mother, even if the stepdaughter is not in his guardianship. Some earlier scholars and the Ahl al-Zahir (literalists) deviated, saying: The stepdaughter is not prohibited to him unless she is in the guardianship of the one who married her mother. So if she is in another city and he separates from the mother after consummation, he may marry her. They argued from the verse: "Allah prohibited the stepdaughter on two conditions: first, that she be in the guardianship of the one who married her mother; second, consummation with the mother. If either condition is absent, the prohibition does not arise." They argued with his (ﷺ) saying: "If my stepdaughter were not in my guardianship, she would not be lawful for me; she is the daughter of my brother through suckling," thus making guardianship a condition. They related from Ali ibn Abi Talib a permission for this. Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Tahawi said: As for the report from Ali, it does not hold, for its transmitter is Ibrahim ibn Ubayd from Malik ibn Aws from Ali, and this Ibrahim is known, and most people of knowledge have rejected it and disagreed with it. Abu Ubayd said: What repels it is his saying: "Do not present to me your daughters or your sisters," where he used the general term and did not say "those in my guardianship," but made them equal in prohibition. Al-Tahawi said: Their attribution to guardianship is only according to what is most common for stepdaughters, not that they are not prohibited when they are not in such a condition.

The tenth issue: His Exalted saying: ﴿But if you have not consummated marriage with them﴾, meaning with the mothers. ﴿Then there is no blame upon you﴾, meaning in marrying their daughters if you have divorced them or they have died before you. The scholars agreed that if a man marries a woman then divorces her or she dies before he consummates with her, it is lawful for him to marry her daughter. They differed concerning the meaning of consummation with the mothers that establishes the prohibition of stepdaughters. Ibn Abbas was reported to have said: Consummation is intercourse; this is also the view of Tawus, Amr ibn Dinar and others. Malik, al-Thawri, Abu Hanifa, al-Awza'i and al-Layth agreed that if he touches her with desire, her mother and her daughter become prohibited to him, and they become prohibited to the father and the son; this is one of the two views of al-Shafi'i. They differed regarding looking. Malik said: If he looks at her hair, her chest, or any of her attractive parts with desire, her mother and her daughter become prohibited to him. The Kufans said: If he looks at her private part with desire, it is like touching with desire. Al-Thawri said: [It becomes prohibited [[the addition from al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit) of Abu Hayyan.]] if he looks at her private part deliberately or touches her, and he did not mention desire. Ibn Abi Layla said: It is not prohibited by looking until he touches, and this is also the view of al-Shafi'i. The evidence that prohibition occurs by looking is that it involves a kind of enjoyment, so it takes the status of marriage, since rulings are attached to meanings, not to words. It may also be said that it is a kind of union through enjoyment, for looking is a meeting and encounter, and among lovers there is enjoyment in it, and poets have exaggerated this, saying:

"Does not the night gather Umm Amr
and us, so that by it we draw near?"

"Yes, and you see the crescent as I see it,
and the day rises over her as it rises over me."

So how about looking, sitting together, conversing and pleasure?

The eleventh issue: His Exalted saying: ﴿And the wives of your sons﴾. Al-Ha'il is the plural of halīla, which means wife. She was named halīla because she "alights" (taḥullu) with the husband wherever he alights. It is on the pattern fa'īla in the sense of fā'ila. Al-Zajjaj and a group went to the view that it derives from the word ḥalāl (lawful), so it is halīla in the sense of muḥallala (made lawful). It was also said: because each of them unties (yaḥillu) the other's waistwrap.

The twelfth issue: The scholars agreed on the prohibition of what fathers have contracted for sons, and what sons have contracted for fathers, whether or not intercourse occurred, because of His saying: ﴿And do not marry what your fathers married of women﴾ and His saying: ﴿And the wives of your sons who are from your loins﴾. If one of them contracts an invalid marriage, the contract with her becomes prohibited for the other just as it is prohibited by a valid one, because an invalid marriage is of two kinds: either it is agreed to be invalid or it is disputed. If it is agreed to be invalid, it establishes no ruling, and its existence is like its non-existence. If it is disputed, then the prohibition attaches to it as it does to a valid one, because it may be a marriage, so it falls under the general wording. When prohibition and permission conflict regarding private parts, prohibition prevails. And Allah knows best.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: All scholars of the regions whose opinions are preserved agreed that if a man has intercourse with a woman in an invalid marriage, she becomes prohibited to his father, his son, his grandfathers and his grandsons.

**Thirteenth issue:** The scholars agreed that a contract of purchase for a slave-girl does not make her forbidden to the buyer's father or son. If a man buys a slave-girl and then touches or kisses her, she becomes forbidden to his father and son. I know of no disagreement on this, so it is obligatory to affirm this prohibition, in deference to them.

Since they differed over whether she becomes forbidden through looking alone, without touching, that is not permissible, because of their disagreement.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: "No report from any of the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) contradicts what we have said."

Ya'qub and Muhammad said: "If a man looks at a woman's private part out of desire, she becomes forbidden to his father and son, and her mother and daughter become forbidden to him."

Malik said: "If he has intercourse with the slave-girl, or sits with her in a position for that purpose even if he does not penetrate her, or kisses her, or caresses her, or squeezes her for pleasure, then she is not lawful to his son."

Al-Shafi'i said: "She is forbidden only by touching, not by looking without touching." This is also the view of al-Awza'i.

**Fourteenth issue:** They differed over whether intercourse through unlawful sexual relations (zina) creates a prohibition. Most scholars said: "If a man has intercourse with a woman through zina, it does not make marriage to her forbidden to him, and likewise his wife does not become forbidden to him if he commits zina with her mother or her daughter. It is enough for him that the prescribed punishment (hadd) be carried out on him, and then he may consummate marriage with his wife." [[Note in the edition: "his wife" — the apparent reading is "who contracted and did not consummate."]]

And if a man commits zina with a woman and then wishes to marry her mother or her daughter, the two are not forbidden to him on that account.

A group said: "She is forbidden to him." This view is reported from Imran ibn Husayn, and al-Sha'bi, 'Ata', al-Hasan, Sufyan al-Thawri, Ahmad, Ishaq and the people of opinion (ahl al-ra'y) said the same. It is also reported from Malik that zina makes the mother and the daughter forbidden, and that it is equal to lawful intercourse. This is the view of the people of Iraq.

The sound view of Malik and the people of the Hijaz is that zina has no legal effect, because God, glorified and exalted, said: ﴿and your mothers-in-law﴾, and the woman he committed zina with is not the mother of his wives, nor is her daughter one of his stepdaughters (rabā'ib). This is also the view of al-Shafi'i and Abu Thawr.

Because when the bride-price (sadaq), the waiting period ('idda), inheritance, the rights of the child, and the requirement of the prescribed punishment are all set aside in zina, it follows that it cannot be ruled to have the legal effect of a valid marriage.

Al-Daraqutni reported from the hadith of al-Zuhri, from 'Urwa, from 'A'isha, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was asked about a man who committed zina with a woman and then wished to marry her or her daughter, and he said: "What is unlawful does not make lawful unlawful; only what is by marriage makes unlawful." (Hadith: "Haram does not make halal haram; only what is by nikah makes haram.")

Among the proof for the other view is the Prophet's (ﷺ) report about Juraij [[Juraij was one of the worshippers among the Children of Israel. They accused him of zina, and God made him see a boy speak, saying that he was the son of the shepherd who had committed zina with his mother. See vol. 2 of Ibn Kathir's History, p. 134 onward.]] and his statement: "O boy, who is your father?" He said: "So-and-so the shepherd."

This indicates that zina makes prohibited just as lawful intercourse does, so the mother of the woman who was committed zina with is not lawful to the father or the sons of the one who committed zina, nor are her daughters. This is the narration of Ibn al-Qasim in the Mudawwana.

It is also used as evidence that a child created from the water of zina is not lawful to the one who committed zina with her mother, and this is the well-known view.

He, peace be upon him, said: "God does not look at a man who looks at the private part of a woman and her daughter." He did not distinguish between lawful and unlawful.

He, peace be upon him, also said: "God does not look at one who uncovers the veil of a woman and her daughter."

Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: "For this reason we say that kissing and all other forms of enjoyment spread the prohibition."

'Abd al-Malik al-Majishun said: "She is lawful, and this is the sound view, because of God, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And it is He who created man from water, then made him [a line of] lineage and marriage﴾, meaning through valid marriage, as its explanation will come in (al-Furqan [[See vol. 13, p. 59.]])."

The way of drawing evidence from the hadith on those two issues is that the Prophet (ﷺ) related from Juraij that he attributed the son of zina to the one who committed zina. God confirmed that attribution by breaking the normal course of nature, making the child speak and testify to it. The Prophet (ﷺ) reported this about Juraij in the context of praise and showing his honor.
