So that attribution was correct by God's confirmation and by the Prophet's (ﷺ) report of it, and therefore the filiation and its legal rulings are established.

If it is said: "Then it follows that the legal rulings of sonship and fatherhood would apply, such as inheritance, guardianship, and other matters, yet the Muslims have agreed that there is no inheritance between them. So how could that attribution be valid?"

The answer: That is a necessary consequence of what we have mentioned. Whatever ruling is established by consensus (ijma') we exclude, and what remains stays on the basis of that evidence. And God knows best.

**Fifteenth issue:** The scholars also differed on this subject concerning the one who commits sodomy (liwat). Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa and their followers said: "Marriage is not forbidden by sodomy."

Al-Thawri said: "If he plays with a boy, his mother becomes forbidden to him." This is also the view of Ahmad ibn Hanbal.

He said: "If he commits sodomy with the son of his wife, or her father, or her brother, his wife becomes forbidden to him."

Al-Awza'i said: "If he commits sodomy with a boy, and a daughter is born to the one who was sodomized, it is not permissible for the sinner to marry her, because she is the daughter of one with whom he had intercourse." This is also the view of Ahmad ibn Hanbal.

**Sixteenth issue:** God's statement: ﴿those [sons] who are from your loins﴾ is a restriction, to exclude everyone whom the Arabs used to adopt who was not from the loins.

When the Prophet (ﷺ) married the wife of Zayd ibn Harithah, the polytheists said: "He married the wife of his son!" The Prophet (ﷺ) had adopted him, as its explanation will come in (al-Ahzab [[See vol. 14, p. 188.]]).

The wife of a son by nursing (rada') becomes forbidden, even if the son is not from the loins, by consensus, based on the Prophet's (ﷺ) statement: "What is forbidden by lineage is forbidden by nursing."

**Seventeenth issue:** God's statement: ﴿and that you should combine two sisters﴾. The position of (fa-in) is in the nominative case, by coordination with ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾.

The term "two sisters" is a general word that includes all cases, whether by marriage or by ownership of the right hand (milk al-yamin).

The community agreed to prohibit combining the two in a single marriage contract, because of this verse, and because of the Prophet's (ﷺ) statement: "Do not offer me your daughters or your sisters."

They differed about two sisters held by right of ownership (milk al-yamin). Most scholars held that it is not permitted to combine the two in intercourse by ownership, although it is agreed that combining them in ownership is permitted. The same applies to a woman and her daughter in a single transaction.

They differed over a marriage contract with the sister of a slave-girl whom he has had intercourse with. Al-Awza'i said: "If he has intercourse with a slave-girl he owns, it is not permitted for him to marry her sister."

Al-Shafi'i said: "Ownership by right of the hand does not prevent marriage to the sister."

Abu 'Umar said: "Whoever treats the marriage contract like a purchase permits it, and whoever treats it like intercourse does not permit it."

They agreed that a contract with the sister of one's wife is not permitted, because of God's statement: ﴿and that you should combine two sisters﴾, meaning two wives by marriage contract.

So consider what they agreed upon and what they differed over, and the correct position will become clear to you, [if God wills].

And God knows best.

**Eighteenth issue:** The people of the outward meaning (Ahl al-Zahir) deviated and said: "It is permitted to combine two sisters held by right of ownership in intercourse, just as it is permitted to combine them in ownership."

They argued with what was reported from 'Uthman concerning two sisters held by right of the hand: "One verse forbade them, and another verse permitted them."

'Abd al-Razzaq mentioned it: Ma'mar related to us from al-Zuhri, from Qabisa ibn Dhu'ayb, that 'Uthman ibn 'Affan was asked about two sisters held by right of the hand, and he said: "I do not command you, nor forbid you. One verse permitted them, and one verse forbade them."

The questioner left and met a man from the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Ma'mar said: "I think he said 'Ali." He said: "What did you ask 'Uthman about?" He told him what he had asked and what 'Uthman had answered him. He said: "But I forbid you. If I had authority over you and you did it, I would make you an example (nakal)."

Al-Tahawi and al-Daraqutni also reported from 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas a view like 'Uthman's.

The verse that permitted them is God's statement: ﴿And lawful to you is what is beyond that﴾.

None of the leading jurists paid attention to this view, because they understood from the interpretation of God's Book something other than this, and it is not permissible to attribute distortion of the interpretation to them.

Among the Companions who held this view were: 'Umar, 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, ['Uthman, [[From edition Ṭ.]]] Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ammar, Ibn 'Umar, 'A'isha and Ibn al-Zubayr. These were the people of knowledge of God's Book, so whoever opposes them is over-strict in interpretation.

Ibn al-Mundhir mentioned that Ishaq ibn Rahawayh prohibited combining the two by intercourse, and that the majority of scholars disliked it, and he counted Malik among those who disliked it.

There is no disagreement on the permissibility of combining the two in ownership, and likewise a mother and her daughter.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It follows from Ishaq's view that whoever combines the two by intercourse should be stoned, and dislike can be inferred from Malik's view: that if he has intercourse with one, then with the other, he is held back from both until he forbids one of them. So he is not subjected to the prescribed punishment (hadd)."

Abu 'Umar said: "As for 'Ali's statement, 'I would make him an example,' he did not say 'I would apply to him the prescribed punishment for the fornicator.' This is because whoever interprets a verse or a Sunna and does not commit what he regards as unlawful is not a fornicator by consensus, even if he is mistaken, unless he claims what cannot be excused by ignorance."

The statement of some of the early generation about combining two sisters by right of ownership, "One verse permitted them and one verse forbade them," is well known and preserved. So how can one who did something with such a strong doubt be subjected to the punishment for fornication?

And success is from God.

**Nineteenth issue:** The scholars differed on the case where a man has intercourse with one woman and then wishes to have intercourse with the other. 'Ali, Ibn 'Umar, al-Hasan al-Basri, al-Awza'i, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Ishaq said: "It is not permitted for him to have intercourse with the second until the private part of the first is made unlawful to him, by removing her from his ownership by sale or manumission, or by marrying her off."

Ibn al-Mundhir said: "There is a second view from Qatada, that if he has intercourse with one and wishes to have intercourse with the other, he should intend to make the first unlawful to himself and not approach her, then refrain from both until he has cleansed the first, who is now forbidden, and then he may approach the second."

There is also a third view: that if he has two sisters, he should not approach either of them. This is what al-Hakam and Hammad said, and a similar meaning is reported from al-Nakha'i.

The view of Malik: If two sisters are held by ownership by a man, he may have intercourse with whichever he wishes, and restraint from the other is left to his trustworthiness. If he wishes to have intercourse with the other, he is obliged to make the first unlawful to himself by an act of removing her from ownership, either by marriage, sale, manumission for a set term, a writing of freedom (kitāba), or long service.

If he has intercourse with one of them and then jumps to the other without making the first unlawful, both are held back, and he may not approach either of them until he makes the other unlawful. This is not left to his trustworthiness, because he is suspected regarding the one he has already had intercourse with, and he was not suspect before, since he had only had intercourse with one.

The view of the Kufans on this subject:

Al-Thawri, Abu Hanifa and his companions held that if a man has intercourse with one of his two slave-women, he may not have intercourse with the other. If he sells the first or marries her off and she then returns to him, he refrains from the other. He may have intercourse with her while her sister is still within the waiting period (iddah) following a divorce or death, but after the waiting period has ended, he may not, until he owns the private part of the one with whom he has not had intercourse. The same meaning is narrated from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him.

They said: Because the ownership that prevented intercourse with the slave-woman at the outset still exists, there is no difference between her returning to him and her remaining in his ownership.

The view of Malik is sound, because it is a valid prohibition at the present moment, and it is not necessary to consider the property. It suffices that when her private part becomes forbidden to him through sale or marriage, she is forbidden to him at that moment.

They did not differ regarding manumission, because it cannot be disposed of in any way. As for the mukatabah (slave-woman under a contract of manumission), she may fail to fulfil the contract and so return to his ownership.

If a man has a slave-woman whom he has intercourse with, and then he marries her sister, there are three opinions on the marriage within the school of Malik. The third, in the Mudawwanah, is that the two are withheld from him when the marriage contract is concluded until he forbids one of them, with disapproval of this marriage, since it is a contract in a situation where intercourse is not permitted.

In this there is an indication that ownership by right of possession (milk al-yamin) does not prevent marriage, as has preceded from al-Shafi'i.

In the same matter there is another opinion: that the marriage is not concluded. This is the meaning of the view of al-Awza'i.

Ashhab said in the Kitab al-Istibra': the contract of marriage with the one is a prohibition on the private part of the slave-woman.

Twentieth: The scholars agreed that if a man divorces his wife with a divorce that allows him to take her back, he may not marry her sister or four others besides her until the waiting period of the divorced woman has ended. They differed where he divorced her with a divorce that does not allow him to take her back. One group said: he may not marry her sister or a fourth wife until the waiting period of the one he divorced has ended. This is narrated from Ali and Zayd ibn Thabit, and it is the view of Mujahid, Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, al-Nakha'i, Sufyan al-Thawri, Ahmad ibn Hanbal and the people of opinion (ashab al-ra'y).

Another group said: he may marry her sister and four others besides her. This is narrated from Ata', and it is the more established of the two reports from him. It is also narrated from Zayd ibn Thabit, and it was said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Hasan, al-Qasim, Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, Ibn Abi Layla, al-Shafi'i, Abu Thawr and Abu Ubayd.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: I do not think it is anything other than the view of Malik, and by it we say.

Twenty-first: The words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿except what has already passed﴾, may mean the same as His words (in another verse): "except what has already passed" in His words: "And do not marry women whom your fathers married, except what has already passed."

It may also carry an additional meaning, which is the permissibility of what has passed: that when such a combination took place in the Jahiliyyah, the marriage was valid, and when it took place in Islam, one is given the choice between the two sisters, according to what Malik and al-Shafi'i said, without applying the contracts of the disbelievers to the requirements of Islam and the demands of the Sharia. It makes no difference whether he concluded one contract combining the two or combined them in two contracts.

Abu Hanifa holds that their marriage is void if he combined them in a single contract.

Hisham ibn Abd Allah narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan that he said: The people of the Jahiliyyah knew all these prohibitions mentioned in this verse except two: one of them is marrying the wife of a father, and the second is combining two sisters. Do you not see that He said: "And do not marry women whom your fathers married, except what has already passed," and "and that you combine two sisters, except what has already passed," while He did not mention "except what has already passed" for the rest of the prohibitions? And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verse 24 (part 1 of 5):

In this verse there are fourteen issues. The first: God's words ﴿And the married women﴾ are a conjunction with the prohibited women and those mentioned before.

Tahsin (protection, chastity) means to guard oneself, and from it comes ḥiṣn (fortress), because one is protected within it. From it is God's words: ﴿And We taught him the making of coats of mail for you, to protect you from your violence﴾ [see vol. 11, p. 320], meaning to guard you. From it also comes ḥiṣān for a horse (with a kasra on the ḥāʾ), because it protects its rider from destruction. And ḥaṣān (with a fatḥa on the ḥāʾ) is a chaste woman, because she protects herself from destruction. One says ḥaṣunat al-mar'ah taḥṣunu fa-hiya ḥaṣān, like jabunat fa-hiya jabān. Ḥassān said about ʿĀʾishah, may God be pleased with her:

A chaste, steadfast woman, never accused of doubt,
who wakes up hungry from the flesh of the heedless.
[Tuzannu: accused. Gharthā: hungry. The meaning is that she does not backbite others.]

The verbal noun is ḥaṣānah (with a fatḥa on the ḥāʾ), and ḥiṣn is like ʿilm [in the lexicon books it is said to have three vowel forms on the ḥāʾ]. So the meaning of al-muḥṣanāt here is those who have husbands. One says imra'ah muḥṣanah, i.e. married, and muḥṣanah, i.e. free. From this is God's words: ﴿And the chaste women from among the believers, and the chaste women from among those who were given the Book﴾ [see vol. 6, p. 75]. And muḥṣanah means chaste: God says, ﴿chaste, not fornicating﴾, and He says, ﴿chaste, not fornicating﴾. Muḥṣanah, muḥaṣṣanah and ḥaṣān all mean chaste, i.e. refraining from immorality. Freedom prevents the free woman from what slaves engage in. God says: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women﴾ [see vol. 12, p. 209], meaning free women. In the pre-Islamic era the custom of slave women was fornication. Do you not see the words of Hind bint ʿUtbah to the Prophet ﷺ when she pledged allegiance to him: "Does a free woman commit fornication?" A husband also prevents his wife from marrying another, so the root ḥ-ṣ-n carries the meaning of prevention, as we have explained. The term iḥṣān was used in Islam because it is a guard and preventer; it is not in the Book but appears in the Sunnah. From it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Faith is a restraint on treachery" [al-fatk: that a man comes upon his companion while he is heedless and unaware, then attacks and kills him. Al-Nihayah]. From it is the saying of the Hudhali:

So it is not like the former state of the house, O Umm Malik,
but chains have encircled the necks.

And the poet said:

She said, "Come, let us talk," I said, "No,
God and Islam forbid it to you."

From it is the saying of Suhaym:

Gray hair and Islam have sufficed a man as a restraint...
[Its first half in the Diwan: ʿUmayrah, leave off if you have prepared to depart. It will come in vol. 15, p. 52, from Abu Bakr: Hurayrah, leave off.]

Second issue: Having established this, the scholars have differed in the interpretation of this verse. Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu Qilabah, Ibn Zayd, Makhul, al-Zuhri and Abu Saʿid al-Khudri said: the meaning of al-muḥṣanāt here is specifically the captured women who have husbands; that is, they are forbidden except what your right hands possess through capture from the land of war, for such women are lawful to the one whose share they fall into, even if they have a husband. This is the view of al-Shafiʿi that capture severs the marriage bond. Ibn Wahb, Ibn ʿAbd al-Hakam, who related it from Malik, and Ashhab also held this view. This is supported by what Muslim related in his Sahih from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri that on the day of Hunayn the Messenger of God ﷺ sent an army to Awtas [Awtas: a valley in the land of Hawazin], and they met the enemy, fought them, prevailed over them and took captives. Some of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ were reluctant to have intercourse with them because of their husbands among the polytheists, so God, mighty and majestic, revealed [concerning that] (﴿and the married women, except those whom your right hands possess﴾), meaning: they are lawful to you once their waiting period is over. This is a clear text that the verse was revealed because of the reluctance of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ regarding intercourse with captured married women, so God the Exalted revealed in answer to them: ﴿except what your right hands possess﴾. This is the view of Malik, Abu Hanifah and his companions, al-Shafiʿi, Ahmad, Ishaq and Abu Thawr, and it is the correct view, God willing. They differed over what establishes their istibra' (purification from pregnancy). Al-Hasan said: the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ would establish the istibra' of a captive woman by one menstrual cycle, and this has been related from the hadith of Abu Saʿid al-Khudri concerning the captives of Awtas: ("A pregnant woman is not to be had until she gives birth, nor a non-pregnant one until she menstruates"). He did not give the bed of the former husband any effect, so as to say that the captive is a slave; rather she was a wife whose marriage had ended, so she observes the waiting period of slave women, as related from al-Hasan ibn Salih, who said: "She has two menstrual cycles as her waiting period if she had a husband in the land of war." The majority of scholars held that her istibra' and the istibra' of a woman without a husband are both one menstrual cycle. The well-known position of the school of Malik is that there is no difference whether the spouses are captured together or separately. Ibn Bukayr related from him that if both are captured together and the man is kept, they remain in their marriage; in this report he saw that keeping him is preserving what he owns, since he has come to have a claim and his wife is among what he owns, so he should not be separated from her. This is the view of Abu Hanifah and al-Thawri, and Ibn al-Qasim also held it and related it from Malik. The first view is the sound one, for the reason we mentioned, and because God the Exalted said: ﴿except what your right hands possess﴾, so He referred the matter to ownership by the right hand and made it the operative factor, so the ruling is attached to it in terms of both generality and causation, except what the evidence specifies.

There is a second view on the verse, stated by ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud, Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab, al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah and Ibn ʿAbbas in the report of ʿIkrimah: that the meaning of the verse is married women, that is, they are forbidden except that a man buys a slave woman who has a husband; for her sale is her divorce, giving her in charity is her divorce, inheriting her is her divorce, and the husband's divorcing her is her divorce. Ibn Masʿud said: when a slave woman is sold while she has a husband, the buyer has more right to her womb, and likewise the captive; all of this necessitates separation between her and her husband. They said: since this is so, the sale of a slave woman must be a divorce for her, because the private part is forbidden to two men at the same time by the consensus of the Muslims. I say: this is refuted by the hadith of Barirah, for ʿĀʾishah, may God be pleased with her, bought Barirah and freed her, then the Prophet ﷺ gave her the choice, and she was married; and in the consensus that Barirah was given the choice while under her husband Mughith after ʿĀʾishah had bought and freed her, this is evidence that the sale of a slave woman is not her divorce [as in the text of D]. This is the position of the majority of jurists of the great cities, from the people of opinion and hadith, and that she has no divorce except a divorce [as in the text of B]. Some have argued by the generality of His words ﴿except what your right hands possess﴾ and by analogy to captive women. What we have mentioned of the hadith of Barirah specifies and refutes this, and that this applies specifically to captive women according to the hadith of Abu Saʿid, and this is the correct and true position, God willing.

There is a third view on the verse: al-Thawri related from Mujahid from Ibrahim [in Awi, H, Z: from Mujahid from Ibrahim; in B, J, D, T: al-Tirmidhi from Mujahid, etc., both of which are in error, since Mujahid narrates from ʿAbd Allah, not from Ibrahim, and the narration of Mujahid is not in al-Tirmidhi concerning this verse. In al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir: al-Aʿmash from Ibrahim from ʿAbd Allah. In al-Tabari also: Hammad from Ibrahim from ʿAbd Allah] that Ibn Masʿud said concerning God's words ﴿And the married women among women, except what your right hands possess﴾: he said: the married women among Muslims and polytheists. ʿAli ibn Abi Talib said: the married women among polytheists. In the Muwatta' from Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab, ﴿and the married women among women﴾ are those who have husbands, and this comes back to God's prohibition of fornication. And a group said: al-muḥṣanāt in this verse means the chaste, that is, all women are forbidden, and the name of chastity is applied to them, whether they have husbands or not, since the laws in themselves require that.

(إِلَّا مَا مَلَكَتْ أَيْمانُكُمْ) They said: its meaning is by marriage or by purchase. This is the view of Abu al-'Aliyah, 'Ubaidah al-Salmani, Tawus, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Ata', and 'Ubaidah narrated it from 'Umar. Thus they included marriage under "what your right hands possess." In their understanding, the meaning of the verse, "except what your right hands possess," is: you own their chastity through marriage and you own their persons through purchase, so that all of them are things possessed by right hand, and whatever lies beyond this is fornication. This is a good view. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Ibn 'Abbas said, "al-Muhsanat" means the chaste women among the Muslims and among the People of the Book. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: By this interpretation the meaning of the verse returns to the prohibition of fornication. Al-Tabari reported with a chain that a man said to Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "Did you not see Ibn 'Abbas when he was asked about this verse and said nothing about it?" Sa'id said: "Ibn 'Abbas did not know it." He also reported from Mujahid that he said: "If I knew someone who could explain this verse to me, I would ride camels' livers to him," referring to His saying, "and the chaste women," up to His saying, "All-Wise." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: I do not know how this statement was attributed to Ibn 'Abbas, nor how Mujahid arrived at this view.

The third point: His saying, ﴿The decree of Allah upon you﴾, is in the accusative as an emphatic infinitive (masdar), meaning: these women have been forbidden to you as a decree from Allah upon you. The meaning of "they have been forbidden to you" is "He prescribed upon you." Al-Zajjaj and the Kufans said: it is in the accusative as an incitement (ighra'), meaning: "Hold fast to the Book of Allah," or "the Book of Allah upon you." In this there is a point of consideration, according to what Abu 'Ali mentioned: in an incitement, the object may not be placed before the particle of incitement, so one does not say "Zaydan 'alayka" or "Zaydan dunaka," but rather "'alayka Zaydan" and "dunaka 'Amran." What he said is correct if it is governed by "'alaykum," but if the verb is omitted it is permissible. It is also permissible to read it in the nominative, meaning: "This is the Book of Allah and His obligation." Abu Haywah and Muhammad ibn al-Sumayqa' read "Kataba Allahu 'alaykum" with the past verb attributed to the name of Allah, and the meaning is: Allah prescribed upon you what He related of prohibition. Ubaidah al-Salmani and others said: His saying, "The Book of Allah upon you," refers to what is established in the Qur'an in His saying, "two, three, or four." In this there is remoteness. The more apparent view is that His saying, "The Book of Allah upon you," refers only to the prohibition that separates people from what the Arabs used to do.

The fourth point: His saying, ﴿And lawful for you is what lies beyond that﴾. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and 'Asim in Hafs's transmission read "wa-uhilla lakum," as a response to "hurrimat 'alaykum." The rest read it with a fatha, as a response to His saying, "The Book of Allah upon you." This would imply that none of the women are forbidden except those mentioned, and this is not so, for Allah has forbidden through the tongue of His Prophet those not mentioned in the verse, so they are added to it. Allah says: "And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it." Muslim and others narrated from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A woman may not be combined with her paternal aunt, nor a woman with her maternal aunt." Ibn Shihab said: "We regard the maternal aunt of her father and the paternal aunt of her father as being in the same position." It has been said that the prohibition of combining a woman with her paternal aunt and maternal aunt is derived from the verse itself, because Allah forbade combining two sisters, and combining a woman with her paternal aunt is in meaning combining two sisters; or because the maternal aunt is in the meaning of the mother and the paternal aunt is in the meaning of the father. The correct view is the first, because the Book and the Sunnah are like one thing; it is as if He said: "I have made lawful for you what lies beyond what We mentioned in the Book, and what lies beyond what I completed in explanation through the tongue of Muhammad (peace be upon him)." Ibn Shihab's statement, "We regard the maternal aunt of her father and the paternal aunt of her father as being in the same position," arose because he extended the maternal and paternal aunts to a general category, and this was sound for him, because "paternal aunt" is the name for every female who shares with your father both his roots or one of them, and the maternal aunt is likewise, as we have explained.

In the Musannaf of Abu Dawud and others, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A woman shall not be married while her paternal aunt is [her co-wife], nor a paternal aunt while the daughter of her brother is, nor a woman while her maternal aunt is, nor a maternal aunt while the daughter of her sister is. The elder shall not be married to the younger, nor the younger to the elder." Abu Dawud also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he disliked combining a paternal aunt with a maternal aunt, or two paternal aunts and two maternal aunts. The narration "لا يجمع" is read with a damma on the ayn, as a report of the legislated ruling, which implies a prohibition. This hadith is agreed upon as binding in prohibiting the combining of those mentioned in it through marriage. The Kharijites permitted combining two sisters, and combining a woman with her paternal aunt and maternal aunt [[This is not authentically reported from them, since it is a rejection of what is explicitly stated, and that is disbelief. If by them the Ibadis are meant, according to their habit of lumping them with the Kharijites, they are innocent of this. Their principle, both earlier and later, is: any two women such that if one of them were male the other would be unlawful to him, combining them in marriage is forbidden, as in the book "Kitab al-Nil wa-Sharhuh." The hadith that is the basis for this is authentic and established among them, and Allah says: "So verify" (fa-tabayyanu). See al-Jassas, vol. 2, p. 134, which contains a difference of opinion regarding this.]], and their disagreement is not taken into account, because they have left the religion and exited it, and because they oppose the established Sunnah. As for his saying, "A woman may not be combined with two paternal aunts or two maternal aunts," it puzzled some scholars, who were perplexed about its meaning, to the point that they interpreted it in ways that are remote or impermissible. They said: "combining between the two paternal aunts" is metaphorical, meaning between the paternal aunt and the daughter of her brother, and so they are called two paternal aunts, just as it is said "the Sunnah of the two 'Umars," meaning Abu Bakr and 'Umar. He said: and between the two maternal aunts is likewise. Al-Nahhas said: This is among the far-fetched interpretations, of a kind hardly ever heard, and it also contains, besides being far-fetched, a repetition without benefit, because if the meaning is a prohibition on combining a woman with her paternal aunt and the daughter of her brother, and between two paternal aunts meaning the paternal aunt and the daughter of her brother, the statement becomes repetitive without benefit. Moreover, if it were as he said, it would have to be "and between the maternal aunt," and the hadith is not so, for the hadith forbade combining the paternal aunt and the maternal aunt. The requirement according to the wording of the hadith is that one may not combine two women, one of whom is the paternal aunt of the other and the other the maternal aunt of the first. Al-Nahhas said: This is explained by a sound meaning: a man and his son marry a woman and her daughter; the man marries the girl and the son marries the mother, and each of them has a daughter from these two wives; the daughter of the father is the paternal aunt of the daughter of the son, and the daughter of the son is the maternal aunt of the daughter of the father. As for combining two maternal aunts, this requires that they be two women each of whom is the maternal aunt of the other, which is when a man marries the daughter of a man and the other marries his daughter, and each has a daughter from them; the daughter of each is the maternal aunt of the other. As for combining two paternal aunts, this requires that one may not combine two women each of whom is the paternal aunt of the other, which is when a man marries the mother of a man and the other marries the mother of the other, and each has a daughter; the daughter of each is the paternal aunt of the other. This is what Allah has forbidden through the tongue of His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ) beyond what is in the Qur'an.

The fifth point: Once this is established, the scholars have set out well who is forbidden to be combined. Ma'mar ibn Sulayman narrated from Fudayl ibn Maysarah, from Abu Jarir, from al-Sha'bi, who said: "Any two women such that if you placed a male in the position of one of them, it would not be lawful for him to marry the other: combining them is invalid." I asked him: "From whom is this?" He said: "From the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." Sufyan al-Thawri said: "Its explanation according to us is that it applies to kinship, and it is not like a woman and her husband's daughter, which one may combine if he wishes." Abu 'Umar said: This is the position of Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifah, al-Awza'i, and all the jurists of the regions, among the people of hadith and others, as far as I know, who do not differ on this principle. Some of the early scholars disliked that a man combine the daughter of a man with his wife, because if one of them were male it would not be lawful for him to marry the other. What the scholars hold is that there is no harm in this, and that what is considered is kinship alone, not other forms of marital relationship. Then in some reports there came an indication of the reason for the prohibition of combining those mentioned, namely that combining leads to severing close kinship ties through the enmity and evils that arise between co-wives because of jealousy. Ibn 'Abbas reported: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade that a man marry a woman together with her paternal aunt or her maternal aunt, and said: "If you do that, you will sever your kinship ties." This was mentioned by Abu Muhammad al-Asili in his Fawa'id, and by Ibn 'Abd al-Barr and others. From the mursal reports of Abu Dawud, from Husayn ibn Talhah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade that a woman be married together with her sisters, for fear of severance. Some of the early scholars extended this reason, forbidding the combining of a woman with any close relative, whether she was a paternal cousin, a paternal aunt's daughter, a maternal cousin, or a maternal aunt's daughter. This was narrated from Ishaq ibn Talhah, 'Ikrimah, Qatadah, and 'Ata' in the transmission of Ibn Abi Najih, but Ibn Jurayj narrated from him that there is no harm in it, and this is the sound view. Hasan ibn Husayn ibn 'Ali married, on one night, the daughter of Muhammad ibn 'Ali and the daughter of 'Umar ibn 'Ali, thus combining two paternal cousins; this was mentioned by 'Abd al-Razzaq. Ibn 'Uyaynah added: "So their women in the morning did not know which of the two to go to." Malik disliked this, though it was not unlawful in his view.

In the narration of Ibn al-Qasim: Malik was asked about two paternal cousins, whether they may be combined. He said: "I do not know it to be unlawful." It was said to him: "Do you dislike it?" He said: "Some people avoid it." Ibn al-Qasim said: "It is lawful and there is no harm in it." Ibn al-Mundhir said: "I know of no one who has invalidated this marriage." Both are included in the general category of what is permitted by marriage, not excluded from it by Book, Sunnah, or consensus; likewise the combining of two daughters of paternal aunts, and of two daughters of maternal aunts. Al-Suddi, regarding His saying, "And lawful for you is what lies beyond that," said: it means marriage in what is other than the private part. It was also said: the meaning is that what lies beyond the unmarriageable female relatives of your kin is lawful. Qatadah said: By this He means ownership by right hand only.

The sixth point: His saying, ﴿that you seek with your wealth﴾ is a word that comprises both marriage and purchase. "An" (that) is in the accusative position as a substitute for "ma" (what), and according to Hamzah's reading it is in the nominative position. It may be that the meaning is "li-an" (so that) or "bi-an" (by that), and the preposition is then omitted, so it is in the accusative position. And "muhsinin" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), meaning: chaste, abstaining from fornication.

**(ghayra musafihin)** means ﴿not committing fornication﴾, that is, not engaging in *zina* (unlawful sexual intercourse). *Al-sifah* (fornication) is the *zina*, and it is derived from *safh al-ma'* (pouring out water and letting it flow), meaning pouring it out and letting it run. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) when he heard the *daffaf* [[As in the originals: *al-zifaf*. *Al-daffaf* is the owner of the *daff* (a frame drum), and the plural of *daff* is *dufuf*. In the hadith: "What separates the lawful from the unlawful is the sound of the *daff*."]] at a wedding feast: "This is marriage (*nikah*), not fornication (*sifah*), nor secret marriage (*nikah al-sirr*)."

It has been said that His saying ﴿chaste, not fornicating﴾ may have two meanings. The first is what we have mentioned: *ihsan* (chastity) through the contract of marriage. Its meaning is: seek the benefits of intimacy with your wealth in the manner of marriage, not in the manner of fornication. On this interpretation, the verse is general in scope. The second possibility is that *muhsinin* (chaste) describes the women, meaning: marry them on the condition that they are chaste. The first meaning is preferable, because whenever it is possible to keep the verse on its general sense and to apply its implication, that is preferable. Also, the implication of the second meaning is that women who fornicate may not be married, and that contradicts the consensus (*ijma'*).

The seventh point: His saying ﴿with your wealth﴾. Allah has permitted intimacy in exchange for wealth without specifying further. Therefore, if intimacy is obtained by other than wealth, the permission should not be effected by it, because it would be outside the permitted condition, just as if one contracted marriage with wine, pork, or something that is not valid to own. It is objected to Ahmad's view that manumission (*'itq*) may serve as a dowry (*sadaq*), because there is no transfer of property in it; there is only the removal of ownership without the woman becoming entitled to the transfer of any property to her. What the master owned has not passed to her; it has merely dropped away. If the husband hands her nothing and she is not entitled to anything from him, but he has merely destroyed his own ownership, then it is not a *mahr* (bridal gift). This is clear from His saying ﴿And give the women their dowries﴾, which is a command implying obligation, and giving manumission does not validly fulfil it. And His saying ﴿But if they give you willingly a part of it, then consume it﴾, which is impossible with manumission. So the dowry can only be property, by His saying ﴿with your wealth﴾.

Those who held this view differed about its amount. Al-Shafi'i relied on the general wording of His saying ﴿with your wealth﴾ to permit a dowry of little or much. This is the correct view, and it is supported by the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying in the hadith of the woman who gave herself in marriage: "Even if it is an iron ring." And by his (ﷺ) saying, repeated three times: "Marry off the single ones (*ayama*)." It was asked: "What are the ties between them, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "What the families agree upon, even a twig of *arak*." Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: "We asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the dowry of women, and he said: 'It is what their families agree upon.'" Jabir reported that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If a man gave a woman a handful of food, it would be lawful for him." Al-Daraqutni recorded both in his *Sunan*.

Al-Shafi'i said: Whatever may be a price for something, or may be a wage, may be a dowry. This is the view of the majority of scholars. The body of hadith scholars from Medina and elsewhere all permitted the dowry to be of little or much property. This is also the view of Abdullah ibn Wahb, a companion of Malik, and it was chosen by Ibn al-Mundhir and others. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: "If he gave her a whip as a dowry, it would be lawful for her, and he married his daughter to Abdullah ibn Wada'a for two dirhams." Rabi'a said: "Marriage is permitted for one dirham." Abu al-Zinad said: "Whatever the families agree upon." Malik said: "The dowry may not be less than a quarter of a dinar or three dirhams by weight." One of our companions gave a reason for this: The thing most similar to this is the amputation of the hand, because the private part (*bud'*) is a limb, and the hand is a limb, and each is permitted in exchange for a specified amount of wealth, which is a quarter of a dinar or three dirhams by weight. So Malik took the private part back to the hand by analogy.

Abu Umar (Ibn Abd al-Barr) said: Abu Hanifa preceded him in this, analogizing the dowry to the amputation of the hand. For Abu Hanifa the hand is not amputated except for a gold dinar or ten dirhams by weight, and he holds that there is no dowry less than that. This is the view of most of his companions and the people of his school, and it is the view of most people of his city regarding amputation of the hand, but not regarding the minimum dowry. Al-Darawardi said to Malik, when he said there is no dowry less than a quarter of a dinar: "You have deviated in this, Abu Abdullah," meaning you have followed the path of the people of Iraq.

Abu Hanifa argued with what Jabir reported, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no dowry less than ten dirhams." Al-Daraqutni recorded it. In its chain is Mubashshir ibn Ubayd, who is abandoned (*matruk*) in hadith. It is also reported from Dawud al-Awdi, from al-Sha'bi, from Ali (peace be upon him): "The dowry may not be less than ten dirhams." Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: Ghiyath ibn Ibrahim taught Dawud al-Awdi, from al-Sha'bi, from Ali: "There is no dowry less than ten dirhams," and so it became a hadith. Al-Nakha'i said: The minimum is forty dirhams. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: fifty dirhams. Ibn Shubruma said: five dirhams. Al-Daraqutni narrated from Ibn Abbas, from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him): "There is no dowry less than five dirhams."

The eighth point: His saying ﴿So for what you have enjoyed from them, give them their wages (*ujur*) as an obligation﴾. *Al-istimta'* is enjoyment and pleasure. *Al-ujur* means the dowries. The dowry was called a wage (*ajr*) because it is the wage for enjoyment. This is an explicit statement that the dowry is called a wage, and that is evidence that it stands in exchange for the private part, because what is exchanged for a benefit is called a wage. Scholars have differed about what is the object of the contract in marriage: is it the woman's body, or the benefit of intimacy, or the lawfulness (*al-hill*)? There are three views. The apparent truth is that all of them together are meant, since the contract requires all of that. And Allah knows best.

The ninth point: Scholars have differed about the meaning of the verse. Al-Hasan, Mujahid, and others said: The meaning is: for what you have benefited from and enjoyed through intercourse with women in valid marriage, ﴿give them their wages﴾, that is, their dowries. So when a man has intercourse with her once, the full dowry becomes due if it was specified, or the dowry of her equivalent (*mahr al-mithl*) if it was not specified. If the marriage was invalid, the transmitted views from Malik differ regarding invalid marriage: does one become entitled to the dowry of equivalence, or to the specified dowry if it was a valid dowry? He said once: the specified dowry, and this is the apparent position of his school, because what they agreed upon is certain, and the dowry of equivalence is an estimate (*ijtihad*). So one must return to what we are certain of, because property is not made due by doubt. The basis of the view that it is the dowry of equivalence is that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Any woman who is married without the permission of her guardian, her marriage is void (*batil*). If he has consummated with her, then she is entitled to the dowry of her equivalent for what he made lawful of her private part [[The text of the hadith is the same in all the originals. It is in Ahmad, Abu Dawud, Ibn Majah, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Hibban, al-Daraqutni, and al-Shafi'i. Its wording in al-Tirmidhi is: "Any woman who is married without the permission of her guardian, her marriage is void, void, void. If he has consummated with her, then she is entitled to the dowry for what he made lawful of her private part..."]]

(The hadith. See al-Daraqutni and his commentary, Hind edition.]]). Ibn Khuwayz Mindad said: It is not permissible to take the verse as permitting mut'ah, because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade mut'ah marriage and prohibited it, and because Allah the Exalted said: "So marry them with the permission of their families." It is known that marriage with the permission of the families is the legally valid marriage, with a guardian (wali) and two witnesses, and mut'ah marriage is not like that. The majority said: What is meant is the mut'ah marriage that existed in early Islam. Ibn 'Abbas, Ubayy and Ibn Jubayr recited: "So for those you enjoy from them, up to a specified term, give them their wages," and then the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade it. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: It was abrogated (mansukh) by the verse of inheritance, since in mut'ah there is no inheritance. 'A'ishah and al-Qasim ibn Muhammad said: Its prohibition and abrogation are in the Qur'an, in His saying: "And those who guard their chastity, except from their spouses or what their right hands possess, for they are not blameworthy" [[See vol. 12, p. 105]], and mut'ah is neither marriage nor ownership by the right hand.

al-Daraqutni narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade mut'ah. He said: It was only for those who could not find (a spouse). When marriage, divorce, the waiting period ('iddah) and inheritance between husband and wife were revealed, it was abrogated. It is also reported from 'Ali (raḍiya Allahu 'anhu) that he said: The fasting of Ramadan abrogated every fast, the zakat abrogated every charity, divorce, the waiting period and inheritance abrogated mut'ah, and the sacrifice abrogated every slaughter. From Ibn Mas'ud: Mut'ah is abrogated; divorce, the waiting period and inheritance abrogated it. 'Ata' narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: Mut'ah was only a mercy from Allah the Exalted, by which He showed mercy to His servants; and had it not been for 'Umar's prohibition of it, none would have committed fornication except a wretch.

Tenth: The scholars differed on how many times mut'ah was permitted and abrogated. In Sahih Muslim, from 'Abd Allah, who said: We used to fight with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and we had no women, so we said: Shall we not castrate ourselves? He forbade us from that, then he permitted us to marry a woman for a garment up to a term. Abu Hatim al-Busti said in his Sahih: Their saying to the Prophet (ﷺ) "Shall we not castrate ourselves?" is evidence that mut'ah was forbidden before they were permitted enjoyment, and had it not been forbidden, their question about this would have had no meaning. Then he permitted them during the military campaign to marry a woman for a garment up to a term; then he forbade it in the year of Khaybar; then he permitted it in the year of the Conquest; then he prohibited it after three days, so it is forbidden until the Day of Resurrection. Ibn al-'Arabi said: As for the mut'ah of women, it is among the strange matters of the Shari'ah, for it was permitted in early Islam, then forbidden on the day of Khaybar, then permitted in the campaign of Awtas, then forbidden after that, and the matter settled on prohibition. It has no counterpart in the Shari'ah except the question of the qiblah, for abrogation applied to it twice and then it was settled afterwards.

Another scholar who gathered the chains of the hadiths on it said: It involves permission and prohibition seven times. Ibn Abi 'Amrah narrated that it was in early Islam. Salamah ibn al-Akwa' narrated that it was in the year of Awtas. From the narration of 'Ali, its prohibition was on the day of Khaybar. From the narration of al-Rabi' ibn Sabrah, its permission was on the day of the Conquest. I say: All these chains are in Sahih Muslim, and in other sources, from 'Ali, is his prohibition of it in the campaign of Tabuk, narrated by Ishaq ibn Rashid from al-Zuhri, from 'Abd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn 'Ali, from his father, from 'Ali; but Ishaq ibn Rashid was not followed in this narration from Ibn Shihab, as Abu 'Umar, may Allah have mercy on him, said. In the Musannaf of Abu Dawud, from the hadith of al-Rabi' ibn Sabrah, is the prohibition of it in the Farewell Pilgrimage, and Abu Dawud held that this is the most authentic of what has been narrated on this. 'Amr [[Apparently 'Amr ibn Maymun, from al-Hasan al-Basri.]] narrated from al-Hasan: Mut'ah was never made lawful except three times, in the 'Umrah of the Qada', it was not lawful before it nor after it. This is also reported from Sabrah. So these are seven occasions in which mut'ah was made lawful and then prohibited.

Abu Ja'far al-Tahawi said: All of those who narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) its unrestricted permission reported that it was during a journey, and that the prohibition afterward reached it during that same journey, so he forbade it. None of them reports that it was during residence, and similarly it is reported from Ibn Mas'ud. As for the hadith of Sabrah in which the Prophet (ﷺ) permits it in the Farewell Pilgrimage, it is outside all its meanings. We examined this phrase and found it only in the narration of 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz alone. Isma'il ibn 'Ayyash narrated it from 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, mentioning that this was at the Conquest of Makkah, and that they complained to him of 'uzbah [[al-'Uzbah (with a silent 'ayn and a zay with a dot) means being cut off from women. It may be with a dotted ghayn and an undotted ra', meaning separation from homelands, because of the separation from family (from Ibn Majah).]], so he permitted it for them. It is impossible that they complained to him of 'uzbah in the Farewell Pilgrimage, because they had made the pilgrimage with their women, and marrying women in Makkah was possible for them, and they were not then in the same condition as in the earlier campaigns. It is possible that, since it was the custom of the Prophet (ﷺ) to repeat such matters in his campaigns and in the gatherings, he mentioned its prohibition in the Farewell Pilgrimage, so that people gathered and whoever had not heard it would hear it, and he emphasized it so that no one claiming its permission would have any pretext; and because the people of Makkah were using it much.

Eleventh: Al-Layth ibn Sa'd narrated from Bukayr ibn al-Ashajj, from 'Ammar, the client of al-Sharid, who said: I asked Ibn 'Abbas about mut'ah: Is it fornication (sifah) or marriage? He said: It is neither fornication nor marriage. I said: Then what is it? He said: Mut'ah, as Allah the Exalted said. I said: Is there a waiting period for it? He said: Yes, one menstrual cycle. I said: Do they inherit from each other? He said: No. Abu 'Umar said: The scholars of the early and later generations did not differ that mut'ah is a marriage up to a term, with no inheritance in it, and separation occurs at the end of the term without divorce.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "Mut'ah was that a man marries a woman with two witnesses and the permission of the guardian, up to a specified term, and on the condition that there is no inheritance between them, and he gives her what they agreed upon. When the term ends, he has no further claim over her, and she must be given a period to ascertain she is not pregnant (istibra' rahim), because a child has no legitimate claim in it without doubt; if she does not become pregnant, she is lawfully free for another." In the book of al-Nahhas there is an error in this, and a child is not attributed to a father in mut'ah marriage. I say: This is what is understood from al-Nahhas's expression, for he said: Mut'ah is that he says to her: "I marry you for a day," or something similar, "on the condition that there is no waiting period upon you, no inheritance between us, no divorce, and no witness who testifies to it." This is fornication itself, and it was never permitted at all in Islam. For this reason 'Umar said: "I will not be brought a man who has married in mut'ah except that I will bury him under the stones."

Twelfth: Our scholars differed: when someone enters into a mut'ah marriage, is he to receive the hadd punishment and the child is not attributed to him, or is the hadd averted because of doubt (shubhah) and the child is attributed to him? There are two views, but he is to be disciplined (yu'azzar [[In manuscripts B, J and D: (yu'zzar).]]) and punished. If in the view of some scholars, holding that it is prohibited, the child is attributed to him today in mut'ah marriage, how then would it not be attributed in that time when it was permitted? This shows that mut'ah marriage was under the rules of valid marriage, differing from it only in the term and inheritance. Al-Mahdawi related from Ibn 'Abbas that mut'ah marriage was without a guardian and without witnesses. There is weakness in what he related, for the reasons we mentioned. Ibn al-'Arabi said: Ibn 'Abbas used to say it was permissible, but then his retraction from it was established, and so the ijma' (scholarly consensus) was concluded on its prohibition; if anyone does it, he is stoned according to the well-known school. In another narration from Malik: He is not stoned, because mut'ah marriage is not forbidden, but because of another principle of our scholars that is unusual, in which they stood alone apart from all other scholars: whether what is prohibited by the Sunnah is the same as what is prohibited by the Qur'an or not. From a narration of some Madinan scholars from Malik, that they are not equal, and this is weak. Abu Bakr al-Tartushi said: None granted a concession for mut'ah marriage except 'Imran ibn Husayn, Ibn 'Abbas, some of the Companions, and a group of the People of the House.

Regarding Ibn 'Abbas's view, the poet says:
"I say to the caravan when our stay was long:
O friend, do you desire the legal opinion of Ibn 'Abbas?
Concerning a fair maiden, soft of extremities, delicate,
who will be your lodging until the people return."

All the other scholars and jurists among the Companions, the Successors and the righteous predecessors hold that this verse is abrogated and that mut'ah is forbidden. Abu 'Umar said: The companions of Ibn 'Abbas from the people of Makkah and Yemen all held mut'ah to be lawful, according to the view of Ibn 'Abbas, while all other people prohibited it. Ma'mar said: al-Zuhri said: People came to detest it so much that a poet said:
"The narrator said when his session grew long:
O friend, do you desire the legal opinion of Ibn 'Abbas?"

As has preceded.

**The Thirteenth Issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿their wages﴾ encompasses wealth and other things, so it is permissible for the *mahr* (bridal gift) to be the benefits of specific items (*manafi' a'yan*). The scholars differed on this. Malik, al-Muzani, al-Layth, Ahmad, Abu Hanifa and his companions prohibited it, except that Abu Hanifa said: if he marries on that basis, the marriage is valid and it is in the ruling of one for whom no dower was specified. She has the *mahr al-mithl* (customary dower) if he consummates with her, and if he does not consummate with her, then she has the *mut'ah* (consolation gift). Ibn al-Qasim disliked it in the *Kitab* of Muhammad, and Asbagh permitted it. Ibn Shas said: if it occurs, it stands according to the view of most of the companions, and this is a narration of Asbagh from Ibn al-Qasim. Al-Shafi'i said: the marriage is valid, and he must teach her what he stipulated for her. If he divorces her before consummation, then for al-Shafi'i there are two opinions: one, that she has half the fee for teaching that surah; the other, that she has half the *mahr al-mithl*. Ishaq said: the marriage is permissible. Abu al-Hasan al-Lakhmi said: the view that all of this is permissible is the better one. *Ijara* (leasing) and *hajj* are like other wealth that is owned, sold and bought. Malik disliked it only because it is recommended that the dower be paid promptly, whereas *ijara* and *hajj* are in the sense of being deferred.

Those who held the first view argued that Allah said ﴿with your wealth﴾, and the reality of wealth is that it is what desires attach to and what is prepared for benefit. The benefit of an object in leasing, and the benefit of teaching the whole of knowledge, are not wealth. Al-Tahawi said: the agreed principle is that if a man hires another to teach him a named surah of the Qur'an for a dirham, it is not permitted, because leases are permitted only for one of two purposes: either for a specific task, such as sewing a garment and the like, or for a known period of time. If he hires him to teach a surah, that is a lease for neither a known period nor a known task; he merely hires him to be taught, and that may be understood as little or much teaching, in short or long periods. Likewise, if he sells him his house on condition that he teach him a surah of the Qur'an, it is not permitted, for the reasons we have mentioned concerning leases. And since teaching does not make benefits or specific items of wealth owned by means of it, it is established by reasoning that marriage (*ab·ḍa'*) cannot be made owned by it. And Allah is the Granter of success.

Those who permitted it argued from the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd concerning the woman who was given (*al-mawhuba*), in which he (ﷺ) said: "Go, I have given her to you in ownership (*mallaktukaha*) in exchange for what you have of the Qur'an." In another narration he said: "Go, I have married her to you, so teach her the Qur'an." They said: this is evidence for the validity of the marriage and the deferral of the dower, which is the teaching. This is according to the apparent meaning of his saying "in exchange for what you have of the Qur'an," for the *ba'* (preposition) denotes exchange, as you say: "take this for that," meaning as a compensation for it. His saying in the other narration, "so teach her," is an explicit command to teach, and the context testifies that it was for the sake of the marriage. No attention should be paid to the one who said that this was an honour to the man for what he had memorised of the Qur'an, that is, *because of* what he had memorised, so that the *ba'* would mean the *lam* (meaning "for"). For the second hadith clearly contradicts that with his words "teach her from the Qur'an."

There is no proof in what is narrated about Abu Talha, that he proposed to Umm Sulaym, and she said: "If he embraces Islam, I will marry him." He embraced Islam and she married him, and no dower is known to be more noble than hers, for her dower was Islam. That is specific to her. Moreover, nothing of benefit reaches her from it, unlike teaching and other benefits. Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) married his daughter to Musa (peace be upon him) on condition that he herd sheep for him as her dower, as its explanation will come in Surat al-Qasas [see vol. 13, p. 271 onwards].

It has been narrated from Ibn Abbas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to a man among his companions: "O so-and-so, have you married?" He said: "No, and I have nothing with which to marry." He said: "Do you not have *Qul huwa Allahu ahad*?" He said: "Yes." He said: "A third of the Qur'an. Do you not have *Ayat al-Kursi*?" He said: "Yes." He said: "A quarter of the Qur'an. Do you not have *Idha ja'a nasrullahi wal-fath*?" He said: "Yes." He said: "A quarter of the Qur'an. Do you not have *Idha zulzilat*?" He said: "Yes." He said: "A quarter of the Qur'an. Marry, marry."

I say: al-Daraqutni narrated the hadith of Sahl from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, and in it there is an addition which clarifies what Malik and others relied upon. In it, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Who will marry this woman?" That man stood up and said: "I, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "Do you have any wealth?" He said: "No, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "Do you recite anything of the Qur'an?" He said: "Yes, Surat al-Baqarah and the *Mufassal* surahs." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I have married her to you on condition that you teach her and instruct her, and when Allah provides for you, you shall compensate her." So the man married her on that basis. This is an explicit text, if it is authentic, that teaching cannot be a dower. Al-Daraqutni said: 'Utbah ibn al-Sakan alone narrated it, and he is abandoned in hadith (*matruk al-hadith*).

*Fariḍatan* is in the accusative as a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥal*), meaning "obligated" (*mafrūḍatan*).

**The Fourteenth Issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿There is no blame upon you in what you mutually agree upon after the obligation﴾, that is, of an increase or decrease in the dower, for that is permissible by mutual consent after the obligation has been established. What is meant is the woman's release of the dower, or the man's payment of the full dower if he divorces her before consummation. Those who said the verse concerns *mut'ah* said: this refers to what they agreed upon regarding an increase in the duration of *mut'ah* in early Islam, for a man would marry a woman for a month for a dinar, for example. When the month ended, he might say: "Extend the term for me, and I will increase the dower for you." So it made clear that this was permissible by mutual consent.

**Part 1 of 4**

There are twenty-one issues in this verse.

**The first issue:** Allah's words, ﴿And whoever among you cannot afford the means (ṭawl) [to marry free women]...﴾ to the end of the verse. He, the Exalted, indicates a concession regarding marriage [[In manuscripts b, d, t, z, and y: "al-manākiḥ" (marriages). It is the plural of "maqʿad" and "maqāʿid." In manuscripts j, a, and j: "al-nikāḥ" (marriage).]], which is the marriage of a slave woman (amah) for one who cannot afford the ṭawl. The scholars differed over the meaning of ṭawl, and there are three opinions.

The first: it means wealth and means. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd, and Malik in al-Mudawwana. It is said: "ṭāla yaṭūlu ṭawlan" in the sense of bounty and capability, and "fulān dhū ṭawl" means he has capacity in wealth (with a fatḥah on the ṭāʾ). "Ṭūlan" (with a ḍammah on the ṭāʾ) is the opposite of shortness. Here it means the ability to pay the dowry. This is the view of most scholars, and it is the position of al-Shafiʿi, Ahmad, Ishaq, and Abu Thawr. Ahmad ibn al-Muʿadhdhal said: ʿAbd al-Malik said: "The ṭawl is anything by which one can be enabled to marry, whether cash, goods, or a debt owed by a solvent debtor." He said: "Anything that can be sold or rented out is ṭawl." He said: "A wife, two wives, or three are not ṭawl." He said: "I have heard this from Malik, may Allah be pleased with him." ʿAbd al-Malik said: "Because a wife cannot be married with, nor can one reach anything else through her, since she is not property." Malik was asked about a man who marries a slave woman while he is one who can afford the ṭawl. He said: "I think they should be separated." It was said to him: "He fears ʿanat." He said: "A whip can be used on him." Then he later relaxed this ruling. The second opinion: ṭawl is a free woman. Malik's view differed regarding whether a free woman counts as ṭawl. In al-Mudawwana he said: "A free woman is not ṭawl that prevents one from marrying a slave woman, if he does not have the means for another and fears ʿanat." In the Book of Muhammad, he said something implying that a free woman is equivalent to ṭawl. Al-Lakhmi said: "This is the apparent meaning of the Qur'an." Something similar is narrated from Ibn Habib, and Abu Hanifah also said it. This implies that whoever has a free wife may not marry a slave woman even if he lacks means and fears ʿanat, because he is seeking desire while he already has a woman. al-Tabari also held this view and argued for it. Abu Yusuf said: "ṭawl is the presence of a free wife under him. So if he has a free wife, he is one who has ṭawl, and it is not permissible for him to marry a slave woman." The third opinion: ṭawl is endurance and self-restraint for one who loves a slave woman and is infatuated with her, to the point that he cannot marry anyone else. In that case he may marry a slave woman if he does not control his desire for her and fears he will commit fornication with her, even if he has the wealth to marry a free woman. This is the view of Qatadah, al-Nakhaʿi, ʿAtaʾ, and Sufyan al-Thawri. According to this interpretation, Allah's words ﴿for him who fears ʿanat among you﴾ describe the lack of endurance. According to the first interpretation, marrying a slave woman is conditional on two things: lack of wealth, and fear of ʿanat. It is not valid unless both are present. This is the explicit position of Malik's school in al-Mudawwana, as transmitted by Ibn Nafiʿ, Ibn al-Qasim, Ibn Wahb, and Ibn Ziyad. Mutarrif and Ibn al-Majishun said: "It is not lawful for a man to marry a slave woman, and they shall not be allowed to remain married unless both conditions are met, as Allah the Exalted said." Asbagh also said so. This view is narrated from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿAtaʾ, Tawus, al-Zuhri, and Makhul, and al-Shafiʿi, Abu Thawr, Ahmad, and Ishaq also held it. Ibn al-Mundhir and others preferred it. If a man has the dowry but lacks the means for maintenance, Malik said in the Book of Muhammad: "It is not permissible for him to marry a slave woman." Asbagh said: "That is permissible, since the maintenance of a slave woman is the responsibility of her owners, if he does not take her into his household."

There is a fourth opinion regarding the verse. Mujahid said: "Among what Allah has granted this community as a blessing is the marriage of a slave woman and of a Christian woman, even if one is wealthy." Abu Hanifah also said this, and he did not require the fear of ʿanat, provided he does not have a free wife. They said: "Because anything with which one can marry a slave woman can also be used to marry a free woman. So according to this, the verse is the basis for the permissibility of marrying a slave woman without restriction." Mujahid said: "Sufyan also holds this view, because I asked him about marrying a slave woman, and he related to me..." from Ibn Abi Layla, from al-Minhal, from ʿAbbad ibn ʿAbd Allah, from ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "If a free woman is married while a slave woman is also married, the free woman has two days and the slave woman has one day." He said: "ʿAli did not see any harm in this." The proof for this view is the general meaning of Allah's words: ﴿And lawful for you is what lies beyond that﴾, and His words: ﴿And whoever among you cannot afford the means [to marry free women]... to His words: that is for him among you who fears ʿanat﴾, based on His words, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿So marry what seems good to you of women, two, three, or four. But if you fear that you will not be just, then only one﴾. All agree that a free man may marry up to four, even if he fears he will not be just. They said: "Similarly, he may marry a slave woman even if he has the means for a free woman and is not fearing ʿanat."

It has been narrated from Malik regarding one who has the means to marry a free woman that he may marry a slave woman while being able to afford a free woman. But this is a weak position from him. He also said at another time: "It is not clearly forbidden, and I permit it." The correct view is that it is not permissible for a free Muslim man to marry a non-Muslim slave woman under any circumstances. He may marry a Muslim slave woman only under the two conditions explicitly stated, as we have explained. ʿAnat means fornication. If he lacks the means and does not fear ʿanat, it is not permissible for him to marry a slave woman. Likewise, if he has the means but fears ʿanat, it is also not permissible. If he is able to afford a free Scripture-people woman (kitabiyyah)...

**The second issue:** Then, may he marry a slave woman? The scholars of our school differed on this. It was said: he may marry a slave woman, because a Muslim slave woman is not equal to a non-believing woman, and a believing slave woman is better than a polytheist free woman. Ibn al-ʿArabi preferred this view. It was also said: he may marry a Scripture-people woman, because although the slave woman surpasses her in faith, the non-believer surpasses her in freedom, and she is a wife. Furthermore, her child will be free and not enslaved, whereas the child of a slave woman will be enslaved. This is what is consistent with the basic principle of the school.

**The third issue:** The scholars differed regarding a man who marries a free woman while already having a slave woman, and the free woman did not know about the slave woman. One group said: the marriage stands. This was said by Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab, ʿAtaʾ ibn Abi Rabah, al-Shafiʿi, Abu Thawr, and the people of opinion (ahl al-raʾy), and it is narrated from ʿAli. It was also said: the free woman has the option (khiyar) if she learns of it. Then regarding what she has the option, al-Zuhri, Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab, Malik, Ahmad, and Ishaq said: she may either remain with him or separate from him. ʿAbd al-Malik said: she may either accept the marriage to the slave woman or annul it. al-Nakhaʿi said: if he marries a free woman while having a slave woman, he must separate from the slave woman, unless he has a child by her; in that case they are not separated. Masruq said: the marriage to the slave woman is annulled, because it is a matter permitted out of necessity, like carrion; when the necessity is removed, the permission is removed.

**The fourth issue:** If he has two slave women under him, and the free woman knows of one of them but not of the other, then she has the option. Do you not see that if a free woman is married to a slave woman and she accepts, then he marries another slave woman and she accepts, then he marries yet another and she objects, she has the right to object? Likewise, here, if she did not know of the two slave women but knew of one. Ibn al-Qasim said: Malik said: "We have given the free woman the option in these cases because of what the scholars before me have said."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verse 25 (part 2 of 4):

He means Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, Ibn Shihab and others. Malik said: "Were it not for what they said, I would consider it permissible, because it is permissible in the Book of Allah." If a free woman does not suffice him and he needs another, and he is unable to pay her dowry, it is permissible for him to marry a slave woman, until he reaches four, by marriage, according to the apparent meaning of the Qur'an. Ibn Wahb narrated this from Malik. Ibn al-Qasim narrated from him: "His marriage is to be annulled." Ibn al-'Arabi said: "The first view is stronger in evidence, and so it is in the Qur'an. For whoever is content with the established cause is content with the effect that follows from it, and she has no option (khiyar), because she knew that he may marry four, and she knew that if he is unable to marry a free woman he will marry a slave woman. What Allah, glorified is He, stipulated for her is as she stipulated for herself, and her knowledge is not taken into account in the stipulations of Allah, glorified and exalted is He. This is the utmost in verification on this matter and the most equitable treatment of it."

The fifth point: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿al-muhsanat﴾ means free women. This is indicated by the division between them and the slave women in His saying: (from your believing slave girls). A group said: its meaning is the chaste. This is weak, because slave women fall under it, and so they permitted marrying the slave women of the People of the Book, while they forbade the adulteresses among the believing women and the women of the Book. This is the view of Ibn Maysara and al-Suddi. The scholars differed concerning what is permissible for a free man who does not find the means (tawl) and fears sinning (al-'anat) to marry slave women. Malik, Abu Hanifa, Ibn Shihab al-Zuhri, and al-Harith al-'Ukli [[al-'Ukli: with a damma and a sukun, a nisba to 'Ukl, a clan of Tamim.]] said: he may marry four. Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman said: he may not marry more than two of the slave women. Al-Shafi'i, Abu Thawr, Ahmad and Ishaq said: he may not marry from among the slave women except one. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Masruq and a group, and they argued with His saying, exalted is He: (That is for him among you who fears sinning), and this condition disappears with marrying one.

The sixth point: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿from what your right hands possess﴾, i.e., let him marry the slave woman of another. There is no disagreement among the scholars that it is not permissible for him to marry his own slave woman, because of the conflict and difference of the rights involved.

The seventh point: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿from your young women﴾, i.e., the enslaved ones, and it is the plural of fataat (young woman). The Arabs call an enslaved male fata (young man) and an enslaved female fataa (young woman). In the authentic hadith: "Let none of you say 'my slave' or 'my slave girl,' but let him say 'my young man' and 'my young woman'," and it will come. The words fata and fataa are also applied to free persons in the beginning of youth [[In J, T and Y: "free persons."]]. As for the enslaved, the terms are applied in youth and in old age.

The eighth point: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿the believing women﴾. By this He made clear that it is not permissible to marry a slave woman from the People of the Book. This qualification is a condition according to Malik and his companions, al-Shafi'i and his companions, al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, al-Hasan al-Basri, al-Zuhri, Makhul and Mujahid. A group of the people of knowledge, among them the people of opinion (ashab al-ra'y), said: marrying a slave woman from the People of the Book is permissible. Abu 'Umar said: I know of no predecessor for their view except Abu Maysara 'Amr ibn Shurahbil, for he said: the slave women of the People of the Book are in the position of their free women. They said: His saying, (believing), is in the manner of a praiseworthy attribute and is not a condition that others be forbidden. This is like His saying, exalted is He: (But if you fear that you will not be just, then one), so if one fears that he will not be just and marries more than one, it is permissible, but the better course is not to marry. Likewise here, the better course is not to marry except a believing woman, but if he marries a non-believing woman, it is permissible. They argued by analogy (qiyas) to free women, for since His saying (believing) did not prevent marrying women of the Book among free women, likewise His saying (believing) regarding slave women does not prevent marrying the slave women of the People of the Book. Ashhab said in the Mudawwana: it is permissible for a free Muslim man to marry a slave woman who is a Christian or Jewish. The prohibition is because the husband would be superior to her in both freedom and religion together. There is no disagreement among the scholars that it is not permissible for a Muslim to marry a Magian (majusiyya) woman or an idolatress, and since marrying them is forbidden by consensus, likewise having intercourse with them by right of ownership is forbidden, by analogy and reasoning. It is narrated from Tawus, Mujahid, 'Ata' and 'Amr ibn Dinar that they said: there is no harm in marrying a Magian slave woman by right of ownership. This is an anomalous, abandoned view, to which none of the jurists of the cities (al-amsar) paid attention. They said: it is not lawful for him to have intercourse with her until she becomes Muslim [[In J and T: "among the jurists of the cities."]]. The discussion of this question has already been given in full under (al-Baqara) [[See vol. 3, p. 69.]]. And praise be to Allah.

The ninth point: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and Allah knows best your faith﴾. The meaning is that Allah is All-Knowing of the inner realities of matters, while you have only their outward appearances. All of you are the children of Adam, and the most honored of you before Allah is the most God-fearing of you. So do not disdain marrying slave women when there is necessity, even if she is recently taken captive, or she is mute, or the like. Thus in the wording there is an indication that the faith of a slave woman may be better than the faith of some free women.

The tenth point: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿some of you are from others﴾. It is a subject and predicate, like your saying "Zayd is in the house." The meaning is: you are the children of Adam. It was also said: you are believers. And it was said: there is inversion in the speech, and the meaning is: "And whoever among you is unable to marry the believing free women, let him marry some of you from others: this one is the young woman of that one, and that one is the young woman of this one." So "some of you" on this reading is in the nominative, governed by its verb, which is "let him marry." The purpose of this statement is to prepare the souls of the Arabs, who used to find the child of a slave woman repugnant and would revile him, calling him a hajin [[Al-hajin: one whose father is Arab and whose mother is not a free woman. Al-Mubarrad: the child of an Arab from a non-Arab woman.]]. When the Law permitted marrying them, they knew that this disparagement had no meaning. The slave woman is lowered in status, so it is not permissible for a free man to marry her except in necessity, because it causes the child to be enslaved, and because the slave woman is not free to devote herself to her husband permanently, since she is occupied with serving her master.

The eleventh point: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿so marry them with the permission of their people﴾, i.e., with the guardianship and permission of their owners. Likewise a slave may not marry except with the permission of his master, because the slave is property with no authority of his own, and his whole person is wholly engaged. But the difference between them is that if a slave marries without his master's permission, and the master then approves, the marriage is valid. This is the position of Malik and the people of opinion, and it is the view of al-Hasan al-Basri, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, Shurayh and al-Sha'bi. But if a slave woman marries without the permission of her people, the marriage is annulled, and it is not validated by the master's approval, because the deficiency of femininity in a slave woman prevents the contract from taking effect at all. A group said: if a slave marries without his master's permission, his marriage is annulled. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, al-Awza'i and Dawud ibn 'Ali. They said: the master's approval is not valid if he is not present, because a void contract cannot be validated by approval, but if he wishes to marry, he must begin again in the proper way. The scholars of the Muslims have agreed that it is not permissible for a slave to marry without his master's permission. Ibn 'Umar used to regard a slave who did this as an adulterer and would apply the hadd punishment to him, and this is the view of Abu Thawr. 'Abd al-Razzaq mentioned, from 'Abd Allah [[He is Ibn Hafs ibn 'Asim ibn 'Umar ibn al-Khattab.]] ibn 'Umar, from Nafi', from Ibn 'Umar, and from Ma'mar, from Ayyub, from Nafi', from Ibn 'Umar, that he took a slave who had married without his permission, flogged him with the hadd, separated them, and annulled her dowry. He said: Ibn Jurayj informed us, from Musa ibn 'Uqba, that he informed him, from Nafi', from Ibn 'Umar, that he regarded a slave's marriage without the permission of his guardian as zina, and held that the hadd applies to him, and he punished those who had married them. He said: Ibn Jurayj informed us, from 'Abd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn 'Aqil, who said: I heard Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah say: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Any slave who marries without his master's permission is an adulterer."
