And from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him: it is a forbidden marriage; if he marries with his master's permission, then divorce is in the hand of the one who makes the private part lawful. Abu 'Umar said: On this is the view of the group of jurists of the cities, in the Hijaz and Iraq. Nothing contrary is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, except that divorce is in the hand of the master. Jabir ibn Zayd and a group followed him in this. It is among the scholars an anomaly not to be relied upon. I think Ibn 'Abbas interpreted in this way the saying of Allah, exalted is He: (Allah strikes a parable: a slave owned, who has power over nothing) [[See vol. 10, p. 146.]]. The scholars have agreed that the marriage of a slave is permissible with his master's permission. If he contracts an invalid marriage, al-Shafi'i said: if he has not consummated it, she is owed nothing; if he has consummated it, then when he is freed he owes the dowry. This is the correct position in his school. It is also the view of Abu Yusuf and Muhammad, who said: no dowry is owed by him until he is freed. Abu Hanifa said: if he has consummated with her, then she is owed the dowry. Malik and al-Shafi'i said: if a slave is jointly owned by two men, and one of them permits him to marry, and he marries, the marriage is void. But if a slave woman informs her people of her wish to marry and they give permission, the marriage is valid, even if she does not conduct the contract herself, but appoints someone to conclude it for her.

The twelfth point: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and give them their wages﴾ is evidence for the obligation of the dowry in marriage, and that it belongs to the slave woman.

(According to what is customary) means according to the Law and the Sunna. This implies that they have more right to their dowries than their masters, and this is the view of Malik. He said in the Book of Pledges (Kitab al-Ruhun): the master may not take the dowry of his slave woman and leave her without provision. Al-Shafi'i said: the dowry belongs to the master, because it is a return (iwad), and so it does not belong to the slave woman. Its basis is the permission of usufruct in the owned person, and it was mentioned only because the dowry became due on account of her. Al-Qadi Isma'il mentioned in his Ahkam: some Iraqis claimed that if a man marries his slave woman to his slave, there is no dowry. This contradicts the Book and the Sunna, and he elaborated on it at length.

The thirteenth point: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿al-muhsanat﴾, i.e., chaste women. Al-Kisa'i read (muhsinat) with a kasra on the sad in the whole Qur'an, except in His saying, exalted is He: (and married women from among women). The rest read it with a fatha throughout the Qur'an. Then He said: (not fornicators), i.e., not prostitutes, that is, not openly committing unlawful intercourse, because in the Jahiliyya there were prostitutes openly, and they had banners raised, like the banner of the farrier.

﴿Nor those who take secret lovers﴾: friends for the purpose of illicit intercourse. The singular is *khidn* or *khadin*, meaning one who keeps company with you (*yukhadinuka*), and a man is *khudanah* when he takes *akhdan*, that is, companions. This is related from Abu Zayd. It is also said that *al-musafihah* is the woman who openly commits fornication, meaning the one who hires herself out for that purpose, and that *dhat al-khidn* is the one who commits fornication in secret. It is also said that *al-musafihah* is the one who is freely available to all, and *dhat al-khidn* is the one who commits fornication with a single man. The Arabs used to condemn open fornication but did not condemn taking secret lovers. Then Islam abolished all of that, and in this regard the words of the Exalted were revealed: ﴿And do not approach immoralities, whether apparent or hidden﴾ [6:151]. This is related from Ibn Abbas and others.

The fourteenth issue: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿When they are chaste﴾ [4:25]. The reading of Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i is with a *fath* on the hamzah (*uhsinna*), while the rest read it with a *damm*. With the *fath* its meaning is "they embraced Islam," and with the *damm* its meaning is "they were married." If a Muslim slave-girl commits fornication, she is lashed half the punishment of a free woman. According to the majority, including Ibn Mas'ud, al-Sha'bi, al-Zuhri and others, her *ihsan* is her Islam. On this view, a disbelieving woman who commits fornication is not subject to the prescribed punishment (*hadd*), and this is the view of al-Shafi'i as transmitted by Ibn al-Mundhir. Others said: her *ihsan* is her marriage to a free man. On this view, if a Muslim slave-girl who has not been married commits fornication, there is no prescribed punishment for her. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan and Qatadah, and it is related from Ibn Abbas and Abu al-Darda', and Abu Ubayd also held this view. He said: In the hadith of Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, he was asked about the punishment of a slave-girl, and he said: "A slave-girl threw her *farwah* (scalp) from behind the house." Al-Asma'i said: *al-farwah* is the skin of the head. Abu Ubayd said: He did not mean the scalp itself, and how could she throw the skin of her head from behind the house? Rather, this is a metaphor. He meant by *al-farwah* the veil, saying that she has no veil or covering, and that she goes out to every place her family sends her to, unable to refrain from that, so she ends up where she cannot refrain from debauchery, such as tending sheep, paying the tax, and the like. So it seems that he held that there is no prescribed punishment for her if she commits fornication, for this reason.

A group said: her *ihsan* is marriage, except that the prescribed punishment is obligatory on the Muslim slave-girl who is not married, by the Sunnah, as in the Sahih of al-Bukhari and Muslim, that it was said: "O Messenger of Allah, what about a slave-girl who commits fornication and is not *muhsanah*?" So he made the prescribed punishment obligatory for her. Al-Zuhri said: The married one is punished by the Qur'an, and the Muslim unmarried one is punished by the hadith. Al-Qadi Isma'il said, regarding the view of those who say that ﴿when they are chaste﴾ means "embraced Islam": this is far-fetched, because faith was already mentioned concerning them in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿from your believing slave-girls﴾ [4:25]. As for those who say that ﴿when they are chaste﴾ means "were married," and that there is no prescribed punishment for a slave-girl until she is married, they followed the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, and I suppose they did not know this hadith. Our position is that if a slave-girl commits fornication after being *uhsinat* (made chaste by marriage), she is lashed by the Book of Allah, and if she commits fornication without being *uhsinat*, she is lashed by the hadith of the Prophet, peace be upon him, and there is no stoning for her, because stoning cannot be halved. Abu Umar said: The apparent meaning of the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, requires that there be no prescribed punishment for a slave-girl, even if she is Muslim, except after marriage. Then the Sunnah came with her lashing even if she is not *uhsinat*, and that was an additional clarification. I say: The back of a believer is a sanctuary that may not be violated except by certainty, and there is no certainty where there is disagreement, were it not for what has come in the authentic Sunnah about lashing in this matter. And Allah knows best. Abu Thawr said, as related by Ibn al-Mundhir: Even if they disagreed about stoning them, both are stoned if they are *muhsan* (married). And if there is a consensus, then consensus takes precedence.

The fifteenth issue: The scholars differed about who establishes the prescribed punishment on them. Ibn Shihab said: The Sunnah has passed that the master's household lashes the slave and the slave-girl for fornication, unless their matter is brought to the ruler, in which case no one may act on his behalf without authorization. This is what is implied by his saying, peace be upon him: "If the slave-girl of one of you commits fornication, let him impose the prescribed punishment on her." Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said in his sermon: "O people, impose the prescribed punishment on your slaves, whether they are married or not, for a slave-girl of the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, committed fornication, and he commanded me to lash her, but she had recently given birth, so I feared that if I lashed her I would kill her. I mentioned that to the Prophet, peace be upon him, and he said: 'You did well.'" Muslim transmitted it as a statement of Ali (mawquf), and al-Nasa'i traced it back to the Prophet, saying in it: The Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, said: "Establish the prescribed punishments on what your right hands possess, whether they are married or not." This is explicit about masters establishing the prescribed punishments on their slaves, whether married or not.

Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, said: A master lashes his slave for fornication, drinking wine and slander, if witnesses testify to that before him, but he does not cut off the hand for theft; only the imam cuts it off. This is also the view of al-Layth. It is related from a group of Companions that they established the prescribed punishments on their slaves, among them Ibn Umar and Anas, and there is no Companion who disagreed with them. It is related from Ibn Abi Layla that he said: "I met the remnants of the Ansar who would lash their slave-girls in their gatherings if they committed fornication." Abu Hanifah said: The ruler, not the master, establishes the prescribed punishments on slaves and slave-girls for fornication and all other prescribed punishments, and this is the view of al-Hasan ibn Hayy. Al-Shafi'i said: The master lashes him for every prescribed punishment and cuts off the limb, and he cited the hadiths we have mentioned. Al-Thawri and al-Awza'i said: He lashes him for fornication, and this is what the hadiths imply. And Allah knows best. The discussion of exiling slaves has already passed in this surah.

The sixteenth issue: If a slave-girl commits fornication and then is freed before her master imposes the prescribed punishment on her, the master has no authority to impose it, and the ruler lashes her if that is established before him. If she commits fornication and then marries, her master has no right to lash her either, for the right of the husband, since that may harm him. This is the position of Malik when the husband is not owned by the master. If he is owned by the master, then the master may do so, because their right is his right.

The seventeenth issue: If the slave confesses to fornication and the master denies it, the prescribed punishment is obligatory on the slave because of his confession, and the master's denial is disregarded. This is agreed upon among the scholars. Likewise for the *mudabbar* (slave freed upon the master's death), the *umm walad* (mother of a child by her master), the *mukatab* (slave under a contract of manumission), and the partly freed slave. They also agreed that if a slave-girl commits fornication and is then freed, she receives the punishment of slave-girls. If she commits fornication while not knowing she has been freed, and then learns of it after she has been punished, the remainder of the free woman's punishment is imposed on her. This was mentioned by Ibn al-Mundhir.

The eighteenth issue: They differed about the master's pardon of his slave or slave-girl if they commit fornication. Al-Hasan al-Basri used to say: He may pardon. Others said: He has no option but to establish the prescribed punishment, just as the ruler has no option to pardon a prescribed punishment once he knows of it; likewise the master has no option to pardon his slave-girl once the prescribed punishment is due to her. This is the position of Abu Thawr. Ibn al-Mundhir said: And this is what we say.

The nineteenth issue: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿then upon them is half the punishment prescribed for the chaste women﴾ [4:25], that is, the lashing. By "the chaste women" here is meant the virgin free women, because the married woman is subject to stoning, and stoning cannot be halved. The virgin is called *muhsanah* even though she is not married, because *ihsan* applies to her, just as it is said of a sacrificial animal "a sacrifice" before it is slaughtered, and as a cow is called "a plougher" before it ploughs. It is also said that *al-muhsanat* means the married women, because on them, according to the hadith, lashing and stoning are imposed, and stoning cannot be halved, so upon them is half the lashing. The purpose in reducing their punishment is that they are weaker than free women. It is said that they do not reach their desires as free women do. It is also said, because punishment is due in proportion to favour. Do you not see that Allah, Exalted is He, said to the wives of the Prophet, peace be upon him: ﴿O wives of the Prophet, whoever of you commits a flagrant immorality, the punishment will be doubled for her, double﴾ [33:30]. Since their favour was greater, He made their punishment more severe. Likewise, since the favour of slave-girls is less, their punishment is less. He mentioned in the verse the punishment of slave-girls specifically and did not mention that of slaves, but the punishment of slaves and slave-girls is the same: fifty lashes for fornication, and forty for slander and drinking wine. This is because the punishment of the slave-girl was reduced only due to the reduction caused by slavery, so male slaves are included in that by the reason of being owned, just as slave-girls were included in his saying, peace be upon him: "Whoever frees his share in a slave" (*shirkan*, meaning a portion and share in him). This is what the scholars call analogy in the sense of the original (*qiyas fi ma'na al-asl*). From it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women﴾ [24:4], the verse, from which the chaste men are included with certainty, as will be explained, if Allah wills, in the surah of *al-Nur*.

The twentieth issue: The scholars agreed that selling a fornicating slave-girl is not an obligatory duty upon her owner, even though they chose that for him, because of his saying, peace be upon him: "If the slave-girl of one of you commits fornication, and her fornication is established, let him lash her with the prescribed punishment, and not reproach her. Then if she commits fornication again, let him lash her with the prescribed punishment and not reproach her. Then if she commits fornication a third time, and her fornication is established, let him sell her even for a rope of hair." Muslim transmitted it from Abu Hurayrah. The Zahiris held that selling her becomes obligatory at the fourth offence, among them Dawud and others, based on His saying: "let him sell her," and his saying: "then sell her even for a braid." Ibn Shihab said: I do not know whether it is after the third or the fourth. The *dafir* is the rope. When he sells her, the buyer is informed of her fornication, because it is a defect, and it is not lawful to conceal it. If it is said: if the purpose of the hadith is to remove the fornicator, and the seller is obliged to inform the buyer of her fornication, then no one should buy her, since we have been commanded to remove her. The answer is that she is property, and property must not be wasted, because wasting property is forbidden; nor is she to be left unrestrained, because that would encourage her to fornicate and enable it; nor is she to be kept confined permanently, because that would deprive her master of her benefit. So only selling her remains. Perhaps the second master will protect her by intercourse, or be extremely careful and prevent her from that. In sum, when owners change, her circumstances vary. And Allah knows best.

The twenty-first issue: His saying, ﴿And that you be patient is better for you﴾, meaning that patience in remaining unmarried (al-'uzba) is better than marrying a slave woman (amah), because it leads to the enslavement of the child, and restraining oneself and being patient in noble character is more fitting than baseness.[[In manuscripts B and D: al-nadhala.]] It is related from Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Whichever free man marries a slave woman, half of him has been enslaved." He means that his child becomes a slave, so patience in refraining from that is better, so that the child does not become a slave. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "Marrying a slave woman is nothing but near to fornication,"[[The wording of Sa'id ibn Jubayr as in Tafsir al-Tabari: "ma izlahafa nakih al-amah 'an al-zina illa qalilan." That is: it does not recede or distance itself.]] and Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And that you be patient is better for you﴾, meaning, refraining from marrying slave women. In the Sunan of Ibn Majah, from al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim, who said: "I heard Anas ibn Malik say: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Whoever wishes to meet Allah pure and purified, let him marry free women.'" Abu Ishaq al-Tha'labi also narrated it from the hadith of Yunus ibn Mirdas, who was a servant of Anas, and he added: Abu Hurayrah said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Free women are the goodness of the household, and slave women are the ruin of the household'" or he said "the corruption of the household."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verse 26:

﴿Allah desires to make clear to you and to guide you to the ways (sunan) of those before you, and to turn to you in forgiveness. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾ (4:26)

That is: to make clear to you the affair of your religion and the welfare of your affairs, and what is lawful for you and what is unlawful for you. This indicates that no incident is devoid of a ruling of Allah the Exalted. From this is His saying: ﴿We have not neglected anything in the Book﴾ [See vol. 6, p. 420 and vol. 7, p. 19.] as will come. Then He said after this: ﴿Allah desires to lighten (yukhaffifa) for you﴾, so this (with "an") came, while the first (with the lam). Al-Farra' said: The Arabs interchange the lam of kay (in order that) and an, so they use the lam that carries the meaning of kay in the place of an with verbs of wanting and commanding, so they say: "I wanted that you do," and "I wanted in order that you do," because both seek the future. It is not permitted to say "I thought in order that you do," because you say "I thought that you had stood." In the Revelation: ﴿And I have been commanded to be just among you﴾ [See vol. 16, p. 13.]

﴿And we have been commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds﴾ [See vol. 6, p. 420 and vol. 7, p. 19.]

﴿They desire to extinguish the light of Allah with their mouths﴾ [See vol. 18, p. 85.]

﴿They desire to extinguish the light of Allah﴾ [See vol. 8, p. 121.] The poet [He is Kuthayyir 'Azza.] said:

"I want to forget her remembrance, but it is as though Layla appears to me on every path."

That is, he wants that I forget. Al-Nahhas said: Al-Zajjaj rejected this view and said: If the lam had the meaning of "an," another lam would enter upon it, as you say: "I came in order that you honor me," then you say "I came in order that you honor me" (li-kay tukrimani). And he recited to us:

"I wanted, in order that people know that it is the trousers of Qays, and the delegations are witnesses."

[The line is by Qays ibn 'Ubada, and after it:

"And lest they say: Qays was absent, and this is the trousers of 'Adi, which Thamud spun."

Ibn Sayyidah said: It has reached us that Qays vied with a Roman before Mu'awiya or another of the commanders, so Qays stripped off his trousers and threw them to the Roman, and they were more than enough for him, so he recited these two verses, apologizing for throwing away his trousers in the assembled gathering.

(From al-Lisan, root s-r-l.)]

He said: The implied meaning is "His desire is to make clear to you." Al-Nahhas said: Some reciters went further with this until they called it "lam of an." It was also said: the meaning is: Allah desires this for the sake of making clear to you.

﴿And to guide you to the ways (sunan) of those before you﴾ — that is, from the people of truth. It was also said: the meaning of "to guide you" is to make clear to you the paths of those before you, from among the people of truth and the people of falsehood. Some scholars of reasoning said: In this is evidence that everything Allah prohibited before this verse for us has also been prohibited for those before us. Al-Nahhas said: This is an error, because the meaning would be: "and He makes clear to you the affair of those before you who used to avoid what was forbidden," and it may be "and He makes clear to you as He made clear to the prophets before you," so it does not point to this specifically. It is said: His saying "Allah desires" is the beginning of the narrative, meaning: Allah desires to make clear to you the manner of obeying Him.

﴿And to guide you﴾ — to acquaint you ﴿with the ways of those before you﴾, that when they abandoned My command, how I punished them; and if you do that, I will not punish you, but I will turn to you in forgiveness. [In manuscript C: "If you do that, I will punish you." And in manuscript Ya: "I will not requite you."]

﴿And Allah is All-Knowing﴾ — of who repents — ﴿All-Wise﴾ — in accepting repentance.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿Allah desires to turn to you in forgiveness﴾ is a subject (mubtada') and predicate (khabar). The word (أَنْ) (an) is in the accusative position governed by (يُرِيدُ) (yurīdu, "desires"). Likewise, ﴿Allah desires to lighten [the burden] for you﴾: (أَنْ يُخَفِّفَ) (an yukhaffifa) is in the accusative position governed by (يُرِيدُ) (yurīdu). The meaning is: He desires your repentance, that is, He accepts it, so He pardons your sins, and He desires to lighten [the burden] for you.

It was said: this applies to all the rulings of the Law (sharī'ah), and this is the sound view. It was also said: the intended lightening is the permission to marry a slave woman, meaning: since We knew your weakness in refraining from women, We lightened [the burden] for you by permitting slave women. This was reported by Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and Tawus. Tawus said: "A person is never weaker in anything than in the matter of women."

The scholars differed in identifying those who follow their desires. Mujahid said: they are the fornicators. Al-Suddi said: they are the Jews and the Christians. A group said: they are specifically the Jews, because they wanted the Muslims to follow them in marrying paternal sisters. Ibn Zayd said: it is general, and this is the most correct view.

Al-mayl (الْمَيْلُ) (inclination) means deviating from the path of uprightness. Whoever is upon it wishes that his peers were upon it too, so that he would not be subjected to blame.[[In ṭ and wāw: "And in its meaning it was said:" then a blank in ī. He did not bring the quoted speech, and perhaps he intended to say: (وَخُلِقَ الْإِنْسانُ) (wa khuliqa al-insānu, "and man was created weak") — the verse is a circumstantial clause (jumlah ḥāliyyah).]]

The Almighty's saying: ﴿and man was created weak﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). The meaning is that his desire inclines him, and his appetite and anger overpower him. This is the utmost weakness, so he needs lightening. Tawus said: this refers specifically to the matter of women. It is reported from Ibn Abbas that he recited (وَخَلَقَ الْإِنْسَانَ ضَعِيفًا) (wa khalaqa al-insāna ḍa'īfan), meaning: and Allah created man weak, that is, unable to refrain from women. Ibn al-Musayyib said: "Eighty years have come upon me, one of my eyes has gone, and I see with the other, and my companion is blind and deaf" — meaning his penis — "and I fear the temptation of women." Similar to this was reported from Ubadah ibn al-Samit, may Allah be pleased with him. Ubadah said: "Do you not see that I cannot stand up except with support, and I do not eat except what is softened for me?" — Yahya said: meaning softened and warmed. "My companion has died long ago" — Yahya said: meaning his penis. "And it does not please me that I be alone with a woman who is not lawful to me, even if I owned all that the sun rises upon, for fear that Satan would come to me and stir it against me. Indeed, it has neither hearing nor sight!"

The Almighty's saying: ﴿O you who have believed, do not consume one another's wealth unjustly, except [in the case of] trade by mutual consent among you. And do not kill yourselves. Indeed, Allah is ever Merciful to you﴾

"And it does not please me that I be alone with a woman who is not lawful to me, even if I owned all that the sun rises upon, for fear that Satan would come to me and stir it against me. The Almighty's saying: ﴿O you who have believed, do not consume one another's wealth unjustly, except [in the case of] trade by mutual consent among you. And do not kill yourselves. Indeed, Allah is ever Merciful to you﴾

**The first issue:** Allah's words ﴿by false means﴾, meaning without right. The ways this occurs are many, as we have explained, and we mentioned them earlier in al-Baqarah [[See vol. 2, p. 338.]]. Among the ways of consuming wealth "by false means" is the *bay' al-'urban* (a sale with a down payment, a deposit sale). This is when someone takes your merchandise, or rents your animal, and gives you a dirham or more, on the condition that if he buys the goods or rides the animal, the payment counts toward the price or the rent, and if he abandons the purchase or the rental, the money is yours to keep. This is not valid and not permissible according to the majority of jurists of the major cities, from the Hijaz and Iraq, because it falls under gambling, uncertainty (*gharar*), and risk, and under consuming wealth by false means without any exchange or gift, and this is null by consensus (*ijma'*). A *bay' al-'urban* of this form is annulled (*mafsukh*) when it is concluded in this manner, both before and after possession. The goods are returned if they still exist; if they have been lost, their value on the day of possession is returned.

It has been reported from a group including Ibn Sirin, Mujahid, Nafi' ibn 'Abd al-Harith, and Zayd ibn Aslam that they permitted the *bay' al-'urban* in the form we have described. Zayd ibn Aslam used to say: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) permitted it." Abu 'Umar (Ibn 'Abd al-Barr) said: "This is not known from the Prophet (ﷺ) through any sound chain. 'Abd al-Razzaq mentioned it only from al-Aslami, from Zayd ibn Aslam, as a *mursal* report (one whose chain omits a companion). Such a report, and others like it, are not a proof."

It is possible that the permitted *bay' al-'urban* is the one interpreted by Malik and the jurists who follow him, namely that the buyer gives a deposit and then counts that deposit toward the price if he chooses to complete the sale. There is no disagreement about its permissibility from Malik and others.

In the *Muwatta'* of Malik, from a trustworthy narrator in his view, from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) "forbade the *bay' al-'urban*." Abu 'Umar said: "People have spoken about the trustworthy narrator in Malik's chain at this point, and the most plausible thing said about him is that Malik took it from Ibn Lahi'ah, or from Ibn Wahb from Ibn Lahi'ah, because Ibn Lahi'ah heard it from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb and transmitted it from him. Ibn Wahb and others narrated it from Ibn Lahi'ah. Ibn Lahi'ah is one of the scholars, except that it is said his books were burned, and so when he narrated afterwards from memory he made errors. What Ibn al-Mubarak and Ibn Wahb narrated from him is considered sound by some, while others weaken all his hadith. He had broad knowledge and narrated much, but his condition among them is as we have described."

**The second issue:** Allah's words ﴿except that it be trade by mutual consent among you﴾. This is a disjunctive exception (*istithna' munqati'*), meaning: "but rather, trade by mutual consent." Trade (*tijarah*) is buying and selling. This is like Allah's words ﴿Allah has permitted trade and forbidden usury﴾, as has already been discussed [[See vol. 3, pp. 356 and 371.]].

It was recited as *tijarah* with a *raf'* (nominative), meaning "except that a trade should occur." On this reading Sibawayh recited the verse:

*Ransom for the Banu Dhuhl ibn Shaybān is my she-camel, on a day of dark clouds, dappled and grey-white.*

This is called *kana al-tammah* (complete *kana*), because it is complete with its subject and does not need an object. It was also recited as *tijaratan* with a *nasb* (accusative). Then *kana* is *naqisah* (incomplete), because it is not complete with the noun alone without the predicate. Its noun is then a pronoun hidden within it. If you prefer, you can supply it, meaning: "except that the wealth be wealth of trade." The modifying word (*mudaf*) is omitted and the modified word (*mudaf ilayhi*) takes its place. This has been mentioned before, and among its instances is Allah's words ﴿and if one is in hardship﴾ [[See vol. 3, pp. 356 and 371.]].

**The third issue:** Allah's words ﴿trade﴾. In the language, *tijarah* refers to exchange (*mu'awadah*). From this is the reward that the Creator, glory be to Him, gives the servant in exchange for righteous deeds, which are part of His own act. Allah says: ﴿O you who believe, shall I guide you to a trade that will save you from a painful punishment?﴾ [[See vol. 18, p. 86.]] And He says: ﴿They hope for a trade that will never perish﴾ [[See vol. 14, p. 345.]]. And He says: ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their properties﴾ [[See vol. 8, p. 266.]], and the verse continues. He called all of that buying and selling in a figurative sense, by analogy with the contracts of exchange and sale through which aims are achieved.

These are of two kinds. One is turning over wealth within the home town without moving or travelling. This is hoarding and monopoly (*tarabbus* and *ihtikar*), which the notable people have shunned and the men of high stakes have avoided. The second is turning over wealth through travel and carrying it to the cities. This is more suited to people of honour and more beneficial in its usefulness, but it carries greater risk and greater uncertainty.

It has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed, the traveller and his wealth are on the brink of ruin (*qalat*), except what Allah protects." This means: at risk. It was said: "In the Torah: O son of Adam, travel, and I will create sustenance for you."

Al-Tabari said: "This verse is the clearest proof against the corruption of the view of those Sufis who deny seeking sustenance through trade and crafts, when Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, says: ﴿O you who believe, do not consume one another's wealth by false means, except that it be trade by mutual consent among you﴾, which is an acquisition that Allah has made lawful for them. See al-Tabari's commentary on this verse, and it will come again on p. 156." ......

**The fourth issue:** Know that every exchange (*mu'awadah*) is a trade, whatever form the consideration takes. However, the words ﴿by false means﴾ exclude from it every consideration that is not lawful in the Shari'ah, whether it involves usury, uncertainty, or the stipulation of an invalid consideration such as wine, pork, and the like. Also excluded is every permissible contract in which there is no consideration, such as a loan, charity, and a gift not given in expectation of reward. The contracts of voluntary giving (*tabarru'at*) are permitted by other evidences mentioned in their places. These are two extremes on which there is agreement.

Also excluded is your brother's invitation to you to eat his food. Abu Dawud narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning Allah's words ﴿Do not consume one another's wealth by false means, except that it be trade by mutual consent among you﴾: a man used to feel uneasy about eating at someone's house after this verse was revealed. This was abrogated (*nusikha*) by the other verse in Surah al-Nur, where He says: ﴿There is no blame upon the blind, nor upon the lame, nor upon the sick, nor upon yourselves that you eat from your own houses﴾, up to His words ﴿or separately﴾ [[See vol. 12, p. 311.]]. A wealthy man would invite a relative to his food, and the guest would say: "I feel a sin (*tajannuh*, meaning *haraj*, blame) in eating from it," and the host would say: "The poor man has more right to it than I do." So it was made lawful for them to eat from what the name of Allah has been mentioned over, and the food of the People of the Book was made lawful.

**The fifth issue:** If you buy something from the market, and its owner says to you before the purchase: "Taste it, and you are free to do so," then do not eat from it, because his permission to eat is for the sake of the purchase. Perhaps no sale will take place between you, and then eating it would be doubtful. However, if he describes it to you and you buy it, but do not find it to be as described, then you have the option (*khiyar*).

**The sixth issue:** The majority hold that cheating (*ghabn*) in trade is permissible. For example, a man may sell a jewel for a dirham while it is worth a hundred. This is permissible, and the owner who is sound in ownership may sell his large wealth for a trivial small amount. There is no disagreement among scholars about this when the amount is known, just as a gift is permissible if one is given something. They disagreed when the amount is not known. Some said: whether he knew the value or not, it is permissible if he is mature (*rashid*), free, and of age. Another group said: if the cheating exceeds one third, it is rejected. Only what is close and customary in trade is permitted, but the excessive and gross is not. Ibn Wahb, one of Malik's companions, said so, may Allah have mercy on him.

The first view is more sound, because of the Prophet's (peace be upon him) words in the hadith about the female slave who committed adultery: "let him sell her, even for a braid of hair," and his words (peace be upon him) to 'Umar: "Do not buy it, even if he gives it to you for one dirham," meaning the horse. His words (peace be upon him) also: "Leave people, and Allah will provide some of them with sustenance through others." And his words (peace be upon him): "A townsman should not sell for a desert dweller." The townsman (*hadir*) is one who resides in cities and villages, and the desert dweller (*badi*) is one who lives in the desert. What is forbidden is that a desert Bedouin comes to town carrying food, intending to rush to sell it cheaply, and the townsman says to him: "Leave it with me, and I will sell it at a higher price." This practice is forbidden because it harms others. A sale that takes place with such overpricing is valid. Ibn 'Abbas was asked about the meaning of the hadith, and he said: "It means he should not act as a broker (*simsar*) for him."

(from Ibn al-Athir) — and there is no distinction in it between a little and a lot, one third or otherwise. Seventh: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿except that it be trade by mutual consent from among you﴾. That is, by consent. Yet it came in the form of mufa'alah (a reciprocal form), since trade is between two parties. The scholars differed concerning mutual consent (tarada). One group said: its completion and its being binding is by the parting of the bodies (iftiraq al-abdan) after the concluding of the sale, or by one of the two saying to his companion, "Choose," and he replies, "I have chosen"; and that too is after the contract, so it becomes binding as well even if they have not parted. This was said by a group of the Companions and the Successors, and al-Shafi'i, al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, al-Layth, Ibn 'Uyayna, Ishaq and others held it. Al-Awza'i said: "The two have the option (khiyar) as long as they have not parted, except for three kinds of sale: the sale of the ruler of the spoils (of war), joint ownership in inheritance, and partnership in trade. When he concludes the deal with him in these three, the sale is binding and they have no option in it." He also said: "The limit of parting is that each of them withdraws from the other out of sight, and this is the view of the people of Syria." Al-Layth said: "Parting is that one of them stands up." Ahmad ibn Hanbal used to say: "They have the option forever as long as they have not parted with their bodies, whether or not they say, 'We have chosen,' until they separate bodily from their place." al-Shafi'i also said this, and it is the sound view in this matter because of the hadiths narrated on it. It is also reported from Ibn 'Umar, Abu Barzah and a group of scholars.

Malik and Abu Hanifa said: the completion of the sale is that the sale is concluded by the tongues, so the contract becomes binding by that and the option is removed. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: the meaning of his saying in the hadith, "The two parties to a sale have the option as long as they have not parted," is that if the seller says, "I have sold you," he may retract as long as the buyer has not said, "I have accepted." This is the view of Abu Hanifa, and it is also the explicit position of the school of Malik, related by Ibn Khuwayz Mandad. It was also said: he may not retract. This has been discussed in (al-Baqarah) [see vol. 3, p. 357].

The first group argued with what is established in the hadith of Samurah ibn Jundab, Abu Barzah, Ibn 'Umar, 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As, Abu Hurayrah, Hakim ibn Hizam and others, from the Prophet ﷺ: "The two parties to a sale have the option as long as they have not parted, or one of them says to the other, 'Choose.'" Ayyub related it from Nafi' from Ibn 'Umar. So his saying, peace be upon him, in this narration, "or one of them says to his companion, 'Choose,'" is the meaning of the other narration, "except a sale of option." And his saying, "unless their sale was by option," and the like, means that one of them says to his companion after the completion of the sale, "Choose whether to enforce the sale or to void it." If he chooses to uphold the sale, the sale is complete between them even if they have not parted. Ibn 'Umar, who was the narrator of the hadith, when he concluded a sale with someone and wished to enforce it, would walk a short distance and then return. In the principles (of jurisprudence) it is said: whoever narrates a hadith is the most knowledgeable of its interpretation, especially the Companions, since they know the wording best and were closest to the circumstances.

Abu Dawud and al-Daraqutni related from Abu al-Wadi' (the name is pronounced with a fatha on the waw and a light kasra on the consonant, with hamza: 'Abbad ibn Nusayb) [from al-Tahdhib] who said: "We were on a journey in an army, and a man came with a horse. A man from among us said to him, 'Will you sell this horse for this boy?' He said, 'Yes,' and he sold it, then spent the night with us. When morning came, he got up to his horse, and our companion said to him, 'What is wrong with you and the horse? Did you not sell it to me?' He said, 'I have no need of this sale.' He said, 'That is your affair; you did sell it to me.' The people said to them both, 'This is Abu Barzah, companion of the Messenger of God ﷺ; go to him.' So they came to him, and he said to them, 'Are you both content with the judgment of the Messenger of God ﷺ?' They said, 'Yes.' He said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said, 'The two parties to a sale have the option as long as they have not parted,' and I do not see that you two have parted." These two Companions knew the point of the hadith and acted by its requirement; indeed, this was the practice of the Companions. Salim said: Ibn 'Umar said: "When we made a bargain, each of us had the option as long as the two parties to the bargain had not separated." He said: "I made a bargain with 'Uthman, and I sold him my property in al-Wadi for property of his in Khaybar. When I sold it to him, I began to back away, fearing that 'Uthman would ask me to cancel the sale before I parted from him." Al-Daraqutni related it, then said: "The lexicographers distinguished between faraqtu (light) and farraqtu (intensive): with the light form for speech, and with the intensive for bodies." Ahmad ibn Yahya Tha'lab said: Ibn al-A'rabi told me from al-Mufaddal, who said: "One says faraqtu bayna al-kalamayn (light form) and they separated (iftaraqa); faraqtu bayna ithnayn (intensive) and they separated. So separation (iftiraq) is used for speech, and parting (tafarruq) for bodies."

The Malikis argued with what has been explained earlier in the verse of debt, and with His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Fulfil the contracts﴾ [see vol. 6, p. 31]. These two have contracted, and in this hadith there is a nullification of fulfilling contracts. They said: parting may also occur by speech, as in the contract of marriage and the occurrence of divorce, which Allah has called separation (firaq). Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿But if they separate, Allah will make each independent from His abundance﴾ [see p. 408 of this part]. And He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And do not be like those who became divided﴾ [see vol. 4, p. 166]. And he, peace be upon him, said: "My community will split" (taftariqu ummati), and he did not say "in their bodies." Al-Daraqutni and others related from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb who said: "I heard Shu'ayb say: I heard 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr say: I heard the Prophet ﷺ say: 'Whoever buys something from a man, each of them has the option until they part from their place, unless it is a transaction with option; then it is not lawful for one of them to leave his companion for fear that he will cancel it.'" They said: this indicates that the sale was completed between them before parting, because cancellation (iqalah) is valid only in sales that have been completed. They said: the meaning of his saying, "The two parties to a sale have the option," is that the two bargainers (mutasawimani) have the option as long as they have not concluded; once they conclude, the option is void.

The answer: as for what they relied on regarding parting by speech, the intended meaning there is the bodies, as we explained in (Al 'Imran); and even if it is valid in some contexts, it is not valid in this context. Its explanation: tell us, the words by which the gathering occurred and the sale was completed, are they the words by which parting is meant, or other words? If they say, "They are other words," they have spoken absurdly and produced what cannot be understood, for there are no other words besides these. If they say, "They are those very words," it is said to them: how can the words by which the two gathered and their sale was completed also be the words by which they parted? This is pure absurdity and corrupt speech. As for his saying, "It is not lawful [kadha fi kull al-usul] for him to leave his companion for fear that he will cancel it," its meaning, if sound, is recommendation (nadb), by the evidence of his saying, peace be upon him: "Whoever cancels a Muslim's (sale), Allah will cancel his stumble." By the consensus of the Muslims it is permissible for the doer of that, contrary to the apparent sense of the hadith; and by their consensus it is permitted for him to leave so that his sale takes effect and not to cancel it unless he wishes. In what they agreed upon concerning this is a refutation of the narration of those who related "lā yahillu" (it is not lawful); if this report is not to be understood as recommendation, then it is void by consensus. As for interpreting "al-mutabayi'an" (the two parties to a sale) as "al-mutasawimani" (the two bargainers), it is a departure from the apparent wording. Its meaning is: the two parties to a sale, after their contract, have the option as long as they are in their session, except for a sale in which one says to the other, "Choose," and he chooses; then the option ends between them even if they have not parted. If an option is stipulated, the meaning is: except a sale of option, for then the option remains after parting of bodies. The completion of this chapter is in the books of juristic disagreement. In the words of 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, "I heard my father say," there is evidence for the soundness of his narration. al-Daraqutni said: Abu Bakr al-Naysaburi told us: Muhammad ibn 'Ali al-Warraq told us, who said: I said to Ahmad ibn Hanbal, "Did Shu'ayb hear anything from his father?" He said, "He says, 'My father related to me.'" I said, "Did his father hear from 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr?" He said, "Yes, I think he did hear from him." Al-Daraqutni said: I heard Abu Bakr al-Naysaburi say: he is 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb ibn Muhammad ibn 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As; and the hearing of 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb from his father Shu'ayb is established, and the hearing of Shu'ayb from his grandfather 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr is established.

Eighth: al-Daraqutni related from Ibn 'Umar who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "The truthful, trustworthy Muslim merchant is with the Prophets, the truthful and the martyrs on the Day of Resurrection." It is disliked for a merchant to swear oaths to promote his goods and beautify them, or to send blessings upon the Prophet ﷺ while displaying his goods, by saying, "May God bless Muhammad! How excellent this is!" It is recommended for a merchant that his trade not distract him from performing the obligatory duties; when the time of prayer comes, he should leave his trade so that he is among the people of this verse: ﴿men whom neither trade nor sale distracts from the remembrance of God﴾ [and it will come, see vol. 12, p. 264]. Ninth: In this verse, together with the hadiths we have mentioned, there is a refutation of the view of the ignorant Sufis who deny seeking sustenance through trade and crafts, because Allah, may He be exalted, forbade eating it by falsehood and made it lawful through trade, and this is clear.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾. In this there is one issue. al-Hasan read "tuqattilu" (intensive). The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) agreed that the intended meaning of this verse is the prohibition of some people killing others. Then its wording includes a man killing himself deliberately, out of greed for worldly gain and the pursuit of wealth, by exposing himself to danger leading to destruction. It may also be said: "Do not kill yourselves" in a state of distress or anger; all of this falls under the prohibition. 'Amr ibn al-'As cited this verse when he refrained from bathing in cold water while in a state of major impurity during the expedition of Dhat al-Salasil, fearing for his own life. The Prophet ﷺ approved his argument, laughed at it, and said nothing. Abu Dawud and others related it, and it will come.

(ذَلِكَ) is a reference to killing, because it is the nearest thing mentioned; this was said by ʿAtaʾ. It was also said that it refers to devouring people's property falsely and to killing a soul, because the prohibition against them came in a connected, continuous sequence, and then the threat came in accordance with the prohibition. It was also said that it is general to everything He forbade of the matters from the beginning of the surah up to His saying, exalted is He: (وَمَنْ يَفْعَلْ ذلِكَ) ("And whoever does that"). Al-Tabari said: (ذلِكَ) refers to what He forbade in the last threat, and that is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, it is not lawful for you to inherit women by force﴾, because every prohibition from the beginning of the surah was accompanied by a threat, except from His saying (يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا لَا يَحِلُّ لَكُمْ), for there is no threat after it except His saying (وَمَنْ يَفْعَلْ ذلِكَ عُدْواناً). And ʿUdwan (transgression) is exceeding the limit. And ẓulm (wrongdoing) is placing a thing in other than its proper place, and this has been mentioned earlier [[See the thirteenth issue, vol. 1, p. 309.]]. The threat was restricted by mentioning ʿudwan and ẓulm so that the act of forgetfulness and error would be excluded from it. ʿUdwan and ẓulm were mentioned together, though their meanings are close, because their wordings differ; and this is good in speech, as the poet said:

وَأَلْفَى قَوْلَهَا كَذِبًا وَمَيْنًا [[This is the second half of a line by ʿAdi ibn Zayd, whose first half is:

فقددت الأديم لراهشيه]]

And the conjunction is good because the two wordings differ, as one says: bu'dan wa suhqan (far away and utterly far). From this is the saying of Yaʿqub: ﴿I only complain of my anguish and my grief to Allah﴾ [[See vol. 9, p. 249.]], so this is good because the wording differs. And (نُصْلِيهِ) means we will make him feel its heat. We have already explained the meaning of combining these verses with the hadith of Abu Saʿid al-Khudri concerning the disobedient and the people of major sins for whom the threat is carried out, so there is no point in repeating that. Al-Aʿmash and al-Nakhaʿi read (نَصْلِيهِ) with a fatha on the nun, on the basis that it is derived from ṣalā nāran, meaning aṣlaytuhu (I made him burn). In a report: (شَاةٌ مَصْلِيَّةٌ) ("a roasted sheep"). And whoever reads the nun with a damma, it is derived with the hamza, like ṭaʿimtu and aṭʿamtu.

This passage has two issues. The first concerns major and minor sins, and the second concerns the words "Madkhalan Kariman" (a noble entrance).

**The first issue:** When Allah, exalted is He, in this surah forbade the major sins (*kaba'ir*) and promised to remove the minor sins (*saghair*) for those who avoid them, this shows that sins are of two kinds: major and minor. This is the view of the commentators (*ahl al-ta'wil*) and of the jurists (*jama'at al-fuqaha'*). The touching of a woman and a glance are expiated by avoiding the major sins, by the certainty of His true promise and His true word, not because it is obligatory upon Him. The parallel to this discussion is what was explained earlier regarding the acceptance of repentance in His words: ﴿Repentance is only upon Allah﴾. Allah forgives minor sins for those who avoid major sins, but with another condition added to avoidance, which is the establishment of the obligatory duties (*al-fara'id*).

Muslim narrated from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The five prayers, and the Friday prayer to the next Friday, and Ramadan to the next Ramadan, are expiations for what lies between them, when major sins are avoided."

Abu Hatim al-Busti narrated in his *Sahih Musnad* from Abu Hurayrah and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sat on the pulpit and then said, "By Him in whose hand my soul is," three times. Then he was silent, and each man among us bowed his head, weeping in sorrow because of the oath of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Then he said: "No servant performs the five prayers, fasts Ramadan, and avoids the seven major sins, except that eight gates of Paradise are opened for him on the Day of Resurrection, so that it [the gate] even claps." Then he recited: ﴿If you avoid the major sins which you are forbidden, We will remove from you your misdeeds﴾.

Thus the Book and the sound Sunnah are in agreement regarding the expiation of minor sins with certainty, such as the glance and the like. The Sunnah has made clear that the meaning of "avoid" (*tajtanibu*) is not avoidance of every major sin entirely. And Allah knows best.

As for the theologians (*al-usuliyyun*), they said: It is not obligatory with certainty that minor sins are expiated by avoiding major sins. Rather, this is to be understood as a strong presumption (*ghalabat al-zann*) and strong hope (*quwwat al-raja'*), while the Will of Allah remains established. What points to this is that if we were to hold with certainty that the one who avoids major sins and complies with the obligatory duties has his minor sins expiated with certainty, then this would be for him in the category of the permissible (*mubah*) about which it is certain there is no consequence, and that would undermine the bonds of the Sharia. For us, there is no minor sin.

Al-Qushayri, Abd al-Rahim, said: "The correct view is that they are all major sins, but some of them are greater in effect than others. The wisdom in not distinguishing is that the servant should avoid all acts of disobedience."

I say: Furthermore, whoever looks at the act of opposition itself, as one of them said: "Do not look at the smallness of the sin, but look at whom you have disobeyed," then all sins in this respect are major sins. In this manner are to be understood the statements of al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-Tayyib, al-Ustadh Abu Ishaq al-Isfara'ini, Abu al-Ma'ali, Abu Nasr Abd al-Rahim al-Qushayri, and others. They said: "Some sins are called minor only in comparison with what is greater than them, just as fornication is called minor in comparison with disbelief, and the forbidden kiss is minor in comparison with fornication. There is no sin for us that is forgiven by avoiding another sin. Rather, all of these are major sins, and the one who commits them is under the Will of Allah, except for disbelief, because of His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾." They argued with the reading of the one who read "If you avoid the major sin (*kabir*) which you are forbidden," as singular, meaning monotheism, and the major sin is shirk. They said: "And according to the plural reading, the meaning is the categories of disbelief." The verse that specifies the ruling, to which all these absolute statements are referred, is His words: ﴿and He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾.

They also argued with what Muslim and others narrated from Abu Umamah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever takes the right of a Muslim man by his oath, Allah has made the Fire obligatory for him and forbidden Paradise to him." A man said to him: "O Messenger of Allah, even if it is a small thing?" He said: "Even if it is a twig of arak-wood." So severe warning has come concerning the small thing just as it has come concerning the large.

Ibn Abbas said: "A major sin is every sin for which Allah has ended with Fire, or wrath [*aw ghadabihi* in another manuscript: or His wrath], or a curse, or a punishment."

Ibn Mas'ud said: "The major sins are what Allah forbade in this surah, up to thirty-three verses, and the confirmation of this is His words: ﴿If you avoid the major sins which you are forbidden﴾."

Tawus said: "It was said to Ibn Abbas, 'Are the major sins seven?' He said: 'They are nearer to seventy.'"

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "A man said to Ibn Abbas, 'Are the major sins seven?' He said: 'They are nearer to seven hundred than to seven, except that there is no major sin with seeking forgiveness, and no minor sin with persistence.'"

It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "The major sins are four: despair of the mercy (*rawh*) of Allah, despair of the mercy of Allah, feeling secure from the plan of Allah, and associating partners with Allah. The Qur'an indicates them."

It is narrated from Ibn Umar: "They are nine: killing a soul, consuming usury, consuming the property of an orphan, accusing a chaste woman [of fornication], bearing false witness, disobedience to parents, fleeing from the battlefield, sorcery, and profaning the Sacred House."

Among the major sins according to the scholars are: gambling, theft, drinking wine, insulting the pious predecessors (*al-salaf al-salih*), rulers deviating from the truth, following desire, the false oath, despair of the mercy of Allah, and a person insulting his parents, namely that a man insults a man so that that man insults his parents, and spreading corruption on the earth, and other things whose enumeration is numerous, as their explanation has come in the Qur'an and in hadiths which the imams have transmitted. Muslim has mentioned a considerable number of them in the Book of Faith.

People have differed about their enumeration and limitation because of the differing reports about them. What I say is: there have come many sound and good hadiths about them which were not intended to be exhaustive. Rather, some of them are greater than others in relation to how great their harm is. Shirk is the greatest of all of them, and it is the one that is not forgiven, by the explicit text of Allah, exalted is He, concerning this. After it is despair of the mercy of Allah, because in it is denial of the Qur'an, since He says, and His word is true: ﴿My mercy encompasses all things﴾, while he says: "He will not be forgiven," so he has restricted what is vast. This is when he holds that belief. For this reason Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, none despairs of the mercy of Allah except the disbelieving people﴾. After it is despair (*al-qunut*). Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And who despairs of the mercy of his Lord except the astray﴾. After it is feeling secure from the plan of Allah, so that one persists in disobedience and relies on the mercy of Allah without action. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Do they feel secure from the plan of Allah? None feels secure from the plan of Allah except the losing people﴾. And He said: ﴿And that is your assumption which you assumed about your Lord; it has destroyed you, and you have become among the losers﴾. After it is killing, because in it is the destruction of souls and the annihilation of existence. Sodomy is in it the cutting off of offspring, fornication in it is the mixing of lineages through waters, wine in it is the loss of the intellect which is the basis of legal responsibility, abandoning prayer and the call to prayer in it is abandoning the manifestation of the rites of Islam, and bearing false witness in it is permitting blood, private parts and property, and so on for what is clearly harmful. So every sin about which the Sharia has greatly emphasized the threat of punishment and made it severe, or whose harm in existence is great as we have mentioned, is a major sin, and whatever else is a minor sin. This ties down this chapter for you and fixes it. And Allah knows best.

**The second issue:** His words: ﴿and We will admit you to a noble entrance﴾. Abu Amr and most of the Kufans read "*mudkhalan*" with a *damma* on the *mim* (*mudkhalan*). It may be a verbal noun (*masdar*), meaning *idkhalan* (causing to enter), and the object is omitted, meaning: "and We will admit you to Paradise by admitting." It may also mean a place, in which case it is the object.

The people of Medina read it with a *fatha* on the *mim* (*madkhalan*). It may be the verbal noun of *dakhala* (to enter), in which case it is in the accusative by an implied verb, the meaning being: "and We will admit you, so you enter an entrance," and the context indicates it. It may also be a noun of place, in which case it is in the accusative as an object, meaning: "and We will admit you to a noble place, which is Paradise."

Abu Sa'id ibn al-A'rabi said: I heard Abu Dawud al-Sijistani say: I heard Abu Abd Allah Ahmad ibn Hanbal say: "All Muslims are in Paradise." I said to him: "And how?" He said: Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿If you avoid the major sins which you are forbidden, We will remove from you your misdeeds, and We will admit you to a noble entrance﴾, meaning Paradise.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I have saved my intercession for the people of major sins from my community."

So if Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, forgives what is less than the major sins, and the Prophet (ﷺ) intercedes for the major sins, then what sin remains upon the Muslims?

Our scholars said: "Major sins according to the people of the Sunnah are forgiven for the one who gives them up before death, as has preceded. And it may be that some Muslims who die upon them are forgiven, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾. And what is meant by this is the one who dies upon sins. For if what is meant were the one who repented before death, there would be no meaning to the distinction between associating partners and other than that, since the one who repents from shirk is also forgiven."

It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "Five verses from Surat al-Nisa' are dearer to me than the whole world: His words: ﴿If you avoid the major sins which you are forbidden﴾, and His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives...﴾ [the verse], and His words: ﴿And whoever does evil or wrongs himself﴾ [the verse], and His words: ﴿And if there is a good deed, He multiplies it﴾, and His words: [﴿And those who believe in Allah and His messengers﴾]."

Ibn Abbas said: "Eight verses in Surat al-Nisa' are better for this Ummah than what the sun rises upon and sets upon: ﴿Allah desires to make clear to you﴾, ﴿And Allah desires to accept your repentance﴾, ﴿Allah desires to lighten for you﴾, ﴿If you avoid the major sins which you are forbidden, We will remove from you your misdeeds﴾ [the verse], ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him﴾, ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong [even] the weight of an atom﴾, ﴿And whoever does evil or wrongs himself﴾, ﴿What would Allah do with your punishment?﴾ [the verse]."

The commentary has four issues (masa'il). The first:

Al-Tirmidhi narrated from Umm Salama that she said: "Men go out to fight, but women do not fight, and we get only half of the inheritance." So Allah revealed ﴿And do not wish for that by which Allah has made some of you exceed others﴾. Mujahid said: "And concerning her Allah also revealed ﴿Indeed, the Muslim men and the Muslim women﴾." Umm Salama was the first woman to arrive in Madina as a emigrant (muhajira).

Abu 'Isa (al-Tirmidhi) said: "This is a hadith mursal (a hadith whose chain omits the Companion). Some narrated it from Ibn Abi Najih from Mujahid, as a mursal, that Umm Salama said such-and-such." (In al-Tirmidhi: "she said such-and-such.")

Qatada said: "In the Jahiliyya they did not give inheritance to women or to children. When they were given inheritance, and the male was given a portion equal to two females, the women wished that their shares were like the men's shares. The men said: 'We hope to be given preference over women in the Hereafter through our good deeds, just as we were given preference over them in inheritance.' So this was revealed: ﴿And do not wish for that by which Allah has made some of you exceed others﴾."

The second issue: the words of His, the Exalted: ﴿And do not wish﴾. Tamanni (wishing) is a kind of will directed at the future, just as al-talahhuf (longing for what is lost) is a kind of it directed at the past. Allah, glorified is He, forbade the believers from tamanni, because it entails the mind becoming fixated and forgetting the appointed term.

The scholars differed as to whether ghibta (wishing to have what another has, without wishing for his loss of it) falls under this prohibition. That is when a man wishes to have the same condition as his companion, without wishing that the other's condition be removed. The majority, including Malik and others, permit this. Some take this to be the meaning of his saying, peace be upon him: "There is no envy except in two: a man whom Allah has given the Qur'an, and he stands with it in the hours of the night and the hours of the day; and a man whom Allah has given wealth, and he spends it in the hours of the night and the hours of the day." The meaning of his saying "there is no envy" is that there is no ghibta greater and more excellent than the ghibta in these two matters.

Al-Bukhari drew attention to this meaning when he titled a chapter on this hadith: "Chapter on ghibta in knowledge and wisdom." Al-Muhallab said: "In this verse Allah clarified what it is not permissible to wish for, which is worldly goods and the like." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "As for wishing for righteous deeds, that is good. As for when a person wishes something from Allah without linking his wish to anything we have mentioned, that is permissible. This is found in the hadith of the Prophet (ﷺ) in his saying: 'I wish I could be given life and then be killed.'"

I say: This is the hadith with which al-Bukhari opened the Book of Tamanni (Wishing) in his Sahih. It indicates the wishing of good and acts of righteousness and eagerness for them. It also shows the excellence of martyrdom over all other acts of righteousness, because he (ﷺ) wished for it above others, due to its high rank and the honour of its people. Allah granted him it, according to his saying: "The poisoned morsel from Khaybar has never ceased to trouble me, and now the time has come when it has cut my aorta." [Footnote: al-akla (with a damma) means a morsel. Tu'adduni means it repeatedly afflicts me, and the pain of its poison returns at known times. Al-abhar is a vessel embedded in the spine and heart, connected to it; when it is severed, there is no life with it. The hadith of the poisoned sheep and his eating from it is mentioned in the Battle of Khaybar; it should be consulted.]

In the Sahih: "The martyr will be told, 'Wish,' and he will say, 'I wish to return to the world so that I may be killed in Your way once more.'"

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to wish for the faith of Abu Talib, and the faith of Abu Lahab and the chieftains of Quraysh, although he knew that it would not happen. He used to say: "Oh, how I long for my brothers who will come after me, who will believe in me though they have not seen me."

All of this indicates that tamanni is not forbidden when it does not lead to envy and hatred. The tamanni forbidden in the verse is of this kind, so it includes a man wishing for another's condition, whether in religion or in worldly affairs, on condition that what the other has be taken away. It makes no difference whether, along with that, you wish it to return to you or not. This is envy itself, and it is what Allah, the Exalted, censured with His saying: ﴿Or do they envy people for what Allah has given them of His bounty?﴾ [See p. 250 of this volume.]

It also includes a man proposing to a woman who is already being proposed to by his brother, and a man selling over his brother's sale, because that leads to envy and hatred.

Some scholars disliked ghibta and held that it falls under the prohibition. The correct view is that it is permissible, as we have explained. And success is from Allah.

Al-Dahhak said: "It is not lawful for anyone to wish for another's wealth. Did you not hear of those who said: ﴿Would that we had the like of what Qarun was given﴾ [See vol. 13, p. 316], until He said: ﴿And those who had wished to be in his place said the next day, when he had been swallowed up by the earth along with his home and his wealth: Had Allah not been gracious to us, He would have swallowed us up﴾?"

Al-Kalbi said: "A man should not wish for his brother's wealth, nor his wife, nor his servant, nor his mount. Rather he should say: 'O Allah, grant me the like of it.' This is so in the Torah, and likewise His saying in the Qur'an: ﴿And ask Allah of His bounty﴾."

Ibn 'Abbas said: "Allah, glorified is He, forbade a man from wishing for the wealth and family of so-and-so, and commanded His believing servants to ask Him of His bounty."

Among the proofs for the majority is his saying (ﷺ): "The world belongs to four kinds of people: a man whom Allah has given wealth and knowledge, so he fears his Lord regarding it, maintains his kinship ties through it, and knows that Allah has a right in it—this one is in the best of ranks; and a man whom Allah has given knowledge but has not given wealth, yet he is sincere in intention and says: 'If I had wealth, I would act with it as so-and-so acts'—he has the reward of his intention, and their rewards are equal." The hadith... al-Tirmidhi narrated it and graded it sound, and it has already been mentioned.

Al-Hasan said: "Let none of you wish for wealth, for what does he know, perhaps his destruction lies in it." This applies only when one wishes for it for worldly purposes. But when one wishes for it for good, the Law has permitted it, so the servant wishes for it in order to reach his Lord through it, and Allah does what He wills.

The third issue: the words of His, the Exalted: ﴿For men is a share of what they have earned﴾. He means reward and punishment, ﴿and for women﴾ likewise, as Qatada said. So for a woman is the reward for a good deed multiplied tenfold, just as it is for men.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "What is meant by this is inheritance." On this view, iktisab (earning) means acquisition, so that for the male is a share equal to the portion of two females. Allah, mighty and majestic, forbade wishing in this manner because of what it contains of the causes of envy, and because Allah, the Exalted, knows their interests better than they do, so He set the division among them with inequality according to what He knew of their interests.

The fourth issue: the words of His, the Exalted: ﴿And ask Allah of His bounty﴾. al-Tirmidhi narrated from 'Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Ask Allah of His bounty, for He loves to be asked, and the best worship is waiting for relief." Ibn Majah also narrated from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever does not ask Allah, He will be angry with him."

This indicates that the command to ask Allah is obligatory. Some scholars took this meaning and versified it, saying:

Allah becomes angry if you abandon asking Him,
while the son of Adam becomes angry when he is asked.

Ahmad ibn al-Mu'adhdhal Abu al-Fadl, the Maliki jurist, said, and excelled:

Seek provision from the One
beside whom everything else is but a gatekeeper.
Whoever hates the one who abandons asking him for generosity
does not approve of the one who seeks it.
And one whose word, once spoken, takes effect
without a signature sent to a scribe.

We have expanded on this meaning at length in the book Qam' al-Hirs bi-l-Zuhd wa-l-Qana'a (Suppressing Greed through Asceticism and Contentment).

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: ﴿And ask Allah of His bounty﴾ means worship; it is not a matter of worldly affairs. It was also said: Ask Him for success in acting in a way that pleases Him.

It is narrated from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, that she said: "Ask your Lord even for a full stomach, for if Allah does not make it easy, it will not be easy."

Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna said: "He did not command asking except in order to give."

Al-Kisa'i and Ibn Kathir recited ﴿wa-salu Allaha min fadlihi﴾ without hamza throughout the Qur'an; the rest recited it with hamza, ﴿wa-s'alu Allaha﴾. The original form has the hamza, but the hamza was dropped for ease. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*) on Surah 4, verse 33:

There are five issues in it.

The first: God, exalted is He, has made clear that every person has heirs and *mawali* (those entitled to inherit). Each one should benefit from what God has allotted to him of the inheritance, and should not wish for the property of another. Al-Bukhari, in the Book of Inheritance (*Kitab al-Fara'id*), narrated through Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas: (*Wa-li-kullin ja'alna mawali mimma taraka al-walidani wal-aqrabuna wal-ladhina 'aqadat* [[(*'Aqadat*) is the reading of Nafi', as it is written in the established copies (*rasm al-usul*), and the other readings will come.]] *aymanukum*) — "And for every one We have appointed heirs (*mawali*) to what the parents and close relatives leave, and those with whom your oaths have bound you." He said: When the Emigrants (*Muhajirun*) came to Medina, the Ansari would inherit from the Emigrant to the exclusion of his blood relatives, because of the brotherhood that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) had established between them. Then when (*Wa-li-kullin ja'alna mawali*) was revealed, he said: it abrogated it (*nasakhatha*), namely, (*wal-ladhina 'aqadat aymanukum*). Abu al-Hasan ibn Battal said: In all the copies it occurs: (*Wa-li-kullin ja'alna mawali*), he said: it abrogated it, (*wal-ladhina 'aqadat aymanukum*). The correct version is that the abrogating verse is (*Wa-li-kullin ja'alna mawali*) and the abrogated verse is (*wal-ladhina 'aqadat aymanukum*), and al-Tabari likewise narrated it in his report.

It has been narrated from the majority of the early generations (*jumhur al-salaf*) that the abrogating verse of His saying (*wal-ladhina 'aqadat aymanukum*) is His saying, exalted is He, in *al-Anfal*: (*Wa-ulu al-arhami ba'duhum awla bi-ba'din*) — "And blood relatives are nearer to one another" [[See vol. 8, p. 58.]]. This was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and al-Hasan al-Basri, and it is what Abu 'Ubayd affirmed in his book *al-Nasikh wal-Mansukh* (On Abrogation). There is another view on it, narrated by al-Zuhri from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, who said: God, mighty and majestic, commanded those who had adopted children other than their own sons in the Jahiliyyah, and who inherited from them in Islam, that they should give them a share in the bequest, and that the inheritance be returned to the blood relatives and the agnatic heirs (*'asaba*). Another group said: His saying, exalted is He, (*wal-ladhina 'aqadat aymanukum*) is decisive (*muhkam*) and not abrogated; God only commanded the believers to give their allies (*hulafa'*) their shares of support, counsel and the like. Al-Tabari mentioned this from Ibn 'Abbas.

(*Wal-ladhina 'aqadat aymanukum fa-atuhum nasibahum*) — "give them their share," meaning of support, counsel, and assistance (*al-rifadah*) [[*Al-rifd* (with a kasra on the ra'): gift and reward.]], and that one should bequeath to them even though the inheritance has gone. This is the view of Mujahid and al-Suddi. I say: al-Nahhas also chose it and narrated it from Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Abrogation is not sound, for combining the two is possible, as Ibn 'Abbas explained, as al-Tabari recorded, and al-Bukhari narrated it from him in the Book of Tafsir. The inheritance of blood relatives (*dhawu al-arham*) will come in *al-Anfal*, God willing.

The second: (*kull*) in the speech of the Arabs means totality and generality. When it comes alone, there must be an ellipsis (*hadhf*) in the sentence according to all the grammarians, to the extent that some of them permitted "*marartu bi-kullin*" (I passed by each one), like *qablu* and *ba'du*. The ellipsis is estimated as: "And for every person We have appointed heirs (*mawali*)," meaning heirs.

(*Wal-ladhina 'aqadat aymanukum*) — meaning by oath (*bil-hilf*), according to Qatadah. That is because a man would make a pact with another man, saying: "My blood is your blood, my destruction is your destruction [[His saying: *hadmi hadmuka* (my destruction is your destruction) means we are one unit in support; you are angered for us and we are angered for you.]], my vengeance is your vengeance, my war is your war, my peace is your peace; you inherit from me and I inherit from you, you seek vengeance through me and I seek it through you, you pay the blood-money (*ta'qil*) for me and I pay it for you." So the ally would receive a sixth (*sudus*) of the ally's inheritance, and then it was abrogated.

The third: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿*mawali*﴾. Know that *al-mawla* is a shared term (*lafz mushtarak*) applied to several meanings. The one who frees (*al-mu'tiq*) is called *mawla*, and the one who is freed (*al-mu'taq*) is called *mawla*. It is also said: the lower *mawla* and the upper *mawla*. The supporter is also called *mawla*, and from it is His saying, exalted is He: (*Wa-anna al-kafirina la mawla lahum*) — "And that the disbelievers have no protector [[See vol. 16, p. 234.]]." The paternal cousin (*ibn al-'amm*) is called *mawla*, and the neighbour is called *mawla*.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿*Wa-li-kullin ja'alna mawali*﴾, it means *'asaba* (agnatic heirs), because of his, peace be upon him, saying: "Give the shares to those entitled to them; what remains is for the nearest male agnate (*awla 'asabatin dhakar*)." Among the agnates is the upper *mawla* and not the lower one, according to the view of most scholars, because what is understood regarding the one who frees is that he is the benefactor of the freed slave, like the one who brought him into being, so he deserves his inheritance for this reason.

Al-Tahawi related from al-Hasan ibn Ziyad that the lower *mawla* inherits from the upper one, and he argued for this with what is narrated: a man freed a slave, then the freer died and left nothing but the freed slave, so the Messenger of God (ﷺ) gave his inheritance to the freed boy. Al-Tahawi said: There is no contrary evidence to this hadith, so it must be held to. Also, when it is possible to establish inheritance for the freer on the supposition that he was like the one who brought him into being, he resembles the father, and the lower *mawla* resembles the son, and this requires equality between them in inheritance; and the principle is that connection (*al-ittisal*) is general. And in the report: "The *mawla* of a people is one of them."

Those who opposed this, and they are the majority, said: Inheritance requires kinship, and there is no kinship here. Rather, we established inheritance for the freer by virtue of his beneficence to the freed slave, so it requires the reciprocation of the benefit with recompense, and that does not reverse for the lower *mawla*. As for the son, he is the most fitting of people to be his father's successor and to stand in his place, whereas the freed slave is not fit to stand in the place of the one who freed him. The freer has bestowed a favour upon him, so the law has reciprocated by making him more entitled to his freer (*mawlahu al-mu'tiq*), and this does not exist in the lower *mawla*. So the difference between them is evident, and God knows best.

The fourth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿*Wal-ladhina 'aqadat aymanukum*﴾. 'Ali ibn Kabshah [[So in Ibn 'Atiyyah, *al-Bahr* and the originals, except D, where it is Ibn Kaysah, and Ali ibn Yazid ibn Kaysah. Perhaps this is the correct one, as in *Tabaqat al-Qurra'* and *al-Taj*.]] narrated from Hamzah (*'aqqadat*) with a shadda on the qaf, for intensification (*al-taktir*). The well-known reading from Hamzah is (*'aqadat aymanukum*) with the qaf unstressed, and this is the reading of 'Asim and al-Kisa'i. This reading is remote, because the act of pact-making (*mu'aqadah*) occurs only between two or more, so its pattern is *fa'ala*. Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: Hamzah's reading is permissible despite its obscurity in Arabic. Its estimate would be: "And those whom your oaths have bound to them (*'aqadat lahum aymanukum*) the alliance," and it is transitive to two objects; its estimate is: "your oaths bound the alliance for them," then the preposition *lam* was omitted, like His saying, exalted is He: (*Wa-idha kaluhum* [[See vol. 19, p. 250.]]) — meaning they measured for them. The second object was omitted, as one says "*kiltuka*" (I measured for you), meaning I measured wheat for you. The first object was omitted because it is connected in the relative clause (*silah*).

The fifth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿*Inna Allaha kana 'ala kulli shay'in shahida*﴾ — meaning He has witnessed your pact with them, and He, mighty and majestic, loves fidelity (*al-wafa'*).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verse 34 (part 1 of 2):

There are eleven issues in it. The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Men are the maintainers of women﴾.
