According to the first reading, *takun* (it is) means "happens," so it is a complete verb (*tammah*). According to the second reading, it is an incomplete verb (*naqisah*), meaning: if his act is a good deed. Al-Hasan read *nudha'if-hā* (We multiply it) with the first-person plural of majesty (nun). The rest read it with *yā'* (third person), which is more sound because of His saying: (and gives). Abu Raja' read *yudha'if-hā* (with doubling of the 'ayn), and the rest read *yudā'if-hā*; both are dialects with the same meaning, which is multiplication. Abu Ubaydah said: *yudā'if-hā* means He makes it into many multiples, while *yuḍa''if-hā* (with the doubled letter) means He makes it into two multiples.

(*Min ladunhu*) means "from Him" (*min 'indihi*). It has four dialectal forms [[In the books of lexicography there are more than four, among them, along with those mentioned: *ladun* and *ludun*.]]: *ladun*, *ludun*, *ladu*, and *ladā*. When they attach it to themselves, they double the nun, and *min* enters upon it, since *min* (used to indicate the starting point) and *ladun* both have this function of indicating the starting point. Because the two are alike, it is good for *min* to enter upon it. For this reason Sibawayh said about *ladun* that it is the place which is the beginning of the endpoint.

(*Ajran 'azhiman*) means Paradise. In Sahih Muslim, in the lengthy hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, the hadith of intercession, it includes: "Until, when the believers are delivered from the Fire, by Him in whose hand my soul is, none of you is more insistent in demanding of Allah the rights of the believers on the Day of Resurrection than they are for their brothers who are in the Fire. They say: 'Our Lord, they used to fast with us, pray with us, and perform Hajj.' It is said to them: 'Bring out those you recognize,' and their forms are forbidden to the Fire. They bring out a great multitude whom the Fire has seized up to the middle of their shins and up to their knees. Then they say: 'Our Lord, no one remains there of those You commanded us (to bring out).' He, Mighty and Majestic, says: 'Return, and whoever you find in his heart the weight of a dinar of good, bring him out.' They bring out a great multitude. Then they say: 'Our Lord, we have not left there anyone of those You commanded us (to bring out).' Then He says: 'Return, and whoever you find in his heart the weight of half a dinar of good, bring him out.' They bring out a great multitude. Then they say: 'Our Lord, we have not left there anyone of those You commanded us (to bring out).' Then He says: 'Return, and whoever you find in his heart the weight of an atom of good, bring him out.' They bring out a great multitude. Then they say: 'Our Lord, we have not left there any good.'" Abu Sa'id al-Khudri used to say: "If you do not believe me in this hadith, then recite, if you wish: (Indeed, Allah does not wrong the weight of an atom, and if it is a good deed He multiplies it and gives from Him a great reward)," and he mentioned the hadith. It is related from Ibn Mas'ud, on the authority of the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "A servant will be brought on the Day of Resurrection and he will be made to stand, and a caller will call out over the heads of all creatures: 'This is so-and-so the son of so-and-so; whoever has a right against him, let him come to his right.' Then He says: 'Give these people their rights.' He says: 'My Lord, from where shall I (give them), when the world has gone from me?' Allah, Exalted is He, says to the angels: 'Look at his righteous deeds and give them from them.' If there remains the weight of an atom of good, the angels say: 'O Lord'—and He knows that better than them—'each person with a right has been given his right, and there remains the weight of an atom of good.' Allah, Exalted is He, says to the angels: 'Multiply it for My servant, and admit him to Paradise by the grace of My mercy.' Its confirmation is (Indeed, Allah does not wrong the weight of an atom, and if it is a good deed He multiplies it). But if he was a wretched servant, the angels say: 'Our God, his good deeds have run out, his evil deeds remain, and many claimants remain.' He, Exalted is He, says: 'Take from their evil deeds and add them to his evil deeds, then write a record for him to the Fire.'" According to this interpretation, the verse concerns disputes: He, Exalted is He, does not wrong even the weight of an atom to an opponent against an opponent, by taking for him from him, and He does not wrong the weight of an atom that remains for him, but rather He rewards him for it and multiplies it for him. This is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if it is a good deed, He multiplies it﴾. Abu Hurayrah related: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Indeed, Allah, glorified is He, gives His believing servant for one good deed two thousand thousand good deeds,'" and he recited: (Indeed, Allah does not wrong the weight of an atom, and if it is a good deed He multiplies it, and gives from Him a great reward). Ubaydah said: Abu Hurayrah said: "When Allah says (a great reward), who can estimate its measure!" It has already been mentioned from Ibn Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud that this verse is one of the verses which are better than what the sun has risen upon.

The letter *fa'* (in *fa-kayfa*) was given a *fatha* because two unvowelled letters (*sakinayn*, consonants without a vowel) came together. *Idha* (when) is an adverb of time, and the verb that governs it is *ji'na* (We come).

Abu al-Layth al-Samarqandi mentioned: al-Khalil ibn Ahmad [[Al-Khalil ibn Ahmad, perhaps al-Asbahani.]] narrated to us, saying: Ibn Mani' narrated to us, saying: Abu Kamil [[From Z, T and Y. In other copies: Ibn Kamil.]] narrated to us, saying: Fudayl narrated to us, from Yunus ibn Muhammad ibn Fadala, from his father, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to them in Bani Zafar [[Bani Zafar (with a vowelled *fa'*) is a clan of the Ansar, and also a clan of Bani Sulaym.]] and sat on the rock that was in Bani Zafar, and with him were Ibn Mas'ud, Mu'adh and some of his Companions. He instructed a reciter to recite, until he reached this verse: ﴿How then, when We bring from every nation a witness, and bring you as a witness against these people?﴾ The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wept until his cheeks were wet, and he said: "O Lord, this one (I bear witness against) those among whom I am present; so how (will it be) for those whom I have not seen?" [[In Ibn Kathir: "This, I have testified against those among whom I am present, so how about those whom I have not seen?"]]

Al-Bukhari narrated from Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: "Recite to me." I said: "Shall I recite to you, when it was revealed to you?" He said: "I like to hear it from someone other than myself." So I recited to him Surah al-Nisa' until I reached: ﴿How then, when We bring from every nation a witness, and bring you as a witness against these people?﴾ He said: "Stop." And behold, his eyes were shedding tears. Muslim also related it, and he said, instead of his saying "Stop": I raised my head (or a man beside me nudged me), so I raised my head and saw his tears flowing.

Our scholars said: The weeping of the Prophet (ﷺ) was only because of the great terror of the scene and the severity of the matter contained in this verse, when the prophets will be brought as witnesses against their nations, regarding their affirmation and denial, and he (ﷺ) will be brought on the Day of Resurrection as a witness.

The reference in His words "against these people" is to the disbelievers of Quraysh and others among the disbelievers. The disbelievers of Quraysh were singled out for mention because the punishment is more severe for them than for others, due to their obstinacy when they saw the miracles and the extraordinary signs that Allah manifested through his hands. The meaning is: how will the condition of these disbelievers be on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿when We bring from every nation a witness, and bring you as a witness against these people﴾: will they be punished or will they be given ease? This is an interrogative whose meaning is rebuke.

It has also been said: the reference is to his whole community. Ibn al-Mubarak mentioned: a man of the Ansar informed us, from al-Minhal ibn Amr, who told him that he heard Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab say: "There is no day but that his community is presented to the Prophet (ﷺ) morning and evening, and he recognises them by their marks and their deeds, and therefore he bears witness against them." Allah, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿How then, when We bring from every nation a witness﴾, meaning, by their prophet, ﴿and bring you as a witness against these people﴾.

The position of *fa-kayfa* is in the accusative, governed by a hidden verb. The estimated meaning is "how will their condition be," as we have mentioned. The hidden verb may stand in place of *idha* (when), and the governing word for *idha* is *ji'na* (We bring). *Shahidan* (as a witness) is a circumstantial accusative (*hal*).

From the hadith, one of the points of jurisprudence is the permissibility of a student reciting to a teacher and presenting to him, and it is also permissible the reverse. Its explanation will come, if Allah the Exalted wills, in the hadith of Ubayy in the commentary on Surah (Lam yakun) [[See vol. 20, p. 142. And he did not come with anything.]].

[*Shahidan* is in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) [[This addition is from J, D and Y.]].]

The waw in (ʿaṣaw) is given a ḍammah because two unvowelled letters meet, but it may also be given a kasrah. Nafi' and Ibn ʿAmir read (tassawwā) with a fatḥah on the tā' and a shaddah on the sīn. Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read it the same way, except that they lighten the sīn. The rest of the readers (al-Bāqūn) put a ḍammah on the tā' and lighten the sīn, in the passive form with the agent unnamed. The meaning is: ﴿if Allah would level the earth with them﴾, that is, make them and the earth equal. Another meaning is: they wished that Allah had not raised them, and that the earth lay level over them, because they were taken from dust. According to the first and second readings, "the earth" is the subject, and the meaning is: they wished that the earth would split open for them so that they would sink into it. This is the view of Qatadah. It has also been said that the bā' has the sense of ʿalā (upon), meaning: ﴿if the earth were leveled upon them﴾, that is, it would split and then close over them. This is the view of al-Ḥasan. So the reading with shaddah is by assimilation (idgham), and the reading with lightening is by omitting the tā'.

It has also been said: they only wished this when they saw the animals turn to dust, and they knew that they would be eternally in the Fire. This is the meaning of His words, exalted is He: ﴿The disbeliever will say: "Would that I were dust!"﴾ [See vol. 19, p. 183.]

It has also been said: they only wished this when this community bore witness for the prophets, as was explained earlier in (al-Baqarah) at His words, exalted is He: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation﴾ [2:143], to the end of the verse. [See vol. 2, p. 153.] Then the earlier nations will say: "Among them are adulterers and thieves, so their testimony is not accepted." Then the Prophet (ﷺ) will vouch for them, and the polytheists will say: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [6:23]. Then their mouths will be sealed, and their hands and feet will bear witness to what they used to earn. This is His words: ﴿On that Day those who disbelieved and disobeyed the Messenger will wish that the earth were leveled over them﴾, meaning they will be swallowed up by the earth. And Allah knows best.

[His words:] ﴿and they will not conceal from Allah any statement﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: Some have said that ﴿and they will not conceal from Allah any statement﴾ is a new sentence, because what they did is manifest to Allah, and they cannot conceal it. Others have said that it is coordinated (with the previous clause), and the meaning is: they wish that the earth were leveled over them, and that they had not concealed from Allah any statement, because their lies had become evident. Ibn ʿAbbas was asked about this verse and about His words: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾. He said: When they saw that no one enters Paradise except the people of Islam, they said: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾. Then Allah sealed their mouths, and their hands and feet spoke, so they did not conceal from Allah any statement. Al-Ḥasan and Qatadah said: The Hereafter has stages; this happens in some of them, and that happens in others. The meaning is that when the matter became clear to them and they were called to account, they did not conceal anything. More detailed explanation of this will come, if Allah wills, in (al-Anʿām). [See vol. 6, p. 401.]

There are forty-four issues in this verse.

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾. Allah, glorified and exalted is He, addressed this address specifically to the believers, because they used to establish prayer after having taken wine, which had clouded their minds, so they were singled out for this address. The disbelievers did not perform it either sober or intoxicated.

Abu Dawud related from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: When the prohibition of wine was revealed, ʿUmar said: "O Allah, make clear to us a healing explanation regarding wine." Then the verse in al-Baqarah was revealed: ﴿They ask you about wine and gambling﴾ [[See vol. 3, p. 51.]]. He said: ʿUmar was summoned and it was recited to him. He said: "O Allah, make clear to us a healing explanation regarding wine." Then the verse in an-Nisa' was revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾. The herald of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), whenever the prayer was called, would proclaim: "Beware, let no intoxicated person approach the prayer." ʿUmar was summoned and it was recited to him, and he said: "O Allah, make clear to us regarding wine a healing explanation." Then this verse was revealed: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ [[See vol. 6, p. 275.]]. ʿUmar said: "We have desisted."

Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: The people remained upon the practices of their jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic ignorance) until they were commanded or prohibited. They used to drink it at the beginning of Islam, until this was revealed: ﴿They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In them is great sin and benefits for people﴾. They said: "We drink it for its benefit, not for its sin." A man drank it, then went forward to lead them in prayer and recited: ﴿Say: O disbelievers, I do not worship what you worship﴾, so this was revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾. They said: "It is about other than the actual prayer."

ʿUmar said: "O Allah, reveal to us regarding wine a healing explanation." Then this was revealed: ﴿Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred...﴾, the verse. ʿUmar said: "We have desisted, we have desisted." Then the herald of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went around proclaiming: "Beware, wine has indeed been prohibited," as will be explained in al-Maʾidah, Allah willing.

At-Tirmidhi related from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, who said: ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf prepared food for us, invited us, and gave us wine to drink. The wine took effect on us, and the prayer time came, so they put me forward, and I recited: ﴿Say: O disbelievers, I do not worship what you worship﴾, while we were worshipping what you worship. He said: Then Allah revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated until you know what you are saying﴾. Abu ʿIsa (at-Tirmidhi) said: This is a hadith that is good and sound.

The connection and arrangement with what precedes it: He, glorified and exalted, said: ﴿And worship Allah and do not associate anything with Him﴾. Then after faith He mentioned prayer, which is the head of the acts of worship. For this reason whoever abandons it is killed, and its obligation does not lapse. The discourse then extended to mention its conditions, without which it is not valid.

The second: The majority of scholars and the group of jurists hold that what is meant by intoxication (sukr) is the intoxication of wine. Except ad-Dahhak, who said: What is meant is the intoxication of sleep, based on his (peace be upon him) saying: "If one of you becomes drowsy during the prayer, let him sleep until the sleep leaves him, for he does not know, perhaps he would seek forgiveness and end up cursing himself." ʿUbaydah as-Salmani said: ﴿While you are intoxicated﴾ means when you are ḥāqin [[al-ḥāqin: one whose urine has accumulated greatly.]], based on his (peace be upon him) saying: "None of you should pray while he is ḥāqin," and in another narration: "while he is pressing between his thighs."

I say: The saying of ad-Dahhak and ʿUbaydah is sound in meaning, for what is required of the one praying is to turn to Allah, exalted is He, with his heart and to abandon attention to anything else, and to be free of everything that disturbs him, such as sleep, the urge to urinate, hunger, and everything that preoccupies the mind and alters the state. He (ﷺ) said: "When the evening meal is served and the prayer is called, begin with the meal." So he (ﷺ) considered the removal of every disturbance that attaches itself to the thought, so that one turns to the worship of his Lord with a free heart and pure intellect, and thus is humble in his prayer. This verse includes: ﴿The believers have succeeded, those who are humble in their prayer﴾ [[See vol. 12, p. 102.]], as will be explained.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾ is abrogated by the verse of al-Maʾidah: ﴿When you rise to prayer, wash...﴾, the verse. According to this view they were first commanded not to pray while intoxicated, then they were commanded to pray in every state. This was before the prohibition. Mujahid said: It was abrogated by the prohibition of wine. Likewise ʿIkrimah and Qatadah said, and this is the sound view on the matter, due to the hadith of ʿAli mentioned above.

It is related that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) said: The prayer was called and the herald of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) proclaimed: "Let no intoxicated person approach the prayer." An-Nahhas mentioned it. According to the view of ad-Dahhak and ʿUbaydah, the verse is muhkam (clear and not abrogated), with no abrogation in it.

The third: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do not approach﴾. If it is said: lā taqrab [[In one copy: taqrabū, talabbasū, tanū.]] with a fatha on the ra', its meaning is "do not engage in the act." If it has a ḍamma on the ra', its meaning is "do not come near it." The address is to the body of the community who are sober. As for the intoxicated person who has lost discernment due to his intoxication, he is not addressed at that time because his intellect is gone, but he is addressed to carry out what is obligatory upon him, and to make up for what he neglected during the time of his intoxication of the rulings whose obligation was established for him before intoxication.

The fourth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The prayer﴾. The scholars differed concerning what is meant by prayer here. One group said: it is the well-known act of worship itself, and this is the view of Abu Hanifa. For this reason He said: ﴿until you know what you are saying﴾. Another group said: what is meant is the places of prayer, and this is the view of ash-Shafiʿi, so the qualifier has been omitted. Allah the Most High has said: ﴿Had it not been for Allah repelling some people by others, there would have been demolished monasteries, churches, and prayers﴾ [[See vol. 12, p. 68.]], so He called the places of prayer "prayer." This interpretation is supported by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿nor one in a state of major impurity, except those passing through [a place of prayer]﴾. This implies permissibility for a junub to pass through the masjid, but not to pray in it. Abu Hanifa said: What is meant by His saying: ﴿nor one in a state of major impurity, except those passing through﴾ is the traveler who does not find water, so he performs tayammum and prays, and this will be explained. Another group said: what is meant is both the place and the prayer together, because at that time they did not come to the masjid except for prayer, and did not pray except in congregation, so the two were mutually connected.

The fifth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿While you are intoxicated﴾. It is an inchoate (mubtada') and predicate (khabar), a sentence in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to ﴿do not approach﴾. And ﴿sukārā﴾ is the plural of sakrān, like kaslān and kusālā. An-Nakhaʿi read sakrā with a fatha on the sin, in the pattern faʿlā, which is a broken plural of sakrān. It was broken into sakrā because intoxication is a calamity that affects the intellect, so it took the pattern of ṣarʿā (the stricken) and its class. Al-Aʿmash read sukrā like ḥublā, so it is a singular adjective, and it is permissible to predicate a singular adjective of a group, as they do when they predicate a collective with the singular.

Sukr (intoxication) is the opposite of ṣaḥw (sobriety). It is said: sakira yaskaru sakran, from the pattern ḥamida yaḥmadu. And sakirat ʿaynuhu taskuru means it became bewildered, and from this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Our eyes have only been dazzled﴾ [[See vol. 10, p. 8.]]. And sakkartu ash-shaqq [[In the sources: sakkartu as-sadd (I blocked the dam); in Ibn ʿAtiyyah: sakkartu al-māʾ (I dammed the water).]] means I blocked it. So the intoxicated person has been cut off from what he was upon of intellect.

The sixth: In this verse there is evidence, indeed an explicit text, that drinking was permissible at the beginning of Islam, up to the point where its drinker reaches intoxication. Some people said: intoxication is forbidden in every intellect and is not permitted in any religion, and they interpreted intoxication in this verse as sleep. Al-Qaffal said: It is possible that they were permitted from drink what stirs the disposition toward generosity, courage, and zeal.

I say: This meaning is found in their poetry, and Hassan said:
"We drink it, and it leaves us as kings."
We have discussed this meaning at length in (al-Baqarah) [[See vol. 3, p. 55 onward.]]. Al-Qaffal said: As for what removes the intellect so that its possessor is in the state of madness and unconsciousness, it is not permitted to intend it. Rather, if it happens without intention, it is lifted from its possessor. I say: This is sound, and it will be explained in (al-Maʾidah), Allah willing, in the story of Hamzah [[See vol. 6, p. 287.]].

When this verse was revealed, the Muslims would avoid drinking at the times of the prayers. When they prayed the ʿishāʾ, they would drink it. They continued in this until its prohibition was revealed in (al-Maʾidah) in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ [[See vol. 6, p. 287.]].

The seventh: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿until you know what you are saying﴾, that is, until you know it with certainty, without error. The intoxicated person does not know what he is saying. For this reason ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan (may Allah be pleased with him) said: The intoxicated person's divorce does not bind him. This is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, Tawus, ʿAta', al-Qasim, and Rabiʿah, and it is the view of al-Layth ibn Saʿd, Ishaq, Abu Thawr, and al-Muzani, and at-Tahawi chose it and said: The scholars agreed that the divorce of one who is mentally incapacitated (maʿtūh) is not valid, and the intoxicated person is mentally incapacitated like the one afflicted with obsessive whisperings is mentally incapacitated by them. They do not differ that whoever drinks henbane and loses his intellect, his divorce is not valid, so likewise whoever becomes intoxicated from drink.

Another group permitted his divorce. It is related from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, Muʿawiyah, and a group of the Successors, and it is the view of Abu Hanifa, ath-Thawri, and al-Awzaʿi. The view of ash-Shafiʿi on it varied. Malik held him liable for divorce and for retaliation for wounds and killing, but did not hold him liable for marriage and sale. Abu Hanifa said: All the actions and contracts of the intoxicated person are valid, like those of the sober, except apostasy. If he apostatizes, his wife is not separated from him, except by juristic preference (istihsan). Abu Yusuf said: He is an apostate in the state of his intoxication, and this is the view of ash-Shafiʿi, except that he does not kill him in the state of his intoxication, and does not ask him to repent.

And Imam Abu 'Abd Allah al-Mazari said: "There has also been transmitted to us [[عندنا ساقط في ط.]] an anomalous (shadhdhah) report that the divorce of an intoxicated person does not take effect." Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Hakam said: "Neither divorce nor manumission binds him." Ibn Shas said: "Shaykh Abu al-Walid restricted the disagreement to the person whose mind is confused but who still retains some of his reason, yet cannot control his confusion, so he errs and is correct by turns. As for the drunkard who does not know the earth from the sky or a man from a woman, there is no disagreement that he is like the insane person in all his acts and conditions, both in his dealings with people and in what lies between him and God Most High, except for the prayers whose time has passed. It has been said that these prayers are not dropped from him, unlike the insane person, because by bringing the intoxication upon himself he is like one who deliberately abandons them until their time has gone out."

Sufyan al-Thawri said: "The limit of intoxication [[في ط وى: السكران.]] is the disturbance of the intellect. If he is asked to recite and he garbles his recitation and speaks what cannot be understood, he is to be flogged." Ahmad said: "When his intellect has changed from its state of soundness, he is intoxicated," and something similar is related from Malik. Ibn al-Mundhir said: "If he garbles his recitation, he is intoxicated," citing the words of God Most High: ﴿until you know what you are saying﴾. So if he is in a state where he does not know what he is saying, he should avoid the mosque for fear of defiling it, and his prayer is not valid; if he prays, he must make it up. But if he is in a state where he knows what he is saying and he performs the prayer, his ruling is the ruling of the sober person.

The eighth matter: God Most High's words ﴿nor in a state of major impurity (junub)﴾ are a conjunction with the position of the phrase in the accusative in His words ﴿until you know﴾, meaning: do not pray while you are in a state of major impurity (ajnabtum). It is said: tajannabtum, ajnabtum and jannabtum all have the same meaning. The word junub is not made feminine, dual or plural, because it is on the pattern of the verbal noun, like bu'd (distance) and qurb (nearness). They sometimes lighten it and say janb, and some people have read it that way. Al-Farra' said: it is said janaba al-rajulu and ajnaba from janaba (impurity). It has also been said that in one dialect junub is pluralized as ajnab, like 'unuq and a'naq, and tunub and atnab. Whoever uses jani' for the singular uses junnab for the plural, as in your saying rakib and rukkab. The root meaning is distance, as if the junub has moved away (ba'uda) from the state of prayer by the emission of the gushing fluid. A poet said:

"So do not forbid a man who has spent the night in a state of impurity (janabah), for I am a stranger in the midst of the tents."

A man who is junub is a stranger, and janabah is the mixing of a man with a woman. [In another copy: al-mujanabah, which is the more evident reading.]

The ninth matter: The majority of the community hold that the junub is one who is not in a state of purity because of emission of semen or because the circumcised parts have met. It is related from some of the Companions that there is no ghusl except from emission of semen, based on the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "Water is only from water," related by Muslim. In al-Bukhari, it is related from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that he said: "O Messenger of God, if a man has intercourse with a woman but does not ejaculate?" He said: "He should wash what touched the woman and then perform ablution and pray." Abu 'Abd Allah [Abu 'Abd Allah: the kunya of al-Bukhari] said: "Washing (ghusl) is more cautious, and that other report I have only mentioned because of their disagreement." Muslim also related it in his Sahih with the same meaning, and at its end he said: Abu al-'Ala' ibn al-Shikhkhir said: "The Messenger of God ﷺ had some of his sayings abrogate others, just as the Qur'an has parts that abrogate other parts." Abu Ishaq said: "This is abrogated." Al-Tirmidhi said: "This ruling was in the early period of Islam and then was abrogated." I say: The community of scholars among the Companions, the Successors and the jurists of the cities holds this view, and that ghusl becomes obligatory by the mere meeting of the two circumcised parts. There was disagreement about it among the Companions, but they then returned to the report of 'A'isha from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "When a man sits between her four limbs (shu'ab) and the circumcised part touches the circumcised part, ghusl has become obligatory." Related by Muslim. In the two Sahihs, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah from the Prophet ﷺ, he said: "When he sits between her four limbs and then exerts himself (jahadaha) upon her, ghusl has become obligatory for him." [Jahadaha: he pushed her and urged her on. It has also been said that jahd is one of the names for intercourse.] Muslim added: "even if he did not ejaculate." Ibn al-Qassar said: "The Successors and those after them, after the disagreement of those before them, agreed (ijma') upon acting on the hadith: 'When the two circumcised parts meet.' When a consensus is established after a disagreement, it removes the disagreement." Al-Qadi 'Iyad said: "We do not know of anyone who held this view after the disagreement of the Companions except what has been related from al-A'mash, and after him Dawud al-Isfahani." It is related that 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, made the people abandon acting on the hadith "Water is from water" when they disagreed. Ibn 'Abbas interpreted it as referring to wet dreams, meaning that ghusl with water is only obligatory because of the emission of water in a wet dream. Whenever there is no emission, even if he sees himself having intercourse, there is no ghusl. There is no disagreement about this among all the scholars.

The tenth matter: God Most High's words ﴿except as travellers (ʿābirī sabīl)﴾. It is said: 'abartu al-tarīq, meaning I crossed it from one side to the other. 'Abartu al-nahr 'ubūran, and this is 'ibr al-nahr, meaning its bank. It is also said: 'ubr (with a damma), and al-ma'bar is that which one crosses by means of a boat or a bridge. And this is 'ābir al-sabīl, meaning one who passes along the road. A she-camel 'ubr asfār is one that is never stopped from travel, and across which one crosses the desert and the midday heat because of the speed of its walk. The poet said:

"A swift she-camel, light of hand and quick, a traveller through the noon heat, like a bustard that has reddened its legs."

['Ayranah among camels: one that is swift in its vigour; sirah: quick of step; shimillah: light, quick and alert. Hazaff: a tall bird among the bustards, or one with long plumage. Khadib: a male ostrich when it has eaten spring grass and its shanks and primaries have reddened.]

And 'abara al-qawm means they died. He recited:

"God's decree overcomes everything, and it toys with the impatient and the patient alike. If we pass over, we have mourners; and if we are left behind, we are on the verge of perishing."

He says: "If we die, we will have successors, and if we remain, we must still face death, as though it were an obligation upon us to come to it."

**The eleventh issue:** The scholars differed over His words ﴿except those passing through [a place]﴾. Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and al-Hakam said: "The one passing through (ʿabir al-sabil) is the traveller." It is not permissible for anyone in a state of major ritual impurity (janabah) to approach the prayer until after performing the ghusl (ritual bath), except the traveller, who performs tayammum (dry ablution with clean earth), and this is the view of Abu Hanifa, because water is generally available in settled areas, so the resident washes when water is present, while the traveller performs tayammum when he cannot find it.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: The people of opinion (ashab al-ra'y) said regarding a traveller in janabah who passes by a mosque that has a spring of water: he performs tayammum on the earth, enters the mosque, draws water from it, and then carries the water out of the mosque.

A group permitted a person in janabah to enter the mosque. Some of them relied on the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The believer is not impure." Ibn al-Mundhir said: "And we hold this view."

Ibn Abbas also said, as did Ibn Masud, Ikrima and al-Nakha'i: "The one passing through is the one who crosses over, the one who merely passes through," and this is the view of Amr ibn Dinar, Malik and al-Shafi'i.

A group said: "The one in janabah may not pass through the mosque, except when he finds no alternative, in which case he performs tayammum and passes through it." This is what al-Thawri and Ishaq ibn Rahawayh said.

Ahmad and Ishaq said regarding the one in janabah: "If he performs wudu (ablution), there is no harm in his sitting in the mosque," as related by Ibn al-Mundhir.

Some narrators reported regarding the cause of revelation of the verse that a group of the Ansar had doors of their houses opening directly into the mosque, so when one of them became junub, he was compelled to pass through the mosque.

I say: This is sound, and it is supported by what Abu Dawud narrated from Jasra bint Dajaja, who said: "I heard Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her) say: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ came while the doors of his companions' houses opened onto the mosque, and he said: 'Turn these houses away from the mosque.' Then the Prophet ﷺ entered, and the people had not done anything, hoping that a concession would be revealed for them. So he went out to them and said: 'Turn these houses away from the mosque, for I do not make the mosque lawful for a menstruating woman or for one in janabah.'"

In Sahih Muslim: "Let no opening (khawkha) remain in the mosque except the opening of Abu Bakr." [[The khawkha (with a fatha on the kha): the small door between two houses or two dwellings.]]

Thus he ﷺ ordered the doors to be closed, because leaving them open would lead to the mosque being used as a passageway and to people crossing through it. He made an exception for the opening of Abu Bakr out of honour for him and as a special distinction, because the two of them were generally not separated.

It has been narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he had not permitted anyone to pass through the mosque or to sit in it, except Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him).

Atiyya al-Awfi narrated it from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "It is not fitting for a Muslim, nor is it proper, to be in janabah in the mosque, except for me and Ali."

Our scholars said: This may be so, because Ali's house was in the mosque, just as the house of the Prophet ﷺ was in the mosque. Even if the two houses were not within the mosque but were connected to it, and their doors opened into the mosque, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ treated them as part of the mosque, and so he said: "It is not fitting for a Muslim..." and the rest of the hadith.

What indicates that Ali's house was in the mosque is what Ibn Shihab narrated from Salim ibn Abd Allah, who said: A man asked my father about Ali and Uthman (may Allah be pleased with them both), which of them was better. Abd Allah ibn Umar said to him: "This is the house of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ!" and he pointed to Ali's house beside it, "and there was nothing in the mosque other than these two," and he mentioned the hadith. They did not become junub in the mosque; they became junub in their houses, and their houses were part of the mosque since their doors opened into it, so when they came out of their houses in a state of janabah they would pass through it.

It is also possible that this was a special privilege for them, since the Prophet ﷺ had been given special privileges, so this was among the things specific to him. Then the Prophet ﷺ gave Ali (peace be upon him) a special concession, permitting him what he did not permit others. And even if the doors of their houses were in the mosque, there were other house doors in the mosque besides theirs, until the Prophet ﷺ ordered them closed, except the door of Ali.

Amr ibn Maymun narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Close the doors, except the door of Ali." So he (peace be upon him) singled him out by leaving his door open in the mosque, and he would be in janabah in his house, and his house was in the mosque.

As for his saying: "Let no khawkha remain in the mosque except the khawkha of Abu Bakr," it was, Allah knows best, doors that opened onto the mosque as small openings, while the doors of the houses lay outside the mosque. So he (peace be upon him) ordered those small openings closed and left the opening of Abu Bakr, out of honour for him. The khawkhat are like kuwa (openings) and mashakin (windows), and the door of Ali was the door of the house through which he would enter and exit.

Ibn Umar explained this by his words: "There was nothing in the mosque other than these two."

If it is said: It has been established from Ata ibn Yasar that he said: "Some men among the companions of the Prophet ﷺ would become junub, then perform wudu, come to the mosque, and converse in it." This indicates that remaining in the mosque is permissible for a junub who has performed wudu, and this is the view of Ahmad and Ishaq, as we mentioned.

The answer: Wudu does not remove the state of janabah. Every place that is designated for worship and honoured from visible impurity should not be entered by anyone who is not fit for that worship, and it is not proper for him to engage in it. The commonly reported practice of those people was that they would perform ghusl in their houses. If it is said: "This would invalidate the argument by analogy with one in a minor state of impurity (muhdith)," we say: That occurs frequently, so performing wudu for it would be burdensome, and His words, exalted is He: ﴿nor [come near while] in janabah, except those passing through﴾ contain what suffices and is enough.

If it is not permissible for him to remain in the mosque, then it is even more fitting that it is not permissible for him to touch the Mushaf or to recite from it, since it has greater sanctity. Its explanation will come in (al-Waqi'a [[See vol. 17, p. 223]]), Allah willing.

**The twelfth issue:** According to our scholars, the one in janabah is generally prohibited from reciting the Qur'an, except for brief verses used for seeking refuge (ta'awwudh). Musa ibn Uqba narrated from Nafi', from Ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The one in janabah and the menstruating woman should not recite anything of the Qur'an." Ibn Majah recorded it.

Al-Daraqutni recorded from the hadith of Sufyan, from Mis'ar and Shu'ba, from Amr ibn Murra, from Abd Allah ibn Salama, from Ali, who said: "Nothing prevented the Messenger of Allah ﷺ from reciting the Qur'an except when he was junub." Sufyan said: Shu'ba said to me: "I do not narrate a hadith better than this one." Ibn Majah also recorded it, saying: Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, Shu'ba narrated to us, from Amr ibn Murra, and he mentioned it in its meaning. This is a sound chain (isnad).

And from Ibn Abbas, from Abd Allah ibn Rawaha, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade any of us to recite the Qur'an while in janabah. Al-Daraqutni recorded it.

He also narrated from Ikrima, who said: Ibn Rawaha was lying beside his wife, then he got up and went to a slave girl of his in a corner of the room and had intercourse with her. His wife was startled and could not find him in his bed, so she got up and went out, and she saw him with his slave girl. She returned to the house, took a knife, and went out again. When he had finished, he got up and met her carrying the knife, and he said: "Mahaym?" [[Mahaym: a Yemeni word used for asking, meaning: what is behind you, what is your matter, what is this I see of you, and similar expressions.]] She said: "Mahaym! If I had caught you where I saw you, I would have struck you between your shoulders with this knife." He said: "Where did you see me?" She said: "I saw you with the slave girl." He said: "You did not see me, for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade any of us to recite the Qur'an while in janabah." She said: "Then recite." [And she did not recite the Qur'an.] He said:

Came to us the Messenger of Allah, reciting his Book,
As the clear light of dawn shines forth.
He brought guidance after blindness, and our hearts
Are certain, by him, that what he said will come to pass.
He keeps his side away from his bed
When the couches grow heavy with the idolaters.

فَقَالَتْ: آمَنْتُ بِاللَّهِ وَكَذَّبْتُ الْبَصَرَ. ثُمَّ غَدَا عَلَى رَسُولِ اللَّهِ (ﷺ) فَأَخْبَرَهُ، فَضَحِكَ حَتَّى بَدَتْ نَوَاجِذُهُ (ﷺ).

Thirteenth issue: His saying, exalted is He, (until you have washed yourselves). Allah, glorified and exalted, forbade prayer except after performing the ghusl (ritual bath, full washing of the body). The ghusl is a meaning that is understood, and its wording is known to the Arabs. It is used to express passing the hand along with the water over the thing washed. For this reason, the Arabs distinguished between their saying "I washed the garment" (ghasaltu al-thawb) and their saying "I poured water over him" (afadtu 'alayhi al-ma'a) and "I immersed it in water" (ghamastuhu fi al-ma'). Having established this, know that the scholars differed concerning a junub (one in a state of major ritual impurity, janabah) who pours water over his body or immerses himself in it without rubbing (tadallук, rubbing the body with the hand). The well-known position of the school of Malik is that it does not suffice him until he rubs, because Allah, glorified and exalted, commanded the junub to perform the ghusl, just as He commanded the one performing wudu' (ablution, wudu') to wash his face and hands, [and there was no escape for the one performing wudu' from passing his hands along with the water over his face and hands. Likewise, the whole body and head of the junub are in the same ruling as the face and hands of the one performing wudu'] [[The addition is from manuscripts T, J and Y.]]. [This is the view of al-Muzani and his preference. Abu al-Faraj 'Amr ibn Muhammad al-Maliki said: This is what is understood from the word ghusl, because al-ghusl in the language is al-iftial, and whoever does not pass his hands does not do anything beyond pouring water, and the people of the language do not call him one who washes (ghasil), but rather one who pours water and one who immerses himself in it. He said: Traditions have come from the Prophet (ﷺ) in this sense, that he said: "Under every hair is janabah, so wash the hair and cleanse the skin." He said: Its cleansing, and Allah knows best, is not achieved except by following it through, in line with what we have mentioned.] I say: There is no proof in what was cited from the hadith, for two reasons. The first: its interpretation has been disputed. Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah said: What is meant by his saying, peace be upon him, "and cleanse the skin" is the washing and cleaning of the private part (farj), and he used "skin" as a euphemism for the private part. Ibn Wahb said: I have not seen anyone more knowledgeable in the interpretation of hadiths than Ibn 'Uyaynah. The second: Abu Dawud included the hadith in his Sunan and said of it: "This hadith is weak," as in the narration of Ibn Dasah [[Ibn Dasah: he is Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Bakr al-Basri al-Dasi, a narrator of the Sunan of Abu Dawud.]]. In the narration of al-Lu'lu'i from him: al-Harith ibn Wajih is weak, his hadith is munkar (rejected). So the argument from the hadith falls, and what remains as the reliance is the language, as we have explained. It is supported by what is established in the sound hadiths: that the Prophet (ﷺ) was brought a child who urinated on him, so he asked for water and poured it over his urine and did not wash it. 'A'ishah narrated it, and Umm Qays bint Mihsan narrated something similar; Muslim recorded both. The majority of scholars and the body of jurists said: pouring water over the junub and immersing himself in it suffices, if he thoroughly and comprehensively covers the body, even if he does not rub, in accordance with the hadith of Maymunah and 'A'ishah concerning the ghusl of the Prophet (ﷺ). The imams narrated both, and that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to pour water over his body. Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Hakam also said this, and Abu al-Faraj returned to it, and he narrated it from Malik. He said: The passing of the two hands in the ghusl is commanded only because one who does not pass his hands over the body is hardly safe from the water missing some part of his body that must be washed. Ibn al-'Arabi said: I am amazed at Abu al-Faraj, who narrated and reported from the founder of the school that the ghusl without this is sufficient! Malik never said this explicitly or by derivation; it is only from his own errors. I say: This has indeed been narrated from Malik explicitly. Marwan ibn Muhammad al-Zahiri, who is trustworthy among the trustworthy Syrians, said: I asked Malik ibn Anas about a man who immersed himself in water while he was junub and did not perform wudu'. He said: His prayer is valid. Abu 'Umar said: This narration includes that he did not rub and did not perform wudu', and it sufficed him according to Malik. The well-known position of his school is that it does not suffice him until he rubs, by analogy with washing the face and hands. The argument of the majority is that everyone upon whom water is poured has indeed washed (ightasala). The Arabs say: "The sky washed me" (ghasalatni al-sama'). 'A'ishah and Maymunah described the manner of the ghusl of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and did not mention rubbing. Had it been obligatory, he would not have left it, because he is the one who makes clear from Allah what He intends. Had he done it, it would have been transmitted from him, just as the rubbing of the roots of his hair with water and his scooping water over his head were transmitted, and other aspects of the manner of his ghusl and wudu', peace be upon him. Abu 'Umar said: It is no objection that in the language of the Arabs, ghusl may sometimes mean rubbing (al-'arkh [[al-'Arkh: rubbing.]]) and sometimes pouring and flowing. If this is so, it is not impossible that Allah, mighty and majestic, required His servants in wudu' to pass their hands over their faces with the water, and that this would be a ghusl; and that they pour water over themselves in the ghusl of janabah and menstruation, and that this would be a ghusl in accordance with the Sunnah without departing from the language; and that each of the two matters is a root in itself, and it is not necessary that one be returned to the other, because roots are not reduced to one another by analogy. This is a matter on which there is no disagreement among the scholars of the Ummah. Only branches (furu') are reduced by analogy to roots. And success is from Allah.

Fourteenth issue: The hadith of Maymunah and 'A'ishah refutes what Shu'bah, the mawla (freedman or client) of Ibn 'Abbas, narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: that when he performed the ghusl from janabah, he washed his hands seven times and his private part seven times. It has also been narrated from Ibn 'Umar that he said: "Prayer was fifty, and the ghusl from janabah was seven times, and washing urine from a garment was seven times. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) kept asking (his Lord) until prayer was made five, and the ghusl from janabah once, and washing from urine once." Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: The chain of this hadith from Ibn 'Umar has weakness and laxity, although Abu Dawud recorded it and the one before it from Shu'bah, the mawla of Ibn 'Abbas, and this Shu'bah is not strong. The hadith of 'A'ishah and Maymunah refutes both of them.

Fifteenth issue: As for one who is not able to pass his hand over his body, Sahnun said: Let someone who is nearby do that for him, or he may treat him with a cloth. In al-Wadihah: he passes his hands over the parts of his body he can reach, then pours water until it covers what his hands did not reach.

Sixteenth issue: The statement of Malik differed concerning the junub's combing (takhlil) of his beard. Ibn al-Qasim narrated from him that he said: "It is not obligatory for him." Ashhab narrated from him that it is obligatory. Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam said: That is more beloved to us, because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to comb his hair in the ghusl of janabah, and that is general, although the most apparent of it is the hair of the head. Scholars hold both of these opinions. From the perspective of meaning: covering the entire body in the ghusl is obligatory, and the skin beneath the beard is part of it, so it is obligatory for water to reach it and for the hand to touch it. The obligation shifts to the hair only in the minor purification (tahara sughra, i.e., wudu'), because it is based on lightening, and substitution (niyabat al-abdal) in it without necessity [[In manuscripts U, J, H, W: "and its explanation is that it is not rubbing." In manuscripts T and Z: "and its explanation is substitution without necessity."]] is permitted; for this reason wiping over the leather socks (khuffayn) is permitted in it and not in the ghusl. I say: This is supported by his saying (ﷺ): "Under every hair is janabah."

Seventeenth issue: Some people went to extremes and made rinsing the mouth (madmadah) and sniffing water into the nose (istinshaq) obligatory, based on His saying, exalted is He, (until you have washed yourselves). Among them is Abu Hanifah, and because they are part of the face, and their ruling is the ruling of the outer face, like the cheeks and forehead. So whoever leaves them and prays must repeat, like one who leaves a patch (lum'ah [[al-Lum'ah: a spot the water does not reach in wudu' or ghusl.]]); and whoever leaves them in his wudu' has no obligation to repeat. Malik said: They are not obligatory, neither in janabah nor in wudu', because they are inner parts [so it is not obligatory], like the interior of the body. This is also the view of Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari, al-Layth ibn Sa'd, al-Awza'i, and a group of the Successors (tabi'un). Ibn Abi Layla and Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman said: They are both obligatory in wudu' and ghusl together. This is the view of Ishaq, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and some companions of Dawud. It was also narrated from al-Zuhri and 'Ata' the same view. It is narrated from Ahmad too that rinsing the mouth is Sunnah and sniffing water into the nose is obligatory, and this was said by some companions of Dawud. The proof of those who did not make them obligatory is that Allah, glorified, did not mention them in His Book, and His Messenger did not make them obligatory, and there was no consensus on them, and obligations are not established except by these means. Those who made them obligatory argued from the verse, and from His saying, exalted is He, (So wash your faces) [[Qur'an 5:6, "So wash your faces"]]. Whatever is obligatory in one washing is obligatory in the other. And it has not been preserved from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he left out rinsing the mouth and sniffing water into the nose in his wudu' or in his ghusl from janabah, and he is the one who makes clear from Allah His intent, in word and in deed. Those who distinguished between them argued that the Prophet (ﷺ) performed rinsing the mouth and did not command it, and his actions which recommend something are not obligatory unless by evidence; but he performed sniffing water into the nose and commanded it, and his command is always for obligation.

Eighteenth issue: Our scholars said: Intention (niyyah) is necessary in the ghusl from janabah, because of His saying, exalted is He, (until you have washed yourselves), and that requires intention. This is the view of Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq, and Abu Thawr. Likewise wudu' and tayammum (dry ablution with earth). They supported this with His saying, exalted is He, (And they were not commanded except to worship Allah, being sincere to Him in religion) [[See vol. 20, p. 144.]], and sincerity (ikhlas) is intention in drawing near to Allah, and aiming for Him by performing what He has obligated upon His believing servants. And he, peace be upon him, said: "Actions are only by intentions," and this is an action. Al-Awza'i and al-Hasan said: wudu' and tayammum are sufficient without intention. Abu Hanifah and his companions said: Every purification with water is valid without intention, but tayammum is not valid except with intention, by analogy with the removal of impurity (najasah) from bodies and garments, which by consensus is done without intention. Al-Walid ibn Muslim narrated this from Malik.

Nineteenth issue: As for the amount of water with which one performs the ghusl, Malik narrated from Ibn Shihab, from 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, from 'A'ishah [Mother of the Believers] [[From manuscripts J and T.]], may Allah be pleased with her, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to bathe from a vessel which is the faraq (a measure of about three sa' [[the faraq is a measure of volume, commonly estimated at about sixteen rotls, equal to three sa']]) for janabah.

(The measure) al-Faraq is moved (its) first letter and (the second) is vowelled with sukun. Ibn Wahb said: al-Faraq is a wooden measure. Ibn Shihab used to say that it holds five qisat, by the qisat of the Banu Umayyah. Muhammad ibn Isa al-A'sha explained al-Faraq as three sa', and said: and it is five qisat, and in the five qisat there are twelve mudd by the mudd of the Prophet ﷺ. In Sahih Muslim, Sufyan said: al-Faraq is three sa'. And from Anas, who said: The Prophet ﷺ used to perform wudu with a mudd and bathe with a sa' up to five mudd. In another narration: he would bathe with five makakik and perform wudu with one makkuk [[al-makkuk (kanjur): a well-known measure among the people of Iraq; its plural is makakik and makaki, and by it he meant the mudd. It is also said: the sa'. The first is more apt, because it came in another hadith explained as the mudd.]]. These hadiths indicate the recommendation of using little water without measuring or weighing, taking from it a person as much as suffices and not exceeding it, for excess in it is extravagance (israf), and extravagance is blameworthy. The school of the Ibadiyya holds in favour of excess in water [[Extravagance (israf) in their view is among the disliked acts of wudu, as recorded.]], and that is from Satan.

The twentieth (issue): His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if you are sick, or on a journey, or one of you comes from the place of relieving oneself, or you have touched women, and you find no water, then take clean earth and wipe your faces and your hands﴾. This is the verse of tayammum (dry ablution). It was revealed concerning ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf, who had sexual impurity (janabah) while wounded, so he was permitted to perform tayammum. Then the verse became general for all people. It was also said: it was revealed because the Companions lacked water in the expedition of al-Muraysi' (al-Muraysi' (diminutive of marsu'): a well or water of Khuza'a, a day from al-Furu', to which the expedition of Banu al-Mustaliq is attributed), when the necklace of ʿAisha broke. Malik transmitted the hadith through the narration of ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn al-Qasim from his father from ʿAisha. Al-Bukhari entitled this verse in the Book of Tafsir: Muhammad narrated to us, saying: ʿAbdah informed us, from Hisham ibn ʿUrwah, from his father, from ʿAisha, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: A necklace belonging to Asma' was lost, so the Prophet ﷺ sent men in search of it. The prayer time came, and they were not in a state of wudu and found no water, so they prayed without wudu. Then Allah, Exalted, revealed the verse of tayammum. I say: this narration contains no mention of the place, and in it the necklace belonged to Asma', contrary to the hadith of Malik. Al-Nasa'i mentioned from the narration of ʿAli ibn Mushhir from Hisham ibn ʿUrwah from his father from ʿAisha that she borrowed a necklace from Asma' while she was on a journey with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and it slipped from her; and that place was called al-Salsal (al-Salsal (with a vowel on the first letter and it may be fatha): a place seven miles from Madinah, from Mu'jam al-Buldan), and he mentioned the hadith.
In this narration from Hisham, the necklace is attributed to Asma', and ʿAisha borrowed it from Asma'.
This explains the hadith of Malik when he said: a necklace of ʿAisha broke, and the hadith of al-Bukhari when he said: a necklace of Asma' was lost. And in it, the place is called al-Salsal.
And al-Tirmidhi transmitted it: al-Humaydi narrated to us, Sufyan narrated to us, Hisham ibn ʿUrwah narrated to us, from his father, from ʿAisha, that her necklace fell off on the night of al-Abwa' (al-Abwa' (with fatha on the hamza): a station between Makkah and Madinah near al-Juhfah on the north side, one stage away), so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent two men in search of it, and he mentioned the hadith.
In this narration from Hisham also, the necklace is attributed to her, but as attribution of a borrower, by the evidence of the hadith of al-Nasa'i.
And he said about the place: al-Abwa', as Malik said, except that he said it without doubt.
In the hadith of Malik he said: We sent the camel I was riding and found the necklace beneath it.
In al-Bukhari it came: that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ found it.
All of this is sound in meaning. The differences of the transmitters regarding the necklace and the 'iqd, and regarding the place, do not undermine the hadith or weaken any part of it, because the meaning intended by the hadith and its purpose is the revelation of tayammum, and the narrations have established the matter of the necklace. [[In manuscripts Z and T: the narrations clarified the matter, etc.]]

As for his saying in the hadith of al-Tirmidhi: "he sent two men," it was said: one of them was Usayd ibn Hudayr.

Perhaps they are what is meant by "men" in the hadith of al-Bukhari, and so it was expressed with a plural form, since the least plural is two; or he followed them with others, and so the use of the word is correct, and Allah knows best.

They sent in search of it and searched, but found nothing in their direction. When they returned, they stirred the camel and found it beneath it. [[The pronoun first refers to the necklace, and second to the 'iqd.]]

It has been reported that the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ suffered a wound which spread among them, then they were afflicted with sexual impurity, and they complained of that to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, so this verse was revealed.

This also is not a contradiction to what we mentioned, for they may have been struck by a wound in that expedition from which they returned, since there was fighting in it, and so they complained; the necklace was lost, and the verse was revealed.

It has been said: the loss of the necklace was in the expedition of Banu al-Mustaliq.

This also is not a contradiction to the view of those who said it was in the expedition of al-Muraysi', since it is one and the same expedition. The Prophet ﷺ raided Banu al-Mustaliq in Sha'ban of the sixth year after the Hijrah, according to what Khalifah ibn Khayyat and Abu ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said, and he appointed Abu Dharr al-Ghifari over Madinah.

It was said: rather, Numaylah ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Laythi.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ attacked Banu al-Mustaliq while they were heedless, at a water called al-Muraysi' on the side of Qudayd (Qudayd: a place between Makkah and Madinah, or a water) on the coastal side. He killed whoever he killed and took captive [the women and the offspring]. Their slogan that day was: "Kill them, kill them."

It has been said: Banu al-Mustaliq had gathered against the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and intended him harm, and when this reached him, he went out to them and met them at a water.

This is what came concerning the beginning of tayammum and its cause.

It has been said: the verse of al-Ma'idah is the verse of tayammum, as will be explained there.

Abu ʿUmar said: Allah, Exalted, revealed the verse of tayammum, which is the verse of wudu mentioned in Surat al-Ma'idah, or the verse in Surat al-Nisa'. Tayammum is not mentioned in any other verses than these two, and both are Madani.

The twenty-first (issue): His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Sick﴾. Illness is an expression for the body's departure from the limit of balance and normality into deviation and abnormality.

It is of two kinds: much and little. If it is much, to the extent that one fears death from the cold of the water, or because of the illness one has, or fears the loss of some limbs, then this one performs tayammum by consensus, except what is narrated from al-Hasan and ʿAta' that he purifies himself even if he dies.

This is refuted by His saying, Exalted is He: (And He has not placed upon you any hardship in religion) [[See vol. 12 p. 99]] and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾.

Al-Daraqutni narrated from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: (And if you are sick or on a journey), he said: if a man has a wound in the way of Allah, or sores, or smallpox, and becomes junub and fears he will die if he bathes, he performs tayammum.

And from Saʿid ibn Jubayr also, from Ibn ʿAbbas, he said: The sick person was permitted to perform tayammum with clean earth.

ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs performed tayammum when he feared he would die from the severity of the cold, and the Prophet ﷺ did not order him to bathe or to repeat.

If it is little, but he fears with it the occurrence of an illness, its increase, or slowness of recovery, then these perform tayammum by consensus of the school.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: as far as I have memorized.

I say: al-Baji has mentioned a difference of opinion in this. al-Qadi Abu al-Hasan said: such as when a healthy person fears a catarrh or fever, and likewise if the sick person fears an increase of illness, and Abu Hanifah said something similar.

Al-Shafi'i said: it is not permissible for him to perform tayammum while water is present, except if he fears destruction; and al-Qadi Abu al-Hasan narrated this from Malik.

Ibn al-ʿArabi said: (Al-Shafi'i said: tayammum is not permitted for the sick except when he fears destruction, because the increase of illness is not certain, for it may occur or may not occur, and it is not permissible to abandon a certain obligation for a doubtful fear.

We say: you have contradicted yourself, for you said that if one fears destruction from cold he performs tayammum; just as fear of destruction permits tayammum, so fear of illness permits it, because illness is a harm just as destruction is a harm.

He said: And how strange is al-Shafi'i, who says: if water exceeds its worth by a single grain, he is not obliged to buy it, to preserve wealth, and he is obliged to perform tayammum, while he fears illness for his body!

And for them (against him) is an objection not worth hearing.)

I say: the sound view of al-Shafi'i's position, as al-Qushayri Abu Nasr ʿAbd al-Rahim mentioned in his tafsir, is:

The illness which permits tayammum is that in which one fears loss of life or loss of some limbs if he uses water.

If he fears the prolongation of the illness, then the sound view of al-Shafi'i is: the permissibility of tayammum.

Abu Dawud and al-Daraqutni narrated, from Yahya ibn Ayyub, from Yazid ibn Abi Habib, from ʿImran ibn Abi Anas, from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Jubayr, from ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs, who said:

I had a wet dream on a cold night in the expedition of Dhat al-Salasil, and I feared that if I bathed I would die, so I performed tayammum and then led my companions in the dawn prayer. They mentioned that to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he said: "O ʿAmr, you led your companions in prayer while you were junub?"

I informed him of what had prevented me from bathing, and I said: "I heard Allah, Mighty and Majestic, say: (And do not kill yourselves; indeed Allah is ever Merciful to you)." The Prophet of Allah ﷺ laughed and said nothing.

This hadith indicates the permissibility of tayammum with fear, not with certainty; and in it the name junub is applied to one who performs tayammum, and the permissibility of a tayammum-performer leading those who performed wudu. This is one of the two opinions in our school, and it is the sound one, [and it is] what Malik recited in his Muwatta' and had read to him until he died.

The second opinion: he does not lead, because he is lower in merit than one who performed wudu, and the imam should be of higher rank. al-Daraqutni narrated from the hadith of Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, who said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The one performing tayammum should not lead those who performed wudu." Its chain is weak.

Abu Dawud and al-Daraqutni narrated from Jabir, who said:

We set out on a journey, and a stone struck a man among us and wounded his head; then he had a wet dream, so he asked his companions: "Do you find a concession for me to perform tayammum?"

They said: "We find no concession for you while you are able to use water." So he bathed and died. When we came to the Prophet ﷺ, he was informed of that and said: "They killed him; may Allah kill them! Why did they not ask when they did not know? The cure for ignorance is asking. It would have sufficed him to perform tayammum and to bind—(Musa was uncertain which)—a cloth over his wound, then wipe over it and wash the rest of his body."

Al-Daraqutni said: Abu Bakr said: this is a sunnah narrated uniquely by the people of Makkah and carried by the people of al-Jazirah. Only al-Zubayr ibn Khurayq narrated it from ʿAta' from Jabir, and he is not strong. al-Awza'i differed from him, narrating it from ʿAta' from Ibn ʿAbbas [and this is the correct one]. Concerning al-Awza'i there are differing reports: it is said from him from ʿAta', and it is said from him:

I heard from ʿAṭāʾ. Al-Awzāʿī transmitted its ending from ʿAṭāʾ, from the Prophet ﷺ, and this is the correct version.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim said: I asked my father and Abū Zurʿa about it, and they said: Ibn Abī al-ʿIshrīn narrated it from al-Awzāʿī, from Ismāʿīl ibn Muslim, from ʿAṭāʾ, from Ibn ʿAbbās, and he traced the hadith back (to the Prophet ﷺ).

Dāwūd said: Anyone to whom the name "sick" applies may perform tayammum (dry ablution), based on the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And if you are sick﴾.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: This is the view of Khalaf. Among the scholars of the Muslim community, it applies only to one who fears harm from using water or from its effect on him, such as one with a skin disease or one with an illness that water may endanger, as has already been reported from Ibn ʿAbbās.

The twenty-second issue: the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿or on a journey﴾. Tayammum is permitted because of travel, whether the journey is long or short, when water is unavailable. It is not required that the journey be one in which the prayer may be shortened. This is the position of Mālik and the majority of scholars. [[In (manuscript) j: "the jurists."]]

Others said: One may perform tayammum only on a journey in which the prayer is shortened.

Others stipulated that the journey must be one of obedience.

All of this is weak.

And Allah knows best.

The twenty-third issue: The scholars agreed on the permissibility of tayammum on a journey, as we have mentioned, and they differed about it while residing at home. Mālik and his companions held that tayammum is permitted both at home and on a journey. This is also the view of Abū Ḥanīfa and Muḥammad.

Al-Shāfiʿī said: It is not permitted for a healthy resident to perform tayammum unless he fears destruction. This is also the view of al-Ṭabarī.

Al-Shāfiʿī, al-Layth and al-Ṭabarī also said: If a person, whether healthy or sick, cannot find water while at home and fears the prayer time will pass, he performs tayammum, prays, and then repeats the prayer.

Abū Yūsuf and Zufar said: Tayammum is not permitted at home, neither for illness nor for fear of the prayer time passing.

Al-Ḥasan and ʿAṭāʾ said: A sick person does not perform tayammum when he finds water. (The ruling concerns) only the sick person and not anyone else.

The cause of the disagreement is their difference over the meaning of the verse. Mālik and those who followed him said: Allah mentioned the sick and the travellers as conditions for tayammum, and this was in reference to what is usual for those who cannot find water. Residents usually have water available, so He did not mention them specifically.

Therefore everyone who cannot find water, or for whom something prevents its use, or who fears missing the prayer time, may perform tayammum: the traveller by explicit text, and the resident by the same reasoning. Likewise, the sick person by explicit text, and the healthy person by the same reasoning.

As for those who prohibited it at home, they said: Allah made tayammum a concession for the sick and the traveller, like breaking the fast and shortening the prayer. He permitted tayammum only under two conditions, illness and travel. So a healthy resident does not enter this ruling, since he falls outside the condition set by Allah the Exalted.

As for the view of al-Ḥasan and ʿAṭāʾ, which prohibited it altogether even when water is present, they said: Allah made it conditional only upon the absence of water, by His words: ﴿but if you find no water, then perform tayammum﴾. So He permitted tayammum to no one except when water is absent.

Abū ʿUmar said: Were it not for the view of the majority and the narration that has come down, the view of al-Ḥasan and ʿAṭāʾ would be sound. And Allah knows best.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ permitted tayammum for ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ while he was travelling, when he feared death if he bathed with water. So the sick person is more deserving of this permission.

I (al-Qurṭubī) say: Among the evidence for the permissibility of tayammum at home when one fears missing the prayer if he goes to the water is the Book and the Sunnah.

As for the Book, it is His words, glorified is He: ﴿or one of you comes from the place of relieving oneself﴾, meaning the resident who cannot find water performs tayammum.

Al-Qushayrī, ʿAbd al-Raḥīm, explicitly stated this, saying: Then the consideration turns to whether repeating the prayer is obligatory, because the absence of water at home is a rare excuse. Regarding repetition, there are two opinions.

I say: Our companions have stated the same ruling about one who performs tayammum at home. Does he repeat (the prayer) when he finds water or not? The well-known position of the school of Mālik is that he does not repeat, and this is the sound view.

Ibn Ḥabīb and Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥakam said: He repeats it indefinitely. Ibn al-Mundhir narrated this from Mālik.

al-Walīd said, on his authority: He performs ghusl (full bath), even if the sun has risen.

As for the Sunnah, it is what al-Bukhārī narrated from Abū al-Juhaym ibn al-Ḥārith ibn al-Ṣimma al-Anṣārī, who said: The Prophet ﷺ came from the direction of Bi'r Jamal [[Bi'r Jamal: a place near Madina.]], and a man met him and greeted him with peace, but the Prophet ﷺ did not return the greeting until he turned to a wall, wiped his face and both hands, and then returned the greeting to him.

Muslim also narrated it, but in his version the phrase "well" (bi'r) does not appear [[In Muslim's version: "from the direction of Bi'r Jamal," as in al-Bukhārī's narration.]].

Al-Dāraquṭnī narrated it from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, and in it: Then he returned the greeting to the man and said: Nothing prevented me from returning your greeting except that I was not in a state of purity.

The twenty-fourth issue: The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿or one of you comes from the place of relieving oneself﴾. Al-ghāʾiṭ (the place of relieving oneself) originally means a low-lying piece of land. Its plural is ghiyṭān or aghwāṭ, and Ghūṭat Dimashq (the Ghouta of Damascus) was named after it.

The Arabs used to go to such low places to relieve themselves, to conceal themselves from people's eyes. Then the discharge that comes out of a person was called ghāʾiṭ by association [[In manuscripts ṭ and z: "by proximity."]].

And "ghāṭa fī al-arḍ, yaghūṭu" means he disappeared into the ground.

Al-Zuhrī recited: ﴿min al-ghayṭ﴾. It may be that its origin is al-ghayṭ, which was lightened, like hayyin and mayyit and similar words.

It may also be from al-ghawṭ, as shown by their saying taghawwaṭa when he went to the ghāʾiṭ. The waw in al-ghawṭ was changed to a yāʾ, as they said in "lā ḥawla lā ḥīla".

The "aw" (or) here has the meaning of "wa" (and). That is: If you are sick or on a journey, and one of you comes from the place of relieving oneself, then perform tayammum. On this reading, the cause requiring tayammum is the minor impurity (ḥadath), not illness or travel. This shows the permissibility of tayammum at home, as we have explained.

The correct view regarding "aw" among the people of reasoning is that it keeps its own meaning. "Aw" has its meaning, and "wa" has its meaning.

According to them, this involves an ellipsis, and the meaning is: If you are sick with an illness that prevents you from touching water, or on a journey and you have not found water while needing water.

And Allah knows best.

The twenty-fifth issue: The word ﴿al-ghāʾiṭ﴾ collectively includes, in meaning, all the impurities that break the minor ritual purity.

People have differed about enumerating them, and the most refined of what has been said is that they are three types, about which there is no disagreement in our school:
loss of reason, an habitual discharge, and touching.

According to the view of Abū Ḥanīfa, it is whatever comes out of the body of impure substances. The exit point is not considered, and touching is not counted.

According to the view of al-Shāfiʿī and Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥakam, it is whatever comes out of the two passages. Habituation is not considered, and touching is counted.

Having established this, know that the Muslims agreed that whoever loses his reason through fainting, madness, or intoxication must perform ablution. They differed…

Is sleep like other breaches of ritual purity, or is it not a breach in itself but a likely cause of one? There are three opinions: two extremes and a middle position.

The first extreme: al-Muzani, Abu Ibrahim Isma'il, held that it is a breach, and that wudu' is obligatory after a little or a lot of it, like other breaches. This is what Malik's statement in the Muwatta' implies, in his saying: "One does not perform wudu' except because of a breach that issues from the private parts or the rear, or sleep." It is also implied by the hadith of Safwan ibn 'Assal, which al-Nasa'i, al-Daraqutni and al-Tirmidhi transmitted, and al-Tirmidhi authenticated it. They all related it from the hadith of 'Asim ibn Abi al-Nujud, from Zirr ibn Hubaysh, who said: "I came to Safwan ibn 'Assal al-Muradi and said: 'I came to ask you about wiping over the leather socks.' He said: [Yes [The addition is from Sunan al-Daraqutni.]] 'I was in the army that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ dispatched, and he commanded us to wipe over the socks when we put them on in a state of purity: three days when we travel, and a day and a night when we stay in one place, and not to remove them because of urination, defecation or sleep [and not to remove them [The addition is from Sunan al-Daraqutni.]] except because of janabah.'" In this hadith and in Malik's statement, the same ruling applies to defecation, urination and sleep. They said: By analogy, since a large amount of it, and what overpowers the intellect, is a breach, its small amount must also be one. It is also narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The tie of the anus is the two eyes, so whoever sleeps let him perform wudu'" (al-sah: the anus; its root is al-sathah with vowelling, the 'ayn of the verb having been dropped; it is also transmitted as al-sat, with the lam of the verb dropped). This is a general statement. Abu Dawud transmitted it, and al-Daraqutni transmitted it from the hadith of Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan from the Prophet ﷺ.

As for the other extreme, it is narrated from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari a report indicating that sleep, in his view, is not a breach in any state, until the sleeper commits a breach other than sleep, because he used to appoint someone to guard him when he slept. If no breach came from him, he would rise from his sleep and pray. It is also narrated from 'Ubaydah, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, and al-Awza'i in the transmission of Mahmud ibn Khalid.

The majority holds opposite to these two extremes. The overall position of Malik is that every sleeper who falls into deep sleep and whose sleep is prolonged, in whatever state, is obliged to perform wudu'. This is also the view of al-Zuhri, Rabi'ah, and al-Awza'i in the transmission of al-Walid ibn Muslim. Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: If the sleep is light, not penetrating the heart and not overwhelming it, it does no harm. Abu Hanifa and his companions said: wudu' is required only of one who sleeps lying on his side or reclining. al-Shafi'i said: whoever sleeps sitting has no obligation of wudu'; Ibn Wahb narrated this from Malik.

The soundest of these opinions is the well-known position of Malik, based on the hadith of Ibn 'Umar that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was occupied one night with [meaning the 'Isha' prayer [The addition is from al-Bukhari.]] and delayed it until we slept [in the mosque [The addition is from al-Bukhari.]], then we awoke, then we slept, then we awoke; then the Prophet ﷺ came out to us and said: "None of the people of the earth is awaiting the prayer except you." The imams transmitted it, and the wording is that of al-Bukhari. It is the most sound of what is related on this subject in terms of chain and practice. As for what Malik said in his Muwatta', and what Safwan ibn 'Assal said in his hadith, its meaning is: heavy sleep that overpowers the self, as shown by this hadith and what is similar to it.

Also, Waki' narrated the hadith of Safwan from Mis'ar, from 'Asim ibn Abi al-Nujud, and said: "[or wind] instead of [or sleep]." al-Daraqutni said: no one but Waki' from Mis'ar said "[or wind]" in this hadith. I say: Waki' is a trustworthy imam, whom al-Bukhari, Muslim and other imams narrated from. So the argument from the hadith of Safwan for those who hold that sleep is a breach falls away.

As for the position of Abu Hanifa, it is weak. al-Daraqutni narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ slept while prostrating, until he snored or blew, then rose and prayed.
