I said: "O Messenger of Allah, you have slept!" He said: "Wudu' is not obligatory except on one who sleeps lying down, for when he lies down his joints relax." Abu Khalid alone transmitted it from Qatadah, and it is not sound, said al-Daraqutni. Abu Dawud also transmitted it and said: the statement "Wudu' is for one who sleeps lying down" is a munkar hadith; none transmitted it except Abu Khalid Yazid al-Dalani from Qatadah, while a group related from Ibn 'Abbas without mentioning any of this. Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: this is a munkar hadith; none of the trustworthy companions of Qatadah transmitted it, and Abu Khalid al-Dalani alone transmitted it, and they rejected it, and it is not a proof in what is transmitted.

As for al-Shafi'i's statement: wudu' is obligatory on every sleeper except one who sits alone, and that whoever departs from the state of upright sitting and sleeps must perform wudu', this is the view of al-Tabari and Dawud, and it is narrated from 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Umar, because one who sits rarely falls into deep sleep, so he is in the sense of light sleep. al-Daraqutni narrated from the hadith of 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever sleeps sitting, there is no wudu' for him; and whoever lays his side down, wudu' is obligatory on him."

As for what leaves the body: our evidence is what al-Bukhari transmitted, saying: Qutaybah told us, saying: Yazid ibn Zurayʿ told us, from Khalid, from 'Ikrimah, from 'A'ishah, who said: a woman of his wives performed i'tikaf with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and she would see blood and yellowish discharge, with the basin beneath her while she prayed. This discharge is outside the usual course; it is a vein that was cut, so it is an illness. Whatever is of this nature and comes from the two passages is not, according to us, obligatory for wudu', in contrast to al-Shafi'i as we have mentioned. And success is from Allah. And it is refuted against the Hanafi, who gave consideration to the impure discharge. Thus the position of Malik ibn Anas, may Allah be pleased with him and with them all, is established and made clear, so that no doubt remains.

The twenty-sixth issue: the words of the Exalted: ﴿or you have touched women﴾. Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read (lamastum). Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (lamastum). Regarding its meaning there are three opinions: first, that lamastum means you have had intercourse; second, lamastum means you have made physical contact; third, it combines both meanings. (Lamastum) has the same meaning according to most people, except that it is related from Muhammad ibn Yazid that he said: the more appropriate in linguistic usage is that (lamastum) means kissed or the like, because each of the two has an action. He said: (lamastum) means covered or touched, and in this the woman has no action. The scholars differed on the ruling of the verse according to five positions. One group said: touching here is specific to the hand, and the one in janabah is only mentioned with water, so he does not enter into the meaning intended by His words: (and if you are sick) the verse, so there is no path for him to tayammum; rather, the janabah person must wash or forgo prayer until he finds water. This view was narrated from 'Umar and Ibn Mas'ud. Abu 'Umar said: none of the jurists of the cities among the people of opinion and the bearers of reports has held the view of 'Umar and 'Abd Allah on this question; and that, Allah knows best, is due to the hadith of 'Ammar and 'Imran ibn Husayn and the hadith of Abu Dharr from the Prophet ﷺ regarding tayammum of the janabah person. Abu Hanifa held the reverse of this view, saying: touching here is specific to touching that is intercourse. So the janabah person performs tayammum, and one who touches with his hand has not had mention made of him, so it is not a breach, nor does it diminish his wudu'. So if a man kisses his wife out of desire, his wudu' is not nullified. They reinforced this with what al-Daraqutni narrated from 'A'ishah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ kissed one of his wives and then went out to prayer without performing wudu'. 'Urwah said: I said to her: who was she, other than you? And she laughed. Malik said: one who touches with intercourse performs tayammum, and one who touches with the hand performs tayammum if he is aroused. If he touches her without desire, there is no wudu'; this is also the view of Ahmad and Ishaq, and it is the implication of the verse. 'Ali ibn Ziyad said: if she has a thick garment on, there is nothing on him; if it is thin, he must perform wudu'. 'Abd al-Malik ibn al-Majishun said: whoever deliberately touches his wife with his hand for playfulness must perform wudu', whether he was aroused or not. Abu al-Walid al-Baji said in al-Muntaqa: what is established from the school of Malik and his companions is that wudu' is obligatory on account of intending desire, not on its occurrence; so whoever intends desire by his touch must perform wudu', whether he was aroused or not, and this is the meaning of what is in al-'Utbiyyah from the transmission of 'Isa from Ibn al-Qasim. As for erection by itself, Ibn Nafi' narrated from Malik that it does not require wudu' nor washing of the penis unless it is accompanied by touch or madhy. Shaykh Abu Ishaq said: whoever has an erection breaks his wudu'; this is Malik's view in al-Mudawwanah. al-Shafi'i said: when a man's body part comes into contact with a woman's body, whether by hand or by another limb, the breaking of purity is attached to it; this is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Umar, al-Zuhri and Rabi'ah. al-Awza'i said: if the touch is with the hand it breaks purity, and if it is with other than the hand it does not break it, based on His words: (then they touched him with their hands) [see vol. 6, p. 392]. These are five positions, the strictest of which is the position of Malik, which is narrated from 'Umar and his son 'Abd Allah, and is the view of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud that lamasah is less than intercourse, and that wudu' is obligatory for it; and to this most jurists went. Ibn al-'Arabi said: this is the apparent meaning of the verse, for His words at its beginning: (nor in janabah) indicate intercourse; His words: (or one of you comes from the place of relief) indicate breach; and His words: (or you have touched) indicate touching and kissing. Thus there are three sentences for three rulings, and this is the utmost in knowledge and explanation. And if the intended meaning of touching were intercourse, it would be repetition in speech.

I say: As for what Abu Hanifah relied on from the hadith of Aisha, it is a mursal (a hadith in which the Successor omits the Companion from the chain), narrated by Waki' from al-A'mash from Habib ibn Abi Thabit from Urwah, from Aisha. Yahya ibn Sa'id said, and he mentioned the hadith of al-A'mash from Habib from 'Amrah, and said: "Sufyan al-Thawri was the most knowledgeable of people about this. He claimed that Habib had not heard anything from Urwah." Al-Daraqutni said this.

If it is said: "You (the Shafi'is) also accept the mursal, so you are obliged to accept it and act upon it." We reply: We set it aside in favour of the apparent meaning of the verse and the practice of the Companions.

If it is said: "The mulamasah (touching) is intercourse, and this has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas." We reply: al-Faruq ('Umar) and his son opposed him, and 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who was from Kufa, followed them both. So why did you oppose him?!

If it is said: "The mulamasah is of the form of mufa'alah (the form III verbal pattern), which can only occur between two parties, whereas touching with the hand occurs from one party only. Therefore it is established that mulamasah is intercourse." We reply: The meaning required by mulamasah is the meeting of two skins, whether it comes from one party or from two, because each of them is described as a toucher (lamis) and one who is touched (malmus).

Another answer: mulamasah may occur from one party only. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade the sale of mulamasah (bay' al-mulamasah, a type of sale in which touching the goods concludes the contract), and the garment is touched but is not a toucher. Ibn 'Umar, reporting about himself, said: "I was then of an age close to puberty (nahaztu al-ihtilam)." And the Arabs say: "'Aqabtu al-lis (I punished the thief)" and "Tara'tu al-na'l (I struck the sandal)," and such usages are numerous.

If it is said: When Allah, glorified is He, mentioned the cause of minor impurity (hadath), which is coming from the toilet (al-gha'it), He mentioned the cause of major impurity (janabah), which is mulamasah, so He explained the ruling for both minor and major impurity when water is absent, just as He explained their ruling when water is present. We reply: We do not deny that the word may be taken to mean intercourse and touching, and that it conveys both rulings as we have explained. And it has been read as ﴿lamastum﴾ (you have touched), as we mentioned.

As for what al-Shafi'i held, that if a man touches a woman with some part of his body, with no barrier between them, whether out of desire or without desire, ablution becomes obligatory for him, this is also the apparent meaning of the Qur'an. Likewise, if she touches him, ablution becomes obligatory for him, except for hair. Whoever touches his wife's hair, whether with desire or without desire, is not required to perform ablution. The same applies to the teeth and the nails, because these are not of the same nature as skin. If he takes precaution and performs ablution when he touches her hair, that is good. If he touches her with his hand, or she touches him with her hand, over a garment, and he feels pleasure from it or does not, neither of them incurs anything unless the contact reaches the skin. This is the same whether he did it deliberately or heedlessly, and whether the woman is alive or dead, provided she is a non-mahram (a woman who is not forbidden to him in marriage).

His view differed when a man touches, with his hand, a little girl or an elderly woman, or one of his mahram women whom he may not marry. Once he said that ablution is nullified, based on the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿or you have touched women﴾, since He did not distinguish. And the second view is that it is not nullified, because desire has no place in such cases. Al-Marwazi said: "The view of al-Shafi'i is closer to the apparent meaning of the Book, because Allah, mighty and majestic is He, said: ﴿or you have touched women﴾ and did not say 'with desire' or 'without desire.' Likewise, those among the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) who made ablution obligatory did not stipulate desire." He said: "Likewise the majority of the Successors (tabi'un)."

Al-Marwazi said: "As for what Malik held, namely that taking into account desire and pleasure through a garment makes ablution obligatory, al-Layth ibn Sa'd agreed with him on this, and we know of no one else who said this." He said: "This is not sound on analysis, because whoever does this is not a toucher of his wife and not in actual contact with her; he is only touching her garment." He said: "They have agreed that if he experiences pleasure and desires to touch, ablution is not obligatory for him. Likewise, whoever touches over a garment, because he is not in contact with the woman."

I say: As for what was mentioned, that no one agreed with Malik on his view except al-Layth ibn Sa'd, Hafiz Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr mentioned that this is the view of Ishaq and Ahmad. It was also narrated from al-Sha'bi and al-Nakha'i, all of whom said: "If he touches and feels pleasure, ablution is obligatory; if he does not feel pleasure, there is no ablution." As for his statement, "This is not sound on analysis," it is not correct. The authentic report from Aisha has come, where she said: "I used to sleep in front of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with my legs towards his qiblah (direction of prayer). When he prostrated, he pressed me, and I drew in my legs; when he stood, I extended them again." [She said:] "The houses at that time had no lamps." This is explicit that the Prophet (ﷺ) was the one who touched, and that he pressed Aisha's legs, as in the narration of al-Qasim from Aisha: "When he wished to prostrate, he pressed my legs and I drew them in." Al-Bukhari transmitted it. This specifies the general wording of His saying: ﴿or you have touched﴾. Therefore, according to the apparent meaning of the verse, the ablution of every toucher would be nullified however he touched. But the Sunnah, which is the explanation of the Book of Allah, indicates that ablution is required for some touchers and not others: namely, one who does not feel pleasure and does not intend it.

It should not be said: "Perhaps there was a garment on her feet, or he struck her legs with his sleeve." We reply: The literal meaning of pressing (ghamz) is with the hand, as in your saying "ghamzuka al-kabsh," meaning you feel the ram to see whether it is fat or not. As for pressing meaning striking with a sleeve, that is not the case. The legs of a sleeping person are generally exposed, especially given how he stretches out and the narrowness of his circumstances. Such was the situation at that time. Do you not see her words: "When he stood, I extended them," and her words: "The houses at that time had no lamps"? She also said explicitly: "I used to stretch my legs towards the qiblah of the Prophet (ﷺ) while he prayed. When he prostrated, he pressed me and I raised them; when he stood, I stretched them out again." Al-Bukhari transmitted it. It is thus evident that the pressing was in its literal sense, in direct contact.

Another proof, which Aisha also narrated, may Allah be pleased with her, she said: "One night I lost the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from the bed, so I searched for him, and my hand fell upon the soles of his feet while he was in the mosque and they were upright," and the hadith continues. When she placed her hand on his foot while he was prostrating and he continued his prostration, this was evidence that ablution is not nullified except for some touchers and not others. It may be said: "There was a barrier on his foot, as al-Muzani said." It is answered: The foot is a foot without a barrier until a barrier is proven, and the default is to adhere to the apparent meaning. Indeed, from the totality of what we have mentioned, a conclusion emerges that is like an explicit text.

It may be said: "The community (ummah) has agreed that if a man forcibly violates a woman and his genitals touch hers, while she does not feel pleasure and does not desire it, or she was asleep and felt no pleasure and no desire, then ghusl (full ritual washing) is obligatory for her. Likewise, the ruling for one who kisses or touches, whether with desire or without desire, is that his purity is broken and ablution becomes obligatory for him, because the meaning in touching, contact and kissing is the act, not the pleasure." We reply: We have mentioned that al-A'mash and others disagreed with the consensus you claim. Even if we grant it, this is an argument from consensus (ijma', scholarly agreement) on the point in dispute, so it does not bind us. We have argued for the soundness of our position with authentic hadiths. Al-Shafi'i, according to your claim, said: "When a hadith is authentic, take it and leave my opinion," but he was not the first to hold this; his teacher Malik had preceded him in it, as is well known among us. Now that the hadith is established on this, why do you not follow it?!

It also follows from your position that if a man strikes his wife with his hand, slapping her to discipline her and to be harsh with her, his ablution is nullified, since what is intended is the occurrence of the act. As far as I know, no one holds this. And Allah knows best.

The imams Malik and others narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to pray while Umamah bint Abi al-'As, the daughter of Zaynab bint the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), was on his shoulder. When he bowed he would set her down, and when he rose from prostration he would lift her again. This refutes what al-Shafi'i said in one of his two opinions: that if he touched a little girl, his purity would not be nullified, relying on the word "women." This view is weak, since touching a little girl is like touching a wall. His view also differed regarding mahram women, because he does not take desire into account, whereas we take desire into account: wherever it exists, the ruling exists, which is the obligation of ablution.

As for al-Awza'i's view of restricting it to the hand alone, it is because touching is most commonly done with the hand, so he confined it to that and not other limbs. Indeed, if a man puts his legs into his wife's garments and touches her genitals or her belly, his ablution is not nullified by that. He also said, concerning a man who kisses his wife: "If he comes asking me, I say he should perform ablution; if he does not perform ablution, I do not blame him." Abu Thawr said: "There is no ablution for one who kisses his wife, or has skin contact with her, or touches her." This is to be derived from the view of Abu Hanifah, and Allah knows best.

The twenty-seventh issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and you find no water﴾. The circumstances in which the traveller does not have water are either the total absence of water or the absence of part of it, or fear of losing a companion, or of losing his mount or baggage because of searching for it, or fear of thieves or predators, or fear of losing the time (of prayer), or thirst for oneself or for another. Likewise, water needed for cooking a meal for the good of one's body. When any of these circumstances applies, he performs tayammum (dry ablution with earth) and prays. For a sick person, water is considered absent if he cannot find someone to bring it to him, or fears harm from using it. Water is also considered absent for a healthy resident when there is a general high price affecting all kinds of goods, or when he is imprisoned or bound. Al-Hasan said: "A man should buy water with all his wealth and remain without it." This is weak, because the religion of Allah is ease. A group said: "He should buy it as long as the price does not exceed a third of the value or more." Another group said: "He should buy it for up to two or three times the value of a dirham," and similar. All of this is in the school of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him. It was asked of Ashhab: "Is a water-skin to be bought for ten dirhams?" He said: "I do not think that is incumbent upon people." Al-Shafi'i said that there should be no increase.

THE TWENTY-EIGHTH ISSUE: Scholars differed as to whether seeking water (talab al-ma') is a condition for the validity of tayammum or not. The apparent position of the school of Malik is that it is a condition, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i. The Qadi Abu Muhammad ibn Nasr held that it is not a condition for the validity of tayammum, and this is the view of Abu Hanifa. It is reported from Ibn 'Umar that when he was on a journey and was within two ghalwahs [[Al-ghalwah (with a fatha on the ghayn, then a sukun, followed by an open waw): the distance of a bowshot; it is said to be about three hundred to four hundred cubits.]] from his path, he did not deviate towards it. Ishaq said: he is only obliged to seek water in his place, and he mentioned the hadith of Ibn 'Umar. The first view is more sound and is the well-known position of the school of Malik in the Muwatta', because of the words of the Exalted: ﴿but you find no water﴾, which implies that tayammum may not be used except after seeking water. Also, by way of analogy, this is a substitute commanded upon inability to perform what it replaces, so its performance is not valid except with certainty that its original is absent, like fasting in expiation when freeing a slave is unavailable.

THE TWENTY-NINTH ISSUE: When this is established and water is absent, the person's situation is one of three cases: either it is strongly probable to the mukallaf's assessment that he will despair of finding water within the time, or it is strongly probable to his assessment that water will be found and his hope in it is strong, or the two possibilities are equal for him. These are three states. The first: it is recommended for him to perform tayammum and pray at the beginning of the time, because if the excellence of water escapes him, it is recommended that he secure the excellence of the beginning of the time. The second: he performs tayammum in the middle of the time; this is related by the companions of Malik from him. So he delays the prayer, hoping to attain the excellence of water, as long as the excellence of the beginning of the time does not escape him, for the excellence of the beginning of the time may be attained by its middle, since it is close to it. The third: he delays the prayer until he finds water at the end of the time, because the excellence of water is greater than the excellence of the beginning of the time; the excellence of the beginning of the time is disputed, while the excellence of water is agreed upon. It is permissible to forgo the excellence of the beginning of the time without necessity, but it is not permissible to forgo the excellence of water except out of necessity. The time in this matter is the end of the preferred time; this was said by Ibn Habib. If he knew that water would be found at the end of the time, and he performed tayammum at its beginning and prayed, Ibn al-Qasim said: it suffices him; if he then found water, he repeats it within the time only. 'Abd al-Malik ibn al-Majishun said: if he finds water after [[In J, Z and T: if he finds water and did not repeat, he repeats forever.]] he has prayed, he repeats forever.

THE THIRTIETH ISSUE: What is considered regarding the finding of water is that he finds from it what suffices for his purification. If he finds less than what suffices him, he performs tayammum and does not use what he has found. This is the view of Malik and his companions, and Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i in one of his two opinions said the same; it is the view of most scholars, because God, Exalted, made His obligation one of two things: either water or dust. If water is not sufficient to dispense with tayammum, it is considered non-existent in the Law, since what is required from its presence is sufficiency. [[As in J, Z and T. In others: finds.]] Al-Shafi'i said in the other opinion: he uses the water he has with him and performs tayammum, because he is one who has water, so the condition of tayammum has not been fulfilled; when he uses it and then lacks water, he performs tayammum for what he did not find. The opinion of al-Shafi'i also differed regarding one who forgets the water in his baggage and performs tayammum; the correct view is that he repeats, because when the water is with him he is one who has found it, and he was only negligent. The other opinion is that he does not repeat, and this is the view of Malik, because when he did not know of it, he did not find it.

THE THIRTY-FIRST ISSUE: Abu Hanifa permitted ablution with water that has changed, based on the words of the Exalted: ﴿but you find no water﴾. He said: this is a negation in an indefinite noun, and it generalizes linguistically, so it indicates the permissibility of ablution with water that has changed and with water that has not changed, since the name "water" applies to it. We say: negation in an indefinite noun does generalize as you say, but within the genus; so it is general over every water, whether from heaven, a river, a spring, sweet or salty. As for what is other than the genus, namely what has changed, it is not included in it, just as the water of boiled beans or rosewater is not included in it. The rulings on waters will come in (al-Furqan [[See vol. 13 p. 39]]), God willing.

THE THIRTY-SECOND ISSUE: They agreed that ablution and ritual bathing are not valid with any drink other than nabidh when water is absent, and the words of the Exalted: ﴿but you find no water, then perform tayammum﴾ refute it. The hadith in which ablution with nabidh is mentioned was narrated by Ibn Mas'ud, and it is not established, because the one who narrated it is Abu Zayd, who is unknown and not recognized as having been a companion of 'Abd Allah; this was said by Ibn al-Mundhir and others. Its explanation will come in (al-Furqan [[See vol. 13 p. 39]]), God willing.

THE THIRTY-THIRD ISSUE: Water whose absence permits tayammum is the pure, purifying water that remains upon the attributes of its creation. Some authors of works on the rulings of the Qur'an said, when the Exalted said: ﴿but you find no water, then perform tayammum﴾, that He permitted tayammum only upon the absence of every part of water, because it is an indefinite word that encompasses every part of it, whether it is mixed with something else or standing alone. No one would deny that date-nabidh is "water"; since it is so, tayammum is not permitted when it is present. This is the view of the Kufans, Abu Hanifa and his companions, and they cited weak reports for this, which will be mentioned in Surat al-Furqan, where the discussion of water will come, God willing.

THE THIRTY-FOURTH ISSUE: The words of the Exalted: ﴿then perform tayammum﴾. Tayammum is among what this Ummah was specially granted as a facility for it. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "We have been favoured over the people in three ways: the whole earth has been made a place of prayer for us, and its dust has been made a purifier for us..." and he mentioned the hadith. Its occasion of revelation has already been mentioned, and it was due to the necklace, as we explained. The reasons which permit it have already been mentioned; the discussion here concerns its meaning linguistically and in the Law, its description and manner, what it is performed with and upon, who may perform it, the conditions of tayammum, and other of its rulings.

Linguistically, tayammum means intending. "Tayammamtu al-shay'" means I intended it; "tayammamtu al-sa'id" means I deliberately aimed at it; "tayammamtuhu bi-rumhi wa-sahmi" means I aimed at it to the exclusion of others. Al-Khalil recited [[The speaker is 'Amir ibn Malik Mula'ib al-Asinnah, meaning Dirar ibn 'Amr al-Dabbi.]]:

"I aimed the spear at him sidelong, then I said to him: 'This is valour, not the game of slides.'"

Al-Khalil said: whoever says "amamtuhu" in this verse has erred, because he said "shazran," and "shazr" is only from one side, and he did not intend it in front of him. Imru' al-Qays said:

"I aimed at her [[So it is in the originals, and it is a variant. The well-known reading, as in his Diwan and the Sharh al-Shawahid of Sibawayh, is "tanawwartuha," meaning: I looked at her fire from Adhri'at. Adhri'at is a town on the borders of Syria, adjoining the land of al-Balqa' and 'Oman, to which wine is attributed. Yathrib: the city of the Messenger (ﷺ) and his family.]] from Adhri'at and its people, at Yathrib, the nearest of its abodes, a looking-glance."

He also said:

"The spring beside Dari' aimed at her, whose moss the shade covers, high."

Another:

"Thus am I, whenever a land displeases me, I turn my camel's face to another land."

Al-A'sha of Bahila said:

"I aimed at Qays, and between me and him are many lands, of a far desert, rugged."

Humayd ibn Thawr said:

"Ask the abode where Umm Tariq aimed, and is it the custom of an abode to speak?"

For al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him:

"My knowledge is with me wherever I aim; I carry it, my belly is its vessel, not the belly of a chest."

Ibn al-Sikkit said: the words of the Exalted, ﴿then aim for good dust [sa'idan tayyiban]﴾ mean "intend." Then their use of this word became frequent, until tayammum came to mean wiping the face and hands with dust. Ibn al-Anbari said regarding their saying "the man has performed tayammum": it means he has wiped dust over his face and hands. I say: this is the legal tayammum when its purpose is drawing near to God. "I performed tayammum for the sick man, so he performed tayammum for prayer." A "muyammam" man is one who attains everything he seeks, related from al-Shaybani. He recited:

"We found 'Asar ibn Sa'd, a muyammam of the house, of lofty glory."

Another said:

"Azhar, not born under the star of avarice, a muyammam of the house, noble of origin."

[[The verse is by Ru'ba. He intended by "al-sankh" the "naskh" (with a ghayn-less kha), and so changed the kha into a ha because of "al-shuh"; some narrate it with a kha, and combined it with the ha because both are throat letters. "Al-sankh" (with a kasra on the sin) is the origin of everything.]]

(from al-Lisan).]] The thirty-fifth issue: The word *tayammum* is mentioned by God, exalted is He, in His Book in (al-Baqarah [[See vol. 2, p. 325.]]) and in this surah, and in (al-Ma'idah [[vol. 6, p. 106.]]). The one in this surah is the verse of *tayammum*. And God knows best. Al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: This is a problem (*mu'dilah*) for which I have found no remedy with anyone. There are two verses in which *tayammum* is mentioned: one of them [[Addition from Ibn al-'Arabi.]] is in (al-Nisa'), and the other is in (al-Ma'idah). We do not know which verse 'Aishah meant by her saying: "Then God sent down the verse of *tayammum*." Then he said: Her narration indicates that *tayammum* was not known before that, nor was it something they were obliged to do. I say: As for his saying, "We do not know which verse 'Aishah meant," it is this verse, as we have mentioned. And God knows best. As for his saying, "Her narration indicates that *tayammum* was not known before that, nor was it something they were obliged to do," this is correct, and there is no disagreement about it among the historians (*ahl al-siyar*), because it is known that the ritual bath of major impurity (*ghusl al-janabah*) was not made obligatory before ablution (*wudu'*). Likewise, it is known to all the historians that the Prophet ﷺ, from the time prayer was made obligatory upon him in Makkah, did not pray except with ablution like our ablution today. This shows that the verse of ablution was revealed so that its earlier obligation would be recited in the revelation. As for his saying, "Then the verse of *tayammum* was revealed," and he did not say "the verse of ablution," this indicates that what came to them of knowledge at that time was the ruling of *tayammum*, not the ruling of ablution, and this is clear, with no difficulty in it.

The thirty-sixth issue: *Tayammum* is obligatory on every accountable person (*mukallaf*) who is bound to pray when he cannot find water and the time of the prayer has entered. Abu Hanifah, his companion, and al-Muzani, the companion of al-Shafi'i, said: It is permissible before that, because seeking water is not a condition according to them, by analogy with the voluntary prayer (*nafilah*). Since *tayammum* is permitted for the voluntary prayer without seeking water, it is also permitted for the obligatory prayer. They cited from the Sunnah the Prophet's ﷺ saying to Abu Dharr: "Clean earth is the ablution of the Muslim, even if he does not find water for ten years." So he ﷺ named the earth an ablution just as water is named, so its ruling is the ruling of water. And God knows best. Our evidence is God's saying: ﴿But if you find no water﴾, and it is not said that one "has not found water" except for the one who has sought and not found it. This meaning has already been mentioned. Also, it is a purification of necessity, like that of the woman with continuous bleeding (*mustahadah*). And also, the Prophet ﷺ said: "Wherever prayer overtakes you, perform *tayammum* and pray." This is the view of al-Shafi'i and Ahmad, and it is related from 'Ali, Ibn 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas.

The thirty-seventh issue: The scholars agreed that *tayammum* does not lift major impurity (*janabah*) or minor impurity (*hadath*), and that the one who performs *tayammum* for them, if he finds water, returns to being in major impurity as he was, or in minor impurity, because of the Prophet's ﷺ saying to Abu Dharr: "When you find water, let it touch your skin." Except for something related from Abu Salamah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, which Ibn Jurayj and 'Abd al-Hamid ibn Jubayr ibn Shaybah related from him, and Ibn Abi Dhi'b related from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Harmalah from him, who said concerning the one in major impurity who performed *tayammum* and then found water while he was still in his state of purity: he needs neither ritual bath nor ablution until he becomes impure again. And it has been related from him concerning one who performed *tayammum*, prayed, and then found water within the time, that he performs ablution and repeats that prayer. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: This is a contradiction and a lack of careful consideration. And Abu Salamah, in their view, did not have the understanding of his fellow Successors (*tabi'un*) in Madinah.

The thirty-eighth issue: They agreed that whoever performs *tayammum* and then finds water before entering the prayer, his *tayammum* is invalid, and he must use water. The majority hold that whoever performs *tayammum*, prays, and finishes his prayer, having sought water diligently and not having it with him, his prayer is complete, because he has discharged his obligation as he was commanded. It is not permissible to require him to repeat without proof. Some of them recommended that he repeat within the time if he performs ablution and bathing. It is related from Tawus, 'Ata', al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, Makhul, Ibn Sirin, al-Zuhri and Rabi'ah, all of whom say: he repeats the prayer. Al-Awza'i recommended this and said: It is not obligatory. This is based on what Abu Sa'id al-Khudri related: Two men set out on a journey, and the prayer came due while they had no water with them, so they performed *tayammum* with clean earth and prayed. Then they found water within the time. One of them repeated the prayer with ablution, and the other did not. Then they came to the Messenger of God ﷺ and mentioned that to him. He said to the one who did not repeat: "You have hit the Sunnah, and your prayer suffices you." And he said to the one who performed ablution and repeated: "You have a double reward." Abu Dawud related it, and said: Other than [Ibn [[Addition from Abu Dawud, because 'Abd Allah ibn Nafi' is the narrator of the hadith.]]] Nafi' narrates it from al-Layth, from 'Umayrah ibn Abi Najiyah, from Bakr ibn Sawadah, from 'Ata', from the Prophet ﷺ, and the mention of Abu Sa'id in this chain is not preserved (*mahfuz*). It was also related by al-Daraqutni, who said in it: "Then he found water after the time [[Addition from al-Daraqutni.]]."

The thirty-ninth issue: The scholars differed if one finds water after entering the prayer. Malik said: He is not obliged to break the prayer and use water; he should complete his prayer and perform ablution for what comes after. This is also the view of al-Shafi'i, and Ibn al-Mundhir preferred it. Abu Hanifah and a group including Ahmad ibn Hanbal and al-Muzani said: He breaks it, performs ablution, and begins the prayer anew, because water has become available. Their argument is that since *tayammum* is invalidated by the finding of water before the prayer, so likewise it is invalidated for what remains of it, and when part of it is invalidated, all of it is invalidated, based on the scholars' consensus concerning the woman whose waiting period (*'iddah*) is counted in months, that if only a small part of it remains and then she menstruates, she begins her waiting period anew with menstrual cycles. They said: What overtakes him, that water becomes available while he is in prayer, is similar by analogy and reasoning. Our evidence is God's saying: ﴿And do not nullify your deeds﴾. All agree on the permissibility of entering the prayer with *tayammum* when water is absent, and they differed about breaking it when water is found. No Sunnah has been established for breaking it, nor is there a consensus. Among their arguments also: whoever is obliged to fast in the case of *zihar* or manslaughter, and fasts most of it, then finds a slave to free, does not nullify his fasting and does not return to freeing the slave. Likewise, whoever enters prayer with *tayammum* does not break it and does not return to ablution with water.

The fortieth issue: They differed whether one may pray several prayers with one *tayammum*, or whether *tayammum* is required for each obligatory and voluntary prayer. Shurayk ibn 'Abd Allah al-Qadi said: He performs *tayammum* for each voluntary and obligatory prayer. Malik said: For each obligatory prayer, because he must seek water for each prayer, so whoever seeks water and does not find it, then he performs *tayammum*. Abu Hanifah, al-Thawri, al-Layth, al-Hasan ibn Hayy and Dawud said: He may pray whatever he wishes with one *tayammum* as long as he does not become impure, because he is pure as long as he does not find water, and he is not obliged to seek water when he has despaired of it. What we have said is more correct, because God, mighty and majestic is He, obliged everyone who stands for prayer to seek water, and obliged *tayammum* when it is absent, to make the prayer permissible before the time has passed. So it is a purification of necessity and deficient, as the consensus of the Muslims on its invalidation when water is found, even if one has not become impure, shows; and purification with water is not like this. This disagreement may also be based on the permissibility of *tayammum* before the time enters. Al-Shafi'i and the people of the first opinion do not permit it, because when God said, ﴿But if you find no water, then perform *tayammum*﴾, it became evident that the parts of *tayammum* are tied to need, and there is no need before the time. On this basis one does not pray two obligatory prayers with one *tayammum*, and this is clear. Our scholars differed about one who prays two obligatory prayers with one *tayammum*. Yahya ibn Yahya related from Ibn al-Qasim: He repeats the second as long as it is within the time. Abu Zayd ibn Abi al-Ghamr related from him: He repeats it forever. Likewise it is related from Mutarrif and Ibn al-Majishun: He repeats the second forever. This is what our companions argue about, because seeking water is a condition. Ibn 'Abdus mentioned that Ibn Nafi' related from Malik concerning one who combines two prayers that he performs *tayammum* for each prayer. Abu al-Faraj said concerning one who makes up several prayers: If he makes them up with one *tayammum*, there is nothing upon him, and that is permissible for him. This is based on the view that seeking water is not a condition. The first view is more correct. And God knows best.

The forty-first issue: God's saying: ﴿clean earth﴾. *Al-sa'id*: the surface of the earth, whether or not it has dust upon it. This is what al-Khalil, Ibn al-A'rabi and al-Zajjaj said. Al-Zajjaj said: I know of no disagreement among the lexicographers about it. God, exalted is He, said: (And We will make what is upon it a barren *sa'id* [[See vol. 10, p. 355 and p. 406.]]), meaning hard ground that produces nothing. And He said: (So it becomes a slippery *sa'id* [[See vol. 10, p. 355 and p. 406.]]). From this is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

As if, in the forenoon, he throws over it the *sa'id*, a drunk with a heavy head [[*Al-sa'id*: dust. *Al-dababah* means wine. *Al-khurtum*: wine and its purest part. He says: the gazelle's fawn does not raise its head, as if he were a drunk man from the heaviness of his sleep at the time of forenoon.]]

Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verse 43 (part 11 of 12):

The word ṣaʿīd is so called because it is the highest part of the earth that one ascends to (yuṣʿadu ilayhi). Its plural is ṣuʿadāt, and from this comes the hadith: "Beware of sitting in the ṣuʿadāt" [[al-ṣuʿadāt: the roads.]]. The scholars [[In j, z and ṭ: the jurists.]] differed concerning it because of its qualification by ṭayyib (pure). One group said: one performs tayammum with the entire surface of the earth, whether it is dust, sand, stones, a mineral or saline ground (sabakha). This is the position of Malik, Abu Hanifa, al-Thawri and al-Tabari. And ṭayyiban means ṭahiran (pure). Another group said: ṭayyiban means ḥalal (lawful), but this view is unsound (qalaq). Al-Shafi'i and Abu Yusuf said: ṣaʿīd is dust that grows plants (al-turab al-munbit), and this is the ṭayyib, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And the good land, its vegetation comes forth by the permission of its Lord﴾ [[See vol. 7, p. 312.]]. Therefore tayammum on anything other than this is not permissible according to them. Al-Shafi'i said: ṣaʿīd applies only to dust that has dust-like particles (dhu ghubar). ʿAbd al-Razzaq reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that he was asked, "Which ṣaʿīd is the purest?" He said: "Tilled land (al-harth)." Abu ʿUmar said: In this statement of Ibn ʿAbbas there is an indication that ṣaʿīd can be other than tilled land. ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, said: it is only dust. In the Kitab of al-Khalil: "Tayammam bi-l-ṣaʿīd" means take from its dust, related by Ibn Faris. This requires tayammum with dust, for a hard rock has no dust on it. Al-Kiya al-Tabari said: al-Shafi'i stipulated that the dust must cling to the hand and that one perform tayammum with it by transferring it to the parts of tayammum, just as water is transferred to the parts of wudu'. Al-Kiya said: There is no doubt that the word ṣaʿīd is not explicit in what al-Shafi'i said, but the saying of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "The earth has been made for me a place of prostration (masjid) and its dust a purifier (ṭahur)" clarifies that. I say: The proponents of this position relied on his peace be upon him saying: "and its soil has been made for us a purifier (ṭahur)," and they said: This is from the category of the general and the particular (muṭlaq and muqayyad), and it is not so; rather, it is from the category of specifying some individuals of a general term, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿In them are fruit, date palms and pomegranates﴾ [[See vol. 17, p. 185.]]. We have mentioned this in al-Baqara at His saying ﴿and His angels, His messengers, Jibril and Mika'il﴾ [[See vol. 2, p. 36.]]. The lexicographers have related that ṣaʿīd is a name for the surface of the earth, as we have mentioned, and this is the explicit text of the Qur'an as we have shown, and there is no clarification after the clarification of Allah. The Prophet ﷺ also said to one in a state of janabah: "Upon you is the ṣaʿīd, for it will suffice you," and it will come. Thus ﴿ṣaʿīdan﴾ according to this is an adverb of place. Whoever takes it to mean dust makes it a direct object, with the preposition (bi) omitted, i.e., "with ṣaʿīd." And ﴿ṭayyiban﴾ is its adjective. Whoever takes ﴿ṭayyiban﴾ to mean ḥalal makes it accusative as a circumstantial (ḥal) or as an infinitive (maṣdar).

The forty-second issue: When this has been established, know that the place of consensus among what we have mentioned is that a man performs tayammum on pure, plant-bearing earth that is not transported and not usurped. The place of consensus in prohibition is that a man performs tayammum on pure gold, silver, rubies, emeralds, foodstuffs such as bread and meat and others, or on impurities (najasat). Opinions differ regarding other things such as minerals: it is permitted, and this is the position of Malik and others; and it is prohibited, and this is the position of al-Shafi'i and others. Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: According to Malik, tayammum on grass is permitted if it is on the ground, and there is a difference of report from him regarding tayammum on snow: in the Mudawwana and the Mabsut it is permitted, and in other works it is prohibited. The school differed regarding tayammum on wood; the majority hold it prohibited. In the Mukhtasar of al-Waqqar [[al-Waqqar (with a kasra-like vowel as in sahhab): the epithet of Zakariyya ibn Yahya ibn Ibrahim al-Misri, the jurist.]] it is stated that it is permissible.

The Eleventh... wait, let me translate the passage as given.

It was said: the ruling depends on whether the surface is detached or attached. Thus it is permitted on what is attached (to the ground) and prohibited on what is detached.

Al-Tha'labi mentioned that Malik said: "If one strikes his hand on a tree and then wipes with it, it suffices him." He said: al-Awza'i and al-Thawri said: "It is permitted with the earth and everything on it of trees, stones, clods and others, to the extent that they said: 'If one strikes his hand on ice and hail [[al-jamad (with a fatha on the mim): frozen water]], it suffices him.'"

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "As for dirt transported from clay or other material, the majority of the school holds that tayammum (dry ablution) with it is permissible. Within the school there is a prohibition, though outside the school it is more common. As for what has been fired, such as plaster and baked brick, there are two opinions within the school: permission and prohibition. And there is disagreement about performing tayammum on a wall."

I say: The correct view is permissibility, based on the hadith of Abu Juhaym ibn al-Harith ibn al-Simma al-Ansari, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came from the direction of Bi'r Jamal, and a man met him and greeted him with salam. The Prophet (ﷺ) did not return the greeting until he turned to a wall and wiped his face and hands, and then returned the salam." Related by al-Bukhari. This is evidence for the validity of tayammum with other than dust, as Malik and those who agree with him say. It refutes al-Shafi'i and those who follow him in their claim that what is wiped with must be pure dust that has fine particles clinging to the hand.

Al-Naqqash related from Ibn 'Ulayya and Ibn Kaysan that both permitted tayammum with musk and saffron. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is pure error from several angles."

Abu 'Umar said: "The body of scholars agrees on the permissibility of tayammum with saline soil (sibakh), except Ishaq ibn Rahawayh."

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning one who finds that the time for tayammum has come while he is in mud: he takes from the mud and smears part of his body with it, and when it dries, he performs tayammum with it.

Al-Thawri and Ahmad said: "Tayammum is permissible with the dust of felt (al-libad)."

Al-Tha'labi said: "Abu Hanifa permitted tayammum with kohl, orpiment, quicklime, plaster, and powdered gemstones." He said: "If one performs tayammum with filings (sihalat) of gold, silver, brass (al-sufr, with a damma: that from which vessels are made), copper, or lead, it does not suffice him, because it is not of the kind of earth."

The forty-third issue: the words of the Exalted: ﴿So wipe your faces and your hands﴾. Al-maskh (wiping) is a homonymous term that can mean intercourse: it is said, "The man wiped the woman (masaha al-rajul al-mar'ah)" when he had intercourse with her. Al-maskh also means passing the sword over something and cutting it with it. "The camels wiped their day (masahat al-ibil yawmaha)" when they traveled. Al-mismah means a woman who is bald and has no buttocks. "So-and-so has a trace of beauty (masah min jamal)."

What is meant here by wiping is a description of passing over the surface being wiped, specifically. If it is done with an implement, it refers to transferring the implement to the hand and drawing it over the surface being wiped. This is what the Exalted's words in the verse of al-Ma'idah require: ﴿wipe your faces and your hands with it﴾ [[see vol. 6, p. 106]]. His words "with it" (minhu) indicate that it is necessary to transfer the dust to the place of tayammum. This is the position of al-Shafi'i, but we do not stipulate it, because when the Prophet (ﷺ) placed his hands on the ground and raised them, he blew on them, and in another narration, he shook them out. This indicates that an implement is not a condition, and his tayammum on the wall clarifies this.

Al-Shafi'i said: "Since there is no escape, in wiping the head with water, from moisture transferred to the head, likewise wiping with dust requires transfer."

There is no disagreement that the rule for the face in both tayammum and wudu' is thoroughness and covering all its places. Some permitted not covering everything thoroughly, such as the folds in boots and what is between the fingers on the head. This is the view of Muhammad ibn Maslama within the school, as related by Ibn 'Atiyya.

The Mighty and Majestic said: (with your faces and your hands), beginning with the face before the hands, and the majority held this view. In al-Bukhari, in a hadith of Ammar in the chapter "Tayammum with one strike," the hands are mentioned before the face. Some scholars said this by analogy to reversing the order of wudu'.

The forty-fourth issue: The scholars differed over how far tayammum extends on the hands. Ibn Shihab said: "Up to the shoulders," and it is related from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq. In the Musannaf of Abu Dawud, from al-A'mash, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wiped up to the middle of his forearms. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "No one has acted on this hadith as far as I have memorized."

It was said: he extends it to the elbows, by analogy to wudu'. This is the view of Abu Hanifa, al-Shafi'i and their companions, al-Thawri, Ibn Abi Salama, and al-Layth. All of them held that reaching the elbows in tayammum is an obligatory duty (fard wajib). This was also the view of Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Hakam and Ibn Nafi', and Isma'il al-Qadi adopted it. Ibn Nafi' said: "Whoever performs tayammum only up to the wrists must repeat the prayer forever." Malik said in al-Mudawwana: "He repeats it within the time."

Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah and Ibn 'Umar related from the Prophet (ﷺ) tayammum up to the elbows, and Ibn 'Umar acted on this. Al-Daraqutni said: Qatada was asked about tayammum while travelling, and he said: "Ibn 'Umar used to say: up to the elbows." Al-Hasan and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i used to say: "Up to the elbows." He said: "A narrator related to me from al-Sha'bi, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abza, from Ammar ibn Yasir, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: '(Up to the elbows).'" Abu Ishaq said: "I mentioned it to Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and he was amazed by it and said: 'How good it is!'"

Another group said: he extends it to the wrists (al-kau'ayn), which are the two joints (al-rusghan). This is related from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, al-Awza'i, 'Ata', and al-Sha'bi in one narration, and it was the view of Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ishaq ibn Rahawayh, Dawud ibn 'Ali, and al-Tabari. It is also related from Malik, and it is the view of al-Shafi'i in his older opinion.

Makhul said: "Al-Zuhri and I met and discussed tayammum. Al-Zuhri said: 'The wiping is up to the armpits.' I said: 'From whom did you take this?' He said: 'From the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. He says: (So wipe your faces and your hands), and it is an entire hand.' I said to him: 'But Allah the Exalted says: (As for the male thief and the female thief, cut off their hands) [[see vol. 6, p. 159]]. So from where is the hand cut?' He said: 'I was defeated in argument.'"

It is related from al-Darawardi [[so in the originals; in Ibn 'Atiyya: al-Dawudi]] that the wrists are obligatory and the armpits are a virtue. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This view is supported by neither analogy nor evidence. Some generalized the word 'hand' and made the shoulder obligatory. Others analogized to wudu' and made the elbows obligatory. Here the majority of the community stands. Others kept to the hadith regarding the wrists, and they were also analogized to amputation, since it is a legal ruling and a purification, just as this is a purification. Others kept to the hadith of Ammar regarding the palms. This is the view of al-Sha'bi."

The forty-fifth issue: The scholars also differed over whether one strike suffices for tayammum or not. Malik in al-Mudawwana held that tayammum is with two strikes: one strike for the face and one strike for the hands. This is the view of al-Awza'i, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa and his companions, al-Thawri, al-Layth, and Ibn Abi Salama. It was related by Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah and Ibn 'Umar from the Prophet (ﷺ).

Ibn Abi al-Jahm said: "Tayammum is with one strike." This is related from al-Awza'i in his most well-known view, and it is the view of 'Ata' and al-Sha'bi in one narration. Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ishaq, Dawud, and al-Tabari also held this. It is the most firmly established of what has been related on this matter from the hadith of Ammar.

Malik said in the Kitab of Muhammad: "If one performs tayammum with one strike, it suffices him." Ibn Nafi' said: "He repeats it forever."

Abu 'Umar said: Ibn Abi Layla and al-Hasan ibn Hayy said: "Two strikes: with each strike he wipes his face, forearms, and elbows." No one among the people of knowledge other than these two held this view.

Abu 'Umar said: "When the reports differed regarding the manner of tayammum and contradicted one another, the obligation in this matter is to return to the apparent meaning of the Book, and it indicates two strikes: one strike for the face, and another for the hands up to the elbows, by analogy to wudu' and following the action of Ibn 'Umar, for he is one whose knowledge is not rejected in relation to the Book of Allah. If something were established from the Prophet (ﷺ) on this matter, it would be necessary to stop at it. And success is from Allah."

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed Allah is ever Pardoning and Forgiving﴾. That is, He has always been One who accepts pardon, and He is the Easy-going (al-sahl), and He forgives sin, meaning He conceals its punishment, so He does not punish.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verses 44–53 (part 1 of 3):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book?﴾ up to His saying, may He be exalted: (Among them are those who believed in it, and among them are those who turned away from it), the verse [[In J, T.]]. It was revealed concerning the Jews of Madinah and those around it. Ibn Ishaq said: Rifa'ah ibn Zayd ibn al-Tabut was one of the great men of the Jews. When he spoke to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he twisted his tongue and said: "Give us your hearing, O Muhammad, until we make you understand." Then he attacked Islam and found fault with it. So Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed: (Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book?) up to His saying: (little). The meaning of (yashtaruna) is "they exchange," and it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal). In the sentence there is an omission, its estimate being "they buy error in exchange for guidance," as He, may He be exalted, said: (Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance). This was said by al-Qutabi and others.

(And they wish that you would stray from the way) is coordinated with it, and the meaning is that you would stray from the path of truth. al-Hasan recited (tudallu) with a fatha on the dad, meaning "led astray from the way."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And Allah is most knowing of your enemies﴾ means: He knows them about you, so do not take them as companions, for they are your enemies. It is also permissible for (a'lam) to carry the meaning of (alim, knowing), as in His saying, may He be exalted: (And it is easier for Him), meaning "easy."

(And sufficient is Allah as protector) — the ba' is superfluous, added because the meaning is "rely on Allah, and He will suffice you against your enemies." (Waliyyan) and (nasiran) are in the accusative as explanation (bayan), and if you wish, as circumstantial clauses (hal).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Among those who are Jews﴾. al-Zajjaj said: If (min) is connected to what precedes it, then one does not stop at His saying (nasiran). If it is made a new beginning (munqati'ah), then a pause on (nasiran) is permissible, and the estimate is: "Among those who are Jews are a people who distort the words," and then it was omitted. This is the view of Sibawayh, and the grammarians cited:

"If I were to say, there is no one among her people
who surpasses her in lineage and in smile..." [[Tayathim (with a kasra on the ta'): a dialect of some Arabs, for they put a kasra on the prefixed letter in forms like ta'allam and ta'lam; when they put a kasra on the ta', the hamza changed into a ya'. The mim (on the pattern of al-majlis): the teeth at the front of the mouth.]]

They said: the meaning is, "If I were to say there is no one among her people who surpasses her," and then it was omitted. al-Farra' said the omitted word is (man), so the meaning is: "Among those who are Jews are those who distort." This is like His saying, may He be exalted: (And there is none of us but has a known station), meaning "there is none of us who has..." Dhu al-Rummah said:

"They remained, and among them is one whose tears are flowing for her,
and another who sheds the tear of the eye with flowing drops..."

[[In the Diwan of Dhu al-Rummah: (ghalib) and (yuthanna). Himlan al-'ayn: its flowing with tears. Yudhri: he sheds.]]

He means: "And among them is one whose tears..." so he omitted the relative pronoun. al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj rejected this, because omitting the relative pronoun is like omitting part of a word. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i recited (al-kalam). al-Nahhas said: (al-kalim) in this place is preferable, because they only distort the words of the Prophet (ﷺ), or what they have in the Torah, and they do not distort all speech. The meaning of (yuharrifuna) is that they interpret it other than its proper interpretation. Allah, may He be exalted, censured them for this because they do it deliberately. It was also said: (from its places) means the description of the Prophet (ﷺ).

(And they say: "We hear and we disobey") means: we hear your words and we disobey your command.

(And hear, without being heard) — Ibn 'Abbas said: They would say to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Hear, may you not hear!" This is what they meant, may Allah curse them, while they showed that they meant: "Hear, without hearing anything disagreeable or harmful." al-Hasan and Mujahid said: its meaning is "without being heard from you," that is, not accepted, and not answered in what you say. al-Nahhas said: If it were so, it would have been "without being heard by you." The discussion of (ra'ina) has already been given [[4]]. The meaning of (laywan bi-alsinatihim) is that they twist their tongues away from the truth, that is, they bend them toward what is in their hearts. The root of (layy) is "killing," and it is in the accusative as an infinitive (masdar). If you wish, it may be an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi). Its original form was (lawyan), then the waw was assimilated into the ya'.

(And slander) is coordinated with it, that is, they slander the religion. That is, they would say to their companions: "If he were a prophet, he would know that we are reviling him." So Allah, may He be exalted, made His Prophet aware of that, and this became one of the signs of his prophethood, and He forbade them from this speech. The meaning of (aqwam) is "more correct for them in judgment." (So they do not believe except a few) means: except a faith that is small, by which they do not deserve the name of faith. It was also said: its meaning is "they do not believe except a few of them." But this is far-fetched, because He, mighty and majestic, has informed us that He cursed them for their disbelief.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who were given the Book, believe in what We have sent down﴾. Ibn Ishaq said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) spoke to leaders among the rabbis of the Jews, among them Abdullah ibn Suriya al-A'war and Ka'b ibn Asad. He said to them: "O assembly of Jews, fear Allah and submit. By Allah, you know that what I have brought to you is the truth." They said: "We do not know that, O Muhammad." They denied what they knew and persisted in disbelief. So Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed concerning them: (O you who were given the Book, believe in what We have sent down, confirming what is with you, before We obliterate faces) up to the end of the verse.

(Confirming what is with you) is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal).

(Before We obliterate faces) — (tams) is the total effacement of a thing's trace, and from it is His saying, may He be exalted: (When the stars are obliterated). (Natmisu) and (natmusu), with kasra and damma on the mim in the future, are two dialects. It is also said in speech: tasama yatsimu and yatsumu, with the meaning of tamasa, one says: tamasa al-athar and tasama, meaning it was effaced. All of these are dialects. From it is His saying, may He be exalted: (Our Lord, obliterate their wealth) meaning: destroy it, according to Ibn 'Arafah. It is said: "I obliterated it," and "tamasa" is both intransitive and transitive. "Tamasa Allah basarahu" and he is "matmus al-basar" when the trace of the eye is gone. From it is His saying, may He be exalted: (And if We willed, We would have obliterated their eyes), meaning: We would have blinded them.

The scholars differed about the intended meaning of this verse: is it literal, so that the face becomes like the back of the neck, and the nose, mouth, brow and eyes are taken away? Or is it an expression for error in their hearts and the removal of success from them? There are two opinions. It was narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that he said: (Before We obliterate faces) means: before We cause you to go astray with a misguidance after which you will not be guided. He holds that it is a figure of speech, and that if they do not believe, this will be done to them as a punishment. Qatadah said: its meaning is: before We make the faces into necks, that is, we take away the nose, the lips, the eyes and the eyebrows; this is its meaning according to the lexicographers. It was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ata' al-'Awfi that the obliteration is that the two eyes alone are removed and returned to the back of the neck, so that this becomes a turning around to the back, and one walks backwards. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The first Islam of Ka'b al-Ahbar was that he passed by a man in the night who was reciting this verse: (O you who were given the Book, believe), so he placed his palms on his face and returned backwards to his house, and embraced Islam on the spot, and said: "By Allah, I feared that I would not reach my house before my face was obliterated." Abdullah ibn Salam did likewise: when this verse was revealed and he heard it, he came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) before he went to his family, and embraced Islam, and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I did not know that I would reach you until my face was turned around on my neck."

If it is asked: how was it permissible for Him to threaten them with the obliteration of faces if they did not believe, and it was not done to them? It is answered: when these believed, and those who followed them, the threat was lifted from the rest. al-Mubarrad said: the threat remains awaited. He said: there must be an obliteration among the Jews and a transformation before the Day of Resurrection.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Or We curse them﴾, that is, the people of the faces (as We cursed the people of the Sabbath). That is, We transform them into apes and swine, according to al-Hasan and Qatadah. It was also said: this is a shift from address (khitab) to third-person reference (ghaybah).

(And the command of Allah is always accomplished) means: it is existent and occurring. "Amr" here may mean "what is commanded," so it is a verbal noun used in the place of a passive participle, and the meaning is that whenever He wills it, He brings it into being. It was also said: its meaning is that every matter that He has informed about its occurrence is bound to occur as He has informed.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him﴾. It was narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited (Indeed, Allah forgives all sins), and a man said to him: "O Messenger of Allah, and what about associating partners!" So (Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, and He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills) was revealed. This is among the clear (muhkam) matters agreed upon, about which there is no disagreement among the community.

(And He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills) is among the ambiguous (mutashabih) matters about which the scholars have spoken. Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: This verse has made clear that every person who commits a major sin is under Allah's will, so that if He wills, He pardons his sin, and if He wills, He punishes him for it, as long as his major sin is not associating partners with Allah, may He be exalted. Some said: Allah, may He be exalted, has explained that in His saying: (If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden, We will remove from you your misdeeds) [[See p. 158 of this part.]]. So know that He wills to forgive the minor sins of those who avoid the major sins, and He does not forgive them for those who commit major sins. Some of the interpreters went to the view that this verse abrogates (naskh, cancelling a earlier ruling by a later revelation) the one at the end of (al-Furqan) [[See p. 158 of this part.]]. Zayd ibn Thabit said: Surah al-Nisa' was revealed six months after al-Furqan. The correct view is that there is no abrogation, because abrogation in reports (akhbar) is impossible. The reconciliation of the verses in this surah with those in al-Furqan will come, if Allah wills [[See vol. 13, p. 77.]]. In al-Tirmidhi, it is narrated from Ali ibn Abi Talib that he said: "There is no verse in the Qur'an more beloved to me than this verse: (Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, and He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills)." He said: This is a hadith that is hasan gharib.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verse 44–53 (part 2 of 3):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Have you not seen those who claim purity for themselves?﴾ There are three issues in this.

The first: Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Have you not seen those who claim purity for themselves?﴾ This wording is general in its outward sense, and none of the exegetes has disagreed that the intended people are the Jews. They differed over the matter by which they claimed purity for themselves. Qatadah and al-Hasan said: it is their saying, "We are the sons of God and His beloved" (Qur'an 5:18), and their saying, "None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians" (Qur'an 2:111). Al-Dahhak and al-Suddi said: it is their saying, "We have no sins; what we did by day was forgiven us by night, and what we did by night was forgiven us by day, and we are like children in being free of sins." Mujahid, Abu Malik and Ikrimah said: it is their putting the young children forward for the prayer, because they have no sins upon them. This is far from the aim of the verse. Ibn Abbas said: it is their saying, "Our fathers who have died intercede for us and purify us." Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said: it is the praise of some of them for others. This is the best of what has been said, for it is the apparent meaning of the verse. And tazkiyah means purification and clearing (tanzih) from sins.

The second: this verse and the saying of Allah the Exalted, ﴿So do not claim purity for yourselves﴾ (Qur'an 53:32), require the disapproval of a person who praises himself with his tongue, and the information that the one who is truly pure is the one whose deeds are good and whom Allah the Exalted purifies. So a person's praise of himself carries no weight; what carries weight is Allah's praise of him. In Sahih Muslim, from Muhammad ibn Amr ibn Ata, who said: I named my daughter Barrah, and Zaynab bint Abi Salamah said to me: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade this name. I had named her Barrah, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not claim purity for yourselves, Allah knows best who among you is righteous." They said: "What shall we name her?" He said: "Name her Zaynab." So the Book and the Sunnah have indicated the prohibition of a person claiming purity for himself. Similar to this is what has spread in these Egyptian lands of people describing themselves with epithets that imply purity, such as Zaki al-Din, Muhyi al-Din and the like. But since the blemishes of those named with these names have multiplied, the disconnection of these epithets from their origin has become apparent, so they no longer convey anything.

The third: as for purifying another and praising him, in al-Bukhari, from the hadith of Abu Bakrah: a man was mentioned in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), and a man praised him highly. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Woe to you, you have cut the neck of your companion" — he said it several times — "If one of you must praise, let him say: I think so-and-so is such, if he sees that he is, and his reckoning is with Allah, and let him not purify anyone before Allah." So he (ﷺ) forbade excessive praise of a man for what is not in him, lest conceit and pride enter him, and he thinks he truly holds that rank, and this leads him to neglect deeds and cease seeking further virtue. For this reason he (ﷺ) said: "Woe to you, you have cut the neck of your companion." In another hadith: "You have broken the back of the man," when they described him with what was not in him. On this basis the scholars interpreted his saying (ﷺ): "Throw dust in the faces of the flatterers," as meaning those who flatter people to their faces with falsehood and with what is not in them, so that they make that a commodity by which they live off the one praised and corrupt him. But praising a man for the good action and commendable matter that is in him, so that it becomes an encouragement for him to the like and an incitement for people to follow him in similar things, is not flattery, even though the speaker has become one who praises by the good words he has spoken about him. This goes back to intentions, and Allah knows the corrupter from the reformer. The Prophet (ﷺ) was praised in poetry, in speeches and in address, and he did not order dust thrown in the faces of those who praised him, nor did he command it. Such as the saying of Abu Talib:

"And a fair one, by whose face rain is sought, the shelter of orphans and the protection of widows."

And like the praise of Abbas and Hassan for him in their poetry, and Ka'b ibn Zuhayr praised him, and he himself praised his companions, saying: "You are few when greed is present and many when fear is present." As for his saying (ﷺ) in the sound hadith: "Do not exaggerate in praising me as the Christians exaggerated in praising Isa son of Maryam; say: the servant of Allah and His Messenger," its meaning is: do not describe me with attributes that are not in me, seeking thereby to praise me, as the Christians described Isa with what was not in him, so they attributed to him that he is the son of God, and thereby they disbelieved and went astray. This implies that whoever raises a person above his level and exceeds his measure with what is not in him is a transgressor and sinful, because if that were permissible for anyone, the most worthy of creation to receive it would be the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And they will not be wronged a whit (fatil)﴾. The pronoun in "they will not be wronged" refers to those mentioned, both those who claimed purity for themselves and those whom Allah the Exalted purifies. Anyone other than these two categories knows from another verse that Allah the Exalted does not wrong him. The fatil is the thread that is in the split of a date-stone, said by Ibn Abbas, Ata and Mujahid. It was said: it is the membrane that surrounds the stone between it and the unripe date. Ibn Abbas also said, as did Abu Malik and al-Suddi: it is the dirt that comes out between your two fingers or palms when you roll them together, so it is fa'il in the sense of maf'ul. All of this returns to an expression of the smallness and insignificance of a thing, and that Allah does not wrong anyone in the least. Similar in this sense of minimizing is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Nor will they be wronged a speck (naqir)﴾ (Qur'an 4:53), which is the pit mark on the back of a date-stone, from which the palm tree grows, and it will come. A poet, dispraising some kings, said:

"You gather an army of thousands and raid, then you do not harm the enemy a whit (fatil)."

Then the Prophet (ﷺ) marvelled at this and said: "Look how they invent lies against Allah," in their saying: "We are the sons of God and His beloved." It was said: their claiming purity for themselves, from Ibn Jurayj. And it was narrated that they said: "We have no sins except like the sins of our children on the day they are born." Iftira' means fabrication, and from it: "So-and-so fabricated against so-and-so," that is, he accused him with what is not in him. And faraytu al-shay' means I cut it.

﴿And sufficient is it as a manifest sin﴾: it is in the accusative as a specification (bayan). The meaning is the magnifying and condemnation of the sin. The Arabs use such a construction both in praise and in blame.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book?﴾ meaning the Jews, ﴿they believe in al-jibt and al-taghut﴾. The exegetes differed over the interpretation of al-jibt and al-taghut. Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and Abu al-Aliyah said: al-jibt is the sorcerer in the language of Abyssinia, and al-taghut is the soothsayer. Al-Faruq Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: al-jibt is magic, and al-taghut is the devil. Ibn Mas'ud: al-jibt and al-taghut here are Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and Huyayy ibn Akhtab. Ikrimah: al-jibt is Huyayy ibn Akhtab and al-taghut is Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, its evidence being the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿They wish to seek judgment before al-taghut﴾ (Qur'an 4:60). Qatadah: al-jibt is the devil and al-taghut is the soothsayer. Ibn Wahb narrated from Malik ibn Anas: al-taghut is whatever is worshipped besides Allah. He said: I heard someone say that al-jibt is the devil; mentioned by al-Nahhas. It was also said: both are every object of worship besides Allah, or every one obeyed in disobedience to Allah, and this is good. The root of al-jibt is al-jibs, which is what has no good in it, and the ta' was substituted for the sin, said by Qutrub. It was said: al-jibt is Iblis and al-taghut are his allies. Malik's view on this matter is good, and it is indicated by the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿That you worship Allah and avoid al-taghut﴾ (Qur'an 16:36), and the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And those who avoided al-taghut from worshipping it﴾ (Qur'an 39:17). Qutn ibn al-Mukhariq narrated from his father who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Tarq, tiyarah and iyafah are of al-jibt." Tarq is divination by lines, and iyafah is the reading of omens from birds. Abu Dawud recorded it in his Sunan. It was also said: al-jibt is everything that Allah has forbidden, and al-taghut is everything that makes a person transgress. And Allah knows best.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And they say to those who disbelieve﴾, that is, the Jews say to the disbelievers of Quraysh: "You are better guided in the way than those who believe in Muhammad." That is because Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf went out with seventy riders from the Jews to Mecca after the battle of Uhud, to form an alliance with Quraysh against fighting the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Ka'b stayed with Abu Sufyan and he treated him generously, and the Jews stayed in the houses of Quraysh, and they made a pact and a covenant that they would unite in fighting Muhammad. Abu Sufyan said: "You are a man who reads the Book and knows, and we are unlettered and do not know; so which of us is better guided in the way and nearer to the truth, we or Muhammad?" Ka'b said: "By Allah, you are better guided in the way than what Muhammad is upon."

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Or do they have a share of sovereignty?﴾ That is: do they have it? The mim is an added particle (silah).

(Naseeb) means a portion (haddh) ﴿of sovereignty﴾. This is in the form of denial, meaning they have nothing of sovereignty; and if they had any of it, they would not have given anyone anything of it, due to their miserliness and envy. It was also said: the meaning is "Rather, do they have a share?", so that am is disjunctive, meaning a turning away from the first and the beginning of a new statement. It was also said: it is conjunctive upon an omitted element, because they were disdainful of following Muhammad (ﷺ). The sense is: "Are they more worthy of prophethood than the one I have sent, or do they have a share of sovereignty?"

﴿Then they would not give people even a speck (naqir)﴾: that is, they withhold rights. Allah the Exalted informed about them with what He knows of them. The naqir is the mark in the back of a date-stone, from Ibn Abbas, Qatadah and others. Also from Ibn Abbas: the naqir is what a man digs with his finger, as one digs the earth. Abu al-Aliyah said: I asked Ibn Abbas about the naqir, and he placed the tip of the thumb on the inner side of the index finger, then raised them and said: "This is the naqir." The naqir is also the root of a piece of wood that is hollowed out and in which something is soaked; and in this the prohibition came and then was abrogated. And "so-and-so is of noble naqir," that is, of noble origin. Here (idhan) is annulled, not operative, because the coordinating fa' has entered upon it; and it could have been put in the accusative. Sibawayh said: "idhan" among the operators of verbs is like "aẓunnu" among the operators of nouns; it is cancelled when the speech does not rely on it, but if it comes at the beginning of the speech and what follows it is in the future, it governs the accusative, as in your saying: "I will visit you," and he replies to you: "Then I will honour you." Abdullah ibn Anamah al-Dabbi said:

"Turn back your donkey, let it not graze in our meadow; otherwise it will be turned back, and the halter of the wild ass is tied."

It governs the verb because what precedes (idhan) is a complete sentence, so it stands at the start of a statement. If it falls between two things, as in your saying "Zayd idhan yazuruka" (Zayd, then, would visit you), it is cancelled (ilgha', meaning it loses its governing effect). If a conjunction particle, either fa' al-'atf or waw al-'atf, precedes it, then both i'mal (its governing effect applied, meaning it governs the verb) and ilgha' (its cancellation) are permitted.

As for i'mal, it is because what follows the waw is resumed as the coordination of one sentence upon another, so it is permissible outside the Qur'an to say ﴿فَإِذًا لَا يُؤْتُوا﴾ [fa-idhan la yu'tu'a]. In the revealed text there is ﴿وَإِذاً لا يَلْبَثُونَ﴾ (And then they would not remain). In the codex of Ubayy it reads ﴿وَإِذًا لَا يَلْبَثُوا﴾ (wa-idhan la yalbathu'a).

As for ilgha', it is because what follows the waw can only occur after a statement to which it is coordinated. According to Sibawayh, the one that governs the verb is idhan, owing to its resemblance to an (that). According to al-Khalil, an is implied after idhan. [In manuscript C: idhan.]

Al-Farra' claimed that idhan is written with an alif and that it takes tanwin (nunation). Al-Nahhas said: I heard Ali ibn Sulayman say: I heard Abu al-Abbas Muhammad ibn Yazid say: "I would like to cauterize the hand of whoever writes idhan with an alif.
