It is also permissible for (a'lam) to carry the meaning of (alim, knowing), as in His saying, may He be exalted: (And it is easier for Him), meaning "easy."

(And sufficient is Allah as protector) — the ba' is superfluous, added because the meaning is "rely on Allah, and He will suffice you against your enemies." (Waliyyan) and (nasiran) are in the accusative as explanation (bayan), and if you wish, as circumstantial clauses (hal).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Among those who are Jews﴾. al-Zajjaj said: If (min) is connected to what precedes it, then one does not stop at His saying (nasiran). If it is made a new beginning (munqati'ah), then a pause on (nasiran) is permissible, and the estimate is: "Among those who are Jews are a people who distort the words," and then it was omitted. This is the view of Sibawayh, and the grammarians cited:

"If I were to say, there is no one among her people
who surpasses her in lineage and in smile..." [[Tayathim (with a kasra on the ta'): a dialect of some Arabs, for they put a kasra on the prefixed letter in forms like ta'allam and ta'lam; when they put a kasra on the ta', the hamza changed into a ya'. The mim (on the pattern of al-majlis): the teeth at the front of the mouth.]]

They said: the meaning is, "If I were to say there is no one among her people who surpasses her," and then it was omitted. al-Farra' said the omitted word is (man), so the meaning is: "Among those who are Jews are those who distort." This is like His saying, may He be exalted: (And there is none of us but has a known station), meaning "there is none of us who has..." Dhu al-Rummah said:

"They remained, and among them is one whose tears are flowing for her,
and another who sheds the tear of the eye with flowing drops..."

[[In the Diwan of Dhu al-Rummah: (ghalib) and (yuthanna). Himlan al-'ayn: its flowing with tears. Yudhri: he sheds.]]

He means: "And among them is one whose tears..." so he omitted the relative pronoun. al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj rejected this, because omitting the relative pronoun is like omitting part of a word. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i recited (al-kalam). al-Nahhas said: (al-kalim) in this place is preferable, because they only distort the words of the Prophet (ﷺ), or what they have in the Torah, and they do not distort all speech. The meaning of (yuharrifuna) is that they interpret it other than its proper interpretation. Allah, may He be exalted, censured them for this because they do it deliberately. It was also said: (from its places) means the description of the Prophet (ﷺ).

(And they say: "We hear and we disobey") means: we hear your words and we disobey your command.

(And hear, without being heard) — Ibn 'Abbas said: They would say to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Hear, may you not hear!" This is what they meant, may Allah curse them, while they showed that they meant: "Hear, without hearing anything disagreeable or harmful." al-Hasan and Mujahid said: its meaning is "without being heard from you," that is, not accepted, and not answered in what you say. al-Nahhas said: If it were so, it would have been "without being heard by you." The discussion of (ra'ina) has already been given [[4]]. The meaning of (laywan bi-alsinatihim) is that they twist their tongues away from the truth, that is, they bend them toward what is in their hearts. The root of (layy) is "killing," and it is in the accusative as an infinitive (masdar). If you wish, it may be an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi). Its original form was (lawyan), then the waw was assimilated into the ya'.

(And slander) is coordinated with it, that is, they slander the religion. That is, they would say to their companions: "If he were a prophet, he would know that we are reviling him." So Allah, may He be exalted, made His Prophet aware of that, and this became one of the signs of his prophethood, and He forbade them from this speech. The meaning of (aqwam) is "more correct for them in judgment." (So they do not believe except a few) means: except a faith that is small, by which they do not deserve the name of faith. It was also said: its meaning is "they do not believe except a few of them." But this is far-fetched, because He, mighty and majestic, has informed us that He cursed them for their disbelief.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who were given the Book, believe in what We have sent down﴾. Ibn Ishaq said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) spoke to leaders among the rabbis of the Jews, among them Abdullah ibn Suriya al-A'war and Ka'b ibn Asad. He said to them: "O assembly of Jews, fear Allah and submit. By Allah, you know that what I have brought to you is the truth." They said: "We do not know that, O Muhammad." They denied what they knew and persisted in disbelief. So Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed concerning them: (O you who were given the Book, believe in what We have sent down, confirming what is with you, before We obliterate faces) up to the end of the verse.

(Confirming what is with you) is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal).

(Before We obliterate faces) — (tams) is the total effacement of a thing's trace, and from it is His saying, may He be exalted: (When the stars are obliterated). (Natmisu) and (natmusu), with kasra and damma on the mim in the future, are two dialects. It is also said in speech: tasama yatsimu and yatsumu, with the meaning of tamasa, one says: tamasa al-athar and tasama, meaning it was effaced. All of these are dialects. From it is His saying, may He be exalted: (Our Lord, obliterate their wealth) meaning: destroy it, according to Ibn 'Arafah. It is said: "I obliterated it," and "tamasa" is both intransitive and transitive. "Tamasa Allah basarahu" and he is "matmus al-basar" when the trace of the eye is gone. From it is His saying, may He be exalted: (And if We willed, We would have obliterated their eyes), meaning: We would have blinded them.

The scholars differed about the intended meaning of this verse: is it literal, so that the face becomes like the back of the neck, and the nose, mouth, brow and eyes are taken away? Or is it an expression for error in their hearts and the removal of success from them? There are two opinions. It was narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that he said: (Before We obliterate faces) means: before We cause you to go astray with a misguidance after which you will not be guided. He holds that it is a figure of speech, and that if they do not believe, this will be done to them as a punishment. Qatadah said: its meaning is: before We make the faces into necks, that is, we take away the nose, the lips, the eyes and the eyebrows; this is its meaning according to the lexicographers. It was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ata' al-'Awfi that the obliteration is that the two eyes alone are removed and returned to the back of the neck, so that this becomes a turning around to the back, and one walks backwards. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The first Islam of Ka'b al-Ahbar was that he passed by a man in the night who was reciting this verse: (O you who were given the Book, believe), so he placed his palms on his face and returned backwards to his house, and embraced Islam on the spot, and said: "By Allah, I feared that I would not reach my house before my face was obliterated." Abdullah ibn Salam did likewise: when this verse was revealed and he heard it, he came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) before he went to his family, and embraced Islam, and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I did not know that I would reach you until my face was turned around on my neck."

If it is asked: how was it permissible for Him to threaten them with the obliteration of faces if they did not believe, and it was not done to them? It is answered: when these believed, and those who followed them, the threat was lifted from the rest. al-Mubarrad said: the threat remains awaited. He said: there must be an obliteration among the Jews and a transformation before the Day of Resurrection.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Or We curse them﴾, that is, the people of the faces (as We cursed the people of the Sabbath). That is, We transform them into apes and swine, according to al-Hasan and Qatadah. It was also said: this is a shift from address (khitab) to third-person reference (ghaybah).

(And the command of Allah is always accomplished) means: it is existent and occurring. "Amr" here may mean "what is commanded," so it is a verbal noun used in the place of a passive participle, and the meaning is that whenever He wills it, He brings it into being. It was also said: its meaning is that every matter that He has informed about its occurrence is bound to occur as He has informed.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him﴾. It was narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited (Indeed, Allah forgives all sins), and a man said to him: "O Messenger of Allah, and what about associating partners!" So (Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, and He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills) was revealed. This is among the clear (muhkam) matters agreed upon, about which there is no disagreement among the community.

(And He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills) is among the ambiguous (mutashabih) matters about which the scholars have spoken. Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: This verse has made clear that every person who commits a major sin is under Allah's will, so that if He wills, He pardons his sin, and if He wills, He punishes him for it, as long as his major sin is not associating partners with Allah, may He be exalted. Some said: Allah, may He be exalted, has explained that in His saying: (If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden, We will remove from you your misdeeds) [[See p. 158 of this part.]]. So know that He wills to forgive the minor sins of those who avoid the major sins, and He does not forgive them for those who commit major sins. Some of the interpreters went to the view that this verse abrogates (naskh, cancelling a earlier ruling by a later revelation) the one at the end of (al-Furqan) [[See p. 158 of this part.]]. Zayd ibn Thabit said: Surah al-Nisa' was revealed six months after al-Furqan. The correct view is that there is no abrogation, because abrogation in reports (akhbar) is impossible. The reconciliation of the verses in this surah with those in al-Furqan will come, if Allah wills [[See vol. 13, p. 77.]]. In al-Tirmidhi, it is narrated from Ali ibn Abi Talib that he said: "There is no verse in the Qur'an more beloved to me than this verse: (Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, and He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills)." He said: This is a hadith that is hasan gharib.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verse 44–53 (part 2 of 3):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Have you not seen those who claim purity for themselves?﴾ There are three issues in this.

The first: Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Have you not seen those who claim purity for themselves?﴾ This wording is general in its outward sense, and none of the exegetes has disagreed that the intended people are the Jews. They differed over the matter by which they claimed purity for themselves. Qatadah and al-Hasan said: it is their saying, "We are the sons of God and His beloved" (Qur'an 5:18), and their saying, "None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians" (Qur'an 2:111). Al-Dahhak and al-Suddi said: it is their saying, "We have no sins; what we did by day was forgiven us by night, and what we did by night was forgiven us by day, and we are like children in being free of sins." Mujahid, Abu Malik and Ikrimah said: it is their putting the young children forward for the prayer, because they have no sins upon them. This is far from the aim of the verse. Ibn Abbas said: it is their saying, "Our fathers who have died intercede for us and purify us." Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said: it is the praise of some of them for others. This is the best of what has been said, for it is the apparent meaning of the verse. And tazkiyah means purification and clearing (tanzih) from sins.

The second: this verse and the saying of Allah the Exalted, ﴿So do not claim purity for yourselves﴾ (Qur'an 53:32), require the disapproval of a person who praises himself with his tongue, and the information that the one who is truly pure is the one whose deeds are good and whom Allah the Exalted purifies. So a person's praise of himself carries no weight; what carries weight is Allah's praise of him. In Sahih Muslim, from Muhammad ibn Amr ibn Ata, who said: I named my daughter Barrah, and Zaynab bint Abi Salamah said to me: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade this name. I had named her Barrah, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not claim purity for yourselves, Allah knows best who among you is righteous." They said: "What shall we name her?" He said: "Name her Zaynab." So the Book and the Sunnah have indicated the prohibition of a person claiming purity for himself. Similar to this is what has spread in these Egyptian lands of people describing themselves with epithets that imply purity, such as Zaki al-Din, Muhyi al-Din and the like. But since the blemishes of those named with these names have multiplied, the disconnection of these epithets from their origin has become apparent, so they no longer convey anything.

The third: as for purifying another and praising him, in al-Bukhari, from the hadith of Abu Bakrah: a man was mentioned in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), and a man praised him highly. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Woe to you, you have cut the neck of your companion" — he said it several times — "If one of you must praise, let him say: I think so-and-so is such, if he sees that he is, and his reckoning is with Allah, and let him not purify anyone before Allah." So he (ﷺ) forbade excessive praise of a man for what is not in him, lest conceit and pride enter him, and he thinks he truly holds that rank, and this leads him to neglect deeds and cease seeking further virtue. For this reason he (ﷺ) said: "Woe to you, you have cut the neck of your companion." In another hadith: "You have broken the back of the man," when they described him with what was not in him. On this basis the scholars interpreted his saying (ﷺ): "Throw dust in the faces of the flatterers," as meaning those who flatter people to their faces with falsehood and with what is not in them, so that they make that a commodity by which they live off the one praised and corrupt him. But praising a man for the good action and commendable matter that is in him, so that it becomes an encouragement for him to the like and an incitement for people to follow him in similar things, is not flattery, even though the speaker has become one who praises by the good words he has spoken about him. This goes back to intentions, and Allah knows the corrupter from the reformer. The Prophet (ﷺ) was praised in poetry, in speeches and in address, and he did not order dust thrown in the faces of those who praised him, nor did he command it. Such as the saying of Abu Talib:

"And a fair one, by whose face rain is sought, the shelter of orphans and the protection of widows."

And like the praise of Abbas and Hassan for him in their poetry, and Ka'b ibn Zuhayr praised him, and he himself praised his companions, saying: "You are few when greed is present and many when fear is present." As for his saying (ﷺ) in the sound hadith: "Do not exaggerate in praising me as the Christians exaggerated in praising Isa son of Maryam; say: the servant of Allah and His Messenger," its meaning is: do not describe me with attributes that are not in me, seeking thereby to praise me, as the Christians described Isa with what was not in him, so they attributed to him that he is the son of God, and thereby they disbelieved and went astray. This implies that whoever raises a person above his level and exceeds his measure with what is not in him is a transgressor and sinful, because if that were permissible for anyone, the most worthy of creation to receive it would be the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And they will not be wronged a whit (fatil)﴾. The pronoun in "they will not be wronged" refers to those mentioned, both those who claimed purity for themselves and those whom Allah the Exalted purifies. Anyone other than these two categories knows from another verse that Allah the Exalted does not wrong him. The fatil is the thread that is in the split of a date-stone, said by Ibn Abbas, Ata and Mujahid. It was said: it is the membrane that surrounds the stone between it and the unripe date. Ibn Abbas also said, as did Abu Malik and al-Suddi: it is the dirt that comes out between your two fingers or palms when you roll them together, so it is fa'il in the sense of maf'ul. All of this returns to an expression of the smallness and insignificance of a thing, and that Allah does not wrong anyone in the least. Similar in this sense of minimizing is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Nor will they be wronged a speck (naqir)﴾ (Qur'an 4:53), which is the pit mark on the back of a date-stone, from which the palm tree grows, and it will come. A poet, dispraising some kings, said:

"You gather an army of thousands and raid, then you do not harm the enemy a whit (fatil)."

Then the Prophet (ﷺ) marvelled at this and said: "Look how they invent lies against Allah," in their saying: "We are the sons of God and His beloved." It was said: their claiming purity for themselves, from Ibn Jurayj. And it was narrated that they said: "We have no sins except like the sins of our children on the day they are born." Iftira' means fabrication, and from it: "So-and-so fabricated against so-and-so," that is, he accused him with what is not in him. And faraytu al-shay' means I cut it.

﴿And sufficient is it as a manifest sin﴾: it is in the accusative as a specification (bayan). The meaning is the magnifying and condemnation of the sin. The Arabs use such a construction both in praise and in blame.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book?﴾ meaning the Jews, ﴿they believe in al-jibt and al-taghut﴾. The exegetes differed over the interpretation of al-jibt and al-taghut. Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and Abu al-Aliyah said: al-jibt is the sorcerer in the language of Abyssinia, and al-taghut is the soothsayer. Al-Faruq Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: al-jibt is magic, and al-taghut is the devil. Ibn Mas'ud: al-jibt and al-taghut here are Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and Huyayy ibn Akhtab. Ikrimah: al-jibt is Huyayy ibn Akhtab and al-taghut is Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, its evidence being the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿They wish to seek judgment before al-taghut﴾ (Qur'an 4:60). Qatadah: al-jibt is the devil and al-taghut is the soothsayer. Ibn Wahb narrated from Malik ibn Anas: al-taghut is whatever is worshipped besides Allah. He said: I heard someone say that al-jibt is the devil; mentioned by al-Nahhas. It was also said: both are every object of worship besides Allah, or every one obeyed in disobedience to Allah, and this is good. The root of al-jibt is al-jibs, which is what has no good in it, and the ta' was substituted for the sin, said by Qutrub. It was said: al-jibt is Iblis and al-taghut are his allies. Malik's view on this matter is good, and it is indicated by the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿That you worship Allah and avoid al-taghut﴾ (Qur'an 16:36), and the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And those who avoided al-taghut from worshipping it﴾ (Qur'an 39:17). Qutn ibn al-Mukhariq narrated from his father who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Tarq, tiyarah and iyafah are of al-jibt." Tarq is divination by lines, and iyafah is the reading of omens from birds. Abu Dawud recorded it in his Sunan. It was also said: al-jibt is everything that Allah has forbidden, and al-taghut is everything that makes a person transgress. And Allah knows best.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And they say to those who disbelieve﴾, that is, the Jews say to the disbelievers of Quraysh: "You are better guided in the way than those who believe in Muhammad." That is because Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf went out with seventy riders from the Jews to Mecca after the battle of Uhud, to form an alliance with Quraysh against fighting the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Ka'b stayed with Abu Sufyan and he treated him generously, and the Jews stayed in the houses of Quraysh, and they made a pact and a covenant that they would unite in fighting Muhammad. Abu Sufyan said: "You are a man who reads the Book and knows, and we are unlettered and do not know; so which of us is better guided in the way and nearer to the truth, we or Muhammad?" Ka'b said: "By Allah, you are better guided in the way than what Muhammad is upon."

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Or do they have a share of sovereignty?﴾ That is: do they have it? The mim is an added particle (silah).

(Naseeb) means a portion (haddh) ﴿of sovereignty﴾. This is in the form of denial, meaning they have nothing of sovereignty; and if they had any of it, they would not have given anyone anything of it, due to their miserliness and envy. It was also said: the meaning is "Rather, do they have a share?", so that am is disjunctive, meaning a turning away from the first and the beginning of a new statement. It was also said: it is conjunctive upon an omitted element, because they were disdainful of following Muhammad (ﷺ). The sense is: "Are they more worthy of prophethood than the one I have sent, or do they have a share of sovereignty?"

﴿Then they would not give people even a speck (naqir)﴾: that is, they withhold rights. Allah the Exalted informed about them with what He knows of them. The naqir is the mark in the back of a date-stone, from Ibn Abbas, Qatadah and others. Also from Ibn Abbas: the naqir is what a man digs with his finger, as one digs the earth. Abu al-Aliyah said: I asked Ibn Abbas about the naqir, and he placed the tip of the thumb on the inner side of the index finger, then raised them and said: "This is the naqir." The naqir is also the root of a piece of wood that is hollowed out and in which something is soaked; and in this the prohibition came and then was abrogated. And "so-and-so is of noble naqir," that is, of noble origin. Here (idhan) is annulled, not operative, because the coordinating fa' has entered upon it; and it could have been put in the accusative. Sibawayh said: "idhan" among the operators of verbs is like "aẓunnu" among the operators of nouns; it is cancelled when the speech does not rely on it, but if it comes at the beginning of the speech and what follows it is in the future, it governs the accusative, as in your saying: "I will visit you," and he replies to you: "Then I will honour you." Abdullah ibn Anamah al-Dabbi said:

"Turn back your donkey, let it not graze in our meadow; otherwise it will be turned back, and the halter of the wild ass is tied."

It governs the verb because what precedes (idhan) is a complete sentence, so it stands at the start of a statement. If it falls between two things, as in your saying "Zayd idhan yazuruka" (Zayd, then, would visit you), it is cancelled (ilgha', meaning it loses its governing effect). If a conjunction particle, either fa' al-'atf or waw al-'atf, precedes it, then both i'mal (its governing effect applied, meaning it governs the verb) and ilgha' (its cancellation) are permitted.

As for i'mal, it is because what follows the waw is resumed as the coordination of one sentence upon another, so it is permissible outside the Qur'an to say ﴿فَإِذًا لَا يُؤْتُوا﴾ [fa-idhan la yu'tu'a]. In the revealed text there is ﴿وَإِذاً لا يَلْبَثُونَ﴾ (And then they would not remain). In the codex of Ubayy it reads ﴿وَإِذًا لَا يَلْبَثُوا﴾ (wa-idhan la yalbathu'a).

As for ilgha', it is because what follows the waw can only occur after a statement to which it is coordinated. According to Sibawayh, the one that governs the verb is idhan, owing to its resemblance to an (that). According to al-Khalil, an is implied after idhan. [In manuscript C: idhan.]

Al-Farra' claimed that idhan is written with an alif and that it takes tanwin (nunation). Al-Nahhas said: I heard Ali ibn Sulayman say: I heard Abu al-Abbas Muhammad ibn Yazid say: "I would like to cauterize the hand of whoever writes idhan with an alif. It is like lan and in, and nunation does not enter particles."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verses 44–53 (part 1 of 3):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book?﴾ up to His saying, may He be exalted: (Among them are those who believed in it, and among them are those who turned away from it), the verse [[In J, T.]]. It was revealed concerning the Jews of Madinah and those around it. Ibn Ishaq said: Rifa'ah ibn Zayd ibn al-Tabut was one of the great men of the Jews. When he spoke to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he twisted his tongue and said: "Give us your hearing, O Muhammad, until we make you understand." Then he attacked Islam and found fault with it. So Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed: (Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book?) up to His saying: (little). The meaning of (yashtaruna) is "they exchange," and it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal). In the sentence there is an omission, its estimate being "they buy error in exchange for guidance," as He, may He be exalted, said: (Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance). This was said by al-Qutabi and others.

(And they wish that you would stray from the way) is coordinated with it, and the meaning is that you would stray from the path of truth. al-Hasan recited (tudallu) with a fatha on the dad, meaning "led astray from the way."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And Allah is most knowing of your enemies﴾ means: He knows them about you, so do not take them as companions, for they are your enemies. It is also permissible for (a'lam) to carry the meaning of (alim, knowing), as in His saying, may He be exalted: (And it is easier for Him), meaning "easy."

(And sufficient is Allah as protector) — the ba' is superfluous, added because the meaning is "rely on Allah, and He will suffice you against your enemies." (Waliyyan) and (nasiran) are in the accusative as explanation (bayan), and if you wish, as circumstantial clauses (hal).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Among those who are Jews﴾. al-Zajjaj said: If (min) is connected to what precedes it, then one does not stop at His saying (nasiran). If it is made a new beginning (munqati'ah), then a pause on (nasiran) is permissible, and the estimate is: "Among those who are Jews are a people who distort the words," and then it was omitted. This is the view of Sibawayh, and the grammarians cited:

"If I were to say, there is no one among her people
who surpasses her in lineage and in smile..." [[Tayathim (with a kasra on the ta'): a dialect of some Arabs, for they put a kasra on the prefixed letter in forms like ta'allam and ta'lam; when they put a kasra on the ta', the hamza changed into a ya'. The mim (on the pattern of al-majlis): the teeth at the front of the mouth.]]

They said: the meaning is, "If I were to say there is no one among her people who surpasses her," and then it was omitted. al-Farra' said the omitted word is (man), so the meaning is: "Among those who are Jews are those who distort." This is like His saying, may He be exalted: (And there is none of us but has a known station), meaning "there is none of us who has..." Dhu al-Rummah said:

"They remained, and among them is one whose tears are flowing for her,
and another who sheds the tear of the eye with flowing drops..."

[[In the Diwan of Dhu al-Rummah: (ghalib) and (yuthanna). Himlan al-'ayn: its flowing with tears. Yudhri: he sheds.]]

He means: "And among them is one whose tears..." so he omitted the relative pronoun. al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj rejected this, because omitting the relative pronoun is like omitting part of a word. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i recited (al-kalam). al-Nahhas said: (al-kalim) in this place is preferable, because they only distort the words of the Prophet (ﷺ), or what they have in the Torah, and they do not distort all speech. The meaning of (yuharrifuna) is that they interpret it other than its proper interpretation. Allah, may He be exalted, censured them for this because they do it deliberately. It was also said: (from its places) means the description of the Prophet (ﷺ).

(And they say: "We hear and we disobey") means: we hear your words and we disobey your command.

(And hear, without being heard) — Ibn 'Abbas said: They would say to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Hear, may you not hear!" This is what they meant, may Allah curse them, while they showed that they meant: "Hear, without hearing anything disagreeable or harmful." al-Hasan and Mujahid said: its meaning is "without being heard from you," that is, not accepted, and not answered in what you say. al-Nahhas said: If it were so, it would have been "without being heard by you." The discussion of (ra'ina) has already been given [[4]]. The meaning of (laywan bi-alsinatihim) is that they twist their tongues away from the truth, that is, they bend them toward what is in their hearts. The root of (layy) is "killing," and it is in the accusative as an infinitive (masdar). If you wish, it may be an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi). Its original form was (lawyan), then the waw was assimilated into the ya'.

(And slander) is coordinated with it, that is, they slander the religion. That is, they would say to their companions: "If he were a prophet, he would know that we are reviling him." So Allah, may He be exalted, made His Prophet aware of that, and this became one of the signs of his prophethood, and He forbade them from this speech. The meaning of (aqwam) is "more correct for them in judgment." (So they do not believe except a few) means: except a faith that is small, by which they do not deserve the name of faith. It was also said: its meaning is "they do not believe except a few of them." But this is far-fetched, because He, mighty and majestic, has informed us that He cursed them for their disbelief.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who were given the Book, believe in what We have sent down﴾. Ibn Ishaq said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) spoke to leaders among the rabbis of the Jews, among them Abdullah ibn Suriya al-A'war and Ka'b ibn Asad. He said to them: "O assembly of Jews, fear Allah and submit. By Allah, you know that what I have brought to you is the truth." They said: "We do not know that, O Muhammad." They denied what they knew and persisted in disbelief. So Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed concerning them: (O you who were given the Book, believe in what We have sent down, confirming what is with you, before We obliterate faces) up to the end of the verse.

(Confirming what is with you) is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal).

(Before We obliterate faces) — (tams) is the total effacement of a thing's trace, and from it is His saying, may He be exalted: (When the stars are obliterated). (Natmisu) and (natmusu), with kasra and damma on the mim in the future, are two dialects. It is also said in speech: tasama yatsimu and yatsumu, with the meaning of tamasa, one says: tamasa al-athar and tasama, meaning it was effaced. All of these are dialects. From it is His saying, may He be exalted: (Our Lord, obliterate their wealth) meaning: destroy it, according to Ibn 'Arafah. It is said: "I obliterated it," and "tamasa" is both intransitive and transitive. "Tamasa Allah basarahu" and he is "matmus al-basar" when the trace of the eye is gone. From it is His saying, may He be exalted: (And if We willed, We would have obliterated their eyes), meaning: We would have blinded them.

The scholars differed about the intended meaning of this verse: is it literal, so that the face becomes like the back of the neck, and the nose, mouth, brow and eyes are taken away? Or is it an expression for error in their hearts and the removal of success from them? There are two opinions. It was narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that he said: (Before We obliterate faces) means: before We cause you to go astray with a misguidance after which you will not be guided. He holds that it is a figure of speech, and that if they do not believe, this will be done to them as a punishment. Qatadah said: its meaning is: before We make the faces into necks, that is, we take away the nose, the lips, the eyes and the eyebrows; this is its meaning according to the lexicographers. It was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ata' al-'Awfi that the obliteration is that the two eyes alone are removed and returned to the back of the neck, so that this becomes a turning around to the back, and one walks backwards. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The first Islam of Ka'b al-Ahbar was that he passed by a man in the night who was reciting this verse: (O you who were given the Book, believe), so he placed his palms on his face and returned backwards to his house, and embraced Islam on the spot, and said: "By Allah, I feared that I would not reach my house before my face was obliterated." Abdullah ibn Salam did likewise: when this verse was revealed and he heard it, he came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) before he went to his family, and embraced Islam, and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I did not know that I would reach you until my face was turned around on my neck."

If it is asked: how was it permissible for Him to threaten them with the obliteration of faces if they did not believe, and it was not done to them? It is answered: when these believed, and those who followed them, the threat was lifted from the rest. al-Mubarrad said: the threat remains awaited. He said: there must be an obliteration among the Jews and a transformation before the Day of Resurrection.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Or We curse them﴾, that is, the people of the faces (as We cursed the people of the Sabbath). That is, We transform them into apes and swine, according to al-Hasan and Qatadah. It was also said: this is a shift from address (khitab) to third-person reference (ghaybah).

(And the command of Allah is always accomplished) means: it is existent and occurring. "Amr" here may mean "what is commanded," so it is a verbal noun used in the place of a passive participle, and the meaning is that whenever He wills it, He brings it into being. It was also said: its meaning is that every matter that He has informed about its occurrence is bound to occur as He has informed.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him﴾. It was narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited (Indeed, Allah forgives all sins), and a man said to him: "O Messenger of Allah, and what about associating partners!" So (Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, and He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills) was revealed. This is among the clear (muhkam) matters agreed upon, about which there is no disagreement among the community.

(And He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills) is among the ambiguous (mutashabih) matters about which the scholars have spoken. Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: This verse has made clear that every person who commits a major sin is under Allah's will, so that if He wills, He pardons his sin, and if He wills, He punishes him for it, as long as his major sin is not associating partners with Allah, may He be exalted. Some said: Allah, may He be exalted, has explained that in His saying: (If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden, We will remove from you your misdeeds) [[See p. 158 of this part.]]. So know that He wills to forgive the minor sins of those who avoid the major sins, and He does not forgive them for those who commit major sins. Some of the interpreters went to the view that this verse abrogates (naskh, cancelling a earlier ruling by a later revelation) the one at the end of (al-Furqan) [[See p. 158 of this part.]]. Zayd ibn Thabit said: Surah al-Nisa' was revealed six months after al-Furqan. The correct view is that there is no abrogation, because abrogation in reports (akhbar) is impossible. The reconciliation of the verses in this surah with those in al-Furqan will come, if Allah wills [[See vol. 13, p. 77.]]. In al-Tirmidhi, it is narrated from Ali ibn Abi Talib that he said: "There is no verse in the Qur'an more beloved to me than this verse: (Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, and He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills)." He said: This is a hadith that is hasan gharib.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verse 44–53 (part 2 of 3):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Have you not seen those who claim purity for themselves?﴾ There are three issues in this.

The first: Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Have you not seen those who claim purity for themselves?﴾ This wording is general in its outward sense, and none of the exegetes has disagreed that the intended people are the Jews. They differed over the matter by which they claimed purity for themselves. Qatadah and al-Hasan said: it is their saying, "We are the sons of God and His beloved" (Qur'an 5:18), and their saying, "None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians" (Qur'an 2:111). Al-Dahhak and al-Suddi said: it is their saying, "We have no sins; what we did by day was forgiven us by night, and what we did by night was forgiven us by day, and we are like children in being free of sins." Mujahid, Abu Malik and Ikrimah said: it is their putting the young children forward for the prayer, because they have no sins upon them. This is far from the aim of the verse. Ibn Abbas said: it is their saying, "Our fathers who have died intercede for us and purify us." Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said: it is the praise of some of them for others. This is the best of what has been said, for it is the apparent meaning of the verse. And tazkiyah means purification and clearing (tanzih) from sins.

The second: this verse and the saying of Allah the Exalted, ﴿So do not claim purity for yourselves﴾ (Qur'an 53:32), require the disapproval of a person who praises himself with his tongue, and the information that the one who is truly pure is the one whose deeds are good and whom Allah the Exalted purifies. So a person's praise of himself carries no weight; what carries weight is Allah's praise of him. In Sahih Muslim, from Muhammad ibn Amr ibn Ata, who said: I named my daughter Barrah, and Zaynab bint Abi Salamah said to me: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade this name. I had named her Barrah, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not claim purity for yourselves, Allah knows best who among you is righteous." They said: "What shall we name her?" He said: "Name her Zaynab." So the Book and the Sunnah have indicated the prohibition of a person claiming purity for himself. Similar to this is what has spread in these Egyptian lands of people describing themselves with epithets that imply purity, such as Zaki al-Din, Muhyi al-Din and the like. But since the blemishes of those named with these names have multiplied, the disconnection of these epithets from their origin has become apparent, so they no longer convey anything.

The third: as for purifying another and praising him, in al-Bukhari, from the hadith of Abu Bakrah: a man was mentioned in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), and a man praised him highly. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Woe to you, you have cut the neck of your companion" — he said it several times — "If one of you must praise, let him say: I think so-and-so is such, if he sees that he is, and his reckoning is with Allah, and let him not purify anyone before Allah." So he (ﷺ) forbade excessive praise of a man for what is not in him, lest conceit and pride enter him, and he thinks he truly holds that rank, and this leads him to neglect deeds and cease seeking further virtue. For this reason he (ﷺ) said: "Woe to you, you have cut the neck of your companion." In another hadith: "You have broken the back of the man," when they described him with what was not in him. On this basis the scholars interpreted his saying (ﷺ): "Throw dust in the faces of the flatterers," as meaning those who flatter people to their faces with falsehood and with what is not in them, so that they make that a commodity by which they live off the one praised and corrupt him. But praising a man for the good action and commendable matter that is in him, so that it becomes an encouragement for him to the like and an incitement for people to follow him in similar things, is not flattery, even though the speaker has become one who praises by the good words he has spoken about him. This goes back to intentions, and Allah knows the corrupter from the reformer. The Prophet (ﷺ) was praised in poetry, in speeches and in address, and he did not order dust thrown in the faces of those who praised him, nor did he command it. Such as the saying of Abu Talib:

"And a fair one, by whose face rain is sought, the shelter of orphans and the protection of widows."

And like the praise of Abbas and Hassan for him in their poetry, and Ka'b ibn Zuhayr praised him, and he himself praised his companions, saying: "You are few when greed is present and many when fear is present." As for his saying (ﷺ) in the sound hadith: "Do not exaggerate in praising me as the Christians exaggerated in praising Isa son of Maryam; say: the servant of Allah and His Messenger," its meaning is: do not describe me with attributes that are not in me, seeking thereby to praise me, as the Christians described Isa with what was not in him, so they attributed to him that he is the son of God, and thereby they disbelieved and went astray. This implies that whoever raises a person above his level and exceeds his measure with what is not in him is a transgressor and sinful, because if that were permissible for anyone, the most worthy of creation to receive it would be the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And they will not be wronged a whit (fatil)﴾. The pronoun in "they will not be wronged" refers to those mentioned, both those who claimed purity for themselves and those whom Allah the Exalted purifies. Anyone other than these two categories knows from another verse that Allah the Exalted does not wrong him. The fatil is the thread that is in the split of a date-stone, said by Ibn Abbas, Ata and Mujahid. It was said: it is the membrane that surrounds the stone between it and the unripe date. Ibn Abbas also said, as did Abu Malik and al-Suddi: it is the dirt that comes out between your two fingers or palms when you roll them together, so it is fa'il in the sense of maf'ul. All of this returns to an expression of the smallness and insignificance of a thing, and that Allah does not wrong anyone in the least. Similar in this sense of minimizing is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Nor will they be wronged a speck (naqir)﴾ (Qur'an 4:53), which is the pit mark on the back of a date-stone, from which the palm tree grows, and it will come. A poet, dispraising some kings, said:

"You gather an army of thousands and raid, then you do not harm the enemy a whit (fatil)."

Then the Prophet (ﷺ) marvelled at this and said: "Look how they invent lies against Allah," in their saying: "We are the sons of God and His beloved." It was said: their claiming purity for themselves, from Ibn Jurayj. And it was narrated that they said: "We have no sins except like the sins of our children on the day they are born." Iftira' means fabrication, and from it: "So-and-so fabricated against so-and-so," that is, he accused him with what is not in him. And faraytu al-shay' means I cut it.

﴿And sufficient is it as a manifest sin﴾: it is in the accusative as a specification (bayan). The meaning is the magnifying and condemnation of the sin. The Arabs use such a construction both in praise and in blame.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book?﴾ meaning the Jews, ﴿they believe in al-jibt and al-taghut﴾. The exegetes differed over the interpretation of al-jibt and al-taghut. Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and Abu al-Aliyah said: al-jibt is the sorcerer in the language of Abyssinia, and al-taghut is the soothsayer. Al-Faruq Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: al-jibt is magic, and al-taghut is the devil. Ibn Mas'ud: al-jibt and al-taghut here are Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and Huyayy ibn Akhtab. Ikrimah: al-jibt is Huyayy ibn Akhtab and al-taghut is Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, its evidence being the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿They wish to seek judgment before al-taghut﴾ (Qur'an 4:60). Qatadah: al-jibt is the devil and al-taghut is the soothsayer. Ibn Wahb narrated from Malik ibn Anas: al-taghut is whatever is worshipped besides Allah. He said: I heard someone say that al-jibt is the devil; mentioned by al-Nahhas. It was also said: both are every object of worship besides Allah, or every one obeyed in disobedience to Allah, and this is good. The root of al-jibt is al-jibs, which is what has no good in it, and the ta' was substituted for the sin, said by Qutrub. It was said: al-jibt is Iblis and al-taghut are his allies. Malik's view on this matter is good, and it is indicated by the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿That you worship Allah and avoid al-taghut﴾ (Qur'an 16:36), and the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And those who avoided al-taghut from worshipping it﴾ (Qur'an 39:17). Qutn ibn al-Mukhariq narrated from his father who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Tarq, tiyarah and iyafah are of al-jibt." Tarq is divination by lines, and iyafah is the reading of omens from birds. Abu Dawud recorded it in his Sunan. It was also said: al-jibt is everything that Allah has forbidden, and al-taghut is everything that makes a person transgress. And Allah knows best.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And they say to those who disbelieve﴾, that is, the Jews say to the disbelievers of Quraysh: "You are better guided in the way than those who believe in Muhammad." That is because Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf went out with seventy riders from the Jews to Mecca after the battle of Uhud, to form an alliance with Quraysh against fighting the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Ka'b stayed with Abu Sufyan and he treated him generously, and the Jews stayed in the houses of Quraysh, and they made a pact and a covenant that they would unite in fighting Muhammad. Abu Sufyan said: "You are a man who reads the Book and knows, and we are unlettered and do not know; so which of us is better guided in the way and nearer to the truth, we or Muhammad?" Ka'b said: "By Allah, you are better guided in the way than what Muhammad is upon."

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Or do they have a share of sovereignty?﴾ That is: do they have it? The mim is an added particle (silah).

(Naseeb) means a portion (haddh) ﴿of sovereignty﴾. This is in the form of denial, meaning they have nothing of sovereignty; and if they had any of it, they would not have given anyone anything of it, due to their miserliness and envy. It was also said: the meaning is "Rather, do they have a share?", so that am is disjunctive, meaning a turning away from the first and the beginning of a new statement. It was also said: it is conjunctive upon an omitted element, because they were disdainful of following Muhammad (ﷺ). The sense is: "Are they more worthy of prophethood than the one I have sent, or do they have a share of sovereignty?"

﴿Then they would not give people even a speck (naqir)﴾: that is, they withhold rights. Allah the Exalted informed about them with what He knows of them. The naqir is the mark in the back of a date-stone, from Ibn Abbas, Qatadah and others. Also from Ibn Abbas: the naqir is what a man digs with his finger, as one digs the earth. Abu al-Aliyah said: I asked Ibn Abbas about the naqir, and he placed the tip of the thumb on the inner side of the index finger, then raised them and said: "This is the naqir." The naqir is also the root of a piece of wood that is hollowed out and in which something is soaked; and in this the prohibition came and then was abrogated. And "so-and-so is of noble naqir," that is, of noble origin. Here (idhan) is annulled, not operative, because the coordinating fa' has entered upon it; and it could have been put in the accusative. Sibawayh said: "idhan" among the operators of verbs is like "aẓunnu" among the operators of nouns; it is cancelled when the speech does not rely on it, but if it comes at the beginning of the speech and what follows it is in the future, it governs the accusative, as in your saying: "I will visit you," and he replies to you: "Then I will honour you." Abdullah ibn Anamah al-Dabbi said:

"Turn back your donkey, let it not graze in our meadow; otherwise it will be turned back, and the halter of the wild ass is tied."

It governs the verb because what precedes (idhan) is a complete sentence, so it stands at the start of a statement. If it falls between two things, as in your saying "Zayd idhan yazuruka" (Zayd, then, would visit you), it is cancelled (ilgha', meaning it loses its governing effect). If a conjunction particle, either fa' al-'atf or waw al-'atf, precedes it, then both i'mal (its governing effect applied, meaning it governs the verb) and ilgha' (its cancellation) are permitted.

As for i'mal, it is because what follows the waw is resumed as the coordination of one sentence upon another, so it is permissible outside the Qur'an to say ﴿فَإِذًا لَا يُؤْتُوا﴾ [fa-idhan la yu'tu'a]. In the revealed text there is ﴿وَإِذاً لا يَلْبَثُونَ﴾ (And then they would not remain). In the codex of Ubayy it reads ﴿وَإِذًا لَا يَلْبَثُوا﴾ (wa-idhan la yalbathu'a).

As for ilgha', it is because what follows the waw can only occur after a statement to which it is coordinated. According to Sibawayh, the one that governs the verb is idhan, owing to its resemblance to an (that). According to al-Khalil, an is implied after idhan. [In manuscript C: idhan.]

Al-Farra' claimed that idhan is written with an alif and that it takes tanwin (nunation). Al-Nahhas said: I heard Ali ibn Sulayman say: I heard Abu al-Abbas Muhammad ibn Yazid say: "I would like to cauterize the hand of whoever writes idhan with an alif. It is like lan and in, and nunation does not enter particles."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verses 44–53 (part 1 of 3):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book?﴾ up to His saying, may He be exalted: (Among them are those who believed in it, and among them are those who turned away from it), the verse [[In J, T.]]. It was revealed concerning the Jews of Madinah and those around it. Ibn Ishaq said: Rifa'ah ibn Zayd ibn al-Tabut was one of the great men of the Jews. When he spoke to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he twisted his tongue and said: "Give us your hearing, O Muhammad, until we make you understand." Then he attacked Islam and found fault with it. So Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed: (Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book?) up to His saying: (little). The meaning of (yashtaruna) is "they exchange," and it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal). In the sentence there is an omission, its estimate being "they buy error in exchange for guidance," as He, may He be exalted, said: (Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance). This was said by al-Qutabi and others.

(And they wish that you would stray from the way) is coordinated with it, and the meaning is that you would stray from the path of truth. al-Hasan recited (tudallu) with a fatha on the dad, meaning "led astray from the way."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And Allah is most knowing of your enemies﴾ means: He knows them about you, so do not take them as companions, for they are your enemies. It is also permissible for (a'lam) to carry the meaning of (alim, knowing), as in His saying, may He be exalted: (And it is easier for Him), meaning "easy."

(And sufficient is Allah as protector) — the ba' is superfluous, added because the meaning is "rely on Allah, and He will suffice you against your enemies." (Waliyyan) and (nasiran) are in the accusative as explanation (bayan), and if you wish, as circumstantial clauses (hal).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Among those who are Jews﴾. al-Zajjaj said: If (min) is connected to what precedes it, then one does not stop at His saying (nasiran). If it is made a new beginning (munqati'ah), then a pause on (nasiran) is permissible, and the estimate is: "Among those who are Jews are a people who distort the words," and then it was omitted. This is the view of Sibawayh, and the grammarians cited:

"If I were to say, there is no one among her people
who surpasses her in lineage and in smile..." [[Tayathim (with a kasra on the ta'): a dialect of some Arabs, for they put a kasra on the prefixed letter in forms like ta'allam and ta'lam; when they put a kasra on the ta', the hamza changed into a ya'. The mim (on the pattern of al-majlis): the teeth at the front of the mouth.]]

They said: the meaning is, "If I were to say there is no one among her people who surpasses her," and then it was omitted. al-Farra' said the omitted word is (man), so the meaning is: "Among those who are Jews are those who distort." This is like His saying, may He be exalted: (And there is none of us but has a known station), meaning "there is none of us who has..." Dhu al-Rummah said:

"They remained, and among them is one whose tears are flowing for her,
and another who sheds the tear of the eye with flowing drops..."

[[In the Diwan of Dhu al-Rummah: (ghalib) and (yuthanna). Himlan al-'ayn: its flowing with tears. Yudhri: he sheds.]]

He means: "And among them is one whose tears..." so he omitted the relative pronoun. al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj rejected this, because omitting the relative pronoun is like omitting part of a word. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i recited (al-kalam). al-Nahhas said: (al-kalim) in this place is preferable, because they only distort the words of the Prophet (ﷺ), or what they have in the Torah, and they do not distort all speech. The meaning of (yuharrifuna) is that they interpret it other than its proper interpretation. Allah, may He be exalted, censured them for this because they do it deliberately. It was also said: (from its places) means the description of the Prophet (ﷺ).

(And they say: "We hear and we disobey") means: we hear your words and we disobey your command.

(And hear, without being heard) — Ibn 'Abbas said: They would say to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Hear, may you not hear!" This is what they meant, may Allah curse them, while they showed that they meant: "Hear, without hearing anything disagreeable or harmful." al-Hasan and Mujahid said: its meaning is "without being heard from you," that is, not accepted, and not answered in what you say. al-Nahhas said: If it were so, it would have been "without being heard by you." The discussion of (ra'ina) has already been given [[4]]. The meaning of (laywan bi-alsinatihim) is that they twist their tongues away from the truth, that is, they bend them toward what is in their hearts. The root of (layy) is "killing," and it is in the accusative as an infinitive (masdar). If you wish, it may be an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi). Its original form was (lawyan), then the waw was assimilated into the ya'.

(And slander) is coordinated with it, that is, they slander the religion. That is, they would say to their companions: "If he were a prophet, he would know that we are reviling him." So Allah, may He be exalted, made His Prophet aware of that, and this became one of the signs of his prophethood, and He forbade them from this speech. The meaning of (aqwam) is "more correct for them in judgment." (So they do not believe except a few) means: except a faith that is small, by which they do not deserve the name of faith. It was also said: its meaning is "they do not believe except a few of them." But this is far-fetched, because He, mighty and majestic, has informed us that He cursed them for their disbelief.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who were given the Book, believe in what We have sent down﴾. Ibn Ishaq said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) spoke to leaders among the rabbis of the Jews, among them Abdullah ibn Suriya al-A'war and Ka'b ibn Asad. He said to them: "O assembly of Jews, fear Allah and submit. By Allah, you know that what I have brought to you is the truth." They said: "We do not know that, O Muhammad." They denied what they knew and persisted in disbelief. So Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed concerning them: (O you who were given the Book, believe in what We have sent down, confirming what is with you, before We obliterate faces) up to the end of the verse.

(Confirming what is with you) is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal).

(Before We obliterate faces) — (tams) is the total effacement of a thing's trace, and from it is His saying, may He be exalted: (When the stars are obliterated). (Natmisu) and (natmusu), with kasra and damma on the mim in the future, are two dialects. It is also said in speech: tasama yatsimu and yatsumu, with the meaning of tamasa, one says: tamasa al-athar and tasama, meaning it was effaced. All of these are dialects. From it is His saying, may He be exalted: (Our Lord, obliterate their wealth) meaning: destroy it, according to Ibn 'Arafah. It is said: "I obliterated it," and "tamasa" is both intransitive and transitive. "Tamasa Allah basarahu" and he is "matmus al-basar" when the trace of the eye is gone. From it is His saying, may He be exalted: (And if We willed, We would have obliterated their eyes), meaning: We would have blinded them.

The scholars differed about the intended meaning of this verse: is it literal, so that the face becomes like the back of the neck, and the nose, mouth, brow and eyes are taken away? Or is it an expression for error in their hearts and the removal of success from them? There are two opinions. It was narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that he said: (Before We obliterate faces) means: before We cause you to go astray with a misguidance after which you will not be guided. He holds that it is a figure of speech, and that if they do not believe, this will be done to them as a punishment. Qatadah said: its meaning is: before We make the faces into necks, that is, we take away the nose, the lips, the eyes and the eyebrows; this is its meaning according to the lexicographers. It was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ata' al-'Awfi that the obliteration is that the two eyes alone are removed and returned to the back of the neck, so that this becomes a turning around to the back, and one walks backwards. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The first Islam of Ka'b al-Ahbar was that he passed by a man in the night who was reciting this verse: (O you who were given the Book, believe), so he placed his palms on his face and returned backwards to his house, and embraced Islam on the spot, and said: "By Allah, I feared that I would not reach my house before my face was obliterated." Abdullah ibn Salam did likewise: when this verse was revealed and he heard it, he came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) before he went to his family, and embraced Islam, and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I did not know that I would reach you until my face was turned around on my neck."

If it is asked: how was it permissible for Him to threaten them with the obliteration of faces if they did not believe, and it was not done to them? It is answered: when these believed, and those who followed them, the threat was lifted from the rest. al-Mubarrad said: the threat remains awaited. He said: there must be an obliteration among the Jews and a transformation before the Day of Resurrection.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Or We curse them﴾, that is, the people of the faces (as We cursed the people of the Sabbath). That is, We transform them into apes and swine, according to al-Hasan and Qatadah. It was also said: this is a shift from address (khitab) to third-person reference (ghaybah).

(And the command of Allah is always accomplished) means: it is existent and occurring. "Amr" here may mean "what is commanded," so it is a verbal noun used in the place of a passive participle, and the meaning is that whenever He wills it, He brings it into being. It was also said: its meaning is that every matter that He has informed about its occurrence is bound to occur as He has informed.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him﴾. It was narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited (Indeed, Allah forgives all sins), and a man said to him: "O Messenger of Allah, and what about associating partners!" So (Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, and He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills) was revealed. This is among the clear (muhkam) matters agreed upon, about which there is no disagreement among the community.

(And He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills) is among the ambiguous (mutashabih) matters about which the scholars have spoken. Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: This verse has made clear that every person who commits a major sin is under Allah's will, so that if He wills, He pardons his sin, and if He wills, He punishes him for it, as long as his major sin is not associating partners with Allah, may He be exalted. Some said: Allah, may He be exalted, has explained that in His saying: (If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden, We will remove from you your misdeeds) [[See p. 158 of this part.]]. So know that He wills to forgive the minor sins of those who avoid the major sins, and He does not forgive them for those who commit major sins. Some of the interpreters went to the view that this verse abrogates (naskh, cancelling a earlier ruling by a later revelation) the one at the end of (al-Furqan) [[See p. 158 of this part.]]. Zayd ibn Thabit said: Surah al-Nisa' was revealed six months after al-Furqan. The correct view is that there is no abrogation, because abrogation in reports (akhbar) is impossible. The reconciliation of the verses in this surah with those in al-Furqan will come, if Allah wills [[See vol. 13, p. 77.]]. In al-Tirmidhi, it is narrated from Ali ibn Abi Talib that he said: "There is no verse in the Qur'an more beloved to me than this verse: (Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, and He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills)." He said: This is a hadith that is hasan gharib.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verse 44–53 (part 2 of 3):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Have you not seen those who claim purity for themselves?﴾ There are three issues in this.

The first: Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Have you not seen those who claim purity for themselves?﴾ This wording is general in its outward sense, and none of the exegetes has disagreed that the intended people are the Jews. They differed over the matter by which they claimed purity for themselves. Qatadah and al-Hasan said: it is their saying, "We are the sons of God and His beloved" (Qur'an 5:18), and their saying, "None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians" (Qur'an 2:111). Al-Dahhak and al-Suddi said: it is their saying, "We have no sins; what we did by day was forgiven us by night, and what we did by night was forgiven us by day, and we are like children in being free of sins." Mujahid, Abu Malik and Ikrimah said: it is their putting the young children forward for the prayer, because they have no sins upon them. This is far from the aim of the verse. Ibn Abbas said: it is their saying, "Our fathers who have died intercede for us and purify us." Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said: it is the praise of some of them for others. This is the best of what has been said, for it is the apparent meaning of the verse. And tazkiyah means purification and clearing (tanzih) from sins.

The second: this verse and the saying of Allah the Exalted, ﴿So do not claim purity for yourselves﴾ (Qur'an 53:32), require the disapproval of a person who praises himself with his tongue, and the information that the one who is truly pure is the one whose deeds are good and whom Allah the Exalted purifies. So a person's praise of himself carries no weight; what carries weight is Allah's praise of him. In Sahih Muslim, from Muhammad ibn Amr ibn Ata, who said: I named my daughter Barrah, and Zaynab bint Abi Salamah said to me: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade this name. I had named her Barrah, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not claim purity for yourselves, Allah knows best who among you is righteous." They said: "What shall we name her?" He said: "Name her Zaynab." So the Book and the Sunnah have indicated the prohibition of a person claiming purity for himself. Similar to this is what has spread in these Egyptian lands of people describing themselves with epithets that imply purity, such as Zaki al-Din, Muhyi al-Din and the like. But since the blemishes of those named with these names have multiplied, the disconnection of these epithets from their origin has become apparent, so they no longer convey anything.

The third: as for purifying another and praising him, in al-Bukhari, from the hadith of Abu Bakrah: a man was mentioned in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), and a man praised him highly. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Woe to you, you have cut the neck of your companion" — he said it several times — "If one of you must praise, let him say: I think so-and-so is such, if he sees that he is, and his reckoning is with Allah, and let him not purify anyone before Allah." So he (ﷺ) forbade excessive praise of a man for what is not in him, lest conceit and pride enter him, and he thinks he truly holds that rank, and this leads him to neglect deeds and cease seeking further virtue. For this reason he (ﷺ) said: "Woe to you, you have cut the neck of your companion." In another hadith: "You have broken the back of the man," when they described him with what was not in him. On this basis the scholars interpreted his saying (ﷺ): "Throw dust in the faces of the flatterers," as meaning those who flatter people to their faces with falsehood and with what is not in them, so that they make that a commodity by which they live off the one praised and corrupt him. But praising a man for the good action and commendable matter that is in him, so that it becomes an encouragement for him to the like and an incitement for people to follow him in similar things, is not flattery, even though the speaker has become one who praises by the good words he has spoken about him. This goes back to intentions, and Allah knows the corrupter from the reformer. The Prophet (ﷺ) was praised in poetry, in speeches and in address, and he did not order dust thrown in the faces of those who praised him, nor did he command it. Such as the saying of Abu Talib:

"And a fair one, by whose face rain is sought, the shelter of orphans and the protection of widows."

And like the praise of Abbas and Hassan for him in their poetry, and Ka'b ibn Zuhayr praised him, and he himself praised his companions, saying: "You are few when greed is present and many when fear is present." As for his saying (ﷺ) in the sound hadith: "Do not exaggerate in praising me as the Christians exaggerated in praising Isa son of Maryam; say: the servant of Allah and His Messenger," its meaning is: do not describe me with attributes that are not in me, seeking thereby to praise me, as the Christians described Isa with what was not in him, so they attributed to him that he is the son of God, and thereby they disbelieved and went astray. This implies that whoever raises a person above his level and exceeds his measure with what is not in him is a transgressor and sinful, because if that were permissible for anyone, the most worthy of creation to receive it would be the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And they will not be wronged a whit (fatil)﴾. The pronoun in "they will not be wronged" refers to those mentioned, both those who claimed purity for themselves and those whom Allah the Exalted purifies. Anyone other than these two categories knows from another verse that Allah the Exalted does not wrong him. The fatil is the thread that is in the split of a date-stone, said by Ibn Abbas, Ata and Mujahid. It was said: it is the membrane that surrounds the stone between it and the unripe date. Ibn Abbas also said, as did Abu Malik and al-Suddi: it is the dirt that comes out between your two fingers or palms when you roll them together, so it is fa'il in the sense of maf'ul. All of this returns to an expression of the smallness and insignificance of a thing, and that Allah does not wrong anyone in the least. Similar in this sense of minimizing is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Nor will they be wronged a speck (naqir)﴾ (Qur'an 4:53), which is the pit mark on the back of a date-stone, from which the palm tree grows, and it will come. A poet, dispraising some kings, said:

"You gather an army of thousands and raid, then you do not harm the enemy a whit (fatil)."

Then the Prophet (ﷺ) marvelled at this and said: "Look how they invent lies against Allah," in their saying: "We are the sons of God and His beloved." It was said: their claiming purity for themselves, from Ibn Jurayj. And it was narrated that they said: "We have no sins except like the sins of our children on the day they are born." Iftira' means fabrication, and from it: "So-and-so fabricated against so-and-so," that is, he accused him with what is not in him. And faraytu al-shay' means I cut it.

﴿And sufficient is it as a manifest sin﴾: it is in the accusative as a specification (bayan). The meaning is the magnifying and condemnation of the sin. The Arabs use such a construction both in praise and in blame.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book?﴾ meaning the Jews, ﴿they believe in al-jibt and al-taghut﴾. The exegetes differed over the interpretation of al-jibt and al-taghut. Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and Abu al-Aliyah said: al-jibt is the sorcerer in the language of Abyssinia, and al-taghut is the soothsayer. Al-Faruq Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: al-jibt is magic, and al-taghut is the devil. Ibn Mas'ud: al-jibt and al-taghut here are Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and Huyayy ibn Akhtab. Ikrimah: al-jibt is Huyayy ibn Akhtab and al-taghut is Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, its evidence being the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿They wish to seek judgment before al-taghut﴾ (Qur'an 4:60). Qatadah: al-jibt is the devil and al-taghut is the soothsayer. Ibn Wahb narrated from Malik ibn Anas: al-taghut is whatever is worshipped besides Allah. He said: I heard someone say that al-jibt is the devil; mentioned by al-Nahhas. It was also said: both are every object of worship besides Allah, or every one obeyed in disobedience to Allah, and this is good. The root of al-jibt is al-jibs, which is what has no good in it, and the ta' was substituted for the sin, said by Qutrub. It was said: al-jibt is Iblis and al-taghut are his allies. Malik's view on this matter is good, and it is indicated by the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿That you worship Allah and avoid al-taghut﴾ (Qur'an 16:36), and the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And those who avoided al-taghut from worshipping it﴾ (Qur'an 39:17). Qutn ibn al-Mukhariq narrated from his father who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Tarq, tiyarah and iyafah are of al-jibt." Tarq is divination by lines, and iyafah is the reading of omens from birds. Abu Dawud recorded it in his Sunan. It was also said: al-jibt is everything that Allah has forbidden, and al-taghut is everything that makes a person transgress. And Allah knows best.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And they say to those who disbelieve﴾, that is, the Jews say to the disbelievers of Quraysh: "You are better guided in the way than those who believe in Muhammad." That is because Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf went out with seventy riders from the Jews to Mecca after the battle of Uhud, to form an alliance with Quraysh against fighting the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Ka'b stayed with Abu Sufyan and he treated him generously, and the Jews stayed in the houses of Quraysh, and they made a pact and a covenant that they would unite in fighting Muhammad. Abu Sufyan said: "You are a man who reads the Book and knows, and we are unlettered and do not know; so which of us is better guided in the way and nearer to the truth, we or Muhammad?" Ka'b said: "By Allah, you are better guided in the way than what Muhammad is upon."

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Or do they have a share of sovereignty?﴾ That is: do they have it? The mim is an added particle (silah).

(Naseeb) means a portion (haddh) ﴿of sovereignty﴾. This is in the form of denial, meaning they have nothing of sovereignty; and if they had any of it, they would not have given anyone anything of it, due to their miserliness and envy. It was also said: the meaning is "Rather, do they have a share?", so that am is disjunctive, meaning a turning away from the first and the beginning of a new statement. It was also said: it is conjunctive upon an omitted element, because they were disdainful of following Muhammad (ﷺ). The sense is: "Are they more worthy of prophethood than the one I have sent, or do they have a share of sovereignty?"

﴿Then they would not give people even a speck (naqir)﴾: that is, they withhold rights. Allah the Exalted informed about them with what He knows of them. The naqir is the mark in the back of a date-stone, from Ibn Abbas, Qatadah and others. Also from Ibn Abbas: the naqir is what a man digs with his finger, as one digs the earth. Abu al-Aliyah said: I asked Ibn Abbas about the naqir, and he placed the tip of the thumb on the inner side of the index finger, then raised them and said: "This is the naqir." The naqir is also the root of a piece of wood that is hollowed out and in which something is soaked; and in this the prohibition came and then was abrogated. And "so-and-so is of noble naqir," that is, of noble origin. Here (idhan) is annulled, not operative, because the coordinating fa' has entered upon it; and it could have been put in the accusative. Sibawayh said: "idhan" among the operators of verbs is like "aẓunnu" among the operators of nouns; it is cancelled when the speech does not rely on it, but if it comes at the beginning of the speech and what follows it is in the future, it governs the accusative, as in your saying: "I will visit you," and he replies to you: "Then I will honour you." Abdullah ibn Anamah al-Dabbi said:

"Turn back your donkey, let it not graze in our meadow; otherwise it will be turned back, and the halter of the wild ass is tied."

It governs the verb because what precedes (idhan) is a complete sentence, so it stands at the start of a statement. If it falls between two things, as in your saying "Zayd idhan yazuruka" (Zayd, then, would visit you), it is cancelled (ilgha', meaning it loses its governing effect). If a conjunction particle, either fa' al-'atf or waw al-'atf, precedes it, then both i'mal (its governing effect applied, meaning it governs the verb) and ilgha' (its cancellation) are permitted.

As for i'mal, it is because what follows the waw is resumed as the coordination of one sentence upon another, so it is permissible outside the Qur'an to say ﴿فَإِذًا لَا يُؤْتُوا﴾ [fa-idhan la yu'tu'a]. In the revealed text there is ﴿وَإِذاً لا يَلْبَثُونَ﴾ (And then they would not remain). In the codex of Ubayy it reads ﴿وَإِذًا لَا يَلْبَثُوا﴾ (wa-idhan la yalbathu'a).

As for ilgha', it is because what follows the waw can only occur after a statement to which it is coordinated. According to Sibawayh, the one that governs the verb is idhan, owing to its resemblance to an (that). According to al-Khalil, an is implied after idhan. [In manuscript C: idhan.]

Al-Farra' claimed that idhan is written with an alif and that it takes tanwin (nunation). Al-Nahhas said: I heard Ali ibn Sulayman say: I heard Abu al-Abbas Muhammad ibn Yazid say: "I would like to cauterize the hand of whoever writes idhan with an alif. It is like lan and in, and nunation does not enter particles."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verses 44–53 (part 1 of 3):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book?﴾ up to His saying, may He be exalted: (Among them are those who believed in it, and among them are those who turned away from it), the verse [[In J, T.]]. It was revealed concerning the Jews of Madinah and those around it. Ibn Ishaq said: Rifa'ah ibn Zayd ibn al-Tabut was one of the great men of the Jews. When he spoke to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he twisted his tongue and said: "Give us your hearing, O Muhammad, until we make you understand." Then he attacked Islam and found fault with it. So Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed: (Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book?) up to His saying: (little). The meaning of (yashtaruna) is "they exchange," and it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal). In the sentence there is an omission, its estimate being "they buy error in exchange for guidance," as He, may He be exalted, said: (Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance). This was said by al-Qutabi and others.

(And they wish that you would stray from the way) is coordinated with it, and the meaning is that you would stray from the path of truth. al-Hasan recited (tudallu) with a fatha on the dad, meaning "led astray from the way."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And Allah is most knowing of your enemies﴾ means: He knows them about you, so do not take them as companions, for they are your enemies. It is also permissible for (a'lam) to carry the meaning of (alim, knowing), as in His saying, may He be exalted: (And it is easier for Him), meaning "easy."

(And sufficient is Allah as protector) — the ba' is superfluous, added because the meaning is "rely on Allah, and He will suffice you against your enemies." (Waliyyan) and (nasiran) are in the accusative as explanation (bayan), and if you wish, as circumstantial clauses (hal).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Among those who are Jews﴾. al-Zajjaj said: If (min) is connected to what precedes it, then one does not stop at His saying (nasiran). If it is made a new beginning (munqati'ah), then a pause on (nasiran) is permissible, and the estimate is: "Among those who are Jews are a people who distort the words," and then it was omitted. This is the view of Sibawayh, and the grammarians cited:

"If I were to say, there is no one among her people
who surpasses her in lineage and in smile..." [[Tayathim (with a kasra on the ta'): a dialect of some Arabs, for they put a kasra on the prefixed letter in forms like ta'allam and ta'lam; when they put a kasra on the ta', the hamza changed into a ya'. The mim (on the pattern of al-majlis): the teeth at the front of the mouth.]]

They said: the meaning is, "If I were to say there is no one among her people who surpasses her," and then it was omitted. al-Farra' said the omitted word is (man), so the meaning is: "Among those who are Jews are those who distort." This is like His saying, may He be exalted: (And there is none of us but has a known station), meaning "there is none of us who has..." Dhu al-Rummah said:

"They remained, and among them is one whose tears are flowing for her,
