Do you not see what was narrated in the report: "The two eyes commit fornication, and the two hands commit fornication." When there is some fulfilment of desire in looking and touching, intercourse decreases; but the pious one does not look or touch, so desire gathers within him and he has more intercourse. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: every desire hardens the heart except intercourse, for it purifies the heart; and for this reason the prophets used to do it.

The meaning: so among the family of Ibrahim is one who believed in him, and among them is one who turned away from him. It was also said: it refers to the Book. And God knows best.

I translate the passage, keeping the system's conventions for Qur'anic quotations, names, and technical terms.

There are four issues in this passage. The first is the words of God, the Exalted: ﴿Or do they envy the people?﴾ meaning the Jews.

(the people) means the Prophet (ﷺ) specifically, according to Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and others. They envied him for prophethood, and his companions for their faith in him. Qatadah said: "the people" means the Arabs; the Jews envied them for prophethood. Al-Dahhak said: the Jews envied Quraysh, because prophethood was among them. Envy (ḥasad) is blameworthy, and its possessor is distressed; it consumes good deeds as fire consumes firewood. This was related by Anas from the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Hasan said: "I have not seen a wrongdoer more like one wronged than the envious: a constant breath, a lasting grief, and a tear that never runs dry." Abdullah ibn Masʿud said: "Do not be hostile to the blessings of God." It was said to him: "And who is hostile to the blessings of God?" He said: "Those who envy people for what God has given them of His bounty." God, the Exalted, says in some of the books: "The envious one is an enemy of My blessing, resentful of My decree, dissatisfied with My portion."

And for Mansur al-Faqih:

Say to whoever has become envious of me:
do you know whom you have wronged in manners?

You have wronged God in His judgment
when you are not content with what He has granted me.

It is said: envy was the first sin disobeyed God in the heavens, and the first sin disobeyed in the earth. In the heavens it was Iblis's envy of Adam; in the earth it was Qabil's envy of Habil. And for Abu al-ʿAtahiya concerning people:

O Lord, people do not deal justly with me,
and how could they, if I dealt justly with them, they would wrong me?

If I have anything, they rush to take it,
and if I want to seek what they have, they deny me.

If my generosity reaches them, there is no gratitude from them,
and if I do not give to them, they revile me.

If a calamity befalls me, they rejoice in it,
and if a blessing accompanies me, they envy me.

I will restrain my heart from yearning for them,
and I will veil from them my gaze and my eyelids.

It is said: if you wish to be safe from the envious, then distress him with your affair. And for a man of Quraysh:

They envied the blessing when it appeared,
so they pelted it with baseless words.

And when God bestows a blessing,
the words of the enemies of blessings do not harm it.

And well said whoever said:

Be patient with the envy of the envious, for your patience will kill them;
fire consumes its own part if it finds nothing else to consume.

Al-Qurtubi, al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran, commentary on surah 4, verses 56–57:

The meaning of ihla' (burning, roasting) has already been explained at the beginning of the surah [[See the second issue, p. 53 of this volume.]]. Humayd ibn Qays recited (nusliyhim) with a fatha on the nun, meaning "We roast them" (nushwiyuhum). It is said: shah masliyyah (a roasted sheep). The accusative of (naran) in this reading is by removal of the preposition, its estimated form being bi-naran (with fire).

(Kullama nadijat julūduhum) It is said: nadija al-shay' nadjan wa-nudjan (the thing became ripe/cooked), and fulan nadijj al-ra'y (a man of mature, firm judgement). The meaning in the verse is: the skins are replaced with other skins. If one of the heretics (zanadiqa) who attack the Qur'an says: how is it right that He punishes a skin that did not disobey? It is said to him: the skin is neither punished nor made to suffer; the pain falls only upon the souls, for they are the ones that feel and perceive, so the replacing of the skins is an increase in the torment of the souls. This is indicated by His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿So that they may taste the punishment﴾ and His saying: (Whenever it dies down, We increase them in blaze [[See vol. 10, p. 333.]]). The purpose, then, is the punishment of the bodies and the pain of the spirits. Had He intended the skins, He would have said: "so that they may taste the punishment" (liyadhuqna al-adhab).

Muqatil said: the fire consumes them every day seven times. Al-Hasan said: seventy thousand times; whenever it consumes them, it is said to them: "Return," and they return as they were. Ibn Umar said: when they are burnt, white skins like sheets of paper are substituted for them. It is also said: by "skins" is meant the garments (sarabil), as He, exalted is He, says: (And you see the criminals that day bound together in fetters; their garments of tar [[See vol. 9, pp. 382, 385.]]). They were called "skins" because they adjoin their skins, by contiguity, as one says of a thing specific to a person: "he is the skin between his eyes." Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, recited:

They blame me concerning Salim, and I blame them... and the skin between the eye and the nose is Salim.

So whenever the garments are burnt, they are restored. The poet said:

Baseness has clothed the Taym tribe in green on their skins, so woe to the Taym because of their green garments.

Here he uses "garments" as a metaphor for "skins." It is also said: the meaning is that We restore the first skin as new, as you say to a goldsmith: "Make me a ring other than this ring," and he breaks it down and fashions for you a ring from it. The ring fashioned is the first, except that the workmanship has changed while the silver is one. This is like the soul when it becomes dust and becomes nothing, then Allah gives it life. It is like your friend whom you knew healthy, and then you see him afterwards sick and wasted, and you say to him, "How are you?" and he says, "I am not the one you knew." He is the same, but his condition has changed. So the saying of the speaker, "I am not the one you knew," and His saying ﴿other than them﴾ are figurative. Its parallel is His saying: (On the day the earth will be changed into a different earth [[See vol. 9, pp. 382, 385.]]), and it is that very earth, except that its hills, mountains, rivers and trees are altered, and its extent is enlarged and levelled, as will be explained in the surah of (Ibrahim [[See vol. 9, pp. 382, 385.]]), peace be upon him. From this meaning is the poet's saying:

The people are no longer the people you knew, nor is the abode the abode that you used to know.

Al-Sha'bi said: A man came to Ibn Abbas and said: "Do you not see what 'A'ishah has done? She has censured her age, reciting the two verses of Labid:

Gone are those among whose flanks one used to live, and I remain among a worthless posterity like the skin of a mangy camel.

They take pleasure in wantonness and abasement, and whoever speaks against them is blamed, even if he does not transgress."

She said: "May Allah have mercy on Labid! How would he be if he saw our time!" Ibn Abbas said: "If 'A'ishah censured her age, then 'Ad censured its age, for a arrow was found in the storehouse of 'Ad a long time after they had perished, as long as the spears of that era, on which was written:

A land in which we once dwelt, and we were its people, when people were people and the land was land."

The land remains as it is, except that its conditions and the conditions of its people have changed and become unrecognisable.

(Inna Allaha kana 'Aziza) i.e., nothing can overpower Him or escape Him.

(Hakima) in His threat to His servants. And His saying, describing the people of Paradise: (And We shall admit them to a shade, deep and ever-extending) means dense, with no sun in it. Al-Hasan said: it is described as "ever-extending" because nothing enters it of the heat, the hot wind and the like that enter the shade of this world. Al-Dahhak said: it means the shade of trees and the shade of their palaces. Al-Kalbi said: (zillan zalilan) means "perpetual."

**Issue one:** The saying of the Exalted: (Indeed, Allah commands you to render the trusts to their owners). This verse is one of the foundational rulings (ummahat al-ahkam), and it encompasses all of the religion and the Law. There is disagreement over who is addressed by it. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Zayd ibn Aslam, Shahr ibn Hawshab and Ibn Zayd said: this is an address specifically to the rulers of the Muslims. It therefore applies to the Prophet (ﷺ) and his commanders, and then extends to those after them. Ibn Jurayj and others said: it is an address specifically to the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning the matter of the key of the Ka'bah, when he took it from 'Uthman ibn Abi Talhah al-Hajabi al-'Abdari, of the Banu 'Abd al-Dar, and from his cousin Shaybah ibn 'Uthman ibn Abi Talhah. Both of them were disbelievers at the time of the Conquest of Mecca. Al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib asked for the key so that the custody of the Ka'bah (al-sidanah) might be combined with the provision of water to the pilgrims (al-siqayah). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered the Ka'bah, broke what was in it of idols, removed the Station of Ibrahim, and Jibril descended upon him with this verse. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came out reciting this verse, and I had not heard it from him before. He summoned 'Uthman and Shaybah and said: "Take it, [a trust] everlasting and enduring, which none will take from you except a wrongdoer." Makki reported that Shaybah wanted not to hand over the key, then he handed it over and said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Take it with the trust of Allah." Ibn 'Abbas said: the verse refers specifically to the rulers, concerning their admonishing women who show rebellion (nushuz) and the like, and returning them to their husbands.

The most evident view regarding the verse is that it is general to all people. It therefore encompasses the rulers in respect of the trusts entrusted to them, such as the division of wealth, the restoration of wrongfully taken property, and justice in judgments. This is the choice of al-Tabari. It also encompasses those beneath them among the people, in the safeguarding of deposits, caution in testimonies, and other matters, such as a man who judges in a particular case or the like. Prayer, zakah and all the acts of worship are the trust of Allah the Exalted. This meaning has been related in a raised (marfu') hadith from Ibn Mas'ud from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Being killed in the way of Allah expiates all sins," or he said: "everything except the trust. The trust is in prayer, the trust is in fasting, the trust is in speech, and the greatest of these is deposits." Abu Nu'aym al-Hafiz mentioned it in al-Hilyah.

Among those who said that the verse is general to all were al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas and Ubayy ibn Ka'b. They said: the trust is in everything: in ablution, prayer, zakah, major ritual impurity (janabah), fasting, measuring and weighing, and deposits. Ibn 'Abbas said: Allah has not permitted the needy or the wealthy to withhold a trust. I say: this is a consensus (ijma'). The scholars agreed that trusts are to be returned to their owners, whether they are righteous or wicked, as Ibn al-Mundhir stated.

The word amanah is a verbal noun used in the sense of the passive participle (maf'ul), and for this reason it is plural. The connection of the verse with what precedes it is that Allah the Exalted informed of the concealment by the People of the Book of the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) and of their saying that the polytheists were better guided in the way. That was a betrayal on their part, so the discourse moved on to the mention of all trusts. Thus the verse, by its wording, includes every trust, and these are many kinds, as we have mentioned. Its foundational rulings are: the deposit (wadi'ah), the found property (luqatah), the pledge (rahn), and the loan of an item (ariyah).

Ubayy ibn Ka'b narrated: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Render the trust to the one who entrusted you, and do not betray the one who betrayed you." Al-Daraqutni reported it. Anas and Abu Hurayrah related it from the Prophet (ﷺ), and its meaning has been mentioned earlier in (al-Baqarah) [[See vol. 3, p. 406 and what follows.]].

Abu Umamah narrated: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say in his sermon during the Farewell Pilgrimage: "The borrowed item must be returned, the gift of milk-animal must be returned, the debt must be paid, and the guarantor is liable." Sahih; al-Tirmidhi and others reported it. Al-Daraqutni added: a man said: "What of the covenant of Allah?" He said: "The covenant of Allah is most deserving of being fulfilled."

Regarding the return of a deposit, and that it is guaranteed (mudmunah) in every case, whether it was something that could be concealed or not, and whether the custodian was negligent or not, those who held this view in accordance with the requirement of this verse and this hadith were 'Ata', al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Ashhab. It is related that Ibn 'Abbas and Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with them both, held the depositary liable for the deposit.

Ibn al-Qasim related from Malik that whoever borrows an animal or other item that cannot be concealed, and it perishes in his possession, is believed concerning its loss and is not liable for it except through negligence (ta'addi). This is the view of al-Hasan al-Basri and al-Nakha'i, and it is the view of the Kufans and al-Awza'i. They said: the meaning of his saying, peace be upon him, "the borrowed item must be returned," is like the meaning of the saying of the Exalted: "Indeed, Allah commands you to render the trusts to their owners." So if a trust perishes, the trustee is not obliged to compensate for it, because he is believed. Likewise a loan, if it perishes without negligence, because he did not take it on the condition of guarantee. But if it perishes through his negligence towards it, he is obliged to pay its value because of his offence against it.

It is related from 'Ali, 'Umar and Ibn Mas'ud that there is no liability for a loan. Al-Daraqutni related from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no liability upon a trustee." Al-Shafi'i, in what he used as evidence, argued from the words of Safwan to the Prophet (ﷺ) when he borrowed the armours from him: "Is it a guaranteed loan or a loan to be returned?" He said: "Rather, a loan to be returned."

**Issue two:** The saying of the Exalted: ﴿And when you judge between people, judge with justice﴾. Al-Dahhak said: "with the evidence upon the claimant and the oath upon the one who denies." This is an address to the rulers, the commanders and the judges. In meaning, all creation is included in it, as we mentioned concerning the rendering of trusts. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, the just ones on the Day of Resurrection will be upon pulpits of light, at the right hand of the Most Merciful, and both His hands are right; they are those who act justly in their judgment, their families and what they are responsible for." And he said: "Each of you is a shepherd and each of you is responsible for his flock. The imam is a shepherd and is responsible for his flock; the man is a shepherd over his household and is responsible for them; the woman is a shepherdess over her husband's house and is responsible for it; the servant is a shepherd over his master's property and is responsible for it. Indeed, each of you is a shepherd and each of you is responsible for his flock." In these authentic hadiths he made all of these shepherds and judges according to their ranks. Likewise the scholar who judges, for when he issues a legal opinion (ifta') he judges, decides and distinguishes between the lawful and the unlawful, the obligatory and the recommended, and the valid and the invalid. All of that is a trust to be rendered and a judgment to be given. The discussion of (ni'imma) has already been presented in (al-Baqarah) [[See vol. 3, p. 332.]].

﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Hearing and Seeing﴾. Allah the Exalted described Himself as Hearing and Seeing, who hears and sees, as He said: ﴿Indeed, I am with you both; I hear and I see﴾ [[See vol. 11, p. 201.]]. This is the way of revelation (sam'). Reason also indicates this, for the negation of hearing and sight implies their opposites, blindness and deafness, since a locus that is receptive to two opposites cannot be free of one of them. He, the Exalted, is sanctified above deficiencies, and it is impossible for perfect acts to proceed from one characterised by deficiencies, such as creating hearing and sight in one who has neither hearing nor sight. The Muslim community (ummah) has agreed on exalting Him above deficiencies. This is also a revealed proof, sufficient together with the explicit text of the Qur'an, in debate with those united by the word of Islam. Exalted is the Lord, blessed and high, above what the imaginers imagine and what the lying fabricators invent: ﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of might, above what they describe﴾ [[See vol. 15, p. 140.]].

There are three issues here.

The first: when the previous verse addressed the rulers, beginning with them, commanding them to render the trusts and to judge between people with justice, this verse addresses the subjects (al-ra'iyyah). It first commands obedience to Allah the Mighty and Majestic, which is compliance with His commands (imtithal amrihi) and avoidance of His prohibitions (ijtinab nawahihi); then obedience to His Messenger concerning what he commanded and forbade; then, thirdly, obedience to the rulers (umara'), according to the view of the majority and of Abu Hurayrah, Ibn 'Abbas and others.

Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah al-Tustari said: "Obey the sultan in seven matters: the minting of dirhams and dinars, the measures and the weights, the judgments, the Hajj, the Friday prayer, the two 'Eids, and jihad." Sahl said: "If the sultan forbids the scholar to issue fatwas, then he is not permitted to issue them; if he does issue them, he is disobedient, even if the ruler is a tyrannical one."

Ibn Khuwayz Mindad said: "As for obedience to the sultan, it is obligatory in what involves obedience to Allah, and it is not obligatory in what involves disobedience to Allah. For this reason we say: the rulers of our time, their obedience is not permitted, nor is assisting them, nor showing them reverence; but fighting with them is obligatory whenever they fight, and so are judgment on their behalf, the appointment to the imamate and to the hisbah (market supervision), and the establishment of these in accordance with the Shari'ah. If they lead us in prayer and they are sinners in respect of their sins, the prayer behind them is valid; but if they are innovators (mubtadi'ah), the prayer behind them is not valid, unless one fears them, in which case one prays with them out of taqiyyah and then repeats the prayer."

I say: It is related from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "It is a right upon the imam to judge with justice and to render the trust. When he does that, it becomes obligatory upon the Muslims to obey him, because Allah the Exalted commanded us to render the trust and justice, and then commanded us to obey him."

Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah and Mujahid said: "Ulu al-amr are the people of the Qur'an and knowledge." This is the choice of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him. Similar is the saying of al-Dahhak, who said: "He means the jurists and the scholars of the religion." It is related from Mujahid that they are the Companions of Muhammad ﷺ specifically. It is related from 'Ikrimah that it refers specifically to Abu Bakr and 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both.

Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah related from al-Hakam ibn Aban that he asked 'Ikrimah about the umm al-walad (slave-mothers), and he said: "They are free." I said: "On what basis?" He said: "On the Qur'an." I said: "What in the Qur'an?" He said: Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you﴾, and 'Umar was among those in authority. He said: "She was freed even by a miscarriage."

This meaning will be explained in detail in Surah al-Hashr, at the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾ [[See vol. 18, p. 10 onward.]].

Ibn Kaysan said: "They are the people of intellect and opinion who manage the affairs of the people."

I say: The most correct of these views are the first and the second. As for the first, because the origin of authority (al-amr) is from them and judgment is referred to them. The two Sahihs relate from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The verse ﴿O you who have believed, obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you﴾ was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Hudhafah ibn Qays ibn 'Adi al-Sahmi, when the Prophet ﷺ sent him in a military expedition." Abu 'Umar said: "'Abd Allah ibn Hudhafah was known for his humor, and among his humor was that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ appointed him over a detachment and commanded them to gather firewood and kindle a fire. When they had kindled it, he commanded them to plunge into it. He said to them: 'Did not the Messenger of Allah ﷺ command you to obey me?' And he said: '(Whoever obeys my commander has obeyed me).' They said: 'We only believed in Allah and followed His Messenger so that we might be saved from the Fire!' So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ approved their act and said: '(There is no obedience to a created being in disobedience to the Creator).'" Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾ [[Previously mentioned on p. 149.]]. This is a hadith of sound chain and well known.

Muhammad ibn 'Amr ibn 'Alqamah related from 'Umar ibn al-Hakam [['Umar ibn al-Hakam ibn Thawban Abu Hafs al-Madani.]] ibn Thawban that Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: "'Abd Allah ibn Hudhafah ibn Qays al-Sahmi was among the companions of Badr, and he had a humor to him." Al-Zubayr mentioned, saying: "'Abd al-Jabbar ibn Sa'id related to me from 'Abd Allah ibn Wahb from al-Layth ibn Sa'd, who said: 'It reached me that he untied the saddle-girth of the Messenger of Allah's ﷺ mount during one of his journeys, so that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ nearly fell.'" Ibn Wahb said: "I said to al-Layth: 'Was it to make him laugh?' He said: 'Yes, he had humor.'"

Maymun ibn Mihran, Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: "Ulu al-amr are the commanders of the detachments."

As for the second view, its correctness is indicated by the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And if you dispute over anything, refer it back to Allah and the Messenger﴾. He commanded that the matter in dispute be referred to the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Prophet ﷺ, and it is not for other than the scholars to know the manner of referring to the Book and the Sunnah. This indicates that asking the scholars is obligatory and that complying with their fatwas is binding.

Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "People will remain in good as long as they honour the sultan and the scholars. When they honour these two, Allah sets right their worldly life and their hereafter; and when they treat these two lightly, He corrupts their worldly life and their hereafter."

As for the third view, it is particular, and more particular than it is the fourth view. As for the fifth, the apparent wording rejects it, although its meaning is correct, for intellect is the foundation of every virtue and the wellspring of every refinement. It is what Allah made the root of the religion and the pillar of the world. Allah made obligation (taklif) binding in its entirety through it, and made the world ordered by His rulings. The person of intellect is nearer to his Lord, the Exalted, than all the mujtahidun without intellect. This meaning was also related from Ibn 'Abbas.

Some people claimed that what is meant by ulu al-amr is 'Ali and the infallible imams. But if that were so, the saying ﴿refer it back to Allah and the Messenger﴾ would have no meaning; rather he would have said: "refer it back to the imam and ulu al-amr," for in their view the saying of the imam is the one that judges over the Book and the Sunnah. This is an abandoned view, opposed to what the majority holds.

The reality of obedience is complying with a command, just as disobedience is its opposite, which is opposing a command. Ta'ah (obedience) is derived from atta'a, meaning to yield, and ma'siyah (disobedience) is derived from 'asa, meaning to become harsh. "Ulu" (the plural) has the singular "dhu" irregularly, like nisa' (women), ibil (camels) and khayl (horses): each is a collective noun with no singular from its own form. It has been said of the singular of khayl: "khail", and this has been discussed previously [[See vol. 4, p. 22.]].

The second issue: the saying of the Exalted ﴿If you dispute over anything﴾, meaning you argue and differ, as if each one of them is pulling away the other's proof and taking it away. Al-naz' is pulling, and munaza'ah is the pulling of proofs against one another. From this is the hadith: "(Why does the Qur'an contend with me?)" [[In Ibn al-Athir's Nihayah and Lisan al-'Arab: "maali unazi'u al-Qur'an". Yunazi'uni: it pulls me in recitation. That is because some of the followers recited loudly behind him, and it contested his recitation and distracted him, so he forbade him from reciting aloud in prayer behind him.]]. Al-A'sha said:

"They contended over the branches of basil, reclining, and a sharp wine whose strainer is moist"

[Al-khadil is the lush plant, and al-khadilah is the garden. [[The addition is in the (j) edition.]]] ﴿in anything﴾, meaning of the matters of your religion.

﴿Refer it back to Allah and the Messenger﴾, meaning: return that ruling to the Book of Allah or to His Messenger by asking him during his life, or by consulting his Sunnah after his death ﷺ. This is the saying of Mujahid, al-A'mash and Qatadah, and it is the correct one. Whoever does not hold this has a defect in his faith, because of the saying of the Exalted: ﴿if you believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾. It has also been said: the meaning is "say: Allah and His Messenger know best," and this is the referring back. This is like the saying of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him: "Returning to the truth is better than persisting in falsehood." The first view is the more correct, because of the saying of 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: "We have nothing except what is in the Book of Allah and what is in this sheet, or an understanding given to a Muslim man." Had it been as this speaker said, the ijtihad with which this community was singled out and the deduction (istinbat) given to it would be void. Rather, examples are struck and the parallel is sought until the correct answer emerges. Abu al-'Aliyah said: "That is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Had they referred it to the Messenger and to those in authority among them, those who deduce it from them would have known it﴾."

Yes, whatever Allah has kept to His own knowledge and has not disclosed to any of His creatures, that is what is said of: "Allah knows best." 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, deduced the minimum period of pregnancy—six months—from the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And his carrying and his weaning are thirty months﴾ [[See vol. 16, p. 192.]] together with the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And mothers suckle their children for two complete years﴾ [[See vol. 3, p. 160.]]. When we subtract the two years from thirty months, six months remain. Many similar examples exist.

In the saying of the Exalted ﴿and to the Messenger﴾ there is evidence that his Sunnah ﷺ is to be acted upon and what it contains is to be complied with. The Prophet ﷺ said: "What I have forbidden you, avoid; and what I have commanded you, do of it as much as you are able. For those before you were destroyed only by the multitude of their questions and their disputing with their prophets." Related by Muslim.

Abu Dawud related from Abu Rafi', from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Let me not find any one of you reclining on his couch, to whom an order from my commands arrives, of what I have commanded or forbidden, and he says: 'We do not know; whatever we find in the Book of Allah, we follow.'" And from al-'Irbad ibn Sariyah, that he was present when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was addressing the people, and he was saying: "Does any one of you think, reclining on his couch, that Allah has forbidden nothing except what is in this Qur'an? Behold, by Allah, I have commanded, admonished and forbidden things which are indeed like the Qur'an or more." [[Saying: "reclining on his couch": sitting on his adorned bed. This is an explanation of his foolishness and bad manners, as is the custom of the pampered and deluded people of wealth. Al-Khattabi said: he meant the people of luxury and ease who stayed in their houses and did not seek hadith from its people by travelling, so that he rejects it where it does not match his desire (from Ibn Majah).]] Al-Tirmidhi related it from the hadith of al-Miqdam ibn Ma'dikarib with a similar meaning, and said: "A good, gharib hadith."

The decisive matter is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿So let those who oppose his command beware lest a trial afflict them﴾ [[See vol. 12, p. 322.]], and the verse continues. It will come.

The third issue: the saying of the Exalted ﴿That is better﴾, meaning your referring what you differ about to the Book and the Sunnah is better than dispute.

﴿And better in result (ta'wil)﴾, meaning in outcome (marji'an), from "aala ila kadha", meaning "became". It has also been said: from "ultu al-shay'" when I gathered and set it right. So ta'wil is the gathering of the meanings of words that are problematic under a word that is not problematic; it is said: "awwala Allahu 'alayka amrak", meaning He gathered it for you. It is also possible that the meaning is "and better than your interpretation (ta'wilukum)."

Yazid ibn Zurayʿ narrated from Dawud ibn Abi Hind, from al-Shaʿbi, who said: There was a dispute between a man from the hypocrites (al-munafiqin) and a man from the Jews. The Jew invited the hypocrite to the Prophet ﷺ, because he knew that he would not accept a bribe. The hypocrite invited the Jew to their judges, because he knew that they took bribes in their rulings. When they disagreed, they agreed to have a soothsayer (kahin) in Juhayna judge between them. So Allah the Exalted revealed concerning that: ﴿Have you not seen those who claim that they believe in what has been revealed to you﴾, meaning the hypocrite, ﴿and in what was revealed before you﴾, meaning the Jew, ﴿they desire to seek judgement before the tyrant (al-taghut)﴾, down to His words: ﴿and submit in full submission﴾.

Qatada and al-Dahhak said: The Jew invited the hypocrite to the Prophet ﷺ, and the hypocrite invited him to Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf, who is "the tyrant" (al-taghut).

Abu Salih narrated it from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: There was a dispute between a man from the hypocrites, called Bishr, and a Jew. The Jew said: "Come with us to Muhammad." The hypocrite said: "No, to Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf," who is the one Allah named "the tyrant" (al-taghut), meaning the possessor of tyranny. The Jew refused to take his case to anyone except the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. When the hypocrite saw that, he went with him to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he ruled in favour of the Jew.

When the two of them left, the hypocrite said: "I am not satisfied. Come with us to Abu Bakr." So the Jew went with him to Abu Bakr, and he ruled in favour of the Jew, but the hypocrite was not satisfied. This was mentioned by al-Zajjaj. The hypocrite then said: "Come with us to Umar." So they both came to Umar, and the Jew said: "We went to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, then to Abu Bakr, but he was not satisfied." Umar said to the hypocrite: "Is that so?" He said: "Yes." Umar said: "Wait for me until I come out to you both." He went inside, took his sword, then struck the hypocrite with it until he was dead (barada) and said: "This is how I judge against the one who is not satisfied with the judgement of Allah and the judgement of His Messenger." The Jew fled. The verse was revealed, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "You are al-Faruq." Jibril descended and said: "Indeed Umar has distinguished between truth and falsehood, so he was named al-Faruq." Concerning this, all the verses were revealed down to His words: ﴿and submit in full submission﴾.

The word ﴿going far astray﴾ (ḍalalan) is in the accusative on the basis of meaning, that is, "so they will go far astray (with a far straying)." Its like is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah has caused you to grow from the earth as a growth﴾ (nabatan). [[See vol. 18, p. 305.]] This meaning has already been discussed fully. [[See vol. 4, p. 69.]] As for ﴿turning away (sududan)﴾, it is a noun of the verbal noun (ism lil-masdar) according to al-Khalil, and the verbal noun is al-sadd. The Kufans say that both are verbal nouns (masdar).

﴿So how will it be when a disaster strikes them because of what their own hands have sent ahead?﴾ (4:62). That is, how will their condition be, or how will they act, when a disaster befalls them, namely being abandoned by you, and the humiliation that will reach them, as in His saying: ﴿Say, "You will never go out with me, and you will never fight with me against an enemy"﴾ (9:83) [See vol. 8, p. 217]. It has also been said: he means the killing of their companion, ﴿because of what their own hands have sent ahead﴾, and the sentence is complete. Then He begins to report their action: when Umar killed their companion, his people came seeking his blood-money (diyah, the compensation paid for a killing), and they swore, "We want nothing by demanding his blood-money except goodness and agreement with the truth." It has also been said: the meaning is, "We did not desire, by turning away from you in the litigation, anything except reconciling between the disputants and kindness in bringing the ruling closer." Ibn Kaysan said: "Justice and truth." A parallel to it is His saying: ﴿And they will surely swear, "We desired nothing but the best"﴾ (9:107) [See vol. 8, p. 252 and what follows]. Then God, exalted is He, says, denying them: ﴿Those are the ones whose hearts God knows what is in them﴾ (4:63). Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is that God has known that they are hypocrites. The benefit for us is: know that they are hypocrites.

﴿So turn away from them﴾ (4:63). It has been said: from punishing them. It has also been said: from accepting their excuses. ﴿Admonish them﴾, that is, frighten them. It has been said: in public.

﴿And speak to them in their souls a far-reaching word﴾ (4:63), that is, rebuke them with the most eloquent rebuke, in private and in seclusion. Al-Hasan said: "Say to them: if you reveal what is in your hearts, I will kill you." Speech has reached eloquence, and a man is eloquent (baligh) when he conveys with his tongue the full reality of what is in his heart. The Arabs say: "A fool who is complete in folly" (ahmaq balgh and bilgh), meaning he is at the extreme of foolishness. It has also been said: the meaning is that he attains what he wants even if he is a fool.

It is said that the saying of God, exalted is He, ﴿So how will it be when a disaster strikes them because of what their own hands have sent ahead﴾ (4:62), was revealed concerning those who built the mosque of harm (Masjid al-Dirar) [This is a mosque at Quba, a village two miles from Madinah on the left of one heading to Makkah; common people used to volunteer to demolish this mosque. (Mu'jam al-Buldan).] When God exposed their hypocrisy and commanded them to demolish the mosque, they swore to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in defense of themselves: "We did not intend by building the mosque anything except obedience to God and agreement with the Book."

The Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verse 64:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We did not send any messenger﴾ — (min) is extra (zā'idah), for emphasis (lil-tawkīd).

(Except to be obeyed) in what He commanded and forbade.

(By the leave of Allah) — by the knowledge of Allah. It is also said: by the enabling (tawfīq) of Allah.

(And if, when they had wronged themselves, they had come to you) — Abu Sadiq [[al-Azdi al-Kufi, who narrated from Ali (mursal).]] related from Ali, who said: A Bedouin arrived among us three days after we had buried the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He threw himself upon the grave of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and scattered some of its dust over his head, and said: "You spoke, O Messenger of Allah, and we heard your words; you received from Allah and we received from you. What Allah revealed to you included: ﴿And if, when they had wronged themselves, they had come to you﴾ — the verse. I have wronged myself, and I have come to you that you might ask forgiveness for me." Then he was called from the grave: "Indeed, you have been forgiven."

And the meaning of ﴿they would have found Allah Accepting of repentance, Merciful﴾ is: Accepting of their repentance. Both of them (tawwāban and raḥīman) are objects (mafʿūlān) and nothing else.

**Fifth issue**... Actually, here is the translation of the passage in order.

There are five issues in it.

**The first issue:** Mujahid and others said: the intended meaning of this verse is those previously mentioned, from among those who wanted to seek judgment from the *taghut* (false judges or idols; a term glossed as "anything worshipped or obeyed besides God"), and it was revealed concerning them. Al-Tabari said: His saying *fa-la* ("but no") is a rejection of what was mentioned before. Its implied meaning is: "The matter is not as they claim, that they believe in what was revealed to you." Then He began an oath with His saying: ﴿By your Lord, they will not believe﴾. Others said: He placed *la* ("no") before the oath only to give emphasis to the negation and to show its strength. Then He repeated it after the oath to confirm the emphasis on the negation. The second *la* could have been dropped, and most of the emphasis would have remained with the first one placed in front. The first *la* could also have been dropped, and the meaning of negation would remain, but the meaning of emphasis would be lost.

*Shajara* means he disagreed and became confused. From it comes *al-shajar* (trees), because of the variety of their branches. The poles of a litter (*hawdaj*) are called *shijar*, because some of them are interlaced with others. The poet said:

"My soul be your ransom, while the spears are interlaced,
and the people are crowded, standing for the encounter."

Tarafa said:

"They are the judges, the lords of guidance,
and the mediators among the people in the disputed matter."

A group said: It was revealed concerning al-Zubayr and a man from the Ansar. The dispute was about irrigating a garden. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said to al-Zubayr: "Irrigate your land, then release the water to your neighbour's land." The opponent said: "You are favouring your cousin (son of your paternal aunt)." The face of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) changed color, and he said to al-Zubayr: "Irrigate, then hold back the water until it reaches the *jadr*." (*Jadr*: that which is raised around the field like a wall.) And the verse was revealed: ﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not believe﴾. The hadith is authentic and sound. Al-Bukhari narrated it from ʿAli ibn ʿAbd Allah, from Muhammad ibn Jaʿfar, from Maʿmar, and Muslim narrated it from Qutayba; both of them from al-Zuhri.

The people of this view differed about the Ansari man. Some of them said: He was a man from the Ansar from the people of Badr. Makki and al-Nahhas said: He was Hatib ibn Abi Balta'a. Al-Tha'labi, al-Wahidi and al-Mahdawi said: He was Hatib. It was also said: Tha'laba ibn Hatib. And it was said other than this. The correct view is the first, because he is not specified or named. Likewise, in al-Bukhari and Muslim, he is described only as a man from the Ansar.

Al-Tabari preferred that the revelation of the verse concerned the hypocrite and the Jew, as Mujahid said, and then its general wording includes the story of al-Zubayr. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: This is the correct view. Whoever accuses the Messenger of God (ﷺ) of injustice in a judgment is a disbeliever. But the Ansari slipped in a slip, so the Prophet (ﷺ) turned away from him and overlooked his error, because he knew the soundness of his faith, and that it was a momentary lapse, and it is not permissible for anyone after the Prophet (ﷺ). Everyone who does not accept the ruling of the judge and criticizes it and rejects it, that is apostasy (*ridda*), and he should be asked to repent. [Ibn al-ʿArabi's wording: Everyone who does not accept the ruling of the judge after him is a disobedient sinner.] As for one who criticizes the judge himself and not the ruling, the judge may discipline him (*taʿzir*, discretionary punishment), and he may pardon him. The explanation of this will come, God willing, at the end of Surah al-Aʿraf. [See vol. 7, p. 344 and following.]

**The second issue:** If the cause of the revelation of this verse is what we have mentioned from the hadith, then its jurisprudential lesson is that he (peace be upon him) took the path of reconciliation with al-Zubayr and his opponent. He said: "Irrigate, O Zubayr," because of his nearness to the water, "then release the water to your neighbour," meaning: be lenient regarding your right, do not claim it in full, and hasten to release the water to your neighbour. So he urged him to forbearance and ease. When the Ansari heard this, he was not pleased and became angry, because he wanted not to hold back the water at all. At that moment he uttered the unjust, destructive and disastrous word: *An kāna ibna ʿammatika?* ("Because he is your cousin?"), with the *alif* of *an* lengthened, in the form of denial, meaning: "Do you judge in his favour against me because he is your relative?" At that, the face of the Prophet (ﷺ) changed color in anger at him, and he ruled for al-Zubayr to take his right in full without any leniency toward him.

Based on this, it is said: How did he judge while angry, when he said: "A judge should not judge while angry"? We say: Because he is protected from error in conveying and in rulings, by the evidence of reason that proves his truthfulness in what he conveys from God, so he is not like other judges. In this hadith is guidance for a judge toward reconciling between disputants even when the right is clear. Malik prohibited it, and the view of al-Shafiʿi on it varied. This hadith is clear evidence for permissibility. If they reconcile, well and good; otherwise he shall take the right of the rightful party in full and the judgment stands.

**The third issue:** The followers of Malik differed about the manner of releasing water from the upper land to the lower land. Ibn Habib said: The owner of the upper land shall let all the water into his plot and irrigate with it, until the water reaches from the floor of the plot up to the ankles of one standing in it. Then he shall close the entrance of the water and divert whatever exceeds the level of the ankles to the one next to him, and he shall do the same with that, until the flood reaches the furthest plots. Thus Mutarrif and Ibn al-Majishun explained it to me, and Ibn Wahb said it. Ibn al-Qasim said: When the water in the plot reaches the level of the ankles, he shall release all of it to the one below him and shall not hold back any of it in his plot. Ibn Habib said: The view of Mutarrif and Ibn al-Majishun is more beloved to me, and they know best about this, because Medina is their home, and the case took place there, and the practice followed there.

**The fourth issue:** Malik narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Bakr that it reached him that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said concerning the torrents of Mahzur and Muthaynib (two valleys in Medina that flow with rainwater only): "He holds it back until the ankles, then releases the upper onto the lower." Abu ʿUmar said: I do not know of this hadith being connected to the Prophet (ﷺ) through any channel. The best of its chains is what Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated from Abu Malik ibn Thaʿlaba, from his father, that the Prophet (ﷺ) [the people of Mahzur came to him and he ruled that when the water reaches the ankles, the upper one shall not hold it back]. And ʿAbd al-Razzaq mentioned, from Abu Hazim al-Qurtubi, from his father, from his grandfather, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) [the addition is from the book *al-Tamhid* by Abu ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-Barr] that he ruled concerning the torrent of Mahzur that it should be held back at every plot until it reaches the ankles, and then released. The other torrents are the same.

Abu Bakr al-Bazzar was asked about the hadith of this chapter, and he said: I do not know of any hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ) in this regard that is established. Abu ʿUmar said: On this meaning, even if not in this wording, there is an established hadith whose authenticity is agreed upon. Ibn Wahb narrated it from al-Layth ibn Saʿd and Yunus ibn Yazid, both from Ibn Shihab, that ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr told him that ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr told him, from al-Zubayr, that he disputed with a man from the Ansar who had witnessed Badr with the Messenger of God (ﷺ), concerning the water channels (*shirāj*) of the *Harra* (the channels of water in the *harra*, a land of black stones), by which both of them irrigated palm trees. The Ansari said: "Release the water." He refused, so they both took their dispute to the Prophet (ﷺ). [He mentioned the hadith.]

Abu ʿUmar said: His saying in this hadith, "He releases," and in the other hadith, "When the water reaches the ankles, the upper one shall not hold it back," supports the view of Ibn al-Qasim. From the standpoint of reasoning: if the upper one released only what exceeds the ankles, the water would not be cut off in a short time, and it would not reach where it reaches when he releases the whole. In releasing all of it, after the upper one has taken what reached the ankles, there is a more general benefit and greater good in what people have been made partners in. So the view of Ibn al-Qasim is preferable in every case. This applies when the origin of the land is not a property belonging to the lower one exclusively. But what is acquired by work, or by valid ownership, or by ancient entitlement and established ownership, then each has his right according to what is in his possession and according to the basis of his case. And success is from God.

**The fifth issue:** God's saying: ﴿then they will not find in themselves any discomfort (*haraj*) from what you have decided﴾: that is, constriction and doubt. From this is said of thick intertwined trees: *haraj* and *harajah*, whose plural is *hirāj*. Al-Dahhak said: That is, sin, through their denial of what you have decided.

﴿And submit in full submission (*taslīman*)﴾: that is, they should yield to your command in judgment. Al-Zajjaj said: *Taslīman* is an emphatic verbal noun. When you say, "I struck a strike," it is as if you said, "I have no doubt about it." Likewise, ﴿and submit in full submission﴾, meaning: and submit to your ruling with a submission in which they introduce no doubt into themselves.

The reason for its revelation is what is reported: Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas boasted, and a Jew said to him: "By God, it was prescribed for us to kill ourselves, so we killed ourselves, and the number of those killed reached seventy thousand." Thabit said: "By God, if God had prescribed for us to kill ourselves, we would have done it."

Abu Ishaq al-Sabi'i said: When the verse ﴿And had We prescribed for them, "Kill yourselves" or "Leave your homes," few of them would have done it﴾ was revealed, a man said: "If we had been commanded, we would have done it, and praise be to God who has spared us." This reached the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he said: "Among my community are men whose faith is firmer in their hearts than the towering mountains."

Ibn Wahb said: Malik said: The one who said that was Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may God be pleased with him). Makki likewise mentioned that it was Abu Bakr. Al-Naqqash mentioned that it was Umar ibn al-Khattab (may God be pleased with him). It is also reported from Abu Bakr (may God be pleased with him) that he said: "If that had been prescribed for us, I would have begun with myself and the people of my household."

Abu al-Layth al-Samarqandi mentioned that the speaker among them was Ammar ibn Yasir, Ibn Mas'ud, and Thabit ibn Qays, who said: "If God had commanded us to kill ourselves or to leave our homes, we would have done it." Then the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Faith is firmer in the hearts of men than the towering mountains."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verse 69–70:

There are three issues in this.

The first: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger﴾. When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the matter which, if the hypocrites had done it when they were admonished with it and turned back to it, would have bestowed favour upon them, He mentioned after that the reward of whoever does it. This verse is an explanation of His saying, exalted is He: (Guide us to the straight path, the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour) [See vol. 1, p. 146.], and it is the meaning intended in his saying, peace be upon him, at his death: (O Allah, the Highest Companion) [al-Rafiq al-A'la]. In al-Bukhari, from A'ishah, she said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: (No prophet falls ill except that he is given the choice between this world and the Hereafter). During his illness in which he died, he was seized by a severe hoarseness [al-buhhah (with a dammah): thickness and roughness in the voice.], and I heard him say: (With those whom Allah has favoured from among the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous). So I knew that he had been given the choice.

A group said: this verse was revealed when Abdullah ibn Zayd ibn Abd Rabbih al-Ansari, the one who was shown the adhan, said: O Messenger of Allah, when you die and we die, you will be in 'Illiyyin, and we will not see you or gather with you, and he mentioned his grief over that, so this verse was revealed. Makki mentioned from this Abdullah that when the Prophet ﷺ died, he said: O Allah, blind me so that I see nothing after him, and he became blind on the spot [من ج]. Al-Qushayri related it and said: O Allah, blind me so that I see nothing after my beloved until I meet my beloved, and he became blind on the spot. Al-Tha'labi related that it was revealed concerning Thawban, the freedman of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who had a strong love for him and little patience in being apart from him. One day he came to him, his complexion had changed and his body had wasted, and sorrow could be recognised in his face. He said to him: (O Thawban, what has changed your colour?) He said: O Messenger of Allah, I have no harm or pain, except that when I do not see you I long for you and feel a severe loneliness until I meet you. Then I remember the Hereafter and I fear that I will not see you there, because I know that you will be raised with the prophets, and if I enter Paradise I will be in a station lower than your station, and if I do not enter, then that is when I will never see you. So Allah, exalted is He, revealed this verse. Al-Wahidi related it from al-Kalbi.

And he narrated with a chain from Masruq, who said: the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: It is not right for us to part from you in this world, for when you part from us you will be raised above us. So Allah, exalted is He, revealed: (And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger, those are with those upon whom Allah has bestowed favour, of the prophets). Obedience to Allah includes obedience to His Messenger, but He mentioned him to honour his rank and to make his name prominent, ﷺ and upon his family.

(Those are with those upon whom Allah has bestowed favour): that is, they are with them in one abode and one bliss, enjoying their company and their presence, not that they are equal to them in rank, for they differ in rank, but they visit one another, following them in this world and emulating them. Each of them has been granted contentment with his own state, and the belief that he is inferior has departed from him. Allah, exalted is He, said: (And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts) [See vol. 7, p. 208 and vol. 10, p. 33.]. As for al-siddiq, it is on the pattern fi'il, meaning one who is exceedingly truthful or exceedingly affirming of the truth, and the siddiq is the one who realises by his deed what he says with his tongue. It is said: they are the excellent followers of the prophets who precede them in affirming, like Abu Bakr al-Siddiq. The derivation of al-siddiq and the meaning of al-shahid have already been mentioned in al-Baqarah [See vol. 1, p. 233, vol. 2, p. 173, and vol. 4, p. 268.]. The intended meaning of the martyrs here is Umar, Uthman and Ali, and the righteous are the rest of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all. It is said: al-shuhada' are those slain in the way of Allah.

(Al-salihin): the righteous of the Ummah of Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. I say: the wording encompasses every righteous person and every martyr, and Allah knows best. Al-rifq is gentleness of disposition. A companion is called rafiq because you derive benefit (irtifaq) from his companionship, and from this comes al-rufqah (a travelling company), for some of them benefit from others. It is permissible to read (wa hasuna ula'ika rufaqa'). Al-Akhfash said: (rafiqan) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state and has the meaning of rufaqa'; and he said: it is in the accusative as a specification, so it is singular for that reason, as if the meaning were: each one of them was a good companion. As Allah, exalted is He, said: (Then We bring you forth as a child) [See vol. 12, p. 11.], meaning We bring forth each one of you as a child. And He, exalted is He, said: (They look with a furtive glance) [and yunzar (they look) means: it faces; the Arabs say: the house of so-and-so faces the house of so-and-so, i.e., it is opposite it and in front of it. See vol. 16, p. 45.]. The meaning of this verse is his saying, peace be upon him: (The best companions are four). Allah, exalted is He, did not mention here except four, so reflect upon it.

The second: In the verse there is evidence for the caliphate of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him. That is because when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the ranks of His friends in His Book, He began with the highest of them, who are the prophets, then followed them with the siddiqin, and did not place any intermediary between them. The Muslims agreed on calling Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, "al-Siddiq," just as they agreed on calling Muhammad, peace be upon him, "Messenger." When this is established and it is confirmed that he is the Siddiq, and that he is the second of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, it is not permissible for anyone to precede him after him. And Allah knows best.

The third: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿That is the bounty from Allah﴾. Allah, exalted is He, informed that they did not attain the rank [al-daraja (from ج و ط و ز: that is, the rank which is companionship with the goodly ones, etc., as evidenced by His saying: "they attained them"). In ان ح و و: "they did not attain the bounty." This is not correct.] by their obedience, but rather they attained it by the bounty and generosity of Allah, exalted is He, contrary to what the Mu'tazilah said: a servant attains that only by his own action. So when Allah, exalted is He, favoured His friends with what He gave them of His bounty, and it is not permissible for anyone to praise himself for what he did not do, this indicates the falsity of their view. And Allah knows best.

(Al-salihin): the righteous of the Ummah of Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. I say: the wording encompasses every righteous person and every martyr, and Allah knows best. Al-rifq is gentleness of disposition. A companion is called rafiq because you derive benefit (irtifaq) from his companionship, and from this comes al-rufqah (a travelling company), for some of them benefit from others. It is permissible to read (wa hasuna ula'ika rufaqa'). Al-Akhfash said: (rafiqan) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state and has the meaning of rufaqa'; and he said: it is in the accusative as a specification, so it is singular for that reason, as if the meaning were: each one of them was a good companion. As Allah, exalted is He, said: (Then We bring you forth as a child) [See vol. 12, p. 11.], meaning We bring forth each one of you as a child. And He, exalted is He, said: (They look with a furtive glance) [and yunzar (they look) means: it faces; the Arabs say: the house of so-and-so faces the house of so-and-so, i.e., it is opposite it and in front of it. See vol. 16, p. 45.]. The meaning of this verse is his saying, peace be upon him: (The best companions are four). Allah, exalted is He, did not mention here except four, so reflect upon it.

The second: In the verse there is evidence for the caliphate of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him. That is because when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the ranks of His friends in His Book, He began with the highest of them, who are the prophets, then followed them with the siddiqin, and did not place any intermediary between them. The Muslims agreed on calling Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, "al-Siddiq," just as they agreed on calling Muhammad, peace be upon him, "Messenger." When this is established and it is confirmed that he is the Siddiq, and that he is the second of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, it is not permissible for anyone to precede him after him. And Allah knows best.

The third: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿That is the bounty from Allah﴾. Allah, exalted is He, informed that they did not attain the rank [al-daraja (from ج و ط و ز: that is, the rank which is companionship with the goodly ones, etc., as evidenced by His saying: "they attained them"). In ان ح و و: "they did not attain the bounty." This is not correct.] by their obedience, but rather they attained it by the bounty and generosity of Allah, exalted is He, contrary to what the Mu'tazilah said: a servant attains that only by his own action. So when Allah, exalted is He, favoured His friends with what He gave them of His bounty, and it is not permissible for anyone to praise himself for what he did not do, this indicates the falsity of their view. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verse 71:

There are five issues in this.

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, take your precautions﴾. This is an address to the sincere believers of the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ), and a command to them to wage jihad against the disbelievers, to go out in the way of Allah, and to defend the Shari'ah. The connection of this verse with what precedes it is that when He mentioned obedience to Allah and obedience to His Messenger, He commanded the people of obedience to rise up to revive His religion and raise high His call, and commanded them not to rush upon their enemy in ignorance until they have spied out what is with them and know how to respond to them, for that is more firm for them. So He said: ﴿take your precautions﴾, teaching them to engage in war. This does not contradict trust in Allah (tawakkul); rather it is the very essence of tawakkul, as has passed in (Al 'Imran) [see vol. 4, p. 189] and as will come. "Al-hidh" and "al-hadhar" are two dialectal forms, like "al-mithl" and "al-mathal." Al-Farra' said: most of the usage is "al-hadhar," and "al-hidh" is also heard; one says: "khudh hadharaka," meaning "be cautious." It was also said: "take up weapons as a precaution," because with them comes caution, and caution does not repel the decree.

The second: Unlike the Qadariyyah in their saying that caution repels and prevents the schemes of enemies. Had it not been so, there would be no meaning to commanding them to be cautious. It is said to them: there is no evidence in the verse that caution benefits at all against the decree, but we have been bound to not cast ourselves into destruction with our own hands, and from this is the hadith (Tie it and trust). And if the decree proceeds according to what has been decreed, and Allah does what He wills, then what is meant is tranquility of the soul, not that this benefits against the decree; and likewise taking precaution. The proof of this is that Allah, exalted is He, praised the companions of His Prophet (ﷺ) by His saying: ﴿Say: nothing will afflict us except what Allah has written for us﴾ [see vol. 8, p. 159]. Had something other than what He decreed for them afflicted them, this statement would have had no meaning.

The third: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so go forth in groups﴾. It is said: "nafara yanfiru" (with a kasra on the fa') "nafir," and "nafarat al-dabbah tanfuru" (with a damma on the fa') "nufur," meaning: rise up to fight the enemy. "Istanfara al-imam al-nas" means he called the people to go forth, i.e., to go out to fight the enemy. "Al-nafir" is a name for the people who go forth, and its root is from "al-nifar" and "al-nufur," which is fright, and from it His saying: ﴿they turned on their backs in aversion﴾ [see vol. 10, p. 271], i.e., fleeing. From it: "nafara al-jild," meaning it swelled; and a man picked his teeth with a reed and "nafara famuhu," meaning his mouth swelled. Abu 'Ubayd said: it is only from the "nifar" of one thing from another, which is its withdrawal from it and its distancing from it. Ibn Faris said: "al-nafar" is a group of men from three to ten. "Al-nafir" is also "al-nafar," and likewise "al-nafr" and "al-nufrah," which al-Farra' related with a ta' marbuta. "Yawm al-nafr" is the day when people depart from Mina.

"Thubat" means groups, dispersed. It is said: "thubin," which is pluralized with the sound plural in both feminine and masculine. 'Amr ibn Kulthum said:

"As for the day we feared for them... that our horses become groups (u'sban) of thubin"

[Al-'usb (plural of 'usbah): groups.]

So His saying, exalted is He: ﴿thubat﴾ is a metaphor for the detachments (sarayaa), singular "thubah," which is a band of people. Originally it was "al-thubyah." And "thabbaytu al-jaysh" means I made them into thubah thubah (in groups). "Al-thubah" is the middle of the pool to which water returns, i.e., comes back. Al-Nahhas said: the weak in Arabic sometimes imagines that they are one and the same, and that one is derived from the other, but there is a difference between them: the "thubah" of a pool, its diminutive is "thuwaybah," because it derives from "thaba yathuubu." And "thubah" meaning a group is said to be "thibah" [from al-Nahhas]. Others said: the "thubah" of the pool is of a hollow with the waw elided, and it is the root of the verb, while the "thubah" meaning group is defective in its final radical, from "thaba yathbu," like "khala yakhlu." It is possible that "thubah" in the sense of group is from "thubat al-hawd," because when water returns it gathers; accordingly, the diminutive of the group would be "thuwaybiyah," and one of the two yas merges into the other. It has also been said that "thubat al-jama'ah" is derived from "thabaytu 'ala al-rajul," when I praise a man during his lifetime and gather the good points of his mention, so it returns to gathering.

The fourth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿or go forth all together﴾. Its meaning is the massed army with the Messenger (ﷺ), as said by Ibn 'Abbas and others. And the detachments (sarayaa) are not sent out except by permission of the leader, so that it may serve as a spy for them and a support from behind them, and they may sometimes need it to repel an attack. The ruling on detachments and their spoils, and the rulings on armies and the obligation of mobilization, will come in (al-Anfal) [see vol. 7, p. 380 and p. 40 onward of vol. 8] and (Bara'ah) [see vol. 8, p. 140 onward, p. 266 onward, and p. 293 onward], if Allah, exalted is He, wills.

The fifth: Ibn Khuwayz Mandad mentioned: it has been said that this verse is abrogated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿go forth, light and heavy﴾, and by His saying: ﴿unless you go forth, He will punish you﴾. And that ﴿go forth, light and heavy﴾ being abrogated by His saying: ﴿so go forth in groups or go forth all together﴾ and by His saying: ﴿And it is not for the believers to go forth all together﴾ is more apt, because the obligation of jihad is established as a collective duty (fard kifayah); so whenever some of the Muslims guard the frontiers, the obligation is dropped from the rest. But the correct view is that both verses are muhkam (non-abrogated), one of them applying at the time when the whole body is needed to be mobilized, and the other when a group suffices without others.

He (the Exalted) said: ﴿And indeed among you is one who will certainly lag behind﴾. He means the hypocrites. Al-tabti'ah and al-ib'a' (both meaning delay or lagging behind) mean ta'akhkhur (holding back). One says, "What has delayed you from us?" and this is intransitive (lazim). It is also permissible to say, "I delayed so-and-so from such-and-such," meaning "I made him late," and this is transitive (muta'addi).

Both meanings are intended in the verse. They would hold back from going out and would also hold others back. The meaning is that among your intimates and your kind [in (j): "your army" (jaysh-kum)], and among those who displayed their faith to you, are such people. In outward appearance the hypocrites are counted among the Muslims, since the rulings for Muslims are applied to them.

The lam in His saying ﴿la-man﴾ is the emphatic lam (lam al-tawkid), and the second is the lam of oath (lam al-qasam). The word ﴿man﴾ is in the accusative position, and its relative clause is ﴿la-yuba''tinna﴾, because it carries the sense of an oath. The predicate is ﴿minkum﴾ ("among you").

Mujahid, al-Nakha'i and al-Kalbi recited ﴿wa-inna minkum la-man la-yubatt'inna﴾ with the letter ta' lightly pronounced (takhfif), and the meaning is the same. It has also been said that the intended meaning of ﴿wa-inna minkum la-man la-yubatt'inna﴾ is some of the believers, because God addressed them with His words ﴿wa-inna minkum﴾, and God distinguished between the believers and the hypocrites with His words ﴿wa-ma hum minkum﴾ [see vol. 8, p. 164]. This view is rejected by the context of the speech and its apparent meaning. He combined them in the address only in terms of kind and lineage, as we have explained, not in terms of faith. This is the view of the majority, and it is the correct one, God willing, and God knows best. What supports it is His saying ﴿fa-in asabatkum musibah﴾, that is, a killing or a defeat, ﴿qala qad an'amallahu 'alayya﴾, meaning, by remaining behind. This can only come from a hypocrite, especially in that noble era, and it is far-fetched for a believer to say it.

Relevant to this verse is what the Imams narrated from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), as a report about the hypocrites: "The heaviest prayers for them are the 'Isha' prayer and the Fajr prayer. If they knew what is in them, they would come to them even crawling on their hands and knees." The hadith continues. In another narration: "If one of them knew that he would find a fat bone, he would attend it," meaning the 'Isha' prayer. He is saying: if any worldly thing that they could take appeared, and they were certain of it, they would hasten toward it. This is the meaning of His saying ﴿wa-la-in asabakum fadlun min Allah﴾, that is, spoils of war and conquest, ﴿la-yaqulanna﴾, this hypocrite says, as one who regrets and envies, ﴿ya laytani kuntu ma'ahum fa-afwuza fawzan 'azima﴾ ("Would that I had been with them, so that I might achieve a great triumph").

﴿ka-al-lam takun baynakum wa-baynahu mawaddah﴾: the speech here contains inversion (taqdim wa-ta'khir). It has been said that the meaning is: ﴿la-yaqulanna ka-al-lam takun baynakum wa-baynahu mawaddah﴾, that is, as if he had never made a covenant with you regarding jihad. It has also been said that this clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial phrase (hal). Al-Hasan recited ﴿la-yaqulunna﴾ with a damma on the lam, according to the meaning of ﴿man﴾, because the sense of ﴿la-man la-yubatt'inna﴾ does not refer to one specific man. Whoever opened the lam (with fatha) returned to the singular form and made the pronoun singular, following the wording of ﴿man﴾. Ibn Kathir, and Hafs from 'Asim, recited ﴿ka-al-lam takun﴾ with the letter ta' (feminine), following the wording of mawaddah. Whoever recited with ya' (masculine), [Nafi' read it with ya'; this is what is in the originals,] made mawaddah carry the sense of wudd (affection). The hypocrite's saying ﴿ya laytani kuntu ma'ahum﴾ is spoken out of envy, or out of grief over missing the spoils, together with doubt about the reward from God.

﴿fa-afwuza﴾ is the answer to the wish (jawab al-tamanni), and that is why it is in the accusative. Al-Hasan recited ﴿fa-afwuzu﴾ in the nominative, on the basis that he wished for the triumph, so it is as if he said: "Would that I might achieve a great triumph." The accusative is in the sense of a conditional answer, and the meaning is: if I were with them, I would triumph. The accusative here is by implicit ﴿an﴾, because it is taken as a verbal noun (masdar) construction. The intended sense is: "Would that I had been present, and so triumphed."

There are three issues in this verse.

The first concerns His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So let them fight in the way of Allah﴾. The address is to the believers, meaning: let them fight in the way of Allah [the disbelievers [[in j and z.]]] (who sell), i.e. who sell, meaning who give up themselves and their wealth to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, (for the Hereafter), i.e. for the reward of the Hereafter.

The second concerns His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever fights in the way of Allah﴾, which is a conditional (shart). (Then he is killed or conquers) is conjoined to it (ma'tuf 'alayh), and the consequent of the condition is (then We will give him a great reward). The meaning of (is killed) is that he is martyred. (Or conquers) means that he prevails and takes spoils. A group read (whoever fights) and (so let him fight) with the lam of the imperative silent (sukun). Another group read (so let him fight) with the lam of the imperative vowelled with kasra. He, Exalted is He, mentioned the two ultimate outcomes of the fighter's situation and was satisfied with these two outcomes over what lies between them, as Ibn 'Atiyya mentioned.

The third concerns the apparent meaning of the verse [[in j and t: the Qur'an.]], which requires equality between the one who is killed as a martyr and the one who returns as a spoil-taker. In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah has guaranteed for whoever goes out in His way, and nothing brings him out except jihad [[in Muslim: jihadan, iman, tasdiqan. al-Nawawi said: it is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu).]] in My way and faith in Me and belief in My messengers [[in j: My messenger.]], that He is a guarantor over Himself to admit him into Paradise or to return him to the dwelling from which he went out, obtaining whatever reward or spoil he has obtained." And he mentioned the hadith.

In it, also on the authority of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No raiding party that raids in the way of Allah and obtains spoil hastens two-thirds of its reward from the Hereafter, and the remaining third is kept for them. If they do not obtain spoil, their reward is completed for them." So his saying, "obtaining whatever reward or spoil he has obtained," requires that for the mujahid who is martyred there is one of two things: either the reward if he takes no spoil, or the spoil with no reward. This differs from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr. Because of this, some people said: the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr is worthless, since its chain includes Humayd ibn Hani', who is not well known, and they preferred the first hadith over it because of its fame. Others said: there is no contradiction or conflict between them. The (aw) in the hadith of Abu Hurayrah has the meaning of (wa), as the Kufans say, and this is indicated by the narration of Abu Dawud, for he said in it: "from reward and spoil" with the comprehensive conjunction (wa). Some narrators of Muslim also related it with the comprehensive wa. Humayd ibn Hani' is Egyptian; he heard Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Hubuli and 'Amr ibn Malik, and Haywah ibn Shurayh and Ibn Wahb related from him. So the first hadith is to be understood as referring to mere intention and sincerity in jihad, and that is what Allah guaranteed for him: either martyrdom, or returning him to his family rewarded and having taken spoil. The second is to be understood as referring to one who intended jihad but also sought the spoil; when his intention was divided, his reward was diminished. The Sunnah has shown that the spoil-taker also has a reward, as the Book has shown, so there is no contradiction. It was then said: the reduction in the reward of the spoil-taker compared with the one who takes no spoil is only because of the worldly goods Allah has granted him, which he enjoys, and which removes from him the hardship of his life; whereas the one who fails and obtains nothing remains in the hardship of his life and in patience over his condition, so his reward remains complete, unlike the first. Similar to this is his saying in the other hadith: "Among us is one who died without eating anything of his reward, among them Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr; and among us is one whose fruit has ripened for him, so he picks it [[Hadaba the date: he picked it, and ihtadaba: he gathered it. Apparently "among them Mus'ab" etc. is from the narrator, as in Usd al-Ghaba.]]."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verse 75:

There are three issues here.

The first: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you fight not in the cause of Allah﴾. It is an exhortation to jihad (striving, here specifically armed struggle in the way of God). It includes rescuing the oppressed from the hands of the disbelieving polytheists who inflict on them the worst torment and tempt them away from the religion. So Allah, exalted is He, made jihad obligatory to raise His word, to manifest His religion, and to rescue the weak believers among His servants, even if that entails the loss of lives. Ransoming captives is obligatory upon the community of Muslims, either by fighting or by wealth, and wealth is more appropriate for this, since it is less than lives, for wealth is lighter than them. Malik said: It is obligatory upon the people to ransom the captives with all their wealth. There is no disagreement on this, due to the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: (Free the captive). This has already passed in (al-Baqarah [see vol. 2, p. 21]). Likewise they said: They must console them, for consolation is less than ransom. If the captive is wealthy, is the one who paid the ransom entitled to reclaim it from him or not? There are two opinions among the scholars, the more sound of which is that he may reclaim it.

The second: His saying, ﴿and of the oppressed﴾ is conjoined to the name of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, meaning "and in the way of the oppressed," for the deliverance of the oppressed is part of the way of Allah. This is the choice of al-Zajjaj, and it was said by al-Zuhri. Muhammad ibn Yazid said: I prefer that the meaning be "and for the oppressed," so it is conjoined to "the way," meaning "and for the oppressed, for rescuing them," so the two ways differ. By "the oppressed" is meant those believers who were in Makkah under the humiliation and harm of the disbelievers of Quraysh, and they are the ones referred to in his saying, peace be upon him: (O Allah, deliver al-Walid ibn al-Walid, Salamah ibn Hisham, Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'ah, and the oppressed among the believers). Ibn Abbas said: I and my mother were among the oppressed. In al-Bukhari, from him: (except the oppressed among the men, the women and the children), and he said: I and my mother were among those whom Allah excused; I was among the children and my mother among the women.

The third: His saying, ﴿from this town whose people are wrongdoers﴾. "The town" here is Makkah, by the consensus of the exegetes. Describing it as "wrongdoing" although the action belongs to its people is due to the connection of the pronoun. This is like your saying: "I passed by the man whose house is spacious, whose father is noble, whose slave-girl is beautiful." He described the man with these because of the verbal connection between them, which is the pronoun. If you said, "I passed by the noble man Umar," it would not be permissible, because nobility belongs to Amr, so it cannot be made an attribute of a man except through a connection, and that connection is the pronoun. This attribute is neither dualized nor pluralized, because it stands in place of the verb, so the meaning is "the one whose people wronged," and for this reason it does not say "the wrongdoers." And you say: "I passed by two men whose father is noble and whose slave-girls are beautiful," and "by men whose fathers are noble and whose slave-girls are beautiful."

(﴿And appoint for us from Yourself﴾) i.e. from Your presence, ﴿a protector﴾ i.e. one who will rescue us, ﴿and appoint for us from Yourself a helper﴾ i.e. one who will give us victory over them.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verse 76:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those who believe fight in the cause of Allah﴾, meaning in His obedience.

(And those who disbelieve fight in the cause of al-Taghut). Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Kisa'i said: al-Taghut is used in both the masculine and the feminine. Abu 'Ubayd said: It was used in the masculine and the feminine because they used to call a male soothsayer (kahin) and a female soothsayer (kahinah) taghut. He said: Hajjaj narrated to us from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Abu al-Zubayr narrated to us that he heard Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah (may Allah be pleased with him) speak about the taghut to which they used to bring their disputes for judgment. He said: There was one in Juhaynah, one in Aslam, and one in every tribe (hayy).

Abu Ishaq said: The evidence that it refers to Satan is His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿So fight the allies of Satan; indeed, the plot of Satan is ever weak﴾, meaning his scheme and the scheme of those who follow him. It is also said: He meant by it the Day of Badr, when he said to the polytheists: ﴿No one among the people can overcome you this day, and I am your protector.﴾ Then when the two hosts sighted each other, he turned on his heels and said: ﴿Indeed, I am free of you﴾, as will come later [[see vol. 8, p. 26]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verse 77:
