Amr ibn Dinar related from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, that Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf and some of his companions came to the Prophet ﷺ in Makkah and said: "O Prophet of Allah, we were in honour while we were polytheists, and when we became believers we became humbled?" He said: "I have been commanded to pardon, so do not fight the people." Then when Allah the Exalted turned him to Madinah, He commanded him to fight, and they held back, and the verse was revealed. Al-Nasa'i related it in his Sunan, and al-Kalbi said it. Mujahid said: "They are the Jews." Al-Hasan said: "It concerns the believers, based on His saying: ﴿they fear people﴾, that is, the polytheists of Makkah, ﴿as they fear Allah﴾, so it is according to what humans are naturally disposed to of fear, not of opposition." Al-Suddi said: "They are a people who embraced Islam before the obligation of fighting, and when it was made obligatory they disliked it." It was also said: "It is a description of the hypocrites, and the meaning is: they fear being killed by the polytheists just as they fear death from Allah."

﴿Or even greater fear﴾: that is, in their estimation and belief. I say: this is more fitting to the context of the verse, given His saying: ﴿And they say: "Our Lord, why have You prescribed fighting for us? If only You had delayed us to a near term"﴾, meaning: "Why not?" and it is followed only by a verb. Far be it that such a statement should come from a noble companion who knows that the terms of life are fixed and the provisions are apportioned; rather, they were obedient to Allah's commands, listening and submissive, regarding arrival at the Hereafter as better than remaining in the transient abode, as is well known of their conduct, may Allah be pleased with them. Except that its speaker may be one whose foot has not been firmly planted in faith, and whose heart has not been expanded by Islam, for the people of faith vary in degree: some are complete and some deficient, and it is the one whose soul recoils from what he is commanded in matters that involve hardship for him and severity that overtakes him. And Allah knows best.

His saying the Exalted: ﴿Say: The enjoyment of this world is little﴾ is a beginning and a predicate. Likewise ﴿and the Hereafter is better for those who fear Allah﴾, that is, those who avoid sins, and the discussion of this has already passed in (al-Baqarah [[see vol. 1, p. 161]]). The enjoyment of the world is its benefit and the pleasure of its delights, and He called it little because it has no permanence. The Prophet ﷺ said: "My likeness and the likeness of the world is like a rider who took a qaylulah [[al-qaylulah: sleep at midday. It was also said: a rest at midday when the heat is intense, even if there is no sleep with it.]] under a tree, then departed and left it." This meaning has already been discussed fully in (al-Baqarah).

**Issue 1 (on the verse 4:78):** There are four issues in this verse.

The first is His saying, ﴿Wherever you may be, death will overtake you﴾. The phrase is a conditional (*shart*) and its response (*mujazah*), and *ma* (مَا) is an extra particle (*za'ida*). This address is general, even if what is meant is the hypocrites or the weak among the believers who said: ﴿Our Lord, why did You not postpone us to a near term?﴾, that is, until we die at our appointed times. This reading fits the hypocrites better, as we mentioned, because of their saying when the people of Uhud were struck: ﴿If they had stayed with us, they would not have died or been killed﴾ [see vol. 4, p. 462]. So God answered them: ﴿Wherever you may be, death will overtake you, even if you are in towers built high﴾. This is the explanation of Ibn 'Abbas in the narration of Abu Salih from him. The singular of *burūj* (البروج) is *burj* (بُرْج), which is a high building and a great palace. Tarafa said, describing a she-camel:

*As if she were a Roman tower, plastered over with gypsum (shīd) and brick and stones.*

[Note: *shīd* (الشيد), with a kasra, is anything the wall is coated with, such as plaster or flagstone.]

Talha ibn Sulayman read ﴿yudrikukum﴾ with a damma on the kaf (يُدْرِكُكُ‍ُم), which is an elision of the fa' (*idmār al-fā'*). This is rare and occurs only in poetry, like the line:

*Whoever does good deeds, God will reward them.*

He meant: "then God will reward them."

The scholars and the interpreters differed about what is meant by these *burūj*. Most of them, and this is the most sound view, said that it means towers in the fortresses on earth, which are built, because these are the utmost of what humans can do in fortification and protection, so God gave them this as an example. Qatada said: "In fortified palaces." Ibn Jurayj and the majority said the same. From this is the saying of 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Would you like a strong fortress and protection?" Mujahid said: "The *burūj* are palaces." Ibn 'Abbas said: "The *burūj* are fortresses, watchtowers and citadels." The meaning of *mushayyadah* (مُشَيَّدَةٍ) is "lofty," said by al-Zajjaj and al-Qutaybi. Ikrima said: "Adorned (*muzayyana*) with *shīd*, which is gypsum." Qatada said: "Fortified." *Mashīd* and *mushayyad* are the same, and from it is ﴿a lofty palace﴾ [see vol. 12, p. 74]. The doubling of the letter (*tashdīd*) indicates intensification. It was also said: *mushayyad* means "lengthened" (*mutawwalah*), and *mashīd* means "coated with shīd." One says *shāda al-bunyān* (شَادَ الْبُنْيَانَ), meaning he built the building, and *ashāda bi-dhikrihi* (أَشَادَ بِذِكْرِهِ), meaning he raised his mention.

Al-Suddi said: "The *burūj* here are towers in the lowest heaven, built." Makki reported this view from Malik, who said: "Do you not see His saying: ﴿By the sky with its towers﴾ [see vol. 19, p. 281], and ﴿He has placed in the sky towers﴾ [see vol. 13, p. 65], and ﴿We have indeed placed in the sky towers﴾ [see vol. 10, p. 6]?" Ibn al-'Arabi also related this from Ibn al-Qasim from Malik. Al-Naqqash related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "﴿In towers built high﴾ means in palaces of iron." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The apparent wording of the verse does not give this meaning."

The second issue: this verse refutes the Qadariyya (those who deny divine predestination) regarding the appointed terms (*ājāl*), because of His saying: ﴿Wherever you may be, death will overtake you, even if you are in towers built high﴾. Through this He informed them that when the appointed terms end, the soul must part from the body, whether that happens by killing, by death, or by something else through which God has made the custom of the soul's departure. The Mu'tazila (a theological school that held that human acts are created by humans and that God is bound by justice) said: "If the one who is killed had not been killed by the killer, he would have lived." This refutation has already been given in (Surat) Al 'Imran [see vol. 4, p. 226] and will come again. By their saying this, they agreed with the disbelievers and the hypocrites.

The third issue: taking cities and building them so that one is protected in them in preserving wealth and lives is the practice (*sunna*) of God among His servants. In this is the clearest proof against the view of those who say: "Trust in God (*tawakkul*) is leaving off the means (*asbāb*)." Taking cities is among the greatest and most important of the means, and we have been commanded to do it. The prophets took cities and dug trenches around them as a preparation and an added measure of defense. It was said to al-Ahnaf: "What is the wisdom of walls?" He said: "To deter the foolish until the wise (*al-ḥakīm* [in some manuscripts: *al-ḥalīm*, the forbearing]) comes and protects it."

The fourth issue: if we accept the view of Malik and al-Suddi that these are the towers of the sky, then the towers of the celestial sphere are twelve towers, lofty and elevated, and they are the great stars. It was said the stars are called *burūj* because of their visibility, from *baraja* (بَرَجَ), which means "to appear and rise high." From this is His saying: ﴿And do not display yourselves as in the display of the former times of ignorance﴾ [see vol. 14, p. 178]. God created them as stations for the sun and the moon, and He set the moon's stations in them. He arranged the times by them, and made them southern and northern, as a sign of benefits and as a guide to the direction of prayer (*qibla*), and a way to know the parts of the night and the parts of the day, for knowing the times of the night prayer (*tahajjud*), and other matters of livelihood.

His saying: ﴿And if good comes to them, they say, "This is from God"﴾. That is: if fertility (*khiṣb*) reaches the hypocrites, they say, "This is from God."

(﴿And if evil comes to them﴾) means drought and famine. They say, "This is from you," meaning: this happened to us because of your ill omen and the ill omen of your companions. It was also said: *al-ḥasana* (the good) is safety and security, and *al-sayyi'a* (the evil) is sickness and fear. It was said: the good is wealth, and the evil is poverty. It was said: the good is blessing, victory and booty on the day of Badr, and the evil is affliction, hardship and killing on the day of Uhud. It was said: the good is happiness, and the evil is hardship. These are the views of the commentators and the scholars of interpretation, including Ibn 'Abbas and others, on the verse. It was revealed concerning the Jews and the hypocrites, because when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) came to Medina among them, they said: "We have continued to notice a decline in our fruits and our farms since this man and his companions came to us."

Ibn 'Abbas said: the meaning of ﴿from you﴾ is "by your poor management." It was also said: ﴿from you﴾ means "by your ill omen," as we mentioned, that is, by the ill omen that has reached us, and they said this as a form of divination by bad omens (*tiyara*). God said: ﴿Say, "All is from God"﴾, meaning hardship and ease, victory and defeat, are all from God, that is, by God's decree and destiny.

﴿Then what is the matter with these people,﴾ meaning the hypocrites, ﴿that they can hardly understand any statement?﴾ That is: what is their condition that they do not understand that all of it is from God?

The Qur'an's words: "Whatever good befalls you is from God, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself" (4:79). Meaning: O Muhammad, whatever fertility, ease, health and well-being reaches you is by God's bounty and kindness toward you, and whatever drought and hardship reaches you is because of a sin you committed, for which you are being punished. The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), but what is meant is his community: whatever fertility and abundance of provision reaches you, O people, is by God's favour upon you, and whatever drought and narrowness of provision reaches you is from yourselves, that is, it befalls you because of your sins. This is the view of al-Hasan, al-Suddi and others, as in God's words: "O Prophet, when you divorce women..." (65:1). [See vol. 18, pp. 174 ff.]

It has also been said that the address is to humankind in general, and that what is meant is the species. This is like God's words: "By time, indeed humankind is in loss" (103:1–2), meaning that people in general are in loss. Do you not see that He made an exception from them, saying "except those who believe" (103:3), and an exception is only made from a whole or a group? According to this interpretation, the phrase "whatever befalls you" (4:79) is a new sentence (isti'naf). [See vol. 20, p. 178.]

It has also been said that there is an ellipsis (hadhf) in the speech, its estimated meaning being "they say," and according to this the speech is connected, the meaning being: "What is the matter with these people that they hardly understand any statement, until they say: whatever good befalls you is from God?" It has also been said that the interrogative alif is implied, and the meaning is: "Is it from yourself?" A similar example is God's words: "And is it a favour that you count upon me?" (26:22), meaning: "Or is it a favour?" Likewise God's words: "When he saw the moon rising, he said: This is my Lord" (6:77), meaning: "Is this my Lord?" [See vol. 13, p. 93; vol. 7, p. 27.]

Abu Khirash al-Hudhali said:

"They pushed me away and said: O Khuwaylid, do not be frightened,
so I said, when I was startled and did not recognise their faces: Are they them? Are they them?"

He meant "Are they them?" (ahum), so he implied the interrogative alif, which is common, and it will come later. [In the lexicon, under the root r-f-ʾ: "rafanuni" means "they calmed me," and Ibn Hani said: he means "rafa'uni," then dropped the hamza. He said: the hamza is only dropped in poetry, and he has dropped it in this verse. Its meaning is that I was startled, my heart flew away, so they gathered my scattered parts together.]

Al-Akhfash said that "mā" (in "mā aṣābaka") means "alladhī" (who/which). It has also been said that it is a conditional particle (shart). Al-Nahhas said: the correct view is the view of al-Akhfash, because the verse was revealed concerning a specific drought, and this is not in any way a sin. If it were a sin, the verse would say "mā aṣabta min sayyi'ah" (what evil you have incurred).

ʿAbd al-Wahhab ibn Mujahid reported from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbas, Ubayy and Ibn Masʿud, the reading: "Whatever good befalls you is from God, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself, and I have written it upon you." This is a reading by way of explanation (tafsir), but some people of deviation (ahl al-zaygh) have included it in the Qur'an. The report of this from Ibn Masʿud and Ubayy is discontinuous (munqati'), because Mujahid did not meet ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) or Ubayy.

According to the view of those who said: the good is the conquest and spoils on the day of Badr, and the evil is what befell them on the day of Uhud, namely that they were punished when the archers disobeyed the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who had commanded them to protect his back and not leave their position. They saw the Quraysh defeated and the Muslims collecting their wealth, so they abandoned their ranks. Khalid ibn al-Walid, who was with the unbelievers that day, looked at the back of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), which had been exposed by the archers' withdrawal. He took a unit of cavalry, circled around until he was behind the Muslims, and attacked them. No one remained behind the Messenger of God (ﷺ) of the archers except the standard-bearer, who kept the Messenger of God's (ﷺ) command, and he stood firm until he was killed in his place. Its explanation has been given before in (the chapter of) Al ʿImran. Then God revealed a verse similar to this one, namely His words: "What? When a calamity befell you, though you had inflicted twice as much (on the enemy)..." (3:165), meaning the day of Uhud, "...you had inflicted twice as much," meaning the day of Badr, "...you said: 'How is this?' Say: it is from yourselves" (3:165).

It is not permissible that "good" here means obedience and "evil" means disobedience, as the Qadariyyah (those who deny divine predestination) say. For if that were so, the verse would read "mā aṣabta" as we mentioned before, since (in their view) it means an act, and (in our view) it means acquisition (kasb). Good means obedience and evil means disobedience only in a verse such as His words: "Whoever comes with a good deed, he will have ten times its like, and whoever comes with an evil deed, he will not be recompensed except with its like" (6:160). As for this verse, it is as we have already explained, concerning fertility and drought, ease and hardship, in the manner of what came in the verse of al-A'raf, which is His words: "We afflicted the people of Pharaoh with years (of drought) and shortage of crops, so that they might take heed" (7:130). [See vol. 7, pp. 150–151.]

"With years" (bi-l-sinin): with drought, year after year. Rain was withheld from them, so their fruits diminished and their prices rose.

"But when good came to them, they said: This is ours; and if evil befell them, they ascribed it to Moses and those with him" (7:131). That is, they took it as an omen against them and said: this is because of our following you and our obedience to you. God answered them with His words: "Surely their omen is with God" (7:131).

That is, the omen of blessing and the omen of ill-fortune, and good and evil, benefit and harm, all come from God Almighty; no created being has any part in them. Likewise His words, reporting about them, that they attribute it to the Prophet (ﷺ): "And if evil befalls them, they say: This is from you. Say: All is from God" (4:78). As He said: "Surely their omen is with God." And as He said: "And what befell you on the day the two hosts met was by God's permission" (3:166), that is, by God's decree, His destiny and His knowledge. The verses of the Book bear witness to one another. Our scholars said: whoever believes in God and the Last Day does not doubt that everything is by God's decree, His destiny, His will and His wish, as He said: "And We test you with evil and with good as a trial" (21:35). And He said: "When God wills evil for a people, there is no turning it back, and they have no protector besides Him" (13:11). [See vol. 11, p. 287; vol. 9, p. 294.]

Issue: Some ignorant people among Ahl al-Sunnah have clung to this verse and used it as evidence, just as the Qadariyyah have clung to it and used it as evidence. The Qadariyyah's basis for using it is that they say: "good" here means obedience and "evil" means disobedience. They argue that in His words "whatever evil befalls you is from yourself" (4:79) He attributed disobedience to the human being and not to God Most High; this is how they cling to it. The other side's basis for clinging to it is His words: "Say: All is from God" (4:78). They say: He has attributed good and evil to Himself rather than to His creation. This verse is only clung to by the ignorant of both parties, because they built their argument on the premise that evil is disobedience, and it is not so, as we have explained. And God knows best.

As for the Qadariyyah: if they say "whatever good befalls you" means "obedience," then "is from God," that is not their belief, because their belief upon which they built their doctrine is that good is the act of the doer of good and evil is the act of the doer of evil. Moreover, if they had any proof in it, the verse would say "mā aṣabta min ḥasanah wa mā aṣabta min sayyi'ah" (whatever good you incurred and whatever evil you incurred), because He is the doer of both good and evil, so it is not attributed to Him except by His doing both, not by the doing of another. This position was affirmed by the Imam Abu al-Hasan Shabib ibn Ibrahim ibn Muhammad ibn Haydara in his book called "Hazz al-Ghalasim fi Ifham al-Khasim" (The Slaying of the Throats in Silencing the Opponent).

God's words: "And We sent you to humankind as a messenger" (4:79). "Messenger" (rasulan) is an emphatic verbal noun (masdar mu'akkad). It may also be that the meaning is "one possessing a message." "And sufficient is God as a witness" (4:79): the accusative is an explicative accusative (naṣb 'alā al-bayān), and the "bi" (in bi-llah) is superfluous. That is, God suffices as a witness to the truthfulness of His Prophet's message and that he is truthful.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verse 80:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has indeed obeyed Allah﴾. Allah informs that obedience to His Messenger ﷺ is obedience to Him. In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: (Whoever obeys me has obeyed Allah, and whoever disobeys me has disobeyed Allah, and whoever obeys the amir (leader) has obeyed me, and whoever disobeys the amir has disobeyed me). This is in one narration.

(And whoever obeys my amir, and whoever disobeys my amir).

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿But whoever turns away﴾, i.e., turns away and refuses.

(So We have not sent you over them as a guardian) i.e., a protector and watcher over their deeds. Your duty is only to convey (the message). Al-Qutaybi said: a reckoner (one who calls to account). Then Allah abrogated this by the verse of the sword, and commanded him to fight those who oppose Allah and His Messenger.

**Verse 81**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿They say, "Obedience." But when they go out from your presence, a group of them plot by night other than what you say, and Allah records what they plot by night.﴾ That is, "Our affair is obedience" (ṭāʿatun). It is also permissible to read it as ṭāʿatan in the accusative, meaning "we obey with obedience" (nuṭīʿu ṭāʿatan). This is the reading of Naṣr ibn ʿĀṣim, al-Ḥasan and al-Jaḥdarī. This verse concerns the hypocrites according to the opinion of most exegetes (mufassirūn). That is, when they are in your presence they say, "Our affair is obedience," or "We obey with obedience." Their saying this is of no benefit, because one who does not hold obedience in his belief is not truly obedient. Allah, the Exalted, did not confirm their obedience on the basis of what they displayed. Had obedience without belief been real, it would have been judged to be theirs. Thus it is established that obedience requires belief alongside its outward existence.

(﴿When they go out﴾) that is, when they leave (﴿from your presence, a group of them plot by night﴾). He mentioned "a group" (ṭāʾifa) because it carries the meaning of "men." The Kufans assimilated the tāʾ into the ṭāʾ, because they share the same place of articulation. Al-Kisāʾī disliked this in the verb, whereas according to the Basrans it is not objectionable. The meaning of (bayyata) is to devise and to disguise. It is also said: to alter, to change and to distort; that is, they altered the words of the Prophet ﷺ concerning what he had entrusted to them and commanded them to do. Al-Tabyīt means alteration (tabdīl), and from it is the saying of the poet [[It is al-Aswad ibn Yaʿfur, as in Lisān al-ʿArab, root (nakar).]]:

They came to me, but I was not pleased with what they altered,
and they had come to me with an unacceptable matter,
to marry their unmarried woman to Mundhir,
and can a slave marry a free woman?

Another [[It is al-Aswad ibn ʿĀmir al-Ṭāʾī, reproaching a man, as in al-Ṭabarī vol. 5 p. 174, Bulaq edition. In al-Baḥr: "and he altered my speech," etc.]]:

ʿAbd al-Malik altered my words; may Allah fight him, a faithless slave.

When a man plots an affair (bayyata al-amr) it means he arranged it at night. Allah the Exalted said: (﴿when they plot by night what does not please Him of speech﴾) [[See p. 379 of this part.]]. The Arabs say: "an affair was plotted by night" when it was made firm. The night was singled out for this because it is a time when one is free. The poet said:

They resolved their affair by night, and when
they awoke, their outcry had come.

From this come (bayyata al-ṣiyām), the planning of fasting. Al-Bayyūt is water that stays overnight, and al-Bayyūt is also a matter over which its owner stays up anxious. Al-Hudhalī said [[See Dīwān al-Hudhaliyyīn vol. 2 p. 190, Dār al-Kutub edition.]]:

I make its (she-camel's) ribs a stock
when I fear the anxious night of a grave matter.

Al-tabyīt and al-bayāt mean that the enemy comes by night. Bāta yafʿalu kadhā means he did it at night, just as one says ẓalla bi-l-nahār (he did it by day). Bayyata al-shayʾ means he determined it. If it is asked: what is the wisdom in beginning with mention of all of them and then saying (﴿a group of them plot﴾)? It is answered: He describes the state of those whom He knew would remain in their disbelief and hypocrisy, and He overlooked those whom He knew would return from that. It is also said: He describes the state of those who were present and were confused about their affair, while as for those who listened and remained silent, He did not mention them. And Allah knows best.

(﴿and Allah records what they plot by night﴾) that is, He records it in the pages of their deeds, in order to requite them for it. Al-Zajjāj said: the meaning is that He sends it down to you in the Book. This verse is evidence that mere utterance benefits nothing, as we have mentioned. They said "obedience," they uttered it, and Allah did not confirm their obedience nor did He judge its soundness for them, because they did not believe in it. Thus it is established that one is not obedient unless he believes in it along with its existence.

**Verses 82**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So turn away from them, and rely upon Allah; and Allah suffices as a Guardian. Do they not then reflect upon the Qur'an?﴾ His saying (﴿so turn away from them﴾) means: do not inform about their names. This is related from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, meaning the hypocrites. It is also said: do not punish them. Then He commanded him to rely upon Him and to trust in Him for victory over His enemy. It is said that this was abrogated (mansūkh) by His saying: (﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾) [[See vol. 8 p. 204.]]. Then He censured the hypocrites for turning away from reflecting on the Qur'an and contemplating it and its meanings. Tadabbartu al-shayʾ means I considered its consequence. In a ḥadīth: (lā tadābarū), meaning that one of you should not turn his back on another. Adbara al-qawm means their affair came to its end. Al-tadbīr is that a person arranges his affair as if looking at what its outcome will be. This verse and His saying: (﴿Do they not reflect upon the Qur'an, or are there locks upon their hearts?﴾) [[See vol. 16 p. 245.]] indicate the obligation of reflecting upon the Qur'an [[In ṭ and j: "on the Qur'an."]] in order to know its meaning. Thus there is in this a refutation of the corrupt view of one who says that nothing may be taken from its tafsir except what is established from the Prophet ﷺ, and who forbids interpreting it in ways permitted by the Arabic language. It also indicates the command to reason and to draw inferences, and the refutation of blind following (taqlīd), and it indicates the establishment of qiyās (analogical reasoning).

His saying: ﴿Had it been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much discrepancy﴾ means variation and contradiction, related from Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah and Ibn Zayd. The variant readings, the differences in wording of similar expressions, the indications, and the lengths of the surahs and verses are not included in this. What is meant is discrepancy of contradiction and variation. It is also said: the meaning is that if what you report were from other than Allah, it would have been discordant. It is also said: there is no speaker who speaks a great deal without there being much discrepancy in his speech, either in its description and wording, or in the quality of its meaning, or in contradiction, or in falsehood. So Allah, mighty and majestic, sent down the Qur'an and commanded them to reflect upon it, because they find in it no discrepancy in its description, no refutation of it in meaning, no contradiction, and no falsehood in what it reports of the unseen and of what they conceal.

**Verse 81**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿They say, "Obedience." But when they go out from your presence, a group of them plot by night other than what you say, and Allah records what they plot by night.﴾ That is, "Our affair is obedience" (ṭāʿatun). It is also permissible to read it as ṭāʿatan in the accusative, meaning "we obey with obedience" (nuṭīʿu ṭāʿatan). This is the reading of Naṣr ibn ʿĀṣim, al-Ḥasan and al-Jaḥdarī. This verse concerns the hypocrites according to the opinion of most exegetes (mufassirūn). That is, when they are in your presence they say, "Our affair is obedience," or "We obey with obedience." Their saying this is of no benefit, because one who does not hold obedience in his belief is not truly obedient. Allah, the Exalted, did not confirm their obedience on the basis of what they displayed. Had obedience without belief been real, it would have been judged to be theirs. Thus it is established that obedience requires belief alongside its outward existence.

(﴿When they go out﴾) that is, when they leave (﴿from your presence, a group of them plot by night﴾). He mentioned "a group" (ṭāʾifa) because it carries the meaning of "men." The Kufans assimilated the tāʾ into the ṭāʾ, because they share the same place of articulation. Al-Kisāʾī disliked this in the verb, whereas according to the Basrans it is not objectionable. The meaning of (bayyata) is to devise and to disguise. It is also said: to alter, to change and to distort; that is, they altered the words of the Prophet ﷺ concerning what he had entrusted to them and commanded them to do. Al-Tabyīt means alteration (tabdīl), and from it is the saying of the poet [[It is al-Aswad ibn Yaʿfur, as in Lisān al-ʿArab, root (nakar).]]:

They came to me, but I was not pleased with what they altered,
and they had come to me with an unacceptable matter,
to marry their unmarried woman to Mundhir,
and can a slave marry a free woman?

Another [[It is al-Aswad ibn ʿĀmir al-Ṭāʾī, reproaching a man, as in al-Ṭabarī vol. 5 p. 174, Bulaq edition. In al-Baḥr: "and he altered my speech," etc.]]:

ʿAbd al-Malik altered my words; may Allah fight him, a faithless slave.

When a man plots an affair (bayyata al-amr) it means he arranged it at night. Allah the Exalted said: (﴿when they plot by night what does not please Him of speech﴾) [[See p. 379 of this part.]]. The Arabs say: "an affair was plotted by night" when it was made firm. The night was singled out for this because it is a time when one is free. The poet said:

They resolved their affair by night, and when
they awoke, their outcry had come.

From this come (bayyata al-ṣiyām), the planning of fasting. Al-Bayyūt is water that stays overnight, and al-Bayyūt is also a matter over which its owner stays up anxious. Al-Hudhalī said [[See Dīwān al-Hudhaliyyīn vol. 2 p. 190, Dār al-Kutub edition.]]:

I make its (she-camel's) ribs a stock
when I fear the anxious night of a grave matter.

Al-tabyīt and al-bayāt mean that the enemy comes by night. Bāta yafʿalu kadhā means he did it at night, just as one says ẓalla bi-l-nahār (he did it by day). Bayyata al-shayʾ means he determined it. If it is asked: what is the wisdom in beginning with mention of all of them and then saying (﴿a group of them plot﴾)? It is answered: He describes the state of those whom He knew would remain in their disbelief and hypocrisy, and He overlooked those whom He knew would return from that. It is also said: He describes the state of those who were present and were confused about their affair, while as for those who listened and remained silent, He did not mention them. And Allah knows best.

(﴿and Allah records what they plot by night﴾) that is, He records it in the pages of their deeds, in order to requite them for it. Al-Zajjāj said: the meaning is that He sends it down to you in the Book. This verse is evidence that mere utterance benefits nothing, as we have mentioned. They said "obedience," they uttered it, and Allah did not confirm their obedience nor did He judge its soundness for them, because they did not believe in it. Thus it is established that one is not obedient unless he believes in it along with its existence.

**Verses 82**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So turn away from them, and rely upon Allah; and Allah suffices as a Guardian. Do they not then reflect upon the Qur'an?﴾ His saying (﴿so turn away from them﴾) means: do not inform about their names. This is related from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, meaning the hypocrites. It is also said: do not punish them. Then He commanded him to rely upon Him and to trust in Him for victory over His enemy. It is said that this was abrogated (mansūkh) by His saying: (﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾) [[See vol. 8 p. 204.]]. Then He censured the hypocrites for turning away from reflecting on the Qur'an and contemplating it and its meanings. Tadabbartu al-shayʾ means I considered its consequence. In a ḥadīth: (lā tadābarū), meaning that one of you should not turn his back on another. Adbara al-qawm means their affair came to its end. Al-tadbīr is that a person arranges his affair as if looking at what its outcome will be. This verse and His saying: (﴿Do they not reflect upon the Qur'an, or are there locks upon their hearts?﴾) [[See vol. 16 p. 245.]] indicate the obligation of reflecting upon the Qur'an [[In ṭ and j: "on the Qur'an."]] in order to know its meaning. Thus there is in this a refutation of the corrupt view of one who says that nothing may be taken from its tafsir except what is established from the Prophet ﷺ, and who forbids interpreting it in ways permitted by the Arabic language. It also indicates the command to reason and to draw inferences, and the refutation of blind following (taqlīd), and it indicates the establishment of qiyās (analogical reasoning).

His saying: ﴿Had it been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much discrepancy﴾ means variation and contradiction, related from Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah and Ibn Zayd. The variant readings, the differences in wording of similar expressions, the indications, and the lengths of the surahs and verses are not included in this. What is meant is discrepancy of contradiction and variation. It is also said: the meaning is that if what you report were from other than Allah, it would have been discordant. It is also said: there is no speaker who speaks a great deal without there being much discrepancy in his speech, either in its description and wording, or in the quality of its meaning, or in contradiction, or in falsehood. So Allah, mighty and majestic, sent down the Qur'an and commanded them to reflect upon it, because they find in it no discrepancy in its description, no refutation of it in meaning, no contradiction, and no falsehood in what it reports of the unseen and of what they conceal.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verse 83:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When there comes to them a matter of security⦆ — In (idhā) there is the meaning of a conditional, and it does not govern a jussive (verb), even if (mā) is added to it, though that usage is rare. Sibawayh said: "The better usage is what Ka'b ibn Zuhayr said:

*"And when you wish, she sends forth from her, toward the sunset, a fleeing, startled she-camel (nāshiṭan maḏ'ūran)"* [[He described his she-camel as lively and swift after traveling the whole day, so he compared her, as she set off swiftly, to a bull (nāshiṭ) that has been startled by a hunter or a beast of prey. The nāshiṭ is the bull that leaves one land for another, which makes it more wild and more frightened.

(From Sharh al-Shawahid.)]]

He means that the better usage does not apply the jussive after idhā mā, just as it was not applied in this line. This was already mentioned at the beginning of (al-Baqarah) [[See vol. 1, p. 2: 1.]]. The meaning is that when they hear any of the matters that contain security, such as the victory of the Muslims and the killing of their enemy, or fear, which is the opposite of this, they spread it (adhā'ū bihi), that is, they divulge it, make it public, and talk about it before they have verified its truth. It was said that this was done by the weaker among the Muslims, according to al-Hasan, because they used to spread the affair of the Prophet ﷺ and thought that there was no harm for them in doing so. Al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd said: it refers to the hypocrites, and they were forbidden from this because of the lies that befall them in spreading rumours.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if they had referred it to the Messenger and to those in authority among them⦆ — that is, they would not have spoken of it or divulged it until the Prophet ﷺ himself was the one who related it and made it public. Or "those in authority" are the people of knowledge and understanding, according to al-Hasan, Qatadah and others. Al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd said: the rulers. It was also said: the commanders of the expeditions.

(﴿Those who would know it from among them who draw it out⦆) — that is, who extract it, meaning they would have known what should be divulged of it and what should be concealed. Istinbat (drawing out) is derived from istanbatu al-ma', meaning when I extract water. Al-nabat is water extracted at first, as it first comes out when a well is dug. The Nabat were so named because they extract what is in the earth. Istinbat in linguistic usage means extraction, and it indicates ijtihad when there is no explicit text or consensus, as has been mentioned. His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And were it not for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy⦆ — it is in the nominative by inception according to Sibawayh, and according to him the predicate cannot be expressed. The Kufans say it is in the nominative by (lawla).

﴿You would have followed Satan, except for a few⦆ — In this verse there are three opinions. Ibn 'Abbas and others said: the meaning is that they spread it, except for a few of them who did not spread it nor divulge it. This was said by a group of grammarians: al-Kisa'i, al-Akhfash, Abu 'Ubayd, Abu Hatim and al-Tabari. It was also said: the meaning is that those who would know it from among them who draw it out [would know it], except for a few of them, according to al-Hasan and others, and al-Zajjaj chose this view, saying: "Because the majority know this istinbat, since it is seeking knowledge of a report." Al-Farra' chose the first view, saying: "Because the knowledge of the expeditions, when it becomes apparent, is known to the one who extracts it and to others, and the spreading occurs in some and not in others." Al-Kalbi said, on his authority: "For this reason I find the exception from the spreading to be preferable." Al-Nahhas said: "These two are opinions based on metaphor, meaning that there is inversion and reordering in the speech." A third opinion, without metaphor: the meaning is, "And were it not for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy, in that He sent among you a Messenger who established the proof among you, you would have disbelieved and associated partners, except for a few of you, for he used to affirm the Oneness of God." There is also a fourth opinion: al-Dahhak said: the meaning is "You would have followed Satan, except for a few," that is, the Companions of Muhammad ﷺ whispered to themselves something from Satan, except for a few, meaning those whose hearts Allah tested for piety. According to this opinion, His saying "except for a few" is an exception from His saying "you would have followed Satan." Al-Mahdawi said: most scholars rejected this opinion, since were it not for Allah's grace and mercy, all people would have followed Satan.

The first fa' here is connected to His words, "And whoever fights in the way of Allah and is killed or overcomes, We will give him a great reward. So fight in the way of Allah" (﴿وَمَنْ يُقاتِلْ فِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ فَيُقْتَلْ أَوْ يَغْلِبْ فَسَوْفَ نُؤْتِيهِ أَجْراً عَظِيماً. فَقاتِلْ فِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ﴾). That is, "for this reason, fight."

It is also said that it is connected to His words, "And why do you not fight in the way of Allah... So fight" (﴿وَما لَكُمْ لَا تُقاتِلُونَ فِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ. فَقاتِلْ﴾). The meaning is as if it said: do not abandon fighting the enemy and seeking victory over them on behalf of the oppressed among the believers, even if you are alone, because He promised him victory. Al-Zajjaj said: Allah the Exalted commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to fight even if he fights alone, because He had guaranteed him victory. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is the apparent meaning of the wording, except that nothing ever came in any report that fighting was obligatory upon him alone, without the community, for any period. So the meaning, and Allah knows best, is that it is an address to him in wording, and it is an example of what is said to each person concerning himself: you, O Muhammad, and each one of your community, the statement is to him, ﴿fight in the way of Allah; you are not burdened except with yourself﴾. For this reason, every believer should strive even if alone. Among this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): 'By Allah, I will fight them until my neck stands alone (until I am killed).'" The "neck" (sālifa) is the side of the neck, and he referred to its standing alone as death, because it is not separated from what is adjacent to it except by death. And Abu Bakr's saying at the time of apostasy: "Even if my right hand opposed me, I would fight it with my left."

It is also said that this verse was revealed concerning the Badr al-Sughra appointment. When Abu Sufyan returned from Uhud, he arranged a meeting with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at the Badr season. When the appointed time came, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out to it with seventy riders, but Abu Sufyan did not attend, and no fighting took place. This is in line with what Mujahid said, as was mentioned earlier in (Āl ʿImrān) [see vol. 4, p. 277]. The connection of the structure of the verses with what precedes it, on this view, is that He described the hypocrites as confused and as spreading rumours. Then He commanded the Prophet (ﷺ) to turn away from them and to be earnest in fighting in the way of Allah, even if no one assists him in that.

His words, ﴿you are not burdened except with yourself﴾. (tukallafu) is in the nominative because it is imperfect (mustaqbal), and it was not put in the jussive because it is not a condition (ʿilla) for the first clause. Al-Akhfash claimed that its jussive form is permissible.

(illā nafsaka) is the predicate of a passive verb (mā lam yusamma fāʿiluhu), and the meaning is: you are not obligated to the act of others, nor are you held accountable for it.

His words, ﴿And urge the believers; perhaps Allah will restrain the might of those who disbelieve﴾. In this there are three issues.

The first: His words, ﴿And urge the believers﴾ mean encourage them to struggle (jihād) and fight. It is said: "I urged so-and-so to do such-and-such" (ḥarraḍtu fulānan ʿalā kadhā) when you command him to it. And "ḥāraḍa fulān ʿalā al-amr" and "akkaba" and "wāẓaba" have the same meaning. In al-Baḥr it says: He, exalted is He, commanded him to rouse the believers to fight and to stir their resolve toward martyrdom.

The second: His words, ﴿perhaps Allah will restrain the might of those who disbelieve﴾ are an expression of hope (ʿasā as a raising of hopes, iṭmāʿ), and hope from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is binding. Moreover, hope has come in the speech of the Arabs with the meaning of certainty. From this is His saying, the Exalted: "And the One from whom I hope that He will forgive me my sin on the Day of Judgment" (see vol. 13, p. 111). Ibn Muqbil said:

"My assumption about them is like ʿasā, while they are in a desert (tanūfa), disputing the prizes of the proverbs."

(tanūfa: a barren expanse of land.)

His words, ﴿And Allah is more severe in might﴾ mean more formidable in power, greater in authority, and more capable in might to do what He wills.

(And more severe in punishment) means in retribution, according to al-Ḥasan and others. Ibn Durayd said: "Allah struck him with a nukla," meaning He struck him with what would make him an example (yunakkiluhu). He said: "And I made an example of the man (nakkaltu bi-l-rajul) with an example (tankīlan), from al-nakāl." And al-mankal is the thing by which a person is made an example of. He said:

"And throw upon their napes a mankal, with a rock or a host of thick, massed troops."

The third issue: If someone says: "We see the disbelievers in might and strength, and you say that ʿasā means certainty, so where is that promise?" It is said to him: this promise has been fulfilled, and its fulfilment does not necessarily mean it persists continuously. So whenever it occurs, even for a moment, the promise has been true. Allah restrained the might of the polytheists at Badr al-Sughra, and they broke the war and fighting they had pledged. ﴿And Allah sufficed the believers in fighting﴾ (see vol. 14, p. 160). Also at Ḥudaybiyya, He restrained them from treachery and from seizing the opportunity they had aimed at. So the Muslims were alert to them, went out, and took them captive, and this happened while the envoys were moving between them in the peace negotiations. This is what is meant by His words, ﴿And it is He who restrained their hands from you﴾, as will come (see vol. 16, p. 280). Allah also cast terror into the hearts of the confederates, and they withdrew without killing or fighting, as He said, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah sufficed the believers in fighting.﴾ The Jews left their homes and wealth without the believers fighting them. All of this is might that Allah restrained from the believers. Moreover, a great number and a vast multitude of Jews and Christians entered under the jizya, humbled, and gave up war, abased. So Allah restrained their might from the believers. And all praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verse 85:

There are three issues in this.

The first: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Whoever intercedes﴾. The root of shafa'ah (intercession), shuf'ah (pre-emption) and similar words is from shaf' (pair, even number, i.e. a counterpart in number), and from it comes shafi' (intercessor), because he becomes a pair (shaf') together with the one in need. From it also comes the phrase naqah shafu' (a she-camel that, when milked, is milked from two udders in one milking), and naqah shafi' (a she-camel whose womb carries a foetus while she also has a suckling offspring following her). [[As in the originals; but the lexicographers' books say: "wa naqah shafi'" etc., and "shah shafu'" and "shafi' shafa'ha waladuha" (a female that has a young one following her).]] Shaf' means joining one to another. Shuf'ah means joining the share of a partner to your own ownership. Thus shafa'ah is joining another to your standing and your means; in reality it is the display of the intercessor's rank before the one who is asked, and the conveying of benefit to the one for whom intercession is made.

The second: The interpreters differed concerning this verse. Mujahid, al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd and others said that it refers to the intercessions people make among themselves concerning their needs: whoever intercedes so as to benefit someone, he will have a share of it, and whoever intercedes so as to harm someone, he will have a portion (kifl) of it. It was said: the good intercession is in righteousness and obedience, and the bad is in sins. Whoever intercedes a good intercession to reconcile two people earns the reward, and whoever spreads tale-bearing (namimah) and backbiting (ghibah) incurs sin; this is close to the first view. It was also said: by good intercession is meant supplication for the Muslims, and bad is supplication against them. In the sound report: "Whoever supplicates for his brother in his absence, the angel appointed over him says: Amin, and for you the like of it." [[As in the originals; the hadith is "Whoever supplicates for his brother in his absence, the angel appointed over him says: Amin, and for you the like of it" (narrated by Muslim); in another narration: "it is answered for him."]] This is the share; likewise in evil, and the evil of his supplication returns upon him. The Jews used to supplicate against the Muslims. It was also said: the meaning is that whoever is a partner (shafi') to his companion in jihad will have his share of reward, and whoever is a partner to another in falsehood will have his share of burden. It is also reported from al-Hasan: the good is what is permissible in religion, and the bad is what is not permissible in it. It seems that this view is comprehensive. Al-Kifl means burden and sin, according to al-Hasan and Qatadah; al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd said it means share. Its derivation is from the kisa' (saddle-cloth) [[In al-Bahr: it is borrowed from kafl al-ba'ir, which is a cloth...]] that the rider of a camel places on its hump so that he does not fall. It is said: iktafaltu al-ba'ir when I put a cloth on its hump and rode on it. It is called iktifal because he did not use the whole back, but used a portion of the back. It is used for a share of good and of evil, and in the Book of Allah, Exalted is He: (He will give you a double portion of His mercy) [[See vol. 17, p. 266.]]. The intercessor is rewarded for what is permissible even if his intercession is not accepted, because He, Exalted is He, said "whoever intercedes" and did not say "whoever is interceded for." In Sahih Muslim: "Intercede, and you will be rewarded, and let Allah decree through the tongue of His Prophet what He loves."

The third: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah is ever Muqit over all things﴾. Muqit means capable (muqtadir). From it is the saying of al-Zubayr ibn Abd al-Muttalib:

"And a man of rancour whom I restrained myself from, though I was over his ill-will muqit"

meaning capable. So the meaning is that Allah, Exalted is He, gives every person his sustenance (quwwah). From it is his saying, peace be upon him: "It is sufficient sin for a man to neglect those whom he sustains (yuqit)." According to the one who narrated it thus, that is, those who are under his power and in his hand, from dependants and others; this was mentioned by Ibn Atiyyah. One says from it: qattahu, aqutuhu, qawtan, and aqatahu, uqituhu, iqatatan, so I am qa'it and muqit. Al-Kisa'i related: aqat yuqit. As for the verse of the poet [[He is al-Samaw'al ibn Adiya', and the full line is: "Ala al-fadl am 'ala idha hu sabat, inni 'ala al-hisab muqit"]]:

"...indeed I am muqit over the reckoning"

al-Tabari said concerning it: it is from a meaning other than the one mentioned earlier, and it means "watching/awaiting." Abu Ubaydah said: al-Muqit is the Guardian (al-hafiz). Al-Kisa'i said: al-Muqit is the Capable (al-muqtadir). Al-Nahhas said: Abu Ubaydah's view is more likely, because it is derived from qut (sustenance), and qut means the measure by which a person is preserved. Al-Farra' said: al-Muqit is the One who gives every man his sustenance. And in the hadith: "It is sufficient sin for a man to neglect those whom he sustains (yaqut)" and (yuqit), mentioned by al-Tha'labi. Ibn Faris related in al-Mujmal: al-Muqit is the Capable, al-Muqit is the Guardian and the Witness, and "ma 'indahu qit laylah wa qut laylah" (he has nothing for a night). And Allah knows best.

There are twelve issues in this passage.

**First issue:** God's words, ﴿When you are greeted with a greeting﴾. *Al-tahiyyah* is a *taf'ilah* form from *hayyaytu*. The original form is *tahiyyah*, like *tardiyah* and *tasmiyah*, and the two yā's were merged (*idgham*). *Al-tahiyyah* means greeting (*al-salam*). Its root meaning is the invocation of life (*al-du'a' bi-l-hayah*). "*Al-tahiyyatu lillah*" means salutations of protection from calamities (*al-salam min al-afat*). It is also said to mean sovereignty (*al-mulk*).

ʿAbd Allah ibn Salih al-ʿIjli said: I asked al-Kisa'i about the phrase "*al-tahiyyatu lillah*," what does it mean? He said: "*Al-tahiyyat* is like *al-barakat*." I asked: "What is the meaning of *al-barakat*?" He said: "I have not heard anything about them." I also asked Muhammad ibn al-Hasan about it, and he said: "It is something by which God has made His servants worship Him." Then I came to Kufa and met ʿAbd Allah ibn Idris and said: "I asked al-Kisa'i and Muhammad about the phrase 'al-tahiyyatu lillah,' and they answered me with such and such." ʿAbd Allah ibn Idris said: "They have no knowledge of poetry or of these matters?! *Al-tahiyyah* is sovereignty." He recited [the line of ʿAmr ibn Maʿdi Karib, preceded by:
*And every wide, white, glossy coat of mail, and every raider who repeats his raids, is a strong one*]:
*I make for Abu Qabus with it, until I halt with my army at his sovereignty.*
Ibn Khuwayz Mandad recited:
*I march with it to al-Nuʿman, until I halt with my army at his sovereignty.*
He means "at his kingdom." Another [poet, who is Zuhayr ibn Junab al-Kalbi] said:
*For everything the youth attained, I have attained it, except the tahiyyah.*

Al-Qutabi said: He said "*al-tahiyyatu lillah*" in the plural form because there were kings on earth who were greeted with various salutations. Some were told: "May you be spared from curse," others: "Be safe and well," and others: "Live a thousand years." So it was said to us: "Say, *al-tahiyyatu lillah*," meaning the expressions which indicate sovereignty and are used as a way of referring to God the Exalted.

The connection with what precedes is that He said: When you go out for jihad, as the command has already been given, and you are greeted during your journey with the greeting of Islam, do not say to the one who offers you peace, "You are not a believer." Instead, return the greeting, for the rulings of Islam apply to them.

**Second issue:** The scholars differed about the meaning and interpretation of the verse. Ibn Wahb and Ibn al-Qasim narrated from Malik that this verse concerns the blessing of one who sneezes (*tashmit al-ʿatis*) and the response to the one who blesses him. This is weak, since there is no indication in the text of this. As for responding to the one who blesses the sneezer, it falls by analogy under the meaning of returning a greeting, and this is the view of Malik, if that is correctly attributed to him. And God knows best.

Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: It may be that this verse is understood as referring to a gift given in exchange for a reward. Whoever is given a gift in exchange for a reward has the choice: if he wishes, he may return it, and if he wishes, he may accept it and give in return its value.

I say: The followers of Abu Hanifa said something similar. They said: "*Al-tahiyyah*" here means a gift, because of His words: "or return it" (*aw rudduha*), and one cannot return Islam itself. The apparent meaning of the text requires delivering the greeting in its very form, which is the gift, so He commanded compensation if one accepts it, or returning it in kind. This is not possible with the greeting of peace (*al-salam*). The ruling on a gift in exchange for a reward and on a present will come in Surat al-Rum, at His words: "and whatever you give in usury" (*wa ma ataytum min riba*), if God wills. [See vol. 14, p. 36.]

The correct view is that *al-tahiyyah* here means the greeting of peace (*al-salam*), because of His words: ﴿And when they come to you, they greet you with what God has not greeted you with﴾. [See vol. 17, p. 292.]

Al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani said:
*White-skinned slave girls greet them among themselves, and coverings of silk brocade are upon the wooden racks.* [Al-walaʾid: female slaves. Al-idrij: red silk, and it was said: yellow silk. Al-mashajib (plural of mashjab, with a kasra on the mim): sticks whose tops are joined and whose legs are spread apart, on which garments are placed.]

He means: "and they greet them with peace." This is the view of the majority of the exegetes.

Once this is established, the jurisprudence (*fiqh*) of the verse is as follows: The scholars agreed that initiating the greeting of peace is a recommended sunnah, and returning it is an obligation, because of His words: ﴿So greet with something better than it, or return it﴾.

They differed when one of a group returns the greeting: is that sufficient or not? Malik and al-Shafiʿi held that it suffices, and that the Muslim has thereby returned the same as his greeting. The Kufans held that returning the greeting is a specific obligation (*min al-furud al-mutaʿayyanah*). They said: "Greeting (*al-salam*) differs from returning it, since initiating it is voluntary, while returning it is obligatory. And if a non-Muslim returns the greeting on them, it does not relieve them of the obligation to return it." This shows that returning the greeting is binding on each person individually. Qatadah and al-Hasan even said that one who is praying returns the greeting verbally if greeted, and this does not break his prayer, because he has done what he was commanded. But people disagree with this.

The first group argued with what Abu Dawud narrated from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "It suffices for a group when they pass by that one of them greets, and it suffices for those seated that one of them returns it." This is an explicit text on the point of disagreement.

Abu ʿUmar said: This is a good (*hasan*) hadith with no contradiction to it. Its chain includes Saʿid ibn Khalid, who is Saʿid ibn Khalid al-Khuzaʿi of Medina, who is considered acceptable by some. Some weakened him, including Abu Zurʿah, Abu Hatim, and Yaʿqub ibn Shaybah, and they regarded this hadith as unacceptable (*munkar*), because he transmitted it alone with this chain, and because ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Fadl did not hear from ʿUbayd Allah ibn Abi Rafiʿ; al-Aʿraj came between them in other hadiths. And God knows best.

They also argued with the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "The few greet the many." And because they agreed that one person greets a group without needing to repeat it according to the number of the group, so likewise one person returns the greeting on behalf of the group and stands in for the rest, like collective obligations (*furud al-kifayah*).

Malik narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The rider greets the pedestrian, and when one of the people greets, it suffices for them." Our scholars said: This indicates that one person suffices for returning the greeting, because it is only said "it suffices for them" regarding what has already become obligatory. And God knows best.

I say: This is how our scholars interpreted this hadith, and they made it a proof for the permissibility of one person returning the greeting, but there is some difficulty in it.

**Third issue:** God's words: ﴿So greet with something better than it, or return it﴾. The best return is to add to it: if someone says "Peace be upon you" (*al-salamu ʿalayk*), you say "Peace and God's mercy be upon you" (*ʿalayka al-salamu wa rahmatu Allah*). If he says "Peace and God's mercy be upon you," you add in your return "and His blessings" (*wa barakatuhu*). This is the limit, so there is no further addition.

God the Exalted said, reporting about the blessed household: ﴿God's mercy and His blessings be upon you, people of the house﴾, which will be explained, God willing. [See vol. 9, p. 70.]

If the greeting reached its utmost limit, you add the conjunction *waw* at the beginning of your reply, so you say: "And upon you be peace, God's mercy and His blessings."

The return in kind is that you say to one who says "Peace be upon you": "And upon you be peace," except that the whole greeting should be in the plural form, even if the one greeted is one person. Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi narrated through al-Aʿmash: When you greet one person, say "Peace be upon you (plural)," for with him are the angels. Likewise the reply should be in the plural form. Ibn Abi Zayd said: The one greeting says "Peace be upon you (plural)," and the one returning says "And upon you (plural) be peace," or says "Peace be upon you (plural)" as he was greeted, and this is the meaning of His words "or return it." Do not say in your reply "Peace be upon you (singular)."

**Fourth issue:** The preferred practice in greeting, and the courtesy in it, is to place the name of God the Exalted before the name of the created being. God said: ﴿Peace be upon the family of Yasin﴾. He said in the story of Abraham (peace be upon him): ﴿God's mercy and His blessings be upon you, people of the house﴾, and He said, reporting about Abraham: ﴿Peace be upon you﴾.

In the Sahih of al-Bukhari and Muslim, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God the Mighty and Majestic created Adam in his own form [al-Nawawi said: This narration clearly shows that the pronoun in 'his form' refers to Adam, and that the meaning is that he was created at the beginning of his existence in the form in which he was on earth and in which he died], his height was sixty cubits. When He created him, He said: 'Go and greet those people, who are a group of angels sitting, and listen to how they greet you, for that will be your greeting and the greeting of your descendants.' He went and said: 'Peace be upon you.' They said: 'Peace be upon you and God's mercy.' They added 'and God's mercy.' Everyone who enters Paradise is in the form of Adam, and his height is sixty cubits. Then creation has continued to decrease since him until now."

I say: This hadith, with its authenticity, contains seven benefits:
The first: information about the description of Adam's creation.
The second: that we enter Paradise in that form by His grace.
The third: that the few greet the many.
The fourth: putting the name of God the Exalted first.
The fifth: returning in kind, to their saying "Peace be upon you."
The sixth: adding to the return.
The seventh: that answering the whole group with the return is as the Kufans say.
And God knows best.

**Fifth issue:** If someone returns the greeting by placing the name of the one greeted first, it is not forbidden nor disliked, because it is established from the Prophet (ﷺ), when he said to the man who did not perform the prayer well, and who had greeted him: "And upon you be peace. Go back and pray, for you have not prayed." [Al-Bukhari narrated it.]

ʿAʾishah said, when the Prophet (ﷺ) told her that Gabriel sends his greetings to her: "And upon him be peace and God's mercy." Al-Bukhari narrated it. From the hadith of ʿAʾishah, one of the points of jurisprudence is that when a man sends his greeting through another to someone, that person must return it as he would if the greeting were delivered to him in person.

A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "My father sends you his greeting." He said: "Upon you and upon your father be peace."

Al-Nasa'i and Abu Dawud narrated from the hadith of Jabir ibn Sulaym, who said: I met the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: "Upon you be peace, O Messenger of God." He said: "Do not say 'upon you be peace,' for 'upon you be peace' is the greeting of the dead, but say 'peace be upon you.'" This hadith is not authentic. However, since it was the custom of the Arabs to place the name of the one invoked upon first in evil, as when they say: "Upon him be God's curse and God's wrath." God the Exalted said: ﴿And indeed upon you is My curse until the Day of Judgment﴾. [See vol. 15, p. 228.] This was also the habit and custom of poets in greeting the dead, as they say:
*Upon you be God's peace, Qays ibn ʿAsim, and His mercy, as much as He wills to have mercy.*
Another, who is al-Shammakh, said:
*Upon you be peace from a prince, and may God's hand bless that torn leather.*

He forbade that, not because that is the legislated wording for the dead, since it was established from him (peace be upon him) that he greeted the dead as he greeted the living, when he said: "Peace be upon you, abode of a believing people, and we, God willing, will join you." ʿAʾishah said: "I said, 'O Messenger of God, how should I speak when I enter the graveyards?' He said: 'Say: Peace be upon you, people of the dwellings from among the believers.'" The hadith continues, and it will come in Surat Alhakum [al-Takathur], God willing.

) ... if Allah wills. I say: It may be that the hadith of ʿAʾishah and others about greeting all the people of the graves when one enters the graveyard and looks over it, and the hadith of Jabir ibn Sulaym, refer specifically to greeting while passing by for the purpose of visiting. And Allah knows best.

The sixth: It is from the Sunnah that the rider greets the one walking, the standing greets the seated, and the few greet the many. This is how it came in Sahih Muslim from the hadith of Abu Hurairah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The rider greets the one walking," and he mentioned the rest. He began with the rider because of the高 elevation of his rank, and because that is further from pride (zahw). Similarly it has been said regarding the one walking. It has also been said: since the one seated is in a state of dignity, stability and calm, he has a distinction over the one walking, because the walker's condition is the opposite of that. As for greeting the few upon the many, it is out of regard for the nobility of the gathering of Muslims and their greater number. Al-Bukhari added to this hadith: "and the young greets the elder." As for the elder greeting the young, Ash'ath reported from al-Hasan that he did not see greeting children as obligatory; he said: because returning the greeting is obligatory and a child is not obliged to return it, so one should not greet them. It is reported from Ibn Sirin that he used to greet children but not make them hear. Most scholars said: greeting them is better than leaving it. In the two Sahihs it is reported from Sayyar who said: I was walking with Thabit, and he passed by children and greeted them. He mentioned that he was walking with Anas and he passed by children and greeted them, and he related that he was walking with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and he passed by children and greeted them. This is the wording of Muslim. This is from his great character ﷺ, and in it is training for the child, encouragement to teach the Sunan, and conditioning them to the manners of the Shariah, so let one follow him. As for greeting women, it is permissible, except for young women, lest there be fear of temptation from speaking to them by a whisper of Satan or a treacherous glance. As for elderly women (al-mutajallat, i.e., the aged and decrepit) and old women, it is good, due to safety in what we have mentioned. This is the view of ʿAtaʾ and Qatadah, and Malik and a group of scholars adopted it. The Kufans prohibited it when none of them are within the prohibited degrees (dhawat mahram), and they said: since the adhan, iqamah and loud recitation in prayer are dropped from women, returning the greeting is also dropped from them, so one does not greet them. The sound view is the first, based on what al-Bukhari transmitted from Sahl ibn Saʿd, who said: We used to rejoice on Friday. I said: Why? He said: We had an old woman who would send to us from her plantation, (Ibn Maslamah said: palm trees in Madinah), and she would take some of the roots of silq and put them in the pot and crush some grains of barley. When we had prayed Jumuʿah we would leave and greet her, and she would present it to us, and we rejoiced because of it. We did not nap nor have lunch except after Jumuʿah. Takarkar means to grind, as said by al-Qutabi.

The eighth: The Sunnah in greeting and in replying is to speak aloud, and gesturing with a finger or palm does not suffice according to al-Shafiʿi; according to us it suffices if the person is at a distance. Ibn Wahb reported from Ibn Masʿud who said: Al-salam is one of the names of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, which He placed on the earth, so spread it among you, for when a man greets a group and they return his greeting, he has a surplus of one degree over them, because he reminded them; and if they do not return his greeting, one better and purer than them will return it. Al-Aʿmash reported from ʿAmr ibn Murrah from ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Harith who said: When a man greets a group he has a surplus of one degree; if they do not return it, the angels return it and curse them. When the one greeted returns the greeting, he should make his reply audible, for if he does not make the greeter hear it, it is not a reply to him. Do you not see that if the greeter greets with a greeting that the one greeted does not hear, it is not a greeting from him? Likewise, if one replies with a reply not heard, it is not a reply. It is related that the Prophet ﷺ said: "When you greet, make it audible; when you return, make it audible; and when you sit, sit calmly, and let none of you raise his voice above another's speech." Ibn Wahb said: Usamah ibn Zayd informed me from Nafiʿ who said: I was riding with a man of the jurists of Syria called ʿAbd Allah ibn Zakariyya, when my animal stopped me because it was urinating; then I caught up with him and did not greet him. He said: Will you not greet? I said: I was with you just now. He said: Even if it is valid, the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to ride together and a tree would separate them, and when they met some of them would greet others.

The ninth: As for the disbeliever, the ruling on returning his greeting is that it is said to him: "Wa ʿalaykum." Ibn ʿAbbas and others said: the meaning of the verse "And when you are greeted with a greeting" is: if it is from a believer, then "greet with what is better than it," and if it is from a disbeliever, then return it as the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: it is said to them, "Wa ʿalaykum." ʿAtaʾ said: the verse concerns believers specifically, and whoever greets from others is told: "ʿAlayka," as came in the hadith. I say: The inclusion and omission of the waw (and) are both found in Sahih Muslim: "ʿAlayka" without waw, which is the clearer version in meaning; but with the waw there is a difficulty, because the conjunctive waw implies sharing, so it would follow that they include themselves in what they invoked against us, namely death or weariness of our religion. The commentators differed on this in several views. The best of them is to say: the waw is on its original basis of conjunction, but we are answered and they are not answered by us, as he ﷺ said. It is also said: it is superfluous. And it is said: it is for resumption. The first is the best. The version omitting the waw is better in meaning, while including it is sounder in transmission and more widely known, and most scholars hold it.

The tenth: There is disagreement about returning the greeting to the people of protection (dhimmis): is it obligatory like returning it to Muslims? Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Shaʿbi and Qatadah held that it is, adhering to the generality of the verse and to the command to return to them in sound Sunnah. Malik, according to what Ashhab and Ibn Wahb transmitted from him, held that it is not obligatory: if you return it, say, "ʿAlayka." Ibn Tawus preferred that one say in replying to them: "ʿAlaka al-salam," meaning: may it be raised from you. Some of our scholars preferred "al-silam" (with a kasrah on the sin), meaning stones. Malik's statement and others' on this is sufficient and adequate, as came in the hadith. The discussion of their being greeted first will come in Surah Maryam at His saying, reporting Abraham's words to his father, "Peace be upon you" (salamun ʿalayka). In Sahih Muslim from Abu Hurairah, from the Prophet ﷺ, he said: "You will not enter Paradise until you believe, and you will not believe until you love one another. Shall I not direct you to something which, if you do it, you will love one another? Spread the greeting among you." This requires spreading it among Muslims, not among polytheists. And Allah knows best. [Supporting this is his ﷺ saying: "Greeting is a salutation for our community and a safety for our protected people." Narrated by al-Qudai from Anas.] And Allah knows best.

The eleventh: One should not greet the one praying. If he greets him, the one praying has the choice: if he wishes he may return with a gesture of his finger, and if he wishes he may wait until he finishes the prayer and then return. One should not greet someone who is relieving himself, and if he does, the latter is not obliged to return it. A man entered upon the Prophet ﷺ in such a state and he said to him: "When you find me or see me in this state, do not greet me, for if you greet me I will not return it to you." One should not greet one who is reciting the Qur'an and thereby interrupt his recitation; he has the choice: if he wishes he returns, and if he wishes he waits until he finishes and then returns. One should not greet someone who has entered the bath while uncovering his nakedness, or who is occupied with what pertains to the bath; and whoever is otherwise, greet him.

The twelfth: His saying, Exalted is He: "Indeed Allah is ever, over all things, a Reckoner" means: Guardian. It is said: Sufficient, from their saying: "ahsabani kadha," i.e., it sufficed me; similar is "hasbuka Allah." Qatadah said: Reckoner, as one says "akil" meaning "muakil" (one who eats with another). It is also said: it is "fa'il" from reckoning, and this attribute is fitting here because the meaning of the verse concerns a person increasing, decreasing, or fully repaying what he brings. Al-Nasa'i reported from ʿImran ibn Husayn who said: We were with the Prophet ﷺ when a man came and greeted, saying: "As-salamu ʿalaykum." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ returned it and said: "Ten." Then he sat. Then another came and greeted: "As-salamu ʿalaykum wa rahmatullah," and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ returned it and said: "Twenty." Then he sat. Then another came and said: "As-salamu ʿalaykum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh," and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ returned it and said: "Thirty." This report has come explained: whoever says to his Muslim brother, "Salamun ʿalaykum," has ten good deeds recorded for him; if he says, "As-salamu ʿalaykum wa rahmatullah," twenty good deeds are recorded for him; if he says, "As-salamu ʿalaykum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh," thirty good deeds are recorded for him, and likewise for the one who returns the reward. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verse 87:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah — there is no deity except Him﴾ is a beginning (mubtada') and a predicate (khabar). The lam in His saying (la-yajma'annakum) is the lam of oath (lam al-qasam). It was revealed concerning those who doubted the resurrection, so Allah, exalted is He, swore by Himself. Every lam that is followed by a shaddah-ed nun is the lam of oath. Its meaning is: in death and beneath the earth (ilaa yawmi al-qiyamah, "until the Day of Resurrection"). Some of them said: "ilaa" is extra (silah) in the speech, meaning: He will surely gather you on the Day of Resurrection. The Day of Resurrection was named "qiyamah" (rising) because people will stand in it before the Lord of the worlds, exalted and mighty is He. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Do they not think that they will be resurrected for a tremendous Day? The Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾ [see vol. 19, p. 252]. It was also said: the Day of Resurrection was named so because people will rise from their graves toward it. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿The Day they emerge from the graves swiftly﴾ [see vol. 18, p. 296]. The root of "qiyamah" is the letter waw.

(Wa-man asdaqu mina Allahi hadithan) is in the accusative as a specification (nasb 'ala al-bayan), and the meaning is: there is no one more truthful than Allah. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "wa-man azdaqu" with the letter zay. The rest read it with the letter sad. Its original form is sad, but because its place of articulation is close to it, a zay was put in its place.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verse 88:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So what is wrong with you that you are divided into two groups concerning the hypocrites?﴾ (fi'atayn) means two differing groups. Muslim narrated from Zayd ibn Thabit that the Prophet (ﷺ) went out to Uhud, and some people who had been with him turned back. The Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) were divided over them into two groups: some said, "We should kill them," and others said, "No." So the verse was revealed: ﴿So what is wrong with you that you are divided into two groups concerning the hypocrites?﴾ And al-Tirmidhi transmitted it with an addition, and he said: (It is good, and it expels evil as the fire expels the impurity of iron). He said: a hasan sahih hadith. And al-Bukhari said: (It is good, it expels impurity as the fire expels the impurity of silver).

The hypocrites meant here are Abdullah ibn Ubayy and his companions, who forsook the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the day of Uhud and returned with their force after having set out, as was mentioned earlier in (Al 'Imran) [see vol. 4, p. 239 below]. Ibn Abbas said: they are a people in Mecca who professed faith but abandoned the emigration (hijrah). Al-Dahhak said: and they said, "If Muhammad (ﷺ) prevails, we know him, and if our people prevail, that is more beloved to us." So the Muslims became divided about them into two groups: a people who befriended them and a people who disassociated themselves from them. Then Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿So what is wrong with you that you are divided into two groups concerning the hypocrites?﴾

Abu Salamah ibn Abd al-Rahman mentioned, from his father, that it was revealed concerning a people who came to Medina and showed Islam, but the plague and fever of Medina afflicted them, so they were turned back and left Medina. A group of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) met them and said, "What is wrong with you, that you have returned?" They said, "The plague of Medina has afflicted us, and we found it unbearable (ijtawaynaha)." They said, "Do you not have in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) a good example?" Some of them said, "They have become hypocrites." Others said, "They have not become hypocrites; they are Muslims." So Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed: ﴿So what is wrong with you that you are divided into two groups concerning the hypocrites, when Allah has overturned them for what they earned?﴾ to the end of the verse. They came to Medina claiming that they were emigrants, then afterwards they apostatized, and they asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for permission to go to Mecca to bring their goods with which they traded. The believers differed about them: one said, "They are hypocrites," and another said, "They are believers." So Allah, exalted, made their hypocrisy clear, revealed this verse, and commanded that they be killed.

I say: these two reports are supported by the context of the end of the verse, His saying, exalted is He: ﴿until they emigrate﴾, and the first is more sound in transmission, and it is the choice of al-Bukhari, Muslim and al-Tirmidhi. (Fi'atayn) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), as one says: "What is the matter with you, standing?" according to al-Akhfash. The Kufans said: it is the predicate of (ma lakum), like the predicate of kana and zanantu, and they permitted the introduction of the definite article into it. Al-Farra' related: (arkasahum, and rakasahum) meaning he turned them back to disbelief and overturned them, and this was said by al-Nadr ibn Shumayl and al-Kisa'i. Al-raks and al-naks mean overturning a thing on its head, or returning its beginning to its end, and al-marku's means the overturned one. In the reading of Abdullah and Ubayy, may Allah be pleased with them both, it is (wa-Allahu rakasahum). Ibn Rawahah said:

They were overturned into a dark trial, like the blackness of night, followed by trials.

That is, they were overturned. And so-and-so was overturned (irtakasa) in a matter from which he had been saved. The Rukusiyyah are a people between the Christians and the Sabians. Al-rakis is the bull in the middle of the threshing floor while the oxen are around it at the time of threshing.

﴿Do you wish to guide him whom Allah has sent astray?﴾ meaning, to lead him to reward by ruling for him the ruling of the believers.

﴿You will not find for him a way﴾ meaning a path to guidance and right direction and the seeking of proof. In this is a refutation of the Qadariyyah and others who say that their guidance is created by them, and it has been mentioned earlier (see vol. 1, p. 149).
