**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 4, verses 89–90:**

This passage contains five issues.

The first concerns His saying (Exalted is He): (They wish that you would disbelieve as they have disbelieved, that you would be equal). That is, they desire that you become like them in disbelief and hypocrisy. God therefore commanded disassociation from them, saying: (So do not take from among them allies until they emigrate [in the way of God]), as He said: (You have nothing of their guardianship until they emigrate) [[See vol. 8, p. 55 and p. 282.]]. Hijra (emigration) is of several kinds. Among them is emigration to Medina to support the Prophet (ﷺ). This was obligatory at the beginning of Islam, to the point that he said: (There is no hijra after the conquest). Likewise is the emigration of the hypocrites with the Prophet (ﷺ) on the military campaigns, and the emigration of one who has become Muslim in the land of war, which is obligatory. Another is the muslim's emigration from what God has forbidden to him, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: (The emigrant is one who abandons what God has forbidden). These two kinds of hijra remain valid now. There is also the abandonment of people of sins until they return, as a means of discipline for them, so they are not spoken to and not associated with until they repent, as the Prophet (ﷺ) did with Ka'b and his two companions [[See vol. 8, p. 282.]].

(Then if they turn away, seize them and kill them) means: if they turn away from monotheism and emigration, then capture them and kill them.

(Wherever you find them) is general with respect to places, both within the sacred precinct and outside it. And God knows best.

Then He made an exception, which is the second issue, saying: (Except those who join a people between you and whom there is a covenant). That is, those who connect with them and enter into their alliance by neighbourhood and pact. The meaning is: do not kill a people between whom and you there is a covenant, for they are upon their covenant. Then the covenants were abrogated (naskh), and so this ruling was abrogated. This is the view of Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and others, and it is the most sound of what has been said about the meaning of the verse.

Abu 'Ubayd said: (yasilun) means (yantasibun), i.e. they claim kinship. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

When she is joined, she says to Bakr ibn Wa'il,
while Bakr has taken her captive and the noses are humbled...

He means: when she claims kinship. Al-Mahdawi said: the scholars rejected this, because kinship does not prevent fighting and killing the disbelievers. Al-Nahhas said: this is a great error, for it implies that God forbade anyone to be fought who had kinship with the Muslims, whereas the polytheists had kinship ties with the earliest believers. Even more ignorant is the claim that this ruling existed and was then abrogated, since the people of interpretation are unanimous that the abrogating text is (Bara'a [the Repentance surah]), which was revealed only after the conquest and after wars had ended. Al-Tabari also gave this meaning.

I say: some scholars understood the meaning of (yantasibun) as safe conduct, i.e. one who attaches himself to the people of safe conduct is secure when all of them are secure, not in the sense of kinship in the meaning of blood relation.

There is disagreement about those who had a covenant with the Prophet (ﷺ). It was said they were the Banu Mudlij. Al-Hasan reported: there was a treaty between them and Quraysh, and between Quraysh and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) there was a covenant. 'Ikrimah said: it was revealed concerning Hilal ibn 'Uwaymir, Suraqa ibn Ju'shum, and Khuzayma ibn 'Amir ibn 'Abd Manaf, who had a covenant with the Prophet (ﷺ). It was also said: Khuza'a. Al-Dahhak reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he meant by the people between you and whom there is a pact the Banu Bakr ibn Zayd ibn Manat, who were in peace and truce.

The third issue: in this verse there is evidence for establishing a truce (muwada'a) between the people of war and the people of Islam when the truce serves the interest of the Muslims, as will be explained in (al-Anfal [[See vol. 8, p. 55.]] and Bara'a [[See vol. 8, p. 71 onwards.]]), God willing.

The fourth issue concerns His saying: (Or those who have come to you, their breasts constricted), i.e. straitened. Labid said:

I descended and stood upright like the trunk of a tall date palm,
bare, around which its harvesters are kept back [[Jurram (plural of jarim), the one who cuts and harvests dates.]].

That is, their breasts become constricted from the length of this palm tree. From this comes (hasr) in speech, meaning the constriction of speech upon the speaker. And (haṣir) means one who keeps a secret. Jarir said:

The slanderers pursued me, and they found me
keeping your secret, O Umaymah, guarded.

The phrase (haṣirat) means (qad haṣirat) [with qad understood]. Al-Farra' said: it is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring back to the pronoun in (jā'ukum), as you say: "So-and-so came, his mind gone," meaning his mind had gone. It was also said it is a predicate following a predicate. Al-Zajjaj said: i.e. they came to you, then He informed about them, saying: (their breasts constricted). On this view, (haṣirat) is an apposition for (jā'ukum). It was also said (haṣirat) is in the genitive position as a qualifier for a people. In the reading of Ubayy: (Except those who join a people between you and whom there is a covenant, their breasts constricted) without (or jā'ukum). Another view: its underlying sense is (or they came to you as men or a people whose breasts are constricted), so it is a qualifier of a noun in the accusative as a circumstantial clause. Al-Hasan read (aw jā'ukum haṣiratan ṣudūruhum), in the accusative as a circumstantial clause, and it is permissible to read it in the nominative as subject and predicate. It is also reported: (aw jā'ukum haṣirātin ṣudūruhum), and the nominative is permissible. Muhammad ibn Yazid said: (haṣirat ṣudūruhum) is a supplication against them, as you say: "God curse the disbeliever." This was also said by al-Mubarrad [[In the originals Muhammad ibn Yazid is al-Mubarrad, as in al-Bahr, Ibn 'Atiyya and others. It is not far-fetched that Ibn Yazid is al-'Ijli al-Kufi, since he is much earlier than al-Mubarrad.]]. Some exegetes rejected this, saying: this would require that they not fight their own people, which is invalid, for they are disbelievers and their people are disbelievers. It was answered that its meaning is sound: non-fighting on behalf of the Muslims is a rendering them powerless, and on behalf of their people is a belittling of them. It was also said: (aw) has the meaning of (wa), as if He said: "to a people between you and whom there is a covenant, and who came to you with their breasts constricted from fighting you and fighting alongside you, so they disliked fighting both parties." It is possible that they were bound by a covenant to this effect, which is a kind of pact, or they said: "We submit and will not fight," and it is possible this was accepted from them at the beginning of Islam until God opens their hearts to piety and expands them for Islam. The first view is more apparent. And God knows best.

(Or they fight) is in the accusative position, meaning: from fighting you [[In Ta and Z: "from that they fight you."]].

The fifth issue concerns His saying: (If God had willed, He would have given them power over you, and they would have fought you). God's empowering of the polytheists over the believers means that He enables them and strengthens them, either as punishment and retribution when wrongdoing is spread openly and sins become apparent, or as a trial and test, as He said: (We will surely test you until We know those who strive among you and the patient, and We test your reports) [[See vol. 16, p. 253.]], or as an expiation of sins, as He said: (And that God may purify those who have believed) [[See vol. 4, p. 219.]]. God may do what He wills, and empower whom He wills over whom He wills, whenever He wills.

As for the arrangement of the verse and its connection with what precedes: that is, kill the hypocrites about whom you have disagreed, except those who emigrate; and except those who join a people between you and whom there is a covenant, for they enter into what those people have entered, and so they have their ruling; and except those who came to you with their breasts constricted from fighting you or fighting their own people, and so they have entered among you, and therefore do not kill them.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 4, verses 89–90:**

This passage contains five issues.

The first concerns His saying (Exalted is He): (They wish that you would disbelieve as they have disbelieved, that you would be equal). That is, they desire that you become like them in disbelief and hypocrisy. God therefore commanded disassociation from them, saying: (So do not take from among them allies until they emigrate [in the way of God]), as He said: (You have nothing of their guardianship until they emigrate) [[See vol. 8, p. 55 and p. 282.]]. Hijra (emigration) is of several kinds. Among them is emigration to Medina to support the Prophet (ﷺ). This was obligatory at the beginning of Islam, to the point that he said: (There is no hijra after the conquest). Likewise is the emigration of the hypocrites with the Prophet (ﷺ) on the military campaigns, and the emigration of one who has become Muslim in the land of war, which is obligatory. Another is the muslim's emigration from what God has forbidden to him, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: (The emigrant is one who abandons what God has forbidden). These two kinds of hijra remain valid now. There is also the abandonment of people of sins until they return, as a means of discipline for them, so they are not spoken to and not associated with until they repent, as the Prophet (ﷺ) did with Ka'b and his two companions [[See vol. 8, p. 282.]].

(Then if they turn away, seize them and kill them) means: if they turn away from monotheism and emigration, then capture them and kill them.

(Wherever you find them) is general with respect to places, both within the sacred precinct and outside it. And God knows best.

Then He made an exception, which is the second issue, saying: (Except those who join a people between you and whom there is a covenant). That is, those who connect with them and enter into their alliance by neighbourhood and pact. The meaning is: do not kill a people between whom and you there is a covenant, for they are upon their covenant. Then the covenants were abrogated (naskh), and so this ruling was abrogated. This is the view of Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and others, and it is the most sound of what has been said about the meaning of the verse.

Abu 'Ubayd said: (yasilun) means (yantasibun), i.e. they claim kinship. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

When she is joined, she says to Bakr ibn Wa'il,
while Bakr has taken her captive and the noses are humbled...

He means: when she claims kinship. Al-Mahdawi said: the scholars rejected this, because kinship does not prevent fighting and killing the disbelievers. Al-Nahhas said: this is a great error, for it implies that God forbade anyone to be fought who had kinship with the Muslims, whereas the polytheists had kinship ties with the earliest believers. Even more ignorant is the claim that this ruling existed and was then abrogated, since the people of interpretation are unanimous that the abrogating text is (Bara'a [the Repentance surah]), which was revealed only after the conquest and after wars had ended. Al-Tabari also gave this meaning.

I say: some scholars understood the meaning of (yantasibun) as safe conduct, i.e. one who attaches himself to the people of safe conduct is secure when all of them are secure, not in the sense of kinship in the meaning of blood relation.

There is disagreement about those who had a covenant with the Prophet (ﷺ). It was said they were the Banu Mudlij. Al-Hasan reported: there was a treaty between them and Quraysh, and between Quraysh and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) there was a covenant. 'Ikrimah said: it was revealed concerning Hilal ibn 'Uwaymir, Suraqa ibn Ju'shum, and Khuzayma ibn 'Amir ibn 'Abd Manaf, who had a covenant with the Prophet (ﷺ). It was also said: Khuza'a. Al-Dahhak reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he meant by the people between you and whom there is a pact the Banu Bakr ibn Zayd ibn Manat, who were in peace and truce.

The third issue: in this verse there is evidence for establishing a truce (muwada'a) between the people of war and the people of Islam when the truce serves the interest of the Muslims, as will be explained in (al-Anfal [[See vol. 8, p. 55.]] and Bara'a [[See vol. 8, p. 71 onwards.]]), God willing.

I descended and stood upright like the trunk of a tall date palm,

It is not far-fetched that Ibn Yazid is al-'Ijli al-Kufi, since he is much earlier than al-Mubarrad.]]. Its meaning is the same as the meaning of the first verse. Qatada said: it was revealed concerning a people from Tihama who sought safety from the Prophet (ﷺ), so that they would be safe with him and with their own people. Mujahid said: it concerns a people from the people of Makkah. Al-Suddi said: it was revealed concerning Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud, who would give security to both the Muslims and the polytheists. Al-Hasan said: this concerns a people among the hypocrites. It was also said: it was revealed concerning Asad and Ghatafan, who came to Madinah and embraced Islam, then returned to their homelands and openly displayed disbelief.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whenever they are returned to strife, they are plunged back into it.﴾ Yahya ibn Wathhab and al-A'mash read (رُدُّوا) with a kasra on the ra', because the original form was (رُدِدُوا), so it was assimilated (idgham, merging of two identical consonants into one) and the kasra was transferred to the ra'.

(إِلَى الْفِتْنَةِ) means: to disbelief (al-kufr). (أُرْكِسُوا فِيها) means: they are plunged back into it. It was also said: meaning, you will find those who show you reconciliation so that they may be safe from you, and whenever an opportunity for strife arises for them, they will be with its people against you. The meaning of (أُرْكِسُوا فِيها) is: they reverted from their covenant, the one they had made (ʿahdahum alladhi ʿahadu). It was also said: meaning, whenever they are called to association (shirk), they return to it and go back to it.

There are twenty issues in this passage. The first: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake﴾. This is one of the mother verses of the rulings. The meaning is: it is not fitting for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake. His saying, ﴿It is not for a believer﴾, is not a negation but a prohibition and a forbidding, like His saying: ﴿It is not for you to harm the Messenger of Allah﴾ [[See vol. 14, p. 223.]]. If it were a negation, no believer would ever have been found to kill a believer, because what Allah has negated cannot exist. Like His saying: ﴿It was not for you to cause its trees to grow﴾ [[See vol. 13, p. 219.]]. So the servants cannot ever cause its trees to grow. Qatadah said: the meaning is, it was not his right to do that during the covenant of Allah. It was also said: it was not his right to do that in the past, just as it is not his right now in any way. Then comes an exception that is disjunctive (munqati'), not part of the preceding, in which "illa" (except) carries the sense of "lakin" (but). The meaning is: it was not his right to kill him at all, but if he kills him by mistake, then upon him is such-and-such. This is the view of Sibawayh and al-Zajjaj, may Allah have mercy on them both. Among the disjunctive exceptions is His saying: ﴿They have no knowledge of it, except the following of conjecture﴾ [[See vol. 6, p. 9.]]. Al-Nabigha said:

*I stopped there at evening, asking it,*
*but it was unable to answer, and there was no one in the abode,*
*except the tethering-ropes, firmly tied,*
*and the pits like cisterns in the wronged, hard ground.*

Since the tethering-ropes (al-awari) are not literally of the kind of "anyone" (ahad), they are not included in the word. A similar line is by another:

*Saqam has become an empty place, with no companion in it,*
*except the beasts of prey and the wind passing through the ghurf trees.*

And another said:

*A land with no companion in it,*
*except the gazelles and the wild cows.*

And another said:

*Some men are like a palm tree that bears no fruit,*
*and gives no shade, except that it is counted among the palms.*

Sibawayh recited this, and many like it occur. Among the most eloquent is the saying of Jarir:

*Of the fair ones who did not travel far, nor did they tread*
*upon the earth, except the trailing hem of a striped mirt.*

It is as if he said: she did not tread upon the earth, except that she trod upon the hem of the garment. The verse was revealed concerning the killing of Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'ah of al-Harith ibn Yazid ibn Abi Unaysah [[It is said: al-Harith ibn Zayd, as Ibn Unaysah is said. See his biography in the book al-Isabah.]] al-Amiri, because of a grudge (hinnah) between them. [Hinnah and ahinnah mean rancour.] When al-Harith emigrated as a Muslim, Ayyash met him and killed him, not knowing of his Islam. When he was informed, he came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "O Messenger of Allah, there has been between me and al-Harith what you know, and I did not know of his Islam until I had killed him." Then the verse was revealed. It was also said: it is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil), meaning: it is not for a believer to kill a believer and not be retaliated against, except that it be by mistake, so no retaliation is taken from him, but there is such-and-such upon him. Another interpretation is that "kana" is taken to mean "istaqarra" and "wujida" (existed, was established), as if he said: it was not found, nor established, nor was it permissible for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake, since he is sometimes overcome in that. On these two interpretations, the exception is not disjunctive. The verse, on this reading, includes magnifying the intentional killing and the gravity of its matter, just as you say: "It was not for you, O so-and-so, to speak of this except forgetfully?" — magnifying the intention and deliberation, along with absolute prohibition of speaking of it. It was also said: the meaning is "and not by mistake either." Al-Nahhas said: "illa" cannot mean "wa" (and), this is not known in Arabic speech, and it is not correct in meaning, because mistake is not prohibited. The address does not imply the permissibility of a disbeliever killing a Muslim, for the Muslim has a sacred blood. The believer is singled out for mention to emphasise his compassion, brotherhood, tenderness and creed. Al-A'mash read "khata'" with a long vowel in the three places. The forms of mistake are many and uncountable; they are bound by the absence of intent, such as one who shoots at the ranks of the polytheists and hits a Muslim, or one who pursues someone who deserves to be killed, such as an adulterer, a warrior, or an apostate, and he chases him to kill him, but meets another and thinks him to be the one, and kills him; that is a mistake. Or one who aims at a target and hits a person, or something of that kind. This is something on which there is no disagreement. Al-khata' is a noun from akhta'a, khata'an and ikhta'an, when one does not act deliberately; so al-khata' (the noun) stands in place of al-ikhta'. It is said of one who intended something and did another: "akhta'a," and of one who did what is not right: "akhta'a." Ibn al-Mundhir said: Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake﴾, up to His saying ﴿and a compensation paid to his family﴾. So Allah, mighty is His praise, ruled concerning the believer who kills by mistake with the blood-money (diyah), and the established Sunnah from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ confirms this, and the scholars have unanimously agreed upon this.

The second issue: Dawud held that there is retaliation (qisas) between the free man and the slave in the case of a life, and in every injury in which retaliation is possible among the limbs, adhering to His saying: ﴿And We prescribed for them therein that a life is for a life﴾ [[See vol. 6, p. 191.]], up to His saying: ﴿and wounds are subject to retaliation﴾, and his saying, peace be upon him: "The Muslims' blood is equal (tatakafa'u dimauhum)." He did not distinguish between free and slave. This is also the view of Ibn Abi Layla. Abu Hanifah and his companions said: there is no retaliation between free persons and slaves except in the case of life, so a free man is killed for a slave, just as a slave is killed for a free man, and there is no retaliation between them in any injury or limb. The scholars agreed that His saying, ﴿It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake﴾, does not include slaves; rather, only free persons are intended, not slaves. Likewise, His saying, peace be upon him, "The Muslims' blood is equal," is intended only for free persons specifically. This is the position of the majority. And if there is no retaliation between slaves and free persons in what is less than life, then life is all the more so. This has already been discussed in (al-Baqarah) [[See vol. 2, p. 246.]].

The third issue: His saying, ﴿then the freeing of a believing slave﴾, meaning: upon him is the freeing of a slave. This is the expiation (kaffarah) which Allah, exalted, obligated for the expiation of killing and also for zihar, as will come [[See vol. 17, p. 272.]]. The scholars differed over what is acceptable from it. Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i, Qatadah and others said: the believing slave is the one who prays and understands faith; a young child is not sufficient in this. This is the correct view in this matter. 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: a young child born between two Muslims is sufficient. A group including Malik and al-Shafi'i said: whoever is judged by a ruling regarding the prayer over him, if he dies and is buried, is sufficient. Malik said: "The one who prays and fasts is more beloved to me." According to the consensus of all scholars, a blind person, a paralysed person, one with both hands or both feet cut off, or both paralysed, is not sufficient. According to most of them, a lame person and a one-eyed person are sufficient. Malik said: except if the lameness is severe. According to Malik, al-Shafi'i and most scholars, one with one hand or one foot cut off is not sufficient, but according to Abu Hanifah and his companions it is sufficient. According to most of them, one who is permanently insane is not sufficient; according to Malik, one who is intermittently insane is not sufficient, but according to al-Shafi'i it is sufficient. According to Malik, a slave freed on condition of payment over years is not sufficient, but according to al-Shafi'i it is sufficient. According to Malik, al-Awza'i and the people of opinion (ashab al-ra'y), a mudabbar (one freed upon the master's death) is not sufficient, but according to al-Shafi'i, Abu Thawr, and what Ibn al-Mundhir chose, it is sufficient. Malik said: one part of whom has been freed is not valid, because of His saying, ﴿the freeing of a slave﴾. One who has freed only a part is not said to have freed a slave, but has freed a part of him. They also differed over its meaning. It was said: it is obligated as a purification and expiation for the killer's sin, and his sin is his failure to take care and caution, until a man whose blood was protected perished at his hands. It was also said: it is obligated as a substitute for the violation of Allah's right regarding the life of the slain. He had a right in his own person, which is enjoying life and managing what is permitted to him in the manner of the living. Allah, glorified is He, also had a right in him, which is that he was a servant of His servants, to whom is owed, by the matter of servitude, whether young or old, free or slave, Muslim or protected non-Muslim, that which distinguishes him from beasts and animals, and it is hoped along with that that from his offspring there will be one who worships Allah and obeys Him. So his killer could not be free of having deprived him of the status we have mentioned and the meaning we have described, and therefore he is liable for the expiation. Whichever of these two meanings is the case, there is a clarification that the text, though it applies to the killer by mistake, the intentional killer is like him, indeed more deserving of the obligation of expiation than he, as its explanation will come. And Allah knows best. The fourth issue: His saying, ﴿and a compensation paid to his family﴾. Diyah (blood-money) is what is given as a substitute for the blood of the slain to his guardian (waliyy).

(مُسَلَّمَةٌ) means handed over and paid in full. God did not specify in His Book what is to be given as diya (blood-money), and the verse only makes diya obligatory in general terms. It does not state whether it is imposed on the 'aqila (the paternal kin who bear the obligation) or on the killer himself. That ruling was derived from the Sunnah. There is no doubt that imposing this mutual support (muwasah) on the 'aqila runs against the analogical principles governing financial penalties and liability for destroyed property. What the 'aqila owe is not owed as an aggravation of punishment, nor is the killer's burden transferred to them; it is pure mutual support. Abu Hanifa held that it is based on the principle of support (nusrah), so he made it obligatory on the people of his diwan [[The diwan is applied to the register of military service and stipends, and to any assembly gathered for the management and consideration of public interests. al-Jassas said in his Ahkam: "It is placed in their stipends if they are among the people of the diwan"; see vol. 2, p. 225 of the Ahkam, which clarifies the matter. It will come at p. 321 that they are the people of the locality who are "the hand".]].

Reports are firmly established from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that the diya is one hundred camels. He (ﷺ) paid it for 'Abdullah ibn Sahl, who was killed at Khaybar, to Huwayyisa [[Huwayyisa and Muhayyisa (with a damma on the first letter, then a fatha, then a shaddah on the ya with kasra, or unstressed; the more well-known is with shaddah).]], Muhayyisa and 'Abd al-Rahman. That was an explanation, through the tongue of His Prophet (peace be upon him), of what was general in His Book. The scholars are unanimous that the people of camels owe one hundred camels. They differed concerning what is owed by those who are not people of camels. One group said: the people of gold owe one thousand dinars, and they are the people of al-Sham, Egypt and the Maghrib. This is the view of Malik, Ahmad, Ishaq, the people of opinion (Ashab al-Ra'y), and al-Shafi'i in one of his two opinions, the earlier one (al-qadim). This was narrated from 'Umar, 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr and Qatada. As for the people of silver, they owe twelve thousand dirhams, and they are the people of Iraq, Persia and Khurasan. This is the position of Malik, based on what reached him from 'Umar, that he assessed the diya on the people of the towns: he made it one thousand dinars for the people of gold and twelve thousand dirhams for the people of silver. Al-Muzani said: al-Shafi'i said: the diya is camels; if they are unavailable, then their value in dirhams and dinars, according to what 'Umar assessed: one thousand dinars for the people of gold and twelve thousand dirhams for the people of silver. Abu Hanifa, his companions and al-Thawri said: the diya in silver is ten thousand dirhams. It was narrated by al-Sha'bi from 'Abida from 'Umar that he made the diya for the people of gold one thousand dinars, and for the people of silver ten thousand dirhams, and for the people of cattle two hundred cows, and for the people of sheep one thousand sheep, and for the people of camels one hundred camels, and for the people of garments two hundred garments. Abu 'Umar said: in this hadith there is what indicates that the dinars and dirhams are a category of the kinds of diya, not as a substitute or a value; and this is the apparent meaning of the hadith from 'Uthman, 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas. Abu Hanifa opposed what was narrated from 'Umar concerning cattle, sheep and garments. This was also the view of 'Ata', Tawus and a group of the Successors, and it is the view of the seven Fuqaha' of Madina. Ibn al-Mundhir said: a group said the diya of a free Muslim man is one hundred camels, and there is no diya other than that, as the Messenger of God (ﷺ) prescribed. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, and Tawus also held it. Ibn al-Mundhir said: the diya of a free Muslim man is one hundred camels at every time, as the Messenger of God (ﷺ) prescribed. The reports differed from 'Umar (may God be pleased with him) concerning the numbers of dirhams, and none of them is authentically transmitted from him, because they are mursal (disconnected) reports. I have already informed you of the position of al-Shafi'i, and by it we say.

The fifth issue: The jurists differed concerning the ages of the camels for the diya. Abu Dawud narrated from the hadith of 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) decreed that whoever is killed by error, his diya is one hundred camels: thirty bint makhad, thirty bint labun, thirty hiqqa, and ten ibn labun [[In Sharh al-Muwatta' of al-Baji: (Muhammad ibn 'Isa al-A'sha said in al-Muzaniyya: bint makhad is the one that follows its mother, and its mother has conceived. Bint labun is also one that follows its mother, and it is still nursing. The hiqqa is the one that is deserving of being mounted. As for the jadha'a among camels, it is what is above twenty-four months.)]]. Al-Khattabi said: I do not know of any jurist who held this hadith; most scholars said: the diya for error is in fifths. So said the people of opinion, al-Thawri, and likewise Malik, Ibn Sirin and Ahmad ibn Hanbal, except that they differed concerning the categories. The people of opinion and Ahmad said: a fifth ibn makhad, a fifth bint makhad, a fifth bint labun, a fifth hiqaq, and a fifth jidha'. This view was narrated from Ibn Mas'ud. Malik and al-Shafi'i said: a fifth hiqaq, a fifth jidha', a fifth bint labun, a fifth bint makhad, and a fifth ibn labun. This view was narrated from 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, Sulayman ibn Yasar, al-Zuhri, Rabi'a and al-Layth ibn Sa'd. Al-Khattabi said: the people of opinion have a report on this, except that its narrator is 'Abd Allah ibn Khashf ibn Malik, who is unknown and is known only through this hadith. Al-Shafi'i refrained from holding it, for the reason we have mentioned concerning its narrator, and because it includes ibn makhad, and ibn makhad has no place in any of the ages of the sadaqat (zakat animals). It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) in the story of the qasama (oath procedure) that he paid the blood-money of the one killed at Khaybar as one hundred camels from the camels of charity, and there is no ibn makhad among the ages of charity camels. Abu 'Umar said: Zayd ibn Jubayr narrated from Khashf ibn Malik, from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) made the diya for error in fifths; but none raised this to the Prophet except Khashf ibn Malik al-Kufi al-Ta'i, who is unknown, because none narrated from him except Zayd ibn Jubayr ibn Harmal al-Ta'i [al-Jushami [[from Ta and Ya.) (]]] of the Banu Jusham ibn Mu'awiya, one of the trustworthy Kufans. I say: al-Daraqutni mentioned in his Sunan the hadith of Khashf ibn Malik from the narration of Hajjaj ibn Artat, from Zayd ibn Jubayr, from Khashf ibn Malik, from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) decreed concerning the diya for error one hundred camels, of which twenty are hiqqa, twenty jadha'a, twenty bint labun, twenty bint makhad, and twenty ibn makhad. Al-Daraqutni said: (This is a weak hadith, not established according to the people of knowledge of hadith, for several reasons. One of them is that it contradicts what Abu 'Ubayda ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud narrated from his father through a sound chain, which has no flaw and no interpretation, and Abu 'Ubayda knows best the hadith of his father and his school and his fatwa [[The addition is from al-Daraqutni.]], more than Khashf ibn Malik and his peers. 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud was too pious toward his Lord and too careful with his religion to narrate from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he decreed a judgment and then himself issued a fatwa contrary to it. Such a thing cannot be imagined of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who said concerning a matter that came before him, about which he had heard nothing from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and no word had reached him: I say about it with my opinion; if it is correct, it is from God and His Messenger, and if it is wrong, it is from me. Then it reached him later that his fatwa in it agreed with the judgment of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in a similar case, and his companions saw him then rejoice with a great joy such as they had never seen him rejoice, because his fatwa agreed with the judgment of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Whoever has this description and this condition, how could it be valid that he narrates from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) [anything [[The addition is from al-Daraqutni.]]] and then contradicts it?) Another point: the marfu' report that mentions the ibn makhad, we do not know anyone who narrated it except Khashf ibn Malik from Ibn Mas'ud, and he is an unknown man, from whom none narrated except Zayd ibn Jubayr ibn Harmal al-Jushami. The scholars of hadith do not argue with a report that is transmitted by a single unknown man. Knowledge is established for them through a report only when its narrator is an upright, well-known person, or a man from whom the name of unknown has been lifted. The name of unknown is lifted from him when two or more narrate from him; when this is his state, the name of unknown is lifted from him and he becomes known. As for one from whom only a single man narrates and who is alone in a report, it is necessary to withhold from that report until someone else agrees with it. And God knows best. Another point: we do not know anyone who narrated the hadith of Khashf ibn Malik from Zayd ibn Jubayr from him except Hajjaj ibn Artat, and Hajjaj is a man well known for tadlis (concealing sources) and for narrating from those he did not meet and did not hear from. Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna, Yahya ibn Sa'id al-Qattan and 'Isa ibn Yunus abandoned narrating from him after they sat with him and tested him, and that is enough to show their knowledge of the man and their nobility. Yahya ibn Ma'in said: Hajjaj ibn Artat's hadith is not used as proof. 'Abd Allah ibn Idris said: I heard Hajjaj say: a man does not become noble until he abandons prayer in congregation. 'Isa ibn Yunus said: I heard Hajjaj say: I go out to prayer and the porters and grocers crowd me. Jarir said: I heard Hajjaj say: love of wealth and status has destroyed me. Al-Daraqutni mentioned other aspects, among them that a group of trustworthy narrators transmitted this hadith from Hajjaj ibn Artat and differed over it. And other points too long to mention; what we have mentioned of what they mentioned suffices as evidence of the weakness of what the Kufans adopted concerning the diya, even though Ibn al-Mundhir, with his eminence, chose it, as will come. Hammad ibn Salama narrated: Sulayman al-Taymi related to us from Abu Mijlaz, from Abu 'Ubayda, that Ibn Mas'ud said: The diya for error is five fifths: twenty hiqqa, twenty jadha'a, twenty bint makhad, twenty bint labun, and twenty male ibn labun. Al-Daraqutni said: This is a sound chain and its narrators are trustworthy, and something similar has been narrated from 'Alqama from 'Abd Allah. I say: This is the position of Malik and al-Shafi'i, that the diya is in fifths. Al-Khattabi said: It has been narrated from a group of scholars that they said the diya for error is in quarters, and they are al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i and al-Hasan al-Basri, and Ishaq ibn Rahawayh also went to this, except that they said: twenty-five jadha'a, twenty-five hiqqa, twenty-five bint labun, and twenty-five bint makhad. This has been narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib. Abu 'Umar said: As for the view of Malik and al-Shafi'i, it is narrated from Sulayman ibn Yasar, and there is nothing from a Companion on it, but the practice of the people of Madina is upon it. Likewise Ibn Jurayj related from Ibn Shihab. I say: We have already mentioned from Ibn Mas'ud what agrees with what Malik and al-Shafi'i adopted. Abu 'Umar said: The ages of camels in the diyat were not taken by analogy or by reasoning; they were taken by following and submission, and whatever is taken from the source of a report has no room for reasoning in it. So each one speaks by what has been authenticated to him from his predecessors, may God be pleased with them all.

I say: As for what al-Khattabi reported, that no one is known to have held the view in the hadith of Amr ibn Shu'ayb, Ibn al-Mundhir did report it from Tawus and Mujahid, except that Mujahid substituted thirty jadha'ah (four-year-old camels) for the bint makhad (one-year-old she-camel). Ibn al-Mundhir said: "I hold the first view." He means the view of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud) and the people of opinion (ashab al-ra'y), which al-Daraqutni and al-Khattabi declared weak. Ibn Abd al-Barr said: "Because it is the least of what has been said, and it agrees with a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) hadith that we have narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ)." [[In manuscript C: "And the hadith is marfu' etc."]]

I say: How strange is Ibn al-Mundhir! Despite his critical acumen and his independent reasoning, how could he hold to a hadith whose authenticity the critics did not agree upon? But forgetfulness and heedlessness may overtake a person, and perfection belongs only to the Might of the Lord of Majesty.

**The sixth issue:** It is established by reports from the Prophet, the chosen Muhammad (ﷺ), that he ruled that the diyah (blood money) for unintentional killing is borne by the 'aqilah (paternal kin who bear the blood money), and the scholars unanimously agreed upon this. In the consensus of the scholars that the diyah for unintentional killing is borne by the 'aqilah, there is evidence that what is meant by the Prophet's (ﷺ) words to Abu Ramthah, when he came to him with his son, "He does not commit a crime against you, nor do you commit one against him," is intentional wrongdoing, not unintentional. They also agreed that whatever exceeds one-third of the diyah is borne by the 'aqilah, but they differed regarding the one-third. The majority of scholars hold that the 'aqilah does not bear intentional killing, nor confession, nor settlement, and it bears from the diyah for unintentional killing only what exceeds one-third, while what is less than one-third is paid from the wealth of the offender. A group said: the diyah for unintentional killing is borne by the 'aqilah of the offender, whether the harm is small or great, because whoever bears the greater amount bears the lesser. Just as intentional killing is imposed on the wealth of the offender, whether small or great. This is the view of al-Shafi'i.

**The seventh issue:** Its ruling is that it is paid in installments over the 'aqilah, and the 'aqilah are the 'asabah (agnatic male relatives). The child of a woman is not among her 'aqilah if he is not from her 'asabah, nor are maternal brothers 'asabah for their full brothers from the father and mother, so they do not bear anything on their behalf. Likewise, the diwan (register of stipends) does not make one an 'aqilah in the view of the majority of the people of the Hijaz. The Kufans said: one who is on the diwan becomes an 'aqilah, so the diyah is paid in installments by the 'aqilah over three years, according to what Umar and Ali decided, because camels may be pregnant and would be harmed by it. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to give it in one installment, for various purposes, among them that he gave it as a settlement and for arrangement, and among them that he hastened it to win hearts. When Islam became firmly established, the Companions set it according to this system, as Ibn al-Arabi said. Abu Umar said: The scholars, ancient and modern, unanimously agreed that the diyah borne by the 'aqilah is not paid except over three years and not in less than that. They agreed that it is imposed on adult men. The people of biography and knowledge unanimously agreed that the diyah in the Jahiliyyah was borne by the 'aqilah, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) confirmed it in Islam. They used to share the 'aqilah obligation through mutual support. Then Islam came and the matter continued in this way until Umar instituted the diwan. The jurists agreed on narrating this and on holding it. They also agreed that there was no diwan in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) or in the time of Abu Bakr, that Umar instituted the diwan and brought people together, made the people of each region one hand, and made it their duty to fight the enemy nearest to them.

**The eighth issue:** I say: Among what falls under this chapter and enters its system is the killing of an unborn child in its mother's womb, by striking the mother's belly so that it is expelled alive and then dies. All the scholars said: the full diyah is due for it in unintentional killing, and in intentional killing after a qasamah (oath procedure). It was also said: without a qasamah. They differed about what establishes its life, after agreeing that if it cries out, or suckles, or breathes a breath, its life is certain, and the full diyah is due. If it moves, al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa said: the movement indicates its life. Malik said: No, unless it is accompanied by a long period of survival. Male and female are equal in the ruling according to all the scholars. If she expels it dead, then there is a ghurrah (a slave or slave-girl as blood money) [[Ghurrah: the slave himself or the female slave; its discussion will come in the ninth issue.]]: a male slave or a female slave. If she does not expel it and dies while it is still in her womb and it does not come out, there is nothing for it. All of this is a consensus without disagreement. It is related from al-Layth ibn Sa'd and Dawud that they said regarding a woman who dies from a blow to her belly, and then the fetus comes out dead after her death: there is a ghurrah for it, whether she expelled it before or after her death. What matters is her life at the time of the striking, and nothing else. All the other jurists said: there is nothing for it if it comes out dead from her belly after her death. Al-Tahawi argued on behalf of the group of jurists, saying: They all agreed, and al-Layth with them, that if someone strikes her belly while she is alive, and she dies while the fetus is in her belly and has not been expelled, there is nothing for it. Likewise if it is expelled after her death.

**The ninth issue:** The ghurrah must be white. Abu Amr ibn al-Ala said regarding the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "For the unborn child, a ghurrah: a male slave or a female slave." If the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had not intended a specific meaning by "ghurrah," he would have said, "For the unborn child, a male slave or a female slave." But he meant whiteness. Therefore, only a white boy or a white girl is accepted in the diyah, and no black male or black female is accepted. The scholars differed about its value. Malik said: It is valued at fifty dinars or six hundred dirhams, which is one-twentieth of the diyah of a free Muslim male, and one-tenth of the diyah of its mother, a free woman. This is the view of Ibn Shihab, Rabi'ah, and all the people of Madinah. The people of opinion said: its value is five hundred dirhams. Al-Shafi'i said: the age of the ghurrah is seven or eight years, and it is not obligatory to accept it if it is defective. The implication of Malik's school is that one is free to choose between giving a ghurrah or one-tenth of the mother's diyah: twenty dinars of gold if the people are gold-owners, or six hundred dirhams of silver if they are silver-owners, or five female camels (fara'id) of camels. [[Fara'id: plural of fari'dah, a camel taken in zakat; it was called fari'dah because it is an obligation imposed on the owner of property, and the term was extended so that a camel is called fari'dah outside of zakat.]] Malik and his companions said: it is from the wealth of the offender. This is also the view of al-Hasan ibn Hayy. Abu Hanifa, al-Shafi'i, and their companions said: it is borne by the 'aqilah. This is more sound, due to the hadith of al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah that two women were married to two men of the Ansar, in one narration they became jealous of each other, so one of them struck the other with a pillar and killed her. The two men brought the dispute before the Prophet (ﷺ). One of the two men said [[In Sunan Abi Dawud: "one of the two men said."]]: "How shall we pay for one who neither cried out, nor ate, nor drank, nor cried out (istahalla), so that such blood is wasted?" He said: "Is this rhymed prose like the rhymed prose of the Bedouins?" Then he ruled a ghurrah for it and made it the responsibility of the woman's 'aqilah. This hadith is authentic and sound, an explicit text on the point of disagreement, and it requires a ruling. Since the diyah of the injured woman is borne by the 'aqilah, the fetus is similarly so by analogy and reasoning. Our scholars argued from the words of the one against whom the judgment was rendered: "How shall I be made to pay?" They said: This indicates that the one against whom judgment was given was specifically the offender. Had the diyah for the fetus been ruled to be borne by the 'aqilah, he would have said, "The one who was ruled against them said." By analogy, every offender bears his own crime, except where a proof that has no contrary opposes it, such as a consensus that may not be opposed, or an explicit sunnah transmitted through reliable individual reports with no contrary, in which case the ruling must follow it. Allah the Most High said: ﴿And no soul earns [blame] except against itself, and no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another﴾. [[See vol. 7, p. 156.]]

**The tenth issue:** Scholars agree without dispute that if a fetus is born alive, there is kaffarah (expiation) in addition to the diyah (blood-money). They differ about expiation if it is born dead. Malik said: there is a ghurrah (a slave, or its equivalent value, due for a fetus) and expiation. Abu Hanifah and al-Shafi'i said: there is a ghurrah and no expiation.

They also differ about the inheritance of the ghurrah from the fetus. Malik, al-Shafi'i and their companions said: the ghurrah for the fetus is inherited from the fetus, according to the Book of Allah, because it is a diyah. Abu Hanifah and his companions said: the ghurrah belongs to the mother alone, because it is a wrong done to her by cutting off one of her limbs, and it is not a diyah. Evidence for this is that the sex of the fetus is not taken into account in it, as it is in the diyah, so this shows that it is like a limb. Ibn Hurmuz used to say: its diyah belongs to its two parents only, two-thirds to its father and one-third to its mother. Whichever of them is alive receives it. If one of them has died, it goes to the surviving one, whether father or mother, and the siblings inherit nothing.

**The eleventh issue:** Allah's words, ﴿unless they forgo it as charity﴾, originally read (an yatasaddaqu), and the ta' was assimilated into the sad. Tasaddaq means to give. The meaning is: unless the guardians (awliya') of the slain man release the heirs of the killer [the killers] from the diyah that Allah has made due to them from them. So this is an exception, not part of the earlier clause.

Abu Abd al-Rahman and Nubayh [[As in the original manuscripts and Ibn 'Atiyyah. The more likely reading is Abu Nujayh, who is 'Ismah ibn 'Urwah al-Basri, who transmitted from Abu 'Amr and 'Asim. As for Nubayh, we have not found him among the reciters. In al-Tahdhib: Nubayh, diminutive, son of 'Abd Allah al-'Anazi, Abu 'Amr al-Kufi. In al-Taj: a Successor (tabi'i). No recitation is attributed to him. And Allah knows best.]] recited it (illa an tasaddaqu) with the sad and the ta' both lightened. Abu 'Amr recited it the same way, except that he doubled the sad. In the reading, the second ta' is deleted, and it is not permissible to delete it in the reading with the ya'. In the codices of Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud it reads (illa an yatasaddaqu).

As for the expiation, which is due to Allah the Exalted, it does not fall away by their release, because the killer has destroyed a person in the worship of Allah the Glorified, so he must free another person for the worship of his Lord. Only the diyah, which is their right, falls away. The expiation is due from the property of the one who committed the crime and is not borne by others.

**The twelfth issue:** Allah's words, ﴿If he is from a people hostile to you and he is a believer﴾. This is an issue concerning a believer who is killed in the lands of the unbelievers or in their wars, while they regard him as one of the unbelievers. The meaning according to Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, al-Suddi, Ikrimah, Mujahid and al-Nakha'i is: if this slain man was a believing man who had accepted Islam but stayed among his people, and they were unbelievers (hostile to you), then there is no diyah for him. His expiation is the freeing of a slave. This is the well-known view of Malik, and Abu Hanifah said the same.

The diyah falls away for two reasons. The first: the guardians of the slain man are unbelievers, so it is not valid to hand it to them, lest they strengthen themselves with it [[In J and T: "they will strengthen themselves with it."]]. The second: the sanctity of this man who accepted Islam but did not emigrate is slight, so there is no diyah, because of Allah's words: ﴿And those who believed but did not emigrate, you owe them no duty of guardianship until they emigrate﴾ [[Vol. 8, p. 55.]].

Another group said: rather, the reason the diyah falls away is that the guardians are only unbelievers. So whether the killing was accidental among Muslims, or among his own people while he had not emigrated, or he had emigrated and then returned to his people, his expiation is the freeing of a slave and there is no diyah for him, since it is not valid to hand it to the unbelievers. And if the diyah were due, it would have to be paid to the public treasury (bayt al-mal). So no diyah is due in this case, even if the killing took place in the lands of Islam. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, and al-Awza'i, al-Thawri and Abu Thawr also held it. According to the first view, if a believer is killed in the lands of the Muslims while his people are at war with them, then there is a diyah for him, paid to the public treasury, and expiation.

I say: among this category is what is reported in Sahih Muslim from Usamah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent us on an expedition, and we attacked al-Huraqat [[al-Huraqat (with the ha' vowelled with a damma or fatha, and the ra' with a fatha or damma): a place in the lands of Juhaynah.]] of Juhaynah at dawn. I caught up with a man who said: "There is no god but Allah," and I struck him. It weighed on my mind, so I mentioned it to the Prophet (ﷺ). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "He said, 'There is no god but Allah,' and you killed him?!" I said: "O Messenger of Allah, he only said it out of fear of the weapon." He said: "Why did you not split open his heart, so that you would know whether he said it or not?" He did not pass judgement on him (ﷺ) for retaliation (qisas) or diyah.

It is also reported from Usamah that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked forgiveness for me three times and said: "Free a slave." He did not judge for retaliation or diyah.

Our scholars said: As for the falling away of retaliation, it is clear, since the killing was not an aggression. As for the falling away of the diyah, there are three reasons. The first: because he had been permitted to take part in the fighting in general, so the destruction of a sacred soul was an error, like the circumciser and the physician. The second: because he was from the enemy, and there was no Muslim guardian to whom his diyah could be paid, according to Allah's words: ﴿If he is from a people hostile to you﴾, as we have mentioned. The third: Usamah confessed to the killing, and no evidence was established for it, and the paternal kin (al-'aqilah) do not bear liability on the basis of a confession. Perhaps Usamah also had no property from which the diyah could be paid. And Allah knows best.

**The thirteenth issue:** Allah's words, ﴿And if he is from a people between you and whom there is a covenant﴾. This concerns a dhimmi (protected non-Muslim) or a mu'ahad (one under a treaty) who is killed by mistake. Then the diyah and the expiation are due. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i and al-Shafi'i, and al-Tabari chose it. He said: However, Allah the Glorified and Exalted left him unspecified and did not say "and he is a believer," as He said about the slain man among the believers and among the people of war. Its absolute wording, which is not restricted as before, indicates that it is the opposite.

Al-Hasan, Jabir ibn Zayd and Ibrahim also said: the meaning is: if the slain man killed by mistake was a believer from a people who are in covenant with you, then their covenant requires that they are entitled to the diyah of their companion, so the expiation is the freeing of a slave and the payment of the diyah. Al-Hasan recited it: ﴿And if he is from a people between you and whom there is a covenant, and he is a believer﴾. Al-Hasan said: If a Muslim kills a dhimmi, there is no expiation for him.

Abu 'Umar said: As for the verse, its meaning according to the people of the Hijaz is that it refers back to His words: ﴿It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake﴾, then He said: ﴿And if he is from a people﴾, meaning that believer. And Allah knows best.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: What I hold is that the clause is to be understood as the absolute being carried over to the restricted. I say: This is the meaning of what al-Hasan said, and what Abu 'Umar related from the people of the Hijaz.

His words, ﴿then a diyah delivered to his family﴾, in the indefinite form, do not require a specific diyah.

It was also said: this refers to the polytheists of the Arabs who had a covenant with the Prophet (peace be upon him) on condition that they accept Islam or be informed of war at a set term. So whoever of them was killed, the diyah and expiation were due for him, and then this was abrogated (naskh) by Allah's words: ﴿A declaration of immunity from Allah and His Messenger to those among the polytheists with whom you made a covenant﴾ [[See Vol. 8, p. 61.]].

**The fourteenth issue:** The scholars are unanimous that the diyah of a woman is half the diyah of a man. Abu 'Umar said: Her diyah became half the diyah of a man, and Allah knows best, because she receives half the inheritance of a man, and the testimony of two women equals the testimony of one man. This applies only to the diyah for accidental killing. As for intentional killing, there is retaliation (qisas) between men and women, because of the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿A life for a life﴾ and ﴿a free man for a free man﴾, as was mentioned earlier in al-Baqarah [[See Vol. 2, p. 246 onwards.]].

**The fifteenth issue:** Al-Daraqutni related from the hadith of Musa ibn 'Ali ibn Rabah al-Lakhmi, who said: I heard my father say: A blind man used to recite poetry at the season of pilgrimage [[The addition is from al-Daraqutni.]] during the caliphate of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), and he would say:

O people, I have met a strange thing:
can a blind man understand one who sees clearly?
Both of them fell together, and both were broken.

Al-Qurtubi's commentary on surah 4, verse 92 (part 5 of 5):

That was because a blind man was being led by a sighted man, and they both fell into a well. The blind man fell on the sighted man, and the sighted man died. ʿUmar judged that the sighted man's blood-money (ʿaql, the compensation paid by the kin of the one responsible) was to be paid by the blind man.

The scholars have differed concerning a man who falls upon another so that one of them dies. It is narrated from Ibn al-Zubayr that the upper one is liable to the lower one, and the lower one is not liable to the upper one. This is the view of Shurayh, al-Nakhaʿi, Ahmad and Ishaq. Mālik said, concerning two men where one of them pulled the other until both fell and died: the diyah (blood-money) is upon the ʿāqilah (the paternal kinsmen who bear the liability) of the one who pulled. Abu ʿUmar said: "I do not think there is any disagreement on this, Allah knows best, except what some of the later scholars of our school and of the school of al-Shafiʿi have said: he is liable for half the diyah, because he died from his own act and from the falling of the one who fell upon him."

Al-Hakam and Ibn Shubrumah said: if a man falls upon another from the roof of a house and one of them dies, they said: the living one among them is liable.

Al-Shafiʿi said, concerning two men where one of them collides with the other and both die: the diyah of the one who was struck is upon the ʿāqilah of the one who struck, and the diyah of the one who struck is void (hadar). He said, concerning two horsemen who collide and both die: upon each of them is half the diyah of his companion, because each of them died from the act of himself and the act of his companion. This was also said by ʿUthman al-Battti and Zufar.

Mālik, al-Awzaʿi, al-Hasan ibn Hayy, and Abu Hanifah and his companions said, concerning two horsemen who collide and both die: upon each of them is the diyah of the other, upon his ʿāqilah.

Ibn Khuwayz Mandād said: "Likewise, according to us, two ships that collide, if the sailor did not turn the ship aside, nor the horseman turn the horse aside." It is narrated from Mālik concerning two ships and two horsemen: upon each of them is the liability for the full value of what he destroyed of his companion's property.

The sixteenth issue: The scholars have differed in this chapter concerning the detailed diyah of the People of the Book. Mālik and his companions said: it is half the diyah of a Muslim, and the diyah of a Magian is eight hundred dirhams, and the diyah of their women is half of that. This view is narrated from ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-Aziz, ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr, and ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal also held it. On this point, Sulayman ibn Bilal narrated from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith ibn ʿAyyash ibn Abi Rabiʿah, from ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Prophet (ﷺ) set the diyah of a Jew and a Christian at half the diyah of a Muslim. This ʿAbd al-Rahman was also narrated from by al-Thawri.

Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Shaʿbi and al-Nakhaʿi said: a person of the covenant (ahl al-ʿahd) killed by mistake, whether he was a believer or an unbeliever, according to the covenant of his people, the diyah is due for him like the diyah of a Muslim. This is the view of Abu Hanifah, al-Thawri, ʿUthman al-Battti and al-Hasan ibn Hayy, who made all the diyat equal: the Muslim, the Jew, the Christian, the Magian, the one under treaty (muʿahad) and the dhimmi. This is also the view of ʿAṭāʾ, al-Zuhri and Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab. Their proof is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿then a diyah﴾, and that requires the full diyah, like the diyah of a Muslim. They strengthened this with what Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated from Dawud ibn al-Husayn, from ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning the story of the Banu Qurayzah and al-Nadir, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made their diyat equal, a full diyah. Abu ʿUmar said: this is a hadith in which there is weakness, and such a narration is not a proof.

Al-Shafiʿi said: the diyah of a Jew and a Christian is one-third of the diyah of a Muslim, and the diyah of a Magian is eight hundred dirhams. His proof is that this is the least that has been said on the matter, and the dhimmah (protected covenant) is free of obligation except by certainty or proof. This view is narrated from ʿUmar and ʿUthman, and Ibn al-Musayyab, ʿAṭāʾ, al-Hasan, ʿIkrimah, ʿAmr ibn Dinar, Abu Thawr and Ishaq also held it.

The seventeenth issue: the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿but whoever does not find [one]﴾, meaning the slave, and whose wealth does not extend to buying one.

(then fasting two months) meaning: then upon him is fasting two months.

(consecutive) so that if he breaks the fast for a single day, he must begin again. This is the view of the majority. Makki narrated from al-Shaʿbi that fasting two months suffices in place of both the diyah and the freeing of a slave for one who cannot find one. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: this view is an error, because the diyah is only upon the ʿāqilah and not upon the killer. Al-Tabari related this view from Masruq.

The eighteenth issue: Menstruation does not prevent the consecutiveness (tatabuʿ) without any disagreement. If she becomes pure and does not delay, she resumes the rest of her fast, connecting it to what preceded, and there is nothing upon her beyond that, unless she was pure before dawn and then leaves the fast of that day knowing she is pure; if she does this, she begins again according to a group of scholars. Abu ʿUmar said this. They differed concerning the sick person who has fasted some of the two months of consecutive fasting, on two views. Mālik said: no one who is obligated to fast two consecutive months under the Book of Allah, the Exalted, may break it except for an excuse, sickness, or menstruation, and he may not travel and break the fast. Among those who said he continues (yabni) in cases of illness were Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab, Sulayman ibn Yasar, al-Hasan, al-Shaʿbi, ʿAṭāʾ, Mujahid, Qatadah and Tawus. Saʿid ibn Jubayr, al-Nakhaʿi, al-Hakam ibn ʿUyaynah and ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurasani said: he begins again in illness. This is the view of Abu Hanifah and his companions and al-Hasan ibn Hayy, and one of the two views of al-Shafiʿi; he also had another view, that he continues as Mālik said. Ibn Shubrumah said: he makes up that day alone if the excuse is overwhelming, like fasting Ramadan. Abu ʿUmar said: the proof of those who say he continues is that he is excused in breaking the consecutiveness due to his illness, and he did not intend it, and Allah has pardoned what is not done deliberately. The proof of those who say he begins again is that consecutiveness is an obligation that does not fall away due to an excuse; only the sin falls away, by analogy with the prayer, for it consists of consecutive units (rakʿat), so if he breaks it due to an excuse, he begins again and does not continue.

The nineteenth issue: the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿a repentance from Allah﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), and its meaning is "a return." The one who erred needed repentance only because he did not take precautions, and it was his duty to be careful. It was also said: it means "let him fast as a lightening from Allah, the Exalted, upon him, by accepting the fast in place of the slave." From this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Allah knew that you were deceiving yourselves, so He turned to you [in forgiveness]﴾, meaning He lightened [the burden]. And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He knew that you would not be able to keep count of it, so He turned to you﴾.

The twentieth: (And Allah is) meaning in His eternity and His everlastingness.

(All-Knowing) of all that is known.

(All-Wise) in what He decrees and determines.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verse 93 (part 1 of 2):**

There are seven issues in this verse.

**The first issue:** God Most High says: ﴿And whoever kills﴾. ("Whoever," *man*, is a conditional particle. Its response is "then his recompense," which will come later.)

The scholars differed over the description of one who kills deliberately. 'Ata' (ibn Abi Rabah), al-Nakha'i, and others said: he is the one who kills with an iron implement, such as a sword, a dagger, the head of a spear, or similar sharpened things that are prepared for cutting, or with something known to cause death, such as heavy stones and the like.

Another group said: the deliberate killer is anyone who kills with an iron implement, or with a stone, a stick, or anything else. This is the view of the majority (*al-jumhur*).

**The second issue:** God, Mighty and Majestic, mentioned in His Book the deliberate killing (*al-'amd*) and the accidental killing (*al-khata'*), and He did not mention quasi-deliberate killing (*shibh al-'amd*). The scholars differed over whether to affirm it. Ibn al-Mundhir said: Malik rejected this, and said: "There is nothing in the Book of God except deliberate and accidental killing."

Al-Khattabi also reported this from Malik and added: "As for quasi-deliberate killing, we do not recognize it."

Abu 'Umar (ibn 'Abd al-Barr) said: Malik and al-Layth ibn Sa'd rejected quasi-deliberate killing. According to them, whoever kills with something that does not ordinarily kill, such as biting, slapping, or striking with a whip, a rod, or the like, it is deliberate killing, and retaliation (*al-qawad*) is required for it.

Abu 'Umar said: A group of the Companions and the Successors (*al-tabi'un*) held the view of these two.

But the majority of the jurists of the major cities held that all of this is quasi-deliberate killing. This view has also been attributed to Malik, and it was said by Ibn Wahb and a group of the Companions and the Successors.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: "Quasi-deliberate killing is acted upon by us."

Among those who affirmed quasi-deliberate killing were al-Sha'bi, al-Hakam, Hammad, al-Nakha'i, Qatadah, Sufyan al-Thawri, the people of Iraq, and al-Shafi'i. This has been transmitted to us from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with them both.

I (al-Qurtubi) say: This is the sound view, for blood is the most deserving of precaution, since the basic principle is to preserve it in its skin (*ahab*, the plural of *ihab*, meaning "hide"), so it may not be violated except by a clear matter without ambiguity. This case is ambiguous, because when it is uncertain whether it was deliberate or accidental, it is judged as quasi-deliberate. The striking was intended, but the killing was not intended; it occurred without intent. Therefore retaliation falls away, and the blood money (*diyah*) is made more severe.

The Sunnah came in accordance with this. Abu Dawud related from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said:

"Indeed, the blood money for accidental killing that is quasi-deliberate, which is by whip and stick, is one hundred camels, of which forty are pregnant (with their young in their wombs)."

Al-Daraqutni related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said:

"Deliberate killing involves retaliation of the hand. Accidental killing involves blood money (*'aql*), and there is no retaliation for it. Whoever is killed in *'immiyyah* (the word *'immiyyah*, with a kasra on the 'ayn and mim and a shadda on the ya', means a situation in which the matter is obscure, and his killer is not clear, nor is the circumstance of his killing) by a stone, a stick, or a whip, then the blood money is severe, in the ages of camels."

It was also related from the hadith of Sulayman ibn Musa, from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said:

"The blood money for quasi-deliberate killing is severe, like the killing of deliberate killing, and its perpetrator is not to be killed."

This is an explicit text.

Tawus said concerning a man who is struck in *al-rimiyya* (the word *rimiyya*, with a kasra, a shadda, and a short vowel, follows the pattern of *al-hujayra* from *al-rami* (shooting), a verbal noun used for emphasis) in battle with a stick, a whip, or the throwing of stones:

"Blood money is paid for him, and he is not killed for it, because it is not known who killed him."

Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: *al-'imiyya* is a blind matter arising from partisanship (*'asabiyyah*), whose nature is not made clear.

Ishaq said: This applies to a people who fall into *taharuj* (meaning they fall into difficulty) and kill one another.

Thus its origin appears to be from *al-ta'miyah*, which means confusion (*al-talbis*). Al-Daraqutni mentioned this.

**Issue:** Those who affirm quasi-deliberate killing differed concerning the severe blood money. 'Ata' and al-Shafi'i said: It is thirty *hiqqah* (a female camel that has entered its fourth year and is ready to be ridden) (the footnote says: Abu Dawud said in his Sahih: Abu 'Ubayd and others said: when a she-camel enters her fourth year, she is a *haqq* and the female is *haqqah*, because it deserves to be carried and ridden. When it enters its fifth year, it is a *jadha'* and *jadha'ah*. When it enters its sixth year and sheds its incisor, it is a *thani*. When it enters its seventh year, it is a *ruba'* and *ruba'iyyah*. When it enters its eighth year and sheds the tooth after the ruba'iyyah, it is a *sadis* and *sadus*. When it enters its ninth year, its milk has dried up and its teeth are full, and it is a *bazil*. When it enters its tenth year, it is a *mukhlif*. Then it has no name, but it is said: "bazil of one year, and bazil of two years, and mukhlif of one year and mukhlif of two years," up to whatever more. And al-Nadr ibn Tuhmul said: *ibnat makhad* for one year, *ibnat labun* for two years, *haqqah* for three, *jadha'ah* for four, *thani* for five, *ruba'* for six, *sadis* for seven, and *bazil* for eight.) and thirty *jadha'ah* and forty *khalifah* (a pregnant she-camel).

This view has been transmitted from 'Umar, Zayd ibn Thabit, al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah, and Abu Musa al-Ash'ari. It is also the doctrine of Malik, since he affirms quasi-deliberate killing. However, the well-known position of his school is that he did not affirm it except in cases like the story of al-Mudlaji with his son, when he struck him with a sword.

It was also said: It is divided into four parts: a quarter *bint labun* (a female camel in her third year), a quarter *hiqaq*, a quarter *jidha'*, and a quarter *bint makhad* (a female camel in her second year). This is the view of al-Nu'man and Ya'qub, and Abu Dawud mentioned it from Sufyan, from Abu Ishaq, from 'Asim ibn Damrah, from 'Ali.

It was also said: It is divided into five parts: twenty *bint makhad*, twenty *bint labun*, twenty *ibn labun*, twenty *hiqqah*, and twenty *jadha'ah*. This is the view of Abu Thawr.

It was also said: forty *jadha'ah* up to the *bazil* of their year, thirty *hiqqah*, and thirty *bint labun*. This was narrated from 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, and al-Hasan al-Basri, Tawus, and al-Zuhri also said it.

It was also said: thirty-four *khalifah* up to the *bazil* of their year, thirty-three *hiqqah*, and thirty-three *jadha'ah*. This is the view of al-Sha'bi and al-Nakha'i. Abu Dawud mentioned it from Abu al-Ahwas, from Abu Ishaq, from 'Asim ibn Damrah, from 'Ali.

**The third issue:** The scholars differed over who is liable for the blood money of quasi-deliberate killing. Al-Harith al-'Ukli, Ibn Abi Layla, Ibn Shubrumah, Qatadah, and Abu Thawr said: It is owed by the killer from his own property.

Al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i, al-Hakam, al-Shafi'i, al-Thawri, Ahmad, Ishaq, and the proponents of opinion (*ashab al-ra'y*, the Hanafis) said: It is owed by the *'aqilah* (the paternal kin who bear the blood money).

Ibn al-Mundhir said: The view of al-Sha'bi is more sound, based on the hadith of Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet (ﷺ) made the blood money for the fetus the obligation of the *'aqilah* of the woman who struck her.

**The fourth issue:** The scholars agreed that the *'aqilah* do not bear the blood money of deliberate killing, and that it is owed from the property of the perpetrator. This has been mentioned previously in (*al-Baqarah* [see vol. 2, p. 252]).

They also agreed that the one who kills by mistake must make expiation (*kaffarah*). They differed concerning expiation for deliberate killing. Malik and al-Shafi'i held that the killer by deliberate act must make expiation as in accidental killing.

Al-Shafi'i said: If expiation is required for accidental killing, then it is more fitting that it be required for deliberate killing. He also said: If prostration is prescribed for forgetfulness, then it is more fitting that it be prescribed for deliberate action. And what God mentioned regarding the expiation for deliberate killing does not cancel what was required for accidental killing.

It was also said: The one who kills deliberately is only obligated to make expiation if he is pardoned and not killed. As for when he is killed by retaliation, there is no expiation upon him to be taken from his property.

Another view says it is obligatory.

And whoever kills himself, expiation is owed from his property.

Al-Thawri, Abu Thawr, and the proponents of opinion said: Expiation is not required except where God has required it.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: We also say this, because expiations are acts of worship, and it is not permissible to analogize them. No one may impose an obligation that binds God's servants except by a Book, a Sunnah, or a consensus (*ijma'*, the scholarly consensus). The one who imposes expiation on the deliberate killer has no proof from the standpoint that it was mentioned.

**The fifth issue:** The scholars differed concerning a group of people who kill a man by mistake. One group said: Each one of them owes an expiation. This was said by al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah, al-Nakha'i, al-Harith al-'Ukli, Malik, al-Thawri, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu Thawr, and the proponents of opinion.

Another group said: All of them together owe one expiation. This is what Abu Thawr said, and it is reported from al-Awza'i.

Al-Zuhri distinguished between freeing a slave and fasting. He said, concerning a group who throw with a catapult (*al-manjaniq*) and thereby kill a man: All of them owe the freeing of one slave. If they cannot find one, then each of them must fast for two consecutive months.

**The sixth issue:** Al-Nasa'i related: Al-Hasan ibn Ishaq al-Marwazi, a trustworthy narrator, informed us, saying: Khalid ibn Khidash told me, saying: Hatim ibn Isma'il told us, from Bashir ibn al-Muhajir, from 'Abd Allah ibn Buraydah, from his father, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said:

"The killing of a believer is greater in the sight of God than the passing away of this world."

It was also related from 'Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said:

"The first thing for which a servant will be held to account is the prayer, and the first thing to be judged among people is blood."

Isma'il ibn Ishaq related from Nafi' ibn Jubayr ibn Mut'im, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas, that a questioner asked him, saying: "O Abu al-'Abbas, is there repentance (*tawbah*) for the killer?"

Ibn 'Abbas said to him, as if amazed at his question: "What are you saying!" twice or three times. Then Ibn 'Abbas said: "Woe to you! How could he have repentance? I heard your Prophet (ﷺ) say:

'The one who was killed will come, his head hanging by one of his hands, and grasping his killer with the other hand, and blood gushing from his jugular vein, until they both are made to stand before God, Glorified and Exalted. The one who was killed will say: "My Lord, this one killed me." God, Exalted, will say to the killer: "You are ruined." And he will be taken to the Fire.'"

And from al-Hasan, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I did not argue with my Lord about anything as much as I argued with Him about the killing of a believer, and He did not answer me."

**The seventh issue:** The scholars differed over whether the killer by deliberate act has any repentance.

Al-Bukhari related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: The people of Kufa differed concerning it, so I traveled to Ibn 'Abbas and asked him about it. He said: "This verse, ﴿And whoever kills a believer deliberately, his recompense is Hell﴾, was the last thing revealed, and nothing abrogated it."

Al-Nasa'i related from him, who said: I asked Ibn 'Abbas: "Is there repentance for one who killed a believer deliberately?" He said: "No." And I recited to him the verse in al-Furqan: ﴿And those who do not invoke with God another god﴾ [see vol. 13, p. 75]. He said: "This is a Meccan verse, abrogated by a Medinan verse: ﴿And whoever kills a believer deliberately, his recompense is Hell, abiding therein, and God will be angry with him﴾."

It was also related from Zayd ibn Thabit something similar, and that the verse of al-Nisa' was revealed six months after the verse of al-Furqan, and in another narration eight months after. Al-Nasa'i mentioned both from Zayd ibn Thabit.

The Mu'tazilah adopted the general sense of this verse together with these reports from Zayd and Ibn 'Abbas, and they said: "This specifies the general sense of His statement: ﴿And He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾." They held that the threat is binding without exception upon every killer. They reconciled the two verses by saying: "The meaning is: and He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills, except one who kills deliberately."

A group of scholars, among them 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar (and this is also reported from Zayd and Ibn 'Abbas), held that there is repentance for him.

Yazid ibn Harun related, saying: Abu Malik al-Ash'ari informed us, from Sa'd ibn 'Ubaydah, who said: A man came to Ibn 'Abbas and said: "Is there repentance for one who killed a believer deliberately?"

He said: "No, except the Fire." When the man left, his companions said to him: "Is this how you used to issue fatwas to us? You used to tell us that there is an accepted repentance for the killer." He said: "I think he is a man in a rage who wants to kill a believer."

He said: So they sent after him and found him to be just that.

This is the doctrine of the People of the Sunnah, and it is the sound view. This verse is specified (*makhsus*), and the evidence for the specification consists of verses and reports.
