**Variant readings and the occasion of revelation:** In the editions and in Ibn 'Atiyya, the word is read as *ṣubāba*, while in the Qamus and its commentary it is *ḥubāba*, with a ḥā'. [Note: the editorial brackets of the source are reproduced here.]

It is related that he (Maqis ibn Subaba) had embraced Islam together with his brother Hisham ibn Subaba. He found Hisham slain among the Banu al-Najjar, and informed the Prophet ﷺ of this. So the Prophet ﷺ wrote to them, instructing them to hand over to him the killer of his brother, and he sent with him a man from the Banu Fihr. The Banu al-Najjar said: "By Allah, we do not know of any killer of his, but we will pay the blood-money." So they gave him one hundred camels. Then the two of them set out returning to Madina, but Maqis attacked the Fihri and killed him in revenge for his brother, took the camels, and went back to Makkah as an unbeliever, an apostate. He began reciting:

"I killed for him Fihr, and I carried his blood-price
(as a burden) upon the chiefs of the Banu al-Najjar, the lords of Fari'
[Fari': a fortress in Madina.]
Through him I have quenched my vengeance, and I have attained my revenge,
and I have been the first to return to the idols."

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I will not grant him safety, in the sacred precinct or outside it." And he commanded that he be killed on the day of the conquest of Makkah, while he was clinging to the Ka'bah.

Since this is established by the transmission of the people of tafsir and the scholars of religion, it should not be applied to the Muslims. Moreover, taking the apparent meaning of this verse is no more preferable than taking the apparent meaning of: ﴿Indeed, good deeds remove evil deeds﴾ [see vol. 9, p. 108], and His saying ﴿He it is who accepts repentance from His servants﴾ [see vol. 16, p. 25 and vol. 8, p. 250], and His saying: ﴿And He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾. Taking both apparent meanings is contradictory, so specification (takhsis) is necessary.

Furthermore, reconciling the verse of al-Furqan with this verse is possible, so there is neither abrogation (naskh) nor contradiction. This is done by taking the unrestricted (mutlaq) verse of al-Nisa' as qualified (muqayyad) by the verse of al-Furqan, so that its meaning becomes: "Then his recompense is such-and-such, except for the one who repents." Especially since the cause (al-mūjib, the killing) and the consequence (al-mūjab, the threat of punishment) are the same.

As for the reports, they are numerous, such as the hadith of 'Ubada ibn al-Samit, in which he said: "Pledge to me that you will not associate anything with Allah, nor commit adultery, nor steal, nor kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right. Whoever among you fulfils it, his reward is with Allah; whoever commits any of that and is punished for it, that is an expiation for him; and whoever commits any of that and Allah conceals it, his affair is with Allah: if He wills He pardons him, and if He wills He punishes him."
(Narrated by the Imams; it is recorded by the two Sahihs.)

And like the hadith of Abu Hurayra from the Prophet ﷺ concerning the man who killed a hundred souls, recorded by Muslim in his Sahih, Ibn Majah in his Sunan, and others, besides other established reports.

Moreover, they agree with us regarding a man who is witnessed to have committed murder, who confesses that he killed intentionally, and whom the heirs bring before the ruler, so that the prescribed punishment is established upon him and he is executed by retaliation (qawad). This man is not followed in the Hereafter, and the threat is not enforced upon him, by consensus, in accordance with the hadith of 'Ubada. Thus what they relied upon, the general wording of the saying of Allah ﷺ: ﴿And whoever kills a believer intentionally, his recompense is Hell﴾, has been broken, and it is subject to specification by what we have mentioned.

Since this is so, the correct view is that this verse is specified as we have explained, or it is to be understood according to what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said: "intentionally" means "deeming it lawful to kill him" (mustahillan li-qatlihi). This too leads to disbelief, by consensus.

A group said: the killer is subject to Allah's will whether he repents or not. This was said by Abu Hanifa and his companions.

If it is said: the saying of Allah ﷺ: ﴿Then his recompense is Hell, abiding therein, and Allah has become angry with him and cursed him﴾ is evidence of his disbelief, since Allah does not become angry except with a disbeliever who has left the faith. We say: this is a threat (wa'id), and breaking a threat is generosity (karam), as the poet said:

"And if I threaten him, or promise him,
I break my threat and fulfil my promise."

And this has already been mentioned.

A second answer: "if He recompenses him with that," i.e., he is deserving of it and merits it because of the greatness of his sin. This was stated by Abu Mijlaz Lahiq ibn Humayd, Abu Salih, and others. It is also related from Anas ibn Malik, from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, that he said: "When Allah promises a servant a reward, He will fulfil it; and if He threatens him with punishment, then it is up to Him: if He wills He punishes him, and if He wills He pardons him."

There is some objection to these two interpretations. As for the first, al-Qushayri said: "In this there is room for consideration, because the speech of the Lord does not admit of breaking, unless what is meant is the specification of the general, which is permissible in speech." As for the second, even though it is related as marfu', al-Nahhas said: "The error in this interpretation is clear, for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has said: ﴿That is their recompense, Hell, because they disbelieved﴾, and no one has said: 'if He recompenses them,' and it is an error in Arabic, because after it comes ﴿and Allah became angry with him﴾, which is to be understood as meaning 'recompensed him.'"

A third answer: "Then his recompense is Hell" if he does not repent and persists in the sin until he meets his Lord in disbelief, by the evil consequences of the sins.

Dhikrullah (Hibat Allah) mentioned in the book *al-Nasikh wa'l-Mansukh* that this verse is abrogated by the saying of Allah: ﴿And He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾. He said: this is the consensus of the people except Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn 'Umar, who said that it is muhkam (not abrogated). There is consideration in what he said, because this is a place of generality and specification, not a place of abrogation, as Ibn 'Atiyya said. I say: this is good, because abrogation does not enter reports; rather the meaning is "so He will recompense him."

Al-Nahhas said in his *Ma'ani al-Qur'an*: the view among the scholars of inquiry is that it is muhkam, and that He will recompense him if he does not repent; but if he repents, His command has been made clear by His saying: ﴿And indeed I am Forgiving to whoever repents﴾, so this does not fall outside it. And eternity (khulud) does not necessarily mean perpetuity. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We did not grant to any human before you eternity (al-khuld)﴾ — the verse. And Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿He thinks his wealth will make him immortal (akhladahu)﴾. And Zuhayr said:

"Nor anything eternal except the firm mountains"
[This is the second half of a verse; its first half is: "Look! I see nothing enduring among the calamities."]

All of this indicates that khulud is applied to a meaning other than perpetuity, for that ends with the ending of this world. Likewise the Arabs say: "I will make so-and-so eternal (la-ukhallidanna) in prison," and the prison ends and perishes, and so does the prisoner. Similar is their saying in supplication: "May Allah make His kingdom eternal (khallada) and His days everlasting (abbada)."

This has all been mentioned before, both in wording and in meaning. And praise be to Allah.

**Issue 1:** There are eleven issues in this verse. The first concerns God's words: ﴿O you who believe, when you go forth in the cause of Allah, then investigate carefully﴾. This is connected to the mention of killing and fighting. *Ḍarb* means traveling across the land. The Arabs say *ḍarabtu fī al-arḍ* ("I struck in the land") when one travels for trade, raiding, or other purposes, with *fī* attached. They say *ḍarabtu al-arḍ* without *fī* when one intends to relieve oneself. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Two men should not go out striking the open ground, talking while uncovering their private parts, for Allah detests that." This verse was revealed concerning a group of Muslims who, during their journey, passed by a man who had a camel and a small flock of sheep that he was selling. He greeted the people and said, "There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." One of them attacked him and killed him. When this was mentioned to the Prophet (ﷺ), he was distressed, and the verse was revealed. Al-Bukhari transmitted it from ʿAṭāʾ, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: Ibn ʿAbbās said: "A man was with his small flock, and the Muslims overtook him. He said, 'Peace be upon you,' but they killed him and took his flock. So Allah revealed concerning that, up to His words ﴿seeking the goods of this worldly life﴾, which refers to that flock." He said: Ibn ʿAbbās recited *al-salām* (the greeting). Outside al-Bukhari: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) paid his blood money to his family and returned his sheep to him.

Scholars differed about identifying the killer and the victim in this incident. The majority view, which is found in Ibn Isḥāq's *Sīrah*, in Abū Dāwūd's *Muṣannaf*, and in Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr's *al-Istīʿāb*, is that the killer was Muḥallim ibn Jaththāmah and the victim was ʿĀmir ibn al-Aḍbaṭ. The Prophet (ﷺ) invoked against Muḥallim, and he did not live after that except for seven days. He was buried, but the earth would not accept him. He was buried again, but the earth did not accept him. He was buried a third time, but the earth did not accept him. When they saw that the earth would not accept him, they threw him into one of those ravines. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed the earth accepts one who is worse than him." Al-Ḥasan said: "Indeed, it confines one who is worse than him, but he (the Prophet) admonished the people not to return to such acts."

In the *Sunan* of Ibn Mājah, from ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent an army of Muslims against the polytheists. They fought them fiercely, and the polytheists turned their backs. A man from my clan charged at a polytheist man with a spear. When the man reached him, he said, "I testify that there is no god but Allah, I am a Muslim," but he struck him and killed him. He came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said, "O Messenger of Allah, I have been destroyed!" He (ﷺ) said, "And what did you do?" He said this once or twice, and the man told him what he had done. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him, "Why did you not split open his belly so that you would know what was in his heart?" He said, "O Messenger of Allah, if I had split open his belly, would I have known what was in his heart?" He said, "No. You did not accept what he said with his tongue, and you do not know what is in his heart." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) then fell silent. Not long after, the man died, and we buried him, but in the morning he was lying on the surface of the earth. We said, "Perhaps an enemy dug him up." We buried him again, then we ordered our boys to guard him, but in the morning he was lying on the surface of the earth. We said, "Perhaps the boys fell asleep." We buried him again and guarded him ourselves, but in the morning he was lying on the surface of the earth, so we threw him into one of those ravines.

It is also said that the killer was Usāmah ibn Zayd and the victim was Mirdās ibn Nahīk al-Ghaṭafānī, then al-Fazārī, from Banū Murrah, from the people of Fadak. Ibn al-Qāsim transmitted this from Mālik. It is also said that this Mirdās had embraced Islam that very night and had informed his family of this. When the Prophet (ﷺ) greatly rebuked Usāmah for this, Usāmah swore at that time that he would never fight a man who says, "There is no god but Allah." This has been discussed before. It is also said that the killer was Abū Qatādah, and it is said it was Abū al-Dardāʾ. There is no disagreement that the one whom the earth rejected when he died was Muḥallim, whom we mentioned. Perhaps these incidents occurred at close times, so the verse was revealed concerning all of them. It has been narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) returned the sheep and the camel to the family of the Muslim man, and paid his blood money as an act of reconciliation. And Allah knows best.

Al-Thaʿlabī mentioned that the commander of that expedition was a man called Ghālib ibn Faḍālah al-Laythī. It is also said it was al-Miqdād. This was related by al-Suhaylī.

**Issue 2:** God's words ﴿then investigate carefully﴾ mean: reflect carefully. The reading ﴿fa-tabayyanū﴾ is that of the majority. It is the preference of Abū ʿUbayd and Abū Ḥātim, and both said: whoever is commanded to *tabayyun* (clarification) is commanded to *tathabbut* (verification). One says *tabayyantu al-amr* ("I clarified the matter") and *tabayyana al-amru bi-nafsihi* ("the matter became clear by itself"), so it is both transitive and intransitive. Ḥamzah read ﴿fa-tathabbatū﴾, from *tathabbut*, with a *thāʾ* (ث) and then a *bāʾ* with one dot.

The form ﴿fa-tabayyanū﴾ is stronger in this context, because a person may verify without the matter becoming clear. The *idhā* (when) carries the meaning of a condition, which is why the *fāʾ* enters ﴿then investigate﴾. It may also be followed by a conditional verb, as the poet said:

*"And if poverty afflicts you, then bear it with grace (fa-tajammal)."* (This is the second half of a line whose first half is: "And be content with whatever Allah has made you rich in.") In the manuscripts *ṭ*, *z*, and *y*, it is read *fa-taḥammal* with the unpointed *ḥāʾ*, and this is a variant reading.

But the better usage is that it is not followed by a conditional verb, as the other poet said:

*"The soul is eager when you make it eager, and when it is brought down to little, it is content."*

Investigation (*tabayyun*, i.e., verifying) in killing is obligatory whether one is at home or traveling, and there is no disagreement on this. The journey was specifically mentioned only because the incident that occasioned the revelation of the verse took place during a journey.

**Issue 3:** God's words ﴿and do not say to one who offers you peace, "You are not a believer"﴾. *As-salam* and *as-salām* are one and the same, as al-Bukhari said. Both readings have been recited. Abū ʿUbayd al-Qāsim ibn Sallām preferred ﴿al-salām﴾. But the scholars of reasoning disagreed with him and said: ﴿al-salam﴾ (with the vowel on the *lām* and the *sīn* unvowelled) is more fitting here, because it means submission and surrender, as in God's words, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿and they will offer peace (al-salam), saying, "We did no evil"﴾. So *al-salam* means submission and yielding. The meaning is: do not say to one who has laid down his arms, submitted to you, and displayed your call, "You are not a believer."

It is also said that *al-salām* refers to the saying "Peace be upon you," and this returns to the first meaning, because greeting with the greeting of Islam indicates obedience and submission. It may also mean withdrawal and abandonment. Al-Akhfash said: One says "so-and-so is *salām*" when he does not mix with anyone. *Al-silm* (with a doubled *sīn*, with a kasra, and with a sukūn on the *lām*) means reconciliation.

**Issue 4:** It is narrated from Abū Jaʿfar that he read ﴿lasta mu'minan﴾ with a *fatḥah* on the second *mīm*, from *āmantuhu*, meaning "I granted him protection," so he is *mu'man* (one who has been granted protection).

**Issue 5:** When a Muslim meets a disbeliever who has no treaty with him, it is permissible for him to kill him. But if the disbeliever says, "There is no god but Allah," it is not permissible to kill him, because he has taken refuge in the firm handhold of Islam, which protects his blood, his property, and his family. If he kills him after that, he is to be executed for it. The killing was waived for those men only because they were in the early period of Islam, and they interpreted that he said it as a way of seeking refuge and out of fear of the weapon, while the thing that protects is saying it with conviction. Therefore the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Usāmah: "Why did you not split open his heart so that you would know whether he said it or not?" This is transmitted by Muslim, meaning: would you look to see whether he was truthful in his words or lying? That is impossible, so nothing remains except that his tongue must reveal what is in him. There is a great principle of jurisprudence in this: rulings are attached to apparent indications and outward signs, not to certainty or knowledge of hidden intentions.

**Issue 6:** If he says, "Peace be upon you," he should not be killed either until what lies beyond this is known, because this is a matter of ambiguity. Mālik said, concerning a disbeliever who is found and says, "I came seeking safe conduct, asking for protection": these are difficult matters. I hold that he should be returned to his place of safety and not be ruled by the rules of Islam, because disbelief has been established for him, so something must appear from him that indicates his claim. Saying "I am a Muslim" or "I am a believer," or praying, is not sufficient, until he utters the word that protects, upon which the Prophet (ﷺ) attached the ruling in his saying: "I have been commanded to fight people until they say, 'There is no god but Allah.'"

**Issue 7:** If he prays or does an act specific to Islam, our scholars disagreed about it. Ibn al-ʿArabī said: We hold that by this he does not become a Muslim. As for asking him what lies beyond this prayer: if he says, "It is the prayer of a Muslim," it is said to him, "Say: there is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah" (in Ibn al-ʿArabī it is "There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah"). If he says it, his sincerity is made clear. If he refuses, we know that this is trickery, and for those who consider his Islam to be apostasy, it would be apostasy. The correct view is that it is original disbelief, not apostasy. Likewise, the one who said "Peace be upon you" is required to utter the word (*yukallaf al-kalimah*). If he says it, his right guidance is established; if he refuses, his obstinacy is made clear and he is killed. This is the meaning of ﴿then investigate carefully﴾, i.e., the difficult matter, or ﴿verify﴾ and do not hasten; the two meanings are the same. If anyone kills him, he has committed what is forbidden.

If it is asked: how does the Prophet's (ﷺ) harshness toward Muḥallim, and the throwing of him out of his grave, fit with this? We say: because he knew from his intention that he did not care about his Islam, and killed him deliberately because of the enmity that existed between them in the time of ignorance.

**Issue 8:** God's words ﴿seeking the goods of this worldly life﴾ mean: seeking to take his property. The goods of this world are called *ʿaraḍ* because they are transient, passing away and not lasting. Abū ʿUbaydah said: All the provision of this worldly life is called *ʿaraḍ* with a *fatḥah* on the *rāʾ*, and from this is the (ḥadīth): "The world is a present *ʿaraḍ* from which the righteous and the wicked both eat."

*Al-ʿArḍ* (with a sukūn on the *rāʾ*) means everything other than dinars and dirhams. So every *ʿaraḍ* is an *ʿaraḍ*, but not every *ʿaraḍ* is *ʿarḍ*. In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Wealth does not lie in having many possessions; wealth is the wealth of the soul." Some scholars took up this meaning and versified it:

*"Be content with what suffices you, and practice contentment, for you do not know whether you will become rich in the morning or in the evening.*
*So richness is not in having abundant wealth; rather, richness and poverty come from the soul."*

This confirms the saying of Abū ʿUbaydah, because wealth includes everything that is valued. In *Kitāb al-ʿAyn*: *al-ʿaraḍ* is what is obtained from this world, and from it is God's words ﴿you desire the goods of this world﴾. Its plural is *ʿurūḍ*. In *al-Mujmal* of Ibn Fāris: *al-ʿaraḍ* is what befalls a person of illness or the like; *ʿaraḍ al-dunyā* is whatever property there is in it, whether little or much. *Al-ʿaraḍ* among household goods is whatever is not cash. *Aʿraḍa al-shayʾ* means the thing appeared and became possible. *Al-ʿarḍ* is the opposite of length.

**Issue 9:** God's words ﴿with Allah are abundant spoils﴾ are a promise from God that He will provide what comes in its proper way and from lawful means without committing what is forbidden. That is, do not rush into destruction.

(Thus you used to be before) — that is, thus you used to conceal your faith from your people out of fear for yourselves, until Allah bestowed His favour upon you by strengthening the religion and granting victory over the polytheists. So now, each one of them is in his own people, waiting to reach you; therefore, when he reaches you, it is not proper for you to kill him until you have clarified his matter. Ibn Zayd said: the meaning is, "Thus you used to be disbelievers" (then Allah bestowed His favour upon you) by your accepting Islam. So do not deny that he may be in that same state, then accept Islam at that very moment when he meets you; therefore you must be careful about his affair.

The tenth issue: Whoever holds that faith is merely speech has taken evidence from this verse, based on the words of the Exalted: ﴿And do not say to one who offers you peace, "You are not a believer"﴾. They said: Since it was forbidden to say to one who says "There is no god but Allah" that "You are not a believer," it was forbidden to kill them merely on the basis of speech. And if faith were not this speech, their saying would not have been censured. We say: The people only doubted the case where that statement was made out of seeking refuge, so they killed him. Allah has not given His servants anything other than judgment according to the outward. The Prophet ﷺ said: "I have been commanded to fight people until they say, 'There is no god but Allah.'" There is nothing in this to indicate that faith is only affirmation. Do you not see that the hypocrites used to say this statement while they were not believers, as was explained earlier in (al-Baqarah [see vol. 1, p. 193]). The clarification in this matter has been revealed by his saying, peace be upon him: "Did you not split open his heart?" So it is established that faith is affirmation and other than it, and that its reality is assent of the heart, but there is no way for a servant to know it except what is heard from him alone.

This verse is also used as evidence by whoever says that a zindiq's repentance is accepted if he manifests Islam. He said: Because Allah, the Exalted, did not distinguish between the zindiq and others once he manifests Islam. The discussion of this has already passed at the beginning of al-Baqarah [see vol. 1, p. 198].

It also contains a refutation of the Qadariyyah, for Allah, the Exalted, informed that He bestowed His favour upon the believers from among all creation by singling them out for success (tawfiq), whereas the Qadariyyah say: He created all of them for faith. Had it been as they claimed, there would be no meaning to the believers being specially favoured from among all creation.

The eleventh issue: His saying, the Exalted, ﴿So verify﴾ repeats the command to clarify for emphasis.

(Indeed, Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted.) This is a warning against disobeying Allah's command; that is, guard yourselves and keep yourselves away from the slip that would ruin you.

**Five issues arise from this verse.**

**The first issue:** His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Those who sit at home among the believers are not equal﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Not equal are those who stayed behind from Badr and those who went out to it." Then He said: ﴿other than those with a disability﴾, and *al-darar* means a chronic affliction. The imams related, and the wording is that of Abu Dawud, from Zayd ibn Thabit who said: "I was beside the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when tranquility (*sakinah*) overcame him, and the thigh of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to rest upon my thigh. I had never felt any weight heavier than the thigh of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Then he recovered from it and said: 'Write.' So I wrote on a shoulder-blade (*katif*) [[The *katif* is a broad bone at the base of the shoulder of animals, among humans and beasts. They used to write on it because of the scarcity of papers among them.]]: ﴿Those who sit at home among the believers are not equal to those who strive in the way of Allah﴾, to the end of the verse. Then Ibn Umm Maktum, who was blind, stood up when he heard the excellence of the strivers and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what about one among the believers who is unable to strive?' When he finished speaking, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was overcome by tranquility, and his thigh came to rest upon my thigh, and I felt its weight the second time just as I had felt it the first time. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recovered and said: 'Recite, O Zayd.' So I recited: ﴿Those who sit at home among the believers are not equal﴾, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: '…other than those with a disability,' the whole verse." Zayd said: "Allah revealed it alone, and I attached it. By Him in whose hand my soul is, it is as though I can see its attachment at a crack in the shoulder-blade."

In al-Bukhari, on the authority of Miqsam, the client of 'Abd Allah ibn al-Harith, that he heard Ibn 'Abbas say: "﴿Not equal are those who sit at home among the believers﴾ refers to those who stayed behind from Badr, and those who went out to Badr."

The scholars said: "The people of *darar* are the people of excuses, since their affliction has harmed them to the point that it prevented them from jihad." It is authentically established in a report that he, peace be upon him, said, when he had returned from one of his expeditions: "There are men in Madinah. You have not crossed a valley nor journeyed any journey except that they were with you. They are people whom excuse has held back." This indicates that the person with an excuse receives the reward of the warrior. It has been said: "It is possible that his reward is equal, and the bounty of Allah is vast; his reward is a bounty, not an entitlement, so He rewards a sincere intention with what He does not reward for the act." And it has been said: "He is given his reward without multiplication, and the warrior surpasses him by the multiplication for the direct act." And Allah knows best.

I say: The first view is more correct, if Allah wills, because of the sound hadith on this matter ("There are men in Madinah"), and because of the hadith of Abu Kabshah al-Anmari, where he, peace be upon him, said: "The world belongs to four kinds of people…" the hadith, which has already been mentioned in the surah of Al 'Imran [[See vol. 4, p. 215, and vol. 8, p. 292.]]. Of this meaning is what has come in a report: "When a servant falls ill, Allah, Exalted is He, says: 'Record for My servant what he used to do in health until he recovers, or I take him to Me.'"

**The second issue:** Some scholars have used this verse to argue that those enrolled in the military register (*ahl al-diwan*) have greater reward than volunteers (*ahl al-tatawwu'*). This is because those on the register are provided for by stipends, are deployed in hardships, and are startled by expeditions and orders. Therefore they are greater than the volunteer, because their hearts are steadied and their minds are at ease in the great summer campaigns (*al-sawa'if*) and the like. [[*Al-sa'ifah*: a raid in the summer.]] Ibn Muhayriz said: "Those who receive stipends are better than volunteers, because they are startled." Makhul said: "The startling of expeditions dispels the startling of the Resurrection."

**The third issue:** Also connected to this verse is the view of those who say that wealth is better than poverty, since Allah mentions wealth through which one reaches righteous deeds. People have differed on this question, though they agree that poverty which leads to destitution is disliked, and wealth which causes arrogance is blameworthy. One group held that the wealthy is superior, because the wealthy is capable and the poor is incapable, and capability is better than incapability. Al-Mawardi said: "This is the position of one who is dominated by love of prominence." Others held that the poor is superior, because the poor man abandons (the world) while the wealthy man is engaged with it, and abandoning the world is better than being engaged with it. Al-Mawardi said: "This is the position of one who is dominated by love of safety." Others held that the middle course is superior, by moving beyond the limits of poverty to the lowest degree of wealth, so that one attains the virtue of both and is spared the blame of both states. Al-Mawardi said: "This is the position of one who favours moderation, and that (the best of matters is their middle)." The wise poet has spoken well when he said:

*Unless I seek refuge in Allah from lack of means,*
*and from a desire, one day, for something not worth desiring.*

**The fourth issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿other than those with a disability﴾. The reading of the people of Kufa and Abu 'Amr is *ghayru* with a *damma*. Al-Akhfash said: it is a qualifier (*na't*) of "those who sit," because they are not intended as specific people, so they are like an indefinite noun, and it is therefore permissible to qualify them with *ghayr*. The meaning is: "Those who sit, other than those with a disability, are not equal," that is, those who sit who are not people of disability are not equal. The meaning is also: "Those who sit who are healthy are not equal," as al-Zajjaj said. Abu Haywah read *ghayri*, making it a qualifier of "the believers," meaning: among the believers who are other than those with a disability, that is, the healthy believers.

The people of the two Sanctuaries (Makkah and Madinah) read *ghayra* with a *fatha*, as an exception from "those who sit" or from "the believers," meaning: except those with a disability, for they are equal to the strivers. If you wish, it may be a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) of "those who sit," meaning: those who sit, from among the healthy, that is, in their state of health. The circumstantial accusative from them is permissible because their wording is definite, as you say: "Zayd came to me not being ill." What we have mentioned about the occasion of revelation indicates the meaning of the accusative. And Allah knows best.

**The fifth issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah has preferred those who strive with their wealth and their lives over those who sit at home by a degree﴾. He said after this: ﴿degrees from Him, and forgiveness and mercy﴾. Some said: the preference by "a degree," then by "degrees," is only emphasis, clarification and reinforcement. It has also been said: Allah preferred the strivers over those who sit among the people of disability by one degree, and He preferred the strivers over those who sit without excuse by degrees. This was said by Ibn Jurayj, al-Suddi and others. It has been said: the meaning of "degree" is elevation, that is, He raised their mention and their rank through praise, commendation and eulogy. This is the meaning of "degree." As for "degrees," it refers to Paradise. Ibn Muhayriz said: "Seventy degrees, between each two degrees the gallop of a noble horse for seventy years." The word "degrees" (*darajat*) is either a substitute for "reward" (*ajr*) and its explanation, and it is permissible to put it in the accusative as well, on the presumption of an adverb (*zarf*), meaning: He preferred them by degrees. It is also permissible that it be an emphasis of His saying ﴿a great reward﴾, since the great reward is the degrees, forgiveness and mercy. It is also permissible to read it in the nominative, meaning: that is degrees. The word "reward" (*ajran*) is in the accusative by "preferred," and if you wish it may be a verbal noun (*masdar*), which is better. It is not governed by "preferred," because the two objects have already been completed: "those who strive" and "over those who sit." Likewise "a degree." So "degrees" are ranks, some higher than others.

In the Sahih, on the authority of the Prophet (ﷺ): "In Paradise there are one hundred degrees which Allah has prepared for those who strive in His way; between each two degrees is the distance between the heaven and the earth."

As for His saying ﴿And to each Allah has promised the best﴾: "each" (*kullan*) is in the accusative by "promised," and "the best" (*al-husna*) is Paradise, meaning: Allah promised each of them the best. Then it has been said: the intended meaning of "each" is the strivers specifically. It has also been said: the strivers and those with a disability are included. And Allah knows best.

**Five issues arise from this verse.**

**The first issue:** His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Those who sit at home among the believers are not equal﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Not equal are those who stayed behind from Badr and those who went out to it." Then He said: ﴿other than those with a disability﴾, and *al-darar* means a chronic affliction. The imams related, and the wording is that of Abu Dawud, from Zayd ibn Thabit who said: "I was beside the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when tranquility (*sakinah*) overcame him, and the thigh of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to rest upon my thigh. I had never felt any weight heavier than the thigh of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Then he recovered from it and said: 'Write.' So I wrote on a shoulder-blade (*katif*) [[The *katif* is a broad bone at the base of the shoulder of animals, among humans and beasts. They used to write on it because of the scarcity of papers among them.]]: ﴿Those who sit at home among the believers are not equal to those who strive in the way of Allah﴾, to the end of the verse. Then Ibn Umm Maktum, who was blind, stood up when he heard the excellence of the strivers and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what about one among the believers who is unable to strive?' When he finished speaking, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was overcome by tranquility, and his thigh came to rest upon my thigh, and I felt its weight the second time just as I had felt it the first time. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recovered and said: 'Recite, O Zayd.' So I recited: ﴿Those who sit at home among the believers are not equal﴾, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: '…other than those with a disability,' the whole verse." Zayd said: "Allah revealed it alone, and I attached it. By Him in whose hand my soul is, it is as though I can see its attachment at a crack in the shoulder-blade."

In al-Bukhari, on the authority of Miqsam, the client of 'Abd Allah ibn al-Harith, that he heard Ibn 'Abbas say: "﴿Not equal are those who sit at home among the believers﴾ refers to those who stayed behind from Badr, and those who went out to Badr."

The scholars said: "The people of *darar* are the people of excuses, since their affliction has harmed them to the point that it prevented them from jihad." It is authentically established in a report that he, peace be upon him, said, when he had returned from one of his expeditions: "There are men in Madinah. You have not crossed a valley nor journeyed any journey except that they were with you. They are people whom excuse has held back." This indicates that the person with an excuse receives the reward of the warrior. It has been said: "It is possible that his reward is equal, and the bounty of Allah is vast; his reward is a bounty, not an entitlement, so He rewards a sincere intention with what He does not reward for the act." And it has been said: "He is given his reward without multiplication, and the warrior surpasses him by the multiplication for the direct act." And Allah knows best.

I say: The first view is more correct, if Allah wills, because of the sound hadith on this matter ("There are men in Madinah"), and because of the hadith of Abu Kabshah al-Anmari, where he, peace be upon him, said: "The world belongs to four kinds of people…" the hadith, which has already been mentioned in the surah of Al 'Imran [[See vol. 4, p. 215, and vol. 8, p. 292.]]. Of this meaning is what has come in a report: "When a servant falls ill, Allah, Exalted is He, says: 'Record for My servant what he used to do in health until he recovers, or I take him to Me.'"

**The second issue:** Some scholars have used this verse to argue that those enrolled in the military register (*ahl al-diwan*) have greater reward than volunteers (*ahl al-tatawwu'*). This is because those on the register are provided for by stipends, are deployed in hardships, and are startled by expeditions and orders. Therefore they are greater than the volunteer, because their hearts are steadied and their minds are at ease in the great summer campaigns (*al-sawa'if*) and the like. [[*Al-sa'ifah*: a raid in the summer.]] Ibn Muhayriz said: "Those who receive stipends are better than volunteers, because they are startled." Makhul said: "The startling of expeditions dispels the startling of the Resurrection."

**The third issue:** Also connected to this verse is the view of those who say that wealth is better than poverty, since Allah mentions wealth through which one reaches righteous deeds. People have differed on this question, though they agree that poverty which leads to destitution is disliked, and wealth which causes arrogance is blameworthy. One group held that the wealthy is superior, because the wealthy is capable and the poor is incapable, and capability is better than incapability. Al-Mawardi said: "This is the position of one who is dominated by love of prominence." Others held that the poor is superior, because the poor man abandons (the world) while the wealthy man is engaged with it, and abandoning the world is better than being engaged with it. Al-Mawardi said: "This is the position of one who is dominated by love of safety." Others held that the middle course is superior, by moving beyond the limits of poverty to the lowest degree of wealth, so that one attains the virtue of both and is spared the blame of both states. Al-Mawardi said: "This is the position of one who favours moderation, and that (the best of matters is their middle)." The wise poet has spoken well when he said:

*Unless I seek refuge in Allah from lack of means,*
*and from a desire, one day, for something not worth desiring.*

**The fourth issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿other than those with a disability﴾. The reading of the people of Kufa and Abu 'Amr is *ghayru* with a *damma*. Al-Akhfash said: it is a qualifier (*na't*) of "those who sit," because they are not intended as specific people, so they are like an indefinite noun, and it is therefore permissible to qualify them with *ghayr*. The meaning is: "Those who sit, other than those with a disability, are not equal," that is, those who sit who are not people of disability are not equal. The meaning is also: "Those who sit who are healthy are not equal," as al-Zajjaj said. Abu Haywah read *ghayri*, making it a qualifier of "the believers," meaning: among the believers who are other than those with a disability, that is, the healthy believers.

The people of the two Sanctuaries (Makkah and Madinah) read *ghayra* with a *fatha*, as an exception from "those who sit" or from "the believers," meaning: except those with a disability, for they are equal to the strivers. If you wish, it may be a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) of "those who sit," meaning: those who sit, from among the healthy, that is, in their state of health. The circumstantial accusative from them is permissible because their wording is definite, as you say: "Zayd came to me not being ill." What we have mentioned about the occasion of revelation indicates the meaning of the accusative. And Allah knows best.

**The fifth issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah has preferred those who strive with their wealth and their lives over those who sit at home by a degree﴾. He said after this: ﴿degrees from Him, and forgiveness and mercy﴾. Some said: the preference by "a degree," then by "degrees," is only emphasis, clarification and reinforcement. It has also been said: Allah preferred the strivers over those who sit among the people of disability by one degree, and He preferred the strivers over those who sit without excuse by degrees. This was said by Ibn Jurayj, al-Suddi and others. It has been said: the meaning of "degree" is elevation, that is, He raised their mention and their rank through praise, commendation and eulogy. This is the meaning of "degree." As for "degrees," it refers to Paradise. Ibn Muhayriz said: "Seventy degrees, between each two degrees the gallop of a noble horse for seventy years." The word "degrees" (*darajat*) is either a substitute for "reward" (*ajr*) and its explanation, and it is permissible to put it in the accusative as well, on the presumption of an adverb (*zarf*), meaning: He preferred them by degrees. It is also permissible that it be an emphasis of His saying ﴿a great reward﴾, since the great reward is the degrees, forgiveness and mercy. It is also permissible to read it in the nominative, meaning: that is degrees. The word "reward" (*ajran*) is in the accusative by "preferred," and if you wish it may be a verbal noun (*masdar*), which is better. It is not governed by "preferred," because the two objects have already been completed: "those who strive" and "over those who sit." Likewise "a degree." So "degrees" are ranks, some higher than others.

In the Sahih, on the authority of the Prophet (ﷺ): "In Paradise there are one hundred degrees which Allah has prepared for those who strive in His way; between each two degrees is the distance between the heaven and the earth."

As for His saying ﴿And to each Allah has promised the best﴾: "each" (*kullan*) is in the accusative by "promised," and "the best" (*al-husna*) is Paradise, meaning: Allah promised each of them the best. Then it has been said: the intended meaning of "each" is the strivers specifically. It has also been said: the strivers and those with a disability are included. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verse 97–99:

The intended ones here are a group of the people of Makkah who had embraced Islam and openly showed their faith in the Prophet ﷺ. When the Prophet ﷺ emigrated, they remained with their people, and a group among them were tested and succumbed to the test. When the matter of Badr occurred, a number of them went out with the disbelievers, and the verse was revealed. It was also said: when they belittled the number of the Muslims, doubt entered their religion and they apostatised, and they were killed while in apostasy. The Muslims then said: these companions of ours were Muslims and were compelled to go out, so they asked forgiveness for them, and the verse was revealed. The first view is more sound. Al-Bukhari narrated from Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, who said: a levy was imposed upon the people of Madinah [[That is, they were obliged to send out an army to fight the people of Sham during the caliphate of Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr over Makkah (from Sharh al-Qastallani).]], so I enrolled in it, then I met Ikrimah, the freedman of Ibn 'Abbas, and informed him, and he forbade me from that most strongly. Then he said: Ibn 'Abbas told me that some people among the Muslims used to be with the polytheists, increasing the numbers of the polytheists [[So it stands in all the manuscripts. What is in al-Bukhari, per al-Asqalani, is: "increasing the numbers of the polytheists against the Messenger of Allah."]] during the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. An arrow would come and be shot, and it would strike one of them and kill him, or he would be struck and killed. So Allah the Exalted revealed: "Indeed, those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves..."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Those whom the angels take in death﴾ may be a past-tense verb not joined to a feminine marker, since the feminine form of the word "angels" is not real feminine. It may also be a future-tense verb meaning "they will take them," with one of the two taa' deleted. Ibn Furak related from al-Hasan that the meaning is "they will gather them to the Fire." It was also said: "they seize their souls," and this is the clearest view. It was also said: the intended "angels" is the Angel of Death, based on the saying of the Exalted: "Say: The Angel of Death who has been entrusted with you will take you" [[See vol. 14, p. 92.]]. The phrase ﴿wronging themselves﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause, meaning "in the state of wronging themselves," and the intended sense is "wronging themselves," so the nun was deleted for lightness and the noun was made genitive by addition [[The original reads: "fa-hudhifat wa-udifa", with the note that this is out of courtesy towards Allah, the Glorified.]], as the Exalted said: "an offering reaching the Ka'bah" [[See vol. 6, p. 314.]]. The angels' words ﴿In what were you?﴾ are a question of rebuke and reproach, meaning: were you among the companions of the Prophet ﷺ, or were you polytheists! The words of these people ﴿We were oppressed in the earth﴾, meaning Makkah, are an invalid excuse, since they were able to devise means and find the way. Then the angels confronted them about their religion with their words ﴿Was not the earth of Allah spacious?﴾. This question and answer indicate that they died as Muslims who wronged themselves by abandoning emigration; otherwise, had they died as disbelievers, none of this would have been said to them. The mention of them among the Companions was set aside because of the severity of what they had committed, and because it was not determined which of them had faith, and because of the possibility of his apostasy. And Allah knows best. Then the Exalted made an exception from the pronoun in ﴿their abode﴾, the hā' and mīm, for those who were truly oppressed, from the disabled men and the weak women and children, such as 'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'ah, Salamah ibn Hisham and others, for whom the Messenger ﷺ supplicated. Ibn 'Abbas said: I and my mother were among those whom Allah meant by this verse, for I was among the children at that time, and his mother was Umm al-Fadl bint al-Harith, whose name was Lubabah, and she was the sister of Maymunah, and her other sister was Lubabah the Younger, and they were nine sisters, of whom the Prophet ﷺ said: "The sisters are believers." Among them were Salma, al-'Asma', Hufaydah, and it is said of Hufaydah: Umm Hufayd, and her name was Hazilah. They were six full sisters and three from the same mother, and they were Salma, Salamah, and Asma' bint 'Umays al-Khath'amiyyah, the wife of Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, then the wife of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, then the wife of 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with them all.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿In what were you?﴾ is a question of reproach, as has already been mentioned. The original is "fīmā," then the alif was deleted to distinguish the interrogative from the declarative, and the pause upon it is "li-allā tuḥdhaf al-alif wa-l-ḥarakah." The intended meaning of his saying: "Was not the earth of Allah spacious?" is Madinah, meaning: were you not able, empowered to emigrate and to distance yourselves from those who oppressed you? In this verse there is evidence for abandoning a land in which sins are committed.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: if sins are committed in a land, leave it, and he recited: "Was not the earth of Allah spacious, so that you might emigrate therein?" It is related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Whoever flees with his religion from one land to another, even if it is a span, has earned Paradise and will be the companion of Ibrahim and Muhammad, peace be upon them both."

His saying: ﴿So their abode is Hell﴾, meaning their dwelling is the Fire. Emigration was obligatory upon everyone who embraced Islam.

﴿And evil is it as a destination﴾ is in the accusative as an explanation. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They are not able to devise a plan﴾: "hilah" (means/plan) is a general term for the kinds of causes of escape. "Sabil" (way) is, as Mujahid, al-Suddi and others mentioned, the way to Madinah, but the correct view is that it is general to all ways. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿As for those, it may be that Allah will pardon them﴾: this one who has no means of emigrating has no sin for which he would need to be pardoned; rather the meaning is that one may suppose that it is obligatory to bear the utmost hardship in emigration, such that whoever does not bear that hardship is punished. So Allah removed that supposition, for it is not obligatory to bear the utmost hardship; rather, it was permissible to leave emigration when lacking provisions and a mount. So the meaning of the verse is: those will not be strictly called to account. For this reason He said: ﴿And Allah is ever Pardoning and Forgiving﴾, and past and future are the same with respect to Him, the Exalted, as has already been mentioned.

**The commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*) on Surah 4, verse 100:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever emigrates in the way of Allah will find on the earth many a refuge and abundance.﴾ And whoever leaves his home as an emigrant to Allah and His Messenger, then death overtakes him, his reward has indeed fallen upon Allah, and Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful (100). In it are five issues.

**The first issue:** His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever emigrates in the way of Allah will find﴾ is a conditional sentence (*shart*), and its response (*jawab*) follows.

(*Fi al-ardi muraghaman*): Scholars differed over the interpretation of *al-muraghim*. Mujahid said: *al-muraghim* is *al-mutazahzih* [[In Ibn 'Atiyya: "the one who moves away from what he dislikes."]]. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, al-Rabi' and others said: *al-muraghim* is *al-mutahawwal* (the one who relocates) and *al-madhhab* (the way or destination). Ibn Zayd said: *al-muraghim* is *al-muhajar* (the place of emigration), and Abu 'Ubayda said the same. Al-Nahhas said: these statements are alike in meaning. *Al-muraghim* is the way out and the relocation undertaken in a state of emigration, and it is the name of the place where one is "rughima" (has his nose rubbed in the dust), and it is derived from *al-raghām* (dust). One says: "Raghima anfuhu" (his nose was rubbed in the dust), meaning he was humbled and lay prostrate in the dust.

And one says: "Raghamtu fulanan" (I shunned someone and became hostile to him), and I did not care if his nose was rubbed in the dust. It was also said: emigrant and *muraghim* were so named because a man, when he accepted Islam, became hostile to his people and shunned them, so his departure was called *muraghaman*, and his arrival at the Prophet ﷺ was called *hijra* (emigration). Al-Suddi said: *al-muraghim* is the one who seeks a livelihood. Ibn al-Qasim said: I heard Malik say: *al-muraghim* is going off into the earth. All of this is interpretation by meaning, and all of it is close to one another. As for the specific sense of the word, *al-muraghim* is the place of *muraghama* (rubbing the opponent's nose in the dust), as we mentioned: each of two disputing parties rubs the nose of the other by overpowering him in his aim. Thus, it is as if the disbelievers of Quraysh humbled the noses of those who were held back in Makkah; so if an emigrant emigrated from among them, he would humble the noses of Quraysh by being in a place of protection away from them, and that protection is the place of *muraghama*. From this is the saying of al-Nabigha:

*Like a lance that is sheltered by its supports,*
*Mighty in its place of humbling and its refuge.*

**The second issue:** His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and abundance﴾, meaning abundance in provision. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Rabi' and al-Dahhak. Qatada said: the meaning is abundance from misguidance to guidance and from poverty to wealth. Malik said: the abundance is the abundance of lands. This is more fitting to the eloquence of the Arabs, for through the vastness of the earth and the multitude of refuges comes abundance in provision, and expansiveness of the breast for one's worries and thoughts, and other forms of relief. A similar meaning is in the saying of the poet:

*Whenever a friend sought to cut me off,*
*I found behind me an open, wide expanse.*

Another:

*I would have had a wide space to move*
*In the earth, long and broad.*

**The third issue:** Malik said: this verse indicates that no one may dwell in a land where the predecessors (*al-salaf*) are reviled and where things are done without right. He also said: *al-muraghim* is going off into the earth, and *al-sa'a* is the vastness of lands, as previously stated. Some scholars also used this verse as evidence that a warrior (*ghazi*) who set out for a raid and then died before the fighting has a share (of the spoils) even though he did not attend the battle. Ibn Lahi'a narrated this from Yazid ibn Abi Habib from the people of Madinah, and it is also reported from Ibn al-Mubarak.

**The fourth issue:** His saying, may He be exalted: (And whoever leaves his home as an emigrant to Allah and His Messenger) — the verse. 'Ikrima, the client of Ibn 'Abbas, said: I searched for the name of this man for fourteen years until I found it. In 'Ikrima's statement is evidence of the nobility of this knowledge in former times, and that concern for it is good and knowing it is a virtue. A similar statement is that of Ibn 'Abbas: I remained for years wishing to ask 'Umar about the two women who conspired against the Messenger of Allah ﷺ; nothing prevented me except my awe of him.

The one 'Ikrima mentioned is Damra ibn al-'Is, or al-'Is ibn Damra ibn Zinba'; this was related by al-Tabari from Sa'id ibn Jubayr. It is also said: Damira. It is said: Jundu' ibn Damra of the Banu Layth, and he was among the oppressed in Makkah and was ill. When he heard what Allah had revealed about emigration, he said: "Take me out." A bed was prepared for him and he was placed upon it and carried out, but he died on the road at al-Tan'im [[al-Tan'im: a place near Makkah within the sacred area (*al-hill*), known as the mosque of 'A'isha. From it the one performing 'umra enters the state of ihram.]], so Allah revealed concerning him: (And whoever leaves his home as an emigrant) — the verse.

Abu 'Umar mentioned that it has been said concerning him: Khalid ibn Hizam ibn Khuwaylid, the nephew of Khadija, and that he emigrated to the land of Abyssinia, but a snake bit him on the road and he died before reaching the land of Abyssinia, so the verse was revealed concerning him. And Allah knows best. Abu al-Faraj al-Jawzi related that he was Habib ibn Damra. It was also said: Damra ibn Jundab al-Damri, from al-Suddi. And it is reported from 'Ikrima that he was Jundab ibn Damra al-Jundu'i. And it is reported from Ibn [[In Ibn 'Atiyya and in all the manuscripts (*al-usul*) A, J, F: "Jabir." Perhaps the "Ibn Jabir" is 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Jabir ibn 'Ateek al-Ansari or his brother Muhammad.]] Jabir that he was Damra ibn Baghid of the Banu Layth. Al-Mahdawi related that he was Damra ibn Damra ibn Nu'aym. It was also said: Damra ibn Khuza'a. And Allah knows best.

Ma'mar related from Qatada, who said: When the verse (Indeed, those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves) was revealed, a man among the Muslims who was ill said: "By Allah, I have no excuse! I am a guide on the road, and I am well-off, so carry me." They carried him, but death overtook him on the road. The Companions of the Prophet ﷺ said: "Had he reached us, his reward would have been complete," and he had died at al-Tan'im. His sons came to the Prophet ﷺ and informed him of the story, so this verse was revealed: (And whoever leaves his home as an emigrant) — the verse. His name was Damra ibn Jundab, and it is said: Jundab ibn Damra, as previously stated.

(And Allah is ever Forgiving) for what he had of polytheism (*shirk*).

(Merciful) when He accepted his repentance.

**The fifth issue:** Ibn al-'Arabi said: The scholars, may Allah be pleased with them, divided going off into the earth into two categories: fleeing (*haraban*) and seeking (*talaban*). The first divides into six categories:

*First*: emigration (*hijra*), which is departure from the abode of war (*dar al-harb*) to the abode of Islam (*dar al-Islam*). This was obligatory in the time of the Prophet ﷺ, and this emigration remains obligatory until the Day of Resurrection. What was discontinued with the conquest (of Makkah) is the intention to go to the Prophet ﷺ wherever he was [[As in the manuscripts. In Ibn al-'Arabi: "whoever accepted Islam in the abode of war was obligated to leave for the abode of Islam."]]. If one remains in the abode of war, he disobeys, and his state is disputed.

*Second*: leaving a land of innovation (*bid'a*). Ibn al-Qasim said: I heard Malik say: it is not lawful for anyone to dwell in a land where the predecessors are reviled. Ibn al-'Arabi said: This is correct, for when you cannot change an evil, then depart from it. Allah the Exalted said: (And when you see those who engage in vain talk about Our signs, turn away from them) — up to His saying (the wrongdoers) [[See vol. 7, p. 12.]].

*Third*: leaving a land in which what is forbidden (*haram*) predominates, for seeking what is lawful (*halal*) is obligatory upon every Muslim.

*Fourth*: fleeing from harm to the body. This is a grace from Allah which He permitted. If one fears for his life, Allah has permitted him to leave that place and flee with himself to save it from that feared harm. The first to do so was Abraham, peace be upon him, for when he feared his people, he said: (Indeed, I am emigrating to my Lord) [[See vol. 13, p. 339 and p. 265.]], and he said: (Indeed, I am going to my Lord; He will guide me) [[See vol. 15, p. 97.]]. And concerning Moses, He said, reporting: (So he left it, fearful, anticipating) [[See vol. 13, p. 339 and p. 265.]].

*Fifth*: fear of illness in unhealthy lands and leaving them for pleasant lands. The Prophet ﷺ permitted the herdsmen, when they found Madinah unhealthy, to go out to the pasture and stay there until they recovered. Exempted from this is leaving because of plague (*ta'un*), for Allah has forbidden it by the authentic hadith from His Prophet ﷺ, and its explanation has already passed in (al-Baqara) [[See vol. 3, p. 230.]]. However, our scholars said: it is disliked (*makruh*).

*Sixth*: fleeing for fear of harm to wealth, for the sanctity of a Muslim's property is like the sanctity of his blood, and his family is similar to it and more binding.

As for the category of seeking, it divides into two: seeking religion and seeking worldly gain. As for seeking religion, it multiplies according to the multiplicity of its kinds, into nine categories:

*First*: travel for reflection (*'ibra*). Allah the Exalted said: (Have they not traveled through the earth and observed how was the end of those before them?) [[See vol. 14, p. 9.]], and this is abundant. It is said that Dhu al-Qarnayn only traveled the earth to see its wonders. And it was said: to enforce the truth in it.

*Second*: travel for Hajj. The first is recommended (*nadb*), but this is obligatory (*fard*).

*Third*: travel for jihad, and it has its rulings.

*Fourth*: travel for livelihood. A man's livelihood may become difficult while he remains at home, so he goes out in its pursuit, not seeking more than it, whether by hunting, gathering firewood, or cutting grass. This is obligatory upon him.

*Fifth*: travel for trade and for earnings beyond sustenance. This is permissible by the bounty of Allah, the Glorified and Exalted. Allah the Exalted said: (There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord) [[See vol. 2, p. 413.]], meaning trade. It is a blessing that Allah bestowed during travel for Hajj, so how much more so when it is undertaken alone.

*Sixth*: travel for seeking knowledge, which is well known.

*Seventh*: visiting places (*qasd al-biqa'*). The Prophet ﷺ said: (Journeys should not be undertaken except to three mosques).

*Eighth*: the frontiers (*thughur*), for garrisoning (*ribat*) in them and increasing their numbers in order to defend them.

*Ninth*: visiting brothers for the sake of Allah, the Exalted. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: (A man visited his brother in another village, so Allah sent an angel to wait for him on his path. The angel said: "Where are you going?" He said: "I want a brother of mine in this village." He said: "Do you have some favor with him that you are looking after?" He said: "No, except that I love him for the sake of Allah, Mighty and Majestic." He said: "Then I am the messenger of Allah to you, that Allah loves you as you have loved him for His sake.") Related by Muslim and others.

There are ten issues in this matter. The first is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When you travel through the land﴾, meaning you journey, and this has already been discussed. The scholars differed over the ruling on shortening the prayer (qasr) while travelling. It is narrated from a group that it is obligatory (fard). This is the view of Umar ibn Abd al-‘Aziz, the Kufans, al-Qadi Isma'il, and Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman. They argued with the hadith of ‘Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her: "The prayer was prescribed as two rak'ahs, two rak'ahs," and the rest of the hadith. There is no proof in it, because she herself used to complete the prayer while travelling, and that weakens it. Also, the consensus of the jurists of the major cities is that it is not a principle that is considered in the case of a traveller praying behind a resident. Other Companions, such as Umar, Ibn ‘Abbas, and Jubayr ibn Mut'im, have said: "The prayer was prescribed in the settled state as four, in travel as two, and in fear as one rak'ah." This was narrated by Muslim from Ibn ‘Abbas.

Furthermore, the hadith of ‘Aisha has been narrated by Ibn ‘Ajlan from Salih ibn Kaysan, from ‘Urwah, from ‘Aisha, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made the prayer obligatory as two rak'ahs, two rak'ahs. Al-Awza'i narrated it from Ibn Shihab, from ‘Urwah, from ‘Aisha, who said: Allah made the prayer obligatory upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) as two rak'ahs, two rak'ahs, and the rest of the hadith. This is an inconsistency (idtirab) in the transmission. Moreover, her saying "the prayer was prescribed" is not to be taken literally, since the Maghrib and Subh prayers are excluded from it: the Maghrib has not been increased or decreased, and likewise the Subh. All of this weakens its text (matn), not its chain (sanad).

Ibn al-Jahm related that Ashhab narrated from Malik that shortening is obligatory. However, the well-known position of his school, most of his followers, and the majority of scholars of the early and later generations is that shortening is a sunnah. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, and it is the correct position, as will be explained, Allah willing. The position of the majority of the Baghdadi Malikis is that the obligation is a choice (takhyir), and this is also the view of al-Shafi'i's followers.

Then they differed over which of the two is better. Some said that shortening is better; this is the view of al-Abhari and others. It was also said that completing the prayer is better, and this is attributed to al-Shafi'i. Abu Sa'id al-Frawi al-Maliki related that the correct position in the school of Malik is that the traveller has the choice between completing and shortening. I say: this is what appears from His saying, glorified and exalted be He: ﴿There is no blame upon you for shortening the prayer﴾. However, Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, recommends shortening for him, and he also holds that he must repeat the prayer within its time if he completes it.

Abu Mus'ab related in his Mukhtasar from Malik and the people of Madinah, who said: Shortening during travel is a sunnah for men and women. Abu ‘Umar said: That suffices as evidence for the school of Malik. Moreover, his position has not varied on the point that whoever completes the prayer while travelling must repeat it as long as the time remains, and that is a recommendation (istihbab) in the view of those who understood, not an obligation (ijab).

Al-Shafi'i said: Shortening outside of fear is by the Sunnah, while in fear combined with travel it is by the Qur'an and the Sunnah. Whoever prays four rak'ahs has no fault, but I do not like anyone to complete the prayer while travelling out of aversion to the Sunnah.

Abu Bakr al-Athram said: I asked Ahmad ibn Hanbal: May a man pray four rak'ahs while travelling? He said: No, I do not approve of it; the Sunnah is two rak'ahs.

In the Muwatta' of Malik, from Ibn Shihab, from a man of the family of Khalid ibn Usayd, that he asked ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Umar: "O Abu ‘Abd al-Rahman, we find the prayer of fear and the prayer of residence in the Qur'an, but we do not find the prayer of travel?" ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Umar said: "O my nephew, Allah, blessed and exalted, sent Muhammad (ﷺ) to us and we know nothing, so we do as we have seen him doing." In this report, shortening the prayer during travel without fear is a sunnah, not an obligation, because it is not mentioned in the Qur'an. The shortening mentioned in the Qur'an applies only when travel and fear occur together, so Allah did not permit shortening in His Book except under these two conditions. A similar case in the Qur'an is: ﴿And whoever among you cannot afford free believing women...﴾ (see p. 135 of this volume), and it has already been mentioned. Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿So when you are secure, establish the prayer﴾, meaning complete it. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) shortened four rak'ahs to two during all his journeys, except the Maghrib, while he was secure and feared none but Allah, the Exalted. So that became a sunnah established by him (ﷺ), an addition to the rulings of Allah, like all the other things he established and explained that are not mentioned in the Qur'an.

His saying, "as we have seen him doing," together with the hadith of ‘Umar, where he asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about shortening during travel without fear, and he said: "It is a charity which Allah has given you, so accept His charity" [[The text of the hadith ("It is a charity which Allah has given you...") as in al-Sahih, al-Tabari, al-Jassas and others, and it will come later. In the originals: "That is a charity..." and in J: "which Allah gave to His servants."]]. This shows that Allah may permit a thing in His Book under a condition, and then permit that same thing through His Prophet without that condition. Hanzalah asked Ibn ‘Umar about the prayer of travel, and he said: "Two rak'ahs." I said: "Then where is His saying: ﴿If you fear that those who disbelieve will tempt you﴾, while we are secure?" He said: "It is the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." So Ibn ‘Umar called it a sunnah without restriction, and Ibn ‘Abbas said the same. Where, then, is the school's position regarding them?

Abu ‘Umar said: Malik did not establish the chain (isnad) of this hadith, because he did not name the man who asked Ibn ‘Umar, and he dropped a narrator from the chain. The man he did not name was Umayyah ibn ‘Abdullah ibn Khalid ibn Usayd ibn Abi al-‘Is ibn Umayyah ibn ‘Abd Shams ibn ‘Abd Manaf, and Allah knows best.

The second issue: The scholars differed over the distance at which the prayer may be shortened.

...Dawud said: one shortens the prayer on every journey, long or short, even if it is three miles from the place where the Friday prayer is held, relying on what Muslim narrated from Yahya ibn Yazid al-Hunna'i, who said: I asked Anas ibn Malik about shortening the prayer, and he said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out a distance of three miles or three farsakh (Shu'ba, the doubter [[One of the narrators of this chain of narration.]]), he would pray two rak'ahs." This has no proof in it, because it is doubtful. Even if we accept one of the two, it may be that he was marking the distance from which shortening begins, and that the journey was longer than that, and Allah knows best. Ibn al-'Arabi said: Some people have played with the religion, saying: whoever leaves the town to its outskirts shortens the prayer and breaks the fast. The one who says this is either a non-Arab who does not know what travel means among the Arabs, or one who treats the religion lightly. Were it not that the scholars have mentioned it, I would not be willing to glance at it even with the corner of my eye, nor think about it with the idle thoughts of my heart. The limit of the journey that makes shortening permissible is not mentioned either in the Qur'an or in the Sunnah. It was so because it was an Arabic term whose meaning was firmly established among the Arabs to whom Allah addressed the Qur'an. We know with certainty that one who goes out of the houses for some matter is not a traveller linguistically or legally [[In vol. T: "legally in it."]], and that if he walks for three days he is certainly a traveller. Likewise we judge that one who walks for a day and a night is a traveller, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "It is not lawful for a woman who believes in Allah and the Last Day to travel a day's journey except with a mahram of hers." This is the sound view, because it is midway between the two states. Malik relied on it, but he did not find this hadith agreed upon (muttafaq 'alayh), and it was narrated once as "a day and a night" and once as "three days." So he went to 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar and relied on his practice, for he used to shorten the prayer up to Ri'm [[Ri'm (with a kasra on its first letter, a hamza on its second letter, and a sukun; it is also said with a ya without hamza): a valley in Medina.]], which is four burud, because Ibn 'Umar was very much in the habit of following the Prophet (ﷺ). Another said: the scholars are unanimous that shortening was legislated as a concession, and it applies only to a long journey which usually involves hardship. Malik, al-Shafi'i and his companions, al-Layth, al-Awza'i, and the jurists of the people of hadith, Ahmad and Ishaq and others, took a full day as the measure. Malik's saying "a day and a night" refers back to the full day, because by his saying "a journey of a day and a night" he did not mean that one travels all the day and all the night, but that one travels a journey in which one spends the night far [[The word بعيدا is enclosed in brackets in the source text.]] from one's family and cannot return to them. In al-Bukhari: Ibn 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas used to break the fast and shorten [the prayer] over four burud, which are sixteen farsakh. This is the school of Malik. Al-Shafi'i and al-Tabari said: forty-six miles. From Malik in al-'Utbiyyah, concerning one who went out to his estate at forty-five miles, he said: he shortens, and this is a close matter. From Malik in al-Kutub al-Manthurah: that he shortens at thirty-six miles, which is close to a day and a night. Yahya ibn 'Umar said: he repeats it forever! Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam said: within the time! [[So it is in all the manuscripts.]] The Kufans said: one does not shorten for less than a three-day journey. This is the view of 'Uthman, Ibn Mas'ud and Hudhayfah. In the Sahih of al-Bukhari, from Ibn 'Umar, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "A woman should not travel three days except with a mahram." Abu Hanifah said: three days and nights by the pace of camels and the walking of feet. al-Hasan and al-Zuhri said: one shortens the prayer on a journey of two days. This view was also narrated from Malik. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated it from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "A woman should not travel a distance of two nights except with a husband or a mahram." Ibn 'Umar shortened at thirty miles, and Anas at fifteen miles. al-Awza'i said: most scholars hold that shortening is tied to the full day, and we follow this. Abu 'Umar said: the reported hadiths on this subject are inconsistent, as you see in their wording, and the summary of them, in my view, and Allah knows best, is that they were given in answer to questioners. Each one narrated the meaning of what he heard. It is as if he was asked at one time: "Does a woman travel a day's journey without a mahram?" and he said: "No." He was asked at another time: "Does a woman travel two days without a mahram?" and he said: "No." Another asked him: "Does a woman travel [a distance of] [[From vols. J and T.]] [three days without a mahram?"] and he said: "No." The same applies to the matter of the night and the barid as they have been reported: each one conveyed what he heard according to its meaning. And Allah knows best. What unites the meanings of the reports on this subject, though their apparent wordings differ, is the prohibition on a woman travelling, without a mahram, a journey in which she is at risk of temptation, whether short or long. And Allah knows best.

The third matter: they differed concerning the type of journey in which the prayer is shortened. People agreed on jihad, hajj, 'umrah, and what resembles them such as maintaining ties of kinship and saving a life. They differed regarding other journeys. The majority hold that shortening is permitted on a permissible journey, such as trade and the like. It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: the prayer is not shortened except on hajj or jihad. 'Ata' said: it is not shortened except on a journey of obedience and one of the paths of goodness. It is also narrated from him: one shortens on every permissible journey, like the view of the majority. Malik said: if one goes out for hunting, not for his livelihood but for recreation, or goes out to look at a town for enjoyment and pleasure, he does not shorten. Most scholars hold that there is no shortening on a journey of sin, such as a rebel or a highway robber and what is in their meaning. It is narrated from Abu Hanifah and al-Awza'i that shortening is permitted in all of these, and it is narrated from Malik. This has already been discussed in (al-Baqarah [[See vol. 2, p. 277.]]). It differs from Ahmad: at one time he held the view of the majority, and at another he said: one shortens only on hajj or 'umrah. The correct view is what the majority said, because shortening was legislated only as a relief for the traveller from the hardships that befall him, and as an aid to what he intends that is permissible. All journeys are equal in this, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when you travel in the land, there is no blame on you if you shorten the prayer﴾, that is, no sin, which is general. The peace be upon him said: "The best of Allah's servants are those who, when they travel, shorten [the prayer] and break the fast." al-Sha'bi said [[This is a hadith narrated by Ahmad and al-Bayhaqi with the wording: "Allah loves that His concessions be taken, as He loves that His obligations be fulfilled."]]: Allah loves that His concessions be acted upon, as He loves that His obligations be acted upon. As for a journey of sin, shortening is not permitted in it, because that would be an aid to him in disobeying Allah, and Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿And cooperate in righteousness and piety, but do not cooperate in sin and aggression﴾ [[See vol. 6, p. 37.]].

The fourth matter: they differed about when one shortens. The majority hold that the traveller does not shorten until he leaves the houses of the village, and at that point he is "striking through the land" (dharib fi al-ard). This is Malik's view in al-Mudawwanah [[The major early Maliki compendium of law.]]. Malik did not set a limit on nearness. It is narrated from him that if the village is one whose people gather together, its people do not shorten until they pass it by three miles, and likewise on the return. If it is not one whose people gather together, they shorten when they pass its orchards. It is narrated from al-Harith ibn Abi Rabi'ah that he intended a journey, and he led them in two rak'ahs in his house, and among them were al-Aswad ibn Yazid and many companions of Ibn Mas'ud. This is also the view of 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah and Sulayman ibn Musa. I say: on this view the meaning of the verse would be: ﴿And when you strike through the land﴾, that is, when you resolve to strike through the land. And Allah knows best. It is narrated from Mujahid that he said: the traveller does not shorten on his first day until night. This is an anomalous view (shadhdh), and it is established from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed Zuhr in Medina as four rak'ahs, and prayed 'Asr at Dhu al-Hulayfah as two rak'ahs. The imams have recorded it. Between Dhu al-Hulayfah and Medina is about six or seven miles [[In vols. J and T: "It is said seven."]].

**The fifth matter:** The traveller must intend shortening (qasr) from the moment of beginning the prayer. If he opens the prayer with the intention of shortening it, then decides to stay (in a place) during the course of his prayer,[[In J, T and Z: "adʻāf" (multiples).]] he makes it a voluntary prayer (nafilah). If this happens after he has prayed one rak'ah of it, he adds another rak'ah to it and gives the salam, and then prays as a resident. Al-Abhari and Ibn al-Jallab said: "This, and God knows best, is a recommendation (istihbab). If he continues his prayer and completes it, his prayer suffices for him." Abu 'Umar said: "In my view it is as they both said, because it is a noon prayer (zuhr), whether it is performed on a journey or at home, and likewise all the five prayers."

**The sixth matter:** The scholars differed on this topic concerning the length of stay which, if the traveller intends it, makes him complete the prayer. Malik, al-Shafi'i, al-Layth ibn Sa'd, al-Tabari and Abu Thawr said: if he intends to stay four days, he completes the prayer. This is also reported from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib. Abu Hanifah, his companions and al-Thawri said: if he intends to stay fifteen nights, he completes the prayer, and if it is less, he shortens. This is the view of Ibn 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas, and there is no dissenter from them among the Companions, according to what al-Tahawi mentioned. It is also reported from Sa'id. Ahmad said: if the traveller combines (jama'a)[[Jama'a: 'azama (resolved).]] the stay of twenty-one obligatory prayers, he shortens; if he exceeds that, he completes. Dawud also held this view.

The correct view is that of Malik, based on the hadith of Ibn al-Hadrami from the Prophet ﷺ, that he allowed the emigrant (muhajir) to stay in Makkah for three days after completing his rites, and then depart. It was narrated by al-Tahawi, Ibn Majah and others. It is known that when emigration (hijrah) was obligatory before the Conquest, staying in Makkah was not permitted. So the Prophet ﷺ granted the emigrant three days to attend to his needs and prepare his affairs. He did not give these days the ruling of residence nor place them within the category of residing, but he kept for him in them the ruling of the traveller, and prevented him from staying a fourth day, thereby giving him the ruling of the present resident. This became a firmly relied-upon principle.
