Similar to this is what 'Umar (may God be pleased with him) did when he expelled the Jews, in accordance with the saying of the Messenger of God ﷺ[[He means his saying ﷺ: "Expel the Jews and Christians from the Arabian Peninsula."]], granting them a stay of three days to settle their affairs.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: "I heard some of the Malikite scholars say: the three days were only excluded from the ruling of residence because God, Exalted, deferred in them the one upon whom punishment had been sent down and who was certain of leaving the world. So God, Exalted, said: (Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days; that is a promise not to be denied).[[See vol. 9, p. 59.]]"

There is another view on this question besides these views: that the traveller shortens forever until he returns to his homeland or settles in a homeland of his own. It is reported from Anas that he stayed two years in Nishapur, shortening the prayer. Abu Mijlaz said: I said to Ibn 'Umar: "I come to Madinah and stay there seven or eight months seeking a need," and he said: "Pray two rak'ahs." Abu Ishaq al-Sabi'i said: "We stayed in Sijistan for two years with men from the companions of Ibn Mas'ud, praying two rak'ahs." Ibn 'Umar stayed in Adharbayjan[[It is said: six months.]] praying two rak'ahs each time, and snow was between them and their return.

Abu 'Umar said: In our view, the meaning of these reports is that none of these residents had an intention (niyyah) to stay this long; rather the case is like one who says: "I will leave today, I will leave tomorrow." When it is like this, there is no firm resolve ('azimah) here to stay.

**The seventh matter:** Muslim narrated from 'Urwah from 'A'ishah, who said: "God made the prayer obligatory as two rak'ahs when He made it obligatory; then it was completed in residence, and the prayer of the journey was kept at the first obligation." Al-Zuhri said: "I said to 'Urwah: 'What is the matter with 'A'ishah that she completes (the prayer) on a journey?' He said: 'She interpreted it as 'Uthman interpreted.'" This is an answer that is not comprehensive.

The people differed concerning the interpretation of 'Uthman's and 'A'ishah's completion (of the prayer), (may God be pleased with them both), in several views. Ma'mar, from al-Zuhri, said: 'Uthman only prayed four rak'ahs at Mina because he had resolved to stay after the Hajj. Mughirah narrated from Ibrahim that 'Uthman prayed four because he had adopted it as a homeland.[[It is established that 'Uthman (may God be pleased with him) completed the prayer at Mina because he had married in Makkah, and Mina is among its outskirts. When the Companions objected to him, he said: "I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say: 'Whoever marries in a town is one of its people,' and I am married to a person of Makkah." See al-Jassas, vol. 2, p. 254.]] Yunus, from al-Zuhri, said: "When 'Uthman acquired properties at al-Ta'if and intended to stay there, he prayed four." He said: "Then the leaders after him adopted it." Ayyub, from al-Zuhri, said: "'Uthman ibn 'Affan completed the prayer at Mina because of the Bedouins, for they had increased that year, so he led the people in four rak'ahs to inform them that the prayer is four." Abu Dawud mentioned all these views in his Musannaf, in the Book of Rites, in the chapter on prayer at Mina. Abu 'Umar mentioned in al-Tamhid: Ibn Jurayj said: "It has reached me that 'Uthman only completed it at Mina because a Bedouin called out to him in the Mosque of al-Khayf at Mina, saying: 'O Commander of the Faithful, I have been praying it as two rak'ahs since I saw you the first year.' 'Uthman feared that the ignorant people would think the prayer is only two rak'ahs." Ibn Jurayj said: "He only completed it at Mina alone."[[It is established that 'Uthman (may God be pleased with him) completed the prayer at Mina because he had married in Makkah, and Mina is among its outskirts. When the Companions objected to him, he said: "I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say: 'Whoever marries in a town is one of its people,' and I am married to a person of Makkah." See al-Jassas, vol. 2, p. 254.]]

Abu 'Umar said: As for the interpretations of 'A'ishah's completion, none of them is narrated from her; they are only assumptions and interpretations not accompanied by evidence. The weakest of what has been said about this is: "She is the Mother of the Believers, and wherever the people were, they were her sons, and their dwellings were her dwellings." But was she not the Mother of the Believers merely because she was the wife of the Prophet ﷺ, the father of the believers (may God bless him and grant him peace)? He was the one who established shortening (of the prayer) during his journeys, his military campaigns, his Hajj and his 'Umrah.[[From T and Ya.]]

In the recitation of Ubayy ibn Ka'b and his codex: (The Prophet is closer to the believers than their own selves, and his wives are their mothers, and he is a father to them).[[See vol. 14, p. 121.]] And Mujahid, concerning His saying, Exalted: (These are my daughters; they are purer for you),[[See vol. 9, p. 73.]] said: "They were not his daughters, but they were the women of his community, and every prophet is the father of his community." I say: This has been objected to on the ground that the Prophet ﷺ was a lawgiver, whereas she was not, and so the two (answers) are separated.

Weaker than this is the view of those who say: "When she completed the prayer, she was not on a permissible journey." This is absolutely false, for she was too fearful of God and too God-conscious to set out on a journey He does not approve. This interpretation about her is among the lies of the innovating Shi'ah and their slanders. Glory be to You! This is a tremendous slander! Rather, she (may God be pleased with her) went out striving, seeking reward, desiring to extinguish the fire of strife, for she is the most deserving to be shown modesty, but the affairs got out of control. The explanation of this meaning will come, God willing, Exalted.

It has also been said: "She completed (the prayer) because she did not see shortening except in Hajj, 'Umrah and military campaign." This is false, for that was not transmitted from her, nor known from her school of thought. Moreover, she did complete (the prayer) during her journey to 'Ali.

The best of what has been said about her shortening and completing is that she took the concession of God, to show the people that completing (the prayer) has no harm in it, even if other than it is more excellent. 'Ata' said: "Shortening is a sunnah and a concession, and he is the narrator from 'A'ishah that the Messenger of God ﷺ fasted and broke his fast, and completed the prayer and shortened it during the journey." It was narrated by Talhah ibn 'Umar. And from him (someone) said:[[In J, T, Ya and Ya: "she said."]] "The Messenger of God ﷺ did all of that: he fasted and broke his fast, shortened the prayer and completed it." Al-Nasa'i narrated with a sound chain that 'A'ishah performed 'Umrah with the Messenger of God ﷺ from Madinah to Makkah,[until when she arrived at Makkah[[Addition from Sunan al-Nasa'i.]]] she said: "O Messenger of God, may my father and mother be your ransom! You shortened and I completed, you broke your fast and I fasted?" He said: "You did well, O 'A'ishah," and he did not blame me. This is how it is vocalised, with a fatha on the first letter and a damma on the second in both words. Al-Daraqutni narrated from 'A'ishah that the Prophet ﷺ used to shorten during the journey, and complete, break his fast and fast. He said: its chain is sound.

**The eighth matter:** His saying, Exalted: ﴿that you shorten some of the prayer﴾. The (particle) "an" is in the accusative position, meaning "in that you shorten." Abu 'Ubayd said: "In it there are three forms: qasartu al-salat, qassartuha and aqsartuha." The scholars differed concerning its interpretation. A group of scholars held that it means shortening four (rak'ahs) to two, in fear and otherwise, based on the hadith of Ya'la ibn Umayyah, as will come. Others said: it is only the shortening of two rak'ahs to one, and the two rak'ahs on a journey are only a complete (prayer). As 'Umar (may God be pleased with him) said: "A complete (prayer), not shortened," and its shortening is that it becomes one rak'ah. Al-Suddi said: "If you pray two rak'ahs on a journey, it is complete, and shortening is not permitted except when you fear." Thus this verse permits that each group pray one rak'ah, adding nothing to it, and the imam has two rak'ahs. A similar view is reported from Ibn 'Umar, Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah and Ka'b, and Hudhayfah did it in Tabaristan when the commander Sa'id ibn al-'As asked him about it. Ibn 'Abbas narrated that the Prophet ﷺ prayed in this way at the battle of Dhat Qarad[[Dhu Qarad (with a fatha on the qaf, the ra and the unmarked dal): a place about a day's distance from Madinah.]], one rak'ah for each group, and they did not make up (the prayer). Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah narrated that the Prophet ﷺ prayed similarly with his companions on the day of Muharib Khasfah and Bani Tha'labah.[[In J, Z, T, Ya: "the day of Harib Hayisah." In al-Bukhari: "the battle of Muharib Khasafah from Tha'labah." Thus in Ibn 'Atiyyah: it is the battle of Dhat al-Riqa', and Bani Tha'labah, Bani Anmar, and Muharib, and its idafah is a specification, because there is another Muharib.]] Abu Hurayrah narrated that the Prophet ﷺ prayed similarly between Dajnan and 'Usfan.[[Dajnan (with vowelling of the jim or its sukun): a mountain in Tihamah; it is said: a small hill at a distance of one barid from Makkah. Al-Waqidi: between Dajnan and Makkah is twenty-five miles.]][[ 'Usfan (with a damma on its first letter and sukun on its second): a watering place on the road between al-Juhfah and Makkah; or a village containing a pulpit, palm trees and farms, thirty-six miles from Makkah, which is the boundary of Tihamah.]]

(Mu'jam al-Buldan).]]. I say: In Sahih Muslim, from Ibn Abbas, who said: Allah prescribed the prayer through the tongue of your Prophet ﷺ: four (rak'ahs) when at home, two when travelling, and one in fear. This supports and strengthens this opinion. However, the judge Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi mentioned in his book called (al-Qabas): Our scholars [may Allah have mercy on them [[In J, T and Y.]]] said: this hadith is rejected by consensus. I say: This is not sound, for he and others have mentioned the disagreement and dispute, so the consensus they claimed is not established. And success is from Allah. Abu Bakr al-Razi al-Hanafi related in (Ahkam al-Quran) that the meaning of shortening here is shortening in the manner of the prayer, by omitting the bowing and prostration in favour of gesturing, and by omitting standing for the bowing. Others said: this verse permits shortening the limits and form of the prayer during close combat and the clash of battle, so one in such a state is permitted to pray by gesture with his head, and to pray one rak'ah wherever he faces, with one takbir [[So it is in some copies, and it is the correct reading, as in Ibn Atiyyah, who said: "and pray one rak'ah wherever he faces, with two takbirs, to one takbir." In J and T: "his takbir." The correction is from Y.]], as previously discussed in (al-Baqarah [[See vol. 3, p. 223.]]). Al-Tabari preferred this opinion and said: it is equivalent to the Almighty's saying: ﴿So when you are secure, establish the prayer﴾, meaning with its complete limits and form. I say: These three opinions are close in meaning, and they are based on the premise that the traveller's obligation is shortening, and that the prayer for him was only revealed as two rak'ahs, so there is no shortening. It is not said of the obligatory (prayer) "there is no blame," and it is not said of what was legislated as two rak'ahs that it is shortened, just as this is not said of the dawn prayer. Allah the Exalted mentioned shortening with two conditions, and the one in which both conditions apply is the prayer of fear. This is what Abu Bakr al-Razi mentioned in (Ahkam al-Quran) and argued with, and it was refuted with the hadith of Ya'la ibn Umayyah, as will come shortly, God willing. The ninth matter: His saying: ﴿If you fear﴾. The speech came out in the usual case, since the usual condition of Muslims was fear while travelling. For this reason Ya'la ibn Umayyah [I said [[From Z.]]] said to Umar: Why do we shorten while we are secure? Umar said: I wondered at what you wondered at, so I asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about it, and he said: (It is a charity which Allah has given you, so accept His charity). I say: The companions of al-Shafi'i and others have argued against the Hanafis with this hadith of Ya'la ibn Umayyah, saying: his saying "Why do we shorten while we are secure?" is a decisive proof that the implication of the verse is shortening in the number of rak'ahs. Al-Kiya al-Tabari said: The companions of Abu Hanifah have not offered an interpretation of this that equals the mention. Then, the two conditions do not apply to the prayer of fear, for if he does not travel over the land and there is no journey, but the disbelievers come to us and we fight in our lands, the prayer of fear is still permitted, so the existence of the two conditions is not required as he said [[So it is in the originals. Perhaps it is: "as they said."]]. In the recitation of Ubayy: (that you shorten the prayer if those who disbelieve fear to tempt you), with the omission of (if you fear). The meaning according to his recitation: lest those who disbelieve tempt you. It is recorded in the Mushaf of Uthman [may Allah be pleased with him [[From J, T and Y.]]] as (if you fear). A group went to the view that this verse only permits shortening during travel for one who fears the enemy, so whoever is secure has no shortening. It was narrated from Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that she used to say about travel: Complete your prayer. They said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to shorten. She said: He was in war and he was afraid, and are you afraid? Ata said: Among the companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, Aishah, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and Uthman used to complete (the prayer). But this is explained by causes, some of which have been mentioned earlier. A group went to the view that Allah the Exalted did not permit shortening in His Book except with two conditions: travel and fear, and outside of fear it is by the Sunnah; among them is al-Shafi'i, and this has been mentioned earlier. Others went to the view that the saying of the Almighty: (If you fear) is not connected to what precedes, and that the speech was complete at His saying: (from the prayer), then He began and said: (If you fear that those who disbelieve will tempt you), so establish for them, O Muhammad, the prayer of fear. And His saying: (Indeed the disbelievers have been to you an open enemy) is a parenthetical clause, said by al-Jurjani, and mentioned by al-Mahdawi and others. This view was refuted by al-Qushayri and the judge Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi. Al-Qushayri Abu Nasr said: There is great strain in reading it this way, even if the man (meaning al-Jurjani) elaborated in estimation and the striking of examples. Ibn al-Arabi said: None of this was needed by Umar, nor his son, nor Ya'la ibn Umayyah along with them. I say: There has come a hadith in accordance with what al-Jurjani said, mentioned by the judge Abu al-Walid ibn Rushd in his Muqaddimat, and Ibn Atiyyah also in his tafsir, from Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: A group of merchants asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: We travel over the land, so how shall we pray? So Allah the Exalted revealed: (And when you travel in the land, there is no blame upon you to shorten the prayer). Then the speech stopped. When a year had passed after that, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out on a campaign and prayed the noon prayer, and the polytheists said: Muhammad and his companions had an opportunity against you from their rear; why did you not press upon them? One of them said: Indeed they have another (prayer) after it. So Allah the Exalted revealed between the two prayers: (If you fear that those who disbelieve will tempt you) up to the end of the prayer of fear. If this report is sound, then no one has any argument against it, and it would be evidence for shortening outside of fear by the Qur'an. It has also been narrated from Ibn Abbas a similar report, who said: The saying of the Exalted: (And when you travel in the land, there is no blame upon you to shorten the prayer) was revealed concerning prayer while travelling. Then (If you fear that those who disbelieve will tempt you) was revealed concerning fear a year later. So the verse on this account contained two matters and two rulings. His saying (And when you travel in the land, there is no blame upon you to shorten the prayer) means while travelling, and the speech is complete. Then he began another obligation and put the condition first, and the meaning: If you fear that those who disbelieve will tempt you, and when you are among them and you establish the prayer for them. The "and" is superfluous, and the answer is (then let a party of them stand with you). His saying: (Indeed the disbelievers have been to you an open enemy) is a parenthetical clause. Some people went to the view that the mention of fear is abrogated by the Sunnah, namely the hadith of Umar, for it is narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said to him: (This is a charity which Allah has given you, so accept His charity). Al-Nahhas said: Whoever makes the Prophet's ﷺ shortening outside of fear, and his practice in that, abrogating the verse, has erred, for there is no prohibition of shortening in security in the verse; rather, it permits shortening only in fear. The tenth matter: His saying: ﴿that those who disbelieve will tempt you﴾. Al-Farra said: The people of the Hijaz say "fatantu al-rajul" (I tempted the man). Rabi'ah, Qays, Asad and all the people of Najd say "aftantu al-rajul." Al-Khalil and Sibawayh distinguished between them, saying: "fatantuhu" means I put temptation in him, like "akhalituhu" (I applied kohl to him), and "aftantuhu" means I made him one who is tempted. Al-Asma'i claimed that "aftantuhu" is not known.
(﻿Indeed the disbelievers have been to you an open enemy) "Aduwwan" here means "a'da'" (enemies). And Allah knows best.

**Part 1 of 3**

There are eleven issues concerning this verse.

**The first issue:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And when you are among them and establish prayer for them﴾. Al-Daraqutni narrated from Abu 'Ayyash al-Zuraqi, who said: "We were with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at 'Usfan, and the polytheists confronted us, led by Khalid ibn al-Walid, and they were between us and the qiblah. The Prophet (ﷺ) led us in the Dhuhr prayer. They said: 'They were in a state in which, had we attacked them unawares, we would have.' He said: Then they said: 'Now a prayer is coming to them which is dearer to them than their children and themselves.' He said: Then Jibril (peace be upon him) descended with this verse between Dhuhr and 'Asr: ﴿And when you are among them and establish prayer for them﴾." He mentioned the hadith, and its complete form will come later, if Allah wills. This was the cause of Khalid's (may Allah be pleased with him) acceptance of Islam.

This verse is connected to what preceded it concerning jihad. The Lord, blessed and exalted, made clear that prayer is not waived by the excuse of travel, nor by the excuse of jihad and fighting the enemy. However, there are concessions in prayer, as previously explained in (al-Baqarah [[See vol. 3, p. 223.]]) and in this surah, and their explanation is a matter of scholarly disagreement.

This verse is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ), and it also includes the leaders after him until the Day of Resurrection. A similar example is His saying: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾ [[See vol. 8, p. 244.]]. This is the view of the entire body of scholars.

Abu Yusuf and Isma'il ibn 'Ulayyah deviated and said: "We do not perform the prayer of fear after the Prophet (ﷺ), because the address was specific to him, by His saying: ﴿And when you are among them﴾. If he is not among them, this does not apply to them, because the Prophet (ﷺ) is not like others in this respect." Everyone wished to be led by him and to pray behind him, and no one after him stands in his excellence. People after him are equal in their conditions and close to one another, so the imam prays with one group and appoints someone to pray with the other group. But for them all to pray behind a single imam is not permitted.

The majority said: "We have been commanded to follow him and to take him as an example in more than one verse and more than one hadith. Allah said: ﴿So let those who oppose his command beware lest a trial strike them﴾ [[See vol. 12, p. 322.]]. And the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Pray as you have seen me pray.' Therefore, following him is required absolutely, unless clear evidence indicates a specific restriction. If what they cited were evidence of specificity, it would necessitate confining all addresses to those to whom they were directed, and then it would follow that the Sharia is limited to those who were addressed by it." Furthermore, the Companions (may the pleasure of Allah be upon them all) dismissed the notion of specificity in this prayer and extended it to others besides the Prophet (ﷺ). They were the most knowledgeable of the words and the most aware of the circumstances. Allah has also said: ﴿And when you see those who engage in vain talk concerning Our verses, turn away from them until they engage in a conversation other than it﴾ [[See vol. 7, p. 12.]]. This is an address to him, while his community is included within it, and there are many similar examples.

And He said: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾, and this does not necessitate restricting it to him alone, nor that whoever comes after him does not stand in his place in this matter. Likewise with His saying: ﴿And when you are among them﴾. Do you not see that Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, along with the body of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them), fought those who interpreted the obligation of zakat in a way similar to how you interpreted the prayer of fear?

Abu 'Umar said: "There is nothing in collecting zakat, in which the Prophet (ﷺ) and those after him among the caliphs were equal, that resembles the prayer of one who prays behind the Prophet (ﷺ) and one who prays behind someone else. This is because the purpose of collecting zakat is to deliver it to the needy, and there is no excellence for the one who gives it, whereas in prayer there is excellence for the one who prays behind the imam."

**The second issue:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So let a group of them stand with you﴾, meaning a company of them standing with you in prayer.

﴿And let them take their weapons﴾ means those who pray with you. It is also said: ﴿And let them take their weapons﴾ refers to those who are facing the enemy, as will be explained. Allah did not mention in the verse more than one rak'ah for each group, but it is reported in the hadiths that they added another, as will come.

The kasrah was dropped from His saying ﴿فَلْتَقُمْ﴾ and ﴿فَلْيَكُونُوا﴾ because of its heaviness. Al-Akhfash, the readers, and al-Kisa'i reported that the lam of command (لَامُ الْأَمْرِ), the lam of purpose (لَامُ كَيْ), and the lam of denial (لَامُ الْجُحُودِ) are vowelled with a fathah. Sibawayh prohibits this for a specific reason, namely the distinction between the lam of genitive (لَامُ الْجَرِّ) and the lam of emphasis (لَامُ التَّأْكِيدِ).

The purpose of this command is division, meaning that the rest of them stand facing the enemy (وُجَاهَ) out of caution against the expectation of its attack. [[(Wujah) with a vowel, meaning facing them and opposite them.]]

The reports differ concerning the form of the prayer of fear, and the scholars differed because of these differences. Ibn al-Qassar mentioned that the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed it in ten places. Ibn al-'Arabi said: It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he prayed the prayer of fear twenty-four times. Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal, who is the leader of the people of hadith and the foremost in knowing the defects in transmission, said: "I do not know that anything was narrated concerning the prayer of fear except one authentic hadith." All of them are sound and authentic, so whichever hadith the worshipper follows in performing the prayer of fear, it suffices, if Allah wills. Abu Ja'far al-Tabari also said the same.

As for Malik and all his companions except Ashhab, they adopted the hadith of Sahl ibn Abi Hathmah. This is what he narrated in his Muwatta' from Yahya ibn Sa'id, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from Salih ibn Khawwat al-Ansari, that Sahl ibn Abi Hathmah told him that the prayer of fear is: the imam stands with a group of his companions, and another group faces the enemy. The imam bows with one rak'ah and prostrates with those who are with him, then he stands. When he has risen to his feet, he remains standing, and they complete the remaining rak'ah for themselves, then they make the salam and turn away while the imam is still standing. Thus they stand facing the enemy. Then the others who did not pray come forward, say the takbir behind the imam, and he leads them in the rak'ah, bowing and prostrating, then makes the salam. They then stand and perform the remaining rak'ah for themselves, then make the salam.

Ibn al-Qasim, the companion of Malik, said: "The practice according to Malik is the hadith of al-Qasim ibn Muhammad from Salih ibn Khawwat." Ibn al-Qasim also said: "He used to act upon the hadith of Yazid ibn Ruman, then he returned to this one."

Abu 'Umar said: "The hadith of al-Qasim and the hadith of Yazid ibn Ruman both come from Salih ibn Khawwat, except that there is a difference between them concerning the salam. In the hadith of al-Qasim, the imam makes the salam with the second group, then they stand and complete the rak'ah for themselves. In the hadith of Yazid ibn Ruman, he waits for them and makes the salam with them." This is the view of al-Shafi'i, and he adopted it. Al-Shafi'i said: "The hadith of Yazid ibn Ruman from Salih ibn Khawwat is the most similar of the hadiths on the prayer of fear to the apparent meaning of the Book of Allah, and this is what I say."

Among Malik's arguments for choosing the hadith of al-Qasim is analogy with all other prayers: the imam is not permitted to wait for anyone who has fallen behind him in any part of the prayer, and the agreed-upon practice is that those who were left behind complete what they missed after the imam's salam.

The position of Abu Thawr on this subject is like that of Malik. Ahmad's view is like that of al-Shafi'i in what he preferred, and he did not criticize anyone who acted upon any of the forms narrated in the prayer of fear.

Ashhab, one of Malik's companions, followed the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed the prayer of fear with one of the two groups, one rak'ah, while the other group faced the enemy. Then they withdrew and took the places of their companions, facing the enemy. Those others came, and the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed one rak'ah with them, then the Prophet (ﷺ) made the salam. Then these completed one rak'ah and those completed one rak'ah." Ibn 'Umar said: "If the fear is greater than that, one prays while riding or standing, making gestures with the head." This was narrated by al-Bukhari, Muslim, Malik, and others.

This form was adopted by al-Awza'i, and it is what Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr approved, saying: "Because it is the soundest of them in its chain of transmission. It has also come through the transmission of the people of Madinah, and the proof lies with them against those who oppose them. Furthermore, it is more consistent with the foundations, because the first and second groups did not complete the rak'ah except after the Prophet (ﷺ) had exited the prayer, which is the known practice of his Sunnah that the scholars agreed upon in all other prayers."

As for the Kufans, Abu Hanifa and his companions, except Abu Yusuf al-Qadi Ya'qub, they adopted the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, which Abu Dawud and al-Daraqutni narrated. He said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed the prayer of fear. They stood in two rows: one row behind the Prophet (ﷺ), and one row facing the enemy. The Prophet (ﷺ) led them in one rak'ah. The others came and took their places, and these faced the enemy. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) led these in prayer and then made the salam. Those then stood and prayed one rak'ah for themselves, then made the salam, and went away to take the places of those others, facing the enemy. Those returned to their positions and prayed one rak'ah for themselves, then made the salam."

This manner and form are the same as those mentioned in the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, except that there is a difference between them. In the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, the completion by the first group appears to have occurred in a single situation, and the imam remains alone like a guard. Here, their completion is spread out according to the manner of their prayer.

Some have interpreted the hadith of Ibn 'Umar in light of what came in the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud.

The hadith of Ibn Mas'ud was adopted by al-Thawri, in one of his three reported positions, and by Ashhab ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, as al-Lakhmi (Abu al-Hasan) mentioned from him. The first was recorded by Abu 'Umar, Ibn Yunus, and Ibn Habib from him.

Abu Dawud narrated, from the hadiths of Hudhayfah, Abu Hurayrah, and Ibn 'Umar, that he (peace be upon him) prayed with each group one rak'ah and they did not complete it. This is what the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas implies, "In fear, one rak'ah." This is the view of Ishaq.

The indication of this was already mentioned in (al-Baqarah [[See vol. 3, p. 123.]]), and that prayer is more deserving of what is taken with caution for it. The hadith of Ibn 'Abbas cannot serve as proof. As for his saying in the hadith of Hudhayfah and others: "And they did not complete—

)I.e., in the knowledge of the one who narrated that, because it has been narrated that they completed one rak'ah in that same prayer, and the testimony of the one who adds is preferable. It is possible that the meaning is that they did not make it up (qada'), i.e., they did not make it up once they were safe, and the benefit would be that the one in fear, when he becomes safe, does not repeat what he prayed in that state of fear among the prayers of fear. Abu 'Umar said all of this.

In Sahih Muslim, from Jabir, that he (ﷺ) prayed with one group two rak'ahs, then they withdrew, and he prayed with the other group two rak'ahs. He said: so the Messenger of God (ﷺ) had four rak'ahs and the people had two rak'ahs. Abu Dawud and al-Daraqutni also narrated it from the hadith of al-Hasan from Abu Bakrah, and both mention in it that he gave the salam after every two rak'ahs. Al-Daraqutni also narrated it from al-Hasan from Jabir that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) prayed with them two rak'ahs and then gave the salam, then prayed with the others two rak'ahs and then gave the salam. Abu Dawud said: al-Hasan used to issue legal opinions according to this, and it is related from al-Shafi'i. By it, everyone who permits a difference of intention between the imam and the follower in prayer argues, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i, al-Awza'i, Ibn 'Ulayyah, Ahmad ibn Hanbal and Dawud. They strengthened this with the hadith of Jabir: that Mu'adh used to pray the 'Isha prayer with the Prophet (ﷺ), then come and lead his people, the hadith... 

Al-Tahawi said: this was only at the beginning of Islam, when it was permissible to pray the obligatory prayer twice, and then this was abrogated (naskh), and God knows best. These are the views of the scholars on the prayer of fear (salat al-khawf).

Third: This prayer mentioned in the Qur'an is only needed when the Muslims have their backs to the qibla and the enemy faces the qibla. This happened only at Dhat al-Riqa'. As for 'Usfan and the other place, the Muslims were facing the qibla. What we have mentioned about the occasion of revelation in the story of Khalid ibn al-Walid does not fit with dividing the people into two groups, for in the hadith, after his saying (you established the prayer for them), he said: the prayer time came, so the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered them to take up their weapons, and we lined up behind him in two rows. He said: then he bowed and we all bowed, he said: then he raised his head and we all raised ours, he said: then the Prophet (ﷺ) prostrated with the row next to him, and the others were standing guarding them. When they had prostrated and stood up, the others sat down and prostrated in their places. He said: then these moved forward to the places of those, and those came to the places of these. He said: then he bowed and they all bowed, then he raised his head and they all raised theirs, then the Prophet (ﷺ) prostrated with the row next to him, and the others were standing, guarding them. When the others sat down, they prostrated, then he gave the salam to them. He said: so the Messenger of God (ﷺ) prayed it twice: once at 'Usfan and once in the land of Banu Sulaym.

Abu Dawud narrated it from the hadith of Abu 'Ayyash al-Zuraqi and said: this is the view of al-Thawri, and it is the most cautious of them. Al-Tirmidhi narrated from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) descended between Dajnan and 'Usfan, the hadith... In it, he (ﷺ) split them into two groups and prayed with each group one rak'ah, so the people had one rak'ah each, and the Prophet (ﷺ) had two rak'ahs. He said: this is a hadith that is hasan, sahih, gharib. On this subject, there are also reports from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, Zayd ibn Thabit, Ibn 'Abbas, Jabir, Abu 'Ayyash al-Zuraqi, whose name is Zayd ibn al-Samit, Ibn 'Umar, Hudhayfah, Abu Bakr and Sahl ibn Abi Hathmah.

I say: there is no contradiction between these narrations. Perhaps he prayed with them one prayer, with them gathered together, as came in the hadith of Abu 'Ayyash, and prayed with them another prayer, with them dispersed, as came in the hadith of Abu Hurayrah. This would be evidence for those who say the prayer of fear is one rak'ah. Al-Khattabi said: the prayer of fear has several forms, which the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed on different days and in different manners, seeking in all of them what is most cautious for the prayer and most effective in guarding.

Fourth: They differed about how the Maghrib prayer is performed. Al-Daraqutni narrated from al-Hasan from Abu Bakrah that the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed the Maghrib prayer with the people three rak'ahs, then they departed, and the others came and he prayed with them three rak'ahs, so the Prophet had six and the people had three each. Al-Hasan also said this. The majority, regarding the Maghrib prayer, differ from this: he prays with the first group two rak'ahs and with the second group one rak'ah, and they complete their prayer according to their principles concerning when this happens, whether before the imam's salam or after it. This is the view of Malik and Abu Hanifa, because it better preserves the form of the prayer. Al-Shafi'i said: he prays one rak'ah with the first group, because 'Ali (may God be pleased with him) did so on the night of al-Harir [[Laylat al-Harir: like the nights of Siffin.]]. And God the Exalted knows best.

Fifth: They differed about the prayer of fear when the battle is joined, the fighting is fierce, and the time is feared to run out. Malik, al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, al-Shafi'i and most scholars said: he prays however he can, based on Ibn 'Umar's saying: "If the fear is greater than that, then pray riding or standing, gesturing." Malik said in the Muwatta': facing the qibla or not facing it. The view of al-Dahhak and Ishaq has already been mentioned at (al-Baqarah [[see vol. 3, p. 223]]). Al-Awza'i said: if the conquest is imminent and they cannot pray, they pray by gesturing, each one for himself; if they cannot gesture, they delay the prayer until the fighting subsides and they are safe, then they pray two rak'ahs; if they cannot do that, one rak'ah and two prostrations; if they cannot do that, the takbir suffices for them, and they delay the prayer until they are safe. Makhul said likewise.

I say: al-Kiya al-Tabari related it in his book Ahkam al-Qur'an from Abu Hanifa and his companions. Al-Kiya said: when the fear is greater than that and the battle is joined, the Muslims pray as they are able, facing the qibla or with their backs to it. Abu Hanifa and his three companions agree that in this state they do not pray, but delay the prayer. If they fight during the prayer, they say the prayer is invalidated. It is related from al-Shafi'i that if he continues stabbing and striking, his prayer is invalid.

I say: this view indicates the soundness of Anas's saying: "I attended the siege of the fortress of Tustar at the break of dawn, and the fighting intensified, so we could not pray until after the sun had risen. We prayed it with Abu Musa, and it was conquered for us." Anas said: "Nothing would please me in exchange for that prayer, this world and all that is in it." Al-Bukhari mentioned it. Our shaykh, the teacher Abu Ja'far Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Muhammad al-Qaysi al-Qurtubi, known as Abu Hijjah, used to hold this view, and it appears to be al-Bukhari's choice, because he followed it with the hadith of Jabir, who said: "'Umar came on the day of the Trench and began cursing the disbelievers of Quraysh, and said: 'O Messenger of God, I did not pray 'Asr until the sun was almost setting.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'By God, I did not pray it either.' He said: so he descended to Batḥan [[Batḥan: a valley in Medina.]], performed ablution, prayed 'Asr after the sun had set, and then prayed Maghrib after it."

Sixth: They differed about the prayer of the pursuer and the pursued. Malik and a group of his companions said they are equal, each one praying on his mount. Al-Awza'i, al-Shafi'i, the jurists of the hadith folk and Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam said: the pursuer does not pray except on the ground. This is the correct view, because pursuit is voluntary, whereas the obligatory prayer is to be prayed on the ground wherever that is possible. No one prays it mounted except one whose fear is severe, and the pursuer is not like that. And God knows best.

Seventh: They also differed about an army that sees a dark shape, thinks it is an enemy, and prays the prayer of fear, then it becomes clear that it is something else. Our scholars have two narrations on this. In one, they repeat the prayer, and this is the view of Abu Hanifa. The second: there is no repetition for them, and this is the stronger of al-Shafi'i's two views. The reasoning of the first is that the error became clear to them, so they returned to what was correct, like the ruling of a judge. The reasoning of the second is that they acted on their own ijtihad (independent judgment), so it was permissible for them, as in the case of someone who mistakes the qibla. This second view is preferable, because they did what they were commanded to do. It may be said: they repeat it within the time, but not after the time has passed. And God knows best.

Eighth: God's saying ﴿And let them take their weapons﴾, and in another reading (And let them take their caution and their weapons). This is a command to be cautious and to take up arms, lest the enemy attain his hope and seize his opportunity. Al-silah (weapons) is that with which a man defends himself in war. 'Antarah said:

"I clothed the curly-haired ones of the Banu Aban
with my weapon, after nakedness and disgrace."

He means: I lent them my weapon so that they could defend themselves after their nakedness (lack of weapons).

Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿And let them take their weapons﴾ means the group that faces the enemy, because the one who is praying does not fight. Others said: it refers to those who are praying, i.e., let those who prayed first take up their weapons, related by al-Zajjaj. He said: it is possible that the group who are in the prayer are commanded to carry weapons, i.e., let a group of them stand with you, and let them take up their weapons, for that is more fearsome to the enemy. Al-Nahhas said: it may apply to all of them, because it is more daunting to the enemy. It may also apply specifically to the group facing the enemy.

Abu 'Umar said: most scholars recommend that the one who is praying take up his weapon when he prays in a state of fear, and they interpret His saying ﴿and let them take their weapons﴾ as a recommendation, since it is something whose taking would not be obligatory were it not for the fear, so the command to take it is a recommendation (nadb). The people of the outward meaning (Ahl al-Zahir) said: taking up weapons in the prayer of fear is obligatory by God's command, except for one who is harmed by rain; if that is the case, he may set down his weapon. Ibn al-'Arabi said: when they pray, they take their weapons at times of fear, and al-Shafi'i said the same, and this is the explicit text of the Qur'an. Abu Hanifa said: they do not carry them, for if carrying them were obligatory, the prayer would be invalidated by leaving them. We reply: carrying them was not obligatory for the sake of the prayer; rather, it was obligatory on them for their strength and prudence.

**The ninth matter:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Then when they have prostrated﴾. The pronoun in "they have prostrated" refers to the group that is praying, the group that should then withdraw. This is according to one of the reported forms of the prayer. It was also said that the meaning is: when they have prostrated in the make-up rak'ah (*raka'at al-qada'*), and this is according to the form narrated from Sahl ibn Abi Hathmah. This verse shows that prostration may be used to refer to the whole prayer, as in the saying of the Prophet ﷺ (peace be upon him): "When one of you enters the mosque, let him prostrate twice" (ﷺ). That is, let him pray two rak'ahs, and this is in the Sunnah. The pronoun in His saying "then let them be" (*fal-yakunu*) may refer to those who prostrated, or it may refer to the group that was standing first, facing the enemy.

**The tenth matter:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿The disbelievers wish that you were negligent of your weapons and your belongings, so they could attack you in one assault﴾. That is, the disbelievers desired and wished that you would be heedless of taking up your weapons, so that they could reach their goal. Through this, Allah the Exalted explains the wisdom behind the command to take up weapons. He mentioned caution regarding the second group and not the first, because the second group is more in need of taking caution, since the enemy would not delay its attack beyond this time, as it is the end of the prayer. Also, the enemy would say that the weapons have burdened them and they have become weary. This verse is the clearest proof of taking the means (*ta'ati al-asbab*), and of adopting everything that saves people of understanding, leads to safety, and reaches the abode of honour. The meaning of "a single assault" (*maylatan wahidah*) is an intensification: a decisive attack that leaves no need for a second one.

**The eleventh matter:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿There is no blame upon you if you put down your weapons because of rain, or because you are ill﴾, and the verse continues. The scholars have differing views on whether carrying weapons during the prayer is obligatory. We have already pointed to this. If it is not obligatory, then it is recommended as a precaution. Then permission was given to set them down in case of rain, because the padded garments become soaked and heavy, and the iron rusts. It was also said that the verse was revealed concerning the Prophet ﷺ on the day of Batn Nakhlah (a village near Madinah), when the polytheists had been defeated and the Muslims had gained booty. That was a rainy day, and the Prophet ﷺ went out to relieve himself, placing his weapon down. The disbelievers saw him separated from his companions, so Ghawrath ibn al-Harith approached him, coming down from the mountain with his sword and saying: "Who will protect you from me today?" He replied: "Allah." Then he said: "O Allah, suffice me against Ghawrath with whatever You will." Ghawrath then swung the sword towards the Prophet ﷺ to strike him, but he fell on his face because of a slip he had made. Al-Waqidi mentioned that Jibril (peace be upon him) pushed him in his chest, as will come in Surat al-Ma'idah (see vol. 2, p. 431), and the sword fell from his hand. The Prophet ﷺ took it and said: "Who will protect you from me now, O Ghawrath?" He said: "No one." He said: "Will you testify to the truth for me, and I will give you your sword?" He said: "No, but I testify that I will not fight you after this, nor will I help an enemy against you." So he handed him the sword, and the verse was revealed granting permission to set down weapons in the rain. 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf became ill from a wound, as is in Sahih al-Bukhari, so Allah the Exalted permitted them to leave aside weapons and preparation against the enemy because of the excuse of rain. Then He commanded them, saying: ﴿Take your precautions﴾ (*khudhu hidhrakum*), meaning: be alert, whether you have put down your weapons or not. This indicates the emphasis on readiness and caution against the enemy in all circumstances, and on not surrendering, for an army has never been struck by a disaster except through negligence in caution. Al-Dahhak said regarding His saying "and take your precautions" that it means: gird on your swords, for that is the appearance of warriors.

Its meaning: you have finished the prayer of fear. This indicates that qada' (fulfilling, completing) is used for what has been done at its proper time. From it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when you have completed your rites﴾, and this has preceded [[see vol. 6, p. 243]].

The second issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So remember Allah standing, sitting, and on your sides﴾. The majority (al-Jumhur) held that this remembrance commanded is only after the prayer of fear, meaning: when you have finished the prayer, then remember Allah with the heart and the tongue, in whatever state you are (﴿standing, sitting, and on your sides﴾), and continue His remembrance by takbir (saying Allahu akbar), tahlil (saying La ilaha illa Allah), and supplication for victory, especially in the state of fighting. Its counterpart is: ﴿When you meet a company, stand firm and remember Allah much, that you may be successful﴾ [[see vol. 8, p. 23]]. It is also said: ﴿And when you have completed the prayer﴾ means: when you pray in the territory of war, pray upon your mounts, or standing, or sitting, or on your sides if you cannot stand, in case of fear or illness, as He, exalted is He, said in another verse: ﴿And if you fear, then on foot or riding﴾ [[see vol. 3, p. 223]]. Some people said: this verse is similar to the one in (Al 'Imran) [[see vol. 4, p. 216]]. It is narrated that 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud saw people making noise in the mosque and said: "What is this clamor?" They said: "Does not Allah, exalted is He, say: ﴿So remember Allah standing, sitting, and on your sides﴾?" He said: "He means by this only the obligatory prayer: if you cannot (pray) standing, then sitting, and if you cannot, then pray on your side." Thus the intended meaning is the prayer itself, because prayer is the remembrance of Allah, exalted is He, and it includes the obligatory and recommended remembrances. The first opinion is more apparent. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when you are secure﴾, i.e., you are safe. And tuma'nina (tranquility) is the calm of the soul from fear.

(So establish the prayer) i.e., perform it with its pillars and with the completeness of its form during travel, and with the completeness of its number while at home.

(Indeed, prayer has been decreed upon the believers as a decree of specified times) i.e., prescribed at fixed times, obligatory. Zayd ibn Aslam said: (mawqutan) means "in installments," i.e., you perform it in its stated times. According to the linguists, the meaning is: obligatory for a specific time; one says waqqatahu, so it is mawqut, and waqqatahu, so it is muwaqqat. This is exactly the statement of Zayd ibn Aslam. He said (kitaban), and the verbal noun is masculine, so for this reason he said (mawqutan).

The fourth issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not falter﴾, i.e., do not weaken. It has been discussed in (Al 'Imran) [[see vol. 4, p. 216]].

(In pursuit of the people) i.e., seeking them. It was said: it was revealed concerning the Battle of Uhud, when the Prophet ﷺ commanded going out in pursuit of the polytheists, while the Muslims had wounds, and he had commanded that none go out with him except those who had been in the battle, as has preceded in (Al 'Imran). It was also said: this applies to every jihad.

The fifth issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If you suffer pain﴾, i.e., you feel pain from the wounds that have afflicted you, yet they also feel pain from what afflicts them, but you have an advantage, which is that you hope for the reward of Allah while they do not hope for it, for whoever does not believe in Allah does not hope for anything from Allah. A parallel to this verse is: ﴿If a wound touches you, a wound has already touched the people like it﴾, which has preceded [[see vol. 4, p. 217]]. 'Abd al-Rahman al-A'raj read (an takunu) with a fatha on the hamza, meaning "because." Mansur ibn al-Mu'tamir read (in takunu ta'lamun) with a kasra on the ta'. According to the Basrans, the kasra on the ta' is not permissible, due to the heaviness of the kasra in it. Then it was said: al-raja' (hope) here means fear, because whoever hopes for something is not certain of obtaining it, so he is not free from fear of losing what he hopes for. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: al-raja' is not used in the sense of fear except with negation, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not expect dignity from Allah?﴾ [[see vol. 18, p. 303]], i.e., you do not fear the greatness of Allah. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For those who do not expect the Days of Allah﴾ [[see vol. 16, p. 160]], i.e., who do not fear. Al-Qushayri said: it is not far-fetched to mention fear without there being negation in the statement, but the two (scholars) claimed that it was not found except with negation. And Allah knows best.

The first issue: this verse honours the Prophet (ﷺ), ennobles him, magnifies him, entrusts judgment to him, and also corrects him for keeping to the right course in judging, and rebukes him over what was brought to him concerning the Banu Ubayriq. They were three brothers: Bishr, Bushayr and Mubashshir. Usayr ibn 'Urwa was their paternal cousin. They broke into a storeroom [[The mashraba (with the ra' vowelled either way) is an upper room or storeroom.]] belonging to Rifa'a ibn Zayd at night, and stole his armour and some food, and it was discovered. It is also said that the thief was Bushayr alone, who was known as Abu Tu'ma, and that he took a coat of mail. It is said that the coat of mail was in a sack containing flour, and the flour kept scattering through a hole in the sack until it reached his house. Then the nephew of Rifa'a, whose name was Qatada ibn al-Nu'man, came to complain of them [[In j, w, y and t: "yashkuhum" (complaining of them). In a, h, z: "yashkuhu" (complaining of him).]] to the Prophet (ﷺ). Usayr ibn 'Urwa came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, these men have deliberately targeted a household who are people of righteousness and religion, and they have accused them of theft and charged them with it without evidence." He kept arguing on their behalf until the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) became angry with Qatada and Rifa'a. So Allah the Exalted revealed: (And do not argue on behalf of those who betray themselves) to the end of the verse. And Allah the Exalted revealed: (And whoever commits a sin or an offence and then throws it upon an innocent person)

The innocent man whom they had accused of the theft was Labid ibn Sahl. It is also said that it was Zayd ibn al-Samin, and it is said that he was a man from the Ansar. When Allah revealed what He revealed, the thief Ibn Ubayriq fled to Makkah and stayed with Sulafa daughter of Sa'd ibn Shahid. Hassan ibn Thabit recited a verse about her, alluding to her, which is:

Sa'd's daughter has housed him, and she has become one
who is pulled by him, and who pulls him, by the skin of her backside.

You thought that what you had done would stay hidden,
but among us is a Prophet, with whom the revelation is set down.

When she heard it she said: "You have only sent me Hassan's poetry," and she took his saddle and threw it outside the house, so he fled to Khaybar and apostatised. Then one night he broke into a house to steal, and the wall fell on him, and he died as an apostate. At-Tirmidhi related this report with many of its wordings and said: "It is a hasan gharib report. We know of no one who transmitted it with a chain except Muhammad ibn Salama al-Harrani." Al-Layth and al-Tabari related it with different wordings. Yahya ibn Salam mentioned the story of his death in his tafsir, and al-Qushayri likewise, adding a mention of the apostasy. Then it is said that Zayd ibn al-Samin and Labid ibn Sahl were Jews. It is also said that Labid was a Muslim. Al-Mahdawi mentioned him, and Abu 'Umar included him in his book on the Companions, which indicates that he was Muslim in his view. Bushayr was a hypocrite who satirised the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) and attributed to others the poetry he composed. The Muslims would say: "By Allah, it is nothing but the poetry of that wicked man." So he composed a poem in which he disclaimed it, and from it is his saying:

Whenever men recite an ode,
it is ascribed to others, and they say: "Ibn Ubayriq composed it."

Al-Dahhak said: The Prophet (ﷺ) wanted to cut off his hand, for he was obeyed, but the Jews came, armed with weapons, took him and fled with him. Then (Here you are, you people) was revealed, referring to the Jews. And Allah knows best.

The second issue: the words of the Exalted, ﴿by what Allah has shown you﴾. Its meaning is according to the principles of the Sharia, either by revelation and explicit text, or by reasoning that follows the patterns of revelation. This is a foundation for qiyas (analogical reasoning). It indicates that when the Prophet (ﷺ) judged by an opinion, he was correct, because Allah the Exalted showed him that. Allah the Exalted guaranteed His prophets 'ismah (protection from error). As for one of us, when he sees something and thinks it to be so, there is no certainty regarding what he saw. The meaning here is not seeing with the eye, because a ruling is not seen with the eye. In the sentence there is an idmar (an implied word): i.e. by what Allah showed you (bi-ma arakahu Allah) [[the implied object: "bi-ma arakahu Allah" meaning by what Allah showed him]]. There is another idmar in it: "and carry out the rulings according to what We have made you know, without being deceived by their arguments" [[As in z. In j, w and t: "istizlalihim" (their misleading).]]. 

The third issue: the words of the Exalted, ﴿and do not be a disputant for the treacherous﴾. Khasiman here is an active participle (ism fa'il), like your saying: "I sat with him, so I am his companion (jalisuhu)." It is not a fa'il here in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ul). The evidence for this is (And do not argue), so al-khasim is the one who argues. The plural of al-khasim is khusama'. It is also said: khasiman, meaning one who disputes, is likewise an active participle. So Allah the Mighty and Majestic forbade His Messenger from supporting people accused of wrongdoing and from defending them with whatever argument their opponent offers. In this there is evidence that acting as a representative for one in the wrong or one accused in litigation is not permitted. It is therefore not permissible for anyone to dispute on behalf of anyone unless he knows that he is in the right. The discourse in the surah has proceeded on the protection of the wealth of orphans and of people, and it clarifies that the wealth of a disbeliever is protected for him just as the wealth of a Muslim is, except in the cases that Allah the Exalted has permitted.

The fourth issue: The scholars said: When the hypocrisy of a people becomes apparent to the Muslims, it is not fitting for a group among them to argue on behalf of those people in order to shield them and ward off consequences from them. This has occurred in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), and concerning them were revealed the words of the Exalted: ﴿and do not be a disputant for the treacherous﴾ and His words: (And do not argue on behalf of those who betray themselves). The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), but what is meant is those among the Muslims who used to do this, not him, for two reasons. The first is that the Exalted made this clear by what He mentioned afterwards in His words: (Here you are, you are those who argued on their behalf in the life of this world). The second is that the Prophet (ﷺ) was a judge among them, and therefore people would apologise to him, and he would not apologise to anyone else. This indicates that the intended addressee is someone other than him.

There is one issue here. Al-Tabari held that the meaning is: "Seek forgiveness from Allah for your sin in disputing on behalf of the treacherous," so He commanded him to seek forgiveness when he intended to defend them and to cut off the hand of the Jew. This is the view of those who permit minor sins (saghair, minor sins) for the prophets, may the peace and blessings of Allah be upon them.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is not a sin, because the Prophet (ﷺ) only defended them outwardly while believing in their innocence." The meaning is: "And seek forgiveness of Allah for the sinners among your community and for those who dispute falsely. Your position among the people is that you hear from the two claimants and judge according to what you hear, and you seek forgiveness for the sinner."

It was also said: it is a command to seek forgiveness in the manner of glorification (tasbih), like a man who says, "I seek forgiveness of Allah," in the form of glorification, without intending repentance from a sin.

It was also said: the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), but the intended people are the Banu Ubayriq, as in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿O Prophet, fear Allah﴾ [See vol. 14, p. 113.] and ﴿So if you are in doubt﴾ [See vol. 8, p. 382.].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verse 107:

And do not argue on behalf of those who betray themselves. Indeed, Allah does not love one who is a habitual traitor, sinful. (4:107)

That is: do not contend on behalf of those who betray their own souls. It was revealed concerning Usayr ibn Urwah, as has already been mentioned. The mujadalah (contention, dispute) is al-khusumah (quarrelling), from al-jadl, which means twisting (al-fatl), and from it comes the phrase rajul majdul al-khalq (a man of slender, well-knit build: "lateef al-qasab, muhkam al-fatl"), and from it al-ajdal for the falcon. It has also been said that it derives from al-jadalah, which is the surface of the earth, since each of the two opponents wants to throw his companion down upon it. Al-Ajjaj said:

I ride the difficulty after difficulty... and I leave the weakling by the jadalah (the ground),
Flung down, with no escape for him.

Al-jadalah is the earth. From this is their saying: "I left him mujaddal," meaning thrown down upon the jadalah.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love﴾, that is, He does not approve of him and does not honour him with mention.

(man kana khawwanan)

Khā'inan (a traitor). And khawwanan (habitual, intensive traitor) is more emphatic, because it is of the patterns of intensification (ibniyat al-mubalaghah), and that is only because of the great magnitude of that betrayal. And Allah knows best.

Al-Dahhak said: When he stole the coat of mail, he dug a hole in his house and placed the coat of mail under the dust, and then this was revealed: ﴿They hide from men, but they cannot hide from Allah﴾.

It says: The place of the coat of mail is not hidden from Allah, ﴿and He is with them﴾,

that is, a watchful Guardian over them. It was also said: ﴿They hide from men﴾ means they conceal themselves, as the Exalted said: ﴿and he who hides himself by night﴾ [[See vol. 9, p. 290.]], that is, concealed. It was also said: they feel shame before men, because shame is the cause of concealment. The meaning of ﴿and He is with them﴾ is with knowledge, sight and hearing; this is the saying of the People of the Sunnah. But the Jahmiyyah, the Qadariyyah and the Mu'tazilah said: He is in every place, holding to this verse and similar ones. They said: Since He said ﴿and He is with them﴾, it is established that He is in every place, because He has affirmed His being with them, exalted is Allah above their saying. This is the attribute of bodies, and Allah the Exalted is far above that. Do you not see the debate of Bishr concerning the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿There is no secret conversation of three but He is their fourth﴾ [[See vol. 17, p. 289.]], when he said: He is in His very essence in every place? His opponent said to him: He is in your skullcap, in your stuffing, and in the belly of your donkey! Exalted is Allah above what they say. Waki' related this, may Allah be pleased with him.

The meaning of ﴿they plot by night﴾ is: they say. Al-Kalbi related it from Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

﴿That which He does not approve of in speech﴾ means that which Allah does not approve for the people of His obedience.

﴿Of speech﴾ means of opinion and belief, as you say: the madhhab of Malik, al-Shafi'i. It was also said: ﴿speech﴾ here carries the sense of "that which is said," because speech itself is not plotted.

His saying, exalted: ﴿Lo, you are those who argued﴾

It refers to the people of Bushayr the thief, when they fled with him and argued on his behalf. Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿Lo, you are those [hā antum hā'ulā'i]﴾ carries the sense of "those who" (alladhina).

﴿You argued﴾ means you disputed.

﴿In the life of this world; but who will argue with Allah on their behalf on the Day of Resurrection?﴾ is an interrogative whose meaning is denial and rebuke.

﴿Or who will be a guardian over them?﴾

The wakil is the one who manages affairs; Allah the Exalted manages His creation. The meaning: there is no one for them who will take charge of their affair when Allah seizes them with His punishment and brings them into the Fire.

Ibn 'Abbas said: God presented repentance to the Banu Ubayriq through this verse, meaning (And whoever does evil)

by stealing, (or wrongs himself)

by associating partners with God, (then seeks forgiveness from God)

meaning through repentance, for seeking forgiveness with the tongue without repentance benefits nothing. We have explained this in (Al 'Imran) [[See vol. 4, p. 38.]]. Al-Dahhak said: the verse was revealed concerning Wahshi, the slayer of Hamza. He associated partners with God and killed Hamza. Then he came to the Messenger of God ﷺ and said: "Indeed I am regretful, so is there repentance for me?" Then it was revealed: (And whoever does evil or wrongs himself)

the verse. It was also said: the intended meaning of this verse is general, encompassing all creation. Sufyan related from Abu Ishaq, from al-Aswad and 'Alqama, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said: Whoever recites these two verses from Surat al-Nisa' and then seeks forgiveness will be forgiven: (And whoever does evil or wrongs himself, then seeks forgiveness from God, will find God Forgiving, Merciful).

.

(And if they, when they wronged themselves, had come to you and sought forgiveness from God, and the Messenger had asked forgiveness for them, they would have found God Accepting of repentance, Merciful.) It is also reported from 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, that he said: "When I heard a hadith from the Messenger of God ﷺ, God benefited me by it as He willed, and when I heard it from someone else, I made him swear by it [[Thus in ʾw j, z, ṭ, y. In j: "khalaftuhu" (I made him swear).]]. And Abu Bakr told me, and Abu Bakr spoke truthfully: he said: 'There is no servant who commits a sin, then performs ablution, prays two rak'as, and seeks forgiveness from God, except that he is forgiven.' Then he recited this verse: (And whoever does evil or wrongs himself, then seeks forgiveness from God, will find God Forgiving, Merciful)."

"And whoever earns a sin" — that is, a sin (dhanb), "then he earns it only against himself" — that is, its consequence returns upon him. Al-kasb (earning) is what a person does for himself to gain benefit or to ward off harm by it; for this reason the act of the Lord, exalted is He, is not called kasb.

His saying, exalted is He: "And whoever earns a fault (khati'ah) or a sin (ithm)."

It was said: both have one meaning, repeated for variation of wording, for emphasis. Al-Tabari said: the difference between khati'ah and ithm is that khati'ah may be committed deliberately or without deliberation, while ithm is only deliberate. It was also said: khati'ah is what one did not intend, such as killing by mistake. It was said: khati'ah is the minor sin, and ithm the major sin. This verse is general in its wording, and those in the particular occasion (al-nazilah) and others are included under it.

His saying, exalted is He: "Then he throws it upon an innocent one (bari'an)."

The meaning of bari' has already been mentioned in al-Baqarah. The pronoun in "bihi" refers either to the sin (ithm) or to the fault (khati'ah), since its meaning is sin, or to both of them together. It was also said that it refers to the earning (kasb).

"Then he has borne a slander (buhtanan) and a manifest sin (ithman mubinan)."

This is a metaphor, for sins are a burden and a load, so they are like things carried. Allah, exalted is He, has said: "And they will surely bear their own burdens and burdens along with their burdens" (see vol. 13, p. 330). Buhtan comes from bahth (bewilderment, being stunned and dumbfounded by the enormity of the lie one is accused of). It is to confront your brother by accusing him of a sin when he is innocent of it. Muslim related from Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Do you know what backbiting (ghibah) is?" They said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "Your mentioning your brother with what he dislikes." It was said: "What if what I say is true of my brother?" He said: "If what you say is in him, you have backbitten him, and if it is not in him, you have slandered him (bahattahu)." This is an explicit text: throwing an innocent person with an accusation is slander (bahtun) against him. One says: bahattuhu bahtan, and bahatan, and buhtanan, when one says about him what he did not do. The one who does it is bahhat, and the one to whom it is said is mabhut. It is said: bahita al-rajul (with kasra) when he was astonished and bewildered; and bahuta (with damma) is similar; and the more eloquent of the two is buhita, as Allah, exalted is He, said: "So the one who disbelieved was dumbfounded" (see vol. 3, p. 286), because one says "rajul mabhut," and one does not say "bahit" or "bahiit." This was stated by al-Kisa'i.
