Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verse 133:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If He wills, He can remove you, O people﴾, meaning by death, ﴿and bring others﴾, meaning others other than you. He intends the polytheists and the hypocrites.

When this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) struck the back of Salman and said: "They are the people of this man." It has also been said that the verse is general, meaning: if you disbelieve, He will remove you and bring a creation more obedient to Allah than you. This is like His saying in another verse: ﴿And if you turn away, He will replace you with another people, then they will not be like you﴾ [see vol. 16, p. 258]. The verse contains a warning and an admonition to everyone who holds authority, leadership or rule, that he should not be just toward his subjects, or to everyone who is a scholar and does not act on his knowledge or advise the people, that He may remove him and bring another in his place.

﴿And Allah is over all things capable﴾. Power (qudrah) is an eternal attribute, whose objects of power have no end, just as His knowledge has no end. The past and the future in His attributes have one meaning. The past tense is mentioned specifically so that it is not supposed that He is renewed (yahduth) in His essence or attributes. Power (qudrah) is that by which an act occurs, and the existence of incapacity (ajz) together with it is not possible.

Meaning: whoever acts in obedience to what Allah has made obligatory upon him, seeking the Hereafter, Allah will grant him that in the Hereafter; and whoever acts seeking the world, He will give him what has been decreed for him in the world, and he has no reward in the Hereafter, because he acted for other than Allah, as the Exalted said: ﴿And he has no share in the Hereafter﴾ [see vol. 6, p. 2]. And the Exalted said: ﴿Those are the ones for whom there is nothing in the Hereafter except the Fire﴾ [see vol. 9, p. 15]. This is on the basis that the intended meaning of the verse is the hypocrites and the disbelievers, and this is the choice of al-Tabari. It is narrated that the polytheists did not believe in the Resurrection, and they only drew near to Allah, the Exalted, so that He would widen their provision in this world and remove its hardships from them. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿Whoever desires the reward of this world, with Allah is the reward of this world and the Hereafter, and Allah is ever Hearing and Seeing﴾, meaning: He hears what they say and sees what they conceal.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verse 135 (part 1 of 2):

God the Exalted says: ﴿O you who believe, be persistently upright in justice, witnesses for God, even against yourselves or parents and relatives. Whether he is rich or poor, God is more entitled to both of them. So do not follow your desires, lest you deviate. And if you distort or refuse, indeed God is ever, of what you do, Acquainted.﴾ (135)

There are ten issues.

The first: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿be persistently upright﴾ (*qawwamin*). It is an intensive form, meaning that standing firm for justice should be repeated from you. Justice (*al-qist*) is fairness in your testimony against yourselves. A person's testimony against himself is his acknowledgment of the rights that are upon him. Then He mentioned the parents, because of the obligation of honouring them and the greatness of their status. Then He followed with the relatives, since they are the place of affection and partisanship. So a stranger among people is more fitting for justice to be established against him and for testimony to be given against him. The discourse in this surah therefore concerns preserving the rights of creatures in their property.

The second: There is no disagreement among the people of knowledge regarding the soundness of the rulings of this verse, and that a child's testimony against his parents, father and mother [from manuscripts ج and ط], is valid. This does not prevent honouring them. Rather, part of honouring them is to testify against them and rescue them from falsehood. This is the meaning of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Guard yourselves and your families from a Fire﴾ [see vol. 18, p. 194].

If he testifies for them or they testify for him, this is the third issue. Regarding it, opinions have differed, in earlier and later times. Ibn Shihab al-Zuhri said: The righteous predecessors (*al-salaf al-salih*) used to permit the testimony of parents [Ibn al-Arabi's note: "the father for his son, the brother for his brother," etc.] and of brothers, and they interpreted in this regard the saying of God, Exalted is He: ﴿be persistently upright in justice, witnesses for God﴾. None of them disagreed about this among the righteous predecessors, may God be pleased with them. Then matters appeared among people which led the rulers to suspect them, so the testimony of those who are suspected was abandoned, and this became impermissible for a child, a parent, a brother, a husband, and a wife. This is the view of al-Hasan, al-Nakha'i, al-Sha'bi, Shurayh, Malik, al-Thawri, al-Shafi'i and Ibn Hanbal.

Some people permitted one of them to testify for another if they were upright (*'udul*). It is narrated from Umar ibn al-Khattab that he permitted it, and likewise it is narrated from Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz. Ishaq, al-Thawri and al-Muzani also said so.

Malik's school permits a brother's testimony for his brother if he is upright, except in matters of lineage. Ibn Wahb narrated from him that it is not permitted if the brother is dependent on him or if he has a share in property that he inherits.

Malik and Abu Hanifa said: The testimony of a husband for his wife is not accepted, because the benefits of their possessions are interlinked between them, and they are the place of testimony. Al-Shafi'i said: The testimony of spouses for one another is permitted, because they are two separate persons, and between them there is only the marriage contract, which is liable to end. The principle is that testimony is accepted, except where it has been restricted, and what is outside the restricted case remains on the principle. This view is weak, for marriage requires tenderness, companionship, intimacy and love, so the suspicion is strong and evident.

Abu Dawud narrated, through the hadith of Sulayman ibn Musa, from Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) rejected the testimony of a treacherous man and a treacherous woman and of *dhu al-ghimr* (one who harbours enmity) against his brother, and he rejected the testimony of a *qani'* (a dependent) for the people of the household, but he permitted it for others. Al-Khattabi said: *Dhu al-ghimr* is one who has evident enmity between himself and the person against whom he testifies, so his testimony against him is rejected because of suspicion. Abu Hanifa said: His testimony against an enemy is accepted if he is upright.

The *qani'* is the beggar, the one who asks for food, and the root of *al-qunut* is asking. It is also said of the *qani'* that he is one attached to a people who serves them and is at their disposal, like a hired worker, an agent, or the like. The reason for rejecting such testimony is suspicion of drawing benefit to oneself, because the *qani'* for the household benefits from what reaches them of gain.

Anyone who draws a benefit to himself by his testimony, his testimony is rejected. For example, someone who testifies for a man concerning the purchase of a house of which he is the pre-emptor (*shafi'*), or someone for whom a judgment was given against a man for a debt while he himself is insolvent, and then the insolvent man testifies against a man for a debt or the like.

Al-Khattabi said: Whoever rejects the testimony of the *qani'* for the household because of drawing benefit, by analogy his position would be to reject the testimony of a husband for his wife, because the suspicion of drawing benefit between them is greater. Abu Hanifa adopted this view.

The hadith is a proof against those who permit a father's testimony for his son, because he draws benefit to himself through him, for the inclination and love he is created with, and because he would use his son's property. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: ﴿You and your property belong to your father﴾.

Among those whose testimony Malik rejects is the Bedouin against the settled inhabitant. He said: Except if both are in the desert or the village. As for the one who testifies in town as a Bedouin and leaves his neighbours from the townspeople, in my view this is suspicious. Abu Dawud and al-Daraqutni narrated from Abu Hurayrah that he heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: ﴿The testimony of a Bedouin against a villager is not permitted﴾. Muhammad ibn Abd al-Hakam said: Malik interpreted this hadith as meaning testimony concerning rights and property, and testimony concerning blood and what is similar to it, for which people seek redress, is not rejected. The general body of scholars said: The testimony of a Bedouin is permitted if he is upright and establishes testimony in its proper form, and God knows best.

This matter has already been discussed in (*al-Baqarah*) [see vol. 3, p. 389 and what follows], and its completion will come in (*Bara'ah*) [see vol. 8, p. 232], God willing.

The fourth issue: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿witnesses for God﴾ is in the accusative as a qualifier of *qawwamin*, and if you wish it may be a second predicate. Al-Nahhas said: Better than these two is that it be in the accusative as a circumstantial (*hal*) clause referring to the *alladhina amanu* contained in *qawwamin*, since this is the same meaning: be persistently upright in justice at the time of your testimony. Ibn Atiyya said: The circumstantial clause here is weak in meaning, because it restricts standing firm for justice to the sense of testimony only. The word *shuhada'* is not declined, because it contains the feminine ending *alif*.

The fifth issue: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿for God﴾ means for the essence of God, for His face, for His good pleasure and for His reward.

﴿Even against yourselves﴾ is connected to *shuhada'*. This is the apparent meaning on which people have commented, namely that this testimony mentioned concerns rights, so one acknowledges them to their owners. That is his standing firm in testimony against himself, as has already been stated.

God, Mighty and Majestic, trained the believers through this, as Ibn Abbas said: They were commanded to speak the truth even against themselves. It is possible that His saying, ﴿witnesses for God﴾, means witnesses to God's oneness, and that ﴿even against yourselves﴾ is connected to *qawwamin*. The first interpretation is clearer.

The sixth issue: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Whether he is rich or poor, God is more entitled to both of them﴾. In the sentence there is an omitted element, which is the subject of *kana* (the pronoun), meaning: if the claimant or the one against whom the claim is made is rich, then he should not be favoured for his wealth nor feared for it; and if he is poor, he should not be favoured out of pity for him.

﴿God is more entitled to both of them﴾ [i.e. (*ayy*) in what He chose for them of poverty and wealth]. Al-Suddi said: A rich man and a poor man came to dispute before the Prophet (ﷺ). The Prophet's inclination (*dal'*, meaning bias) was with the poor man, because he saw that the poor man would not wrong the rich man, so this verse was revealed.

The seventh issue: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿God is more entitled to both of them﴾. He said ﴿both of them﴾ and did not say ﴿him﴾, although *aw* (or) only indicates one of the two alternatives, because the meaning is: God is more entitled to each one of them. Al-Akhfash said: *Aw* here has the sense of *wa* (and), meaning: if he is rich and poor, God is more entitled to the two litigants however they are. But this view is weak. It is also said: He said ﴿both of them﴾ because their mention has already preceded, as He said, Exalted is He: ﴿And if a man or a woman has a brother or sister, then for each one of them is a sixth﴾ [see p. 71 of this volume].

The eighth issue: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So do not follow your desires﴾ is a prohibition. Following desire is destructive (*mardin*), meaning ruinous. God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿So judge between the people in truth and do not follow desire, lest it lead you astray from the way of God﴾ [see vol. 15, p. 188]. Following desire leads to testimony without truth, to injustice in judgment, and to other things besides that.

Al-Sha'bi said: God, Mighty and Majestic, bound the judges to three things: that they not follow desire, that they not fear people while He is the one to be feared, and that they not sell His signs for a small price.

(an taʿdilū) is in the accusative position. Ninth point: God Most High says: ﴿And if you distort [the testimony] or turn away﴾. It has been read as (wa-in talwū), from lawaytu fulānan ḥaqqahu layyan (I twisted someone's right for him, meaning I pushed him off with it). The verb is (lawā), and its original form is (lawā), where the yā' was changed to an alif because of its vowel and the vowel of what precedes it. The verbal noun is (layyan), originally (lawyan), and (liyyānan), originally (liwyānan), then the wāw was assimilated into the yā'. Al-Qutabi said: (talwū) is from al-layy (twisting) in testimony and inclining toward one of the two litigants. Ibn ʿAmir and the Kufans read (talū), meaning: you took charge of the matter [and turned away], from your saying: I assumed the matter (wallaytu al-amr), so the sentence carries the sense of rebuke for turning away from taking charge of the matter. [From the manuscripts j, ṭ, z.] It is also said that the meaning of (talū) is turning away. So the reading with a damma on the lām conveys two meanings: authority (wilāyah) and turning away, while the reading with two wāws conveys one meaning, which is turning away. Some grammarians claimed that whoever reads (talū) has committed a grammatical error, because there is no sense of authority here. Al-Naḥḥās and others said: this does not follow; rather (talū) means (talwū), since its original form is (talwū). The damma was heavy on the wāw followed by another wāw, so the vowel was moved onto the lām and one of the two wāws was deleted because of the meeting of two silent letters. It is like the reading with a sukūn on the lām and two wāws. Makkī mentioned this. Al-Zajjāj said: the meaning according to this reading (wa-in talwū), then he hamzated the first wāw so it became (tilwū), then the hamza was lightened by moving its vowel onto the lām, so it became (talū), and its origin is (talwū). Thus the two readings agree under this interpretation. Al-Naḥḥās, Makkī, Ibn al-ʿArabī and others mentioned this. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it concerns two litigants sitting before the judge, so the judge's twisting and turning away is toward one of them over the other. Thus the twisting in this sense is stalling the speech and dragging it out until the decisive judgment is lost and its enforcement is lost in favor of the one the judge leans toward. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: I have witnessed some judges doing this, and God is the reckoner of all. Ibn ʿAbbas also said, as did al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Mujāhid: it concerns witnesses, where the witness twists the testimony with his tongue and distorts it so that he does not speak the truth in it, or he turns away from delivering the truth in it. The wording of the verse covers both judging and testimony, and every person is commanded to be just. In a hadith: "The procrastination of the wealthy man makes his honor and his punishment lawful." Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: his punishment is his imprisonment, and his honor is his being complained about. Tenth point: Some scholars used this verse as evidence for rejecting the testimony of a slave, saying: God Most High made the judge a witness in this verse, and this is the strongest proof that a slave is not among those eligible for testimony, because what is intended from it is independent undertaking of this important matter when the need calls for it, and that cannot be achieved from a slave at all; therefore testimony is rejected from him.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verse 136:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, believe﴾ — the verse [continues]. It was revealed concerning all the believers, and the meaning is: O you who have affirmed (ṣaddaqū), persist in your affirmation and remain steadfast upon it.

(And the Book which He sent down upon His Messenger) — that is, the Qur'an.

(And the Book which He sent down before) — that is, every book sent down upon the prophets. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir recited (nuzzila) and (unzila) with a ḍammah (on the first letter). The rest recited (nazzala) and (anzala) with a fatḥah. It has also been said: it was revealed concerning those who believed in those prophets who preceded Muhammad (ﷺ), peace be upon them. It has been said: it is an address to the hypocrites, and the meaning according to this is: O you who have believed outwardly, be sincere to Allah. It has also been said: the intended are the polytheists, and the meaning is: O you who have believed in al-Lat, al-'Uzza and al-Taghut, believe in Allah, that is, affirm Allah and His books.

It was said: the meaning is that they believed in Musa, then disbelieved in Uzair, then believed in Uzair, then disbelieved in Isa, then increased in disbelief toward Muhammad (ﷺ). And it was said: those who believed in Musa then believed in Uzair, then after Uzair they disbelieved in the Messiah, and the Christians disbelieved in what Musa brought and believed in Isa, then they increased in disbelief toward Muhammad (ﷺ) and what he brought of the Qur'an.

If it is said: Allah the Exalted does not forgive any disbelief, so how did He say: ﴿Indeed, those who believed, then disbelieved, then believed, then disbelieved, then increased in disbelief — Allah would not have been to forgive them﴾? The answer is that when a disbeliever believes, his disbelief is forgiven; but when he returns and disbelieves, the first disbelief is not forgiven for him. This is as came in Sahih Muslim from Abdullah, who said: Some people said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): [O Messenger of Allah,] will we be held accountable for what we did in the Jahiliyyah (the period of ignorance before Islam)? He said: "As for whoever among you does good in Islam, he will not be held accountable for it; and whoever does evil, he will be held accountable for his deeds in the Jahiliyyah and in Islam." And in another narration: "Whoever does evil in Islam will be held accountable for the first and the last." The "evil" here means disbelief, since it is not correct to mean by it here the committing of a bad deed; for that would entail that Islam does not wipe out what preceded it except for one who is protected from all bad deeds until his death, and that is false by consensus. The meaning of ﴿then increased in disbelief﴾ is that they persisted in disbelief.

﴿Allah would not have been to forgive them, nor to guide them﴾ — to guide them, i.e., to set them on the right path.

﴿A way﴾ — a path to Paradise. It was also said: He does not single them out with success as He singles out His friends. In this verse there is a refutation of the Qadariyyah (those who deny divine predestination), for Allah the Exalted has made clear that He does not guide the disbelievers to the path of good, so that the servant knows that he attains guidance only through Allah the Exalted, and that guidance is withheld by the will of Allah the Exalted as well. The verse also includes the ruling concerning apostates, and the discussion of them has already passed in (al-Baqarah [see vol. 3, p. 47]) at His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And whoever of you turns back from his religion and dies while he is a disbeliever﴾ [[Recited with unassimilated idgham (ﯾَرْتَدِدْ) according to Nafi'; see vol. 3, p. 40.]].

Al-tabshir (giving good news) is the informing of something whose effect becomes visible on the skin (al-bashara). Its explanation has already been given in (al-Baqarah [[see vol. 1, pp. 198, 238]]), along with the meaning of nifaq (hypocrisy).

**The Qur'anic verse (4:139):** "Those who take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers."

"Those who" is a qualifier (*na't*) describing the hypocrites (*munafiqun*, those who outwardly profess Islam while concealing disbelief).

This indicates that whoever among the monotheists (*muwahhidun*, those who affirm the oneness of God) commits a sin is not a hypocrite, because he does not take the disbelievers as allies. The verse also includes a prohibition against allying with a disbeliever and against taking disbelievers as helpers in matters related to the religion.

In the authentic collection, it is narrated from ʿAisha (may Allah be pleased with her) that a man among the polytheists joined the Prophet (ﷺ) to fight alongside him, and he said to him: "Return, for we do not seek help from a polytheist."

**"Al-ʿIzza"** means dominance, from the verb *ʿazza, yaʿizzu, ʿizzan*, meaning he overcame him.

**"Fa-inna al-ʿizzata lillahi jamiʿan":** that is, dominance and power belong entirely to Allah.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: **"Yabtaghuna ʿindahum"** ("Do they seek [honour] with them?"), meaning with the Banu Qaynuqa, because Ibn Ubayy used to be allied with them.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 4, verses 140–141:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And He has already sent down to you in the Book that when you hear the verses of Allah being denied and mocked﴾. The address is to everyone who professes faith, whether sincere or hypocritical, because whoever professes faith is bound to comply with the commands of the Book of Allah. The revelation referred to is His saying, may He be exalted: (And when you see those who engage in vain talk concerning Our verses, turn away from them until they engage in a different discourse [see vol. 7, p. 12]). The hypocrites used to sit with the rabbis of the Jews and mock the Qur'an.

ʿĀṣim and Yaʿqub read (wa-qad nazzala) with a fatḥah on the nūn and the zāy and a shaddah on the zāy, because the name of Allah, majestic is His majesty, precedes it in His saying, may He be exalted: (for all honour belongs to Allah). Ḥumayd read it the same way, except that he pronounced the zāy without the shaddah. The rest read (nuzzila), in the passive voice.

As for (an idhā samiʿtum āyāti Allāh), the grammatical position (iʿrab) of (an idhā samiʿtum) is in the accusative according to the reading of ʿĀṣim and Yaʿqub, as it is the object of the verb. According to the reading of the rest it is in the nominative, as it is the substitute for the subject of the passive verb.

(yukfaru bihā): that is, when you hear disbelief and mockery directed at the verses of Allah. The verb "hearing" is applied to the verses, but what is meant is the hearing of disbelief and mockery, just as you say: "I heard ʿAbd Allah being blamed," meaning: "I heard blame directed at ʿAbd Allah."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So do not sit with them until they engage in a different discourse﴾, meaning a discourse other than disbelief.

(Indeed, you would then be like them). From this is derived the obligation to avoid the people of sin when wrongdoing appears from them, because whoever does not avoid them has approved of their conduct, and approval of disbelief is disbelief. Allah, mighty and majestic, said: (Indeed, you would then be like them). Therefore, whoever sits in a gathering (majlis) of disobedience without denouncing it is equal to them in sin. He ought to denounce them when they speak of disobedience and act upon it. If he is unable to denounce them, he should rise and leave them, so that he is not among the people of this verse. It has been related from ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz, may Allah be pleased with him, that he seized a group of people drinking wine. It was said to him concerning one of those present that he was fasting, so he imposed the discipline upon him as well, and he recited this verse: (Indeed, you would then be like them). That is, approval of disobedience is itself disobedience. For this reason, both the doer and the one who approves are held accountable for the punishment of sins, to the extent that they all perish together. This likeness is not in all attributes; rather, it is a binding of a kind, likened to the apparent judgment derived from association, as the poet said:

*"Every companion follows the example of the one he accompanies."*

This has already been mentioned [see p. 194 of this part]. Since the avoidance of the people of sin is established as explained, avoiding the people of innovation and desires is all the more fitting. Al-Kalbi said: His saying, may He be exalted, (So do not sit with them until they engage in a different discourse) was abrogated (nusikha) by His saying, may He be exalted: (And there is nothing upon those who fear Allah concerning their accountability [see vol. 6, p. 431]). The majority of the exegetes said: it is muḥkam (decisive, not abrogated). Juwaybir related from al-Ḍaḥḥāk who said: Every innovator in the religion who introduces something new is included in this verse until the Day of Resurrection.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah will gather the hypocrites﴾. The original form is (jāmiʿun) with tanwīn, but it was elided for lightness, since it means "yajmaʿu" (will gather).

(Those who wait for you): meaning the hypocrites, that is, they await for you the turns of fortune.

(If you have a victory from Allah): that is, dominance over the Jews and spoils of war.

(They say: "Were we not with you?"): that is, give us a share of the spoils.

(And if the disbelievers have a portion): that is, a success.

(They say: "Did we not gain mastery over you?"): that is, did we not overcome you, so that the Muslims feared you and we turned them away from you. It is said: *istaḥwadha ʿalā kadhā* means he overcame it. From this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Satan has gained mastery over them﴾ [see vol. 17, p. 305]. It has also been said: the root of *istiḥwādh* is *ḥawṭ* (protection/encompassing); one says *ḥāḏahu yaḥūdhuhu ḥawdhan* when he surrounds him. This verb came according to its original form; had it undergone i'lāl (morphological weakening), it would have been *alam nastaḥidh*. The verb in the form with i'lāl is *istāḥa yastīḥu*, and in the form without i'lāl it is *istaḥwadha yastaḥwidhu*.

(And we protected you from the believers): that is, by our discouraging them from you and our dividing them from what they intended against you. The verse indicates that the hypocrites used to go out with the Muslims on the military expeditions (ghazawāt), and for this reason they said: "Were we not with you?" It also indicates that they were not giving them a share of the spoils, and for this reason they demanded it and said: "Were we not with you!" It is also possible that by their saying "Were we not with you?" they intended to remind the Muslims of their favour, that is, "We used to inform you of their news and we were helpers for you."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And Allah will never give the disbelievers a way over the believers﴾. Concerning this there are three issues.

**The first:** His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And Allah will never give the disbelievers a way over the believers﴾. The scholars have five interpretations of it:

The first: what was related from Yusayʿ (also given as Yuthayʿ or Usayʿ) al-Ḥaḍramī, who said: I was with ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may Allah be pleased with him, when a man said to him: "O Commander of the Faithful, what do you say about the saying of Allah: (And Allah will never give the disbelievers a way over the believers)? How is that, when they fight us and prevail over us at times?" ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Its meaning is on the Day of Resurrection, the Day of Judgment." Likewise Ibn ʿAbbās said: "That is the Day of Resurrection." Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "All the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wīl) said this." Ibn al-ʿArabī said: "This is weak, because the report has no benefit in that case, and the opening of the speech may mislead one about its meaning, due to His saying, may He be exalted: (So Allah will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection). He postponed the judgment until the Day of Resurrection, and made affairs in this world a succession of turns, in which the disbelievers prevail at one time and are overcome at another, according to the wisdom He sees and the word that has preceded. Then He said: (And Allah will never give the disbelievers a way over the believers). So whoever imagines that the end of the speech returns to its beginning has nullified its benefit, for it would then be a repetition."

The second: Allah, glory be to Him, does not grant them a means by which they can wipe out the dominion of the believers, erase their traces and seize their domain. This is as in the authentic Ṣaḥīḥ of Muslim, from the ḥadīth of Thawbān, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "I asked my Lord that He not destroy my community by a general calamity, and that He not give over them an enemy from outside themselves, who would seize their domain. My Lord said: 'O Muḥammad, when I decree a decree it is not turned back. I have granted you for your community that I will not destroy them by a general calamity, and I will not give over them an enemy from outside themselves who would seize their domain, even if all who are in its regions were gathered against them, until some of them destroy others and some of them take others captive.'"

The third: Allah, glory be to Him, does not give the disbelievers a way over the believers (from Him), except when they conspire together in falsehood, do not forbid one another from wrongdoing, and hold back from repentance. Then the enemy's domination comes from their own side, as He, may He be exalted, said: (And whatever misfortune befalls you is for what your hands have earned [see vol. 16, p. 30]). Ibn al-ʿArabī said: "This is extremely precious." I say: The saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him, in the ḥadīth of Thawbān supports it: "until some of them destroy others and some of them take others captive." For "until" (ḥattā) indicates a limit, so the apparent meaning of the speech is that He does not give their enemy power over them to seize their domain, except when some of them destroy others and some of them take others captive. This has occurred in these times through the strife between the Muslims, so the might of the disbelievers grew strong, they seized the lands of the Muslims, and nothing of Islam remained but a little. We ask Allah to make up for us with His pardon, His help and His gentleness.

The fourth: Allah, glory be to Him, does not give the disbelievers a way over the believers by the Law (shar'an). If it occurs, it is contrary to the Law.

The fifth: (And Allah will never give the disbelievers a way over the believers): that is, no rational or legal proof by which they could gain strength, except that it is nullified and refuted.

**The second:** Ibn al-ʿArabī said: Our scholars derived from this verse the argument that a disbeliever does not own a Muslim slave. This was also the view of Ashhab and al-Shafiʿi, because Allah, glory be to Him, negated a way for the disbeliever over him, and ownership by purchase is a way, so it is not legislated for him, and the contract is not valid by it. Ibn al-Qāsim, from Mālik, and it is also the view of Abū Ḥanīfah, said: The meaning of (And Allah will never give the disbelievers a way over the believers) concerns the continuation of ownership, because we find that the initial acquisition of it may belong to him over him [and that is by inheritance]. Its form: a disbelieving slave who has become Muslim is in the possession of a disbeliever, and it is necessary for a judgment to be given for his sale. Before the judgment for his sale was issued, the owner died, and the Muslim slave inherits from the disbeliever. This is a way that has been established by compulsion, without intention. But if ownership is acquired by purchase, it is established through the intention of the will, for the disbeliever wished to possess him by his own choice. If a judgment is given for the validity of the sale and the establishment of his ownership, his intention has been fulfilled, and a way has been made for him over the slave.

Abū ʿUmar said: The Muslims have agreed that the manumission of a Christian or Jewish master of his Muslim slave is valid and effective. They also agreed that if a disbeliever's slave becomes Muslim and is sold against his master's will, his price is paid to him. This indicates that he was sold while still in his master's ownership, and the manumission took effect while he was in that ownership, except that it is an ownership that is not stable, because of the obligation to sell him. This, Allah knows best, is based on the saying of Allah, mighty and majestic: (And Allah will never give the disbelievers a way over the believers), meaning enslavement, ownership and servitude that is stable and permanent.

The scholars differed concerning a disbelieving slave's purchase of a Muslim slave, on two views: first, the sale is annulled; second, the sale is valid and he is sold against the buyer.

**The third:** The scholars also differed on this same question concerning a Christian man who made a slave of his, a Christian, a *mudabbar* (a slave freed upon his master's death), and the slave then became Muslim. Mālik and al-Shafiʿi, in one of his two views, said: He is to be kept away from the slave and removed from his Christian master's possession, and he is not to be sold until his affair is clarified. If the Christian dies while owing a debt, his debt is paid from the price of the *mudabbar* slave, unless there is in his estate what can cover the debt, in which case the *mudabbar* is freed. Al-Shafiʿi, in the other view, said: He is to be sold immediately when he becomes Muslim. This was the view adopted by al-Muzanī, because the *tadbīr* is a bequest, and it is not permissible to leave a Muslim in the possession of a polytheist who humiliates him and removes him from his home, since by becoming Muslim he has become an enemy to him. Al-Layth ibn Saʿd said: The Christian is sold to a Muslim, who frees him, and his *walāʾ* (right of patronage) belongs to the one who bought and freed him, and his price is given to the Christian. Sufyān and the Kufans said: If the *mudabbar* of the Christian becomes Muslim, he is valued at his worth and he works to pay that value. If the Christian dies before the *mudabbar* has finished his work-payment (si'āyah), the slave is freed and the work-payment is annulled.

The fifth: (And Allah will never give the disbelievers a way over the believers): that is, no rational or legal proof by which they could gain strength, except that it is nullified and refuted.

This was also the view of Ashhab and al-Shafiʿi, because Allah, glory be to Him, negated a way for the disbeliever over him, and ownership by purchase is a way, so it is not legislated for him, and the contract is not valid by it. Ibn al-Qāsim, from Mālik, and it is also the view of Abū Ḥanīfah, said: The meaning of (And Allah will never give the disbelievers a way over the believers) concerns the continuation of ownership, because we find that the initial acquisition of it may belong to him over him [and that is by inheritance]. Its form: a disbelieving slave who has become Muslim is in the possession of a disbeliever, and it is necessary for a judgment to be given for his sale. Before the judgment for his sale was issued, the owner died, and the Muslim slave inherits from the disbeliever. This is a way that has been established by compulsion, without intention. But if ownership is acquired by purchase, it is established through the intention of the will, for the disbeliever wished to possess him by his own choice. If a judgment is given for the validity of the sale and the establishment of his ownership, his intention has been fulfilled, and a way has been made for him over the slave.

Abū ʿUmar said: The Muslims have agreed that the manumission of a Christian or Jewish master of his Muslim slave is valid and effective. They also agreed that if a disbeliever's slave becomes Muslim and is sold against his master's will, his price is paid to him. This indicates that he was sold while still in his master's ownership, and the manumission took effect while he was in that ownership, except that it is an ownership that is not stable, because of the obligation to sell him. This, Allah knows best, is based on the saying of Allah, mighty and majestic: (And Allah will never give the disbelievers a way over the believers), meaning enslavement, ownership and servitude that is stable and permanent.

The scholars differed concerning a disbelieving slave's purchase of a Muslim slave, on two views: first, the sale is annulled; second, the sale is valid and he is sold against the buyer.

**The third:** The scholars also differed on this same question concerning a Christian man who made a slave of his, a Christian, a *mudabbar* (a slave freed upon his master's death), and the slave then became Muslim. Mālik and al-Shafiʿi, in one of his two views, said: He is to be kept away from the slave and removed from his Christian master's possession, and he is not to be sold until his affair is clarified. If the Christian dies while owing a debt, his debt is paid from the price of the *mudabbar* slave, unless there is in his estate what can cover the debt, in which case the *mudabbar* is freed. Al-Shafiʿi, in the other view, said: He is to be sold immediately when he becomes Muslim. This was the view adopted by al-Muzanī, because the *tadbīr* is a bequest, and it is not permissible to leave a Muslim in the possession of a polytheist who humiliates him and removes him from his home, since by becoming Muslim he has become an enemy to him. Al-Layth ibn Saʿd said: The Christian is sold to a Muslim, who frees him, and his *walāʾ* (right of patronage) belongs to the one who bought and freed him, and his price is given to the Christian. Sufyān and the Kufans said: If the *mudabbar* of the Christian becomes Muslim, he is valued at his worth and he works to pay that value. If the Christian dies before the *mudabbar* has finished his work-payment (si'āyah), the slave is freed and the work-payment is annulled.

**Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 4, verse 142:**

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites try to deceive Allah, but it is He who deceives them.﴾

The meaning of *khada'* (deception) has already been discussed in (al-Baqarah) [[See vol. 1, p. 195.]]. Allah's deception of them is His requital for their deceiving His friends and His messengers. Al-Hasan said: On the Day of Resurrection, every person, whether believer or hypocrite, is given a light. The hypocrites rejoice and think they have been saved. But when they reach the Bridge (al-Sirat), the light of every hypocrite is extinguished. This is the meaning of their saying: ﴿Wait for us, that we may borrow from your light﴾ [[See vol. 17, p. 245, where there is a discussion of this.]].

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And when they stand up for prayer, they stand lazily﴾, meaning they pray for show, while they are lazy and reluctant. They do not hope for reward, nor do they believe that abandoning it brings punishment. In the authentic hadith: "The heaviest prayers for the hypocrites are the 'Isha' and the Fajr." For the 'Isha' comes when their work of the day has exhausted them, so standing up for it is burdensome to them. The Fajr comes when sleep is dearer to them than anything they could be happy about, and were it not for the sword they would not have stood up. *Riya'* (showing off, ostentation) is displaying good deeds so that people will see them, not for obedience to the command of Allah; its explanation has already been given [[See vol. 3, p. 312.]]. Then He described them with scant remembrance of Allah when they are showing off and when they are afraid. The Prophet ﷺ said, censuring one who delays the prayer: "That is the prayer of the hypocrites—three times—one of them sits watching the sun until, when it is between the two horns of the Devil, or on the two horns of the Devil, he rises and pecks out four rak'ahs, remembering Allah in them only a little." Narrated by Malik and others. It was said: He described them with scant remembrance because they did not remember Allah with recitation or glorification, but only with *takbir* (saying "Allahu akbar"). It was also said: He described it as scant because Allah does not accept it. And it was said: because it lacks sincerity.

Here there are two issues.

**The first:** In this verse Allah explained the prayer of the hypocrites, and His Messenger Muhammad ﷺ also explained it. Whoever prays as they pray and remembers as they remember is joined to them in non-acceptance, and falls outside the scope of His words: ﴿Successful indeed are the believers, who are humble in their prayer﴾ [[See vol. 12, p. 10.]], which will come. Except if he has an excuse, in which case he is limited to the obligatory part, according to what the Prophet ﷺ taught the Bedouin when he saw him neglecting the prayer. He said to him: "When you stand up for prayer, perfect the ablution, then face the qiblah, say takbir, then recite what you can of the Qur'an, then bow until you are at rest in bowing, then rise until you stand upright, then prostrate until you are at rest in prostration, then rise until you are at rest sitting, then do this throughout your prayer." Narrated by the Imams. He ﷺ also said: "There is no prayer for one who does not recite the Umm al-Qur'an [al-Fatihah]." And he said: "A prayer in which a man does not straighten his spine in bowing and prostration is not valid." Al-Tirmidhi transmitted it and said: "A hasan sahih hadith, and the practice among the people of knowledge from the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ and those after them is that a man should straighten his spine in bowing and prostration." Al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Ishaq said: Whoever does not straighten his spine in bowing and prostration, his prayer is invalid, on account of the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "A prayer in which a man does not straighten his spine in bowing and prostration is not valid." Ibn al-'Arabi said: Ibn al-Qasim and Abu Hanifah held that tuma'nina (tranquillity in the postures) is not obligatory. This is an Iraqi narration which none of the Malikis should busy himself with. This matter has already been discussed in (al-Baqarah) [[See vol. 1, p. 170, and pp. 103–4 of vol. 12.]].

**The second:** Ibn al-'Arabi said: Whoever prays a prayer so that people will see him and see him in it, and so that they will testify to his faith, or who desires status and prominence in order to have his testimony accepted and to be permitted to lead the prayer, this is not the prohibited *riya'*, and there is no sin upon him. The *riya'* that is disobedience is to display it as a snare for people and a means to obtain food. This is an intention that does not suffice, and he must repeat the prayer.

I say: His words "or who desires status and prominence in order to have his testimony accepted" are open to question. Its explanation has already been given in (al-Nisa') [[See p. 180 onward in this part, and p. 212 of vol. 20.]], so reflect on it there.

This verse indicates that *riya'* enters both the obligatory and the voluntary prayer, because of Allah's words: ﴿And when they stand up for prayer, they stand﴾, which is general. Some people said: it enters only the voluntary prayer, because the obligatory is binding upon all people, while the voluntary is exposed to it. It was also said the opposite, because if he did not perform the voluntary prayers, he would not be held accountable for them.

Al-Mudhabdhab: one who wavers between two matters. The dhabdhabah is agitation or unsteadiness. It is said: "I made him waver (dhabdhabtuhu), so he wavered (fa-tadhabdhaba)." From this is the verse of al-Nabigha:

"Did you not see that God has given you a sovereignty, before which every king is seen wavering?"

Another poet said:

"A phantom for Umm al-Salsabil, and between her and it is a month's journey for the wavering courier."

It is so narrated with the second dhal pronounced with a kasra. Ibn Jinni said: meaning the trembling (al-muhtazz), the restless one who neither settles nor takes his time. [[In the originals: "al-mumtarr". The correction is from Ibn 'Atiyyah. In al-Raghib: dhabdhabah is the imitation of the sound of a moving suspended thing, then it was borrowed for every agitation and movement.]] These hypocrites are wavering between the believers and the polytheists, neither sincerely holding to faith nor openly declaring disbelief.

In Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The likeness of the hypocrite is like that of a wavering sheep (al-sha'ah al-ta'irah) between two flocks of sheep; it goes toward this one at one time and toward that one at another time." In another narration, "takurru" (it turns back) is used instead of "ta'irru" (it wanders).

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "mudhabdhabina" with a damma on the mim and fatha on both dhals. Ibn 'Abbas read with a kasra on the second dhal. In the codex of Ubayy it is "mutadhabdhibina." It is permissible to assimilate (idgham) in this reading, as "mudhdhabdhibina," with a shadda on the first dhal and a kasra on the second. From al-Hasan it is "madhabdhabina," with a fatha on the mim and on both dhals.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verse 144:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, do not take the disbelievers as allies﴾ — the two objects (of "take") are: that is, do not make them your inner circle and confidants (bitanah) from among them. This meaning has already been mentioned [see vol. 4, p. 178].

(﴿Do you wish to give Allah a clear authority against yourselves?﴾) — that is, to (give Him the right to) punish you by establishing His proof against you, since He has already forbidden you (to do so).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verse 145:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿In the lowest depth of the Fire﴾. The Kufans read (al-Darki) with a sukun on the rā’, but the first (al-Darka, with a fatha) is more eloquent, because its plural is said to be adrak, like jamal and ajmal. This was said by al-Nahhas. Abu ‘Ali said: they are two dialects, like al-sham‘ and al-sham‘ and the like, and the plural is adrak. It was also said: the plural of darak is adruk, like fals and aflus. The Fire has seven darakat, that is, levels and stations, except that the Arabs' usage for everything that is lower is adrak. It is said: for a well there is adrak, and for what is high there is daraj, so for Paradise there is daraj, and for the Fire there is adrak. This has already been mentioned [[See p. 344 of this part.]]. So the hypocrite is in the lowest depth, which is the Hawiyah, because of the severity of his disbelief, the abundance of his treachery, and his power to harm the believers. The highest of the darakat is Jahannam, then Laza, then al-Hutamah, then al-Sa‘ir, then Saqar, then al-Jahim, then al-Hawiyah. All of them may be called by the name of the first level. May God protect us from its punishment by His grace and generosity.

It is related from Ibn Mas‘ud, regarding the interpretation of His saying (in the lowest depth of the Fire), that he said: they are iron coffins locked within the Fire, which are shut upon them.

Ibn ‘Umar said: Indeed the people most severely punished on the Day of Resurrection are three: the hypocrites, those among the People of the Table who disbelieved, and the family of Pharaoh. The confirmation of this is in the Book of God, may He be exalted. God, may He be exalted, said: (Indeed the hypocrites will be in the lowest depth of the Fire). And He, may He be exalted, said regarding the People of the Table: (For I will punish him with a punishment with which I shall not punish anyone among the worlds). And He said regarding the family of Pharaoh: (Admit the family of Pharaoh to the severest punishment) [[See vol. 6, p. 398.]] [[See vol. 15, p. 318.]].

Istithna' (an exception) from those who were hypocrites. Among the conditions for a hypocrite who repents is that he reform his words and deeds, hold fast to Allah, meaning he makes Him his refuge and shelter, and make his religion sincerely for Allah, as this verse explicitly states. Otherwise he is not a penitent. For this reason, the reward of the believers is placed in the expression of uncertainty (al-taswif) because the hypocrites have joined them. And Allah knows best.

Al-Bukhari [In manuscript J: "and Muslim"] narrated from al-Aswad, who said: "We were in the circle of Abdullah [ibn Mas'ud], when Hudhayfah came, stood over us, greeted us, and then said: 'Hypocrisy has descended upon a people better than you.' Al-Aswad said: 'Subhan Allah! Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest depths of the Fire﴾.' Abdullah smiled, and Hudhayfah sat down in a corner of the mosque. Then Abdullah stood up, and his companions dispersed. He threw pebbles at me, so I went to him. Hudhayfah said: 'I am amazed at his laughter, though he knows what I said: Hypocrisy was indeed sent down upon a people who were better than you, then they repented, so Allah accepted their repentance.'"

Al-Farra' said: The meaning of ﴿then those are with the believers﴾ is: from among the believers. Al-Qutabi said: He turned away from their speech out of anger toward them, so He said ﴿then those are with the believers﴾ and did not say: "they are the believers," [In the source: it was not judged that they were the believers, etc., as a warning away from the great disbelief of hypocrisy that they had been in.]

The letter yā' was omitted from ﴿yu'ti﴾ in the writing just as it is omitted in pronunciation, because it is sukun (vowelless) and the lām after it is also sukun. Similar to it are ﴿the day the caller calls﴾ (yawma yunādi al-munādi) [see vol. 17 p. 26, p. 125, and vol. 20 p. 126], ﴿We shall call the guards of Hell﴾ (sanad'u al-zabāniyah), and ﴿the day the caller calls﴾ (yawma yad'u al-dā'i): the waw's were omitted because of the meeting of two sukun letters.

Interrogation in the sense of affirmation addressed to the hypocrites. The implied meaning: what benefit does He gain from punishing you if you give thanks and believe? So He, exalted is He, makes clear that He does not punish the grateful believer, and that His punishing His servants does not increase His dominion, and His leaving off their punishment for their deeds does not diminish His authority.

Makhul said: "Four qualities, whoever has them, they are for him; and three, whoever has them, they are against him. The four that are for him: gratitude, faith, supplication and seeking forgiveness." God the Exalted said: ﴿What would Allah do with your punishment if you are grateful and believe?﴾ And God the Exalted said: ﴿But Allah would not punish them while you are among them, nor would Allah punish them while they seek forgiveness.﴾ [[See vol. 7 p. 398.]] And God the Exalted said: ﴿Say: My Lord would not care for you were it not for your supplication.﴾ [[See vol. 13 p. 84.]] As for the three that are against him: deceit, transgression and breaking of covenant. God the Exalted said: ﴿So whoever breaks his oath, he breaks it only to his own detriment.﴾ [[See vol. 16 p. 268.]] And God the Exalted said: ﴿And the evil plotting encompasses only its own people.﴾ [[See vol. 14 p. 259.]] And God the Exalted said: ﴿Your transgression is only against yourselves﴾ [[See vol. 8 p. 324.]]. ﴿And Allah is Shakir, Knowing﴾: meaning, He rewards His servants for their obedience. The meaning of "He rewards them" (yashkuruhum) is that He gives them recompense, accepting the little deed and granting a great reward for it, and that is His "thanks" for their worship. In the language, shukr (gratitude) means manifestation; it is said: "a shakur beast" when it shows fatness beyond what it is given of fodder. This meaning has been discussed fully earlier [[See vol. 1 p. 397.]]. The Arabs say in a proverb: "More grateful than a barwaqah" [[al-Buruq: what covers the earth of the first greenness of plants. It is said: it is a known plant.]], because it is said that it turns green and bright in the shade of clouds without rain. And Allah knows best.

The fifth volume of Tafsir al-Qurtubi is complete; it is followed, God willing, by the sixth volume, beginning with His words: ﴿Allah does not like the public mention of evil speech﴾

Corrected by Abu Ishaq Ibrahim Itfayyish. Volume six.

[Continuation of the commentary on Surah an-Nisa]

In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

**First issue: the verse and the exception.** There are three matters here. The first concerns His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah does not like the public mention of evil speech﴾, and the sentence is complete. Then He, Majestic and Mighty, says "except one who has been wronged" (*illā man ẓulima*). This is an exception (*istithnā'*) that is not part of the first clause, and it occupies the accusative position. The sense is: "But whoever has been wronged, he may say, 'So-and-so wronged me.'" It is also permissible that it occupies the nominative position, with the implied meaning: "Allah does not like that anyone should publicly mention evil, except one who has been wronged."

The recitation of the majority (*qira'at al-jumhur*) is *ẓulima* with a *ḍammah* on the *ẓā'* and a *kasrah* on the *lām*, and it is permissible to make the *lām* quiescent (*iskān*). Whoever recites *ẓalama*, with a *fatḥah* on both the *ẓā'* and the *lām*, namely Zayd ibn Aslam, Ibn Abi Ishaq and others, as will come, is not permitted to make the *lām* quiescent, because of the lightness of the *fatḥah*.

According to the first recitation, one group said: the meaning is, "Allah does not like that anyone publicly mention evil speech, except one who has been wronged; for him, publicly mentioning it is not disliked."

Then they differed over the manner of publicly mentioning evil and what is permitted of it. Al-Hasan said: it is the man who wrongs another man, and he does not invoke a curse upon him [[In the manuscripts: nahā; the apparent reading is with a waw: khabar.]], but rather says: "O Allah, help me against him. O Allah, extract my right. O Allah, come between him and what he intends of my wronging." This is a supplication in self-defence, and that is the least degree of evil speech.

Ibn Abbas and others said: what is permitted for one who has been wronged is that he may invoke a curse upon the one who wronged him, though if he is patient, that is better for him. This is a general permission regarding the kind of supplication against the wrongdoer.

He also said, together with al-Suddi: there is no harm for one who has been wronged to take revenge against the one who wronged him with the like of his wrong, and to speak openly to him of evil speech.

Ibn al-Mustanir said: "except one who has been wronged" means: except one who has been compelled to publicly utter evil speech, such as disbelief or the like; that is permitted. According to this, the verse concerns compulsion.

Qutrub said likewise: "except one who has been wronged" refers to the one who is compelled, because he is wronged, and so that is lifted from him even if he disbelieves. He said: it is also permissible that the meaning of "except one who has been wronged" is by way of substitution (*al-badal*), as if he said: "Allah does not like anyone except one who has been wronged," meaning: Allah does not like the wrongdoer; so it is as though he says: "He loves the one who has been wronged," meaning: He rewards the one who has been wronged. The reckoning according to this view is: "Allah does not like the one who publicly mentions evil, except one who has been wronged, by substitution."

Mujahid said: it was revealed concerning hospitality, so he was given leave to speak about it. Ibn Jurayj said, from Mujahid: it was revealed concerning a man who hosted a man in a desert wasteland, but the host did not entertain him, so "except one who has been wronged" was revealed. Ibn Abi Najih also narrated it from Mujahid, who said: this verse, "Allah does not like the public mention of evil speech, except one who has been wronged," was revealed concerning a man who passes by a man and he does not host him, so he was given leave to say about him that he did not treat him hospitably.

Those who hold hospitality to be obligatory have used this verse as evidence. They said: because wrongdoing is forbidden, this indicates its obligation. This is the view of al-Layth ibn Sa'd. The majority hold that it is among the noble characteristics (*makārim al-akhlāq*), and its explanation will come in *Hud* [[See vol. 9, p. 64.]].

What the apparent meaning of the verse requires is that the one who has been wronged may take redress against his wrongdoer, but with moderation, if the wrongdoer is a believer, as al-Hasan said. As for answering slander with slander or the like, that is not permitted, and it has already been mentioned in *al-Baqarah* [[See vol. 2, p. 360.]]. If the wrongdoer is a disbeliever, then let your tongue loose and invoke upon him whatever destruction you wish, and every kind of supplication, as the Prophet ﷺ did when he said: "O Allah, press down Your foot upon Mudar, and make upon them years like the years of Yusuf." And he said: "O Allah, upon You be (the requital) against so-and-so and so-and-so," naming them. If the wrongdoer openly commits wrong, he may be invoked against openly, and he has no respected honour, no respected body, and no respected property.

Abu Dawud narrated from Aisha that she said: something of hers was stolen, so she began to invoke a curse against the thief [[i.e., the thief.]]. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do not lighten him (*lā tusabbikhī 'anhu*)." That is: do not lighten his punishment by your supplication against him.

It is also narrated from Amr ibn al-Sharid, from his father, from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who said: "The procrastination (*laiy*) of the one who is able [[Al-layy: delay. Al-wājid: the one able to pay his debt.]] is an injustice that makes lawful his honour and his punishment." Ibn al-Mubarak said: "makes lawful his honour" means he is treated harshly; "his punishment" means he is imprisoned (*yuḥbas*).

In Sahih Muslim: "The procrastination of the wealthy is injustice." So the affluent, capable man, when he is asked to pay and procrastinates, is an oppressor, and that permits speaking about his honour, that it may be said of him: "So-and-so delays people and withholds their rights," and it permits the ruler to discipline him and to impose a discretionary punishment (*ta'zīr*) until he desists from that. The meaning of this has been related from Sufyan, and it is the meaning of the saying of Ibn al-Mubarak, may Allah be pleased with them both.

**The second matter:** Not among this category is what occurred in Sahih Muslim concerning al-Abbas's words about Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, in the presence of Umar, Uthman, al-Zubayr and Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf: "O Commander of the Faithful, judge between me and this liar, sinful, treacherous, deceitful one." The hadith [continues]. None of them rebuked him, because it was a dispute, each of them holding it for himself, until Umar carried out the obligation in it upon them. So said Ibn al-Arabi.

Our scholars said: this applies only when the ranks are equal or close; but when they differ, the rabble is not permitted to lord it over the excellent (*al-fuḍalā'*). They only claim their right by mere assertion, without explicit accusation of injustice or anger. This is correct, and the reports indicate it.

There is another explanation: that this statement proceeded from al-Abbas out of anger and the assertiveness of the paternal uncle's authority. For the paternal uncle is the twin (*ṣinw*, i.e., the equal) of the father, and there is no doubt that when a father uses such expressions toward his child, it is taken as intending harshness and deterrence, to the extent of exaggeration in discipline, not that the child is described by those qualities. Added to this, they were in a dispute over a religious authority (*wilāyah dīniyyah*), so al-Abbas believed that opposing him in it was not permitted, and that opposing him in it leads to the opponent being characterised by those qualities. So in the fury of anger he uttered them in these respects. When those present knew this, they did not object to him. Al-Mazari, al-Qadi Iyad and others pointed to this.

**The third matter:** As for the one who reads *ẓalama* with a *fatḥah* on the *ẓā'* and the *lām*, which is the recitation of Zayd ibn Aslam, who was among the scholars of the Qur'an in Medina after Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, and the recitation of Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-Ḍaḥḥak, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib, then the meaning is: "except one who has wronged in deed or speech; so speak openly to him of evil speech," in the sense of forbidding his action, rebuking him and refuting him. The meaning is: "Allah does not like that it be said to one who has repented of hypocrisy, 'Did you not practise hypocrisy?' except one who wronged, that is, persisted in hypocrisy." This is indicated by His saying: ﴿except those who repent﴾.

Ibn Zayd said: that is because when He, Exalted, informed concerning the hypocrites that they are in the lowest level of the Fire, that was a public mention of evil speech. Then He said to them after that: ﴿What would Allah do with your punishment?﴾ [An-Nisa': 147], in the sense of making them at ease and inviting them to gratitude and faith. Then He said to the believers: "Allah does not like the public mention of evil speech, except one who has been wronged" in persisting in hypocrisy; for it is said to him: "Are you not the hypocrite, the disbeliever, for whom in the Hereafter is the lowest level of the Fire?" and similar words.

Some said: the meaning of the statement is: "Allah does not like that anyone should publicly mention evil speech," then He made a disjunct exception (*istithnā' munqaṭi'*): that is, "But whoever has been wronged, he will publicly mention evil by way of injustice and aggression, and he is a wrongdoer in that." I say: this is the practice of many wrongdoers and their habit, for with their injustice they behave arrogantly with their tongues and attack the honour of those they wronged with what is forbidden to them.

Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj said: it is possible that the meaning is: "except one who has been wronged, who said an evil thing; for you ought to restrain his hands," and the exception is not part of the first clause. I say: this is indicated by hadiths, among them his peace be upon him saying: "Restrain the hands of your foolish ones," and his saying: "Help your brother, whether he is a wrongdoer or one wronged." They said: "We help him when he is wronged, so how do we help him when he is a wrongdoer?" He said: "You restrain him from wronging."

Al-Farra' said: "except one who has been wronged" means "nor one who wronged."

**His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah has always been Hearing and Knowing﴾.** This is a warning to the wrongdoer, lest he wrong, and to the one who has been wronged, lest he exceed the limit in taking redress. Then He followed this with His saying: ﴿If you disclose good or conceal it, or pardon an evil﴾, so He urged toward pardon and encouraged it. Pardon is an attribute of Allah, Exalted, together with His power to take revenge, and the excellence of those who pardon people has already been mentioned in *Al 'Imran* [[See vol. 4, p. 207.]]. In these few words there are many meanings for one who reflects upon them.

It has been said: if you pardon, then Allah will pardon you. Ibn al-Mubarak narrated, saying: "Someone who heard al-Hasan say informed me: When the nations are brought before the Lord of the Worlds on the Day of Resurrection, a call will be made: 'Let stand whoever has his reward from Allah.' No one will stand except one who pardoned in the world." What confirms this report is His saying: ﴿So whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah﴾ [Ash-Shura: 40] [[See vol. 16, p. 38.]]

**First issue: the verse and the exception.** There are three matters here. The first concerns His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah does not like the public mention of evil speech﴾, and the sentence is complete. Then He, Majestic and Mighty, says "except one who has been wronged" (*illā man ẓulima*). This is an exception (*istithnā'*) that is not part of the first clause, and it occupies the accusative position. The sense is: "But whoever has been wronged, he may say, 'So-and-so wronged me.'" It is also permissible that it occupies the nominative position, with the implied meaning: "Allah does not like that anyone should publicly mention evil, except one who has been wronged."

The recitation of the majority (*qira'at al-jumhur*) is *ẓulima* with a *ḍammah* on the *ẓā'* and a *kasrah* on the *lām*, and it is permissible to make the *lām* quiescent (*iskān*). Whoever recites *ẓalama*, with a *fatḥah* on both the *ẓā'* and the *lām*, namely Zayd ibn Aslam, Ibn Abi Ishaq and others, as will come, is not permitted to make the *lām* quiescent, because of the lightness of the *fatḥah*.

According to the first recitation, one group said: the meaning is, "Allah does not like that anyone publicly mention evil speech, except one who has been wronged; for him, publicly mentioning it is not disliked."

Then they differed over the manner of publicly mentioning evil and what is permitted of it. Al-Hasan said: it is the man who wrongs another man, and he does not invoke a curse upon him [[In the manuscripts: nahā; the apparent reading is with a waw: khabar.]], but rather says: "O Allah, help me against him. O Allah, extract my right. O Allah, come between him and what he intends of my wronging." This is a supplication in self-defence, and that is the least degree of evil speech.

Ibn Abbas and others said: what is permitted for one who has been wronged is that he may invoke a curse upon the one who wronged him, though if he is patient, that is better for him. This is a general permission regarding the kind of supplication against the wrongdoer.

He also said, together with al-Suddi: there is no harm for one who has been wronged to take revenge against the one who wronged him with the like of his wrong, and to speak openly to him of evil speech.

Ibn al-Mustanir said: "except one who has been wronged" means: except one who has been compelled to publicly utter evil speech, such as disbelief or the like; that is permitted. According to this, the verse concerns compulsion.

Qutrub said likewise: "except one who has been wronged" refers to the one who is compelled, because he is wronged, and so that is lifted from him even if he disbelieves. He said: it is also permissible that the meaning of "except one who has been wronged" is by way of substitution (*al-badal*), as if he said: "Allah does not like anyone except one who has been wronged," meaning: Allah does not like the wrongdoer; so it is as though he says: "He loves the one who has been wronged," meaning: He rewards the one who has been wronged. The reckoning according to this view is: "Allah does not like the one who publicly mentions evil, except one who has been wronged, by substitution."

Mujahid said: it was revealed concerning hospitality, so he was given leave to speak about it. Ibn Jurayj said, from Mujahid: it was revealed concerning a man who hosted a man in a desert wasteland, but the host did not entertain him, so "except one who has been wronged" was revealed. Ibn Abi Najih also narrated it from Mujahid, who said: this verse, "Allah does not like the public mention of evil speech, except one who has been wronged," was revealed concerning a man who passes by a man and he does not host him, so he was given leave to say about him that he did not treat him hospitably.

Those who hold hospitality to be obligatory have used this verse as evidence. They said: because wrongdoing is forbidden, this indicates its obligation. This is the view of al-Layth ibn Sa'd. The majority hold that it is among the noble characteristics (*makārim al-akhlāq*), and its explanation will come in *Hud* [[See vol. 9, p. 64.]].

What the apparent meaning of the verse requires is that the one who has been wronged may take redress against his wrongdoer, but with moderation, if the wrongdoer is a believer, as al-Hasan said. As for answering slander with slander or the like, that is not permitted, and it has already been mentioned in *al-Baqarah* [[See vol. 2, p. 360.]]. If the wrongdoer is a disbeliever, then let your tongue loose and invoke upon him whatever destruction you wish, and every kind of supplication, as the Prophet ﷺ did when he said: "O Allah, press down Your foot upon Mudar, and make upon them years like the years of Yusuf." And he said: "O Allah, upon You be (the requital) against so-and-so and so-and-so," naming them. If the wrongdoer openly commits wrong, he may be invoked against openly, and he has no respected honour, no respected body, and no respected property.

Abu Dawud narrated from Aisha that she said: something of hers was stolen, so she began to invoke a curse against the thief [[i.e., the thief.]]. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do not lighten him (*lā tusabbikhī 'anhu*)." That is: do not lighten his punishment by your supplication against him.

It is also narrated from Amr ibn al-Sharid, from his father, from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who said: "The procrastination (*laiy*) of the one who is able [[Al-layy: delay. Al-wājid: the one able to pay his debt.]] is an injustice that makes lawful his honour and his punishment." Ibn al-Mubarak said: "makes lawful his honour" means he is treated harshly; "his punishment" means he is imprisoned (*yuḥbas*).

In Sahih Muslim: "The procrastination of the wealthy is injustice." So the affluent, capable man, when he is asked to pay and procrastinates, is an oppressor, and that permits speaking about his honour, that it may be said of him: "So-and-so delays people and withholds their rights," and it permits the ruler to discipline him and to impose a discretionary punishment (*ta'zīr*) until he desists from that. The meaning of this has been related from Sufyan, and it is the meaning of the saying of Ibn al-Mubarak, may Allah be pleased with them both.

**The second matter:** Not among this category is what occurred in Sahih Muslim concerning al-Abbas's words about Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, in the presence of Umar, Uthman, al-Zubayr and Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf: "O Commander of the Faithful, judge between me and this liar, sinful, treacherous, deceitful one." The hadith [continues]. None of them rebuked him, because it was a dispute, each of them holding it for himself, until Umar carried out the obligation in it upon them. So said Ibn al-Arabi.

Our scholars said: this applies only when the ranks are equal or close; but when they differ, the rabble is not permitted to lord it over the excellent (*al-fuḍalā'*). They only claim their right by mere assertion, without explicit accusation of injustice or anger. This is correct, and the reports indicate it.

There is another explanation: that this statement proceeded from al-Abbas out of anger and the assertiveness of the paternal uncle's authority. For the paternal uncle is the twin (*ṣinw*, i.e., the equal) of the father, and there is no doubt that when a father uses such expressions toward his child, it is taken as intending harshness and deterrence, to the extent of exaggeration in discipline, not that the child is described by those qualities. Added to this, they were in a dispute over a religious authority (*wilāyah dīniyyah*), so al-Abbas believed that opposing him in it was not permitted, and that opposing him in it leads to the opponent being characterised by those qualities. So in the fury of anger he uttered them in these respects. When those present knew this, they did not object to him. Al-Mazari, al-Qadi Iyad and others pointed to this.

**The third matter:** As for the one who reads *ẓalama* with a *fatḥah* on the *ẓā'* and the *lām*, which is the recitation of Zayd ibn Aslam, who was among the scholars of the Qur'an in Medina after Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, and the recitation of Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-Ḍaḥḥak, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib, then the meaning is: "except one who has wronged in deed or speech; so speak openly to him of evil speech," in the sense of forbidding his action, rebuking him and refuting him. The meaning is: "Allah does not like that it be said to one who has repented of hypocrisy, 'Did you not practise hypocrisy?' except one who wronged, that is, persisted in hypocrisy." This is indicated by His saying: ﴿except those who repent﴾.

Ibn Zayd said: that is because when He, Exalted, informed concerning the hypocrites that they are in the lowest level of the Fire, that was a public mention of evil speech. Then He said to them after that: ﴿What would Allah do with your punishment?﴾ [An-Nisa': 147], in the sense of making them at ease and inviting them to gratitude and faith. Then He said to the believers: "Allah does not like the public mention of evil speech, except one who has been wronged" in persisting in hypocrisy; for it is said to him: "Are you not the hypocrite, the disbeliever, for whom in the Hereafter is the lowest level of the Fire?" and similar words.

Some said: the meaning of the statement is: "Allah does not like that anyone should publicly mention evil speech," then He made a disjunct exception (*istithnā' munqaṭi'*): that is, "But whoever has been wronged, he will publicly mention evil by way of injustice and aggression, and he is a wrongdoer in that." I say: this is the practice of many wrongdoers and their habit, for with their injustice they behave arrogantly with their tongues and attack the honour of those they wronged with what is forbidden to them.

Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj said: it is possible that the meaning is: "except one who has been wronged, who said an evil thing; for you ought to restrain his hands," and the exception is not part of the first clause. I say: this is indicated by hadiths, among them his peace be upon him saying: "Restrain the hands of your foolish ones," and his saying: "Help your brother, whether he is a wrongdoer or one wronged." They said: "We help him when he is wronged, so how do we help him when he is a wrongdoer?" He said: "You restrain him from wronging."

Al-Farra' said: "except one who has been wronged" means "nor one who wronged."

**His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah has always been Hearing and Knowing﴾.** This is a warning to the wrongdoer, lest he wrong, and to the one who has been wronged, lest he exceed the limit in taking redress. Then He followed this with His saying: ﴿If you disclose good or conceal it, or pardon an evil﴾, so He urged toward pardon and encouraged it. Pardon is an attribute of Allah, Exalted, together with His power to take revenge, and the excellence of those who pardon people has already been mentioned in *Al 'Imran* [[See vol. 4, p. 207.]]. In these few words there are many meanings for one who reflects upon them.

It has been said: if you pardon, then Allah will pardon you. Ibn al-Mubarak narrated, saying: "Someone who heard al-Hasan say informed me: When the nations are brought before the Lord of the Worlds on the Day of Resurrection, a call will be made: 'Let stand whoever has his reward from Allah.' No one will stand except one who pardoned in the world." What confirms this report is His saying: ﴿So whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah﴾ [Ash-Shura: 40] [[See vol. 16, p. 38.]]

**Issue 1:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾. When He mentioned the polytheists and the hypocrites, He mentioned the disbelievers among the People of the Book, the Jews and the Christians, who disbelieved in Muhammad (ﷺ). He explained that disbelief in him is disbelief in all [the prophets], because there is no prophet who did not order his people to believe in Muhammad (ﷺ) and in all the prophets, peace be upon them. The meaning of ﴿and wish to make distinction between Allah and His messengers﴾ is: between belief in Allah and His messengers. So He, glorified is He, expressly stated that making distinction between Allah and His messengers is disbelief. It was disbelief because Allah, glorified is He, obligated people to worship Him by what He legislated for them through the tongues of the messengers. So when they deny the messengers, they reject their laws and do not accept them from them, and so they refuse to bind themselves to the servitude they were commanded to uphold. This is like denying the Creator, glorified is He, and denying the Creator is disbelief because it involves abandoning the commitment to obedience and servitude. Likewise, distinguishing between His messengers in belief in them is disbelief. And this is:

**Issue 2:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and say, "We believe in some and disbelieve in others"﴾. They are the Jews, who believed in Moses and disbelieved in Jesus and Muhammad. This statement of theirs has already been mentioned in al-Baqarah [[See vol. 2, p. 92.]]. And they say to their common people: "We did not find mention of Muhammad in our books."

﴿and wish to adopt a way between that﴾, i.e., they wish to take a path between faith and denial, meaning an innovated religion between Islam and Judaism. He said "that" (dhalika) and did not say "dhaynika" (the dual form), because dhalika is used for the dual as well; had He said dhaynika it would also have been permissible. [[In k: "had he said." i.e., outside the Qur'an.]]

**Issue 3:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those are the disbelievers in truth﴾. This is an emphasis that removes the suspicion of their faith when He described them as saying "We believe in some," and that this does not benefit them when they disbelieve in His messenger. When they disbelieve in His messenger, they have disbelieved in Him, mighty and majestic is He, and they have disbelieved in every messenger who gave good tidings of that messenger. Therefore they became the disbelievers in truth. And ﴿for the disbelievers﴾ takes the place of the second object of ﴿We have prepared﴾, i.e., We have prepared for all their categories ﴿a humiliating punishment﴾, i.e., one that degrades.
