It means by it the Prophet (ﷺ) and his community (ummah).

The Jews asked Muhammad ﷺ to ascend to the sky while they watched, and to bring down to them a written book, in which he would claim his truthfulness, all at once, as Musa had brought the Torah, out of obstinacy towards him ﷺ. Allah, mighty and majestic, informed them that their forefathers had been obstinate with Musa, peace be upon him, with something greater than this, when they said: ﴿Show us Allah openly﴾, that is, face to face. This has already been discussed in "al-Baqarah" [[see vol. 1, p. 403.]]. "Jahratan" (openly) is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning a seeing that is open. They were punished with the thunderbolt because of the enormity of what they had brought of questioning and wrongdoing, after they had seen the miracles.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then they took the calf﴾. There is an omission in the speech, its implied meaning being: "Then We revived them, and they did not stop, and they took the calf." This has already been discussed in "al-Baqarah" [[see vol. 1, p. 693]], and its mention will come in "Ta-Ha" [[see vol. 11, p. 23.]], if Allah wills.

(After the clear signs had come to them): that is, the proofs, the indications and the manifest miracles, such as the hand and the staff, the splitting of the sea and others, showing that there is no god but Allah, mighty and majestic.

(Then We pardoned that): that is, their obstinacy.

(And We gave Musa a clear authority): that is, a clear proof, namely the signs with which he came. It was called "sultan" (authority) because the one who brings it prevails by argument, and it prevails over hearts, in that one knows that it is not within the power of humans to bring the like of it.

The Almighty's words: ﴿And We raised the mountain above them for their covenant﴾, meaning: because of their breaking the covenant that was taken from them, which was to act by what is in the Tawrah (Torah). The raising of the mountain and their entering the gate have already been discussed in *al-Baqarah* [[See vol. 1, pp. 410, 436.]]. "Sujjadan" (prostrating) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl).

Warsh alone recited "We said to them, do not transgress on the Sabbath" with a fatha on the ʿayn, from *ʿadā yaʿdū* (to transgress), *ʿadwan*, *ʿudwānan*, *ʿudūwan* and *ʿadāʾan*, meaning by hunting fish, as has been mentioned in *al-Baqarah* [[See vol. 1, p. 439.]]. The original form of it [[i.e., of what Warsh recited.]] is *taʿtadū*, and the *tāʾ* was assimilated into the *dāl*. Al-Nahhas said: it is not permissible to make the ʿayn quiescent, nor can one reach a join of two quiescent letters here, and the one who recites it this way only intends to avoid error [[In Z: "yadfaʿuhu" (he repels it).]].

﴿And We took from them a solemn covenant﴾ means the covenant that was taken from them in the Torah. It was also said: it is a covenant confirmed by oath, and so it was called "solemn" (ghalīẓ) for that reason.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verses 155–156:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So for their breaking their covenant﴾. "Fa-bi-ma naqdihim" is in the genitive by the preposition bi, and "fa-bima" is a superfluous (za'idah) emphatic particle, like His saying: ﴿So by mercy from Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 159], and this has already been discussed [see vol. 4, p. 248]. The bi is connected to an omitted element, the sense being: "So for their breaking their covenant, We cursed them," related from Qatadah and others. This was omitted because the listener already knows it. Abu al-Hasan Ali ibn Hamzah al-Kisa'i said: it is connected to what precedes it, and the meaning is: "the thunderbolt seized them for their wrongdoing," up to His saying, "for their breaking their covenant." He said: so He explained their wrongdoing, for which the thunderbolt seized them, by what follows it, namely their breaking of the covenant, their killing of the prophets, and the other things He mentioned in which they wronged themselves. Al-Tabari and others rejected this, because those seized by the thunderbolt were in the time of Musa, whereas those who killed the prophets and accused Maryam of a grave slander lived long after Musa. So the thunderbolt did not seize those who were seized for their slandering of Maryam. Al-Mahdawi and others said: this objection does not hold, because it is permissible that He speaks of them while meaning their forefathers, as has been discussed in al-Baqarah [see vol. 1, p. 246]. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: "For their breaking their covenant, We forbade them good things that had been made lawful for them," because this account extends to His saying: ﴿for the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We forbade them good things that had been made lawful for them﴾ [al-Nisa': 160]. Their breaking of the covenant was that it was taken from them that they would make known the description of the Prophet ﷺ. It was also said: the meaning is: "For their breaking their covenant, and their doing such and such, and their doing such and such, Allah set a seal upon their hearts." It was also said: the meaning is: "For their breaking their covenant ... they do not believe except a little," and the fa' is superfluous (muqhamah). "Their disbelief" is conjoined, and likewise "their killing." By "the signs of Allah" is meant their scriptures which they distorted. "Ghulf" is the plural of ghilaf, i.e., "our hearts are vessels for knowledge, so we have no need of knowledge other than what we have." It was also said: it is the plural of aghlaf, meaning covered by a covering, i.e., "our hearts are in coverings, so we do not understand what you say," and this is like His saying: ﴿Our hearts are in coverings﴾ [Fussilat: 5] [see vol. 15, p. 339]. This has already been discussed in al-Baqarah [see vol. 2, p. 25]. Their aim in this was to repel the proof of the Messengers. "Al-taba'" means the sealing, which has been discussed in al-Baqarah [see vol. 1, p. 185]. "Bi-kufrihim" means: as a recompense for them for their disbelief, as He said: ﴿Rather, Allah has cursed them for their disbelief, so they believe only a little﴾ [al-Baqarah: 88] [see vol. 5, pp. 243 and 381], i.e., only a little faith, namely in some of the prophets, and that is of no benefit to them. Then He repeated "and for their disbelief" to inform that they disbelieved with one disbelief after another. It was also said: the meaning of "and for their disbelief" is their disbelief in Maryam (the Messiah, Maryam), so it was omitted because what follows indicates it. The governing element of "bi-kufrihim" is the same as the governing element of "naqdihim," since it is conjoined to it, and it is not permissible that its governing element be "taba'a." The "grave slander" is their accusing her of [an offence with] Yusuf the carpenter, who was among their righteous. "Al-buhtan" is an extreme falsehood that is marvelled at, and this has already been discussed [see vol. 5, pp. 243 and 381]. [And Allah, glory be to Him, knows best.]

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verses 157–158:**

Allah's words: ﴿And their saying, "Indeed, we killed the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, the Messenger of Allah"﴾. The "inna" (إِنَّ) is kasra-vowelled because it begins a new clause after a verb of saying (al-qawl). Opening it with a fatha is also a valid dialect (lughah). The derivation of the word "al-Masih" (the Messiah) has already been discussed in "Al 'Imran" (see vol. 4, p. 88).

"Rasul Allah" (رَسُولَ اللَّهِ, the Messenger of Allah) is in apposition (badal). If you prefer, it can be read as in the sense of "a'ni" (meaning "I mean").

﴿But they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him﴾: this is a refutation of their claim.

﴿But it was made to appear so to them﴾: that is, his likeness was cast upon another, as has been discussed in "Al 'Imran" (see vol. 4, p. 100). It is also said: they did not know his person, and they killed the one they killed while they were in doubt about him, as Allah says: ﴿And indeed, those who differ concerning it are in doubt about it﴾. As for the report (al-ikhbar), it is said that it refers to all of them. It is also said that only their common people (awamm) differed about it. The meaning of their disagreement is that some of them said he was a god, and some said he was the son of Allah. This is the view of al-Hasan. It is also said that their disagreement was that their common people said, "We killed Jesus," while those who witnessed his being raised to the heavens said, "We did not kill him." It is also said that their disagreement was that the Nestorians (al-Nusturiyyah) among the Christians said: Jesus was crucified in respect of his humanity (nasut), not in respect of his divinity (lahut). The Melkites (al-Malakaniyyah) said: the crucifixion and killing fell upon the Messiah entirely, both his humanity and his divinity. It is also said that their disagreement was that they said: "If this is our companion, where is Jesus? And if this is Jesus, where is our companion?" It is also said that their disagreement was that the Jews said: "We killed him," because Yahudha (Judas), the head of the Jews, was the one who strove for his killing. A group of the Christians said: "Rather, we killed him." Another group of them said: "Rather, Allah raised him to the heavens, and we were looking at him."

﴿They have no knowledge of it except the following of assumption﴾: "min" (مِنْ) here is extra (ziyadah, redundant), and the sentence is complete at this point. Then He, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿except the following of assumption﴾. This is an exception that is not part of the former clause (istithna' munqati'), and it is in a accusative position (fi mawdi' nasb). It may also be in a nominative position as a substitution (badal), meaning: "They have no knowledge of it, but only the following of assumption." Sibawayh recited:

*"And a land in which there is no companion, except the ya'afir, and except the 'ais"*

(Note: al-ya'afir are the young of gazelles, singular ya'fur. Al-'ais is the white wild cattle, named for its whiteness; the word originally refers to camels, and the poet borrowed it for cattle.)

Allah's words: ﴿And they did not kill him with certainty﴾. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi said: the meaning is that they did not kill their assumption with certainty, just as you say, "I killed him knowingly" when you know him with complete knowledge. In this case, the pronoun (ha') refers to the assumption (al-zann). Abu 'Ubayd said: If the meaning were "they did not kill Jesus with certainty," then it would say only "wa ma qataluhu" (and they did not kill him). It is also said that the meaning is: they did not kill the one who was made to appear to them as Jesus with certainty; in this case the pause falls on "yaqinan" (with certainty). It is also said that the meaning is: they did not kill Jesus, and the pause falls on "wa ma qataluhu," while "yaqinan" is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (masdar mahdhuf), with two possible estimates. One is: they said this as a certain statement, or Allah said this as a certain statement. The other is that the meaning is: they did not know him with certain knowledge. Al-Nahhas said: if you take the meaning to be "Rather, Allah raised him to Himself with certainty," that is an error, because what follows "bal" does not govern what precedes it, due to its weakness. Ibn al-Anbari permitted pausing on "wa ma qataluhu," with "yaqinan" in the accusative governed by an implied verb which is the answer to an oath, its estimate being: "And you have indeed spoken with certainty," that is, with certain truthfulness.

Allah's words: ﴿Rather, Allah raised him to Himself﴾: this begins a new independent statement, meaning "to the heaven." Allah, Exalted is He, is far above place. The manner of his being raised has already been discussed in "Al 'Imran" (see vol. 4, p. 99 and what follows).

﴿And Allah is ever Mighty﴾: that is, powerful in exacting retribution from the Jews. He therefore gave authority over them to Butrus (Peter) son of Astisanus the Roman, who killed among them a great slaughter.

﴿Wise﴾: He passed judgment upon them with curse and wrath.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verse 159:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And there is none of the People of the Scripture but that they will surely believe in him before his death﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid and ʿIkrimah said: the meaning is that they will believe in al-Masih (the Messiah), "before his death", i.e. the Kitabi's death. So the first pronoun refers to ʿIsa (Jesus), and the second refers to the Kitabi (the People of the Scripture). This is because there is no one among the Jews and Christians who does not believe in ʿIsa, peace be upon him, when he sees the angel, but this is a faith that does not benefit, because it is faith at the time of despair and at the moment of being overtaken by the state of death. So the Jew at that time acknowledges that he was a Messenger of Allah, and the Christian acknowledges that he was a Messenger of Allah.

It is related that al-Hajjaj asked Shahr ibn Hawshab about this verse, and he said: "I am brought a captive from among the Jews and Christians, and I order his neck to be struck, and I look at him at that time, and I do not see faith from him." Shahr ibn Hawshab said to him: "When he witnesses the matter of the Hereafter, he acknowledges that ʿIsa is the servant of Allah and His Messenger, so he believes in him, but it does not benefit him." Al-Hajjaj said to him: "From where did you take this?" He said: "I took it from Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah." Al-Hajjaj said to him: "You took it from a clear spring."

It is related from Mujahid that he said: "There is none of the People of the Scripture but that he believes in ʿIsa before his death." It was said to him: "If he drowns, or burns, or is eaten by a predator, does he believe in ʿIsa?" He said: "Yes!"

It was also said: both pronouns refer to ʿIsa, peace be upon him, and the meaning is that whoever is alive at his descent, near the Hour (i.e. close to the establishment of the Final Hour), will believe in him. This was said by Qatadah, Ibn Zayd and others, and al-Tabari chose it.

Yazid ibn Zurayʿ related from a man, from al-Hasan, regarding His saying, the Exalted: "And there is none of the People of the Scripture but that they will surely believe in him before his death," that he said: "Before the death of ʿIsa. By Allah, he is alive with Allah now, but when he descends, they will all believe in him." Similar was related from al-Dahhak and Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

It was said: "they will surely believe in him" means in Muhammad, peace be upon him, even though he has not been mentioned, because these narratives were revealed to him, and the intended object is belief in him; and belief in ʿIsa includes belief in Muhammad, peace be upon him and his family as well, since it is not permissible to differentiate between them.

It was said: "they will surely believe in him" means in Allah, the Exalted, before he dies, and faith will not benefit him at the moment of witnessing. The first two interpretations are more apparent.

al-Zuhri related from Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The son of Mary will surely descend as a just judge, and he will surely kill the Dajjal, and he will surely kill the swine, and he will surely break the cross, and there will be one prostration for Allah, Lord of the worlds." Then Abu Hurayrah said: "Recite, if you wish: ‘And there is none of the People of the Scripture but that they will surely believe in him before his death.’" Abu Hurayrah said: "Before the death of ʿIsa," repeating it three times.

The construction of the verse according to Sibawayh: "And there is none of the People of the Scripture, any one, but that they will surely believe in him." The construction according to the Kufans: "And there is none of the People of the Scripture except those who will surely believe in him," and this is objectionable, because it involves deleting the relative pronoun, and the relative clause is a part of the relative pronoun, so it is as if part of the noun were deleted.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection he will be a witness against them﴾, i.e. by denying the one who denied him and affirming the one who affirmed him.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verse 160–161:

There are two issues here. The first concerns His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So for the wrongdoing of those who were Jews﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: this is a substitution (badal) for "for their breaking of their covenant". As for "the good things" (al-tayyibat), its explicit ruling is in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And for those who were Jews We forbade every animal with claws﴾ [al-An'am: 146] [[See vol. 7, p. 124.]]. He placed the wrongdoing before the prohibition, since it is the purpose that was intended to be reported, namely that it was the cause of the prohibition.

(And for their turning many away from the way of Allah) meaning: and for their turning away themselves and others from following Muhammad (ﷺ).

(And their taking of usury, though they were forbidden from it, and their consuming of people's wealth by falsehood) all of this is an explanation of the wrongdoing they committed. Likewise what precedes it, their breaking of the covenant, and what follows it. It has already passed in "Al 'Imran" [[See vol. 4, p. 134 and following.]] that the scholars differed about the cause of the prohibition in three opinions, and this is one of them.

The second issue: Ibn al-Arabi said: There is no disagreement in the school of Malik that the disbelievers are addressed (by the divine law). This verse makes clear that they have been forbidden from usury and from consuming wealth by falsehood. If this is a report of what was revealed to Muhammad in the Qur'an, and they are included in the address, then well and good. But if it is a report of what Allah revealed to Musa in the Torah, and that they altered, distorted, disobeyed and opposed, then is it permissible for us to deal with them, since they have corrupted their wealth through their religion, or not? A group thought that dealing with them is not permissible, because of the corruption found in their wealth. The correct view is that it is permissible to deal with them, even with their usury and their committing what Allah, glorified is He, prohibited for them, for conclusive evidence for this has been established from the Qur'an and the Sunnah. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And the food of those who were given the Book is lawful for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 5] [[See p. 75 of this volume.]], and this is an explicit text. The Prophet (ﷺ) dealt with the Jews, and he died while his armour was pledged to a Jew for barley he took for his dependents [[This is noted despite its fame, together with what is authentically reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered the distribution of seven dinars that he had with Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her) while he was in the state of dying. See Nihayat al-Arab, vol. 18, p. 380.]]. What decisively ends the disease of doubt and disagreement is the consensus of the Muslim community on the permissibility of trade with the people of war, and the Prophet (ﷺ) travelled to them as a merchant, and that from his journeys is a conclusive matter establishing the permissibility of travelling to them and trading with them. If it is said: that was before prophethood, we say: he was not tainted before prophethood by anything unlawful, as is established by continuous transmission, nor did he apologize for it after he was sent, nor did he forbid it after he was made a prophet, nor did any of the Companions cut it off during his lifetime, nor did any of the Muslims after his death. They used to travel for the ransoming of captives, which is obligatory, and for reconciliation, as 'Uthman and others sent, and this may be obligatory and may be recommended. As for travelling to them merely for trade, it is permissible.

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 4, verse 162:**

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿But those firmly grounded in knowledge among them﴾. He made an exception for the believers among the People of the Book. The reason is that the Jews denied this and said: "These things were prohibited originally, and you are making them lawful, and they were not prohibited because of our wrongdoing." So it was revealed: "But those firmly grounded in knowledge." The *rasikh* (one firmly grounded) is the one who excels in knowledge of the Book and whose knowledge is firmly established in it. *Rusukh* means firm establishment. This was discussed earlier in Surah Al 'Imran [[See vol. 4, p. 16 and following.]]. The intended persons are 'Abd Allah ibn Salam, Ka'b al-Ahbar, and their counterparts.

"And the believers" means the Muhajirun and the Ansar, the Companions of Muhammad, peace be upon him.

"And those who establish the prayer." Al-Hasan, Malik ibn Dinar, and a group read: "and the establishers" (*al-muqimun*) in the nominative, on the basis of coordination (*'atf*). It is also so in the reading (*harf*) of 'Abd Allah. As for the reading of Ubayy, it has "*wal-muqimina*" (in the accusative), as in the codices (*al-masahif*).

Its case-ending has been disputed, with six opinions. The most correct of them is the view of Sibawayh, that it is in the accusative by way of praise (*al-madh*), meaning "and I mean those who establish." Sibawayh said: "This is a section on what is put in the accusative for emphasis of praise, and among that is 'and those who establish the prayer.'" He recited:

*And every people obeyed the command of their chief,*
*except Numayr, which obeyed the command of its misleader.*

It is also transmitted as: "the command of their guide" (*murshidihim*).

*al-Zaʻinin* [[Its meaning: "They fear their enemy because of their small number and humiliation, so they migrate, and their enemy does not fear them so as to leave their dwellings out of fear of them." And his words, "to one whose house we vacate": that is, when they move away from a dwelling, they do not know who will settle in it after them, because of their fear of all the tribes. The two verses are by Ibn Khayyat.]] *and they do not drive anyone out* ... *and those who say, "To whom does this dwelling belong that we vacate?"*

He also recited [[The two verses are by Khirnaq bint 'Affan of the Banu Qays. She described her people as being victorious over the enemy, slaughtering camels for guests, being constant in war, and being chaste regarding indecency.]]:

*May my people never be lowered, those who are*
*the poison of enemies and the bane of the slaughtered camels,*
*who descend upon every battlefield,*
*and who are the good ones at the knots of the loincloths.*

Al-Nahhas said: "This is the most correct thing said about *al-muqimin*."

Al-Kisa'i said: "*Wal-muqimin*" is coordinated with "*bi-ma*" (in the phrase "what was revealed to you"). Al-Nahhas said: Al-Akhfash said: "This is remote, because the meaning would be 'and they believe in those who establish the prayer.'"

Muhammad ibn Jarir [[In the original sources: Muhammad ibn Yazid.]] reported that it was said to him that *al-muqimin* here are the angels, peace be upon them, because of their constancy in prayer, glorification, and seeking forgiveness. He chose this view. He also reported that the accusative by way of praise is remote, because praise comes only after the completion of the predicate, and the predicate of "those firmly grounded in knowledge" is "those, We shall give them a great reward" [4:162], so *al-muqimin* cannot be in the accusative by way of praise.

Al-Nahhas said: Sibawayh's view on His words "*wal-mu'tuna*" (and those who give the zakat) is that it is in the nominative, being the subject of an inchoative (*mubtada'*). Others said: it is in the nominative by supposing an implied subject, meaning "they are the ones who give the zakat."

It was also said: "*wal-muqimin*" is coordinated with the *kaf* in "*qablika*" (before you), meaning "before you and before those who establish." It was said: "*al-muqimin*" is coordinated with the *kaf* in "*ilayka*" (to you). It was also said: it is coordinated with the *ha'* and *mim* (the pronoun of "*minhum*"), meaning "from them and from those who establish." These three answers are not permissible, because they involve coordinating a noun with an unmarked pronoun in the genitive.

The sixth answer: it is narrated that 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, was asked about this verse, and about His words "Indeed these two are certainly magicians" [20:63] [Ta-Ha: 63] [[See vol. 11, p. 215.]], and His words "and the Sabians" [[See vol. 6, p. 246 of this part.]] in al-Ma'ida [5:69]. She said to the questioner: "O son of my nephew, the scribes made mistakes."

Aban ibn 'Uthman said: The scribe would be dictated to and would write. He wrote "But those firmly grounded in knowledge among them and the believers" and then said to him: "What shall I write?" It was said to him: "Write 'and those who establish the prayer.'" So this error occurred.

Al-Qushayri said: This line of explanation is false, because those who collected the Book were models in the language, so it is not to be supposed that they would insert into the Qur'an what was not revealed.

The most correct of these opinions is the view of Sibawayh, and it is also the view of al-Khalil. The view of al-Kisa'i is the choice of al-Qaffal and al-Tabari. [And Allah knows best.] [[From manuscript K.]]

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an) on Surah 4, verse 163:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah﴾. This is connected to His saying: ﴿The People of the Book ask you to bring down to them a Book from heaven﴾ [al-Nisa': 153]. God informs that the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ) is like the matter of the prophets who came before him. Ibn 'Abbas said, as reported by Ibn Ishaq: it was revealed concerning a group of Jews, among them Sukayn and 'Adi ibn Zayd, who said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "God has not revealed anything to anyone after Moses." So God refuted them.

Al-wahy (revelation) is informing in concealment. It is said: waha ilayhi bil-kalam yahi wahyan, and awha yuhi ihaa'an. ﴿To Noah﴾: He mentioned him first because he was the first prophet on whose tongue the sharia (religious law) was prescribed. It has been said otherwise: al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar reported: Abu al-Hasan 'Ali ibn al-Mughira told me, from Hisham ibn Muhammad ibn al-Sa'ib, from his father, who said: "The first prophet whom God, blessed and exalted is He, sent to the earth was Idris, whose name was Akhnukh [Note: Akhnukh, with a fatha on the hamza; the author of Taj al-'Arus reported from his teacher that it is with a damma]. Then the messengers ceased until God sent Nuh ibn Lamak [Note: Lamak, with two fathas; it is also said with a fatha and then a sukun] ibn Mattushalakh [Note: Mattushalakh, with a damma on the mim, a fatha on the ta', a waw, a sukun on the shin, and it is also said with a fatha on the mim, a damma on the doubled ta', a sukun on the waw, and a fatha on the lam and kha'; from Ruh al-Ma'ani] ibn Akhnukh. Sam ibn Nuh was also a prophet. Then the messengers ceased until God sent Ibrahim as a prophet and took him as a close friend (khalil). He is Ibrahim ibn Tarakh, and the name of Tarakh was Azar. Then Isma'il ibn Ibrahim was sent and he died in Makkah. Then Ishaq ibn Ibrahim, who died in al-Sham. Then Lut, and Ibrahim was his paternal uncle. Then Ya'qub, who is Isra'il ibn Ishaq. Then Yusuf ibn Ya'qub. Then Shu'ayb ibn Yawbab [Note: Yawbab, with a two-dot letter below and a waw, both with shadda, on the pattern of Ja'far (from Ruh al-Ma'ani)]. Then Hud ibn 'Abd Allah. Then Salih ibn Asif. Then Musa and Harun, the two sons of 'Imran. Then Ayyub. Then al-Khidr, who is [Note: in MS Z: Khadirun] Khadirun. Then Dawud ibn Iasha. Then Sulayman ibn Dawud. Then Yunus ibn Matta. Then Ilyas [Note: in MS Z: then Ilyas, then Bashir, etc. Bashir is not known among the prophets]. Then Dhu al-Kifl, whose name was 'Uwaydina, from the tribe of Yahudha ibn Ya'qub."

He said: "Between Musa ibn 'Imran and Maryam bint 'Imran, the mother of 'Isa, there were one thousand and seven hundred years, and neither of them was from the tribe [Note: They mentioned among the prophets of the Arabs Handhalah ibn Safwan, a messenger to the people of al-Rass, and Khalid ibn Sinan al-'Absi]. Then Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, the Prophet (ﷺ)."

Al-Zubayr said: every prophet mentioned in the Qur'an is from the descendants of Ibrahim, except Idris, Nuh, Lut, Hud and Salih. No prophets among the Arabs existed except five: Hud, Salih, Isma'il, Shu'ayb, and Muhammad, may God's blessings and peace be upon him and upon all of them [Note: They mentioned among the prophets of the Arabs Handhalah ibn Safwan, a messenger to the people of al-Rass, and Khalid ibn Sinan al-'Absi]. They were only called Arabs because no one other than them spoke Arabic.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the prophets after him﴾. This includes all the prophets. Then He said: ﴿And We revealed to Ibrahim﴾, singling out certain people by mention to honour them, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿His angels and His messengers, Jibril and Mika'il﴾ [Note: See vol. 2, p. 63]. Then He said: ﴿and 'Isa and Ayyub﴾. He placed 'Isa before peoples who came before him, because the particle waw does not necessarily imply order. Also, in it is the singling out of 'Isa, as a rebuttal to the Jews. In this verse there is an indication of the rank and nobility of our Prophet (ﷺ), since He mentioned him first among His prophets. A similar example is His saying: ﴿And when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you, and from Nuh﴾ [al-Ahzab: 7], to the end of the verse [Note: See vol. 14, p. 126].

Nuh is derived from al-nawh (lamentation). It has already been mentioned in full in Surah Al 'Imran [Note: See vol. 4, p. 62]. It is inflected (yunsarif) and it is a non-Arabic name, because it consists of three letters, so it is light. As for Ibrahim, Isma'il [and Ishaq] [Note: The addition is from I'rab al-Qur'an by al-Nahhas], they are non-Arabic and definite (ma'rifa), and therefore they are not inflected. Likewise Ya'qub, 'Isa and Musa, except that in 'Isa and Musa the alif may be a feminine marker, so they are not inflected whether definite or indefinite. As for Yunus and Yusuf, it is narrated from al-Hasan that he read "wa-Yunisa" with a kasra on the nun, and likewise "Yusifa" with a kasra, treating them as derived from anasa and asafa. According to this, they should be inflected and hamzated, and the plural of them would be ya'anis and ya'asif. Whoever does not hamza says: Yawanis and Yawasif. Abu Zayd related: Yunasa and Yusafa with a fatha on the nun and the sin. Al-Mahdawi said: It seems that "Yunisa" was originally a verb in the active voice, and "Yunasa" a verb in the passive voice, and they were named by them.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We gave Dawud the Zabur﴾. The Zabur is the Book of Dawud. It consisted of one hundred and fifty surahs, in which there is no ruling, nor any permitted or forbidden matter, but only wisdom and admonitions. Al-zubur means writing, and al-zabur, in the sense of al-mazbur (that which is written), is like al-rasul, al-rakub and al-halub. Hamza read "Zubura" with a damma on the zay, the plural of zabr, like fals and fulus, and zabr in the sense of al-mazbur, as one says: hadha al-dirham darb al-amir, that is, madrubuhu (this dirham is the minting of the amir, i.e., his minted coin). The original meaning of the word is securing, as one says: bi'r mazbura, meaning a well lined with stones. A book is called zabur because of the strength of the bond it provides. Dawud, peace be upon him, had a beautiful voice, and when he began to recite the Zabur, humans, jinn, birds and wild beasts gathered to him because of the beauty of his voice. He was humble and ate from the work of his hands. Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shayba reported to us: Abu Usama reported to us, from Hisham ibn 'Urwa, from his father, who said: "Dawud (ﷺ) would address the people while in his hand was a basket of palm-leaf fibres. When he finished, he would give it to one of those beside him to sell. He used to make coats of mail, and it will come [Note: See vol. 11, p. 330]."

In a hadith: "Blueness in the eye is a blessing (yumn)." And Dawud was blue-eyed.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verse 164:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And messengers We have already related to you before﴾, meaning in Makkah. "Wa-rusulan" (and messengers) is in the accusative by an implied verb, i.e., "and We sent messengers," because the meaning of "We revealed to Nuh" is "We sent Nuh." It was also said: it is in the accusative by a verb indicated by "qasasnahum" (We related them), i.e., "and We related messengers." Similar to this is what Sibawayh recited [[The two verses are by al-Rabi' ibn Id' al-Fazari, one of the long-lived, describing the end of his youth and the loss of his strength.]]:

I have become one who no longer bears arms, nor can I hold the reins of a camel if it bolts,

and I fear the wolf if I pass by it alone, and I fear the winds and the rain.

That is, "and I fear the wolf." In the reading of Ubayy, "wa-rusulun" (and messengers) is in the nominative, on the assumption of "wa-minhum rusulun" (and among them are messengers). Then it was said: when Allah, exalted is He, related in His Book the names of some of His prophets and did not mention the names of others, and those mentioned have a virtue over those not mentioned, the Jews said: "Muhammad mentioned the prophets and did not mention Musa." So it was revealed: ﴿And Allah spoke to Musa directly﴾. "Taklimான" (direct speech) is a verbal noun whose meaning is emphasis, indicating the falsity of one who says that Allah created speech for Himself in a tree and Musa heard it; rather, it is the true speech by which the speaker is a speaker. Al-Nahhas said: The grammarians agreed that when you emphasize the verb with a verbal noun, it is not metaphorical, and that it is not permissible, in the saying of the poet:

The basin was filled and said, "Enough for me,"

that he should say "said a saying"; so likewise, when He said "takliman" (direct speech), it must be speech in the true sense of speech that is understood. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Musa, peace be upon him, said: "My Lord, by what did You take me as a confidant (kalim)?" He sought the deed by which Allah had made him happy, so that he might increase in it. Allah, exalted is He, said to him: "Do you remember when a kid of your flock ran off, and you pursued it for most of the day and wearied yourself; then you caught it, kissed it, pressed it to your chest, and said to it: 'You have tired me and tired yourself'; and you were not angry with it? For that reason I have taken you as a confidant."

"His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Messengers as bearers of good news and as warners﴾. It is in the accusative case as a substitution (badal) for "and messengers We have related to you before". It is also permissible for it to be accusative by implying a verb, and its accusative can be as a circumstantial state (hal), meaning: as We revealed to Nuh and the prophets after him, messengers.

(So that people will have no argument against God after the messengers.) They would say, "You did not send us a messenger, nor did You send down to us a Book." In the revelation: ﴿And We would never punish until We send a messenger﴾ [al-Isra' 17:15] [[See vol. 10, p. 230.]], and His saying, the Exalted: "And if We had destroyed them with a punishment before it, they would have said, 'Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger so that we might follow Your signs'" [Ta-Ha 20:134] [[See vol. 11, p. 264.]]. In all of this there is clear evidence that nothing is obligatory by reason ('aql). It was narrated from Ka'b al-Ahbar that he said: The prophets were two thousand and two hundred thousand [[In K: one hundred.]]. Muqatil said: [[This narration is attributed by (al-Bahr) and (Ruh al-Ma'ani) to Ka'b al-Ahbar.]] The prophets were one million, four hundred thousand, and twenty-four thousand. Anas ibn Malik narrated from the Messenger of God ﷺ that he said: "I was sent upon the trail of eight thousand prophets, among them four thousand from the Children of Israel." Abu al-Layth al-Samarqandi mentioned it in his Tafsir, then he traced it back through Shu'bah from Abu Ishaq from al-Harith al-A'war from Abu Dharr al-Ghifari who said: I said, "O Messenger of God, how many were the prophets, and how many were the messengers?" He said: "The prophets were one hundred thousand and twenty-four thousand prophets, and the messengers were three hundred and thirteen." I say: This is the most authentic of what has been narrated on this matter; al-Ajurri and Abu Hatim al-Busti in his Musnad Sahih transmitted it.

Allah said: ﴿But Allah bears witness﴾. It is in the nominative case as the subject of a nominal sentence (raf' bi'l-ibtida'). If you wish, you may emphasize the nun (shaddidta al-nun) and put it in the accusative (wa nasabta).

There is an omission in the statement, which the context indicates. It is as if the disbelievers said: "We do not bear witness to you, O Muhammad, regarding what you say; so who bears witness for you?" Then it was revealed: ﴿But Allah bears witness﴾. The meaning of ﴿He has sent it down with His knowledge﴾ is: while He knows that you are worthy of its being sent down to you. The verse indicates that Allah, exalted is He, is knowing with a knowledge.

﴿And the angels bear witness﴾. He mentioned the witness of the angels to set against it the denial of their witness.

﴿And sufficient is Allah as a witness﴾. That is, Allah is sufficient as a witness, and the bāʾ (bi-) is superfluous (zāʾidah).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verse 167:

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved﴾ means the Jews [i.e., they wronged themselves].

(And hindered from the way of Allah) i.e., from following the Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ), by their saying: "We do not find his description in our book; prophethood is only among the offspring of Harun and Dawud, and in the Torah it is stated that the law of Musa will not be abrogated."

(They have certainly gone far astray) because they disbelieved and, along with that, prevented people from embracing Islam.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and wrong⁠﻿ [themselves]⁠﻿ ...﴾. He means the Jews. That is, they wronged Muhammad (ﷺ) by concealing his description, and they wronged themselves by disbelieving, and they wronged the people by concealing it from them.

(﴿Allah would never forgive them﴾) This applies to those who die upon their disbelief without repenting.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and wrong⁠﻿ [themselves]⁠﻿ ...﴾. He means the Jews. That is, they wronged Muhammad (ﷺ) by concealing his description, and they wronged themselves by disbelieving, and they wronged the people by concealing it from them.

(﴿Allah would never forgive them﴾) This applies to those who die upon their disbelief without repenting.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verse 170:

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿O mankind﴾. This is an address to all people.

(﴿The Messenger has certainly come to you﴾) 170. He means Muhammad (ﷺ).

(﴿with the truth﴾) with the Qur'an. It is also said: with the true religion. It is also said: with the testimony that there is no god but Allah. It is also said: the bāʾ (bi-, "with") is for transitivity, meaning "he came to you while the truth was with him," so it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿So believe; it is better for you﴾ 170. In the speech there is an implied element (iḍmār), meaning "and bring about what is better for you." This is the view of Sibawayh. According to the view of al-Farra', it is an attribute (naʿt) of an omitted verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning "a belief that is better for you." According to the view of Abu ʿUbayda, the phrase means "it would be better for you" (yakun khayran lakum).

**Al-Qurtubi's Commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 4, Verse 171 (Part 1 of 2)**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿O People of the Scripture, do not commit excess (ghuluw, going beyond the limit) in your religion﴾. This is a prohibition of ghuluw. Ghuluw is exceeding the limit. From it comes the expression "the price rose (ghala al-si'r yaghlu ghala'an)," and "the man went to extremes in the matter (ghala al-rajul fi al-amr ghuluwwan)," and "the girl's flesh and bones grew (ghala bi-al-jariyah lahmuha wa 'azmuha)" when she matured quickly and surpassed her peers [[al-lidat (plural of lidah, like 'iddah): the peers, that is, the one who was born with you and raised with you.]]. By this, as the exegetes have mentioned, is meant the excess of the Jews regarding 'Isa (Jesus), to the point that they slandered Maryam (Mary), and the excess of the Christians regarding him, to the point that they made him a lord. Excess and deficiency are all a fault and disbelief. For this reason Mutarrif ibn 'Abd Allah said: "The good deed lies between two evil deeds." And the poet said:

*Fulfil your right entirely and do not delay it, and shake hands; a generous man never fully demands his due.*

*Do not go to extremes in any matter, but be moderate, for both extremes of the matter are blameworthy.*

And another said:

*Keep to the middle course of affairs, for it is salvation, and do not ride either a tame mount or a wild one.*

In the Sahih of al-Bukhari, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Do not overpraise me as the Christians overpraised 'Isa (Jesus). Say: 'the servant of Allah and His messenger.'" [[al-Iftira': exceeding the bounds in praise, and lying in it.]]

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿and do not say about Allah except the truth﴾, that is, do not say that He has a partner or sons. Then Allah the Exalted explained the state and description of 'Isa (peace be upon him), saying: "The Messiah, 'Isa son of Maryam, is only the messenger of Allah and His word." In this there are three issues.

The first: the words of Allah the Exalted ﴿The Messiah﴾. "al-Masih" is in the nominative case as the subject (mubtada'), and "'Isa" is an apposition (badal) to it, and likewise "ibn Maryam." It is also permissible for it to be the predicate (khabar) of the subject, and the meaning would be: "The Messiah is only the son of Maryam." By His words "'Isa son of Maryam," He indicated that one who is ascribed to his mother cannot be a god, since the essence of a god is to be eternal, not created. And "messenger of Allah" is a second predicate after the first.

The second: Allah the Mighty and Majestic did not mention any woman by her name in His Book except Maryam daughter of 'Imran, for He mentioned her name in about thirty places, for a wisdom that some of the shaykhs have mentioned. Kings and nobles do not mention their free women in public, nor do they make their names common; rather they refer to a wife by "the bride," "the family," "the dependents," and the like. If they mention slave-women, they do not use such allusions for them, nor do they guard their names from mention and explicit naming. So when the Christians said about Maryam what they said, and about her son, Allah named her explicitly and did not refer to her by motherhood and servanthood, which are her attributes, and He let the speech follow the custom of the Arabs in mentioning their slave-women.

The third: the belief that 'Isa (peace be upon him) has no father is obligatory. So when his name is repeated ascribed to his mother, hearts perceive what they must believe: the negation of a father for him, and the purification of the pure mother from the claim of the Jews, may Allah curse them.

And Allah knows best.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿and His word which He cast to Maryam﴾, that is, he was brought into being by the word "Be" (kun), so he was a human without a father. The Arabs name a thing after another thing when it proceeds from it. It was also said: "His word" is the good tidings that Allah the Exalted gave to Maryam (peace be upon her), and His message to her through Jibril (Gabriel) (peace be upon him) [[From K.]], and that is His saying: "When the angels said: 'O Maryam, Allah gives you good tidings of a word from Him'" [[See vol. 4, p. 88.]] (Al 'Imran: 45). It was also said: "the word" here means "the sign (ayah)." Allah the Exalted says: "And she affirmed the words of her Lord" [[See vol. 18, p. 23.]] (al-Tahrim: 12), and "the words of Allah would not be exhausted" [[See vol. 14, p. 76.]] (Luqman: 27). 'Isa had four names: al-Masih, 'Isa, Kalimah (the Word), and Ruh (the Spirit), and it was said other than this, which is not in the Quran. The meaning of ﴿He cast it to Maryam﴾ is that He commanded it to Maryam [[In al-Bahr: "He cast it to Maryam" means He brought this event into being in Maryam and realized it in her.]].

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿and a spirit from Him﴾. This is what led the Christians into misguidance, for they said: "'Isa is a part of Him," so they were ignorant and went astray. Concerning this there are eight answers.

The first: Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: Allah created the spirits of the children of Adam when He took the covenant from them, then He returned them to the loins of Adam, and He kept with Himself the spirit of 'Isa (peace be upon him). When He willed to create him, He sent that spirit to Maryam, and 'Isa (peace be upon him) came into being from it. So for this reason He said: "and a spirit from Him." It was also said: this ascription is for honour, although all spirits are of His creation. This is like His saying: "and purify My House for those who circumambulate" [[See vol. 2, p. 110.]] (al-Hajj: 26). It was also said: one from whom wondrous things appear may be called a spirit, and it is ascribed to Allah the Exalted, so it is said: "This is a spirit from Allah," meaning from His creation, as it is said of a blessing that it is from Allah. 'Isa used to heal the blind and the leper and raise the dead, so he deserved this name. It was also said: he is called a spirit because of the breath of Jibril (peace be upon him), and breath is called a spirit, because it is wind that comes out from the spirit. The poet, who is Dhu al-Rummah, said:

*I said to him: "Raise it to yourself and love it by your spirit (breath)," and light for it a little fire, a measured one.*

[[Bi-ruhika: by your breathing. (Wa-qititu lahu qitatan qadra): he commands him to be gentle and to blow lightly on the fire, and to feed it little firewood, little by little.]]

It has been reported that Jibril blew into the garment of Maryam, and she conceived from it by the permission of Allah. On this view, "and a spirit from Him" is in apposition (ma'tuf) to the pronoun in "cast," which refers to the name of Allah, so the meaning is: "Allah and Jibril cast the word to Maryam." It was also said: "a spirit from Him" means "from His creation," as He said: "And He subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, all from Him" [[See vol. 16, p. 160.]] (al-Jathiyah: 13), that is, from His creation. It was also said: "a spirit from Him" means "a mercy from Him," so 'Isa was a mercy from Allah to whoever followed him, and from this is His saying: "and He strengthened them with a spirit from Him" [[See vol. 17, pp. 308 and 232.]] (al-Mujadilah: 22), meaning with mercy. It is recited "fa-ruhun wa rayhan" [[See vol. 17, pp. 308 and 232.]]. It was also said: "and a spirit from Him" and "a proof from Him," and 'Isa was a proof and an argument against his people (ﷺ).

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So believe in Allah and His messengers﴾, that is: believe that Allah is one God, the Creator of the Messiah and the One who sent him, and believe in His messengers, among whom is 'Isa, so do not make him a god.

﴿And do not say: "Three"﴾ [Our gods are three]. This is from al-Zajjaj. Ibn 'Abbas said: by the Trinity is meant Allah, His consort, and His son. Al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubayd said: that is, do not say "They are three," like His saying: "They will say: 'Three'" [[See vol. 10, p. 322.]] (al-Kahf: 22). Abu 'Ali said: the estimate is "Do not say: He is the third of three," so the subject and the genitive (al-mudaf) were omitted. The Christians, with all their sects, agree on the Trinity, and they say: "Allah is one essence (jawhar wahid) and has three hypostases (aqanim)." So they make each hypostasis a god, and by the hypostases they mean existence, life, and knowledge. Sometimes they express the hypostases as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, meaning by the Father existence, by the Spirit life, and by the Son the Messiah, in a discourse of theirs that is confused, the explanation of which belongs to the principles of religion. The summary of their speech comes down to holding that 'Isa is a god because of what Allah the Glorified and Exalted caused to occur at his hands of extraordinary events (kharq al-'adat), according to His intentions and will. They said: "We know that these matters are beyond human capacity, so the one who is capable of them must be described as divine." It is said to them: If that were within his capacities and he were independent in it, then saving himself from his enemies and repelling their evil from himself would be within his capacities, and it is not so. If the Christians acknowledge this, then their claim and assertion that he used to do these things independently has fallen. And if they do not accept that, they have no proof either, because they are opposed by Musa (Moses) (peace be upon him) and what occurred at his hands of great matters, such as the turning of the staff into a serpent, the splitting of the sea, the white hand, the manna and the quails, and other things. Likewise what occurred at the hands of the prophets. If they deny that, we deny what they claim of its manifestation at the hands of 'Isa (peace be upon him) too, and then they cannot establish any of that for 'Isa, for the path to establishing it for us is the texts of the Quran, and they deny the Quran and reject the one who brought it. So they cannot establish that by reports of mass transmission (tawatur).

It has been said that the Christians were upon the religion of Islam for eighty-one years after 'Isa was raised, praying toward the qibla and fasting the month of Ramadan, until war broke out between them and the Jews. Among the Jews there was a brave man called Bulus (Paul), who killed a group of the companions of 'Isa. He said: "If the truth is with 'Isa, then we have disbelieved and denied, and our end is the Fire, and we are cheated [[In J and Z: "tricked."]] if they enter Paradise and we enter the Fire. I will scheme against them and misguide them, so they will enter the Fire." He had a mare called al-'Uqab. He showed remorse, put dust on his head, and said to the Christians: "I am Bulus, your enemy. I have been called from heaven: there is no repentance for you except that you become a Christian." So they brought him into a chamber in the church, and he remained in it for a year, not coming out night or day, until he learned the Gospel. Then he came out and said: "I have been called from heaven: Allah has accepted your repentance." So they believed him and loved him. Then he went to Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) and appointed Nustura over them, and informed him that 'Isa son of Maryam is a god. Then he traveled to the Romans and taught them the divine nature (lahut) and the human nature (nasut), and said: "'Isa was not a human who became humanized, nor a body that became embodied, but he is the son of Allah." He taught this to a man called Ya'qub. Then he called a man called al-Malik [[As in the originals: what is in the book "al-Milal wa al-Nihal" is that the Malkaniyyah are the followers of Malka, who appeared in the lands of the Romans and seized them. In "Subh al-A'sha," the Malkaniyyah are the followers of Malkan, who appeared in the lands of the Romans, so it is Malka or Malkan. The mention of the Malkaniyyah will come on p. 118.]] and said to him: "The God has always been, and still is, 'Isa." When he had gained power over them, he called these three one by one and said to each: "You are my chosen one. I have seen the Messiah in a dream, and he was pleased with me." He said to each of them: "Tomorrow I will slaughter myself and draw near to Allah by it, so call the people to your sect." Then he entered the slaughterhouse and slaughtered himself. When the third day came, each of them called the people to his own sect, and each one was followed by a group. They fought and differed until this day of ours, so all the Christians belong to the three sects. This, it is said, was the cause of their associating partners with Allah, and Allah knows best. I have related this story in explanation of the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿So We cast among them enmity and hatred until the Day of Resurrection﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 14) [[See p. 116 of this volume.]], and it will come, Allah willing.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Cease; it is better for you﴾. "Khayran" is in the accusative according to Sibawayh by an implied verb, as if he said: "Do what is better for you," because when He forbade them from associating partners, He commanded them to do what is better for them. Sibawayh said: Among what is in the accusative by an omitted verb whose appearance is left out is "Cease, it is better for you," because when you say "Go to it," you are removing him from one matter and placing him in another. And he recited:

*So promise her the two trees of Malik, or the rising ground between them, which is level.* [[The verse is by 'Umar ibn Abi Rabi'ah. "Sarhatan Malik": a specific place; the two sarhah are two trees by which the place became known; al-Ruba: plural of rabwah, the elevated part of the land.]]

Abu 'Ubayda's view is: "Stop, it will be better for you" (intahu yakun khayran lakum). Muhammad ibn Yazid said: this is an error, because it implies the conditional clause and its response, and this does not occur in the speech of the Arabs. The view of al-Farra' is that it is an adjective (na't) of a deleted verbal noun (masdar). 'Ali ibn Sulayman said: this is a gross error, because the meaning would become: "Stop the stopping which is better for you."

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah is but one God.﴾ This is a subject and predicate (mubtada' and khabar), and "one" (wahid) is its attribute (na't). It is also permissible for "God" (ilah) to be a substitute (badal) for the name of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, with "one" (wahid) as its predicate; the implied meaning is: "Indeed, the one worshipped is one."

(Glorified is He above that He should have a child) meaning: exalting Him (tanzihan) (above) having a child. When "'an" (from) is dropped, "an" (that) is in a position of accusative through the removal of the preposition, meaning: how could He have a child? A man's child resembles him, and there is no likeness to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

(To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth) so He has no partner. Jesus and Mary are among what is in the heavens and what is on the earth, and whatever is in them is created. How then could Jesus be a god when he is created? And if a child were permissible, then offspring would be permissible too, so that everyone upon whom a miracle appeared would be His child.

(And sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs) meaning: as a guardian for His allies, as has been mentioned previously.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verse 172–173:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Never will the Messiah disdain﴾ means: he will never be too proud nor ashamed. ﴿To be a servant of Allah﴾ means: from being [a servant of Allah], so it is in the accusative position. Al-Hasan recited: "in yakūna" (إِنْ يَكُونُ) with a kasra on the hamza, taking it as a negation (nafy) [[from z.]] in the sense of "mā", and the meaning is: it is not fitting for Him to have a son. It is also said that yakūna should be in the nominative case, but the transmitters did not mention it [[In Mukhtasar al-Shawadhdh of Ibn Khalawayh: "in yakūna" with a kasra on the hamza and a raf' on yakūna. Al-Hasan, Qatadah and Abu Wafid made in mean mā.]]. ﴿Nor the angels brought near﴾ means: [brought near] to the mercy of Allah and His good pleasure. By this it is indicated that the angels are superior to the prophets, may the blessings of Allah be upon them all, and likewise [the verse] ﴿And I do not say, "Indeed, I am an angel"﴾ [[See vol. 9, p. 27.]]. This meaning has already been alluded to in (al-Baqarah) [[See vol. 1, p. 289.]].

Then: ﴿Whoever disdains﴾

that is, refuses ﴿His worship and is proud﴾

so does not do it. ﴿He will gather them to Himself﴾

that is, to the place of gathering. ﴿All together﴾

so He will recompense each according to what he deserves, as He explained in the verse after this: ﴿And as for those who believed and did righteous deeds, He will give them their rewards in full and increase them from His bounty﴾

up to His saying: ﴿a helper﴾. The root of "yastankif" is "nakif", so the yā', sīn and tā' are additions. It is said: nakiftu min al-shay' and istankaftu minhu and ankaftuhu, i.e., I exalted him above what is disdained from it. From this is the hadith: he was asked about "Subhan Allah" and said: "Inkāf Allāh min kulli sū'" meaning His exaltation and sanctification above rivals and offspring. Al-Zajjaj said: istankafa means anifa (was too proud), taken from nakaftu al-dam'a when you wipe the tear with your finger from your cheek. From this is the hadith: "mā yunkafu al-'araq 'an jabīnih," i.e., what does not cease. Also the hadith: "He came with an army whose last part does not cease" (lā yunkafu ākhiruh), i.e., its last part does not stop. It was also said: it is from al-nakf, which is a defect; one says: "mā 'alayhi fī hādhā al-amr nakfun wa lā wakf," i.e., no defect. So the meaning is: the Messiah will not refuse, will not exalt himself from servitude, will not cease from it, and will not consider it a defect.

"Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O mankind, there has certainly come to you a proof (burhan) from your Lord﴾ — meaning Muhammad (ﷺ), according to al-Thawri. He was called a proof (burhan) because with him is the clear evidence (al-burhan), which is the miracle (al-mu'jizah). Mujahid said: the burhan here is the argument (al-hujjah). The meaning is close, for the miracles are his argument (ﷺ). And the light that was sent down (al-nur al-munazzal) is the Qur'an, according to al-Hasan. He called it light because by it rulings are made clear and by it one is guided out of error, so it is a manifest light (nur mubin), i.e., clear and evident."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 4, verse 175:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿As for those who believe in Allah and hold fast to Him﴾, i.e., to the Qur'an, to keep away from its disobedience. And if they hold fast to His Book, then they have held fast to Him and to His Prophet. It was also said: "held fast to Him" means to Allah. And al-'işma (protection, safeguarding) is restraint (al-imtina'), and it has been discussed previously [see vol. 4, p. 156]. ﴿And He will guide them﴾, i.e., and He guides them; He is made implicit so as to show that the sentence is cut off from what precedes it.

(ilayhi) i.e., to His reward. It was also said: to the truth, so that they may recognize it.

(ṣirāṭan mustaqīman), i.e., a straight religion. "Ṣirāṭan" is in the accusative by an implied verb indicated by "wa-yahdīhim", the estimated sense being: "and He makes them know a straight path." It was also said: it is a second object, with the estimated sense: "and He guides them to His reward, a straight path." It was also said: it is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl). As for the pronoun in "ilayhi", it was said: it refers to the Qur'an; it was said: it refers to grace (al-fadl); and it was said: it refers to grace and mercy, because both carry the meaning of reward. It was also said: it refers to Allah, exalted and majestic, with an elided genitive (al-muḍāf), as previously mentioned, the meaning being "and He guides them to His reward." Abu 'Ali said: the pronoun refers to the name of Allah, exalted and majestic, mentioned earlier, and the meaning is "and He guides them to His path." If we take "ṣirāṭan mustaqīman" as accusative of circumstance, then the circumstance is from this elided element. In His saying, "(wa-faḍlin)" there is evidence that He, exalted is He, bestows His grace upon His servants with His reward, for if it were in exchange for the deed, it would not be grace. And Allah knows best.

The First issue: al-Bara' ibn 'Azib said, "This is the last verse to be revealed of the Qur'an," as is recorded in the Sahih of Muslim. It was also said that it was revealed while the Prophet (ﷺ) was preparing for the Farewell Pilgrimage (Hajjat al-Wada'). It was revealed on account of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: "I fell ill, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and Abu Bakr came to visit me on foot. I lost consciousness, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) performed ablution, then poured some of his ablution water over me, and I regained consciousness. I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, how should I dispose of my property?' He gave me no answer until the verse of inheritance was revealed: 'They ask you for a ruling. Say: Allah gives you a ruling concerning the kalalah.'" [Narrated by Muslim.] And he (Muslim) said: "The last verse to be revealed was: ﴿And fear a Day when you will be returned to Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 281]." [See vol. 3, p. 375.] This has already been mentioned. The discussion of the kalalah (one who dies leaving neither ascendants nor descendants) has been dealt with fully at the beginning of the surah [See vol. 5, p. 76 and following], and that the term "brothers" here refers to full brothers or paternal brothers [from j, w and k]. Jabir had nine sisters.

The Second issue: The words of Allah, "If a man dies leaving no child," mean: leaving no child and no parent; the verse mentions only one of them. Al-Jurjani said: The word "walad" (child) applies both to the parent and to the offspring. The parent is called "walid" because he begot (walad), and the offspring is called "walad" because he was born (wulida). It is like "dhurriyyah" (offspring), which derives from "dhara," and is applied both to the offspring and to the parent. Allah says: ﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring in the laden ship﴾ [Ya-Sin: 41]. [See vol. 15, p. 34.]

The Third issue: The majority of scholars, from among the Companions and the Successors, make sisters 'asabah (residuary heirs) of daughters even if there is no brother with them. The exception is Ibn 'Abbas, who did not make sisters 'asabah of daughters. Dawud (al-Zahiri) and a group also held this view. Their evidence is the apparent meaning of Allah's words: ﴿If a man dies leaving no child and has a sister, she has half of what he left﴾. The sister is only given inheritance when the deceased has no child. They said: It is known that a daughter is a child, so a sister should not inherit alongside her. Ibn al-Zubayr used to hold the view of Ibn 'Abbas on this question, until al-Aswad ibn Yazid informed him that Mu'adh had ruled in the case of a daughter and a sister, dividing the estate between them equally.

The Fourth issue: This verse is called the "verse of summer" (ayat al-sayf), because it was revealed in the summer. 'Umar said: "By Allah, I will not leave any matter more important to me than the matter of the kalalah. I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about it, and he was never as harsh with me about any matter as he was about it, until he struck my side or my chest with his finger and said: 'O 'Umar, does not the verse of summer, which was revealed at the end of Surat al-Nisa', suffice you?'" And from him (may Allah be pleased with him) who said: "Three matters, had the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) explained them, would be dearer to me than the world and all that is in it: the kalalah, usury (riba), and the caliphate." Ibn Majah recorded it in his Sunan.

The Fifth issue: Some of the Rafidah (Shi'a) criticized 'Umar's words, "By Allah, I will not leave..." (the hadith).

The Sixth issue: Concerning Allah's words ﴿Allah makes clear to you, lest you go astray﴾. Al-Kisa'i said: The meaning is "Allah makes clear to you so that you do not go astray." Abu 'Ubayd said: I related to al-Kisa'i a hadith narrated by Ibn 'Umar from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "None of you should invoke curse upon his child, lest it coincide with an answer from Allah." He found it admirable. Al-Nahhas said: According to Abu 'Ubayd, the meaning is "lest it coincide with an answer from Allah." This view is considered an error by the Basrans, because they do not permit the implicit omission of "la" (not). According to them the meaning is: "Allah makes clear to you the dislike that you should go astray," and then it is omitted, as in His words: ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82]. [See vol. 9, p. 245.] The same applies to the meaning of the Prophet's (ﷺ) hadith, i.e., "out of dislike that it should coincide with an answer from Allah."

﴿And Allah is All-Knowing of everything﴾ has been mentioned in more than one place. And Allah knows best. The surah of "al-Nisa'" is complete, and all praise is due to Allah, who granted success.
